Covenants Evidence Ledger

Everything extracted from John Andrew Morrow's The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (Angelico Press, 2013), with printed page and PDF page for every item, followed by every fact-check report with its verdicts and source links. This is the complete record behind the summary report.

1336 rows merged from the nine extraction files. 'Sort year' is computed only to order the rows (AH years converted approximately; centuries placed at mid-century); it is not a claim. Rows with only a relative date (an age, 'the same journey') take the sort year of the row before them in the same extraction and are marked with ≈. Rows with no usable year at all are at the end.

1. Section summary

The front matter frames the book as a recovery of "a third foundational source of Islam": documents the Prophet Muhammad is said to have issued to Christian communities. Charles Upton's Foreword and the blurbs make this claim. The book is also framed as a contemporary call to Muslim–Christian solidarity against "Wahhabi/Salafi" extremism and a secular "New World Order". "Concerning the Covenants" traces the European printing history of the Testamentum et pactiones / al-'Ahd wa al-shurut (the Covenant with the Christians of the World). It covers Sionita and Vitré in 1630, the further 1630 editions, Fabricius in 1638, Nissel in 1655, Nagy de Harsány in 1672 and Hinckelmann in 1690, then the translations by Rycaut, Briot, Grassi, Miltitz and Van Dyke. It also gives the earlier publication history of the Sinai, Najran, Assyrian, Persian and Armenian covenants. "The Covenants Initiative" prints a declaration and about 41 named Muslim signatories, and "Chasing History" adds news items from 2011 and 2013.

Chapter 1 reconstructs Muhammad's early life with a focus on his contacts with Christians:

  • recognition stories from childhood (Jews testing him with a hen; Syrian and Abyssinian Christians);
  • the Bahira episode at Busrah, defended against skeptical and polemical readings;
  • the monk Nastur on Khadijah's caravan, and Waraqah ibn Nawfal.

The chapter's most distinctive argument is that the "twenty-five years of silence" in the sirah can be filled by the monks of Mount Sinai's tradition. On that tradition, Muhammad stayed at or worked for St Catherine's Monastery as a youth (shepherd, caravaneer, camel driver) and gave the monks a palm-printed promise of protection. That promise would be the origin of the Sinai achtiname. A long excursus covers:

  • the history and dating of the mosque inside the monastery and the one on the summit of Jebel Musa;
  • Muslim pilgrimage to Sinai and the reasons for its rise and decline (Fatimid interest; Crusades; Ottoman and Wahhabi/Salafi factors; closure in the 1980s; the 2013 closure);
  • shared Muslim–Christian–Jewish devotion.

The chapter then summarizes the revelation and the Meccan period (610–622 CE). It prints a translation of the Constitution of Medina (from Ibn Ishaq 233) and argues that the Constitution created a pluralist ummah. In that ummah, Jews and Christians belonged to the "Community of Believers", and the author argues it was superior to Athenian democracy and the Roman Republic. He also rebuts Donner's thesis that "Islam" as a confessional identity emerged only under 'Abd al-Malik.

B. Foreword (Charles Upton's claims)
  1. The two foundational sources of Islam are the Qur'an and hadith; sirah "has never held the same pre-eminent position". — xi [PDF 12] — (Upton)
  2. Asked after the Prophet's death what his character was like, 'A'ishah answered: "It was exactly like the Qur'an." — xi [PDF 12] — (Upton) T
  3. The book may mark "the emergence of a third foundational source for Islam". The documents have "been known to a few scholars for many centuries" but neglected. — xi [PDF 12] — (Upton)
  4. Morrow includes original sources in Arabic and Persian and corrected versions of "most of these" in modern Arabic typescript. — xi [PDF 12] — (Upton)
  5. Rhetorical questions: before the Crusades, Muslims on hajj visited Christian and Jewish sites. In the Prophet's time Christians were also called al-mu'minin ("the faithful"). Christian knights sometimes fought alongside Muslim armies. Crusaders received safe-conduct for pilgrimages. — xii [PDF 13] — (Upton)
  6. Morrow argues that Muhammad's original intent was "a confederation of the People of the Book", with rights extended "even to pagan polytheists" in some circumstances. — xii [PDF 13] — (Upton)
  7. Qur'an 2:256 ("no compulsion in religion"): the principle was established by the Prophet, repeated by the Caliphs and enshrined in the shari'ah. — xii [PDF 13] — (Upton)
  8. The covenants were "rediscovered in obscure monasteries and collections". They forbid attacking or robbing Christians, stopping church repairs, tearing down churches to build mosques, and preventing Christian wives from going to church. — xii [PDF 13] — (Upton)
  9. Wahhabi/Salafi Islam is "willful and militant ignorance", the "seed-bed" of "Islamic" terrorism, and vulnerable to manipulation by Western powers. — xii–xiii [PDF 13–14] — (Upton) opinion
  10. St Paul's definition of faith is quoted as "the presence of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen". — xii [PDF 13] — (Upton)
  11. Qur'anic verses quoted: 3:3, 3:64, 29:46, 2:62. — xiii [PDF 14] — F
  12. Morrow block-quoted: "there is unity in religious diversity, there is no place for syncretism … Each religion is an ecosystem … Jews, Christians, and Muslims must defend each other from the onslaught of the secular New World Order". — xiii [PDF 14] — (Morrow, quoted)

  1. Latin title Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Mohammedem et Christianae fidei cultores; Arabic al-'Ahd wa al-shurut allati sharataha Muhammad rasul Allah li ahl al-millah al-nasraniyyah, "The Treaty and Covenant which Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, Concluded with the Christian Community". — xv [PDF 16] — F
  2. Vitré's surname was also spelled "Vitray". — xv [PDF 16] — F

  4. The Sionita edition includes the original Arabic, a Latin translation and the Pact of 'Umar. — xv [PDF 16] — F
  5. Nissel's 1655 work is held at Columbia University Library (NYC) and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Their catalogues list Robert of Chester, Hermann of Carinthia and du Ryer as co-translators; the author calls this "silly" and explains that their Qur'an translations were included in the volume. — xv [PDF 16] — F / I/O
  6. Nissel's translation was "published in several runs", and some libraries speak of three editions. Copies listed: British National Library; British Library, St Pancras; Bibliotheek Universiteit Leiden; Herzog August Bibliothek Wolfenbüttel; Niedersächsische Staats- und Universitätsbibliothek Göttingen (listed twice); Universitätsbibliothek Rostock; Herzogin Anna Amalia Bibliothek/Klassik Stiftung Weimar; Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin–Preussischer Kulturbesitz; Thüringer Universitäts- und Landesbibliothek; Universitäts- und Forschungsbibliothek Erfurt/Gotha; Universitäts- und Landesbibliothek Sachsen-Anhalt/Zentrale; Universitätsbibliothek Greifswald; Bibliothèque Cantonale et Universitaire–Lausanne; Koninklijke Bibliotheek; Bibliothèque nationale de France; Zentralbibliothek Zürich; Bayerische Staatsbibliothek. — xv–xvi [PDF 16–17] — F

  8. Sionita's Arabic type uses fa with no dot above and three dots below for "p", writes alif maqsurah as ya, and omits final hamzas. Omitting final hamzas "was a trait of the Prophet's Arabic, which was not accepted when Classical Arabic grammar was standardized". — xvi [PDF 17] — F / I/O
  9. Sionita's edition was printed by Vitré using Brèves' Arabic types (Hamilton and Richard 47). These fonts "had actually been molded in Istanbul" (Bernard 45, note 1). — xvi [PDF 17] — A
  10. Nissel's Arabic is printed in fully vocalized 'Uthmani script, "as found in contemporary Qur'ans". — xvi [PDF 17] — F
  11. "To be blunt, both Latin translations are poor." — xvi [PDF 17] — I/O

  14. Sionita is "single-handedly responsible" for spreading word of the covenant to the West. — xvii [PDF 18] — I/O

H. Bahira and Busrah
  1. Busrah is 145 km south of Damascus; spellings Busrah, Bosra, Bosrah, Bostra, Bustra, Bustrah. — p. 2 [PDF 25] — F
  2. Yusuf 'Ali's "another Busra in Edom, north of Petra in Transjordania" (7) "is certainly not the correct site". — p. 2 [PDF 25] — I/O
  3. Sawma'ah (cell) = "the dwelling place of a solitary monk and probably a vertical, tower-like structure" (Roggema 38, n. 4). Roggema apparently did not see Bahira's hermitage (45, n. 33); her definition matches the site on the south-west side of the city. — p. 2 [PDF 25] — A + I/O
  4. Reza Shah-Kazemi: "Can we see here a luminous anticipation of the mutual recognition between the Prophet and the monks …?" — p. 2 [PDF 25] — A
  5. Bahira was "probably a title of respect such as 'Reverend'". Some sources call him "Rabbi" (Sprenger 578), a term Nestorians also use for clerics. — p. 2 [PDF 25] — I/O + A
  6. Bahira story elements: a cloud over Muhammad; Quraysh men left him under a tree; "Do not ask me by al-Lat and al-'Uzza …"; the seal of prophethood between his shoulders; "guard him carefully against the Jews" (Ibn Ishaq 81). — p. 2–3 [PDF 25–26] — A (Ibn Ishaq)
  7. Rogerson: Bostra was the seat of the Byzantine governor and a legion commander, its Archbishop "lorded over some thirty-three junior bishops", and it had a "newly completed domed cathedral". It lay in the Hauran, with roads to Antioch, Damascus, Palmyra and the Red Sea. The mosque of Mabrak marks where Muhammad dismounted; "an old Roman basilica" is considered Bahira's church. — p. 3 [PDF 26] — A (Rogerson 63–64)
  8. Bahira's hermitage and church "remain places of religious and historical importance in southern Syria". — p. 3 [PDF 26] — F
  9. The Bahira story lacks a complete chain of transmission and is "cautiously introduced by 'it is supposed'". — p. 3 [PDF 26] — F
  10. Al-Dhahabi dismissed the versions in Tarikh al-Islam as "munkar jiddan or very weak" (Roggema 46). — p. 3 [PDF 26] — A
  11. Bell: "[n]o credence can be given to the stories …" (21). Armstrong: "pious legends" (1993: 48; OCR "1993- 48"). — p. 3 [PDF 26] — A
  12. Polemicists called Bahira a Bahrani Nestorian, an Arian or a Jacobite, and named him Sergius, Georgius or Nestorius, later Baeira or Pakhyras. — p. 4 [PDF 27] — A
  13. Robert Irwin: polemicists "invented tales about how a monk (in some versions actually a renegade cardinal) instructed Muhammad" (20). — p. 4 [PDF 27] — A
  14. "many have claimed that Bahira was the actual author of the Qur'an" (Vernet, 1991: 233). — p. 4 [PDF 27] — A
  15. Bahira may have been a Unitarian Christian (Thomson and 'Ata'ur-Rahim). Rhodes: "Arian influence on Islam would be more believable than Nestorian influence" (150, n. 265). — p. 4 [PDF 27] — A / I/O
  16. Supportive quotes: Roggema, a "historical kernel" (51); R. A. Gabriel accepts encounters with monks (56); Peters, Muhammad "well acquainted with the customs of Christian monks" (166); Goddard, "no good reason to discount the accounts" (19); Glubb (70–71); Betts, "Rahib al-Buhayra may have been a wandering Syrian monk" (5); Safi, "A simple answer might be because they happened" (80); Sprenger, al-Waqidi's account "bears equally the stamp of high antiquity" (592). — p. 4 [PDF 27] — A
  17. Donner: Arabia "may also have been home to some communities of Jewish Christians called Nazoreans" (30–31). Schoeps: Arabian Christianity was "schismatic … characterized by Ebionite and Monophysite views" (136–137), and Jewish Christianity and Islam share an "extensive similarity in structure" (139). — p. 5 [PDF 28] — A
  18. Pococke alleged that the Greek monk Sergius helped Muhammad write the Qur'an during a visit to St Catherine's (151; Stanley 326, n. 111). Thévenot claimed the Qur'an was patchworked by Sergius (72). — p. 5 [PDF 28] — A, rejected
  19. Thévenot "was abysmally ignorant of all matters Arabic and Islamic". — p. 5 [PDF 28] — I/O
  20. A hermit called Sargarius supposedly lived in a grotto on Mount Sinai; "no evidence" of any such person in the Prophet's time. — p. 5 [PDF 28] — F / I/O

I. Trade routes and geography
  1. Routes: south to Yemen; north to the Levant and Syria; east to Basrah (Iraq); to Gerrha (Bahrayn); and a route through Medina to 'Aqabah, then Nakhl in central Sinai, to Alexandria, where the Arabian routes met the trans-Saharan ones (Porter 93). — p. 7 [PDF 30] — F / A
  2. Meccan caravans passed Medina, Mada'in Salih and Tabuk, crossing into the Sinai from 'Aqabah toward Alexandria; the southern Sinai is very mountainous. — p. 9 [PDF 32] — F
  3. A route ran from Aylah/'Aqabah down the east coast of the Sinai and up the west coast. Near Nuwaybah a route crossed inland toward St Catherine's, passed Fayran [Pharan] and reached the Gulf of Suez. — p. 9 [PDF 32] — F
  4. Heading south into the Sinai on the way to Alexandria "more than doubled the distance". — p. 9 [PDF 32] — F / I/O
  5. Affagart put Mecca–Mount Sinai at 14 days by camel caravan (203); the author says this "is inaccurate" and the trip "would have been substantially longer". — p. 9 [PDF 32] — A + I/O
  6. Aylah was the intersection of the Silk Road, the Spice Route and the Incense Road in Roman times (Franck and Brownstone, endpapers). The western Sinai remained a major part of the Spice Route. — p. 10 [PDF 33] — A / F
  7. The great fair at Daba (Oman) drew traders from China, Hind and Sind, Persia, and the East and West every year. — p. 8 [PDF 31] — A (Hamidullah, citing Ibn al-Kalbi)
  8. The Qur'an names Sinai by the ancient name Jabal Tur; chapter 52 is al-Tur, "a synonym for al-Sina' or Sinai". — p. 15 [PDF 38] — F
  9. Other proposed Sinai sites are Jabal Lawz (Arabia) and Jabal Shara (Jordan). Some contemporary Islamic sources identify Jabal Lawz with Sinai, including a map of Muhammad's caravan routes. — p. 22 [PDF 45] — F
  10. Maqnah oasis is "accessible by foot from Jabal Lawz". — p. 22 [PDF 45] — F
  11. Hazleton: "Jebel Musa is generally acknowledged as the true peak, and is accepted by all three of the religions" (5). — p. 22 [PDF 45] — A
  12. Al-Tur is "the port city in proximity to the Monastery of Saint Catherine". — p. 23 [PDF 46] — F
  13. The Fountains of Moses is an oasis 12 km from El-Shatt (Champdor 58). — p. 21–22 [PDF 44–45] — A
  14. Atiya's description of the summit: to the east the Gulf of Aqaba, "from which Solomon once sent his trading ships"; to the north the wilderness of Zin; a chapel and a mosque at the top; the cave where Moses lived 40 days near the mosque (Atiya x–xi). — p. 15 [PDF 38] — A
J. St Catherine's Monastery, the covenant and the travellers' accounts
  1. Atiya: Muhammad "is said to have visited the Monastery during his early peregrinations" and "later rewarded them by issuing a covenant whereby their lives and property became secure under Moslem rule" (xviii). — p. 8–9 [PDF 31–32] — A
  2. A monk told Hobbs: "Muhammad and his companions were taken in by the monastery … he guaranteed the safety and protection of this place. That is one of the reasons for its longevity" (159). — p. 8–9 [PDF 31–32] — A
  3. Monconys: Muhammad, a friend of one of the monks, gave a charter of privileges and tax exemptions, "subjected all the Arabs who serve them", and required the monks to feed all Arabs who came; he signed "with the figure of his hand". — p. 9 [PDF 32] — A (228–229)
  4. Thévenot (Greek monks' version): Muhammad was the monks' camel driver; an eagle circled his sleeping head; the Abbot obtained a palm-print promise on "white paper". — p. 9–10 [PDF 32–33] — A (Relation 322–323; Voyages 536–537)
  5. Morison: Muhammad "stayed there for a few years … taking care of the camels", gave gifts out of regard for a monk he was fond of, and granted perpetual privileges, a total tax exemption and "absolute power over the Arabs". The monastery was required to give bread to poor Arabs, "who (as I have seen myself) come in rather large numbers". — p. 10 [PDF 33] — A (105–106)
  6. Cantemir: the account comes only "in a fabulous treatise by a Sinaitic monk" (168). Muhammad promised to free monks ("Rubban, (Keepers of the Life or Course)") from all tribute, in "an Arabic writing … confirm'd … for want of a Seal, with the Palm of his hand". — p. 10–11 [PDF 33–34] — A
  7. Fazakerley: the original document was signed by 'Ali and Abu Bakr and many of Muhammad's chieftains, "the Prophet having consecrated it with his own seal". — p. 11 [PDF 34] — A (375–378)
  8. Henniker: the superior said the hand-impression "is now at Constantinople, for the Gran Seignor having desired to look at it, retained it". Muhammad "swore by the token that the convent should remain forever sacred; that the country, as far as eye can scan, should belong to it". — p. 11 [PDF 34] — A (233–234)
  9. Arundale: the monastery library held "the copy of an edict from the Prophet, addressed to all Christians". The original was "written in Cufic characters upon the skin of a gazelle", with marks of the Prophet's fingers, and is "at present in the possession of the Sultan". — p. 12 [PDF 35] — A (28)
  10. Gazelle skin "is consistent with the period of the Prophet", and Kufic script "is consistent with Imam 'Ali personal artistic preference". — p. 12 [PDF 35] — I/O
  11. The Ottoman Caliph, "guided by his Grand Vizier, and counseled by the greatest scholar of Islam", would not have paid such a sum for a spurious document. — p. 11 [PDF 34] — I/O
  12. The monk population was "much greater than imagined": 6,000–7,000 monks in the Sinai at the conquest (Burckhardt 546). — p. 9 [PDF 32] — A
  13. Ratliff: "[t]ravel to visit holy places and holy figures flourished in the century before the Arab occupation" ("To Travel to the Holy" 87). The "See of Jerusalem and the monasteries of Mar Saba … and Saint Catherine … were important intellectual centers" ("Christian…" 38). — p. 15 [PDF 38] — A
  14. The monastery was built over the traditional site of the Burning Bush; a nearby sacred tree is said to have sprung from Aaron's rod (Atiya x–xi). — p. 15 [PDF 38] — A
  15. Origin of the achtiname: before the declaration of prophecy, as an oral promise sealed with a palm-print, or "according to another version, a document redacted by the monks and sealed by Muhammad" (Mouton 177). — p. 15 [PDF 38] — A + I/O
  16. The Virgin-and-Child image in the Ka'bah and the St Catherine icon are "This very same image". — p. 13 [PDF 36] — I/O
  17. Women are prohibited from entering the monastery, "as is true of any Eastern Orthodox monastery where even female animals are not admitted". — p. 24 [PDF 47] — F (author)
  18. The monastery draws "thousands of tourists per day along with a small number of true pilgrims". — p. 24 [PDF 47] — F
  19. St Catherine's "is the only monastery in the world to embrace both a church and a mosque". — p. 20 [PDF 43] — F (author)
K. The two mosques (monastery and summit)
  1. Cave of Moses: "Ten steps lead down into the cave, where there is a small altar and a mihrab niche indicating the direction of Mecca" (Hobbs 169). Mouton: the niche was carved when the mosque was built, and Bedouins never stopped Christians praying there (181). — p. 16 [PDF 39] — A
  2. The Jami' Fatimah [Mosque of Fatimah] (OCR "Fatiniah") stands 10 m south of the church on top of Jebel Musa. — p. 16 [PDF 39] — A (Hobbs 169)
  3. Mouton is "certain" the summit mosque was built on the foundations of an ancient Christian chapel (181). The mosque and the earlier fort used the remains of an ancient church or convent (Dahari 153), and the remains of four earlier churches can be seen in the debris (153). — p. 16 [PDF 39] — A
  4. Stanley: the monks "allowed the Mahometan devotees to pray side by side with Christian pilgrims". — p. 16 [PDF 39] — A (120)
  5. Henniker: the mosque "sanctifies the place in the eyes of the Musulman, and professes to acknowledge his superiority" (224). — p. 17 [PDF 40] — A
  6. Early Muslims built mosques next to existing churches and sometimes attached small churches to prayer halls. — p. 17 [PDF 40] — F (author)
  7. The construction of mosques "accompanied all of the early Muslim conquests". — p. 17 [PDF 40] — F (author)
  8. Lindsay: "Close to the church rises a minaret of a mosque! Built, for the nonce, three centuries ago … seldom used unless some Turkish pilgrim of rank visits" (290). — p. 17 [PDF 40] — A
  9. "There was, of course, no Sultan in Egypt; he ruled from Istanbul." The Fatimids "did not employ the title of Sultan". — p. 17 [PDF 40] — F (author)
  10. Dumas: "the Greek convent in token of servitude has been compelled to erect a Turkish edifice" (246). — p. 18 [PDF 41] — A
  11. Arabic News (2004): the mosque has six rooms divided by two pillars; the minaret is 12 m high, square in its upper part with a round dome, and "very much like that of al-Gioshi Mosque in Cairo". Its floor is wood carried by wooden beams ("rams"). — p. 18 [PDF 41] — A
  12. The monastery minbar is one of only three surviving Fatimid-era minbars; the other two are at Kous (Upper Egypt) and Hebron (Palestine) (Champdor 48). — p. 18 [PDF 41] — A (Skrobucha 61; Champdor 48)
  13. Inscription titles of Shahan Shah: "Prince of the Army, Sword of Islam, Helper of Islam, Protector and Judge of Humankind, Guide and Protector of the Faithful". — p. 18 [PDF 41] — A
  14. Champdor: "the church bell and the minaret, side by side, are a moving symbol" (47). The mosque was built for the Muslim vassals of the monastery and the people of the Sinai (47). Only the minaret was new; a chapel was converted (34). — p. 19 [PDF 42] — A
  15. J. Daumas: the mosque was built on the site of a chapel of St Basil, "the founder of the Order of Greek Monks" (qtd. Champdor 47–48). — p. 19 [PDF 42] — A
  16. "To become a Mameluke" means both "to embrace Islam" and "to become an apostate". — p. 19 [PDF 42] — F
  17. Thenaud's text shows that the mosque "was built or re-built by a head monk who converted to Islam", and that the Fatimids granted him its administration. — p. 19 [PDF 42] — I/O
  18. Only two ancient mosques remain at Mount Sinai, one in the monastery and one on the summit. — p. 19 [PDF 42] — F
  19. 'Abd al-Malik: the mosques "were built for Muslims passing through the Sinai: pilgrims on the way to Mecca or to Mount Moses". — p. 19 [PDF 42] — A
  20. The Shi'ite Fatimids showed the most interest in Mount Sinai, more than the Sunni Ayyubids, Mamluks and Ottomans; pilgrim flow was "far greater during Shi'ite times". — p. 19 [PDF 42] — I/O
  21. Mosque staff were appointed by the chief qadi in Cairo: one or two people serving as imam, muezzin and superintendent. The mosque was "always closed to the troublesome local Bedouins". — p. 20 [PDF 43] — A (Mouton 179)
  22. Arabic News: "During the Ayyubid and Mamluk ages, only little was known about the mosque." — p. 20 [PDF 43] — A
  23. Arabic News: "[a] budget has been allocated for the mosque for periodical maintenance." — p. 20 [PDF 43] — A
L. Other sacred sites and shared devotion
  1. Tomb of the Prophet Salih in Wadi al-Shaykh (Skrobucha 55). A several-day festival for Nabi Salih ends with a sacrifice on Jabal Musa (55). — p. 20 [PDF 43] — A
  2. A camel-hoofprint hollow about 200 m northwest of the summit is the "Print of the She-Camel (Matabb an-Naaga) of Nabi Saalih Rashiid". Earlier Bedouins said it belonged to Muhammad's she-camel, whose other legs rested in Mecca, Jerusalem and Damascus, or in Mecca, Cairo and Damascus (Hobbs 169–170). — p. 20 [PDF 43] — A
  3. Others attribute the print to Buraq (Freeman-Grenville 210; Skrobucha 56; Clayton 20; Van Egmont and Heyman 166–167; Stanley 246; Henniker 233). The author prefers the Buraq accounts "due to their antiquity". — p. 20 [PDF 43] — A + I/O
  4. Authenticated ahadith say Muhammad was physically carried from Mecca to the precinct of the Temple of Solomon in Jerusalem on Buraq; "the Family of the Prophet always insisted that it was physical". — p. 20–21 [PDF 43–44] — T
  5. Champdor: Bedouins sacrifice a goat (or, in good years, a camel) at the rock each year and smear the blood on the lintel and side-posts (50). — p. 21 [PDF 44] — A
  6. Arundale: monks avoid effacing the print because its veneration "serves to check the constant inclination of the Arabs to plunder the Convent" (32). — p. 21 [PDF 44] — A
  7. Skrobucha's list of Sinai holy sites (27–28): Moses' cave; Horeb, where Elijah fled from Ahab; Elijah's cave and altar; where Aaron and the seventy stood; the Burning Bush; the golden-calf sites; the stone where the tablets were broken; the water-rock; manna and quails. — p. 21 [PDF 44] — A
  8. More sites: the Monastery of the Forty Saints; where St Catherine's body rested three centuries; a monastery with no bells from which bells sounded; the bushes used for Moses' walking-sticks (Freeman-Grenville 212); the valley of the Amalekite defeat (Affagart 197); twelve fountains for the twelve tribes (198); golden-calf sites (199); Aaron's footprint and shrine (Hobbs 173). — p. 21 [PDF 44] — A
  9. Jabali tradition: Catherine lived on Mount Sinai in early Islamic times, became a Muslim, and was beheaded by her Christian father; angels took her body to Jabal Katerina. — p. 22 [PDF 45] — T
  10. Arab tradition: the monastery's foundation goes back to Moses (57; Bernstein 123). Skrobucha calls this an "incongruous legend" (57) and Arab beliefs "naive" (62). — p. 22 [PDF 45] — A
  11. Marquis of "Labode" admired the accuracy of Arab traditions (204). — p. 22 [PDF 45] — A
  12. "Jewish people eventually lost the geographic details of their wanderings in the Sinai, leaving scarcely any documentation." — p. 22 [PDF 45] — F (author)
  13. Tschanz: some outlying hajj routes "were intended to allow the pilgrim to visit mosques and holy places". The Sinai route was feasible only for pilgrims from North Africa and Egypt. — p. 23 [PDF 46] — A / F
  14. Affagart: Turks and Moors revere "the holy virgin Catherine". His "church with a priest" means a mosque with an imam. — p. 23 [PDF 46] — A + I/O
  15. Ratliff: "[a]ll of the preserved documents mention the monastery receiving … pilgrims, who in the Mamluk period are identified as Muslims traveling to and from Mecca" (15). — p. 24 [PDF 47] — A
  16. Muslims of Christian ancestry kept major Christian holidays for centuries. Some communities celebrated Christmas, Easter and Eid together and slaughtered a sheep in honor of the Virgin Mary (Berkey 160). — p. 24 [PDF 47] — A / F
  17. "the Alavis, celebrate Christmas, Easter, and Epiphany to this day, along with Persian holy days". Christmas was later "replaced by mawlid al-nabi". — p. 24 [PDF 47] — F (author)
  18. Stephens: "on this sacred spot the followers of Christ and Mohammed have united in worshipping the true living God" (219). — p. 25 [PDF 48] — A
  19. Salafism "holds that pilgrimage to other than Mecca is a prohibited form of polytheism"; "pseudo-Sunnis rarely show their respect for sacred sites". — p. 25 [PDF 48] — I/O
  20. Shi'ites visit the graves of the Fourteen Infallibles (the Prophet, Fatimah, the Twelve Imams) and sites of Biblical prophets in Iran, Iraq, Syria, Jordan, Palestine and Egypt. Qur'an 22:32; 40:81; 5:29; 31:32 are cited. — p. 25 [PDF 48] — F
  21. Holy Land sites revered by Muslims: the Tomb of David on Mount Zion (Limor 223); the tombs of St Pelagia, Rabi'ah al-'Adawiyyah and the prophetess Huldah on the Mount of Olives (227); the Tomb of the Virgin Mary in the Vale of Jehoshaphat; the Church of the Ascension (220); the Temple Mount. — p. 25 [PDF 48] — A
  22. The Great Mosque of Damascus was built "on the site of the basilica of Saint John the Baptist" (Ratliff 34). In Ottoman times Muslims visited the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (Faroqhi 170–171). — p. 25 [PDF 48] — A
  23. Hobbs: "Through the Angel Gabriel, God revealed the Mount Sinai tradition to the Prophet Muhammad … it forms part of the bedrock on which Islam is founded" (33). — p. 26 [PDF 49] — A
  24. Muhammad himself made pilgrimages to holy sites before and after his proclamation of prophecy and visited the graves of the martyrs of Islam. — p. 26 [PDF 49] — F (author)
  25. "The Prophet Muhammad, it is reported, performed his prayers on a clay tablet": a tradition among Sunnis, "treated as obligatory" by the Shi'ites. — p. 26 [PDF 49] — T / F
  26. Carrying clay tokens from pilgrimage sites was a pre-Islamic Christian custom, believed to have spiritual and medicinal power (Flood 250). Believers touched them to their eyes, mouth and forehead (Ratliff, "To Travel to the Holy" 86). — p. 26 [PDF 49] — A
  27. "the Prophet had rendered the earth clean for prostration by his sacred steps and had rendered the soil of Medina curative by means of his saliva." — p. 26 [PDF 49] — T
M. Medina and the Constitution
  1. Yathrib was "rich but self-destructive", divided between warring Arab tribes and their Jewish allies. — p. 27–28 [PDF 50–51] — F / I/O
  2. "The Jews were not clients, as so many have claimed, but powerful and influential allies of the Arabs" (Lecker 2000: 67). — p. 28 [PDF 51] — A
  3. Greater Medina = Yathrib plus nearby towns. The Banu Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa' lived in al-Quff and Zuhra (eastern Medina) (Lecker 2010: 66, 70); the Banu Qurayza in the southeast (65). — p. 28 [PDF 51] — A
  4. Lecker: the Nadir, Qurayza and Qaynuqa' "are not listed among the participants … for the simple reason that they were not part of it" (68). — p. 28 [PDF 51] — A
  5. These tribes may have come from Khaybar, "as stipulated in early Islamic sources" (Scholler 30, n. 44). — p. 28 [PDF 51] — A (possibility)
  6. Clans named in the printed Constitution: Banu 'Awf, Sa'ida, al-Harith, Jusham, al-Najjar (1.1); Banu 'Amr b. 'Awf, al-Nabit, al-'Aws (1.2). Jews of Banu 'Awf, al-Najjar, al-Harith, Sa'ida, Jusham, al-Aws, Tha'laba, "the Jafna, a clan of the Tha'laba", and al-Shutayba (6.2); the freedmen of Tha'laba (6.3); the Jews of al-'Aws (8.5). — p. 29–31 [PDF 52–54] — A (Ibn Ishaq 233)
  7. The Constitution is printed with editorial bracketed headings: Preamble; 1 The Blood-Wit; 2 Loyalty and Unity of the Ummah; 3 Rules of Engagement; 4 Code of Conduct; 5 The Guardianship of the Prophet; 6 The War Effort, Military Matters, and Support; 7 Rights of Women; 8 Binding Nature of the Covenant; Epilogue. Clauses run 1.1–1.3, 2.1–2.5, 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4, 5.1, 6.1–6.10 (6.1 printed "6:1"), 7.1 and 8.1–8.9. — p. 29–31 [PDF 52–54] — F
  8. Key clauses: "They are one community [ummah] to the exclusion of all men" (Preamble); "To the Jew who follows us belong help and equality" (2.5); "The Jews of Banu 'Awf are one community with the believers, the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs" (6.2); "Yathrib shall be a sanctuary for the people of this document" (6.9); "A woman shall only be given protection with the consent of her family" (7.1); "Quraysh and their helpers shall be given no protection" (8.3); peace must be kept "except in the case of holy war" (8.4). — p. 29–31 [PDF 52–54] — A (Ibn Ishaq 233)
  9. Hoyland: "[i]ts authenticity has been accepted by most scholars" (2000: 290, n. 58). Crone admitted its authenticity in Slaves on Horses (7). — p. 31 [PDF 54] — A
  10. Donner, Muhammad and the Believers: the "umma document … seems to be of virtually documentary quality … all students of early Islam, even the most skeptical, accept it as authentic" (72). — p. 31 [PDF 54] — A
  11. The Constitution aimed to end infighting between "the Arab war-lords of the tribe of Khazraj and their Jewish rivals", and in doing so "established the first Islamic State". — p. 32 [PDF 55] — F / I/O
  12. Peters: if the Jews could practise their religion within the ummah, "then Muhammad's original Medina 'community' was a purely secular one" (201). — p. 32 [PDF 55] — A
  13. Armstrong: "In the Qur'anic vision there is no dichotomy between the sacred and the profane … The aim was tawhid" (2000: 14–15). — p. 32 [PDF 55] — A
  14. In Islam, slaves can earn freedom "by work or conversion", "all children born of slaves are free", and freeing slaves is a pious act and sometimes a required expiation. — p. 32 [PDF 55] — F (author)
  15. Roman Republic: consuls "acted like kings"; the People's Assembly was composed of representatives of military units; the Senate represented the aristocracy; plebeians "could not rule, elect rulers or make use of land". — p. 32 [PDF 55] — F (author)
  16. Under the Constitution, "all privileges of class were abolished": rich and poor, Arabs and non-Arabs, blacks and whites, men and women, children and adults "all had the same rights". — p. 33 [PDF 56] — I/O
  17. "In the time of the Prophet, the ahl al-dhimmah, both Jewish and Christian, belonged to the community of believers." The term kuffar was reserved for those who actively attacked Islam. — p. 33 [PDF 56] — F (author)
  18. Qur'an 3:19 ("Inna al-dina 'inda Allahi al-Islam") and 5:3: the definite form al-Islam refers to a religion, not "submission". — p. 33 [PDF 56] — F / I/O
  19. O'Shea: "The message given to Muhammad, the last in a long line of prophecy, improved and supplanted all that had come before" (15). — p. 33 [PDF 56] — A
  20. "Muhammad clearly identified himself as the Prophet and Messenger of Allah, his religion as Islam, and his followers as Muslims in the many letters he sent". The sentence continues past the end of this chunk. — p. 33 [PDF 56] — F (author)

5. Covenant and document details in this section

5.1 Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (Testamentum et pactiones / al-'Ahd wa al-shurut)
  • Claimed date of the document (AH/CE): not given in this section. The contents give three versions: 1630 CE (Sionita's printed text), 1538 CE (the "possible source covenant") and 1655 CE (Nissel). — contents [PDF 8–9]; xvii [PDF 18]
  • Original or source copy: "what appears to be the original covenant brought from Palestine to Paris by Father Pacifique Scaliger in 1629. This possible source covenant, which dates to 1538, has never been previously published." — xvii–xviii [PDF 18]
  • Origin "especially obscure": Sionita may have obtained it from a Levantine community or through church channels. Nissel's connection is "even less clear". The Ottomans, French allies, "had encouraged the dissemination" (author inference). — xvi [PDF 17]
  • Editions: (1) 1630, Paris, Vitré, ed. Sionita, Arabic + Latin + Pact of 'Umar; 3 copies (Notre Dame, Chicago, Oklahoma). (2) 1630, Paris, no names; 1 copy, Harvard. (3) 1630, Paris, ed. François Hotman, Sionita's Latin, Vitré; copy at Marburg. (4) 1638, J. Fabricius, Latin only. (5) 1655, Leiden, Nissel, Latin + vocalized Arabic + Surahs 14–15; Columbia, VU Amsterdam and many European libraries. (6) 1672, Nagy de Harsány, Latin only, in Colloquia familiar[ia] turco-latina. (7) 1690, Hinckelmann, German. — xv–xvi [PDF 16–17]
  • Translations: Rycaut (English, History of the Ottoman Empire) → Briot (French, 1670) → Grassi, Charte Turque (1826) → Miltitz, Manuel des Consuls (1838) → Van Dyke, Capitulations of the Ottoman Empire (1881), "not a direct translation". — xvii [PDF 18]
  • Survival: fewer than 30 copies printed in 1600s Europe survive; never published in the Muslim world; not in Arabic for 3.5 centuries. — xvii–xviii [PDF 18–19]
  • This book's contents: Texts I–IV; corrected Arabic originals from 1630 and 1538; reproductions of the 1538, 1630 and 1655 documents (Ch. 10); commentary on the 1630 and 1538 covenants (Ch. 5). — contents [PDF 8–9]
5.2 Covenant with the Monks of Mount Sinai (Achtiname)
  • Origin (monks' tradition as the author reconstructs it): a promise by the young Muhammad before his prophecy, either oral and sealed with a palm-print, or a document written by the monks and sealed by him (Mouton 177). The formal charter dates to "the early days of Islam". — p. 15 [PDF 38]
  • Physical description: "contract of protection, drawn up on the skin of a gazelle" signed with an inked hand-print ("(344)", p. 8 [PDF 31]); "written in Cufic characters upon the skin of a gazelle … marks of the Prophet's fingers" (Arundale 28, p. 12 [PDF 35]); a palm-print on "white paper" (Thévenot, p. 10 [PDF 33]); "an Arabic writing … Palm of his hand" for want of a seal (Cantemir 168, p. 11 [PDF 34]).
  • Signatories/witnesses: "The original was signed by 'Ali, and Abu Bekr, and many of Mahomet's chieftains, the Prophet having consecrated it with his own seal" (Fazakerley 375–378). — p. 11 [PDF 34]
  • Scribe: not named. The author links the Kufic script to "Imam 'Ali['s] personal artistic preference". — p. 12 [PDF 35]
  • Recipients: the monks of Mount Sinai. Arundale calls it an edict "addressed to all Christians"; Thenaud says the privileges were granted "the monks of the Church of the East". — p. 12 [PDF 35]; p. 19 [PDF 42]
  • Terms (as travellers report them): privileges and tax exemptions; Arabs who serve the monks subjected to them; the monks to feed the Arabs (Monconys); freedom from all tribute (Cantemir); perpetual privileges and "absolute power over the Arabs" (Morison); convent "forever sacred", land "as far as eye can scan" (Henniker).
  • Custody:
    • in the monastery mosque, in Muslim hands, from the 12th to the 14th century (author's inference from Thenaud 1512 and Affagart 1533–34); earliest copies possibly taken to Cairo by the Fatimids and lost in Salah al-Din's destruction of the library (author speculation) — p. 19 [PDF 42]; p. 23 [PDF 46]
    • removed by Selim I: "demanded" in 1517 after the conquest of Egypt (Arundale); "purchased … for four thousand gold crowns" with a Chatisherif (Cantemir), the version the author accepts; "taken" by Selim (Monconys, Fazakerley); placed "in the Treasury of the Serrail in Constantinople" (Morison); retained by the "Gran Seignor" at Constantinople (Henniker) — p. 9–12 [PDF 32–35]
    • Selim left the monks a certified or signed copy (parchment, per Arundale); in 1831 it was in the library archives (Arundale) — p. 10–12 [PDF 33–35]
  • Turkish copy: a Turkish-language copy of 1638, reproduced on the cover by permission of St Catherine's Monastery, Egypt. — copyright [PDF 7]
  • Publications: 1902 English translation by Anton F. Haddad (from Naufal Effendi Naufal's Arabic translation of a Turkish copy); complete Arabic versions by Shuqayr (1916) and Bernhard Moritz (1918). This book includes six translations (Texts I–VI) and a corrected Arabic original (Ch. 8). — xvii [PDF 18]; contents [PDF 8]
5.3 Covenant with the Christians of Najran
  • Published in Arabic and French in 1919; French translation by Archbishop Addai Scher. Arabic reprinted in 1956 (Hamidullah, Majmu'ah al-watha'iq al-siyasiyyah) and 2002 ('Amarah, al-Islam wa al-akhar). — xviii [PDF 19]
  • The contents list a "Corrected Arabic Original from the 9th Century CE" (Ch. 11, p. 301). — contents [PDF 9]
  • The covenant proclaims "the need to follow the laws that God had imposed on the Children of Israel". — p. 13 [PDF 36]
5.4 Covenant with the Assyrian Christians
  • "a work widely unknown", first published in Persian and English by George David Malech in 1910. The book includes a "Reproduction of Original Document" (Ch. 12, p. 315). — xviii [PDF 19]; contents [PDF 9]
5.5 Covenant with the Christians of Persia
  • Published in English by Leon Arpee in 1948 (Ch. 9 text, p. 223). — xviii [PDF 19]; contents [PDF 9]
5.6 Covenant with the Armenian Christians of Jerusalem
  • Has circulated "to a limited extent" among Armenian clerics and educated members (front matter spells it "Propet" [sic]). Ch. 7 (p. 191); no text chapter for it appears in Part II. — xviii [PDF 19]; contents [PDF 9]
5.7 Covenants listed in the Introduction
  • "with the Christians of Mount Sinai, Najran, Assyria, Persia, Palestine, Egypt, Armenia, and the World". — p. 1 [PDF 24]
5.8 Constitution of Medina (Sahifat al-Madinah, Charter of Medina)
  • Issuer: "a document from Muhammad, the Prophet". Parties: "the believers and Muslims of Quraysh and Yathrib, and those who followed them", named clans and the Jews of named clans (see §4 #200–202).
  • Date: presented after arrival in Yathrib in 622 CE (author). Sirah: immediately on arrival. Peters: within a few months (200). Esposito: 622–624 CE (80). Author: possibly later, after the Jewish tribes' expulsion. — p. 27–28 [PDF 50–51]
  • Omission: Banu Qurayzah, Nadir and Qaynuqa' are absent (Lecker 68). — p. 28 [PDF 51]
  • Text source: Ibn Ishaq 233; the bracketed headings and clause numbers are editorial. — p. 29–31 [PDF 52–54]
  • Authenticity: Hoyland ("accepted by most scholars"), Crone, Donner. — p. 31 [PDF 54]
5.9 Other treaties and agreements mentioned
  • A possible treaty between Quraysh and the Ansar to prevent bloodshed (Lecker 2000: 157–167). — p. 27–28 [PDF 50–51]
  • An agreement between the Prophet and "the Jews, all of them" on his arrival in Medina, attaching every tribe to its confederates (al-Waqidi 87). The author says it is distinct from the Constitution. — p. 28 [PDF 51]
  • Treaty of Maqnah with the Jewish inhabitants of the oasis, signed 631 CE. — p. 22 [PDF 45]
  • Pact of 'Umar, printed in Sionita's 1630 edition. — xv [PDF 16]
5.10 Other dated documents and inscriptions
  • Fatimid minbar inscription at St Catherine's: "month of Rabi I, of the year 500 [AH]" (book: minbar 1106 CE). It names Abu 'Ali al-Mansur al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah, and the minbar was ordered by Abu al-Qasim Shahan Shah (qtd. Skrobucha 61). — p. 18 [PDF 41]
  • Arabic manuscript at the monastery (seen by Burckhardt in 1816): Turkish hajjis made mosque servants in "the year of the Hedjra 783" (Burckhardt: 1381 CE). — p. 18 [PDF 41]
  • Manuscript at the monastery library: monks conferred in the mosque "round AD 1508" (Arabic News). — p. 20 [PDF 43]

6. The author's key arguments and opinions

  1. Christian–Muslim conflict "has been artificially ignited by the forces of imperialism", and the covenants can inspire "insuperable harmony" among the three Abrahamic religions. — p. 1 [PDF 24]
  2. Majlisi's account of two childhood trips to Syria should be believed "in this case". — p. 2 [PDF 25]
  3. The Bahira event is historically plausible. A missing chain of transmission does not make it untrue, since the episode predates the hadith period. Skeptics (Bell, Armstrong, al-Dhahabi) are wrong or unsupported, and Gabriel "cannot, in good faith, ignore centuries … of sources". — p. 3–4 [PDF 26–27]
  4. Secular scholars' "default setting" is denial, then distortion. The polemical labels for Bahira (Nestorian, Arian, Jacobite, renegade cardinal) are distortions. — p. 4 [PDF 27]
  5. Bahira could not have written the Qur'an: it would have had to resurface 25–31 years later. The relationship "is not one of influence but one of recognition". — p. 4–5 [PDF 27–28]
  6. Arian or Nazorean Christians, not Trinitarian ones, were more likely to be awaiting a final prophet; the monks Muhammad met may have been followers of Jesus who kept the Mosaic law. — p. 5 [PDF 28]
  7. No one at St Catherine's could have taught Muhammad Arabic, judging from Antoninus Martyr's list of languages. — p. 5 [PDF 28]
  8. Ibn Ishaq condensed his account, "perhaps suppressing elements that sounded too mythological". — p. 7 [PDF 30]
  9. Muhammad was well travelled; the claim that he made only two trips is "a logical impossibility". The image of an illiterate Muhammad with little Christian contact stems from "an over-reaction" to Orientalist ideas. — p. 8 [PDF 31]
  10. Muhammad probably combined religion and commerce in travelling to Sinai, may have been the monks' contracted caravaneer, and may have set off for Sinai for religious reasons or carried pilgrims. — p. 9–10, 15 [PDF 32–33, 38]
  11. The Cantemir version "appears to be the oldest of all". It shows a cloud, not an eagle, and a hand-print used for lack of a seal, not because of illiteracy; the illiteracy charge "appears to be a later development". — p. 10–11 [PDF 33–34]
  12. Selim I bought the covenant rather than seizing it, and would not have paid so much for a spurious document. — p. 11 [PDF 34]
  13. Central thesis of this part: 25 years of Muhammad's life (ages 15–25 and 25–40) are "unaccounted for". When news of him "disappears in the Hijaz, news of him reappears in the Sinai", and the monks' account "fits" and "completes the picture". The monks were "experts in sirah literature, extremely lucky, or honest and truthful. The evidence points to the latter." — p. 12 [PDF 35]
  14. The Qur'an "seems to support" a Sinai sojourn (93:6–8; 95:1–6; 52:1). The orphan sheltered (93:6) is read as the monks' care, and the "man created in the best of moulds" as the Prophet. — p. 13–15 [PDF 36–38]
  15. "I would prefer a Muhammad who was mentored by monotheistic holy men than a Muhammad who cared for the idols in the Ka'bah." Islam is not weakened by continuing the Judeo-Christian tradition; "The issue … is not of borrowing, but rather of belonging". — p. 13, 15 [PDF 36, 38]
  16. Muhammad's praying in caves may have begun in the cave of Moses on Sinai, "the immediate precursor to the cave of Hirah". — p. 16 [PDF 39]
  17. By protecting the Virgin icon in the Ka'bah, the Prophet "re-enacted" the Sinai icon's Hand of God; "it was not truly the Hand of Muhammad, but rather, the Hand of Allah". — p. 13 [PDF 36]
  18. The Bedouin belief that the mosque dates from the Prophet's time is untrue literally but "founded by his footstep", and expresses nostalgia for lost Muslim–Christian unity: "Something … had gone wrong". — p. 16–17 [PDF 39–40]
  19. Placing churches inside Islamic complexes protected them, and the early Muslims "embodied the teachings of the covenants". — p. 17 [PDF 40]
  20. Physical evidence (the minbar) "must always prevail over speculation"; the mosque dates to the early 12th century, while its "origin … appears to be lost in time". — p. 18 [PDF 41]
  21. Thenaud shows the mosque was built or rebuilt by a convert prior. The Fatimids made Muslims the custodians of the covenant, and the earliest copies may have perished under Salah al-Din. — p. 19 [PDF 42]
  22. Shi'ite (Fatimid) Islam had a "greater appreciation for sacred sites and spiritual pilgrimages", and Shi'ites alone still treat Sinai as a pilgrimage site. Salafis and "pseudo-Sunnis" do not, while "true, traditional Sunnis" do. — p. 19, 22, 25 [PDF 42, 45, 48]
  23. Skrobucha applies "double standards" by treating Jewish and Christian traditions as fact and Arab ones as "naive". — p. 22 [PDF 45]
  24. The decline of Muslim pilgrimage to Sinai is linked to the Crusades, trade shifts, suppression of inter-religious ties, the rise of Ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab, and Salafism, which "rendered the region unsafe". — p. 23–25 [PDF 46–48]
  25. The Alawis of Syria and Alevis of Turkey may practise "a primitive form of Islam which has remained frozen in time". — p. 24 [PDF 47]
  26. Muhammad was always a prophet, even before Creation. His early encounters with Christians confirmed his status and gave him confidence in "the spiritual solidarity of the People of the Book" (against Salahi). — p. 26 [PDF 49]
  27. The Prophet visited holy sites and may have prostrated on soil brought back from Sinai. — p. 26 [PDF 49]
  28. The Constitution of Medina created "a tolerant, pluralistic government which protected religious freedom". It was "a unique system which had never existed before and which has never been seen since"; calling it a kingdom, theocracy or secular state is "incorrect". — p. 32 [PDF 55]
  29. The Constitution was more egalitarian than Athenian "slave-master democracy" or the Roman Republic, and the resemblance of Greek democracy to today's Western "liberal" democracies is "no coincidence". — p. 32–33 [PDF 55–56]
  30. In the Prophet's time Jews and Christians were part of the "Community of Believers"; the post-prophetic labelling of the People of the Book as kuffar is a later development. — p. 33 [PDF 56]
  31. Donner misunderstands "basic Arabic" (definite al-Islam vs indefinite islam), and his 'Abd al-Malik thesis has "no basis". Islam came "to correct … and complete" earlier religions. — p. 33 [PDF 56]
  32. Donner's theories on Islam's origins "can and should be criticized as utterly unfounded". Crone has "little love towards Islam and Muslims". — p. 31 [PDF 54]
  33. Front matter: Nissel's and Sionita's Latin translations are both "poor"; Haddad's and Naufal's reliance on a Turkish copy was "academically inexcusable". — xvi–xvii [PDF 17–18]
  34. Front matter: Sionita's unusual orthography (no final hamza) "may have been a faithful transcription of the original text", reflecting the Prophet's Arabic. — xvi [PDF 17]
  35. Front matter (Covenants Initiative): Muslims should publicly defend persecuted Christians "in the name of the Prophet Muhammad himself"; "Peace is … made by facing and enduring conflict". — xix [PDF 20]

7. Internal inconsistencies within this section

  1. Date of Muhammad's marriage to Khadijah. p. 6 [PDF 29]: Bahira "in 582 CE" and marriage "in 595 CE"; "In 595 … hired by Khadijah". p. 12 [PDF 35]: "from his voyage to Syria with his uncle Abu Talib in 582 CE to his marriage to Khadijah in 582 CE". Same event, two dates. p. 26 [PDF 49] ("wife … for fifteen years" by 610) agrees with 595.
  2. Start of the "unaccounted" period. p. 6 [PDF 29]: "from the age of twelve to the age of twenty-five" he kept leading caravans. p. 12 [PDF 35]: "a period of ten years … from the time he was fifteen to the time he was twenty-five, that is unaccounted for".
  3. Muhammad's age at the Bahira meeting. p. 2 [PDF 25]: "nine years old" in some Sunni accounts, "twelve" in others. p. 4 [PDF 27]: "an illiterate boy of nine or fifteen years". p. 6 [PDF 29] gives 582 CE, i.e. age 12 by the book's 570 birth date.
  4. Harb al-fijar participation. p. 6 [PDF 29]: "spurious allegations that he participated … when he was twenty years of age". p. 12 [PDF 35]: Safdar Husayn "wrongly alleges … the Sacriligious War in 585 CE", which is age 15 on the book's chronology. The two passages also spell it differently: "Sacrilegious" vs "Sacriligious".
  5. Age at the Sinai visit. p. 12 [PDF 35] places the Sinai stay within ages 15–25, before the marriage; p. 21 [PDF 44] speaks of a visit "at the age of twenty-five"; p. 8 [PDF 31] puts the Sinai contact in "this obscure decade" between the marriage and the revelation. That gives three different placements.
  6. Fatimid caliph name and reign dates. p. 16 [PDF 39]: summit mosque built "during the reign of Abu 'Ali al-Mansur (r. 996-1021 CE), the tenth of the Fatimid Caliphs". p. 17 [PDF 40]: al-Hakim is "(r. 996-1021 CE)", and the monastery mosque was built under al-Hakim's "fourth successor, Abu Ali al-Mansur, al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah, who ruled from 1102 to 1131 CE". The same name, "Abu 'Ali al-Mansur", gets two different reigns, 996–1021 and 1102–1131.
  7. Al-Amir's reign. p. 17 [PDF 40]: "1102 to 1131 CE". p. 18 [PDF 41]: "al-Amir (r. 1101-1130 CE)".
  8. Certainty on the mosque's date, p. 18 [PDF 41]. "the origin of the mosque appears to be lost in time … the mystery of the Jami' mosque remains to be resolved". On the same page: "There can be little doubt that the mosque was built at the beginning of the 12th century". p. 17 [PDF 40] says "In reality, the existing structure was built" under al-Amir.
  9. Citation that looks like a date. p. 16 [PDF 39]: the Jabaliyyah "believe it dates from the rule of Caliph 'Umar" is cited as "(Hobbs 634-644)", which looks like 'Umar's reign dates rather than Hobbs page numbers. Hobbs is otherwise cited at pp. 159–173 and 219.
  10. Number of covenants in the volume. xvii [PDF 18]: "includes six of the covenants" but lists five (Sinai, Najran, World, Persia, Assyrian). Contents: six Part I chapters (with Armenian, Ch. 7) but only five text chapters in Part II. p. 1 [PDF 24]: covenants with Christians of "Mount Sinai, Najran, Assyria, Persia, Palestine, Egypt, Armenia, and the World" (eight).
  11. Route of the Night Journey. p. 21 [PDF 44]: stops for prayer at "Medina, Mount Sinai, Bethlehem, and Jerusalem" (date "around the year 621 CE"). p. 27 [PDF 50]: "from Mecca to Syria … then to Palestine … and then to Mount Sinai" (date "620/621 CE").
  12. Closure of the monastery mosque. p. 20 [PDF 43]: "officially closed in 1986" (Mouton; 'Abd al-Malik), and in the same paragraph "The SCA carried out a restoration process of the mosque in 1986" (Arabic News). p. 25 [PDF 48]: closure "in the mid-1980s" from a "chill in relations". p. 19 [PDF 42]: "In recent decades … the closing of the mosque by the monks and the planting of a cross on its dome".
  13. Waraqah's Gospel language. The two Bukhari versions quoted on p. 27 [PDF 50] differ: "used to read the Gospel in Arabic" vs "would write from the Gospel in Hebrew". This is a variance between quoted sources, not the author's own claim.
  14. Fate of Sa'ib. p. 8 [PDF 31]: Ibn 'Abbas says he swore fealty and received Hunayn booty, and Ibn Hisham says he "became an excellent Muslim". Ibn Ishaq says he was killed among the polytheists at Badr (338). The author notes this conflict between sources.
  15. How Selim obtained the Sinai covenant. Sources disagree, and the author picks one: "demanded" in 1517 (Arundale, p. 12); "taken" (Monconys p. 9; Fazakerley p. 11); "purchased … for four thousand gold crowns" (Cantemir p. 11); "retained" after asking to look at it (Henniker p. 11). Author: "Rather than being seized, it was purchased" (p. 11 [PDF 34]).
  16. Which account is "oldest". p. 10 [PDF 33] calls the Cantemir version "the oldest of all", although Cantemir (1673–1723) is later than Monconys (1646–47) and Thévenot (1655–63). The author ties its age to the "fabulous treatise by a Sinaitic monk" it is said to draw on. p. 11 [PDF 34] hedges: "If this is indeed the oldest account". The book also gives no date for Arundale's or Henniker's sources.
  17. Pococke vs Thévenot chronology, p. 5 [PDF 28]. Pococke (1704–1765) is said to have alleged the Sergius story, and "This fanciful fabrication was spread widely centuries before" Thévenot (1633–1667). This is not strictly contradictory (the fabrication may be older than both), but the passage reads oddly because Pococke postdates Thévenot.
  18. Arundale dates appear only once each. p. 11 [PDF 34]: "Francis Arundale, the British architect, visited … in 1831" (no lifespan). p. 21 [PDF 44]: "Francis Arundale (1807-1853)" (no "CE", unlike the book's usual style).
  19. Spelling variants of key names. Nissel / "Nisell" (xvi); Rycaut / Ricaut (xvii); Vitré / Vitray (xv); Dar Rahe Haqq (p. 1) / Dar Rah Haqq (p. 6); Bahira / Baheera (Salahi quote, p. 26); Jebel Musa / Jabal Musa; Morison's "Chanoine de Bar le Due" (OCR); "Hesburg" Library; minbar as "mimbar", "tnitibar" (OCR) and "minibars"; Omid Safi / "Saji" (signatory list, xix); "Mount Saint Catherine" (p. 14) for the monastery; "Propet" (xviii); "Zaffulla" Khan. The Göttingen library is listed twice (xv–xvi).
  20. Era phrase. p. 25 [PDF 48]: Muslim Brotherhood influence "in the second decade of the second millennium". As printed; context (2013 events) suggests the 21st century was meant. No correction is made here; flagged only.
  21. Chunk page marker. PDF 56 is labelled "printed p.31" by the chunk header, but the page foot reads "33" (see header note).

1. Section summary

This part finishes the author's reading of the Constitution of Medina. He sets it against Athenian democracy and the Roman Republic and calls the Medinan ummah a pluralistic "Free State" in which Jews, Christians and even pagans counted as one community, against Orientalist readings such as those of Peters and Donner. He rejects Donner's thesis that "Islam" as a distinct religion took shape under 'Abd al-Malik, while granting that relations with Christians hardened under that caliph (Dome of the Rock, Arabicization, the Standing Caliph coins). Under "The Judeo-Christian Response to the Advent of Islam" he recounts conversions: Salman the Persian, 'Abd Allah ibn Sallam, Addas, a party of Abyssinian Christians possibly from Najran, Qays 'Abd al-Rashid and Mukhayriq. He contrasts these with most Jews, who he says rejected Muhammad because he descended from Ishmael. The section on the Jewish opposition tells the "orthodox" Ibn Ishaq sequence for Banu Qaynuqa' (after Badr, 624), Banu Nadir (exiled 625) and Banu Qurayzah (627; men allegedly executed). He then sets out revisionist doubts (Donner, Scholler, al-Kalbi, Barakat Ahmad) and contextualizes the executions with Karen Armstrong. "Consolidating the Monotheistic Movement" lists about 90 raids and expeditions and argues that the Prophet used the threat of force rather than violence, unifying Arabia at the cost of about 1,000 casualties. "The Prophet's Domestic and Foreign Policy" quotes treaties and letters at length: Banu Damrah (2 AH), Ashja' (5 AH), Najran per the Chronicle of Seert, Saint Catherine (6 AH/628 CE), Yamamah, the Negus, Heraclius, Muqawqis, Chosroes, Bahrayn, Oman, Ghassan, Dumat al-Jandal/Ukaydir, Abd al-Qays (8 AH/630 CE), Maqnah (9 AH), Adhruh, Aylah, Himyar, Jurash and Najran/'Amr ibn Hazm (10 AH). His aim is to show a consistent policy: convert, or ally and pay tax, and no compulsion in religion. The section then follows how Christians received the early conquests (Sinai, Egypt, Spain), Muslim magnanimity (Saladin, Selim I's decrees for Saint Catherine's, Ottoman protection) and the Sinai Bedouins. The "Conclusions" cover the Umayyads, Imam 'Ali's instructions on Christian subjects, later Shi'i figures (Zayn al-'Abidin, al-Sadr, Khomeini) and Hizbullah. The section closes with a polemic that the West under-reports colonialism, and with Qur'an 3:113–115 as an epigraph on p. 64.
