4. Factual claims (non-date)

A. Comparative politics; slavery (pp. 32–33)
  1. In Athenian democracy, "the majority of peasants, who represented more than 50% of the population," were excluded from citizenship; it was in effect "pro-slavery democracy." p. 32 [PDF 57]. FACT/OP.
  2. "Islam did not abolish slavery in a single stage," but "established a system that would gradually eradicate it"; in Islam slavery "is not a permanent state"; slaves can earn freedom "by work or conversion"; "all children born of slaves are free in Islam"; freeing slaves is pious and "in many cases … a required act of expiation for certain sins." p. 32 [PDF 57]. FACT.
  3. Roman consuls "presided over the Senate and the People's Assembly, which was composed of representatives of military units"; the Senate "represented the aristocracy"; plebeians "could not rule, elect rulers or make use of land," which "was reserved for the patricians or nobles." p. 32 [PDF 57]. FACT.
  4. The resemblance between Greek democracy and current Western "liberal" democracies "is no coincidence." p. 32 [PDF 57]. OP.
B. Constitution of Medina and the early Medinan community (pp. 32–35)
  1. The Prophet prepared the Constitution of Medina "Determined to bring an end to the bitter in-fighting between the Arab war-lords of the tribe of Khazraj and their Jewish rivals," and so "established the first Islamic State." p. 32 [PDF 57]. FACT.
  2. Under the Constitution, identity was no longer based on "family, tribe, kinship, or even religion"; citizens were "one and indivisible regardless of religion," whether heathen, People of the Book or Muslims. p. 32 [PDF 57]. FACT/OP.
  3. Clause quoted: "The Jews of Banu 'Awf are one community with the believers." p. 32 [PDF 57]. FACT (quoting the Constitution).
  4. Peters quote: "If the Jews were permitted from the outset to practice their religion within the newly constituted ummah, then Muhammad's original Medina 'community' was a purely secular one…" p. 32 [PDF 57]. ATTR Peters 201.
  5. The original Islamic State has been called "a kingdom, a theocracy, or even a secular state, all of which definitions are incorrect." p. 32 [PDF 57]. OP.
  6. Armstrong quote: "In the Qur'anic vision there is no dichotomy between the sacred and the profane … The aim was tawhid (making one)…" p. 32 [PDF 57]. ATTR Armstrong 2000: 14–15.
  7. In the Medinan community "all privileges of class were abolished"; rich and poor, Arabs and non-Arabs, black and white, men and women, children and adults "all had the same rights." p. 33 [PDF 58]. FACT/OP.
  8. The Prophet said, as a rhetorical question, that even if his daughter Fatimah were to steal he would give her the punishment for theft. p. 33 [PDF 58]. FACT (hadith paraphrased; no source given).
  9. "In the time of the Prophet, the ahl al-dhimmah [OCR "ahi aldhimmah"], both Jewish and Christian, belonged to the community of believers. The term kuffar was reserved for those who actively attacked and plotted to destroy Islam." p. 33 [PDF 58]. FACT/OP.
  10. In "post-prophetic interpretations," People of the Book are considered kuffar, and only the best Muslims mu'minin. p. 33 [PDF 58]. FACT/OP.
  11. Constitution of Medina: blood money replaces the lex talionis; it "devoted great detail to the peace process and fostering stable tribal relations." p. 34–35 [PDF 59–60]. FACT.
  12. "The Arabs of Medina were known to be violent and bellicose warlords with a deeply-ingrained culture of revenge." p. 34 [PDF 59]. FACT/OP.
  13. "Hypocrites" (munafiqin), "among both the Arabs and the Jews," tried to undermine the peace; defined as "those who outwardly professed Islam but secretly held different beliefs." p. 35 [PDF 60]. FACT.
  14. "The Qur'an and the Sunnah were enshrined as the sole basis for legislation." p. 35 [PDF 60]. FACT.
  15. Non-Muslims had the same rights, autonomy in religious matters, and "were not obliged to participate in the religious wars of the Muslims" ("rights without obligations"); Muslims and Jews were bound to defend each other, with "the cost of war … equally shared." p. 35 [PDF 60]. FACT.
  16. Protection extended "to both combatants and non-combatants so long as they had not engaged in any crimes or atrocities." p. 35 [PDF 60]. FACT.
  17. The Medinan state was "the first of its kind in the intellectual and political history of human civilization," founded "more than thirteen hundred years before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)." p. 35 [PDF 60]. ATTR Khan 1.
  18. Joining the ummah "was particularly appealing to the pagan Arabs, a few Jews, and an important number of Christians." p. 35 [PDF 60]. FACT/OP.
C. Islamic identity and the Donner debate (pp. 33–34)
  1. Donner argued Islam was not (originally) a distinct faith (58); the author rejects this. p. 33 [PDF 58]. ATTR Donner 58 / OP.
  2. Donner quote: islam and muslim "did not yet have the sense of confessional distinctness we now associate with 'Islam' and 'Muslim'" (71); the author says this "demonstrates a misunderstanding of basic Arabic." p. 33 [PDF 58]. ATTR Donner 71 / OP.
  3. Indefinite islam/muslim = "submission"/"one who submits"; definite al-Islam = the religion; Qur'an 3:19 ("Inna al-dina 'inda Allahi al-Islam") and 5:3 cited. p. 33 [PDF 58]. FACT/OP.
  4. O'Shea quote: "The message given to Muhammad, the last in a long line of prophecy, improved and supplanted all that had come before." p. 33 [PDF 58]. ATTR O'Shea 15.
  5. Donner's belief that 'Abd al-Malik "helped convert the Believer's movement into 'Islam'" (194–224) has "no basis." p. 33 [PDF 58]. ATTR Donner / OP.
  6. Muhammad identified himself as Prophet, his religion as Islam and his followers as Muslims "in the many letters he sent which still exist in museums to this date." p. 33–34 [PDF 58–59]. FACT.
  7. Some wrongly assert Islam was "a Jewish or Christian heresy" ("as some Orientalists have asserted"). p. 33 [PDF 58]. ATTR unnamed Orientalists.
  8. Mattson quote: "Muslims seem to have been articulating a more distinct identity with respect to the People of the Book…" p. 34 [PDF 59]. ATTR Mattson 149.
D. The Prophet's letters (counts); 'Abd al-Malik and the coins (p. 34)
  1. "Of the sixty-two letters said to have been sent by the Prophet Muhammad in Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic" (Zeitlin 131), "the texts of twenty-nine of them are available" (Dar Rah Haqq 133–134). p. 34 [PDF 59]. ATTR Zeitlin 131; Dar Rah Haqq 133–134.
  2. The 29 do not include the covenants with: the Monks of Mount Sinai; the Christians of Najran; the Assyrian Christians; the Christians of Persia; the Armenian Christians of Jerusalem; and "the two versions of the Covenant … with the Christians of the World, among possible others." p. 34 [PDF 59]. FACT.
  3. "Hence, over thirty-five letters of the Prophet appear to have survived." p. 34 [PDF 59]. INF/OP.
  4. Donner "devotes his time casting doubt on sources produced in the centuries immediately after the Prophet while completely ignoring the sources produced by the Messenger of Allah himself." p. 34 [PDF 59]. OP.
  5. 'Abd al-Malik "constructed the Dome of the Rock as a symbol of Muslim superiority," "imposed Arabic as the official language of the administration," removed "the cross from coinage, in favor of religious slogans exclusively in Arabic," and "printed a couple of controversial coins." p. 34 [PDF 59]. ATTR Foss 136.
  6. Coin "numbered 89A" shows a man on the obverse, "believed by some to be the Standing Caliph but said by Foss and Hoyland to be the Prophet Muhammad himself." p. 34 [PDF 59]. ATTR some / Foss and Hoyland.
  7. Reverse: for some a qutb or pole symbolizing the Caliph as center of the community (Foss 137, 142, 287 note 8); for others a broken cross; the author "can only conclude that it represents a broken cross" (142, 89a), comparing earlier coins (140, fig. 65, 86a). p. 34 [PDF 59]. ATTR Foss / INF/OP.
  8. The reverse "may also be an allusion to the hadith … which asserts that Jesus Christ would break the crosses during his second coming." p. 34 [PDF 59]. INF/OP.
  9. Foss quote on coin 89c: "Their inscription names Muhammad messenger of God … Could this be the image of the Prophet himself?" (137). p. 34 [PDF 59]. ATTR Foss 137.
  10. The Standing Caliph coins "were the last to depict a human image." p. 34 [PDF 59]. FACT.
E. Conversions and Jewish/Christian responses (pp. 35–39)
  1. Salman: "Originally a Zoroastrian, he had converted to Christianity and had served two bishops and three priests, the last of whom informed him of the imminent arrival of the predestined prophet." p. 35 [PDF 60]. FACT.
  2. A pious priest told Salman the awaited one would rise from Mecca, migrate to "a city full of date trees," bear "the seal of prophecy between his shoulder blades," and eat food only as a gift, not charity. p. 35 [PDF 60]. FACT (story).
  3. Salman paid "some Arabs from the tribe of Kalb" to take him to Arabia; they sold him to a Jewish man, who sold him to "his nephew who belonged to the Banu Qurayzah of Yathrib." p. 35 [PDF 60]. FACT.
  4. Islam was "very much a revival of the true teachings of Judaism" in monotheism, ritual purity, dietary laws and prayer toward Jerusalem. p. 36 [PDF 61]. OP.
  5. Ibn Sallam's first words heard from the Prophet: "O people! Spread peace…. Share food…. Pray during the night while people (normally) sleep … and you will enter Paradise in peace…." p. 37 [PDF 62]. ATTR Islamic Web.
  6. The Jews said of Ibn Sallam: "He is our chief, and the son of our chief; our rabbi, and our most learned man." p. 38 [PDF 63]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq 241.
  7. Ibn Sallam's integrity "is even attested to in the Qur'an, which presents him as a Jewish witness to the truth" (Qur'an 46:10 quoted). p. 38 [PDF 63]. FACT/INF.
  8. Abyssinian Christians' reply to Abu Jahl: "We have our religion and you have yours." p. 37 [PDF 62]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq.
  9. Najran Christians "were followers of Monophysite Christianity" (Goddard 16) vs "at first Monophysites … turned to Nestorianism … in 575" (Betts 5). p. 37 [PDF 62]. ATTR Goddard 16; Betts 5.
  10. Nestorians were "'olive oil and water' Christians" (two natures cannot mix); Monophysites "'wine and water' Christians" (natures mixed, "impenetrable to theological analysis"). p. 37 [PDF 62]. ATTR Rogerson 82.
  11. Najran Christians "shared much in common with the Muslims, a fact that may have helped precipitate their proselytization." p. 37 [PDF 62]. INF/OP.
  12. Qays 'Abd al-Rashid is "alleged to have been a 37th descendant of King Saul through Malak Afghanah, a grandson of King Saul." p. 38 [PDF 63]. TRAD.
  13. "While many other Jewish people acknowledged that Muhammad was the Messenger of Allah, most of them opted to oppose him due to the fact that he descended from Isma'il [Ishmael] as opposed to Ishaq [Isaac]." p. 38 [PDF 63]. FACT/OP.
  14. Safiyyah bint Huyyay ibn Akhtab is "the Jewish wife of the Prophet"; she was "the favorite child of my father and my uncle Abu Yasir." p. 38 [PDF 63]. FACT; ATTR Ibn Ishaq 242.
  15. "Besides 'Abd Allah ibn Sallam, the only other prominent Jew to embrace Islam was another rabbi by the name of Mukhayriq." p. 38 [PDF 63]. FACT.
  16. Mukhayriq "was a learned rabbi owning much property in date palms"; the Prophet "used to say 'Mukhayriq is the best of the Jews'" ("I am told"). p. 38 [PDF 63]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq 241 (TRAD within).
  17. The rest of Medina's Jews "allied themselves with the hypocrites." p. 38 [PDF 63]. FACT.
F. Jewish tribes: Qaynuqa', Nadir, Qurayzah, Khaybar (pp. 39–42)
  1. Prophet to Qaynuqa': "O Jews! Beware lest God bring upon you the vengeance that He brought upon Quraysh and become Muslims…" p. 39 [PDF 64]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq 363.
  2. Qaynuqa' "had broken their treaty obligations and threatened the Prophet"; "might act as fifth column allies of the polytheists"; Muhammad "would have been within his military rights to put them to the sword." p. 39 [PDF 64]. FACT/OP.
  3. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy was "the chief of the hypocrites." p. 39 [PDF 64]. FACT.
  4. The Qurayzah plot was "to combine an external attack by the polytheists with an internal attack by the Banu Qurayzah." p. 40 [PDF 65]. FACT.
  5. "The Muslims had signed two treaties with them, one was Charter of Medina and the other signed at the time of the battle with the Banu Nadir." p. 40 [PDF 65]. ATTR Qureshi 261.
  6. Some Qurayzah "recognized that Muhammad was indeed the prophet that their elders had testified about." p. 40 [PDF 65]. ATTR Waqidi 247.
  7. The mass execution "had been decided by a judge appointed by the Jewish people, and who had ruled on the basis of the Torah." p. 40 [PDF 65]. FACT (in the context of Donner 73).
  8. "The clashes between the Prophet and the Jews of Medina may have been greatly exaggerated and some of the details may have been completely fabricated." p. 40 [PDF 65]. ATTR Donner 73.
  9. Scholler: the evidence "does seem to imply that there was neither a B. Qaynuqa' nor a B. al-Nadir episode as we know it from the 'orthodox' sira version" but a single larger conflict (28–29), which "may have taken place in Medina or, maybe, even in Khaybar" (30). p. 40 [PDF 65]. ATTR Scholler.
  10. Ibn Ishaq's sequence "has become the 'orthodox' version." p. 40 [PDF 65]. FACT.
  11. Khaybar is "located 150 kilometers from Medina where other Jewish tribes resided." p. 40 [PDF 65]. FACT.
  12. The Muslims of Medina were "surrounded by enemies on all sides: the Jews of Khaybar and their Arab polytheistic allies to the north and the Arab pagans of Quraysh in Mecca to the south." p. 40 [PDF 65]. FACT.
  13. Prophet to Safiyyah: "If you will be in your religion, we will not compel you; but if you choose God and His Messenger I will take you for myself"; she: "Rather, I will choose God and His Messenger." p. 41 [PDF 66]. ATTR Waqidi 348.
  14. Three claims about Khaybar's land: (1) left to the Jews for crop-sharing; (2) some kept by the Prophet, the rest distributed to combatants; (3) "Fadak fell to Muhammad alone, but he left the land to the Jews on condition of share-cropping." p. 41 [PDF 66]. ATTR Scholler 38–39.
  15. The third version "is the most sound and supported by the impeccable testimony of Fatimah." p. 41 [PDF 66]. OP.
  16. Syed Barakat Ahmad's book "cast doubts on the credibility of Ibn Ishaq's account … which may have been colored by 'Abbasid ideas"; the author calls it "not entirely convincing." p. 41 [PDF 66]. ATTR Ahmad / OP.
  17. "As far as Ahmad is concerned, no Jews were executed or expelled from Medina during Muhammad's life." p. 41 [PDF 66]. ATTR Ahmad.
  18. The historical record "only indicates that he had problems with a number of them" [of 20+ Jewish tribes]. p. 41 [PDF 66]. INF (after Levy 158).
  19. Armstrong quote: "In seventh-century Arabia an Arab chief was not expected to show mercy to traitors like the Qurayzah … The struggle did not indicate any hostility towards Jews in general, but only towards the three rebel tribes … Smaller Jewish groups continued to live in Medina." p. 41 [PDF 66]. ATTR Armstrong 2000: 21.
  20. The Hebrew majority "rejected Muhammad's message for what they admitted were racist reasons"; "claiming that polytheists were preferable to Muslims." p. 41 [PDF 66]. FACT/OP.
  21. "The real danger to Islam was from the polytheists and the Jews because the Christians were not active in Arabia." p. 41 [PDF 66]. ATTR Qureshi 274.
  22. "The polytheists and Jews among the people of Medina hurt the Prophet and his companions grievously … God, Most High, commanded His Prophet … to be patient and forgiving." p. 41 [PDF 66]. ATTR al-Waqidi 91.
  23. The sequence of the Prophet's approach to the Jews: treaties, then calls to repent, then calls to submit and pay taxes; military action only after "the Jews themselves had chosen war." p. 41–42 [PDF 66–67]. FACT/OP.
G. Military campaigns and numbers (pp. 42–43)
  1. Badr: "just over 300 Muslims overwhelmed 900 enemy combatants." p. 42 [PDF 67]. FACT.
  2. Raids and expeditions the Prophet took part in (30, as printed): Waddan, Buwat, Safwan, Dhul Ashir, the First Badr, Kudr, Sawiq, Qaynuqa', Ghatafan, Bahran, Uhud, al-Asad, Najd, the Second Badr, the First Jandal, the Trench, Qurayzah, the Second Lahyan, Mustaliq, Hudaybiyyah, Khaybar, Fadak, the Third Qurah, Dhat al-Riqa, Baqra, Mecca, Hunayn, Awtas, Ta'if, Tabuk. p. 42 [PDF 67]. FACT.
  3. Forays he sent troops on but did not take part in (61, as printed): Nakhlah, Najd, the First Asad, the First Lahyan, al-Raji, Umayyyah [sic], Bir Mauna, the Assassination of Abu Rafi, Maslamah, the Second Asad, the First Thalabah, the Second Thalabah, Dhu Qarad, Jumum, al-Is, the Third Thalabah, Hismah, the First Qurah, the Second Jandal, the First 'Ali, the Second Qurah, Uraynah, Rawaha, 'Umar, Abu Bakr, Murrah, Uwwal, the Third Fadak, Yemen, Sulaym, Kadid, Banu Layth, Amir, Dhat Atlah, Mu'tah, Amr, Abu 'Ubaydah, Abi Hadrad, Edam, Khadirah, the First Khalid ibn Walid, the "Demotion" [sic] of Sumwa, the Demolition of Manat, the Second Khalid ibn Walid, the Demolition of Yaghuth, the First Awtas, the Second Awtas, Banu Tamim, Banu Khatham, Banu Kilab, Jiddah, the Third 'Ali, Adhruh, the Third Khalid ibn Walid, the Fourth Khalid ibn Walid, Abu Sufyan, Jurash, the Second 'Ali, the Third 'Ali, Dhul Khalasa, the Army of Usamah. p. 42–43 [PDF 67–68]. FACT.
  4. Most raids "took place with little to no bloodshed"; "The bulk of these were short actions, not long campaigns." p. 43 [PDF 68]. FACT.
  5. "It is estimated that during his entire life Muhammad spent no more than 89 days in battle." p. 43 [PDF 68]. TRAD/estimate (unsourced).
  6. "He single-handedly brought the entire Arabian Peninsula under Islamic rule at the cost of approximately one thousand casualties." p. 43 [PDF 68]. FACT.
  7. "[E]ven Western skeptics may wonder about the divine nature of the Islamic conquest." p. 43 [PDF 68]. ATTR Nafziger and Walton 24.
  8. "only one possible explanation remains for the Arab success—and that was the spirit of Islam." p. 43 [PDF 68]. ATTR Nafziger and Walton 34.
  9. "Muhammad's proclamation of a fresh revelation … together with his political theory and practice, that created such a powerful expansionist impulse." p. 43 [PDF 68]. ATTR Fowden qtd. Zeitlin 164.
  10. Early Muslims created "the first cosmopolitan culture." p. 43 [PDF 68]. FACT/OP.
  11. It is said that the Muslims "were like lambs among the believers, they were like lions among unbelievers in the battlefield." p. 42 [PDF 67]. TRAD ("It is said").
H. Policy statements, sayings, Qur'anic principles (pp. 43–44)
  1. The Prophet's saying "Both I smile and I fight." p. 43 [PDF 68]. ATTR Ibn Taymiyyah qtd. Hamidullah, Muslim Conduct 157.
  2. Opponents resisted because Islam "was a threat to their vested economic interests." p. 44 [PDF 69]. OP.
  3. Policy: "Whoever was at peace with Muslims, Muslims were at peace with them"; generous covenants offered "to any tribes or nations, be they pagan, Jewish or Christian." p. 44 [PDF 69]. FACT.
  4. Hostile nations were told: "submit to Islam or suffer conquest," but conquered peoples "would still not be compelled to convert" (taxed instead). p. 44 [PDF 69]. FACT.
I. Treaties and letters: content claims (pp. 44–57). Full document data is in §5.
  1. After more families joined, the Banu Damrah treaty was expanded "from non-aggression to include a pact of mutual aid and neutrality in certain circumstances." p. 44 [PDF 69]. FACT.
  2. "As a result of the Prophet's military and diplomatic efforts, many Arab populations submitted to Islamic rule without fighting." p. 45 [PDF 70]. FACT.
  3. The Banu Ghatafan had "long-standing hostility towards the Prophet" and took part "in numerous wars against the Muslims of Medina." p. 45 [PDF 70]. FACT.
  4. Najran's people "did not embrace Islam"; they "offered to support him and to fight under his banner." p. 45 [PDF 70]. ATTR Chronicle of Seert 281/601.
  5. With Najran and Sinai, the Prophet "did not expect the Christians … to embrace Islam. He simply sought their solidarity." p. 45 [PDF 70]. OP.
  6. Hawdah's reply: "I am a famous orator and poet … If you include me in your government, I am prepared to follow you." p. 45 [PDF 70]. FACT (quoted, no separate cite).
  7. "It was the custom of the Prophet to contact world leaders, invite them to Islam or … ask them to enter into an alliance." p. 46 [PDF 71]. FACT.
  8. Heraclius was "pressured by his ecclesiastic advisors to reject Muhammad's invitation." p. 47 [PDF 72]. FACT.
  9. Jizyah definition: "collective military tax paid by tribes who did not have to share in the Muslims military engagements, but in exchange for which the Muslim authority was to ensure their defense…" p. 47 [PDF 72]. ATTR Ramadan 189.
  10. The jizyah system "was very advanced"; "No such tolerance existed in Christendom, where Jews, Muslims, and other Christians … were subjected to forced conversion, persecution, or expulsion." p. 47 [PDF 72]. ATTR Esposito 71.
  11. "[O]ver the centuries it was generally better to be a Christian or a Jew in an Islamic society than a Jew or Muslim in a Christian society." p. 47 [PDF 72]. ATTR Armour 29.
  12. After Heraclius's 632 baptism order, "Jewish sympathies would hardly have been with the Byzantines"; Jews and persecuted Christian groups sided with the Muslim armies. p. 48 [PDF 73]. ATTR Armour 27 / FACT.
  13. "[M]any Jews saw the Islamic invaders as nothing less than harbingers of the Messiah, rescuing them from 'the Evil Empire'…" p. 48 [PDF 73]. ATTR Steven Fine 103.
  14. The letter to Muqawqis "is preserved in a library in Egypt." p. 48 [PDF 73]. FACT.
  15. Chosroes was "incensed that the Prophet addressed him on equal terms: 'From Muhammad ibn Abd Allah to Chosroes, the Emperor of Persia.'" p. 48–49 [PDF 73–74]. FACT.
  16. Egyptian, Roman and Persian leaders "were considered enemy powers that would be dealt with at some future point." p. 49 [PDF 74]. FACT/OP.
  17. Bahrayn's inhabitants are described as "the Persian inhabitants of the island nation"; the Prophet claimed the "Temple of Fire" for "demolition or conversion into a place of prayers" once they embraced Islam. p. 49 [PDF 74]. FACT.
  18. Bahrayn conditions: zakat, ushr on dates and half ushr on grain, not converting progeny to Magianism; otherwise jizyah. p. 49 [PDF 74]. ATTR qtd. Qureshi 35.
  19. Zakat = "2.5% tax on livestock and agriculture"; khums = "20% of one's yearly profit after expenses"; non-Muslims pay per capita tax "in exchange for not participating in Muslim military service." p. 50 [PDF 75]. FACT (author's glosses).
  20. Oman is a "kingdom in the southeastern Arabian Peninsula"; its two ruling brothers "played an important role in the spread of the Muslim faith." p. 50 [PDF 75]. FACT.
  21. "The Ghassanid kings were great supporters of the Monophysite Jacobite Church." p. 51 [PDF 76]. ATTR Rogerson 82.
  22. Dumat al-Jandal = "modern al-Jawf," "located five hundred miles from Medina, and some seven days by caravan south of Damascus," "at the southern end of the Wadi Sirhan"; "an important route connecting northern Arabia and southern Syria"; "a major intersection of trade routes from Mesopotamia, Syria, and the Arabian Peninsula." p. 51 [PDF 76]. FACT; quote ATTR Hoyland 2001: 68.
  23. Prophet's orders to 'Abd al-Rahman: "Do not be deceitful with the spoils; do not be treacherous; nor mutilate, nor kill children." p. 52 [PDF 77]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq 672.
  24. Ukaydir's treaty "appears in a slightly different version in the Faizer's English translation" and "is said to have been sealed with the thumb-print of the Messenger of Allah as he did not have his seal with him at the time." p. 52 [PDF 77]. ATTR Waqidi 505 (TRAD "is said").
  25. "[I]mages of Jesus and Mary were included among the idols of the Ka'bah." p. 53 [PDF 78]. FACT (unsourced).
  26. Abd al-Qays was "a branch of the Banu Rabi'ah," "settled in Bahrayn and included some Christians." p. 53 [PDF 78]. FACT.
  27. Maqnah is "the port city on the Gulf of Aqabah"; "near Aylah" (Gil version). p. 53–54 [PDF 78–79]. FACT; ATTR Gil.
  28. Maqnah terms (Qureshi version): woven clothes, slaves, horses and coats of armour to the Messenger, plus "one fourth of the products from your oases, the fish caught by your boats, and whatever is spun by your wives"; exempted "from jizyah and compulsory labor." p. 53 [PDF 78]. ATTR qtd. Qureshi 182.
  29. Maqnah terms (Gil version): arms, slaves and rings to the Messenger; "a quarter of your date harvest and a quarter of your fishing yield, and a quarter of the yarn spun by your women"; free of any other levy. p. 54 [PDF 79]. ATTR Gil 29.
  30. Measures: "A wasq equals sixty saa'; a saa' is four mudds, and a mudd is what an average man can scoop up with two hands." p. 54 [PDF 79]. ATTR bracketed gloss within Moshe [Gil] 28–30.
  31. Yuhanna letter: "give Harmal three wasqs of barley"; "clothe Zayd in fine robes"; messengers "Shurahbil and Ubayy and Harmala and Hurayth b. Zayd who is one of the sons of the Banu Tayy'"; threat to "take the young as captives and slay the elderly" if envoys not satisfied. p. 54 [PDF 79]. ATTR Moshe [Gil] 28–30.
  32. Aylah treaty covers "their ships and their caravans by land and sea … men of Syria and Yemen, all seamen." p. 55 [PDF 80]. ATTR qtd. Qureshi 180; Peters 241.
  33. Himyar letter: poll tax "for every adult, male or female, free or slave, one full dinar … or its equivalent in clothes." p. 55 [PDF 80]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq 643–644.
  34. Himyar letter zakat scale: tithe on land watered by fountains/rain, one-twentieth by bucket; "for every forty camels, a milch camel; for every thirty camels, a young male camel; for every five camels, a sheep; for every ten camels, two sheep; for every forty cows, one cow; for every thirty cows, a bull calf or a cow calf; for every forty sheep at pasture, one sheep." p. 55 [PDF 80]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq 643–644.
  35. Himyar letter: messengers Mu'adh ibn Jabal (leader), 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd, Malik ibn Ubadah, 'Uqbah ibn Nimr, Malik ibn Murra; "The alms tax is not lawful to Muhammad or his Household." p. 55–56 [PDF 80–81]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq 643–644.
  36. Mu'adh ibn Jabal "was known for his excessive fervor." p. 56 [PDF 81]. FACT.
  37. Instructions to Mu'adh: "[m]ake things easy for them and do not put them into difficulty…" (Bukhari); "You are going to People of the Book … five prayers every day and night … zakat … Do not take their best properties" (Bukhari); "Make your character good for the people, Mu'adh ibn Jabal" (Malik). p. 56 [PDF 81]. ATTR Bukhari; Malik.
  38. Surad was "vulnerable to attacks from the enemies of Islam"; Jurash's people "had attacked Muslims without provocation" and "refused the peace settlement"; only armed combatants were killed. p. 56 [PDF 81]. FACT.
  39. The one-dinar sum "is repeated in numerous letters, treaties, and covenants." p. 56 [PDF 81]. FACT.
  40. 'Amr ibn Hazm letter zakat scale: "for every one camel, two sheep; and for every twenty camels, four sheep; for every forty cows, one cow; for every thirty cows, a bull or cow calf; for every forty sheep at grass, one sheep"; tithe/twentieth on land; non-converting Jew or Christian "must pay a golden dinar or its equivalent in clothes." p. 57–58 [PDF 82–83]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq 647–648.
  41. 'Amr ibn Hazm letter: "the greater hajj is the greater hajj and the lesser hajj is the 'umra"; the five prayer times; ablutions; ban on appeals "to tribes and families." p. 57 [PDF 82]. ATTR Ibn Ishaq 647–648.
J. Treaty violations; Islamic State; early conquests (pp. 58–61)
  1. "many polytheists, Jews, and Christians did not honor their treaties, as was the case with the Banu Kuza'ah, Banu Mudlij, Banu Bakr, Banu Damrah, and Banu Sulaym." p. 58 [PDF 83]. FACT.
  2. The rightly-guided Companions followed the Prophet's precedent with Christians and Jews of the Middle East, North Africa and Europe, and "the Hindus and Buddhists of South-East Asia." p. 58 [PDF 83]. FACT.
  3. "the Prophet, it needs emphasizing, had established the Islamic State in Madinah"; "in following the Sunnah, Muslims are obliged to live in the Islamic State or, if one does not exist, to strive to establish one." p. 58 [PDF 83]. ATTR Bangash, "Following the Lead."
  4. Chronicle of Seert: "Muhammad ibn Abd Allah was strong and powerful" (280/600). p. 58 [PDF 83]. ATTR Chronicle of Seert (Nestorian monks).
  5. Hagarism is "a book written by infidels for infidels" (viii); Crone and Cook argue the conquerors' indifference to converting monks "suggests that the Arabs were not 'Muslims' in the sense we understand the term today" (8). p. 58 [PDF 83]. ATTR Crone and Cook.
  6. "the Qur'an instructed Muslims to respect the People of the Book, and that is precisely what they did." p. 58 [PDF 83]. ATTR Karabell 28.
  7. 'Amr ibn al-'As "took advantage of the fact that the Coptic Christians were Monophysites … to stress their similarity with Islam," which "would explain why Egypt fell quickly to an army of less than five thousand soldiers." p. 58 [PDF 83]. ATTR Karabell 28.
  8. "[T]he Muslims, with their mild tax, were generally welcomed as liberators, not conquerors." p. 60 [PDF 85]. ATTR Nafziger and Walton 33.
  9. Michael the Syrian, "a Patriarch of the non-Chalcedonian Syrian Church": "The God of vengeance … led the sons of Ishmael from the region of the south to deliver us from Roman hands." p. 60 [PDF 85]. ATTR Binns, qtd. 172.
  10. "the coming of the Arabs must have been a relief" for the Assyrian Christians. p. 60 [PDF 85]. ATTR Wigram, The Assyrians 33.
  11. Cahen: in the East "certain sects professed the continued coming of prophets, even after Jesus." p. 60 [PDF 85]. ATTR Cahen 57.
  12. Fletcher: "the record of such capitulation treaties as survive shows that the leadership sought to observe Koranic precept" (20–21); "To the persecuted Monophysite Christians of Syria and Egypt … the Muslims could be presented as deliverers. The same could be said of the persecuted Jews of Spain" (16). p. 60 [PDF 85]. ATTR Fletcher.
  13. Esposito: some Christian sects persecuted as "heretics" by "'official' Christianity, that is, Catholicism" welcomed the Muslims, who imposed "lighter taxes" (82); Muslim rule in Spain "offered … the opportunity to become prosperous small landholders" (83). p. 60–61 [PDF 85–86]. ATTR Esposito.
K. Sinai monastery, Ottoman documents, Bedouins (pp. 61–62)
  1. Saladin "granted its people clemency and allowed freedom of movement to Christian pilgrims throughout his domain." p. 61 [PDF 86]. ATTR Hobbs 226.
  2. "Muslims have a better record of religious tolerance than Christians, as is best proven by the fact that the monastery … has an unbroken tradition." p. 61 [PDF 86]. ATTR John Galey 13.
  3. "The Monastery of Saint Catherine was protected by the Prophet as well as by the Caliphs and Sultans that followed him." p. 61 [PDF 86]. FACT.
  4. Selim's charter (Cantemir trans.): Muhammad "being heretofore by their Monastery hospitably receiv'd in his travails … graciously exempted this community of Nazaraean Monks from their annual tribute … was pleas'd to give an holy writing signed with his own hand"; Selim orders "an authentic copy of the Instrument of God's Holy Prophet, confirm'd by our Inscription"; refers to "our Chatifsherif [hatt-i sherif] and mandate." p. 61 [PDF 86]. ATTR Cantemir 168–169.
  5. Documents from the Islamic government in Cairo "reference the tradition of Islamic beneficence towards the monastery." p. 61 [PDF 86]. ATTR Ratliff 15.
  6. "Generally speaking … the Moslems respected the Monastery"; "This tolerance … is attributed to the famous Achtiname, the 'Testament' of the Prophet Mohammed who protected the monks from many dangers and exempted them from heavy taxation." p. 61 [PDF 86]. ATTR Tomadakis 14.
  7. Affagart: the Bedouins "claim to be Muslims; however, they do not observe Islamic law" (186); a "detestable and tyrannical band of brigands" raiding caravans "of five or six thousand merchants" (186); sedentary Muslims of Egypt "truthful, trustworthy (186), and honest gentlemen (188)." p. 61–62 [PDF 86–87]. ATTR Affagart.
  8. Bedouins of Sinai "represent, more often as not, a category of Muslims who escape the control of both the monks and that of the Muslim authorities" (180); "a long history of pestering the monks" (181); Islamic authorities repeatedly ruled for the monks (179–181). p. 62 [PDF 87]. ATTR Mouton.
  9. The Bedouins' behaviour "was consistent with their description in the Qur'an" (49:14). p. 62 [PDF 87]. OP.
L. Umayyads, Imam 'Ali, later Imams, modern figures (pp. 62–63)
  1. "Muslim rule … has almost always assured protection for members of minorities, a policy that did not always extend to all Islamic schools and sects." p. 62 [PDF 87]. FACT/OP.
  2. Despots such as Yazid II "oppressed all of their subjects, Muslim or non-Muslim." p. 62 [PDF 87]. OP.
  3. Imam Ali to Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr: "I recommend to you to be equitable to the [Christian] subjects…" (186); to Ma'qal ibn Qays: "Do not be unjust to the Muslims … and do not oppress the [Christian] subjects" (185); "neither Muslim nor [Christian] subject will be oppressed" (185); to Malik al-Ashtar: "some are your brethren-in-faith … and others are creatures of God like you" (183). p. 62 [PDF 87]. ATTR qtd. Jordac.
  4. Jordac/Zaydan: "A Muslim is the brother of a Christian whether he likes it or not, because a man is the brother of a man whether he admits it or not." p. 62 [PDF 87]. ATTR Jordac 184.
  5. "Ali was loved very much for his justice by the knowledgeable Christians"; Ibn Abu al-Hadid in Sharh Nahj al-balaghah: "What should I say about that man ['Ali] whom the [Christian] subjects loved ardently…" p. 62–63 [PDF 87–88]. ATTR Jordac 186.
  6. The Umayyads were an example of "the inherent Islamic tolerance toward Christians." p. 63 [PDF 88]. ATTR Shboul 127.
  7. "[I]t had always been a point of honor among Arabs to treat their clients well." p. 63 [PDF 88]. ATTR Armstrong 2000: 31.
  8. "the Imams after 'Ali were politically powerless." p. 63 [PDF 88]. FACT.
  9. Al-Sadr (al-Rikabi 258) and Khomeini (42) "insisted … that any Islamic system must guarantee the rights and liberties of all citizens, regardless of religion." p. 63 [PDF 88]. ATTR.
  10. Khomeini: "Jews are different from Zionists; if the Muslims overcome the Zionists, they will leave the Jews alone…" p. 63 [PDF 88]. ATTR Khomeini 42.
  11. Hizbullah "called for constant dialogue between Muslims and Christians and … a non-confessional political system"; "It is both policy and practice to back Sunni and Christian candidates." p. 63 [PDF 88]. ATTR Mamdani 172.
  12. Western media report Muslim terrorism "liberally" but not "the long history of European colonialism, and European and American neo-colonialism"; "the periods of greatest intolerance have coincided with Western imperialist occupation." p. 63 [PDF 88]. OP.

  5. "Leave the Abyssinians in peace, so long as they do not take the offensive." p. 47 [PDF 72]. Abu Dawud and Nisa'i.
  6. "Even so, O Lord, tear from him his kingdom." p. 49 [PDF 74]. No source.
  7. "Fight everyone in the way of Allah … kill those who disbelieve in Allah … This is Allah's ordinance and the practice of his Prophet among you." p. 52 [PDF 77]. Ibn Ishaq 672.
  8. To the Qaynuqa' (claim 58); to Safiyyah (claim 70); to Mu'adh (claim 132).

Factual claims: 194 numbered items (186 claims plus 8 sayings in group N).

6. The author's key arguments and opinions

  1. The Constitution of Medina created a "tolerant, pluralistic government which protected religious freedom," more genuinely progressive than Athenian democracy or the Roman Republic; he asks why it "is ignored in favor of" them. pp. 32–33 [PDF 57–58].
  2. The original Islamic State was "a unique system which had never existed before and which has never been seen since"; it was neither kingdom, theocracy nor secular state. p. 32 [PDF 57].
  3. The Prophet's Community of Believers included Jews and Christians, yet Islam had a distinct identity from the start. He partly agrees and partly disagrees with Donner. p. 33 [PDF 58].
  4. Donner misreads Arabic on islam/al-Islam; his 'Abd al-Malik thesis has "no basis," since the Prophet's own surviving letters name Islam and Muslims. pp. 33–34 [PDF 58–59].
  5. Islam came "to correct" and "complete" Judaism and Christianity, which had "gone astray in matters of orthodoxy and orthopraxy." p. 33 [PDF 58].
  6. The reverse of coin 89A "represents a broken cross" and marks "a monumental change in the relationship between Islam and Christianity." p. 34 [PDF 59].
  7. The Prophet hoped the Jews of Yathrib would convert, because the learned Christian Salman had recognized him. p. 36 [PDF 61].
  8. The Prophet showed mercy in exiling, rather than killing, the Qaynuqa' and Nadir, though killing them was "within his military rights." p. 39 [PDF 64].
  9. The Qurayzah execution may be unhistorical ("increasingly, the evidence suggests that we cannot" believe it). If it happened, it "must not be judged according to the standards of our times." p. 41 [PDF 66].
  10. Ibn Hisham, rather than Ibn Ishaq, was "More likely" responsible for the polemical view of the Jews. p. 41 [PDF 66].
  11. The Prophet's harder treatment of the Jews compared with the Christians is explained by Jewish hostility and alliance with the polytheists (with Qureshi: Christians "were not active in Arabia"). p. 41 [PDF 66].
  12. Both the Orientalist view (Islam spread by forced conversion) and the apologist view ("peace jihad") are wrong. The Prophet offered benefits, or else conditions, "a time honored political and military strategy." p. 42 [PDF 67].
  13. The Prophet "did not use violence per se to bring people into his fold" but "use[d] the threat of violence as a stratagem." p. 43 [PDF 68].
  14. Being a "man of peace" does not conflict with waging war, because social interests override individual ones and "the essential and irreplaceable ingredient for peace was justice." pp. 43–44 [PDF 68–69].
  15. The Prophet was "a visionary long-term planner" who knew the spread of Islam "could take centuries." p. 44 [PDF 69].
  16. Religious diversity is God-willed: no compulsion; the conquered pay taxes but are not forced to convert. p. 44 [PDF 69].
  17. Jizyah "may seem startling to modern minds" but was "quite revolutionary." p. 48 [PDF 73].
  18. By rejecting the Prophet and forcing baptism, Heraclius "sealed his fate" as Jews and persecuted Christians sided with the Muslims. p. 48 [PDF 73].
  19. "Those who embrace Islam have nothing to fear and nothing to lose" (from the Bahrayn letters). p. 49 [PDF 74].
  20. "Islam should be introduced in stages and taught by example" (from the instructions to Mu'adh). p. 56 [PDF 81].
  21. Ukaydir treaty: Qureshi's translation is "poor." "False gods" may refer to Jesus as worshipped by Christians and "idols" to statues of Jesus, Mary and the saints. The Ghassanids may have been only partly Christianized or have ruled a mainly pagan population, so the Prophet was "helping purify Christianity from invasive pagan influences." pp. 52–53 [PDF 77–78].
  22. The Prophet "was clearly no imperialist"; he aimed at a "United States of Islam" or "Islamic Union" in which regional rule was encouraged as long as solidarity with Islam came first. p. 58 [PDF 83].
  23. Muslims must live in, or strive to set up, an Islamic State. Muslims preferring "monarchy, despotic dictatorship or 'democracy'" contradict the Qur'an and Sunnah, and a scholar opposing Islamic rule "calls his own orthodoxy into question." p. 58 [PDF 83].
  24. Against Crone and Cook, the conquerors' indifference to converting monks shows they were "Qur'anically-conscious, bona fide, believing, Muslims." p. 60 [PDF 85].
  25. Karabell's Monophysite-similarity explanation for Egypt's quick fall "is not completely convincing," since most Iberian Catholics also embraced Islam. p. 59 [PDF 84].
  26. Trinitarians fall "short of strict monotheism" but are not polytheists. It would be "absurd" today to make Unitarianism vs Trinitarianism a "life or death" question. Muhammad tolerated Christian beliefs about Jesus' divinity and kept out of sectarian disputes so as to build a unified ummah, while being stricter with Muslims. This tolerance "is exactly one of the characteristics of the covenants" and is why Christians accepted them. pp. 59–60 [PDF 84–85].
  27. Those who sow Christian–Muslim discord follow the "Machiavellian slogan of 'divide and you will rule.'" p. 59 [PDF 84].
  28. Why Egyptian and nearby Christians sided with the Muslims "has not been satisfactorily answered." p. 60 [PDF 85].
  29. "The historical literature is simply replete with evidence of Muslim military mercy." p. 61 [PDF 86].
  30. The Sinai Bedouins' attacks cannot be blamed on Islam; they are the "desert Arabs" of Qur'an 49:14. pp. 61–62 [PDF 86–87].
  31. Injustices against Christians under Muslim rule "rarely lasted long and were soon rectified." If the Umayyads, "the most wretched rulers of Islam," behaved well, the treatment by the Prophet and Imam Ali was "exalted." p. 62 [PDF 87].
  32. Hizbullah's support for Christian candidates shows "an enormous amount of forbearance" given Christian atrocities in the Lebanese Civil War. p. 63 [PDF 88].
  33. Muslims had the "fullest rights, protections, and liberties" under Islamic rule, not Western liberal democracy, and the "periods of greatest intolerance have coincided with Western imperialist occupation." p. 63 [PDF 88].

7. Internal inconsistencies within this section

  1. Coin issue dates. "These Standing Caliph coins, issued between 694/95 and 692/697 CE": the second date range (692/697) starts before the first (694/95). Possibly OCR or typesetting. p. 34 [PDF 59].
  2. Coin numbering. "the image of the man who appears on the back of coin 89c and the front of 89c" names the same coin twice. The other coins cited are 89A and 89a; possibly 89b was meant. p. 34 [PDF 59].
  3. Heraclius timing. The letter to Heraclius was "probably sent in 627 CE" (p. 47), and Heraclius "took the opposite attitude a couple of years later," illustrated with "In AD 632" (p. 48). On the book's own dates that gap is about five years. pp. 47–48 [PDF 72–73].
  4. Muqawqis's attitude. On p. 48 Muqawqis is praised for "tact," keeps the letter in an ivory casket and sends gifts. On p. 49: "both the Egyptian, Roman, and Persian leaders expressed anger and hostility towards the Prophet." pp. 48–49 [PDF 73–74].
  5. Ja'far's relationship. In the Prophet's letter he is "my cousin Ja'far" (p. 46); in the Negus's reply "your nephew and his companions" and "your nephew" (pp. 46–47). The inconsistency lies within the quoted documents. pp. 46–47 [PDF 71–72].
  6. Camel zakat rates. Himyar letter: "for every five camels, a sheep; for every ten camels, two sheep" (p. 55). 'Amr ibn Hazm letter: "for every one camel, two sheep; and for every twenty camels, four sheep" (p. 57). The cattle and sheep rates match. pp. 55, 57 [PDF 80, 82].
  7. Esposito's middle initial. "John L. Esposito (b. 1940 CE)" (p. 47) and "John L. Esposito" (p. 61), but "John F. Esposito (b. 1940 CE)" (p. 60). pp. 47, 60, 61 [PDF 72, 85, 86].
  8. Expulsion and execution of the Jews: author's narrative vs endorsed doubts. The author narrates the exiles of Qaynuqa' and Nadir (p. 39), says the Prophet "forced them into exile" (p. 41) and writes "With his Jewish opponents sent into exile" (p. 42). He also reports, without fully endorsing ("not entirely convincing"), Ahmad's view that "no Jews were executed or expelled from Medina during Muhammad's life," and Scholler's that the Qaynuqa' and Nadir episodes may not have happened "as we know it." He says "increasingly, the evidence suggests" the Qurayzah killings cannot be believed (p. 41), though p. 40 narrates them as "alleged." pp. 39–42 [PDF 64–67].
  9. Khaybar: fighting or not. "The Muslims marched on Khaybar, surrounded the city, and compelled the Jews to surrender. One of the captives of the battle…" (p. 40), versus "the Jews of Khaybar surrendered without any significant fighting" (p. 41). pp. 40–41 [PDF 65–66].
  10. Jewish converts. "Besides 'Abd Allah ibn Sallam, the only other prominent Jew to embrace Islam was … Mukhayriq" (p. 38). Elsewhere: Ibn Sallam's household and aunt converted (p. 38); "Some members of the Banu Qurayzah embraced Islam" (p. 40); Rayhannah and Safiyyah converted (pp. 40–41); "he won a small segment of the Jewish community" (p. 41). The word "prominent" may reconcile these.
  11. Bahrayn ruler's title. "Letter to the King of Bahrayn" (p. 49), "Mundhir ibn Sawa, the ruler of Bahrayn" and "the leader of Bahrayn" (p. 49), versus caption "Mundhir ibn Sawa, Governor of Bahrain" (p. 50). Spelling also varies: Bahrayn/Bahrain. pp. 49–50 [PDF 74–75].
  12. Abyssinian ruler's title. "King of Abyssinia" (text, p. 46); captions "Emperor of Abyssinia" and "al-Najashi, Ruler of Abyssinia" (p. 46). p. 46 [PDF 71].
  13. Spelling variants for the same person. Hawdah / Hawda ibn 'Ali (p. 45); Yuhanna ibn Ru'bah / Yuhannah b. Ru'bah / Yuhanna bin Ru'bah (pp. 54–55); Qureshi / "Qureishi" (p. 48); Rayhannah (single spelling); Muadh / Mu'adh ibn Jabal (p. 56); 'Amr ibn al-'As / Amr ibn al-As (p. 58).
  14. Gil cited as "Moshe." Introduced as "Moshe Gil in his History of Palestine" (p. 53), then cited as "(qtd. Moshe 30)" and "(Moshe 28–30)" (p. 54), using his first name as surname. p. 54 [PDF 79].
  15. Duplicates in the forays list. "the Third 'Ali" appears twice (p. 42 after "Jiddah," and p. 43 after "the Second 'Ali"), and "the Second 'Ali" follows the first "Third 'Ali." "Najd" appears in both the Prophet's own list and the forays list; "Awtas" in the Prophet's list and "the First Awtas, the Second Awtas" among the forays. "the Third Fadak" appears with no First or Second Fadak in the forays list. pp. 42–43 [PDF 67–68].
  16. Banu Damrah. The 2 AH treaty is presented as a model of mutual aid (pp. 44–45), but on p. 58 the Banu Damrah are listed among those who "did not honor their treaties." This is not a contradiction in itself; it is noted for checkers. pp. 44, 58 [PDF 69, 83].
  17. Najran's denomination. Goddard calls them Monophysite (16) and Betts says they turned Nestorian in 575 (5), p. 37. On p. 51 Rogerson lists Najran among Christian sites in a passage on the Monophysite Jacobite network of the Ghassanids. The author does not resolve this. pp. 37, 51 [PDF 62, 76].
  18. Joachim's lifespan. "Joachim, the Patriarch of Alexandria (c. 1448-1567 CE)" implies a life of about 119 years (arithmetic on the printed dates only). p. 61 [PDF 86].
  19. Order of Najran events. The Najran covenant via Sayyid Ghassani "apparently predates" the 6 AH Sinai treaty (p. 45), but "The year 10 AH also saw the complete submission of the Christians of Najran" (p. 57). These may be two stages, but the book does not connect them. pp. 45, 57 [PDF 70, 82].
  20. Ukaydir's religion. The treaty text says Ukaydir "has embraced Islam, forsaking false gods and idols" (p. 52), while the narrative calls him "the Christian prince." The author raises this himself (p. 52–53). pp. 52–53 [PDF 77–78].
  21. Affagart's description. He is "the French pilgrim" (p. 61) and "the French knight" (p. 62). Not contradictory; noted only.
  22. Unclear citation. "(39)" after the Khaybar emissaries claim (p. 41) presumably means Scholler. "(12)" for the southern Jordan treaties (p. 53) follows a Qureshi 288 citation, but the source is not stated (Shoup 12 is cited on p. 51). pp. 41, 53 [PDF 66, 78].

  • Basis tags: fact = the author states it as fact in his own voice; attr. [X] = the author attributes it to source X (page cited by the book in parentheses where given); trad. = the book presents it as tradition, "some accounts", "it is said", "reportedly"; inference/opinion = the author's own inference, hypothesis or opinion.
  • "(OCR)" marks an obvious OCR misreading, with the likely reading given. "[sic]" marks a spelling or citation that appears exactly that way in the printed text and is not an OCR problem.
  • The scan is two-column, and on several pages (pp. 72, 78, 80, 81, 88, 93, 97) the OCR mixes up the order of the columns. Where I had to rebuild which quotation goes with which attribution, the item says so.
  • No Arabic or Persian script appears in this chunk; none was skipped.

1. Section summary

Chapter 2 argues that the Achtiname (also "Akd Name", "Patent of Muhammad") kept at St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, is authentic. The author says it was concluded in the second year of the hijrah, written by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, sealed with the Prophet's handprint, and dated 3 Muharram 2 AH, which he gives as July 7, 623. Most of his sources say Sultan Selim I took the original to Istanbul/Constantinople in 1517 and left certified copies. The author raises Greffin Affagart's report (pilgrimage 1533–34) that the original was still in the monastery's mosque, and suggests Sulayman the Magnificent may have taken it instead. He also suggests the original may survive in Topkapi or another palace. He lists Atiya's surviving Arabic and Turkish copies (six Arabic scrolls dated 1737/38–1800/01 or undated, codices of 1561 and 1683–84, and 43 Turkish translations). He then points to the long series of Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman decrees (975 to 1888) and fatwas from all four Sunni schools, plus the Fatimid school, as a millennium of Muslim recognition. Next he takes on the critics: Burckhardt (the document says it was written at Medina, was addressed to all Christians, and has 22 witnesses), Moritz and Skrobucha (date, style and content; no duties imposed; taxes fixed by the Christians themselves; possible forgery under al-Hakim), Mouton (anachronistic witnesses Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Darda'; the hijri calendar not yet in existence; derivation from the 878 Najran letter forged by the Banu Makhlad), Ratliff (the convert-abbot 'Abd al-Masih) and Hobbs's unnamed "observers" (a monks' forgery c. 1010). His answers rest on the early use of the hijri calendar, scribal re-dating, and the later addition of dates and witnesses. He also attacks Moritz's character as a German imperial agent and Nazi collaborator. He discusses the eagle legend, Latin anti-Islamic legends of the 9th century, Napoleon's 1798 decree, and a 1403 treaty that mentions St. Catherine. A "Commentary on the Content" section goes through the covenant's 18 items (11 for the Sinai monks, 7 for Christians generally) and links them to modern political themes. The Conclusions call the covenant authentic in the absence of definitive proof of forgery.

4. Factual claims (non-date), numbered and grouped by theme

A. Status and reception of the document
  1. The Covenant "is a controversial and highly disputed document"; "many Orientalists summarily dismiss it as spurious". — p. 65 [PDF 90] — fact/opinion
  2. "the venerable Greek Orthodox Church and generations of Muslim scholars from all schools of law have insisted upon its authenticity." — p. 65 [PDF 90] — fact
  3. The Covenant "is virtually unknown to most Muslims and has historically received greater circulation and recognition among Arabic, Latin, and English-speaking Christians." — pp. 65–66 [PDF 90–91] — fact
  4. "This may be the most important document in the monastery's vast collection." — p. 66 [PDF 91] — attr. Hobbs (160)
  5. Albert Champdor counts "the Akd Name or Achtiname of Muhammad as one of the most famous works found at the Monastery". — p. 66 [PDF 91] — attr. Champdor
  6. "As custodians of the Covenant ... the monks of Mount Sinai have always unanimously and unequivocally endorsed its authenticity, their assertions spanning centuries." — p. 70 [PDF 95] — fact
  7. Napoleon "endorsed its authenticity." — p. 70 [PDF 95] — fact
  8. The Covenant's authenticity "was confirmed by the Fatimids ..., the Ayyubids ..., the Mamluks ..., and the Ottomans ... through a long series of decrees". — p. 70 [PDF 95] — attr. Atiya (32-35; 80)
  9. The Covenant "was accepted by both Shi'ites and Sunnis"; there is "no evidence at all" that Sunnis rejected it as a rafidi Shi'ite imposture or that Shi'ites rejected it as a nasibi Sunni fabrication. — p. 72 [PDF 97] — fact/opinion
  10. Chain of transmission between dynasties: the Ottomans (Sunni) received it from the Mamluks (Sunni, but seen by the Turks as "heretics and apostates for supporting the Safavid Shi'ites"); the Mamluks from the Fatimids (Shi'ite); the Fatimids from "their enemies, the Sunni 'Abbasids"; the 'Abbasids from the Umayyads; the Umayyads from Imam 'Ali. — p. 72 [PDF 97] — fact (author's construction)
  11. Definitions given: rafidi = "extremist," "critic," "heretic," "innovator," "misguided," "renegade," "deserter"; nasibi = those who hate the Household of the Prophet; "Muqtada al-Sadr uses it to refer to the Salafis." — p. 72 [PDF 97] — fact
  12. "While some doubt that the Achtiname is genuine, the fact that it was always respected by Moslem leaders, the Arabs to begin with, and later the Turks, indicates that the Moslems did consider it the will of the Prophet." — p. 72 [PDF 97] — attr. Tomadakis (14)
  13. "In general ... the Caliphs of Baghdad, Cairo or Damascus respected the clauses of this Gentleman's agreement and confirmed them on numerous occasions." — p. 73 [PDF 98] — attr. Champdor (32)
  14. The Arabs of the Sinai Peninsula "questioned its authenticity or ignored its existence as a pretext to assault and pillage the powerless monks". — p. 73 [PDF 98] — attr. Champdor (32-33)
  15. Father Makarios, a monk at Mount Sinai: "Where would the monastery be today if it had turned Muhammad away when he came?" — p. 73 [PDF 98] — attr. qtd. Hobbs (280-281)
  16. "The preservation of the Monastery's Greekness" was due to the monks gaining the protection of "the Arabs, the Turks and the Egyptians by means of the famous Charter or Achtiname given by ... the Prophet Mohammed himself". — p. 73 [PDF 98] — attr. Konstantinos A. Manafis (22) (attribution rebuilt from the column layout)
  17. "The monastery of Sinai could not possibly have survived without the protection afforded by Mohammed and his successors.... the great number of decrees ... must have resulted from the fact that Mohammed himself had granted protection to Sinai". — p. 71 [PDF 96] — attr. Amantos, "the Greek historian" (qtd. Shah-Kazemi)
  18. The authenticity of the Patent has been "attested to by John Davenport in his Apology for Mohammed and the Koran (148)"; Davenport: its "facts and arguments" refute the charge that Islam was spread by the sword, which is "both false and scandalous" (151). — pp. 96–97 [PDF 121–122] — attr. Davenport
  19. Authenticity "recognized by a long list of Muslim scholars, including, Dr. A. Zahoor, Dr. Z. Haq, Dr. Muqtedar Khan, Dr. Reza Shah-Kazemi", and "endorsed by numerous Islamic associations such as the Islamic Supreme Council of Canada." — p. 97 [PDF 122] — fact
  20. Many Muslims "would even discard the covenants because they were preserved and passed down by Christians"; "the anti-intellectual Wahhabis" dismiss historical books without isnads. — p. 77 [PDF 102] — opinion
  21. The Covenant's content "is roundly rejected by certain groups of Islamist extremists" ("Wahhabis"), because it has no isnad and is not in the hadith collections. — p. 77 [PDF 102] — attr. Salafis/Wahhabis (as reported); characterization is opinion
  22. The Covenant "is ... found in partial form in classical Islamic historical literature" (Tabari, Ibn Sa'd). — p. 77 [PDF 102] — fact
  23. "the Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World ... has only reached us thanks to Arab and European Christians from the 1500s and 1600s." — p. 77 [PDF 102] — fact
  24. Many millions of Muslims "have no knowledge of this covenant or its intentions." — p. 96 [PDF 121] — fact/opinion

  3. Atiya: the Monastery holds "six Arabic copies of the Covenant ... dating from unknown periods to 1800/01 CE." — p. 66 [PDF 91] — attr. Atiya

Atiya (xxix)
  10. "The only difference between the various copies involves decorative elements." — p. 74 [PDF 99] — fact
  11. "Some of the later copies ... apart from the depiction of the Monastery and Mt. Sinai," include "the imprint of a palm and five fingers, namely the symbol of the Prophet Mohammed and his blood relatives Fatima, Ali, Hasan, and Hussein". — p. 74 [PDF 99] — attr. Digbassanis (361)
  12. The handprint symbolism: five fingers = Muhammad, Fatimah, Ali, Hasan and Husayn; "the fourteen bones" = "the fourteen infallibles, namely, the Prophet, his daughter, and the Twelve Imams". — p. 74 [PDF 99] — inference/opinion
  13. "Digbassanis ... is wrong to suggest that the hand-print was a latter addition ... as it is attested in many ancient sources." — p. 74 [PDF 99] — opinion
  14. "the presence of the Hand of Muhammad or khamsah on the Covenant has been attested to in all of the ancient sources"; "The sole exception appears to be the account of Van Egmont and John Heyman which claims that the Prophet simply dipped one of his fingers in the ink and signed the covenant with a fingerprint (161)." — p. 75 [PDF 100] — fact/opinion + attr. Van Egmont & Heyman
  15. Van Egmont and Heyman: "neither of these men seems to have actually seen the Covenant, their version can be discounted as a mere misunderstanding." — p. 75 [PDF 100] — opinion
  16. Skrobucha describes the writing as "signed by him with two fingers of his hand". — p. 78 [PDF 103] — attr. Skrobucha (58-59)
  17. Affagart: Muhammad "dipped his hand in ink, and pressed it against a piece of paper"; the Turks offered "a great deal of money in exchange for that sign, which is in the form of his hand, in order to make it a relic", but the monks refused "since, by means of it, they are free from [paying] any tribute." — p. 68 [PDF 93] — attr. Affagart (191), author's translation from Middle French
  18. M.L.M.D.C.: the Prophet "used to soak his hand in a big basin full of ink and would press his hand against the parchment" and "never used any feather or writing instrument apart from his hand". — p. 75 [PDF 100] — attr. Jeux d'esprit (86)
  19. The Marshal (in M.L.M.D.C.): "It was a double and true Patent since it was covered with all of its forms and ... it was the exact figure of the Hand of Muhammad which is the greatest Relic of the Ottomans." — p. 75 [PDF 100] — attr. Jeux d'esprit (87)
  20. Burckhardt: Muhammad "confirmed it by impressing his extended hand, blackened with ink, upon the parchment." — p. 81 [PDF 106] — attr. Burckhardt (Chapter 7)
  21. Stanley: a "contract of protection, drawn up on the skin of a gazelle". — p. 76 [PDF 101] — trad., attr. Stanley (344-345)
  22. Scribal note: "A copy of this covenant has been deposited in the treasury [khizanah] of the Sultan. It was signed with the seal of the Prophet ... It was written on a piece of leather from Ta'if." — p. 97 [PDF 122] — attr. the note on the display copy
  23. "The Arabic version in my possession clearly states that the covenant was written on jild or leather which is consistent with early prophetic practice"; "The surviving segments of the Qur'an, which were written by the scribes of Revelation, are all found on leather." — p. 97 [PDF 122] — fact (author's claim)
  24. Sidney H. Griffith translated the word as "parchment" (63); author: "this is not the accurate rendition of the Arabic word found on the covenant", though the original "possible[y]" was parchment. — p. 97 [PDF 122] — attr. Griffith + opinion
  25. The meaning of "seal" is "somewhat ambiguous": the palm-print, or "the actual seal from his ring which he would dip in ink". — p. 97 [PDF 122] — opinion
  26. The display copy's note: "This copy, which is copied from the original, is sealed with the signature of the noble Sultan [sharif al-Sultani]. This reproduction was copied from the copy that was copied from the copy written in the handwriting of the Leader of the Believers, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib". — p. 97 [PDF 122] — attr. note (author's translation)
  27. The display copy's note: the Sultan's order was given "because the copy, which was copied from the copy written by the Leader of the Believers, was lost, in order that his document be a support of the Sultan's royal decrees". — pp. 97–98 [PDF 122–123] — attr. note
  28. The display copy's pious formula: "Blessed be he who abides by its contents. Blessed be he for he belongs to those who can expect the forgiveness of Allah." — p. 97 [PDF 122] — attr. note
  29. "This copy of the covenant is not dated but this could easily be done by determining the lifespan of the scribe and judge who are signatories." — p. 97 [PDF 122] — fact/opinion
  30. "The copy of the covenant that has been commented upon in this book is the one which is on display in the Holy Monastery of Saint Catherine at Mount Sinai and which was copied by Moritz." — p. 97 [PDF 122] — fact
  31. Burckhardt's note on the copy he saw: "in a note it is expressly stated that the original, written by 'Ali, was lost, and that the present was copied from a fourth successive copy taken from the original". — p. 68 [PDF 93]; p. 82 [PDF 107] — attr. Burckhardt (Chapter 7)
  32. A copy "written in Turkish Arabic script", made in 1858, "bears the seal of the Sinai dependency of Canea, Crete". — p. 98 [PDF 123] — fact
  33. In terms of "spelling, style, and usage, the covenant in question contains many archaic traits." — p. 84 [PDF 109] — opinion
  34. Moritz's Arabic rendition is full of "sic" markings (6-8), "suggesting that such shortcomings were somehow suspicious". — p. 83 [PDF 108] — attr. Moritz + inference
  35. "The covenant from the Sinai is more direct while the covenant from Iraq is much more elaborate, at least in the long introductory section which precedes the actual list of privileges"; both are "written in the Classical Arabic of the period". — pp. 86–87 [PDF 111–112] — fact (author's comparison)
C. Location, custody and removal of the original
  1. Géramb: the Covenant "had been kept in the Convent of the Holy Transfiguration of God at the Monastery of Saint Catherine". — p. 65 [PDF 90] — attr. Géramb (Pèlerinage 294; Pilgrimage 245)
  2. The original was "guarded preciously by the monks at Mount Sinai for nearly nine centuries." — p. 65 [PDF 90] — fact
  3. The monks keep a display copy "in one of the most heavily traveled corridors in the monastery, where all visitors may see it". — pp. 65–66 [PDF 90–91] — attr. Hobbs (160)
  4. Affagart says the original was kept "not in the monastery, but in the mosque", and that the Turks "had not yet convinced the monks to sell the original". — pp. 68–69 [PDF 93–94] — attr. Affagart, as read by the author
  5. The author asks whether Affagart actually saw the Covenant in the mosque, was told it was there, or assumed so. — p. 69 [PDF 94] — opinion
  6. Selim I's Chamber of the Relics (Topkapi) holds "the Prophet's mantle, his swords, and the letter he wrote to Muqawqis, the ruler of Egypt", hairs from his beard, soil from his tomb, one of his teeth, and imprints of his footstep, from the treasuries of the Mamluk State, the 'Abbasid Caliphate and the Hijaz Emirate. — p. 69 [PDF 94] — fact
  7. "several of them specify that it was stored in the Serrail (Morison 105-106) or Seraglio (Van Egmont and Heyman 161)"; these terms mean mainly Topkapi but also other Turkish palaces. — p. 69 [PDF 94] — attr. Morison; Van Egmont & Heyman
  8. "the search must start at the Topkapi Museum, it should be extended to other ancient palaces as well." — p. 69 [PDF 94] — opinion
  9. Stanley: the Covenant was "taken by Sultan Selim to Constantinople, and exchanged for a copy, which, however, no traveler has ever seen". — p. 67 [PDF 92] — attr. Stanley (344-344 [sic])
  10. Tomadakis: the original "must still exist in the archives" of Constantinople. — p. 68 [PDF 93] — attr. Tomadakis (16)
  11. "the firman of Selim I has actually been located in the Turkish collection; and, although it does not contain the text of the covenant at all, it is nevertheless a clear guarantee of safe conduct for the monks". — p. 74 [PDF 99] — attr. Atiya (xxix)
  12. Burckhardt saw the copy "certified with his [Selim's] own cipher" and says it "is kept in the Sinai convent at Cairo". — p. 81 [PDF 106] — attr. Burckhardt (Chapter 7)
  13. The Covenant "eventually went missing from the Treasury in Istanbul"; "It is possible that the enemies of ahl al-bayt destroyed it on grounds that it was too favorable to the Shi'ite cause." — p. 74 [PDF 99] — inference/opinion
  14. "The original copy of the Covenant ... was lost. Hence, all we have are the copies produced by generations of monks over the centuries." — p. 77 [PDF 102] — fact
  15. The Arabic note says "the original covenant was lost, and that the copy was provided by the Sultan to replace it"; author: "Was it not simply taken by the Sultan as opposed to lost?" — p. 98 [PDF 123] — attr. note + opinion
  16. The Monastery of Saint Catherine "contains the largest collection of Christian documents and codices after the Vatican Library" and is a "veritable conservatory of the Christian Orient". — p. 96 [PDF 121] — fact + attr. Géhin (163)
D. The monastery's archive, decrees, fatwas and the mosque
  1. "The oldest Arabic document housed in the library at Mount Sinai belongs to the Fatimid period and was perhaps written in 1106 CE". — p. 68 [PDF 93] — attr. Digbassanis (361)
  2. "the Arabic section of the Archive contains documents which inform us about the relations of the Monastery with the Arab chiefs and with the centers of the Islamic world from a very early date"; copies of the "Achtiname' (the Holy Testament)" are kept, "the first guarantee given by Mohammed which, according to tradition, the Prophet himself sanctified by stamping his palm over it." — p. 76 [PDF 101] — attr. Digbassanis (361)
  3. Atiya: privileges "upheld by the imams of the four Islamic rites: Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali, and Hanafi. The subject of each fatwa is presented at the top, and this is succeeded by a signed opinion of each of the imams". — p. 71 [PDF 96] — attr. Atiya (xxx)
  4. Atiya: "The decrees are the charters of liberties granted by the caliphs and sultans of mediaeval Egypt"; "they are supposed to be following in the steps of the Prophet in his famous covenant"; the oldest date from the Fatimid period; they increase greatly under the Mamluks, and some sultans issued several in one reign; signatures of sultans, "vizirs and their diwans at the royal court of Cairo". — p. 71 [PDF 96] — attr. Atiya (xxix)
  5. Ottoman viceroys of Egypt issued "166 decrees safeguarding the Monastery and the monks". — p. 71 [PDF 96] — attr. Atiya (xxxi)
  6. "A total of 1,742 Arabic and Turkish firmans are housed in the library at Saint Catherine's Monastery, including 210 royal mandates or decrees from twenty-one Ottoman sultans in succession". — p. 71 [PDF 96] — attr. Atiya (xxxi)
  7. Atiya: "A survey of the monumental Firman collection ... proves that the covenant of the Prophet, whether forged or authentic, was renewed by the successive Moslem potentates in Egypt, and the privileges of protection and safe-conduct to the monks of St. Catherine were freely upheld throughout the Islamic period". — p. 71 [PDF 96] — attr. Atiya (xviii)
  8. The Christians of Sinai "also obtained edicts, rulings, or fatwas from the four Sunni schools of jurisprudence as well as the Fatimid school". — p. 71 [PDF 96] — fact
  9. Mosque within the monastery walls "atop a spot where they would say the Prophet Muhammad had stood" (the version "today's monks relate"); "apparently constructed around 1106 during the reign of ... al-Afdal". — p. 75 [PDF 100] — attr. Hobbs (161)
  10. There is "no record of any such decree" ('Umar's forced-conversion decree) "in the archives of the Monastery at Mount Sinai." — p. 76 [PDF 101] — fact (author's claim)
  11. "the monks of Mount Sinai were prolific and prodigious scribes. Copying and recopying documents was their raison d'etre." — p. 68 [PDF 93] — fact/opinion
  12. Skrobucha: firmans (al-Hafiz 1132-49 and others) "contain explicit references to a holy letter of protection of the Prophet's." — p. 79 [PDF 104] — attr. Skrobucha (57-58)
  13. Hieromonk Justin of Sinai: "[t]hese documents, considered old at the time, must have already existed for some centuries" (51). — p. 79 [PDF 104] — attr. Justin
E. Napoleon and the European period
  1. Napoleon "claimed not only to be a Muslim but the manifestation of the Mahdi". — p. 70 [PDF 95] — fact
  2. Napoleon's decree (as described by Tomadakis): confirmed the privileges of Sinai; allowed the monks "free communication"; exempted them "from various financial obligations"; Napoleon helped rebuild the collapsed north wall. — p. 70 [PDF 95] — attr. Tomadakis (16)
  3. Champdor: "this order of protection and privilege ... matches, corresponds to, and acts as a counterpart to the Akd Name of Muhammad" (35). — p. 70 [PDF 95] — attr. Champdor
  4. Napoleon's decree "stresses the French Republic's respect for the Law of Moses, the Jewish Nation, and the educated inhabitants of the monastery"; its articles stop warring Bedouins from seeking asylum in the monastery, guarantee freedom of religious practice, and release the monks from "tribute, taxes, or duty on any goods" (99-100). — p. 70 [PDF 95] — attr. Fazakerley (378) / unclear source for "(99-100)"
  5. "Since the region was invaded by the French from 1798 to 1801 and subjected to British rule from 1882 to 1952, the monks of the Sinai had over a century and a half of European Christian domination to come clean". — p. 70 [PDF 95] — fact/inference
F. Travelers and Western writers
  1. Burckhardt: "It is a favorite belief of the monks of Mount Sinai, that Mohammed himself, in one of his journeys, alighted under the walls of the convent" and, "impressed with due veneration for the mountain of Moses", gave a Firmahn; "Ali is said to have written it". — p. 81 [PDF 106] — attr. Burckhardt (Chapter 7, 546-47)
  2. Burckhardt: "None of the historians of Mohammed ... mention his having been at Mount Sinai"; "it is totally contrary to history that he should have granted to any Christians such privileges", e.g. that "Moslems are bound to aid the Christian monks in rebuilding their ruined churches". — pp. 81–82 [PDF 106–107] — attr. Burckhardt
  3. Burckhardt: the document "states itself to have been written by Ali, not at the convent, but in the mosque of the Prophet at Medina"; it "is addressed, not to the convent of Mount Sinai in particular, but to all the Christians and their priests"; "The names of twenty-two witnesses, followers of Mohammed, are subscribed to it"; "the former is a fable and the latter a forgery." — p. 82 [PDF 107] — attr. Burckhardt (Chapter 7, 546-47)
  4. Burckhardt was "Known also as John Lewis or Jean Louis", "converted to Islam, sincerely or otherwise, dressed as an Arab, and went by the name of Shaykh Ibrahim ibn 'Abd Allah"; his family "always rejected claims" he converted; "he was indeed buried as a Muslim in Cairo". — p. 82 [PDF 107] — fact
  5. Paul Lunde believes Burckhardt's conversion was genuine; if so, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land "would represent the first Islamic critique of the Covenant". — p. 82 [PDF 107] — attr. Paul Lunde + inference
  6. "In all likelihood, Lewis simply pretended to be a Muslim ... to facilitate his travels throughout the Holy Land, including the sacred city of Mecca." — p. 82 [PDF 107] — opinion
  7. Arundale: the Bedouins "are amongst the largest of the tribes, and governed by their own Emir and Sheikhs. They have a contempt for the Turks ... Their religion is a reformation of the Mahomedan ... being for the most part followers of 'Ali." — p. 74 [PDF 99] — attr. Arundale (6-7)
  8. Stanley: the Koran's "repeated allusions ... to the stone of Moses ... to the holy valley of Tuwa ... and to the special addresses made to Moses on the western, and on the southern slopes of the mountain" make the visit possible; "Nowhere else probably in the Christian world is to be found such a cordial ... feeling towards the Arabian prophet". — p. 76 [PDF 101] — attr. Stanley (344-345)
  9. M.L.M.D.C. (1697): the Prophet gave great gifts to the Monastery "motivated by the friendship he had with one of the monks", including "an exemption from taxation" (85-86), by means of "a Patent signed with his hand" (86). — p. 75 [PDF 100] — attr. Jeux d'esprit
  10. Cantemir "both read and transcrib'd" the instrument of Exemption, which the monks brought to Adrianople. — p. 72 [PDF 97] — attr. Cantemir (169)
G. Critics and their arguments (as the author presents them)
  1. Critics argue "that the oldest extant copies of the Covenant date to the 16th century". — p. 66 [PDF 91] — attr. unnamed critics
  2. Hobbs: "some scholars suggest that the Covenant of the Prophet may have merely been a ruse (160)". — p. 75 [PDF 100] — attr. Hobbs
  3. "The idea of 'monkish impostures' has a long history among Protestant scholars due to their hatred of Catholics." — p. 75 [PDF 100] — opinion
  4. Hobbs: "There are conflicting accounts of the Prophet Muhammad's contact with the monastery, and there are questions about whether contact took place at all" (159). — pp. 75–76 [PDF 100–101] — attr. Hobbs
  5. J. Muehleisen Arnold: "Were the celebrated Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Mohammedem et Christianae fidei cultores (Paris 1630 and Hamb. 1690) a genuine document, which it is not, it would only be a 'snare and delusion'"; Arnold is described as "a reverend and missionary" whose book cover said "the entire proceeds of this work will be given towards founding a 'society for propagating the gospel among the Mohammedans'". — pp. 71–72 [PDF 96–97] — attr. Arnold
  6. Moritz offers "the most detailed criticism" (after the Salafis); he "wrote in German", so the author uses Skrobucha's summary. — p. 78 [PDF 103] — fact
  7. Skrobucha/Moritz: authenticity "disproved by Moritz on grounds of date, style, and content"; chief argument: "in contrast to the Prophet's surviving genuine letters of protection, there is no demand for the fulfillment of any single duty"; "the Christians themselves are empowered to fix the amount of their taxes", which "is contrary to Muslim government practice and is unparalleled in our sources"; "the monastery of Sinai is not expressly mentioned"; passages on "women, military service, and commerce, have no relevance to the monastery". — pp. 78–79 [PDF 103–104] — attr. Skrobucha (58-59)
  8. Skrobucha: the forgery was "not a very skilful" one, explained by "'the Mohammedans' lack of critical sense in religious matters and their reverence' for the Prophet"; "there had been undoubtedly genuine letters of protection ... to the Jewish community at Maqnah on the Gulf of Aqaba". — p. 79 [PDF 104] — attr. Skrobucha
  9. Skrobucha: "the Muslim rulers made it their principle in doubtful cases to favor the presumption of authenticity, even to the extent of renewing the right of protection in the absence of documentary evidence". — p. 79 [PDF 104] — attr. Skrobucha
  10. Skrobucha: "Improbable as the existence of a letter of protection from the Prophet is, the effect in history ... did not depend on any questions about the reality, the authenticity of the document." — p. 79 [PDF 104] — attr. Skrobucha (58-59)
  11. Moritz "had served as the director of the Khedivial Library in Cairo"; "He was a German imperial field agent and propagandist". — p. 79 [PDF 104] — attr. McMeekin (88, 92, 96, 147, 372, note 12)
  12. Frobenius on Moritz: "in his innermost heart a despiser of Oriental peoples". — p. 79 [PDF 104] — attr. qtd. McMeekin (147)
  13. "Moritz worked on behalf of the German Propaganda Ministry"; "Moritz was a man who wanted Muslims to kill and persecute Christians". — p. 80 [PDF 105] — fact/opinion
  14. German agents paid "Sunni and Shi'ite religious authorities as some sort of jizyah" to obtain fatwas for the German jihad against the Allies. — p. 80 [PDF 105] — attr. McMeekin (200, 201-209, 214-15, 233)
  15. German "Orientalists/covert operatives gathered armies of Islamists" and insisted it was an obligation "to kill Jewish and Christian infidels, excluding, of course, the Deutschen dhimmis". — p. 80 [PDF 105] — attr. McMeekin (86-93, 96-99, n8, 124-37, 160-161, 172-179, 181, 202-209, 216, 258, 263-265, 267-268, 271, 273-274, 333, 338)
  16. Mouton: "The lists of witnesses attesting to the authenticity of the document is also suspect: some of them, such as Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Darda had not yet converted to Islam at this date and even fought against it". — p. 82 [PDF 107] — attr. Mouton (177)
  17. Mouton: the hijri calendar "did not yet exist; it was only established in 637 by the Caliph 'Umar who, in retrospect, made it start in 622". — p. 84 [PDF 109] — attr. Mouton (177)
  18. Mouton: the Sinai document "contains nothing really original" and belongs to a body of similar documents from the medieval Near East, all from the 878 Iraqi letter, which "was also false and was, without a doubt, forged on the order of the Banu Makhlad, a family of viziers of Nestorian origin"; "There was no visible effort of adaptation on the part of the monks who forged the firman of Saint Catherine". — p. 86 [PDF 111] — attr. Mouton (177)
  19. Ratliff: the document "bears close resemblance to a number of other documents found in religious communities in the Near East", "remarkably similar to the letter of Muhammad addressed to the Christians of Najran"; the letter grants "protection against acts of violence, protection for Christian cult sites, and exemption from taxes". — p. 81 [PDF 106] — attr. Ratliff (15)
  20. Author's reading of Ratliff: "Ratliff alleges that Abd al-Masih, an Arab and former Muslim, had both the linguistic skills and religious knowledge to forge the famous Patent" ("While she is not bold enough to come out and say it directly"). — p. 81 [PDF 106] — inference/opinion
  21. Stanley: "No one can now prove or disprove the tradition". — p. 76 [PDF 101] — attr. Stanley
  22. The Jabaliyyah Arabs "mistakenly believe that the Covenant was written by Caliph 'Umar ibn al-Khattab". — p. 76 [PDF 101] — attr. Hobbs; "mistakenly" is opinion
  23. Father Golubovich called Turkish administrators "accomplices" of the Orthodox Christians. — p. 88 [PDF 113] — attr. Golubovich (L'École Pratique d'Études Bibliques 637)
  24. Jeffery: legendary development in Hayat al-qulub is "of Christian origin" (352). — p. 88 [PDF 113] — attr. Jeffery
