H. Calendar and dating background
  1. "the ancient Arabs ... were not familiar with calculation in years" (195). — p. 84 [PDF 109] — attr. Lammens
  2. Hudayfah ibn al-Yaman: "We are Arab people; when we report, we predate and postdate, we add and we subtract at will, but we do not mean to lie". — p. 84 [PDF 109] — attr. Ibn Qutaybah, qtd. Berkey (58)
  3. Peters: "Later Muslim authorities seem to give tacit recognition to the uncertainty of any of the chronological indications ... about the Prophet's life at Mecca"; "the historical ground grew firm only at Muhammad's migration to Medina" (103). — p. 85 [PDF 110] — attr. Peters
  4. Hashim Amir 'Ali: "there is more calendrical confusion connected with these ten years of Muhammad's mission in Medina than with any other decade of human history". — p. 85 [PDF 110] — attr. qtd. Peters (253)
  5. The early lunisolar calendar used intercalation (a leap month); "It is not known exactly when the Prophet suppressed this intercalary month". — p. 85 [PDF 110] — attr. "Lammers" [sic/OCR for Lammens] (204)
  6. The pushed-back era start introduced "a degree of anarchy into the Muslims' recollection of the date of events during the intercalation era at Medina". — p. 85 [PDF 110] — attr. Peters (253)
  7. Dates were adjusted to match auspicious astrological dates or sacred days; mnemonic devices were used; ages were altered, including Muhammad's birth date, Khadijah's age at marriage and the birth of Fatimah al-Zahra. — p. 85 [PDF 110] — fact; attr. Faizer (xv) for mnemonics
  8. Caetani: a "possibility of error of three years in the Prophet's chronology" (Lammens 188). Lammens: "a full ten years may have been added to Muhammad's existence" (197). — p. 85 [PDF 110] — attr.
  9. Kasim Sulum: "the calendar must also be regarded as a part of the developments in calendar practices of the period of Holy Prophet"; 'Umar's "official Islamic calendar" was based on the "original Islamic calendar". — p. 84 [PDF 109] — attr. Sulum
  10. "it was Imam 'Ali ibn Abi Talib ... who proposed the hijri calendar to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab". — p. 84 [PDF 109] — fact (author's claim)
  11. "some Muslim scholars believe that the hegira dating system was developed by the Prophet himself." — p. 84 [PDF 109] — attr. unnamed Muslim scholars
  12. "It is also widely accepted in Shi'ite scholarly circles that Imam 'Ali, and the eleven Imams who followed him, had inherited the knowledge of the Prophet." — p. 84 [PDF 109] — attr. Shi'ite scholarly circles
  13. Isnads: "In many instances, these chains of narration were produced centuries after the fact"; "only Muslims have used these chains of narration"; "the Muslim methodology of documentation is unsurpassed even by modern researchers (Azami 75)". — p. 83 [PDF 108] — fact/opinion + attr. Azami
  14. "the Qur'an was the first book committed to writing in the Arabic alphabet"; grammar and orthography took centuries to formalize. — p. 83 [PDF 108] — fact
  15. Shakespeare's will was signed "Shakspere" and "Shakspeare"; Raleigh's name was spelled Raleigh, Raliegh, Ralegh, Raghley, Rawley, Rawly, Rawlie, Rawleigh, Raulighe, Raughlie, or Rayly. — p. 84 [PDF 109] — fact (analogy)
I. Parallel covenants, the Islamic sources and other documents
  1. "a copy of a treaty with the Monastery of Saint Catherine does indeed exist in Islamic sources"; Ibn Sa'd's version "is far shorter than the Covenant on display"; Ibn Sa'd "is a secondary source". — p. 69 [PDF 94] — fact/opinion
  2. "Since the Prophet made and remade numerous treaties with the same parties ... it is quite possible that more than one treaty was signed with the monks". — pp. 69–70 [PDF 94–95] — inference
  3. "out of over one hundred official letters sent by the Prophet Muhammad as part of his diplomatic campaign, the texts of only sixty or so have survived in ancient historical sources and less than ten original copies have endured". — p. 67 [PDF 92] — fact
  4. Treaty of Maqnah purchased by al-Saffah for 300 dinars; the people of Aylah also kept the Prophet's cloak. — p. 78 [PDF 103] — attr. Gil (29, note 25)
  5. Letter to Muqawqis found in 1850 in a Coptic Bible cover at Ahmin, near Saide (Barthlmy); "many Muslims, including the Sultans of the Ottoman Empire and scores of Muslim scholars, have accepted this letter". — p. 78 [PDF 103] — attr. Aydin (96) / fact
  6. Existing treaties of the Prophet: the Constitution of Medina; the treaties with the Meccans at al-Hudaybiyyah, the Jews of Khaybar and the Christians of Najran. — p. 81 [PDF 106] — fact
  7. Waardenburg: the Prophet's peace treaties "served as models for treaties during and after the Arab conquest" (17, note 22). — p. 81 [PDF 106] — attr. Waardenburg
  8. Sa'id ibn Makhlad's "career came to an abrupt end as a result of his Christian brother's attempt to obtain special concessions for the Christian subjects of the Caliphate." — p. 86 [PDF 111] — fact
  9. The 'Abbasids were careful not "to give the People of the Book too much influence over the court and the empire". — p. 86 [PDF 111] — attr. Karabell (46)
  10. The 1403 treaty of the Order of St. John with the Sultan of Egypt mentions pilgrims to St. Catherine and gives permission to repair and build. — p. 88 [PDF 113] — attr. Laborde (332-333)
  11. "If one looks at the laws implemented by the early Caliphs (Fortescue 226), they are virtually identical to those contained in the covenants." — p. 89 [PDF 114] — attr. Fortescue + opinion
  12. The Prophet: "Narrate [traditions] from the Children of Israel for there is nothing objectionable in that" (Shafi'i); "Seek knowledge, even in China" (Bayhaqi). — p. 78 [PDF 103] — attr. Shafi'i; Bayhaqi
  13. "out of the millions of sayings attributed to the Prophet, only a small number are genuine." — p. 78 [PDF 103] — fact/opinion
J. Eagle story and early legends
  1. Eagle symbolism: in Judaism "divine powers of deliverance and watchful protection"; in Christianity "one of the Four Living Creatures surrounding the Throne of the Lamb in the Apocalypse and the symbol of Saint John the Evangelist"; in Islam "associated with the Angel Gabriel". — p. 87 [PDF 112] — fact
  2. Buraq "is also described as having the wings of a giant eagle"; Muhammad's Black Standard was called rayat al-'uqab, "the Banner of the Eagle," "even though it was solid black." — p. 87 [PDF 112] — fact
  3. "The image of the eagle is particularly rare in Sunni sources"; "In the story of Bahira, it was a cloud, and not an eagle"; "The story of the eagle seems to be uniquely associated with Muhammad and the monks of Mount Sinai." — p. 87 [PDF 112] — fact/opinion
  4. The anonymous author of the Istoria "appears to have had a 'significant degree of familiarity with Islam'". — p. 87 [PDF 112] — attr. Gervers (95)
  5. "The story of Muhammad at Mount Sinai does not exist in any of the surviving Arabic and Islamic sources." — p. 87 [PDF 112] — fact (author's claim)
  6. In the Eulogius account, the evil angel had Ozim preach "Allah is Great, Allah is Great, there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is his Messenger" (95). — p. 88 [PDF 113] — attr. Gervers
  7. The Legend of Sergius Bahira "makes mention of a revelation that Bahira received on Mount Sinai"; "no Islamic account of Bahira associates him with the Sinai". — p. 88 [PDF 113] — fact
K. Covenant content (Commentary section; quotations attributed to the Covenant)
  1. The opening: "As God is great and governs, from whom all the prophets are come, for there remains no record of injustice against God." — p. 89 [PDF 114]
  2. Addressees: the Prophet "has written the present instrument to all those who are in his national people, and of his own religion, as a secure and positive promise to be accomplished to the Christian nation"; to every Christian "whosoever they may be, whether they be the noble or the vulgar, the honorable or otherwise." — p. 89 [PDF 114]
  3. Item I (warning): "Whosoever of my nation shall presume to break my promise and oath ... destroys the promise of God, acts contrary to the oath, and will be a resister of the faith, (which God forbid) for he becomes worthy of the curse...."; "whether he be the King himself, or a poor man." — p. 90 [PDF 115]
  4. Protection: "whenever any of the monks in his travels shall happen to settle upon any mountain, hill, village, or other habitable place, on the sea, or in deserts, or in any convent, church, or house of prayer, I shall be in the midst of them, as the preserver and protector of them...." — p. 90 [PDF 115]
  5. "jointly with all my national people"; "they are a part of my own people, and an honor to me". — p. 90 [PDF 115]
  6. Tax exemption: "I command all officers not to require any poll-tax of them, or any other tribute, because they shall not be forced or compelled to anything of this kind." — p. 90 [PDF 115]
  7. Officials: "None shall presume to change their judges or governors, but they shall remain in their office, without being deported." — p. 91 [PDF 116]
  8. "The fifth item": freedom of movement: "No one shall molest them when they are travelling on the road." — p. 91 [PDF 116]
  9. Item six: "Whatever churches they are possessed of, no one is to deprive them of them." — p. 91 [PDF 116]
  10. Item seven (repeated warning): "Whosoever shall annul any of one of these my decrees, let him know positively that he annuls the ordinance of God." — p. 91 [PDF 116]
  11. Item eight: "Neither their judges, governors, monks, servants, disciples, or any others depending on them, shall pay any poll-tax, or be molested on that account." — p. 92 [PDF 117]
  12. "I am their protector, wherever they shall be, either by land or sea, east or west, north or south; because both they and all that belong to them are included in this my promissory oath and patent." — p. 92 [PDF 117]
  13. Hermits: "And of those that live quietly and solitary upon the mountains, they shall exact neither poll-tax nor tithes from their incomes, neither shall any Muslim partake of what they have; for they labor only to maintain themselves." — p. 93 [PDF 118]
  14. Provision: "Whenever the crop of the earth shall be plentiful in its due time, the inhabitants shall be obliged out of every bushel to give them a certain measure." — p. 93 [PDF 118]
  15. Item eleven: "Neither in time of war shall they take them out of their habitations, nor compel them to go to the wars, nor even then shall they require of them any poll-tax." — p. 93 [PDF 118]
  16. Structure: "the previous eleven items applied specifically to the monks of Mount Sinai. The seven items which follow are applicable to Christians as a whole." — p. 93 [PDF 118] (i.e. 18 items in all)
  17. Item twelve: "Those Christians who are inhabitants, and with their riches and traffic are able to pay the poll-tax, shall pay no more than twelve drachms." — p. 94 [PDF 119]
  18. Item thirteen: "Excepting this, nothing shall be required of them, according to the express order of God, that says, 'Do not molest those that have a veneration for the books that are sent from God, but rather in a kind manner give of your good things to them, and converse with them, and hinder everyone from molesting them.'" — p. 95 [PDF 120]
  19. Item fourteen: "If a Christian woman shall happen to marry a Muslim, the Muslim shall not cross the inclination of his wife, to keep her from her church and prayers, and the practice of her religion." — p. 95 [PDF 120]
  20. Item fifteen: "that no person hinder them from repairing their churches." — p. 95 [PDF 120]
  21. Item sixteen: "Whosoever acts contrary to my grant, or gives credit to anything contrary to it, becomes truly an apostate to God, and to his divine apostle, because this protection I have granted to them according to this promise." — p. 96 [PDF 121]
  22. Item seventeen: "No one shall bear arms against them, but, on the contrary, the Muslims shall wage war for them." — p. 96 [PDF 121]
  23. Item eighteen: "And by this I ordain, that none of my nation shall presume to do or act contrary to this my promise, until the end of the world." — p. 96 [PDF 121]
  24. The English translation quoted in the Commentary is not identified in this chapter. — pp. 89–96 — note
L. Religious, legal and economic claims in the Commentary
  1. "The Prophet never imposed shari'ah law on non-Muslims. Jewish people were judged on the basis of Jewish law and Christians ... of Christian law." — p. 90 [PDF 115] — fact
  2. Imam 'Ali: "Question me before you lose me ... I could give judgments to the people of the Torah by their Torah, to the people of the Gospels by their Gospels, to the people of Psalms by their Psalms, and to the people of the Furqan ... by their Furqan". — p. 90 [PDF 115] — attr. Mufid (21)
  3. "the building of synagogues and churches actually flourished during the Golden Age of Islam." — p. 91 [PDF 116] — fact
  4. An Islamic State does not allow proselytization among Muslims; non-Muslims may spread the Gospel "among pagans and polytheists". — pp. 91–92 [PDF 116–117] — opinion
  5. Qur'an references cited for obeying Allah and His Messenger: 2:285; 3:32; 4:13; 4:14; 8:1; 8:20; 8:24; 8:46; 9:71 [OCR "971"]; 24:51; 24:52; 33:33; 33:66; 33:71; 48:17; 49:14; 58:13; 64:12; 72:23. Also 49:13 (diversity) and 56:77-80 ("hidden scriptures"). — p. 92 [PDF 117]; p. 90 [PDF 115]; p. 94 [PDF 119]
  6. Dalrymple: "Islam has traditionally been tolerant of religious minorities ... that Islamic tradition of tolerance is today wearing distinctly thin"; "things are suddenly becoming difficult for the last Christians of the Middle East" (19). — p. 92 [PDF 117] — attr. Dalrymple
  7. Humphreys: "Many of these texts are quite late ... and represent a period when the status of non-Muslims had sharply degenerated from earlier times" (259). — p. 92 [PDF 117] — attr. Humphreys
  8. Hamidullah: ten dirhams "represented the expenses of an average family for ten days" (Introduction 149); contrasted with Habib Levy's "exorbitant annual poll-tax" (165). — p. 94 [PDF 119] — attr.
  9. "the jizyah did not exist in the early days of Islam and ... many jurists believe that it can legally be discontinued (Hamidullah 149-150)"; "the poll-tax was eventually abolished". — p. 94 [PDF 119] — attr./fact
  10. The poll-tax "is actually much lower than the 2.5% zakat paid by Sunni Muslims and vastly less than the 20% of khums [OCR "khutns"] paid by Shi'ite Muslims." — p. 94 [PDF 119] — fact/opinion
  11. Islamic law does not tax the poor (not mentioned in the covenant); "People are considered poor if they do not have enough savings to survive for an entire year without working." — p. 94 [PDF 119] — fact
  12. Some argued dhimmi status "also embraced Zoroastrians, Manicheans, Buddhists, and even Hindus"; Imam 'Ali told his governor in Egypt to treat all subjects as "equals in creation" (278); Moghul emperors "gave like justice to all" (Lybyer 298). — p. 94 [PDF 119] — attr.
  13. "Twelver Shi'ite Islam prohibits permanent marriages between Muslims and the People of the Book" but "does allow for fixed-term marriage, which can legally apply for a lifetime." — p. 95 [PDF 120] — fact
  14. A Christian wife may consume wine or pork and dress as she pleases; children of mixed unions must be raised Muslim; Catholic Canon Law "is more restrictive than the shari'ah in this regard". — p. 95 [PDF 120] — fact/opinion
  15. Modern comparisons the author makes: Soviet Union and China destroyed "tens of thousands of mosques"; France denies Muslims places of worship "through deliberate governmental policies"; Saudi women "cannot even drive"; Moroccan grand taxis need special authorization to leave the city outskirts; Malaysia seeks to stop Christians from using "Allah"; Australia "now advocates assimilation"; Puerto Ricans "are deprived of the right to vote". — pp. 90–92 [PDF 115–117] — fact/opinion

5. Covenant details

5.1 Names used for the document
  • "The Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Monks of Mount Sinai" (author's standard title) — throughout
  • "Achtiname" (Griffith, Tomadakis, Evans, Manafis, Digbassanis; the author) — pp. 65, 67–68, 69, 72, 73, 76, 98; "achtiname" p. 70, p. 98
  • "Akd Name" (Champdor, p. 66, p. 70) / "Akd Nâme" (Champdor quotation, p. 73)
  • "firman" / "original firman" (Hobbs, p. 65; author, p. 68); "firman of Saint Catherine" (Mouton, p. 86); "Firmahn" (Burckhardt, pp. 81–82)
  • "Patent of Muhammad" / "Patent" (Pococke, p. 69; M.L.M.D.C., p. 75; author, pp. 73, 81, 96–97); "Relic and Patent", "a double and true Patent" (Marshal in M.L.M.D.C., p. 75)
  • "Charter" / "the original charter" (author, pp. 67, 71); "Muhammad's Charter" (p. 72); "famous Charter or Achtiname" (Manafis, p. 73)
  • "writ of protection" (p. 65); "letter of protection" (Skrobucha, p. 79; Ratliff, p. 81; Monastery statement, p. 96); "contract of protection" (Stanley, p. 76)
  • "Diploma"; "instrument of Exemption" (Cantemir, p. 72)
  • "Pact of Muhammad" (p. 73); "this Gentleman's agreement" (Champdor, p. 73); "Akd Name ... diplomatic decree"; "this Decree" (Champdor quotation, p. 73)
  • "the Holy Testament" (Digbassanis, p. 76); "the Testament" (Griffith, p. 98)
  • "promise of protection ['ahd]" (scribal note, p. 97); "this my promissory oath and patent" (covenant text, p. 92)
  • Related but distinct (as the author treats them): "Treaty of Saint Catherine, which was signed in the year 6 AH" (the shorter Ibn Sa'd version, p. 70); Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Mohammedem et Christianae fidei cultores (Paris 1630, Hamburg 1690), named by Arnold (p. 71)
5.2 Claimed date
  • "in the second year of the hijrah" — p. 65 [PDF 90] (author); "on the second year of the hijrah" — p. 70 [PDF 95]
  • "the third of Muharram of the second year of the hijrah, which corresponds to July 7th, 623 of the Gregorian calendar" — p. 83 [PDF 108] (author's conversion)
  • Scribal note on the display copy: "on the third of Muharram in the second year of the Prophet's Hegira" — p. 97 [PDF 122]
  • Burckhardt: "in the second year of the Hedjra" — p. 82 [PDF 107]
  • Hobbs: "written by his cousin and son-in-law 'Ali in 623 CE" — p. 76 [PDF 101]
  • Monastery statement: "In the second year of the Hegira, corresponding to AD 626" (date of the delegation's request) — p. 96 [PDF 121]
  • Related: monks' delegation to Medina "in 625 CE ... the second to third year of the hijrah" — p. 70 [PDF 95]
  • Author's caveats: the year "may be a later addition" (p. 97); "In all probability ... the dates ... were added at a later time" (p. 85); Davenport: the original probably had no date (p. 85)
  • Balagna: manuscripts "attributed to 'Ali, which were written in the second year" are "plausible or likely"; manuscripts witnessed by Mu'awiyyah "in the fourth year of the hijrah are anomalous" (66-67) — p. 85 [PDF 110]
5.3 Place issued
  • "in the Mosque of the Prophet" (scribal note, p. 97 [PDF 122]); "not at the convent, but in the mosque of the Prophet at Medina" (Burckhardt, p. 82 [PDF 107])
  • Rival traditions: given at the monastery during Muhammad's visit (Affagart, p. 68; Stanley, p. 76, contract "deposited in the archives of the convent"; Burckhardt reporting the monks' "favorite belief", p. 81; Hobbs, "By some accounts ... on that visit", p. 70); or given to a delegation that went to Medina in 625 CE (Hobbs, p. 70) / AD 626 (Monastery statement, p. 96)
5.4 Scribe
  • Imam 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (d. 661 CE): "scribed by the hand of Imam 'Ali" (p. 68); "written by the hand of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib" (p. 70); "written by 'Ali" (p. 77); "Ali is said to have written it" (Burckhardt, p. 81); "Akd Name redacted by ['Ali ibn] Abu Talib" (Champdor, p. 73); "the Caliph 'Ali" (Atiya, p. 74); "it is accurate that 'Ali acted as the Prophet's scribe, as he did on many occasions" (p. 97)
  • Caveat: "In all probability ... the name of the scribe ... [was] added at a later time" (p. 85 [PDF 110])
  • Folk variant: the Jabaliyyah Arabs think it was written by Caliph 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (Hobbs; "mistakenly" in the author's view) — p. 76 [PDF 101]
  • Note: the later copyist/scribe and a judge who signed the display copy are unnamed ("the lifespan of the scribe and judge who are signatories") — p. 97 [PDF 122]
5.5 Witnesses
  • Count: "twenty-two witnesses, followers of Mohammed" (Burckhardt, p. 82 [PDF 107]); "the issue of the twenty-two witnesses" (author, p. 82)
  • Names given in this chapter (7 of 22):
    1. Abu Bakr (listed first) — p. 85 [PDF 110]
    2. 'Umar (second) — p. 85
    3. 'Uthman (third) — p. 85
    4. 'Ali (fourth) — p. 85
    5. Muawiyyah / Mu'awiyyah (fifth) — p. 85
    6. Abu Hurayrah — p. 82 [PDF 107], p. 83 [PDF 108] (Mouton)
    7. Abu al-Darda' — p. 82, p. 83 (Mouton)
    • The other fifteen witnesses are not named in this chapter.
  • The author says the primary document was "witnessed by other Companions" (p. 77 [PDF 102]).
5.6 Recipients
  • "the Monks of Mount Sinai" (title); "a community of monks who inhabit the Mountain of Tur-Sina'i" (scribal note, p. 97)
  • Burckhardt: "addressed, not to the convent of Mount Sinai in particular, but to all the Christians and their priests" (p. 82)
  • Pococke: granted "not only to the Monks of Mount Sinai, but to Christians in general" (289) (p. 69)
  • Skrobucha: "the monastery of Sinai is not expressly mentioned" (p. 79)
  • Author: the first eleven items apply to the Sinai monks and the seven that follow to "Christians as a whole" (p. 93); the covenant is "directed, not only to the entire Muslim ummah, but to the Christian Nation as well" (p. 89); "The principles the Prophet set forth applied not only to the monks of Mount Sinai, but to Christians around the world" (p. 82); yet "the Prophet made a treaty with a specific monastery out of gratitude for their kindness. Nowhere else is this the case" (p. 80)
5.7 Seal / signature
  • Handprint (Affagart, p. 68; M.L.M.D.C., p. 75; Stanley, p. 76; Burckhardt, p. 81; Atiya "sealed by the hand of the Prophet", p. 74; Digbassanis "stamping his palm", p. 76; Monastery statement "placed his hand upon the document", p. 96); "khamsah" (p. 75)
  • Two fingers (Skrobucha, p. 78); one fingerprint (Van Egmont & Heyman, p. 75)
  • "signed with the seal of the Prophet" (scribal note, p. 97); the author says "seal" could mean the palm-print or the ring seal (p. 97)
5.8 Location of the original
  • At the monastery until 1517 (Hobbs, Tomadakis, Monconys, Pococke, Oumanetz/Volkoff, Skrobucha, Burckhardt, Digbassanis, Monastery statement; "every authority" per the author citing Ratliff 14-15), "for nearly nine centuries" (p. 65)
  • In the monastery's mosque in 1533–34 (Affagart) — pp. 68–69
  • Taken to the palace of Selim I in Istanbul (Hobbs, p. 65); Constantinople archives (Tomadakis, p. 68); "imperial treasury at Constantinople" (Burckhardt, p. 81); "royal treasury in Constantinople" (Monastery statement, p. 96); "the treasury [khizanah] of the Sultan" (scribal note, p. 97); "Serrail" (Morison) / "Seraglio" (Van Egmont & Heyman) (p. 69); author: possibly Topkapi or "other ancient palaces" (p. 69)
  • Possibly taken by Sulayman the Magnificent instead (author's hypothesis, p. 69)
  • "lost" (Burckhardt's note, p. 68; scribal note, p. 98; author, p. 77); "went missing from the Treasury in Istanbul", possibly destroyed by enemies of ahl al-bayt (author, p. 74); Stanley: "has long since disappeared", if it ever existed (p. 67)
5.9 Copies
  • Six Arabic scroll copies (Atiya; table p. 65): dated 1737-38, 1778 and 1800-01 CE, and three undated
  • Arabic/Turkish codices 695 and 696 (dates 1561 CE and 1683–1684 CE; alignment unclear) — p. 65
  • Turkish translations numbered 1 to 43 (Atiya 80) — p. 66
  • Display copy in a corridor (Hobbs) — pp. 65–66; the book comments on the display copy "copied by Moritz", "not dated", "appears ... to date from 1800/01 CE", certified "with the signature of the noble Sultan" — p. 97
  • Certified copy with Selim's cipher, seen by Burckhardt at "the Sinai convent at Cairo" — p. 81
  • "certified copies ... each depicting the hand print" given by Selim (Monastery statement) — p. 96
  • "the first official copy, provided by Selim I ... in 1517 CE, was sealed with his signature" (author's inference) — p. 97
  • Copies "certified in court by judges of Islam" (Atiya) — p. 74
  • Turkish Arabic-script copy of 1858 with the seal of the Sinai dependency of Canea, Crete — p. 98
  • Selim I's firman (not containing the covenant text) "located in the Turkish collection" (Atiya) — p. 74; listed as support in the Conclusions, p. 98
  • "Arabic version in my possession" (author) — p. 97
5.10 Who published, translated or transcribed it, and when (as named in this chapter)
  • Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Mohammedem et Christianae fidei cultores, Paris 1630 and Hamburg 1690 (named via Arnold) — p. 71; "the covenant of the Prophet published in Paris in 1630 CE" — p. 78
  • Cantemir "read and transcrib'd" the instrument of Exemption at Adrianople (time of Soliman II) — p. 72
  • Burckhardt described it in Travels in Syria and the Holy Land ("Chapter 7, 546-47"); he visited in 1816 — pp. 68, 81–82
  • Bernhard Moritz: Arabic rendition (6-8) in Beiträge zur Geschichte des Sinai-Klosters im Mittelalter nach arabischen Quellen (1918); copied the display copy — pp. 79, 83, 97
  • Skrobucha summarized Moritz (57-59) — pp. 78–79
  • Sidney H. Griffith translated it (renders jild as "parchment", 63; 1858 copy heading 63-64) — pp. 97–98
  • The author translated Affagart's Relation de Terre Sainte from Middle French (191) — p. 68
  • English translation used in the Commentary: source not named in this chapter — pp. 89–96
5.11 The author's authenticity verdict

Verdict: authentic. "most academics not bound to 'the hermeneutics of suspicion' have good grounds for considering The Covenant ... to be authentic in the absence of definitive evidence of forgery. To date, no scholar has presented any solid proof that the covenant is a fake." The covenant "has passed the test" of content analysis. — p. 98 [PDF 123]

Supporting arguments (in the author's words where possible):

  1. The date (2 AH) "is consistent with the chronicles kept by the monks since the early days of Islam" (p. 65); "the Covenant's date is confirmed by Islamic sources as well as the chronicles from the Monastery" (p. 80).
  2. Late copies prove nothing about the date of composition (Iliad, Tanakh, Codex Sinaiticus, Qur'an and hadith analogies) (p. 66); "Simply because a covenant was copied in 1630, 1561, 1538 or ... the 10th century CE does not mean it was created on that date" (p. 89).
  3. Material decay: paper lasts about a century at best, so copies were remade roughly every century; the copies are identical in content, so the chain of faithful transcription reaches back to 'Ali's original (p. 68); the original would have "turned to dust" had it stayed (p. 67).
  4. Undated copies may be older than 1561, and one may be the first copy made from the original (p. 66).
  5. Affagart's 1533–34 eyewitness report places the original at the monastery's mosque (p. 68).
  6. A shorter version of the treaty with St. Catherine exists in Islamic sources (Ibn Sa'd, 6 AH); the Prophet renewed treaties, so there may have been more than one (pp. 69–70).
  7. Monastery records of a 625 CE delegation to Medina; traditions of earlier visits (p. 70).
  8. The monks have always upheld it; they had over a century and a half of European rule in which to "come clean" and did not (p. 70).
  9. Napoleon endorsed it; his 1798 decree mirrors it (p. 70).
  10. Unbroken confirmation by Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman decrees (975–1888) and fatwas of the four Sunni schools plus the Fatimid school: "recognized ... for more than a millennium" (pp. 70–71).
  11. Accepted by both Sunnis and Shi'ites despite their mutual hostility (p. 72).
  12. Even Kara Mustapha Pasha, who called it a forgery, conceded the immunity and kept the monastery exempt (p. 72).
  13. Champdor: it existed under 'Umar (r. 634–644), who endorsed it (p. 73).
  14. Already confirmed in 975 CE, so a 1517 or 1010 origin is impossible (p. 73); the al-Hafiz firman of 1134 calls the agreements "ancient" (Justin: "for some centuries"), so it cannot be a forgery made a century earlier under al-Hakim (p. 79).
  15. A forgery would have been a "formidable feat": the penalty would be death, and nobody at the monastery could have imitated the Prophet's speech or 'Ali's handwriting (pp. 73–74).
  16. Atiya, "who was Christian", accepts that the copies are identical and presumably reproduce 'Ali's original (p. 74).
  17. The handprint is attested "in all of the ancient sources" (p. 75).
  18. Several versions of the contact "suggest that an event took place" (p. 76); the monastery archives chronicle early contacts, so critics would have to show the archives are forged; "The onus of proof is on the accuser" (p. 76).
  19. Stanley: the visit is "at least not impossible" (p. 76).
  20. No isnad is needed for a primary document (pp. 77, 98).
  21. Style and content are "consistent with other authenticated accords" (p. 80); no demands were made because the recipients were monks, not a commercial city-state (p. 80).
  22. The monks had no motive to forge: existing treaties (Medina, Hudaybiyyah, Khaybar, Najran) were precedents, and a forger would have named the monastery (p. 81).
  23. A common origin with the Najran letter is explained by a common author (the Prophet); "no 'cut and paste' job ever took place"; the styles differ (p. 86).
  24. There is no evidence for Mouton's Banu Makhlad forgery theory (p. 86).
  25. The eagle story and Latin legends of c. 850 CE show the Sinai stories circulating by the mid-9th century (pp. 87–88).
  26. The 1403 treaty "allusion" predates the 16th century (p. 88).
  27. The covenant's injunctions match the laws of the early Caliphs (Fortescue) (p. 89).
  28. The scribe's pious formula shows the copyist believed it authentic (p. 97).
  29. The 1858 Canea copy, and Griffith's statement that it was confirmed up to Abdul Hamid II in 1904 (p. 98).
  30. Conclusions list: Muhammad's travels in the Greater Levant; his confirmed contacts with Christians; the "remarkable stability" of the account; recognition by the monks and by Muslim scholars of all schools; the discovery of Selim I's firman; and comparison with the Prophet's other treaties (p. 98).

Counter-arguments addressed, and the author's replies:

Counter-argument (as presented) Who Author's answer Page
The oldest extant copies date only to the 16th century unnamed critics Specious: compare the Iliad, Tanakh, NT and Qur'an; paper decays; undated copies may be older; Affagart saw the original in 1533–34 pp. 66–68
The original "if ever it existed, has long since disappeared"; the copy has never been seen Stanley Tomadakis is confident it still exists; "it must still exist in the archives" pp. 67–68
Covenant forged by the monks to save themselves; "ruse"; drafted c. 1010 when a Muslim army threatened the monastery Hobbs's unnamed "observers"; "some scholars" Hobbs names neither the observers nor their evidence; "monkish impostures" is a Protestant prejudice; confirmed already in 975 pp. 73, 75
Testamentum (1630/1690) not genuine; a "snare and delusion" Arnold Contradictory reasoning from a missionary pp. 71–72
Tax exemption unbelievable Moritz Then Napoleon's decree would also be suspect; "how often does any politician abolish taxes?" p. 70
Disproved "on grounds of date, style, and content"; no duties imposed; Christians fix their own taxes; monastery not named; irrelevant clauses on women, military service, commerce Moritz via Skrobucha Date is confirmed by sources and chronicles; style matches other accords; no demands because these were monks; the case was exceptional; the Prophet issued "direct, but distant" rulings applicable to all pp. 78–82
Possibly forged in Egypt under al-Hakim (996–1020) Skrobucha "without foundation"; the 1134 firman calls the agreements ancient p. 79
Moritz's scholarship (general) Moritz Moritz was a German imperial agent and propagandist, later allied with the Nazis, so his scholarship is "propaganda" pp. 79–80
Moritz's "sic" markings imply suspicious errors Moritz Arabic orthography was not yet fixed; Shakespeare and Raleigh spelling analogies; variants may be scribal slips pp. 83–84
Derived from similar Near-Eastern documents; the convert-abbot 'Abd al-Masih could have forged it Ratliff (as the author reads her) Ratliff ignores the most likely cause (common origin with the Prophet) p. 81
No historian records Muhammad at Mount Sinai; the privileges are "totally contrary to history"; the document says it was written at Medina, is addressed to all Christians, and states the original was lost (fourth successive copy); "a fable and ... a forgery" Burckhardt Little is known of Muhammad's pre-prophetic life and few witnesses survived; the Bahira story may echo the Sinai visit; the Prophet issued many protection edicts; his rulings were addressed generally pp. 81–82
Anachronistic witnesses: Abu Hurayrah (joined 7 AH) and Abu al-Darda' (converted after Badr, 624) Mouton (also Ratliff) Abu Hurayrah reportedly visited the Prophet in Mecca earlier; Abu al-Darda' was a Medinan, friendly to Islam, and may have converted in 623; also, witnesses "may have been added after the fact" pp. 82–83
Order of witnesses (Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Mu'awiyyah) is suspicious (the Sunni caliph order) the author raises it himself The list was attached later, "no earlier than" 'Umar II (717–720) pp. 85–86
The hijri calendar did not exist in 2 AH (only established 637, backdated to 622) Mouton 'Ali proposed the calendar to 'Umar and may have used it earlier; 'Ali inherited the Prophet's knowledge; Sulum says the Prophet used it from 2 AH; later copyists re-dated documents; the year may be a later addition; early Arab dating was unreliable pp. 84–85, 97
Nothing original; copied from the 878 Iraqi (Najran) letter forged by the Banu Makhlad; no adaptation effort Mouton No proof; points similar but not identical; styles differ; no evidence the Banu Makhlad forged anything; such a scandal would have been recorded p. 86
No isnad; not in the hadith collections Salafis/Wahhabis Isnads arose a century later; a primary document needs none; hadith scholars ignored treaties and rarely reached the Sinai p. 77
Muslims cannot rely on Christian sources unnamed Islamic tradition draws on Jewish and Christian material; hadith literature also contains forgeries p. 78
Ottomans (some Turks) rejected the covenants unnamed Their motives were fiscal and political, not doubts about authenticity; just as many accepted them p. 88
Conflicting accounts; doubt whether contact happened at all Hobbs Many versions imply an event took place; repeated visits merged into one narrative pp. 75–76

Fingerprint, not handprint Van Egmont & Heyman They never saw the document p. 75
Jabaliyyah: written by 'Umar; 'Umar's forced-conversion decree survives Hobbs (Jabaliyyah) They confuse it with the Pact of 'Umar; no such decree exists in the archives p. 76
Achtiname dates from the first Muslim advance into Sinai Evans It was only renewed under 'Umar p. 73
1517 date of the Covenant "some scholars" Already confirmed in 975 p. 73
Legends of Christian origin (Hayat al-qulub) Jeffery The same argument can be turned to confirm the encounters p. 88

6. The author's key arguments and opinions (kept separate from facts)

  1. Orientalists who reject the Covenant rely on "specious arguments"; their reasoning is "intellectually inadmissible"; "an attitude of rejection has preceded any investigation". — p. 66 [PDF 91]
  2. He compares this to Lewontin's admitted a-priori materialism: some historians reject the true positions of Islam on Christianity for "political and ideological considerations" or "worldly benefits". — pp. 66–67 [PDF 91–92]
  3. The copies are reliable because monks recopied the original about once a century, and all copies are identical. — p. 68 [PDF 93]
  4. Affagart's account means the chronology "must be modified": Selim may have seized it later, or Sulayman the Magnificent may have taken it, which is "perfectly plausible" given his good relations with the French and Protestant princes. — p. 69 [PDF 94]
  5. Selim I "would have taken the Covenant ... to the Treasury at Topkapi Palace"; its rediscovery "would mark a monumental event in Islamic history, reconfirming ... the historicity of the Prophet". — p. 69 [PDF 94]
  6. Ibn Sa'd's shorter text does not prove a forgery, since it is a secondary citation; the 6 AH treaty reaffirmed the 2 AH covenant. — pp. 69–70 [PDF 94–95]
  7. Muhammad "appears to have visited the Monastery prior to receiving his first revelation"; "it seems virtually certain that the Prophet provided the monks with a treaty". — p. 70 [PDF 95]
  8. "If the monks of Mount Sinai perpetrated a fraud, it would be one of the best held secrets in history." — p. 70 [PDF 95]
  9. If Moritz rejects the tax exemption, he should also reject Napoleon's decree. — p. 70 [PDF 95]
  10. "To summarily dismiss one thousand years of scholarly consensus ... may ... be the product of some political and ideological prejudice." — p. 71 [PDF 96]
  11. The Covenant "brought Sunnis and Shi'ites together". — p. 72 [PDF 97]
  12. Champdor's admission is "a rare moment of objectivity in the history of Western Orientalism"; the covenant is "the antithesis of the discriminatory demands of the so-called Pact of 'Umar". — p. 73 [PDF 98]
  13. A palm-print representing the five members of the Holy Household (and fourteen infallibles) "would certainly support the Shi'ite claim" to 'Ali's succession; this "may explain the suppressed history of Shi'ism in Egypt". — p. 74 [PDF 99]
  14. Sinai Bedouins were "followers of 'Ali", which may be why later dynasties portrayed them badly ("wrong kind of Muslims"); this "may also explain why the Covenant ... eventually went missing from the Treasury in Istanbul", possibly destroyed by enemies of ahl al-bayt. — p. 74 [PDF 99]
  15. "If there are many versions of an event, it suggests that an event took place"; historians should not question a renowned document "by mere hypothesis"; "there is no ijtihad ... against the text". — p. 76 [PDF 101]
  16. "The onus of proof is on the accuser and, so far, no serious repudiation of the Covenant has ever been formulated." — p. 76 [PDF 101]
  17. "The text must take precedence over oral tradition." — p. 76 [PDF 101]
  18. The Wahhabi/Salafi isnad argument is "utter absurdity"; "Any 'alim ... worth the turban on his head can easily forge an isnad". — p. 77 [PDF 102]
  19. Muslims should use all sources, including Christian ones; the Muqawqis letter (found 1850) is accepted, so older covenants (1630, 878/879, 1538, 750–754) deserve "the same, if not greater, acclaim". — p. 78 [PDF 103]
  20. Moritz was not "an objective, impartial, man"; "his scholarship can be dismissed precisely as that: propaganda"; "Of course he dismissed the Covenant ... It was against German imperial interests for Muslims to treat the People of the Book with tolerance." — pp. 79–80 [PDF 104–105]
  21. The British spread Wahhabism and Salafism, and the US inherited the Salafi movement. — pp. 79–80 [PDF 104–105]
  22. Moritz's "no demands" claim "is as clear as clouds"; the Prophet "catered to the specific conditions of particular communities". — pp. 80–81 [PDF 105–106]
  23. Ratliff "fail[s] to follow the scientific method"; the Prophet's authorship "is apparently unpalatable to Ratliff". — p. 81 [PDF 106]
  24. Orientalists like Ratliff and Mouton "merely ingest them, digest them, and redeliver them". — p. 82 [PDF 107]
  25. Burckhardt's claim is "manifestly untrue"; his conversion was "In all likelihood" pretended. — p. 82 [PDF 107]
  26. Witnesses, dates and the scribe's name were probably added later "to meet the scholarly demands of the day and to silence doubters"; this is an honest scholarly practice, not fraud. — pp. 83, 85 [PDF 108, 110]
  27. The hijri date can be defended because 'Ali, who conceived the calendar, was the scribe; and some say the Prophet himself used it from 2 AH. — p. 84 [PDF 109]
  28. Mouton "operates in a world of groundless assumptions and conjectures"; "Having carefully compared both documents, I can confirm that no 'cut and paste' job ever took place." — p. 86 [PDF 111]
  29. The eagle may have marked Muhammad as the Paraclete foretold by St. John, and the "Banner of the Eagle" may allude to his "divine appointment at Mount Sinai" ("only God and the Prophet could say"). — p. 87 [PDF 112]
  30. The Latin legends (c. 850) "may actually serve to corroborate the true, traditional, account"; the Bahira legend's Sinai link suggests its Christian forgers knew of Muhammad's visit to the monastery. — p. 88 [PDF 113]
  31. Muslim tolerance of pilgrims during the Crusades shows obedience "to commands of a higher order". — p. 89 [PDF 114]
  32. Commentary themes: the covenant rejects "classism, elitism, and racism"; the Prophet was "not a centrist but rather a federalist" ("Islamic Federalism"); freedom of movement; protection of places of worship; non-Muslims "taxed far less than Muslims"; "True Islam is actually tolerant to the extreme"; Islam protects itself "from the cancerous spread of secularism, liberalism, and materialism"; "It is only through a righteous Islamic Republic that Muslims can reach their highest potential". — pp. 89–95 [PDF 114–120]
  33. The protection "was contingent upon the Christians upholding their side of the bargain"; aiding Crusaders, colonizers or "American imperialists" would annul it for them; yet it is not currently void, and remains "a model for relations between Muslims and Christians". — pp. 95–96 [PDF 120–121]
  34. The library at Mount Sinai "is precisely the place where one would expect to find a priceless document like the Patent". — p. 96 [PDF 121]
  35. With a document, "authority, or lack thereof, must be exclusively determined on the basis of content analysis", and "the covenant has passed the test". — p. 98 [PDF 123]
  36. The establishment of the State of Israel "ruined a millennium and a half of conviviality"; Western colonialism and missionary campaigns explain Muslim suspicion of Christians. — p. 92 [PDF 117]

7. Internal inconsistencies within this section (only what is in the text)

  1. CE equivalent of the Covenant's date. The author gives 3 Muharram 2 AH as "July 7th, 623" (p. 83 [PDF 108]); Hobbs gives "623 CE" (p. 76 [PDF 101]). The Monastery statement says "the second year of the Hegira, corresponding to AD 626" (p. 96 [PDF 121]). The monks' delegation is "625 CE ... the second to third year of the hijrah" (p. 70 [PDF 95]).
  2. Date of Napoleon's decree. Tomadakis (quoted): "8 December, 1798"; the author on the same page: "the decree issued by Napoleon on 19 December 1798". — p. 70 [PDF 95]
  3. Reign of al-Hakim. Author: "(r. 996-1021 CE)"; Skrobucha's quotation: "(AD 996-1020)". — p. 79 [PDF 104]
  4. Reign of al-Mu'tamid. "the nominal Caliph 878-885 CE" vs "(r. 877; 878-879 CE)", same page. — p. 86 [PDF 111]
  5. End of Ottoman confirmations. "Ottomans (1517-1805 CE)" (p. 70); Ottoman decrees "from 1519 to 1818/19 CE" (p. 71); latest edict "issued by Ottoman Sunni scholars in 1888" (p. 71); Griffith: confirmed "to the time of Sultan Abdul Hamid II in 1904" (p. 98).
  6. Fatimid decree of 1134. Skrobucha's "firman of 1134" and the author's "In 1134 CE ... al-Hafiz" (p. 79) are not in the list of Fatimid decree years (975, 1109, 1110, 1135, 1154, 1156) on p. 71.
  7. Is the display copy dated? p. 68: Burckhardt's copy was "in all probability ... the one dated from 1800/01 CE"; the table (p. 65) shows a roll dated 1215 AH / 1800-01 CE. But p. 97 says the display copy "is not dated" and only "appears ... to date from 1800/01 CE".
  8. Where Burckhardt saw the copy. The author says Burckhardt "visited the monastery in 1816" and examined "the copy ... on display" (p. 68). Burckhardt's own quoted words say the certified copy he saw "is kept in the Sinai convent at Cairo" (p. 81).
  9. Fate of the original. p. 69: it may "remain stored in some forgotten archive, perhaps in the Palace of Topkapi"; the search "must start at the Topkapi Museum". p. 74: it "eventually went missing from the Treasury in Istanbul", possibly destroyed. p. 77: "The original copy ... was lost." p. 98: the author questions the note's word "lost": "Was it not simply taken by the Sultan as opposed to lost?"
  10. Which Sultan sealed the display copy. p. 97: the note "confirms that the first official copy, provided by Selim I ... in 1517 CE, was sealed with his signature". p. 98: "Since the name of the Sultan is not stipulated, it is unclear if it refers to Selim I or the Sultan who reigned when this copy, dating from the 1800s was made."
  11. Handprint unanimity. p. 75: the handprint is "attested to in all of the ancient sources", with Van Egmont & Heyman's fingerprint the "sole exception". But Skrobucha (p. 78) says "signed by him with two fingers of his hand". Digbassanis (p. 74) says the palm imprint appears in "Some of the later copies", while the Monastery statement (p. 96) says Selim's certified copies "each" depict the handprint.
  12. Writing material. The note and the author's Arabic version say leather (jild) "from Ta'if" (p. 97). Affagart says "a piece of paper" (p. 68); M.L.M.D.C. (p. 75), Burckhardt (p. 81) and Griffith (p. 97) say "parchment"; Stanley says "the skin of a gazelle" (p. 76). The author's own durability argument on p. 67 discusses paper and parchment.
  13. Witnesses: genuine or later additions? The author calls the document "witnessed by other Companions" (p. 77) and argues Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Darda' could really have been witnesses (pp. 82–83). He also says witnesses "may have been added after the fact" (p. 83), that "In all probability ... both the dates, the name of the scribe, and those of the witnesses were added at a later time" (p. 85), and that the list was attached "no earlier than" 'Umar II (p. 86).
  14. Scribe's name: fact or later addition? 'Ali as scribe is stated as fact (pp. 68, 70, 97: "it is accurate that 'Ali acted as the Prophet's scribe"), yet p. 85 says "the name of the scribe" was "In all probability" added later.
  15. Date: confirmed or added later? The 2 AH date is "consistent with the chronicles" (p. 65) and "the Covenant's date is confirmed by Islamic sources as well as the chronicles" (p. 80). Yet "the dates ... were added at a later time" (p. 85) and "the year of composition may be a later addition" (p. 97).
  16. Dating the witness list. p. 85: 'Ali was added to the "rightly-guided" Caliphs only "during the time of Imam Ahmad ibn al-Hanbal (780-855 CE) two centuries after his rule"; that is the basis for calling the order suspicious. p. 86 then concludes the list was attached "no earlier than the rule of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (r. 717 to 720 CE)", which is earlier than Ibn Hanbal's time.
  17. Stable vs conflicting accounts. The Conclusions cite "the remarkable stability of the account of his contact with the Monastery" (p. 98). Earlier the author called Hobbs's "There are conflicting accounts" "a sound historical assessment" (p. 75) and spoke of "various conflicting versions" that "differ in details and dates" (p. 76).
  18. "All" versions include the eagle. p. 87: "According to all of the various versions which narrate the pilgrimage of Muhammad to Mount Sinai, an auspicious eagle appeared". Among the versions quoted in this chapter, only Stanley's (p. 76) mentions the eagle; Affagart (p. 68), M.L.M.D.C. (p. 75), Hobbs (pp. 70, 75), Burckhardt (p. 81) and the Monastery statement (p. 96) do not.
  19. Islamic sources on the Sinai contact. p. 69: "a copy of a treaty with the Monastery of Saint Catherine does indeed exist in Islamic sources" (Ibn Sa'd). p. 77: it is "found in partial form in classical Islamic historical literature". p. 80: the date is "confirmed by Islamic sources". p. 87: "The story of Muhammad at Mount Sinai does not exist in any of the surviving Arabic and Islamic sources." (Treaty and story may be different things, but the statements pull against each other.)
  20. Item numbering in the Commentary. p. 91: "The fifth item promised by the Prophet was freedom of movement". p. 92: "Expanding upon the fifth item, the Prophet addresses the issue of taxation, for a second time, in item eight", and successors might read "item five" as granting tax-free status only to the monks.
  21. "Over a century and a half of European Christian domination." The periods the author gives on the same page, French 1798–1801 and British 1882–1952, add up to about 73 years. — p. 70 [PDF 95]
  22. Recipients: specific monastery or all Christians? p. 80: "the Prophet made a treaty with a specific monastery out of gratitude for their kindness. Nowhere else is this the case." p. 81: a forger "would have had the common sense to include direct references to themselves" (implying the text lacks them). p. 82: the principles "applied not only to the monks of Mount Sinai, but to Christians around the world". p. 93: the first eleven items "applied specifically to the monks of Mount Sinai".
  23. Age of the oldest copies. pp. 66 and 68: the oldest copies at the monastery date from Sulayman's reign (16th c.). p. 89 lists covenants "copied in 1630, 1561, 1538 or at some point in the 10th century CE", and in the same paragraph says "the oldest extant copies date from the 9th, 16th, and 17th centuries" (10th vs 9th century in one paragraph; this refers to the covenants as a group).
  24. "Every authority has accepted 1517." p. 68 says so (citing Ratliff), but p. 73 reports "some scholars still suggest that the Covenant ... dates to 1517 CE", i.e. composed then, and Atiya frames the 1517 removal as "The story is circulated" (p. 74).
  25. Anachronism inside a quoted source. Hobbs's quotation (p. 75) says the mosque, built "around 1106", may have been "a device to ward off an attack by Ottoman troops"; everywhere else in the chapter the Ottomans arrive in 1517.
  26. Poll-tax amounts. Item twelve fixes the maximum at "twelve drachms" (p. 94). The author's economic note that follows asks "What exactly did ten dirhams represent in the time of the Prophet?" (p. 94). Ten vs twelve is not reconciled.
  27. Citation and spelling variants: "Bernard Moritz" (p. 78) vs "Bernhard Moritz" (p. 79); "Ratfliff" (p. 68) vs "Ratliff" (pp. 81, etc.); "Lammers 204" (p. 85) vs "Lammens" elsewhere; Stanley cited "(344-344)" (p. 67) vs "(344-345)" (p. 76); "John Lewis Burckhardt" (p. 68) vs "Johann Ludwig Burckhardt" (p. 81) (the book itself notes "Known also as John Lewis or Jean Louis", p. 82); "Moritz, 190: 91 & 96" (p. 66; probably 1918, OCR or misprint).
  28. Burckhardt's age. "(1784-1817 CE)" (p. 81) and "buried ... at the age of 32" (p. 82). These are consistent only if he died before his birthday in 1817; this is noted only for the checkers, since the book gives no birth or death day.

Book extraction

Chapters 3–4: Persia and Najran (pp. 99–138)

236 table rows · source file 04_ch3_ch4.md

Extraction: Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013)

Chapter 3 "The Prophet Muhammad and the Christians of Persia" (pp. 99–108) and Chapter 4 "The Prophet Muhammad and the Christians of Najran" (pp. 109–138)

Source file: book/chunks/04_ch3_ch4.txt (PDF pp. 124–163), read in full (lines 1–3918).

Conventions

  • Citations are p. M [PDF N].
  • Basis tags: [F] = the author states it as fact; [A: …] = attributed to a source, as the book cites it; [T] = tradition / the covenant's own text; [O] = the author's inference or opinion.
  • Quoted text is reproduced as printed, OCR spellings included. "(OCR)" marks an obvious OCR reading.
  • The OCR text of the two-column pages is sometimes out of order (for example, on p. 99 column 2 comes before column 1). I re-sequenced it by sense. Page assignments are unaffected, because each page marker covers both columns.
  • p. 111 [PDF 136] carries "[3 illustrations on this page]", captioned "The Fatwa of Husayn ibn 'AH [=‘Ali], the Sharif of Mecca, Commanding Muslims to Protect the Armenian Christians". The Arabic text of the fatwa came through as unreadable garbled characters (file lines ~1116–1271). It may contain a date, names or signatures that cannot be read from the OCR.
  • The text of neither covenant is reproduced in these chapters. Ch. 3 says the Persia covenant is "included in this work" (p. 99), presumably elsewhere in the book. Ch. 4 quotes long excerpts of the Najran covenant but gives no witness list.

1. Section summary

Chapter 3: Christians of Persia
  1. Morrow introduces the "Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of Persia". It is a Persian-language covenant that "survives only in English translation" and is strikingly similar to the Sinai covenant; some scholars call it a Persian translation of that document (p. 99).
  2. He gives three possibilities: a very free translation of the Arabic, Shi'ite tampering, or (in his words "far-fetched as it may seem") the Arabic Sinai covenant being a translation from a Persian original (p. 99).
  3. His main source is Leon Arpee (1877–1947), who in 1946 reported that the document "was preserved in the archives of the Armenian Bishop of New Julfa", had been granted to the bishop in the 17th century by the Shah (identified as Abbas I), and was rendered "from the version of Johanianz (New Julfa, 1881)" (pp. 99, 102).
  4. He sets the covenant against Shah Abbas's 1606 relocation of Armenians to New Julfa (Isfahan) and Safavid diplomacy with Europe. He considers how the Shah might have obtained a copy: from Armenians, Christian monks, envoys such as the Maronite Petrus de Monte (1516), Father Scaliger (1628–1629), or Twelver scholars from Jabal 'Amil (pp. 99–102).
  5. He answers Seta B. Dadoyan, who calls Arpee's claim "highly dubious" and says no such document exists in the cited book or the New Julfa archives. He argues that Arpee had no motive or ability to forge it, that a referencing error is possible, and that the New Julfa library had been "robbed" (pp. 102–103).
  6. He relays Arpee's report that Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (8th century) authenticated the text against the original "in his own hand". He calls this "probably the single most important endorsement any covenant of the Prophet can receive" and says it would make the Persian version the original (p. 103).
  7. The commentary covers: Christians as believers; Muslims' duty to protect Christians even outside Muslim lands; a tax of four dirhams per adult male (no more than twelve for the wealthy); the ruler called "Imam" rather than "Sultan"; marriage "permanently or only for a time" (which he takes as mut'ah, with an extended defence of mut'ah); Christians' obligations; and 'Alid formulae (pp. 104–107).
  8. He notes that the covenant is dated to the fourth year of the hijrah, a date he thinks a scribe probably added (p. 107).
  9. Conclusion: authenticity "cannot be established" (Dadoyan), but in Morrow's view "neither can it be disproved". The document seems to have gone missing, and Dadoyan's remarks on the Tanzimat (1839, 1856) are presented as evidence of legal continuity (pp. 107–108).
Chapter 4: Christians of Najran
  1. The chapter opens with Archbishop Addai Scher's verdict (282/602) that the covenant is "certainly apocryphal" and was forged by Christians. The covenant came to light in Scher's Arabic/French Histoire nestorienne inédite: Chronique de Seert, published posthumously in Patrologia Orientalis five years after his death at the hands of the Young Turks (p. 109).
  2. According to the Chronicle, the copy was made from a document found in 265 AH (878/879 CE) with Habib the Monk in Birmantha. Habib said it came from an original in the Library of Philosophy, written on yellowed cow-hide and bearing the Prophet's seal (p. 109).
  3. Morrow rebuts Scher point by point. He then digresses at length on the Young Turks (1906 party, 1908 coup, 1915 Assyrian massacres, "1916" republic, 1922 abolition of the Caliphate), the Armenian massacres, and Western or German sponsorship of extremism (pp. 109–112).
  4. He names the "strongest argument" against authenticity: the covenant's absence from surviving classical Islamic sources. Against it he sets the Prophet's many contacts with Najran: a delegation in Mecca before 621 CE, a delegation in 630 CE/8 AH, the mubahalah, a 9 AH treaty, and a 10 AH "Treaty of Najran" (witnesses named) quoted from Qureshi (pp. 112–114).
  5. He disputes Hitti's claim that 'Umar expelled the Najran Christians, citing evidence of Christians there into the late 9th, 10th and 13th centuries (p. 114).
  6. On the witness list (thirty-two Companions on p. 115, thirty on p. 138), he answers critics' objections about Abu Hurayrah, Mu'awiyah, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. Using Shaykh al-Mufid's account (quoted at length), he dates the covenant to "the last year of the Prophet's life", since Fatimah would have been too young earlier (pp. 115–118).
  7. He rejects other critics: Claude Cahen ("pious fraud of Nestorian monks of the 9th century"), Vrej Nersessian, Brandie Ratliff, Louis Massignon and Barbara Roggema. He explains textual variants as different readings of unpointed early Arabic script, using the two versions of the Treaty of Maqnah (Ibn Sa'd and Baladhuri) as an example (pp. 119–121).
  8. The commentary (pp. 121–138) covers several topics:
    • the exordium and the covenant proper;
    • the Prophet's literacy, argued at length;
    • the hostility of the Jews of Medina versus Christian loyalty, with digressions on anti-Semitism, Jewish converts, Donner's "Believers" movement, and the names and numbers of the Najran delegation;
    • taxes: four dirhams, a twelve-dirham maximum, clerics exempt, and Thevenot's Ottoman evidence;
    • exemption from military service, freedom of religion, consent in marriage, and Muslim help in repairing churches;
    • the ban on using Christians as spies;
    • Christians' obligations, including three days' hospitality.
  9. Conclusion: the covenant is "a historical find of momentous importance". It was first published in 1919 and reprinted by Hamidullah (1956) and 'Amarah (2002), but remains little known (p. 138).
