4. Factual claims (non-date)

CHAPTER 3: Persia

A. Framing and the covenant's textual status

  • C3-1. Only "a small number of scholars and educated readers" know of the covenants with St Catherine's and Najran; "far fewer" know those with the Armenian Christians, "the foremost of which is the Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of Persia". p. 99 [PDF 124] [O/F]
  • C3-2. The Persia covenant is "strikingly similar" to the Sinai covenant, "so much so that some scholars assert it to be a Persian translation of the same". p. 99 [PDF 124] [A: unnamed "some scholars"]
  • C3-3. "This Persian-language covenant ... survives only in English translation" and contains components not found in the Arabic covenant it is said to derive from. p. 99 [PDF 124] [F]
  • C3-4. Three possibilities: (1) a very free translation of the Arabic; (2) tampering by Shi'ite scholars; (3) "as far-fetched as it may seem", the Arabic Sinai covenant is a translation from the Persian original. p. 99 [PDF 124] [O]
  • C3-5. Morrow says that his "intimate knowledge" of the Sinai covenant allows him to "confirm that the Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of Persia is not a complete and accurate translation of the former document". p. 99 [PDF 124] [O/F]
  • C3-6. The Persia covenant "was supposedly written in Persian". p. 102 [PDF 127] [A: implied tradition]

B. Arpee's account

  • C3-7. Arpee: the covenant "reproduces a charter, purporting to be ... originally granted by Mohammed ... to the Monastery of St. Catherine, at Mount Sinai, and intended by the Prophet to be valid for Christians everywhere" (355). pp. 99 [PDF 124] [A: Arpee 355]
  • C3-8. Arpee: "New Julfa ... was the seat of a Bishop recognized as the spiritual head of all the Armenians of Persia, India and Java, and holding a charter after the Prophet's reputed original defining the rights and obligations of a Christian community under Shiite law" (235). p. 99 [PDF 124] [A: Arpee 235]
  • C3-9. "To all evidence, Arpee was operating on assumptions." p. 99 [PDF 124] [O]
  • C3-10. Arpee claims to have taken the covenant from the History of New Julfa at Isfahan. p. 102 [PDF 127] [A: Arpee, as reported by Dadoyan]
  • C3-11. "Having read Arpee's works, he comes across as a serious historian and his own works are often cited by specialists in the field." p. 103 [PDF 128] [O]
  • C3-12. Arpee "did not have sufficient linguistic proficiency as to replicate a 17th-century Persian edict nor ... enough knowledge of Shi'ism to produce a convincing product", and "had nothing to gain". p. 103 [PDF 128] [O]
  • C3-13. Possible error: "It is possible that Arpee, a typist, an editor, or a printer made a mistake in referencing the Covenant." p. 103 [PDF 128] [O]
  • C3-14. "Many archives contain works in their collections that are not listed in their catalogue." p. 103 [PDF 128] [F/O]

C. Dadoyan's critique as presented

  • C3-15. Dadoyan on Arpee's view: "the Safavid Shah Abbas made a Medinan-style commitment to the Armenians", an agreement "ratified by a copy of an old Medinan oath allegedly given to the Syrian Christians" (60–61). p. 100 [PDF 125] [A: Dadoyan 60–61]
  • C3-16. Dadoyan: Arpee's claim is "highly dubious yet intriguing" (60). p. 102 [PDF 127] [A: Dadoyan 60]
  • C3-17. Dadoyan: "[n]o such document exists in this book, and no record exists of any such document in the archives of the Prelacy of New Julfa" (64, note 56); "[n]o documents that he refers to are found in the archives of the Armenian Bishopric of New Julfa" (61). p. 102 [PDF 127] [A: Dadoyan]
  • C3-18. Morrow: Dadoyan's allegations "seem absolute and factually-based" but "are seen to be grounded on assumptions". p. 102 [PDF 127] [O]
  • C3-19. Dadoyan: authenticity "cannot be established" (61). Morrow: "neither can it be disproved". p. 107 [PDF 132] [A: Dadoyan 61] / [O]
  • C3-20. Dadoyan "admits that 'the history of New Julfa in an Islamic state somehow proves this extravagant hypothesis'" (61). p. 107 [PDF 132] [A: Dadoyan 61]
  • C3-21. "As Dadoyan intimates, the Covenant ... must have existed at some point." pp. 107–108 [PDF 132–133] [A/O]

D. New Julfa, the Armenians and Safavid policy

  • C3-22. Abbas built the Armenians of New Julfa a new cathedral, granted religious liberties, offered interest-free loans and allowed them to elect their own mayor. p. 99 [PDF 124] [F]
  • C3-23. Van Gorder: "It is probable that Safavids treated Armenians better than Ottomans [did] and were thus seen as allies, if not liberators" (63). pp. 99–100 [PDF 124–125] [A: Van Gorder 63]
  • C3-24. "In the view of Persian Jews, 'Christians—especially the Armenians—lived in comfort'" under Shah Abbas (Levy 265). p. 100 [PDF 125] [A: Levy 265]
  • C3-25. Bournoutian (209), block quote: Persian masons and Armenian craftsmen built the settlement. Of its many churches, "thirteen of which survive today". Armenians "elected their own mayor ... rang church bells, had public religious processions, established their own courts, and had no restrictions on clothing or the production of wine. No Muslims could reside in New Julfa." The mayor "was given one of the shah's royal seals" and "had jurisdiction over the two-dozen Armenian villages around Isfahan". p. 100 [PDF 125] [A: Bournoutian 209]
  • C3-26. The Armenians of Julfa and New Julfa "controlled an extensive international trading network" with contacts in Europe, including France (Bournoutian 209). p. 100 [PDF 125] [A]
  • C3-27. "most Western diplomats, visitors, and merchants who visited Persia were housed in New Julfa" (209). p. 100 [PDF 125] [A: Bournoutian 209]
  • C3-28. Shah 'Abbas "was greeted as a liberator by both the Christians and the Shi'ites of Nakhichevan province" (208). p. 102 [PDF 127] [A: Bournoutian 208]
  • C3-29. "a certain Shi'ite-Christian solidarity seems to have existed under Ottoman rule." p. 102 [PDF 127] [O]
  • C3-30. Abbas the Great's tolerance of Christians "formed part of his policy of establishing ties with European powers in order to combat the Ottomans". p. 101 [PDF 126] [O/F]
  • C3-31. The Ottomans were doing "the very same with the French": "Both Sunnis and Shi'ites were brandishing copies of the Covenant of the Prophet to win the sympathy and support of antagonistic Western Christian powers." p. 101 [PDF 126] [O]
  • C3-32. Spanish Christians "may have reciprocated by supporting the spread of Shi'ism among the North African Moriscos in an attempt to destabilize the Ottomans who ruled there" (Cutillas Ferrer 49–64). p. 101 [PDF 126] [A]
  • C3-33. "If Shi'ite clerics ruled at home, 'Abbas the Great employed Christians to represent him abroad." p. 101 [PDF 126] [F/O]
  • C3-34. Shah 'Abbas received delegations from Spain and Portugal (Jurdi Abisaad 80). p. 101 [PDF 126] [A]
  • C3-35. Levy: Persia had become a "circus of European spies" (259); "It was not long ... before European spies and agitators disguised as merchants, travelers, painters, artists, ambassadors, princes, advisors, representatives, functionaries, missionaries, and teachers descended upon Iran" (263). p. 101 [PDF 126] [A: Levy]
  • C3-36. Shah 'Abbas "imposed Shi'ism as the official religion of his empire" (in the course of a hypothesis that he "Shi'itized" the covenant). p. 102 [PDF 127] [F, embedded in hypothesis]

E. How the Shah could have obtained the covenant

  • C3-37. "How and where the Shah obtained this covenant is unclear." p. 100 [PDF 125] [O]
  • C3-38. "Although I have access to virtually every Shi'ite source in existence, I failed to locate the Covenant ... with the Monks of Mount Sinai in any of them." It "may also have existed in a Shi'ite work which is no longer extant". It "is not found in any Sunni sources either". p. 100 [PDF 125] [F/O]
  • C3-39. That leaves the Christian community as the source: either another Christian community in the empire or the Arabic-speaking world, "most likely the Monastery of Saint Catherine". p. 100 [PDF 125] [O]
  • C3-40. Four possibilities: (1) the Armenians of Julfa gave Shah Abbas a copy to dissuade him from uprooting them; (2) Armenians seeking refuge presented a copy to gain refugee status; (3) the Safavids got a copy from Christian monks; (4) they got it from Arab Shi'ite scholars of the Levant who moved to Persia "in masse" under Shah Abbas. p. 100 [PDF 125] [O]
  • C3-41. The Armenians may have received a covenant from the Prophet and passed it down until the 20th century, or held a copy of the Sinai covenant, "addressed to 'the Christians of the world'". p. 100 [PDF 125] [O]
  • C3-42. Isma'il received many ambassadors, including Petrus de Monte (Maronite, Mount Lebanon, ambassador from Louis II of Hungary, 1516), and an envoy from Charles V. p. 100 [PDF 125] [F]
  • C3-43. "The Maronite monk, in particular, stands out as a prime suspect." p. 101 [PDF 126] [O]
  • C3-44. Petrus del Monte came from Mount Lebanon, "the very same region where Father Scaliger was given a copy of the Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World by Arab Capuchin monks". p. 101 [PDF 126] [F/O]
  • C3-45. "Still, Mount Carmel stands out as a source of diffusion." p. 101 [PDF 126] [O]
  • C3-46. The Christian denominations "operated large diplomatic networks and were represented in most Muslims governments". p. 101 [PDF 126] [F]
  • C3-47. Since the Capuchins operated openly, "the possibility that they were perpetrating a fraud ... seems slim". p. 101 [PDF 126] [O]
  • C3-48. "If anything, Abbas the Great appears to have obtained the covenant from Safavid state archives." p. 101 [PDF 126] [O]
  • C3-49. A copy may have come with the Twelver scholars. If it is not in surviving Shi'ite sources, that may be because Jamal Pasha burned the Jabal 'Amil books. p. 101 [PDF 126] [O + A: Jurdi Abisaad 218 n.12]
  • C3-50. If authenticated by Ja'far al-Sadiq and containing Shi'ite elements, it may have been brought by Twelver scholars rather than monks. The 'Amili scholars may themselves have got copies from Christian clerics. p. 102 [PDF 127] [O]
  • C3-51. "remote possibility" that the covenant belonged to the Shi'ite Muslims of Julfa. p. 102 [PDF 127] [O]

F. Arabic, Turkish and Persian versions

  • C3-52. "some of the Arabic versions of the Covenant ... with the Monks of Mount Sinai are actually translations of the Turkish copies". p. 102 [PDF 127] [F]
  • C3-53. Anton E [as printed; possibly OCR for an initial "F."] Haddad's Oath of the Prophet Mohammed is an English translation of an Arabic translation by Naufal Effendi Naufal, "a Christian from Tripoli, Syria". That Arabic translation, in Naufal's book Sunnajat al-tarab, "was based on a Turkish copy". p. 102 [PDF 127] [F]
  • C3-54. "The Arabic versions of the Covenant of the Prophet also contain many mistakes." p. 102 [PDF 127] [F]
  • C3-55. Hypothesis: the Arabic original was translated into Turkish or Persian and then lost, and some surviving Arabic versions are poor retranslations; or the mistakes are "the errors of non-Arab scribes". p. 102 [PDF 127] [O]
  • C3-56. Hypothesis: "the original Covenant of the Prophet was written in Persian, and the mistakes found in the Arabic are the result of a poor translation." p. 102 [PDF 127] [O]
  • C3-57. "evidence of Umayyad tampering appears evident in many covenants, at least where the list of witnesses are concerned." p. 102 [PDF 127] [O]
  • C3-58. "Why is Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan, a die-hard enemy of Islam, listed as the scribe of the Prophet on documents which date prior to his professed conversion?" p. 102 [PDF 127] [F (listing) / O]

G. Arpee and Vartabed on early authentication

  • C3-59. Arpee: "Ja'far, sixth Shi'ite Imam (8th century), testifies to its authenticity after comparing the text with the original in his own hand" (355). p. 103 [PDF 128] [A: Arpee 355]
  • C3-60. For Shi'ites, Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is "an infallible, divinely-guided and inspired Imam, and the rightful successor of the Prophet". The copy passed down to him came through Imam Muhammad al-Baqir, Imam 'Ali Zayn al-'Abidin, Imam Husayn, Imam Hasan, Imam 'Ali and the Prophet. p. 103 [PDF 128] [F re Shi'ite belief / O]
  • C3-61. Giragos Vartabed: Catholicos John of Otzun's threefold petition granted by the Caliph (identified with Hisham) (Arpee 355). p. 103 [PDF 128] [A]
  • C3-62. Arpee: Omar II, Hisham, John of Otzun and "the Imam Mohammed Jafar" "were all contemporaries" (355). p. 103 [PDF 128] [A]
  • C3-63. The Prophet "was actually preparing the ground for the future conquest of Persia by aligning the oppressed Christians with the Muslims against the pagan oppressors." p. 103 [PDF 128] [O]

H. Content of the Persia covenant (as quoted or paraphrased)

  • C3-64. Opening: "By the will of God! In the name of God Merciful!" p. 104 [PDF 129] [T]
  • C3-65. It begins with the obligation of obedience imposed on "all Christian nations ... throughout the world" who live in eastern Arabia and Persia, whether or not in contact with Muslims. Unlike some other covenants, it states Christians' obligations first. p. 104 [PDF 129] [T/F]
  • C3-66. "it behooves all Moslems also to observe its provisions." Whoever obeys it "had perfect faith"; whoever corrupts or annuls it is punishable regardless of religion, status or rank. p. 104 [PDF 129] [T]
  • C3-67. The covenant's words are divinely inspired; no past prophet nor "angels standing nigh" was burdened with its like; "[t]he words... of this covenant... must be obeyed". p. 104 [PDF 129] [T]
  • C3-68. Moses' covenant "applied to the Children of Israel"; he "was not burdened with the obligation of protecting the members of other religious communities". p. 104 [PDF 129] [O]
  • C3-69. "All pious believers ... shall deem it their bounden duty to defend believers and to aid them wheresoever they may be, whether far or near." p. 104 [PDF 129] [T]
  • C3-70. Treating Christians as muminin is "consistent with the Constitution of Medina" and "a sure sign of the antiquity" of the covenant. p. 104 [PDF 129] [O]
  • C3-71. The duty to defend Christians extends beyond dar al-islam into Christendom (churches, monasteries, monks, priests). p. 104 [PDF 129] [T/O]
  • C3-72. Hamidullah: "A document of the time of the Umayyad caliph 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (reported by Ibn Sa'd), says, that the payment of the ransoms by the Muslim government includes liberating even the non-Muslim subjects who ... have been made prisoners by the enemy" (Introduction 127). p. 104 [PDF 129] [A]
  • C3-73. The Umayyads were "the greatest liars in the history of Islam"; 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz was "the only righteous ruler the Umayyads ever produced". p. 104 [PDF 129] [O]
  • C3-74. "According to traditional Islamic political theory, a citizen is a citizen, regardless of religion." p. 104 [PDF 129] [F/O]
  • C3-75. Muslims are to care for Christians "to the same extent that they honor and respect the Prophet himself"; Christians are to be taxed fairly. p. 104 [PDF 129] [T/O]
  • C3-76. Block quote: building enterprises not interfered with; priests not molested; no persecution; worship according to their rites; churches not dismantled; homes and mansions not confiscated "for mosques or residences, without their consent". Violators are "a despiser of this Compact, and a gainsayer of the word of God and of his Prophet". p. 105 [PDF 130] [T]
  • C3-77. Tax: "four dirhams per adult male", payable in cash or goods, placed in the Treasury for public use. Merchants, the wealthy, pearl divers, mine operators and large estate owners pay no more than twelve dirhams. p. 105 [PDF 130] [T]
  • C3-78. "the Prophet states that non-Christians would be taxed at four dirhams per year", so Jews, Zoroastrians, polytheists, animists and "even atheists" had the same rights. p. 105 [PDF 130] [T + O]
  • C3-79. Land taxes "apply only to sedentary populations, not to nomads." p. 105 [PDF 130] [F/T]
  • C3-80. The Persia covenant uses "Imam" for the ruler where other covenants use "Sultan". Morrow thinks "Imam" was the Prophet's original term, changed to "Sultan" "to suit Arab and Ottoman Sunni sentiment", and says "Imam", not "Sultan", is the term "employed in the Qur'an and most of the Sunnah". p. 105 [PDF 130] [F / O]
  • C3-81. Christians have no military obligations, paying "taxes in lieu of service". p. 105 [PDF 130] [T/O]
  • C3-82. "No Christians shall be brought by force to confess Islam"; "no Christians shall be tyrannized over or oppressed". Christians shall not "on their part tyrannize over Moslems or oppress them, from this time forth even until such time as God shall ordain". p. 105 [PDF 130] [T]
  • C3-83. Morrow reads this as possibly foreshadowing the final conflict of Christ's followers and Imam Muhammad al-Mahdi against the Anti-Christ. p. 105 [PDF 130] [O]
  • C3-84. "Moslems shall not take the women and maidens of the Christians by force", which Morrow says proves "categorically" that crimes against Berber women by early conquerors and slave-traders "are outlawed in Islam". p. 105 [PDF 130] [T + O]
  • C3-85. Christian women may marry Muslim men "permanently or only for a time", which refers "indubitably" to both nikah and mut'ah. p. 105 [PDF 130] [T + O]
  • C3-86. Temporary marriage "was not only permitted during the time of the Prophet but actually promoted". p. 105 [PDF 130] [O, "As all honest Muslim scholars are aware"]
  • C3-87. "none of the traditions prohibiting fixed-term marriages have sound chains of narration" (Kashif al-Ghita' 84). p. 105 [PDF 130] [A]
  • C3-88. Companions who held mut'ah permissible: "'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari, Salmah ibn al-Akwa', Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mughirah ibn Sha'hab, Sa'id ibn Jarir, and Ibn Jarih" (Kashif al-Ghita' 85). p. 106 [PDF 131] [A]
  • C3-89. "Imam 'Ali and his eleven descendants ... always insisted that mut'ah was Islamically sanctioned and pointed at Caliph 'Umar as the cause of its prohibition." The prohibiting tradition "was thus forged". p. 106 [PDF 131] [T / O]
  • C3-90. Qur'an 4:24 is quoted ("And those of whom ye seek content [istamta'tum ...] ... give unto them their portions as a duty"). Its prohibition "has no binding value as it contradicts the Qur'an". p. 106 [PDF 131] [Qur'an + O]
  • C3-91. "Even some eminent Sunni scholars, such as Zamakhshari and Hakam ibn 'Ayniyah, report that the verse of mut'ah was not abrogated" (Kashif al-Ghita' 79). p. 106 [PDF 131] [A]
  • C3-92. A Christian wife may keep her faith, so "the custom of requiring Christian women to convert, prior to marrying a Muslim man, is unfounded". Pressuring her into a "conversion of convenience" is "a serious sin". p. 106 [PDF 131] [T/O]
  • C3-93. "the Prophet mentions that the main criteria for marriage is love and that there can be no marriage for a woman who does not want it." p. 106 [PDF 131] [T]
  • C3-94. Christians may repair churches, chapels and monasteries, with Muslims free to help, and are encouraged to help Muslims in construction. p. 106 [PDF 131] [T]
  • C3-95. Unlike the Sinai covenant, where monks were not expected to act as scouts, spies or agents, "the Prophet lifts this restriction from lay Christians": "If any one of them shall be sent as an envoy to negotiate peace between Moslems and Infidels, no one shall prevent his going, and if he should prove of service to our cause, let the service be accepted." p. 106 [PDF 131] [T]
  • C3-96. Ormanian: the Caliphs "had an interest in seeing the Armenians regulate their own religious affairs in a spirit which was opposed to Greek ideas" (44). p. 107 [PDF 132] [A: Ormanian 44]
  • C3-97. Block quote of Christians' obligations: no aid to infidels; no harbouring enemies or enemy troops; no supplying "spear, arrow, sword or horse"; no acting as guides; no safekeeping enemies' possessions; no communication "except only under duress". A Muslim guest "may there be entertained three days and three nights". Christians are to "avert from Moslems the abuse and oppressions of tyrants", hide Muslims if necessary, and not betray Muslim women and children. p. 107 [PDF 132] [T]
  • C3-98. A Christian who acts contrary to the covenant "shall be accounted as annulling the same", "is loathsome to God, and the Prophet shall visit upon him his just retribution". The covenant is binding "so long as God wills". p. 107 [PDF 132] [T]
  • C3-99. 'Alid element: Muhammad's name is followed by "blessings of God rest upon him and his posterity". p. 107 [PDF 132] [T]
  • C3-100. In the witness list of the Covenant with the Assyrian Christians, 'Ali's name is followed by 'alayhi al-salam. Some early Sunni authorities occasionally used the phrase for 'Ali, but it "eventually became solely associated with Shi'ism". p. 107 [PDF 132] [F]
  • C3-101. Dadoyan: "the two rescripts of the Ottoman Tanzimat ... (1839, 1856) were not more than modernized versions of the early Islamic or Medinan system of regulating the status of non-Muslims or dhimmi subjects" (61). p. 108 [PDF 133] [A]
  • C3-102. "Tolerance of Christians who are at peace with Muslims forms an intrinsic part of the Islamic tradition." p. 108 [PDF 133] [O]
CHAPTER 4: Najran

A. Scher and the Chronicle of Seert

  • C4-1. Epigraph (Scher, 282/602): "This covenant is certainly apocryphal. It was forged by the Christians so that the Muslims would spare them. Every Christian sect in the Orient possesses a copy which is more or less different one to the other.... This one is written in a language which is unsure and incorrect." p. 109 [PDF 134] [A: Scher]
  • C4-2. The covenant is "virtually unheard of outside a small circle of mostly non-Muslim Orientalists" and "castigated by both the Orientalist who brought it to light and by the few others who are familiar with it". p. 109 [PDF 134] [O/F]
  • C4-3. It came to light in the Arabic/French Histoire nestorienne inedite: Chronique de Seert by Addai Scher, "the Assyrian Chaldean Catholic archbishop of Siirt, a city in southeastern Turkey", "published posthumously in Patrologia Orientalis, five years after his death at the hands of the Young Turks". p. 109 [PDF 134] [F]
  • C4-4. The Chronicle's provenance account (265 AH; Habib; Birmantha; Library of Philosophy; cow-hide; Prophet's seal) is set out in §2B 4.30–4.31. p. 109 [PDF 134] [A: Scher 281/601]
  • C4-5. Scher "did not advance a single argument to support his allegations and did not present a shred of proof". Qur'an 2:111 is cited: "Produce your proof if ye are truthful". p. 109 [PDF 134] [O; Qur'an]
  • C4-6. "history has shown that Muslims generally respected the rights of other religious communities"; it was not in their interest "to massacre subject populations". p. 109 [PDF 134] [O]
  • C4-7. "The covenant which is in circulation among the Greek Orthodox is identical." p. 109 [PDF 134] [F]
  • C4-8. Covenants of the communities in Najran, Iraq and Syria differ "because the Prophet made different accords with different denominations". p. 109 [PDF 134] [O]
  • C4-9. The covenants with "the monks of Mount Sinai, Najran, Assyria, Persia, Armenia, and the World" were "authored by the same individual: Muhammad". p. 110 [PDF 135] [O]
  • C4-10. "Muslims actually abide by the dictates of such covenants", a fact "Scher does not mention". p. 110 [PDF 135] [F/O]
  • C4-11. Scher "asserts that the Covenant is written in flawed Arabic, yet does not avail himself of his linguistic expertise". p. 110 [PDF 135] [O]
  • C4-12. Scher "refused to avail himself of a document that might have saved him". p. 110 [PDF 135] [O]

B. Young Turks, the Ottomans and the Armenians (digression)

  • C4-13. The Ottoman Empire, "The last Muslim Empire", collapsed through "incompetence, corruption, and ignorance". The Western world "employed ... the infamous military officers from the 'Young Turk Movement'", "Westernized atheists" forming "a Fifth Column at the core of the Caliphate". p. 110 [PDF 135] [O]
  • C4-14. The Young Turks manipulated the Sultan "like a puppet" after the 1908 coup. p. 110 [PDF 135] [F/O]
  • C4-15. "it was not the Muslims who were responsible for the crimes committed against the Assyrians and the Armenians; but the 'Young Turks' who were Westernized anti-Islamic atheists". pp. 110–111 [PDF 135–136] [O]
  • C4-16. Lewy: "[t]he Armenian community in Turkey was not simply 'an unarmed Christian minority'" (268–269). p. 111 [PDF 136] [A]
  • C4-17. "Comparing the disputed Armenian Genocide with the Jewish Holocaust is simplistic, factually inaccurate, and misleading." p. 111 [PDF 136] [O]
  • C4-18. European powers were eager to partition the Muslim world, "promising homelands for European Jews, Arabs, Kurds, Assyrians, and Armenians" (Bournoutian 301). p. 111 [PDF 136] [A]
  • C4-19. "The Turks may have committed massacres; however, there is no evidence that they intended to exterminate entire groups of people"; their plan was to relocate "potentially dangerous and disloyal Christians" (Lewy 150–161). p. 111 [PDF 136] [O + A]
  • C4-20. Vahakn N. Dadrian, German Responsibility in the Armenian Genocide: the massacres were "to a large extent, the product of German policy". p. 111 [PDF 136] [A]
  • C4-21. "the British had created, encouraged, and exploited Islamic extremism ... so had the Germans, laying the foundations of modern-day Islamic terrorism." pp. 111–112 [PDF 136–137] [O]
  • C4-22. The same methods were used "by Western powers in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Palestine, and Nigeria, as well as India, Pakistan, and Iraq". p. 112 [PDF 137] [O]
  • C4-23. "Required reading" (with page lists as printed): Mamdani, Good Muslim, Bad Muslims; Labévière [printed "Labevi&re"], Dollars for Terror; Napoleoni, Terror Incorporated; Peter Lance, 1000 Years of Revenge. p. 112 [PDF 137] [O]
  • C4-24. Illustration: "The Fatwa of Husayn ibn 'Ali, the Sharif of Mecca, Commanding Muslims to Protect the Armenian Christians" (3 illustrations; Arabic unreadable in OCR). p. 111 [PDF 136] [F]

C. Absence from classical sources; early contacts with Najran

  • C4-25. "The strongest argument that can be made against the Covenant ... resides in the fact that mention of this document appears to be completely absent in the classical Islamic sources which have survived ... It is on this basis that most scholars dismiss it." p. 112 [PDF 137] [F/A]
  • C4-26. "the Messenger of Allah met with delegations of Christians from Najran on numerous occasions." p. 112 [PDF 137] [F]
  • C4-27. Ibn Ishaq (179), block quote: "some twenty Christians" came to the Prophet in Mecca, wept on hearing the Qur'an, and accepted his call; "It is said that these Christians came from Najran, but God knows whether that was so." p. 112 [PDF 137] [A]
  • C4-28. Ibn Ishaq (271): Najran's Christians entered the mosque at the afternoon prayer "clad in Yamani garments, cloaks, and mantles, with the elegance of men of B. al-Harith b. Ka'b". The Companions "never saw their like"; "They prayed towards the east." pp. 112–113 [PDF 137–138] [A]
  • C4-29. The Prophet and the Bishop debated Christian dogma, reaching "an impasse". A revelation instructed mutual imprecation; Bishop Abu Haritha ibn 'Alqama judged cursing such figures "an act of suicide" (Mufid 118). p. 113 [PDF 138] [A]
  • C4-30. Letter to the People of Najran: "In the Name of Allah, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I invite you to worship God instead of men. If you refuse, you must pay jizyah. Otherwise, I will declare war on you. And peace be upon you" (qtd. Qureshi 54). p. 113 [PDF 138] [A]
  • C4-31. The 9 AH treaty (Qureshi 117) and the 10 AH Treaty of Najran (Qureshi 182–183): terms in §5C. p. 113–114 [PDF 138–139] [A]
  • C4-32. Qureshi: the Treaty of Najran "conferred on the non-Muslims ... autonomy, both religious and administrative". Quoting Syed Amir 'Ali: "This document ... has furnished the guiding principle to all Muslim rulers in their mode of dealing with their non-Muslim subjects ..." (183). p. 114 [PDF 139] [A]
  • C4-33. "there exists no logical reason for them to falsify a covenant which is essentially the same as the ones that were granted to them previously." p. 114 [PDF 139] [O]
  • C4-34. Despite Hitti, "the Christian community of Najran resided there for centuries after (Goddard 42-43)". p. 114 [PDF 139] [A]
  • C4-35. Hitti, "As an Arab Christian", has scholarship "noted for its subjectivity and his persistent attempt to present Muslims in a poor light"; "Jafri appears to have come to the correct conclusion". pp. 114–115 [PDF 139–140] [O]
  • C4-36. Kufah was "a stronghold of the partisans of 'Ali"; migrants "may have opted to move there feeling that their rights would be better respected". p. 114 [PDF 139] [F/O]
  • C4-37. "Still, the historicity of these documented events has been called in to question." p. 114 [PDF 139] [O]

D. The witness list and dating

  • C4-38. The Prophet's treaties, "with rare exceptions, ... were not signed by witnesses. These treaties were short dispatches." p. 115 [PDF 140] [F/O]
  • C4-39. The covenant notes "the names of thirty-two witnesses from the Companions of the Prophet", which is "anomalous". p. 115 [PDF 140] [F]
  • C4-40. "the movements of the Prophet's Companions were well-known and duly documented", so forgers would have been taking "a huge risk". p. 115 [PDF 140] [O]
  • C4-41. Critics ("Scholars who have superficially perused the Covenant") say Abu Hurayrah and Mu'awiyyah were not yet Muslims, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was dead, and Ja'far ibn Abi Talib was in exile in Ethiopia. p. 115 [PDF 140] [A: unnamed critics]
  • C4-42. The Sinai, Najran and World covenants may have been "designed to be anomalous": "long and detailed", perhaps "models for millennia to come", hence the long witness lists. p. 115 [PDF 140] [O]
  • C4-43. "As with the case of the Covenant ... with the Monks of Mount Sinai, there also exists the possibility that the chain of authorities was appended at a later date." p. 115 [PDF 140] [O]
  • C4-44. Abu Hurayrah: originally "'Abd al-Shams, the Sun-Worshipper", a Yemenite of the Banu Daws. He embraced Islam through Tufayl ibn 'Amr, his tribe's leader, who had met Muhammad in Mecca, and went with Tufayl to Mecca to meet the Prophet, who "renamed him 'Abd al-Rahman". He returned to his tribe "for several years" before migrating (628/629). He "may very well have been present" at the signing. p. 115 [PDF 140] [F/O]
  • C4-45. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh: "in medieval times, most deaths did not take place on the battlefield"; they came "weeks or months later" from infection and gangrene. The Sirah "has not accurately recorded" his death year, possibly. If the Banu Qurayzah story is false, details of his role and death "might therefore be fabrications". pp. 115–116 [PDF 140–141] [O]
  • C4-46. Mu'awiyyah, "along with his father, Abu Sufyan, ... used to regularly travel back and forth between Mecca and Medina on diplomatic missions"; he may have been asked to witness. p. 116 [PDF 141] [F/O]
  • C4-47. Abu Riyya (Light on the Muhammadan Sunnah or Defense of Hadith): there "were those who would not fabricate text of hadith, but would bring in a correct authentic chain of transmission" (144). p. 116 [PDF 141] [A]
  • C4-48. "the Umayyads and 'Abbasids opened wide the doors of innovation and creative editing and wasted no opportunity when it came to falsifying the prophetic sunnah." p. 116 [PDF 141] [O]
  • C4-49. al-Nawawi: traditions were falsified by the zanadiqah (heretics) "out of favoritism, religiosity, rebellion, bigotry, partisanship, or fanaticism, as well as a desire for fame [printed "feme"] or for monetary reward" (Abu Riyya 144). Abu Riyya adds further motives (disunity, schools or schism, neglect, pleasing the powerful, error, faulty memory, confusion, ego, popularity). p. 116 [PDF 141] [A]
  • C4-50. "some Jewish people were notorious for forging false ahadith, creating an entire genre of Israiliyyat"; Christians "played a very minor role". Christian concepts entered mostly via "misguided Sufi Muslims" (Rizvi 41). p. 116 [PDF 141] [O + A]
  • C4-51. A pre-Badr dating "makes little sense as the Prophet was still relatively unknown in Arabia". p. 116 [PDF 141] [O]
  • C4-52. Mufid, Kitab al-irshad (116–118), extended quote:
    • Abu Haritha, bishop of Najran, came "with thirty of the Christians who included the deputy (al-'aqib), the chief (al-sayyid) and 'Abd al-Masih", arriving at the afternoon prayer "wearing robes of silk and crosses".
    • The Jews and Christians traded accusations, and Q 2:113 was revealed.
    • The Prophet called the Messiah "a servant of Allah"; Q 3:61 was revealed "in Surat Al 'Imran".
    • The next morning the Prophet held 'Ali's hand, with al-Hasan and al-Husayn in front and Fatimah behind.
    • The bishop said: "if it was not for the position of Caesar (i.e. the Byzantine emperor), I would submit to him", and addressed the Prophet as "Abu al-Qasim".
    • Terms: "two thousand protective breastplates, each breastplate being forty standard dirham (in value)".
    • pp. 116–118 [PDF 141–143] [A: Mufid]
  • C4-53. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi cites the Archbishop: "O Christians! I surely see faces of men who, if they were to ask Allah to move a mountain, He would surely do it ... no Christian will remain on Earth until the Day of Resurrection". The Prophet: "had I cursed you, Allah would not have left a Christian on the fact [sic] of the earth" (qtd. Ordoni 158). p. 118 [PDF 143] [A]
  • C4-54. Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi, working "under the watchful eye of the oppressive rulers of the age", "skipped or glossed over the identification and spiritual status of the ahl al-bayt", the "Purified Five". p. 118 [PDF 143] [O]
  • C4-55. Shi'ite biographers like Mufid summarize the theological debate "which is much stressed by Ibn Ishaq (270-277)". "The debate between the Jews and Christians ... is not mentioned by Ibn Ishaq, and is shortened to two sentences by Shaykh al-Mufid"; the covenant treats it "in much greater length". p. 118 [PDF 143] [F/A]
  • C4-56. Sunni and Shi'ite writers "were all clearly relying on the same complete sources which they altered to serve their own ideological interests". p. 118 [PDF 143] [O]
  • C4-57. The Prophet's letters, treaties and covenants "grew steadily longer". Witnesses grew "exponentially over time from a couple to over thirty", which "may also be explained by the increase in the literacy rate among the Companions". p. 118 [PDF 143] [O]

E. Modern critics

  • C4-58. Claude Cahen dismissed the covenant as "a pious fraud of Nestorian monks of the 9th century" (qtd. Nercessian), an opinion "blindly accepted by Vrej Nerses Nersessian", who calls it "a patent fabrication, probably the work of some Nestorian priest or monk". p. 119 [PDF 144] [A]
  • C4-59. "the Covenant is preserved by two oriental Christian sources, the Chronicle of Seert and the Ecclesiastical chronicle of Bar Hebraeus." p. 119 [PDF 144] [F]
  • C4-60. Brandie Ratliff "relies on Scher (1867-1915 CE) (602, note 1) and Louis Massignon (1883-1962 CE) (250-257)" and "provides no new evidence of her own". p. 119 [PDF 144] [A/O]
  • C4-61. Quote from "The Monastery of Saint Catherine at Mount Sinai and the Christian Communities of the Caliphate" (17, note 11): "(a)spects of this letter have also been questioned; it seems to have been produced by viziers of the 'Abbasid period, who were of Nestorian origin and wanted protection for their community". The text introduces it with "she", right after naming both Ratliff and Roggema, so whose article it is remains ambiguous. p. 119 [PDF 144] [A]
  • C4-62. Massignon's "sympathy towards Islam was ambivalent (Irwin 224)"; "he once wrote that he studied the language of the Qur'an in order to demolish it (225)". p. 119 [PDF 144] [A: Irwin]
  • C4-63. "The Christians in the Islamic world did not have a history of falsifying prophetic traditions or documents." "virtually all falsifications originated from the center of power". p. 119 [PDF 144] [O]
  • C4-64. Roggema mentions the covenant "in passing as part of her study on the story of Bahira". She calls the Prophet's declaration "clearly fictitious" (116) and the pact "certainly penned by Christians" (117), but says it "should not be dismissed as an absolute forgery, because it includes a list of obligations for Christians known also from the Pact of 'Umar, and it also echoes some of the Prophet's demands and promises to the people of Najran as contained in Muslim sources" (117). p. 119 [PDF 144] [A]
  • C4-65. Roggema (117), block quote: the Chronicle's covenant has obligations similar to the Pact of 'Umar (three days' hospitality; no shelter for enemies). Abu Yusuf Ya'qub and al-Baladhuri include a Prophet–Najran agreement with the same pledge of non-interference in monastic and church affairs. The option to pay a garment's value in money is "in all likelihood a response to the stipulation ... that the community of Najran must pay 2000 garments each year". p. 119 [PDF 144] [A]
  • C4-66. Roggema notes that some Jews were accused of the same (118, note 68) and asks whether the "Christian authors of these edicts" wanted to prescribe a policy "which in reality did not exist in such clear-cut terms" (118). p. 120 [PDF 145] [A]
  • C4-67. "one may not question original, authenticated documents: namely, the existing copies of similar pacts sealed by the Prophet himself." p. 120 [PDF 145] [O]
  • C4-68. For Roggema the covenant is "a cut and paste job drawn from previous prophetic agreements and the Pact of 'Umar". Morrow: "would it not be simpler ... to attribute them to the same single author?" p. 120 [PDF 145] [A/O]

F. Script and variants

  • C4-69. "the letters of the Prophet Muhammad were written in a very elementary form of Arabic script." The Sinai and Najran covenants "were copied from early Arabic script into the more expressive 'Uthmani script". p. 120 [PDF 145] [F]
  • C4-70. The Treaty of Maqnah survives in two variants, in Ibn Sa'd and in Baladhuri. Gil: "Certain expressions were already unfamiliar in Ibn Sa'd's time, and he tried to explain them ... not quite accurately" (29–30, note 27). p. 120 [PDF 145] [A]
  • C4-71. Baladhuri names the tribe "Habibah", Ibn Sa'd "Janbah"; both readings are possible because ha, jim and kha, and ba, ta, tha and nun, were indistinguishable without dots. p. 120 [PDF 145] [F]
  • C4-72. Baladhuri "obtained a copy of the document from an Egyptian who had seen the original in Maqnah". It was "written on red parchment, the script of which was already faded" (Gil 29–30, note 27). pp. 120–121 [PDF 145–146] [A]
  • C4-73. The originals were probably in poor condition when copied; any mistakes "were made in good faith". p. 121 [PDF 146] [O]
  • C4-74. "proliferation of transmitters ... is considered a mode of authentication" in hadith studies (Azami 33–42). p. 121 [PDF 146] [A]

G. Structure and exordium of the Najran covenant

  • C4-75. The Najran covenant "is the longest of all the accords concluded by the Messenger of Allah". "Unlike the other two", it begins with the basmallah, and "Unlike the covenants concluded with the monks of Mount Sinai and the Assyrian Christians" it has two sections: an exordium and the covenant itself. p. 121 [PDF 146] [F]
  • C4-76. Exordium: "covenant of protection granted by Allah and His Messenger to the People of the Book, the Christians, who belong to the religion of Najran or any other Christian sect". pp. 121 [PDF 146] [T]
  • C4-77. It was "written by Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah to all of humanity, as a guarantee of protection ...". The verb kataba troubles Muslims who believe the Prophet was illiterate. p. 121 [PDF 146] [T/F]
  • C4-78. Morrow quotes his own "Pre and Early Islamic Period" (A Cultural History of Reading, 526):
    • ummi (Q 7:157–58) can mean "an inhabitant of Mecca, known as Umm al-Qura", "Gentile", or "unlettered".
    • "According to the Prophet's Family, Muhammad could read and write in seventy languages."
    • "Maxine [sic] Rodinson, W. Montgomery Watt, and Albert Guillaume" hold the Prophet was literate before Islam.
    • The quote lists sayings on knowledge, including "Seek knowledge, even in China".
    • Prisoners of war who taught two Muslims to read were freed.
    • pp. 121–122 [PDF 146–147] [A: Morrow's own work]
  • C4-79. The Imams said: "By Allah, he could read and write in seventy languages" (Majlisi). Hadith al-tariq: "The Imam is blessed in his majesty with the knowledge of all languages spoken by all living things." Sunni traditions show the Prophet, Hasan and Husayn speaking Persian; Imams are cited speaking Hebrew. p. 122 [PDF 147] [T/A]
  • C4-80. qara'a means "to read" while sama', alqa and sarada mean "to recite". p. 122 [PDF 147] [F]
  • C4-81. Pre-Islamic illiteracy would show he "could not have forged the Qur'an" (Saleh 33) and would explain "why he signed an early engagement with the monks of Mount Sinai with his palm-print". p. 122 [PDF 147] [A + F]
  • C4-82. Bihar al-anwar: the Prophet was given knowledge of all languages when Gabriel first descended, and taught 'Ali the scripts of previous prophets (xviii, 266, 278–282). p. 122 [PDF 147] [A]
  • C4-83. Exordium quotations:
    • "it is forbidden for any man, whether he is a governor or holder of authority, to revoke it or infringe upon it"
    • "the Believers must not charge them with other conditions than those which are included in this document"
    • a violator "will carry his crime on his head ... he will thus be an imposter in the eyes of Allah", compared with Q 55:41 and 96:15–16
    • "the religion of Allah has been imposed and the covenant which he has made has rendered protection obligatory"
    • Q 2:159 cited
    • "The reason for which the Christians have been found worthy of this covenant ... is because it is a right they have earned."
    • p. 123 [PDF 148] [T]
  • C4-84. The covenant "has not been concluded by equal parties"; "they were terms of surrender and submission". p. 123 [PDF 148] [O]
  • C4-85. "the ancient religions" alludes to "the Sabians, to the Magians, and perhaps even to the polytheists". "the ancient Books" means the People of the Book, "unanimously agreed upon to include the Jews and the Christians, and extended to the Zoroastrians and even Hindus and Buddhists by a minority of scholars". Q 22:17. p. 124 [PDF 149] [O/F]
  • C4-86. Hamidullah: "the practice of the Prophet and that of the Orthodox Caliphs has... decided that all non-Muslims may be tolerated as subjects" (Muslim Conduct 112–13). This was the opinion of al-Shaybani, al-Sarakhsi, Abu Hanifah and Abu Yusuf (113). p. 124 [PDF 149] [A]
  • C4-87. The Qur'an uses metaphors of hard and sick hearts (2:10; also 2:74; 3:7; 5:13; 5:52; 6:43; 8:49; 9:77; 9:125; 22:53; 24:50; 33:12; 33:60; 39:22; 47:20; 47:29; 74:31; 83:14). The Jewish people "slew the prophets in defiance of right" (3:112; 4:155). p. 124 [PDF 149] [Qur'an]
  • C4-88. The Prophet "seems to be alluding quite clearly to the Jews of Medina". Jews and Christians were "eagerly awaiting the arrival of a long-awaiting prophet". p. 124 [PDF 149] [O]
  • C4-89. Hayat al-qulub by 'Allamah Majlisi includes "a large number of prophecies concerning the birth, status, and signs of Muhammad" (Chapter 2). The Jews "rejected him on the basis that he was an Arab rather than a Jewish person". pp. 124 [PDF 149] [A/O]
  • C4-90. Recommended books: Muhammad in the Bible ('Abdul 'Ahad Dawud), What the Bible Says about Muhammad (Ahmed Deedat), Muhammad in the Bible (Jamal Badawi). p. 124 [PDF 149] [O]

Arabs or foreigners, known or unknown'". p. 132 [PDF 157] [T]

5. Covenant details

5A. Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of Persia (Ch. 3)
Field As stated in the book
Names used "Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of Persia" (throughout); "the Covenant with the Persians" (p. 107); Arpee: "a charter" (p. 99); Dadoyan: "a Medinan-style commitment" ratified by "a copy of an old Medinan oath allegedly given to the Syrian Christians" (p. 100); "a 17th-century Persian edict" (p. 103). Among "the covenants he concluded with the Armenian Christians, the foremost of which" (p. 99)
Language "This Persian-language covenant"; "supposedly written in Persian"; "survives only in English translation" (pp. 99, 102)
Claimed date "dated on the fourth year of the hijrah" (p. 107). No CE equivalent given. Morrow: probably added by a scribe
Place issued Not stated
Scribe Not stated
Witnesses None listed in this chapter. (The Assyrian covenant's witness list, with 'Ali + 'alayhi al-salam, is mentioned for comparison, p. 107)
Recipients / addressees "all Christian nations... throughout the world" who live in eastern Arabia and Persia (p. 104); Armenian Christians of Persia (pp. 99, 103)
Grant / transmission Granted to the Armenian Bishop of New Julfa in the 17th century by the Shah of Persia (Arpee 355), identified by Morrow as Abbas I (p. 99)
Location of original / copies "was preserved in the archives of the Armenian Bishop of New Julfa" (Arpee, 1946, 355) (p. 99). The New Julfa library was "now robbed of its most valued treasures" (Arpee 235) (p. 103). Dadoyan: no record in the Prelacy/Bishopric archives (p. 102). "appears to have gone missing" (p. 107). The original or copy "apparently went missing" in the 20th century (p. 100). The existing copy "dates from the 17th century" (p. 103)
Textual source used by Arpee "from the version of Johanianz (New Julfa, 1881)" (Arpee 355) (p. 102). Arpee claimed to have taken it from the History of New Julfa at Isfahan (per Dadoyan) (p. 102)
Published / translated Arpee, 1946 (p. 99); "1948" on p. 103 (see §7). English translation. Morrow includes it "in this work" (p. 99)
Early authentication claim Ja'far al-Sadiq "testifies to its authenticity after comparing the text with the original in his own hand" (Arpee 355) (p. 103)
Related early evidence Vartabed: the Prophet's grant to Persia's Armenians for four dirhams etc. (p. 99); the John of Otzun petition under Hisham (p. 103)
Key content See C3-64 to C3-99: obedience; divine inspiration; protection beyond Muslim lands; tax of 4 dirhams per adult male (max 12 for the wealthy); non-Christians 4 dirhams; "Imam" not "Sultan"; no forced conversion; marriage "permanently or only for a time"; envoy clause; Christians' obligations (three days' hospitality); 'Alid blessing on Muhammad "and his posterity"
Author's verdict Not proven either way: Dadoyan says authenticity "cannot be established", Morrow replies "neither can it be disproved" (p. 107). He leans towards authenticity: "documented evidence that it was being adhered to and emulated in the 8th century", and Ja'far al-Sadiq's endorsement would make it "the original" (p. 103). Not a "complete and accurate translation" of the Sinai covenant (p. 99)
Arguments for (1) Arpee was a serious historian with no motive, no Persian proficiency and too little knowledge of Shi'ism to forge it (p. 103). (2) Fabrication in 1946/1948 "would have been scholarly suicide" (p. 103). (3) Over sixty years passed before he was challenged (p. 103). (4) A referencing error by Arpee, a typist, editor or printer is possible; half a dozen 1880–81 Armenian histories might contain it (pp. 102–103). (5) The New Julfa library was robbed; archives hold uncatalogued works (p. 103). (6) Ja'far al-Sadiq's authentication (p. 103). (7) The 8th-century John of Otzun petition shows the terms in practice (p. 103). (8) Christians as muminin is consistent with the Constitution of Medina, "a sure sign of the antiquity" (p. 104). (9) 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz's ransom policy likely followed it (p. 104). (10) Dadoyan herself admits New Julfa's history "somehow proves this extravagant hypothesis" (p. 107)
Counter-arguments addressed (a) It is merely a Persian translation of the Sinai covenant (pp. 99, 102). (b) Shah 'Abbas "Shi'itized" it (tahrif), answered with possible Turkish/Arab/Umayyad purging of 'Alid elements (p. 102). (c) Dadoyan: no such document in the cited book or the archives; "highly dubious" (pp. 102–103). (d) It is not found in Shi'ite or Sunni sources; perhaps a lost work, or destroyed by Jamal Pasha (pp. 100–101). (e) The "fourth year of the hijrah" date, attributed to a later scribe (p. 107)
5B. Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of Najran (Ch. 4)
Field As stated in the book
Names used "Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of Najran"; Scher: "This covenant" (apocryphal); "the pact or patent" (p. 109); self-descriptions: "covenant of protection", "an authoritative contract", "authentic certificate", "inviolable pact", "this edict" (pp. 121, 132, 137)
Published edition Addai Scher, Histoire nestorienne inedite: Chronique de Seert, Arabic/French edition, published posthumously in Patrologia Orientalis "five years after his death" (p. 109); "first published in an obscure Orientalist journal in 1919" (p. 138). Cited as Scher 281/601, 282/602, 602 n.1
Reprints 1956: Muhammad Hamidullah, Majmu'ah al-watha'iq al-siyasiyyah li al-'ahd al-nabawi wa al-khilafah al-rashidah. 2002: Muhammad 'Amarah, al-Islam wa al-akhar (p. 138)
Manuscript provenance Copy made from a document found in 265 AH (878/879 CE) in the possession of Habib, the Monk, in Birmantha. Habib's copy came from an original in the Library of Philosophy, where he was curator before becoming a monk. The original was on cow-hide "turned yellow with age" and "bore the seal of the Prophet Muhammad" (Scher 281/601) (p. 109)
Preserved in "two oriental Christian sources, the Chronicle of Seert and the Ecclesiastical chronicle of Bar Hebraeus" (p. 119)
Claimed date No date from the document is given in this chapter. Datings discussed: critics, "early years after the hijrah" / before Badr (p. 116); Morrow's initial reading, just after the Trench or Khaybar (p. 115); Shi'ite sources, "after the conquest (of Mecca)" (p. 116); Morrow's conclusion, "the last year of the Prophet's life" (p. 118)
Place Implied Medina: the forgers would have had to assume all witnesses "were present in Medina at the same time on the same date" (p. 115)
Scribe Not named. "Whether it was written by the hand of the Prophet or that of one of his scribes" (p. 123); the text says "written by Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah" (p. 121)
Witnesses: count "thirty-two witnesses from the Companions of the Prophet" (p. 115); "over thirty" (p. 118); "thirty prominent Companions of the Prophet" (p. 138); "his closest Companions as well as the leaders of the Christians" (p. 131)
Witnesses: names given here Only those disputed: Abu Hurayrah; Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan; Sa'd ibn Mu'adh; Ja'far ibn Abi Talib (p. 115). Full list not reproduced in this section
Recipients "the People of the Book, the Christians, who belong to the religion of Najran or any other Christian sect" (p. 121); "Sayyid Ibn Harith ibn Ka'b, his co-religionists, and all those who profess the Christian religion, be they in East or West ..." (p. 132); ratified "not only with the Nestorian Christians, but with all 'the different Christians sects'" (p. 131)
Requesters / delegation named in text "three people (from Sayyid Ghassani)" asked for a safe-conduct document (p. 131). Visitors: "The Sayyid 'Absiso, Ibn Hijrah, Ibrahim the monk, and 'Isa the Bishop ... accompanied by forty horsemen from Najran" (p. 126)
Structure The longest of all the accords; begins with the basmallah; two sections, an exordium and the covenant (p. 121)
Key terms See C4-126 to C4-153: universal protection; no removal of clergy; no seizure of churches; clergy tax-exempt; 4 dirhams a year (or a striped outfit or embroidered Yemeni turban); max 12 dirhams for the wealthy; travellers exempt; no military service or forced equipment; no forced conversion (29:46); consent in marriage and respect for a Christian wife's faith; Muslim help with church repairs; no Christian used as spy/scout/guide/messenger; Christians not to aid enemies; three days' hospitality "with their animals"; hide Muslims; violators "cast out of the alliance"; valid "until the hour of the Resurrection"
Critics' positions Scher: apocryphal, forged so Muslims would spare Christians, every sect has a differing copy, faulty language (p. 109). Cahen: "a pious fraud of Nestorian monks of the 9th century" (p. 119). Nersessian: "a patent fabrication, probably the work of some Nestorian priest or monk" (p. 119). Ratliff: relies on Scher and Massignon (p. 119). Massignon (via the 17 n. 11 quote): produced by 'Abbasid-era viziers of Nestorian origin (p. 119). Roggema: declaration "clearly fictitious", pact "certainly penned by Christians", but "should not be dismissed as an absolute forgery" (p. 119). Most scholars: dismiss it because it is absent from classical Islamic sources (p. 112). Superficial critics: anachronistic witnesses (p. 115)
Author's verdict Authentic: "a historical find of momentous importance" (p. 138). The covenants share one author, "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah" (p. 110)
Arguments for (1) Scher gave no proof (p. 109). (2) Different covenants for different denominations explain the variation; the Greek Orthodox copy is identical (p. 109). (3) Independent forgers would differ radically, collaborating forgers would agree exactly; the mixture points to one author (pp. 109–110). (4) Muslims abide by such covenants (p. 110). (5) Many documented contacts with Najran (Mecca before 621; 630/8 AH; mubahalah; 9 AH; 10 AH) mean it "does not appear in a vacuum" (pp. 112–114). (6) Najran's Christians already had treaties, so there was no motive to forge (p. 114). (7) A long witness list would endanger forgers, so its presence may confirm authenticity (p. 115). (8) Each disputed witness can be accounted for (pp. 115–116). (9) Fatimah's role means the last year of the Prophet's life, when most witnesses could be present (p. 118). (10) It is preserved in two Christian sources (p. 119). (11) Christians had no history of forging prophetic documents; forgeries came from the centre of power; the 'Abbasids had no need to forge (p. 119). (12) Variants are good-faith misreadings of unpointed script, as with Maqnah (pp. 120–121). (13) Proliferation of transmitters across regions points to a common origin (Azami) (p. 121). (14) The delegation's names and numbers match early Islamic sources (p. 127)
Counter-arguments addressed Absence from classical sources (p. 112); 'Umar's expulsion (Hitti) (p. 114); anomalous witness list and anachronisms (pp. 115–116); pre-Badr chronology (p. 116); later chains of narration possible (pp. 115–116); Roggema's "cut and paste" thesis (p. 120); Jews accused of similar forgeries (p. 120); the Prophet's illiteracy versus "written by Muhammad" (pp. 121–123); "Islamists" calling it a Christian fabrication of a "soft" Prophet (p. 137)
5C. Other Najran agreements reported in Ch. 4
Document Date Terms as quoted Scribe / witnesses Source Page
Treaty after the mubahalah undated "The Prophet granted them a treaty and bid them farewell" — Mufid 118 p. 113 [PDF 138]
Letter to the People of Najran undated, after the accord was not honoured invitation to worship God; else jizyah; else war — qtd. Qureshi 54 p. 113 [PDF 138]

Qureshi 117 p. 113 [PDF 138]

6. The author's key arguments and opinions

Chapter 3
  1. The Persia covenant is not just a translation of the Sinai covenant. It may be a free translation, a Shi'itized version, or even the original of which the Arabic is a translation. pp. 99, 102
  2. Arpee was "operating on assumptions" in calling it a reproduction of the Sinai charter. p. 99
  3. The Shah most likely got the covenant from the Christian community (most likely St Catherine's) or from Safavid state archives. Envoys, Capuchins and Twelver scholars are possible carriers. The Maronite Petrus de Monte is "a prime suspect". pp. 100–102
  4. Ottomans and Safavids both "brandish[ed]" covenant copies to win Western Christian support, so which version is most authentic "begs to be answered". p. 101
  5. Missionaries working openly were unlikely to commit fraud, since they circulated covenants "known since the early days of Islam". p. 101
  6. Dadoyan's objections rest on assumptions. Arpee had no motive or means to forge, and the missing reference may be a clerical error. pp. 102–103
  7. Ja'far al-Sadiq's endorsement, if real, is "probably the single most important endorsement any covenant of the Prophet can receive" and would make the Persian version "the original". p. 103
  8. Umayyad tampering is evident in witness lists, for example Mu'awiyyah as scribe before his conversion. p. 102
  9. The Prophet's treaty-making with Persian Christians was "brilliant and visionary", "preparing the ground for the future conquest of Persia". p. 103
  10. Muslims must protect Christian friends of Islam everywhere, not "Crusaders, colonizers or imperialists"; Salafis, Wahhabis and Takfiris will be outraged. p. 104
  11. The Umayyads were "the greatest liars in the history of Islam"; 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz followed the Prophet's precedent. p. 104
  12. Overtaxation of Christians was the exception; the idea of routine oppressive taxes or church bans "is not accurate". p. 105
  13. "Imam" was the Prophet's original term for the ruler, changed to "Sultan" for Sunni or Ottoman sentiment. p. 105
  14. Mut'ah is Islamically valid; the prohibiting tradition was forged to support 'Umar's ban. pp. 105–106
  15. The custom of requiring Christian brides to convert is unfounded; there is "a chasm the size of the Grand Canyon" between Islamic theory and practice. p. 106
  16. Mu'awiyyah's 650 Armenian settlement shows Muslim forces rescuing autonomous Christian allies. pp. 106–107
  17. The "fourth year of the hijrah" date was probably added by a scribe. p. 107
  18. Authenticity "cannot be disproved". The document may be "misplaced" or "stolen" and should be rediscovered. p. 107
  19. Dadoyan's Tanzimat remarks show "a clear-cut case of continuity in the legal canon". p. 108
Chapter 4
  1. Scher's claims are unsupported. His dismissal portrays Muslims as "imbeciles" and the churches as fraudsters. pp. 109–110
  2. Consistency mixed with variation across all the covenants shows a single author, the Prophet. p. 110
  3. Scher's death is "a lesson": denying Islamic ethics "may contribute to a self-fulfilling prophecy". p. 110
  4. The Young Turks were Western-backed "Westernized atheists", not Muslims. The Armenian Genocide comparison with the Holocaust is "simplistic"; there is no evidence of intent to exterminate. pp. 110–111
  5. Western powers (British, German, later others) created and use Islamic extremism; "Islamic fundamentalism" is a colonial-era ideology. pp. 111–112
  6. Absence from classical sources is the strongest objection, but dismissing the covenant on that basis is "eminently reactionary and intransigent". pp. 112–113
  7. Najran's Christians had no motive to forge something they had already been granted. p. 114
  8. Hitti is biased; Jafri is correct; Christians stayed in Najran for centuries. 'Umar may have exiled only the elite. p. 114
  9. The long witness list is paradoxically evidence of authenticity, since forgers would not take such a risk. The covenants were "designed to be anomalous". p. 115
  10. Each disputed witness can be reconciled: Abu Hurayrah was an early convert; Sa'd may have died later, or the Qurayzah story is doubtful; Ja'far returned in 626; Mu'awiyyah travelled to Medina. pp. 115–116
  11. The Shi'ite chronology (after the conquest of Mecca) is "most sensible"; the Sunni pre-Badr placement "makes little sense". p. 116
  12. The covenant dates from the Prophet's last year, because of Fatimah's age. p. 118
  13. Sunni writers (Ibn Ishaq, al-Waqidi) suppressed and Shi'ite writers emphasized ahl al-bayt material. A full picture needs Sunni, Shi'ite and Christian sources together. p. 118
  14. Massignon was ambivalent about Islam and Ratliff adds nothing; the "'Abbasid Nestorian viziers" theory is speculation. p. 119
  15. Christians did not forge prophetic documents. Forgery came from the centre of power, and the 'Abbasids had no need to forge. p. 119
  16. Roggema's "cut and paste" observation better supports a single author. p. 120
  17. Variants arise from good-faith readings of unpointed early script and damaged originals, not interpolation. pp. 120–121
  18. The Prophet was literate after revelation (Qur'an "his grammar school"); ummi means Meccan/Gentile/unschooled; the Prophet and Imams knew all languages. pp. 121–123
  19. The covenant was terms of submission from a position of power, not a mere goodwill gesture. p. 123
  20. Jews of Medina were hostile while Christians were loyal. The Prophet was not anti-Semitic; the conflict was not racial; modern accusations project present values on the past. pp. 124–128
  21. The covenant supports Donner's view that early Islam was a broad movement of believers including Christians and Jews. "Christian Islamists" served as emissaries. pp. 128–129
  22. Qureshi confused names; differences in names and numbers are "a non-issue"; numbers are symbolic in Semitic languages. p. 127
  23. The tax provisions laid "the bases of the Islamic economic system" with "much thought and contemplation inspired by revelation". pp. 135
  24. The ban on aiding enemies applies today: hosting foreign military bases or a Muslim serving in an army fighting Muslims is kufr. p. 137
  25. The covenant is "a historical find of momentous importance", neglected because Scher called it spurious and because of Muslim "scholarly stagnation". p. 138

7. Internal inconsistencies within this section

  1. Year of Arpee's publication. "At the time of publication, namely, 1946" (p. 99 [PDF 124]) versus "introducing a fabricated Covenant of the Prophet in 1948 would have been scholarly suicide" (p. 103 [PDF 128]). Arpee's dates are given as "(1877—1947 CE)" (p. 99), so a 1948 introduction would fall after his death. Also on p. 103: "Most scholars in the 1950s did not type", offered to explain a mistake in a work dated 1946.
  2. Date of the Battle of Khaybar. Ch. 3 gives "the Conquest of Khaybar (629 CE)" (p. 105 [PDF 130]; the date is attributed to Sunni sources). Ch. 4 says Ja'far "returned to Medina in 626 CE at the very moment that Muhammad was returning from the Battle of Khaybar" (p. 116 [PDF 141]).
  3. Number of witnesses on the Najran covenant. "thirty-two witnesses from the Companions" (p. 115 [PDF 140]); "from a couple to over thirty" (p. 118 [PDF 143]); "witnessed ... by thirty prominent Companions" (p. 138 [PDF 163]). p. 131 [PDF 156] says it was witnessed by "his closest Companions as well as the leaders of the Christians", whereas pp. 115 and 138 speak only of Companions.
  4. Scher's death and the first publication. Scher died in 1915 (pp. 109–110, 112, 119) and the Chronicle was published "five years after his death" (p. 109 [PDF 134]), which implies about 1920. Yet the covenant "was first published in an obscure Orientalist journal in 1919" (p. 138 [PDF 163]).
  5. Ibn Ishaq and the Jewish–Christian dispute. "The debate between the Jews and Christians, which took place in the presence of the Prophet, is not mentioned by Ibn Ishaq" (p. 118 [PDF 143]) versus "Ibn Ishaq mentions that a dispute between Christians and Jews took place in the presence of the Prophet (258)" (p. 130 [PDF 155]).
  6. Did Najran's Christians keep faith? "When the Christians of Najran did not honor their accord with the Prophet, the Messenger of Allah sent them a stern, clear warning" (p. 113 [PDF 138]) versus "Unlike many others, this particular group of Christians from Najran had not betrayed the trust of the Prophet" and the quoted text "they did not break their covenant" (p. 127 [PDF 152]).
  7. Dating of the Najran covenant.
    • Initially "the immediate aftermath of the Battle of the Trench or the Battle of Khaybar" (p. 115).
    • Then the Shi'ite "after the conquest (of Mecca)" chronology is called most sensible (p. 116).
    • Then "must necessarily date from the last year of the Prophet's life" (p. 118).
    • Morrow's defence of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh as witness rests on the covenant being concluded "after the Battle of the Trench", when Sa'd "may still have been in a position to ratify it" (p. 115). That sits uneasily with the last-year dating, given his reported death after the Trench (p. 115).
    • The delegation dates are 630 CE/8 AH (p. 112), with the jizyah treaty in 9 AH and the further delegation in 10 AH (p. 113).
  8. Number of Najran delegations. "the Christians of Najran sent two delegations to Medina" (p. 126 [PDF 151], per early Islamic sources / Qureshi 85). But the chapter also describes a Mecca delegation before 621 (p. 112), a 630/8 AH delegation of sixty riders (p. 112) followed by the mubahalah (p. 113), the 9 AH treaty, and a 10 AH delegation (p. 113). Qureshi places the sixty-person delegation second, after the mubahalah delegation (p. 127). Morrow's p. 112 account appears to treat Ibn Ishaq's sixty riders as the mubahalah delegation.
  9. Size of the delegation. "sixty riders, led by fourteen nobles" (p. 112, Ibn Ishaq); "thirty of the Christians" (Mufid, p. 117); "forty horsemen" (covenant, p. 126); "sixty persons ... twenty-four famous chiefs" (Qureshi, p. 127); "some twenty Christians" in Mecca (Ibn Ishaq, p. 112). Morrow acknowledges and reconciles these on p. 127 (numbers "symbolize a large amount").
  10. 'Abd al-Masih and the 'Aqib. Morrow: "'Abd al-Masih, who was the 'Aqib, deputy or leader" (p. 127 [PDF 152]). His own Mufid quotation lists them separately: "thirty of the Christians who included the deputy (al-'aqib), the chief (al-sayyid) and 'Abd al-Masih", and "The bishop looked at the deputy, the chief and 'Abd al-Masih" (p. 117 [PDF 142]). Morrow cites "Mufid 116" for his identification.
  11. Names of the Najran leader / recipient. The exordium names "The Sayyid 'Absiso" (p. 126); the covenant proper is "concluded with Sayyid Ibn Harith ibn Ka'b" (p. 132); the requesters are "three people (from Sayyid Ghassani)" (p. 131); Qureshi has "Abu al-Harith al-Ayham" (p. 127); Morrow names the Sayyid "al-Ayham" (p. 127). Morrow reconciles only 'Absiso, Ibn Hijrah and 'Isa.
  12. Name spellings for the same person. "Petrus de Monte" (p. 100) / "Petrus del Monte" (p. 101). "Girangos Vartabed" (p. 99) / "Giragos Vartabed" (p. 103). "Nercessian" in the citation versus "Nersessian" in the text (p. 119). "'Abassid" versus "'Abbasid" (p. 119). Some may be OCR.
  13. Mount Lebanon versus Mount Carmel. The diffusion argument centres on Mount Lebanon (Petrus del Monte; Scaliger's Capuchins). Then: "Still, Mount Carmel stands out as a source of diffusion" (p. 101 [PDF 126]), with Mount Carmel not otherwise introduced in this section.
  14. Textual status of the Persia covenant. "survives only in English translation" (p. 99) versus "the existing copy of the Covenant ... dates from the 17th century" (p. 103) versus "the covenant in question appears to have gone missing" (p. 107).
  15. Hitti versus Morrow on 'Umar. Morrow rejects Hitti's claim that 'Umar expelled Najran's Christians to Syria (p. 114). On the same page he proposes that 'Umar "offered the Christians the option to pay the jizyah or relocate to Syria with monetary compensation", that "some Christians immigrated to Syria" and "the majority" went to Kufah, and that 'Umar "exiled only the hierarchs and nobles".
  16. Witness practice. "with rare exceptions, they were not signed by witnesses" (p. 115) sits beside the 10 AH Treaty of Najran, quoted as witnessed by five named Companions (p. 114).
  17. Spy and envoy clauses: a contrast between covenants, not strictly a contradiction. Ch. 3 says the Persia covenant "lifts this restriction from lay Christians", allowing a Christian envoy whose "service be accepted" (p. 106). Ch. 4's Najran covenant forbids employing "any Christian as a messenger, scout, guide or spy" (p. 137).
  18. Ambiguous attribution. The quote "(a)spects of this letter have also been questioned ... viziers of the 'Abbasid period" (17, note 11) is introduced with "she" right after "Brandie Ratliff ... and ... Barbara Roggema" (p. 119). Morrow then discusses Ratliff, and turns to Roggema "in passing" at the end of p. 119.
  19. Date attached to Nafziger and Walton. Printed "George F. Nafziger and (b. 1949 CE) Mark W. Walton" (p. 128), so it is unclear which co-author the birth date belongs to.

1. Section summary

Chapter 5 deals with the "Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World" (Arabic al-'Ahd wa al-shurut allati sharataha Muhammad rasul Allah li ahl al-millah al-nasraniyyah; Latin Testamentum et pactiones, Testamentum Mahometi, etc.). The author says it has no extant Islamic sources and an obscure origin, but was circulating in the Ottoman Empire and Europe by the early 17th century. He traces how it reached Europe. The Capuchin Pacifique Scaliger (René de l'Escale, Pacifique de Provins, 1588–1648) obtained it, probably in the Levant in 1627–1628. He brought it to France in 1629, and through François Hotman it went to the Maronite Gabriel Sionita, who published an Arabic–Latin edition in Paris in 1630 (printed by Antoine Vitray). The author disputes the story that it was found at a Mount Carmel monastery "one day's journey from Mecca" (Ricaut), and he rejects the allegation that Scaliger forged it. His key claim: he followed the chain of custody and found in the Bibliothèque nationale de France an Arabic Christian anthology, MS Arabe 214, copied in 1538 (1254 of the Martyrs / 945 AH) by Girgis al-Ifrangi, with the covenant on its final folios. He argues it bears Sionita's reading mark ("Gabriyal Sahyun al-Ziftawi") and so must be Sionita's source. Yet he also notes that its beginning, end, witness list (30 names) and scribe ('Ali rather than Mu'awiyah) differ from the 1630 print, and that it may instead be a covenant for the Christians of Egypt. He then surveys the reception of the text over four centuries, organised as defenders (Salmasius, Hinckelmann, Ricaut, Renaudot, Layard, Madrazo, Grassi, Twiss and others), neutral figures (Hottinger, Layard, Luke) and opponents (Grotius, Mosheim, Döllinger, Gieseler, Jacques and others). Along the way he covers the 1795 plans of the French Revolutionary Committee of Public Instruction to print it. He sets all this in the context of the Franco-Ottoman alliance and the history of Arabic printing. Finally he comments clause by clause on the 1630 text and then the 1538 text, drawing out possible Shi'ite and Sufi lexical features. He concludes that the covenant is a distinct treaty from the Najran covenant and that its variants point to authenticity. Whether the 1538 text is the forerunner of the 1630 text he leaves "to be determined".
