4. Factual claims (non-date)

A. Names and titles of the covenant
  1. Arabic title: al-'Ahd wa al-shurut allati sharataha Muhammad rasul Allah li ahl al-millah al-nasraniyyah, "literally, the Treaty and Covenant which Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, Concluded with the Christian Community". p. 139 [PDF 164]. fact
  2. The same title is rendered "The Covenant which Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, Concluded with His Christian Subjects" (p. 146 [PDF 171]) and "...with the Christian Community" (p. 149 [PDF 174]). fact
  3. Latin names: Testamentum et pactiones, Testamentum Muhammedis, Muhammedis Testamentum, Testamentum Mahometi. English: "Treaty of Muhammad" or "Patent of Muhammad". p. 139 [PDF 164]. fact
  4. The English titles are "identical to those applied to the Pactum Muhammedis", the covenant with the monks of Mount Sinai. The author therefore uses "Covenant ... with the Monks of Mount Sinai", "...with the Christians of Najran", and "...with the Christians of the World" (the last because it is addressed to all Christians). p. 139 [PDF 164]. fact/inf
  5. The Turks called it the Prophet's "hand or signature" ("Hand of Muhammad", "Signature of Muhammad"). p. 141 [PDF 166]. attr: Scaliger 407
  6. Layard: it "is usually called the 'Testamentum Mahometi'". p. 151 [PDF 176]. attr: Layard 207
  7. BnF index title: "Charte accordée à tous les chrétiens, par Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib 12. F. 257-261 (foliotation)". p. 145 [PDF 170]. attr: BnF index
  8. Other titles quoted: "Traité de Mahomet avec les Chrétiens" (Grassi); "Privilège accordé par Mahomet aux Chrétiens" (Miltitz); "Pact of Muhammad in Favor of the Christians" (Committee/Guillaume); "Original du traité de Mahomet, prophète des Arabes avec ceux qui font profession de la foi de Jésus" (Marana); "Testament de Mahomet" (Nagy de Harsany); "Pièce très rare et curieuse qui est le Testament de Mahomet" (Scaliger's chapter title). pp. 140, 152, 153, 155, 160. attr: various
  9. Gieseler's titles: "Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Mohammedem et Christianae fidei cultores" and "Pactum Muhammedis, quod indulsit Monachis montis Sinai et Christianis in universum". p. 158 [PDF 183]. attr: Gieseler 563 n. 7
  10. Salmasius wished "the translator had not given it that name; for it is nothing like a Testament. It is a league and a covenant". p. 152 [PDF 177]. attr: Salmasius, qtd. Bayle 1737: 38
B. Origin, sources and discovery stories
  1. The covenant "does not exist in any extant Islamic sources" (like the Sinai and Najran covenants). p. 139 [PDF 164]. fact
  2. It shares "remarkable similarities" with the Najran covenant. p. 139 [PDF 164]. fact/inf
  3. Its early trajectory is unknown. p. 139 [PDF 164]. fact
  4. Fortescue: "This is the famous Testament of Mohammed, published by Gabriel Sionita (Paris, 1630)". p. 139 [PDF 164]. attr: Fortescue 92 n. 5
  5. Bayle: the covenant was "found in a monastery at Mount Carmel"; the author says this would place the discovery in Palestine, close to Lebanon. p. 139 [PDF 164]. attr: Bayle 241; inf
  6. The Carmelites are "one of the oldest orders of Catholic monks in the Holy Land". p. 139 [PDF 164]. fact
  7. The Carmelites "may have obtained a copy of a covenant concluded by the Prophet with their predecessors". p. 139 [PDF 164]. inf
  8. Ricaut: the treaty was found in a convent of the monks of Mount Carmel, "close to Mount Lebanon, and at one day's journey from Mecca, where Muslim pilgrims perform their Qurban, or sacrifice, prior to entering the City". p. 140 [PDF 165]. attr: Ricaut 320
  9. It "takes approximately forty days to go from the Hijaz to Syria or Iraq by caravan". p. 140 [PDF 165]. fact
  10. Reaching Ghadir Khumm ("Khumrn", OCR), "a marsh or pond in the Wadi Rabigh", in under three days is "virtually inconceivable". p. 140 [PDF 165]. fact
  11. Ta'if is within one day's travel of Mecca, but "there is no record of Christians living there". p. 140 [PDF 165]. fact
  12. The only major town north of Mecca is Medina; the only major town south is Najran. p. 140 [PDF 165]. fact
  13. The place of sacrifice within a day of Mecca is "the tent city of Mina", "really but a neighborhood of the sacred city"; "There were never any Christian monasteries in Mina." p. 140 [PDF 165]. fact
  14. Mar Saba is "the longest continually inhabited monastery in the Middle East", "often described as a convent", and contains many ancient manuscripts, perhaps including a copy of a covenant. p. 140 [PDF 165]. fact; inf
  15. Ricaut said "On dit" ("It is said") of the transfer to the King's Library and "quoiqu'il en soit" ("whatever the truth may be"), calling the document "ancient and curious". p. 140 [PDF 165]. attr: Ricaut 320
  16. Scaliger's Relation du voyage de Perse (1631) does not mention a discovery at Mount Carmel. p. 140 [PDF 165]. fact
  17. Scaliger: the Testament "fortuitously fell into my hands, as a result of my spirit of curiosity". p. 140 [PDF 165]. attr: Scaliger 405–406
  18. Scaliger describes it as made by Muhammad "in favor of the Christians before dying, and in the presence of the witnesses who have signed below, who were his disciples, & authenticated by the Secretary or Notary Public". p. 141 [PDF 166]. attr: Scaliger 407
  19. Rehatsek: "[t]he first copy of this diploma was brought to Europe by Pacificus Scaliger, who had obtained it from Arab Capuchin monks". p. 141 [PDF 166]. attr: Rehatsek 97 n. 141a
  20. Marana's spy: a Latin note at the bottom of the Royal Library manuscript said "this document was found in the Convent of the Christian brothers of Mount Carmel". p. 160 [PDF 185]. attr: Marana 156
  21. The 1538 manuscript "trace[s] back to Cairo". p. 168 [PDF 193]. fact/inf
C. Scaliger: biography and character
  1. Full French name: René de l'Escale dit Pacifique de Provins; born in France in 1588. p. 141 [PDF 166]. fact
  2. Itinerary: Constantinople 1622; Egypt, Holy Land, Syria; Italy 1623 (Pope Gregory XV); Paris; Syria and Mount Lebanon 1628; missions in Aleppo and Cyprus; Persia (Baghdad, Isfahan); Europe 1629; French Antilles 1645; Paris 1646; died en route to French Guiana 1648. p. 141 [PDF 166]. attr: Pouillon 734
  3. Scaliger established diplomatic ties between the French and the Persians. p. 141 [PDF 166]. attr: Pouillon 734
  4. Murad IV's 1627 edicts gave the Capuchins protection, freedom of movement and religious practice, and liberty to preach and teach in their churches, "on grounds that they belong to an allied nation"; the author says they "contain echoes of the covenant". p. 142 [PDF 167]. attr: Scaliger, Relation 233–236; inf
  5. "the Capuchins acted as diplomats, ambassadors, and even covert operatives and spies on behalf of the French King". p. 142 [PDF 167]. fact
  6. A Capuchin friar's description: from "the noble and ancient family which bears this name"; joined "the Capuchins of the province of French Guiana"; known for mortification, fasts and austerities; charged with teaching theology; travelled to Persia and America; "numerous conversions". p. 143 [PDF 168]. attr: "un religieux du même ordre" 433–434
  7. No evidence exists that Scaliger was proficient in Classical Arabic or Islamic Studies. p. 142–143 [PDF 167–168]. fact/inf
  8. Scaliger "left no mark on the manuscript" (MS Arabe 214). p. 145 [PDF 170]. fact
  9. From bringing it to light until his death in 1648, Scaliger "never disavowed this document". p. 142 [PDF 167]. fact
  10. Scaliger published his own French translation in 1631 as the last section of the Relation. p. 142 [PDF 167]. fact
  11. Allegation (Bayle 1735: 241) that Scaliger personally forged the manuscript. p. 142 [PDF 167]. attr: Bayle
D. Transmission in France: Hotman, Sionita, the King
  1. Schefer: "a copy of this act of Muhammad was sent from the East to François Hotman, Counselor in the parliament of Paris by father Pacifique". p. 142 [PDF 167]. attr: Schefer (Thenaud 72 n. 2)
  2. Hotman (or Scaliger; the referent of "he" is ambiguous in the text) is called "the personal representative of the King of France to the Parliament of Paris". p. 142 [PDF 167]. fact
  3. Hotman was Sionita's host and entrusted him with translating the covenant from Arabic into Latin. p. 142 [PDF 167]. attr: Bernard 43; Thenaud 72 n. 2
  4. Goujet: Hotman "hired Sionita to put it into Latin"; "this erudite Maronite was well liked by this magistrate who housed him in his home for a long time". p. 142 [PDF 167]. attr: Goujet 100
  5. The covenant was "eventually entered into the library of the French King". p. 142 [PDF 167]. attr: Goujet 100
  6. That Scaliger brought it to France is "a fact which all scholars agree upon". p. 142 [PDF 167]. attr: Bayle 1737: 38; Bayle 1735: 241
  7. "François Hotman de Mar-fontaine, a Magistrate" was close to Du Ryer and his "circle of Islamologists" and to the King, and "was provided with the manuscript which had been discovered by Scaliger". p. 152 [PDF 177]. fact
  8. Sionita was criticised for "correcting" what seemed to him the bad Arabic of the New Testament, and had conflicts with colleagues, but was also much praised. p. 152 [PDF 177]. attr: "(M 254)"; Goujet 100
  9. Sionita (Jibra'il al-Sahyuni), "learned Maronite priest", is "famous for publishing the Parisian polyglot of the Bible". p. 143 [PDF 168]. fact
  10. Savary de Brèves, former French ambassador to Turkey with an interest in Oriental Studies, "may have played a role in bringing the Arabic version of the Covenant to France". p. 143 [PDF 168]. inf
  11. Göçek: "[m]anuscripts on Christianity and Greek civilization, along with those in Ottoman, Persian, and Arabic were collected avidly" in France during the Franco-Ottoman alliance; this "led to the development of large royal collections and libraries"; the King commissioned travellers to "search for rarities". p. 143 [PDF 168]. attr: Göçek 98
  12. In Marana's novel: "Cardinal de Richelieu ... had a large quantity of Persan, Syrian, and Arabic books". p. 143 [PDF 168]. attr: Marana 155
  13. Chain of possession: Scaliger to the King, the King to Hotman, Hotman to Sionita. p. 143 [PDF 168]. inf/fact
  14. Toomer: such manuscripts "eventually ended up in major libraries in France, the majority in the Royal Library, thus forming the basis of the splendid collection of Arabic manuscripts in the Bibliothèque nationale". p. 144 [PDF 169]. attr: Toomer 35
  15. Unless Sionita returned it at once through Hotman or Du Ryer, he "was the last person to have it". p. 144 [PDF 169]. inf
  16. Balagna: Sionita was "a friend of Savary de Braves"; "Louis III [sic] still maintains the policy of Henri IV and Savary, pro-Ottoman friendship, support for Eastern Christians"; Vitray's preface thanks Michel Le Jay, "the king's printer for Oriental languages", for Arabic, Syriac and Samaritan characters; "The Arabic ones were those of Savary." pp. 149–150 [PDF 174–175]. attr: Balagna 67
  17. Sionita "published the Covenant without full vocalization and case endings". p. 146 [PDF 171]. fact
  18. The work was also translated into Latin, French and German. p. 150 [PDF 175]. fact
  19. Sionita "had the Christians of the Arab world in mind when he published the Testamentum et pactiones". p. 150 [PDF 175]. inf
E. MS Arabe 214 (the 1538 manuscript), Bibliothèque nationale de France
  1. Guillaume's note: an apocryphal "Pact of Muhammad in Favor of the Christian[s]", part of a 262-sheet Arabic manuscript. p. 144 [PDF 169]. attr: Guillaume 831 B
  2. De Slane (pp. 54–55) via Guillaume: catalogued as no. 214; contains several works; the document is "the twelfth and last" and "takes up folios 245-246"; dated "1254 of the martyrs (1538 CE)". p. 144 [PDF 169]. attr: Guillaume / de Slane
  3. Notes at folios 114 and 125: copyist named George, "belonged to the Jacobite religion", "of European origin". p. 144 [PDF 169]. attr: de Slane via Guillaume
  4. Catalogue entry: "N° 214... 12° (Fol. 245). Copy of the charter granted by Muhammad, the son of 'Abd Allah, and grand-son of 'Abd al-Muttalib, to all Christians, featuring the signatures of approximately thirty Companions. It is one of many redactions of this apocryphal document." p. 144 [PDF 169]. attr: Guillaume 831 B
  5. Lefebvre de Villebrune translated this text. p. 144 [PDF 169]. attr: Guillaume
  6. Current catalogue: Anthology; Arabic 214 (serial number); 385 (Regius) (old number); Ancient Arab Collection 88 (old number); 1538. p. 144 [PDF 169]. attr: BnF catalogue
  7. Physical description: 17 lines per page; written surface 210 x 135 mm; Western paper; 262 fol. (f. 261v and 262v blank); paginated in Coptic numerals; "Oriental writing (Egyptian)"; title headings; 285 x 210 mm; binding of reddish-brown calf leather, back of red morocco "with the numbers of Napoleon the 1st"; in Arabic; BnF, Department of Manuscripts. p. 144 [PDF 169]. attr: BnF catalogue
  8. "Copy made for the library of Yuhanna ibn Ishaq al-Batanuni (f. 256 v), by Girgis al-Ifrangi (f. 114,125)". p. 144 [PDF 169]. attr: BnF catalogue
  9. History of conservation: a note by Renaudot; "Purchased by Vansleb in the Orient"; seals with Vansleb's numbers; pen marks (f. 1); reader's mark of Girgis ibn Yuhanna al-Tamawi (f. 1v); reading marks of Butrus ibn Diyab al-Halabi (1673 CE) and Mansur ibn Sulayman Sahyun al-Ramadi (14 Baba 1336 of the Martyrs, 1620 CE) (f. 2); note of a missionary's arrival in Old Cairo (9 Hatur 1380 of the Martyrs, 1592 CE) and mark of Gabriyal Sahyun al-Ziftawi (f. 2v); ownership mark of Sim'an ibn Fadl ("Fadi") Allah al-Barallusi (f. 262). pp. 144–145 [PDF 169–170]. attr: BnF catalogue
  10. De Slane: "nothing in his writing indicates that he was a French writer" (55); the author says the handwriting "was not that of a European". p. 145 [PDF 170]. attr: de Slane 55; fact
  11. In Arabic, ifranj, like rumi, "is applied indiscriminately to all Europeans". p. 145 [PDF 170]. fact
  12. Renaudot inferred Vansleb's purchase from the Vansleb seal; the author calls this "chronologically incorrect". p. 145 [PDF 170]. attr: Renaudot; inf
  13. The mark of "Gabriyal Sahyun al-Ziftawi" is "that of Gabriel Sionita himself!" p. 145 [PDF 170]. inf (stated as certain)
  14. "there is no question that this is the actual document that he [Scaliger] brought back"; "dates from 1538. It was already nearly one hundred years old." p. 145 [PDF 170]. inf (stated as certain)
  15. The covenant "occupies sheets 257 to 262, that is, the last eleven pages". p. 146 [PDF 171]. fact
  16. The work "appears to have been a mushaf or stack of sheets". p. 146 [PDF 171]. inf
  17. The Latin table of contents lists theological treatises and commentaries of the Eastern Church; an anonymous doctrinal exposition; a debate with one 'Abd al-Rahman on the truth of Christianity; an epistle; a debate with a Jew; a work on the wisdom of Solomon; a Christian–Jewish debate; an exposition of the Nicene Creed; an exposition of Sunday prayers; extracts from various authors; questions and responses. The Covenant is not listed. p. 146 [PDF 171]. fact
  18. It is "an obscure manuscript of which but a single copy remains in existence". p. 146 [PDF 171]. fact/inf
  19. The book has no title; it is "a work of Christian apologetics" to prepare monks, priests and missionaries to face Jews and Muslims. p. 146 [PDF 171]. inf
  20. The 1538 text "has never been previously published". p. 146 [PDF 171]. fact
  21. The manuscript is "written in beautiful Arabic handwriting" and "vocalized", as are all the documents in the book. p. 168 [PDF 193]. fact
  22. The Covenant is "the last folio in an Arab Christian anthology of apologetic literature which was copied in 1538". p. 168 [PDF 193]. fact
  23. "a large number of the [witness] names are misspelled"; Arabic readers can check this against "the scanned copy from 1538". p. 173 [PDF 198]. fact
  24. Partway through the witness list "the handwriting changes". p. 173 [PDF 198]. fact
  25. The BnF librarians note that the script shows no sign of a European hand. p. 175 [PDF 200]. attr: BnF librarians
  26. Yuhanna ibn Ishaq al-Batanuni was "the owner of the library for which the manuscript was copied". p. 175 [PDF 200]. fact
F. Political context: Franco-Ottoman alliance and capitulations
  1. Since 1536, "[t]he French had secured in the Levant a position of absolute pre-eminence". p. 145 [PDF 170]. attr: Hadjiantonious 53
  2. Before this, "the Greek Orthodox, the Armenians, and the Assyrians" had claimed privileges granted by the Prophet, "to the exclusion of the Byzantines"; now the French asserted them for the Roman Catholic Church. p. 145 [PDF 170]. fact/inf
  3. The alliance was denounced as "the impious alliance" or "the sacrilegious union of the Lily and the Crescent". p. 148 [PDF 173]. fact
  4. Ambassadors were exchanged; trade, religious, military and financial agreements were concluded; joint campaigns were conducted. p. 148 [PDF 173]. fact
  5. "[t]he alliances that Sulayman cemented with the Catholic French did not lead anyone to question his bona fides as a Muslim". p. 148 [PDF 173]. attr: unnamed source, p. "(179)"
  6. Boullata: "the Qur'an has specifically prescribed kindness and tact and gracious manners for Muslims when dealing with people of other faiths". p. 148 [PDF 173]. attr: Boullata 51
  7. Coffee drinking, Ottoman clothing (turban, caftan) and reclining on Persian rugs were "all the rage" in Paris. p. 148 [PDF 173]. fact
  8. Francis I wanted to protect Christians in the Ottoman Empire through Capitulations. p. 148 [PDF 173]. fact
  9. During Ottoman rule, "the Christians had never had it better"; "some would say that they were favored over other minorities". p. 143 [PDF 168]. fact/inf
  10. The 1630 publication "was motivated by political, economic, military, religious, and cultural considerations". p. 149 [PDF 174]. inf
  11. "many leading figures in French society embraced Islam" over the centuries of the alliance. p. 150 [PDF 175]. fact
G. Printing history
  1. "much Islamic literature was printed in Europe, particularly in Italy and France". p. 148 [PDF 173]. fact
  2. For ultra-conservative clerics the press was a prohibited innovation. p. 148 [PDF 173]. attr: "(83-84)". No author is named; the nearest preceding citations are to Chejne ("(101)"), and the next one is Göçek 113.
  3. Muteferrika explained that the religious dignitaries had forbidden the invention; they feared more books would threaten public order and religion. pp. 148–149 [PDF 173–174]. attr: Göçek 113
  4. Only minorities could print, and only in Hebrew or Latin characters. p. 149 [PDF 174]. attr: Göçek 111
  5. "[t]he Ottoman state was favorable to the trade and printing of books by foreigners". p. 149 [PDF 174]. attr: Göçek 111
  6. Three Italian Arabic presses: the Medici Press (Gospels, Arabic grammar, Greek authors in Arabic, Islamic science); the press of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (Arabic Bibles and Christian works); the Tipografia del Seminario in Padua (Qur'an with Arabic text and Latin translation); all marketed in the Ottoman Empire. p. 149 [PDF 174]. attr: Göçek 110
  7. "If printing the Qur'an was cause for capital punishment in the Ottoman Empire so was the publication of any other works". p. 149 [PDF 174]. fact/inf
  8. "the first machine-printed Arabic Qur'an was produced in Europe". p. 149 [PDF 174]. fact
  9. "That the French were the first to machine press the Qur'an is indicative of their interest in Islam." p. 149 [PDF 174]. inf (presented as fact)
  10. Postel advocated a universalistic religion integrating Jews, Muslims and Christians into "a broader ... Christian creed"; Bodin recognised that religions could coexist in one state and advocated pluralism. p. 149 [PDF 174]. fact
  11. "[t]he printing presses in the West started printing religious books in Arabic script by the sixteenth century for religious and trade purposes". p. 150 [PDF 175]. attr: Göçek 110
  12. Such books "served to maintain the faith among Arabic-speaking Christian communities in the Middle East and to help spread Christianity". p. 150 [PDF 175]. attr: Göçek 110
  13. "While they had led the Western world into the Renaissance, the Muslims were now centuries behind European Christians." p. 148 [PDF 173]. inf
H. Reception: defenders
  1. The covenant "was rejected by many authorities" but "defended by even larger numbers of them, the first of whom were Muslims". p. 151 [PDF 176]. inf
  2. Mosheim: "though some learned men doubt the authenticity of this instrument, yet the Mohammedans do not call it in question". pp. 151–152 [PDF 176–177]. attr: Mosheim 254
  3. Layard: "rejected as a forgery by several European critics" but "its authenticity is admitted by early Mohammedan and Eastern Christian writers". p. 152 [PDF 177]; repeated p. 156 [PDF 181]. attr: Layard 207
  4. Luke: "generally regarded in the West as of dubious authenticity", but "accepted by early Moslem writers as genuine". p. 152 [PDF 177]; p. 156 [PDF 181]. attr: Luke 68
  5. Féraud-Giraud: "the authenticity of this document is called into question", but the Treaty of 'Umar alludes to an earlier covenant of the Prophet with the Christians. p. 152 [PDF 177]. attr: Féraud-Giraud 36 and n. 1
  6. Layard: "[t]he substance of this treaty is given by three Syriac authors—Bar Hebreaus, Maris, and Amrus (Assemani, vol. iv, p. 59)". p. 151 [PDF 176]. attr: Layard 207
  7. Bar Hebraeus "has been described as the most learned and versatile man from the Syriac Orthodox Church". p. 151 [PDF 176]. attr: unnamed
  8. "Christian and Muslim Arabs had upheld the Covenant ... for centuries prior to its rediscovery". p. 152 [PDF 177]. inf/fact
  9. "Arabs aside, the first European scholar to stand behind the covenant was Father Pacificus Scaliger." p. 152 [PDF 177]. fact
  10. After Scaliger, Sionita and Hotman argued for the covenant's authenticity. p. 152 [PDF 177]. fact
  11. Salmasius: "I lately saw Mahomet's Testament: I have no doubt of its being genuine"; he cites Elmacin's Life of Mahomet on the Prophet favouring Christians, taxing them and covenanting with them. p. 152 [PDF 177]. attr: qtd. Bayle 1737: 38
  12. Salmasius was "a person of considerable learning" with "extensive acquaintance" with Hebrew, Arabic and Persian. pp. 152–153 [PDF 177–178]. attr: Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge 362
  13. Nagy de Harsany treated the covenant as trustworthy; he was well versed in Oriental languages and perfected his Turkish and Arabic in the Ottoman Empire. pp. 152–153 [PDF 177–178]. fact
  14. Bayle: "Mr. Hinkleman, is of the same opinion with Salmasius; and so was also Sir Paul Ricaut". p. 153 [PDF 178]. attr: Bayle 38
  15. Ricaut: "very good authors" believe it genuine and made "at the time set down at the end of it", when Muhammad's empire was weak and at war with the Arabians and he feared the Christians; "he made this treaty with them in the monastery of the monks of Mount Carmel, from whence these austere friars derive their name". p. 153 [PDF 178]. attr: Ricaut, qtd. Bayle 1737: 38
  16. Renaudot accepted it as genuine. He knew Arabic from his youth, examined the original manuscript at the Bibliothèque nationale, and left notes on it. p. 153 [PDF 178]. attr: Rehatsek 98; fact
  17. Treated as factual by Layard, Pedro de Madrazo, the Société d'Amis de la Religion et de la Patrie, and James Thayer Addison; Madrazo saw it as an example of Islamic tolerance. p. 153 [PDF 178]. attr: Layard 207; Madrazo 123
  18. Annales de la Religion: "history has preserved a treaty of Muhammad with the Christians which protects their religious property for he was less cruel in establishing his false religion than our persecutors have been to destroy the true one". p. 153 [PDF 178]. attr: Société d'Amis 112–113
  19. Bayle's summary of Dr. Addison: one of "Mahomet's artifices to support his authority"; once established, he "changed his language, and added several chapters to his Koran" denouncing death, imprisonment and slavery against infidels, "by which expression he particularly meant the Christians". p. 153 [PDF 178]. attr: Bayle 241
  20. Grassi describes the Prophet as "the greatest of geniuses" (66) and the Testament as "a political and moral masterpiece" (75). p. 153 [PDF 178]. attr: Grassi
  21. Grassi: "Most historians, all of whom are Christian, have viewed Muhammad with the kind of contempt that only an impostor ... can inspire". p. 153 [PDF 178]. attr: Grassi 66
  22. Grassi: "The Charter of Muhammad only is inviolable ... The laws of this Charter are obligatory for the rich, for the poor, and even for the prince himself". p. 155 [PDF 180]. attr: Grassi (front page)
  23. Miltitz's version "was not a new translation" but "the French translation of the English translation of the original Arabic that had been included in Ricaut's ... Histoire de l'état present de l'empire ottoman (316-358)". pp. 153–154 [PDF 178–179]. fact
  24. Van Dyke's English translation "was made on the basis of the French translation found in Ricaut"; Van Dyke noted it "is considered by many as apocryphal" (87) but "himself believed that it was genuine". p. 154 [PDF 179]. fact; attr: Van Dyke 87
  25. Van Dyke: Muhammad at first proclaimed toleration, "either out of real feelings of toleration ... or through adroit and well-calculated hypocrisy", and "afterwards changed the tone". p. 154 [PDF 179]. attr: Van Dyke 85
  26. Van Dyke refers readers to Muir's Life of Mahommed "[f]or other treaties with the Christians". p. 154 [PDF 179]. attr: Van Dyke 87
  27. Van Dyke, "Plagiarizing Grassi (75)": the treaty is "a masterpiece of political forethought and ... a rare monument of wisdom, morality, and toleration". p. 154 [PDF 179]. attr: Van Dyke 85; author's charge
  28. Basnage de Beauval (review of the 1690 Hamburg edition): "It is true that Grotius doubted it and that it looks like pious fraud. However, Mr. Hinkleman assures us that scholars have set aside their suspicions since the Arabic text was first brought from the East by Father Pacifique Scaliger." p. 158 [PDF 183]. attr: Basnage de Beauval 81–82
  29. Basnage: Hinkleman "is far too well-versed in Oriental languages to be duped". p. 158 [PDF 183]. attr: Basnage
  30. Basnage's summary of content: Muhammad calls himself the Messenger of God; promises to defend Christians, protect and help rebuild churches and monasteries, and exempt them from taxes, on condition they do not give his enemies weapons or an escape route; "it is signed by thirty-three Muslims". p. 158 [PDF 183]. attr: Basnage
  31. Basnage: Muhammad "inserted in his Qur'an favorable sentiments for all religions", declaring that Jews, Christians and others who believe in God and the Last Day and do good "had nothing to fear". p. 158 [PDF 183]. attr: Basnage
  32. Twiss: the term "conditions" in the pact is "perfectly harmonious with the Qur'an" (431), and is also found in the Treaty of 'Umar, "the second oldest Islamic covenant" (432). pp. 159–160 [PDF 184–185]. attr: Twiss
  33. Twiss: if the Testament (625) and the Capitulations of 'Umar (636) were both inauthentic, monks forging them would have avoided language contradicting Muslim law. p. 160 [PDF 185]. attr: Twiss 432
  34. Twiss: the privileges for the People of the Book need not have been a unilateral concession; they could have been "a treaty between two parties". p. 160 [PDF 185]. attr: Twiss 432
  35. Twiss's analysis: both the Testament and the Treaty of 'Umar "show clear signs of authenticity". p. 160 [PDF 185]. attr: Twiss (per author)
I. Reception: neutral figures and opponents
  1. Hottinger "adopted a cautious attitude and remained neutral". p. 156 [PDF 181]. fact
  2. Layard admits a treaty was made between the Prophet and the Nestorians. p. 156 [PDF 181]. attr: Layard 207
  3. Opponents: Hugo Grotius, Gisbertus Voetius, Johannes Hoornbeek, Bespier, Humphrey Prideaux, Pierre Bayle, Ignaz von Döllinger, Johann Lorenz von Mosheim. p. 156 [PDF 181]. fact
  4. Mosheim: those who side with Grotius suppose it "fabricated by the monks living in Syria and Arabia, to circumvent their hard masters"; the Sinai monks had a similar edict "beyond all controversy fraudulently drawn up by themselves" (citing Cantemir, Hist. de l'Empire Ottoman, tome ii, p. 269); the Mohammedans' acceptance proves little since they are "rude and illiterate"; the style argument is weak because Muhammad "might have employed his secretary"; yet "Mohammed originally would allow no injury to be offered to the Christians and especially to the Nestorians". p. 156 [PDF 181]. attr: Mosheim 255
  5. Editor's footnote in Mosheim: "a formal compact between Mohammed on the one part, and the Nestorians and Monophysites on the other"; protection and religious freedom in exchange for loyalty and support; it may have aimed at subduing Asian lands under the Greek emperors. p. 157 [PDF 182]. attr: Mosheim 254–255 (editor)
  6. Döllinger: the Testament brought by Scaliger, "printed in Paris since 1630", and the Sinai document "all shows signs of being fictitious"; they "would have placed Christians in a better position than the Muslims themselves as Tychsen observes" (De Muhammede aliarum religionum sectatores tolerante, T. XV des Mémoires de la société de Goettingue). p. 157 [PDF 182]. attr: Döllinger 291
  7. Döllinger admits that the Prophet made a covenant with the Christians of Najran and with other communities. p. 157 [PDF 182]. attr: Döllinger 291
  8. An Arabic-skilled person, asked by Addison, said the treaty felt spurious, did not resemble the Qur'an, and that the preface said Scaliger brought it from the East; he concluded Scaliger had very probably forged it. p. 157 [PDF 182]. attr: Bayle 241
  9. Jacques: "both the existing documents, the Testamentum and the Pactum Muhammedis, assuring liberal privileges to all Christians, are spurious". p. 158 [PDF 183]. attr: Jacques 203
  10. Gieseler: both documents "are spurious". p. 158 [PDF 183]. attr: Gieseler 563 n. 7
  11. Ricaut: "the Turks deny that this Treaty was made [by] Muhammad with the Christians". p. 161 [PDF 186]. attr: Ricaut 332
  12. Guillaume: "The Pact of Muhammad in Favor of the Christians ... is an apocryphal Arab document" (831 B); "the so-called Treaty or Pact of Muhammad with the Christians" (858 n. 4). p. 155 [PDF 180]. attr: Guillaume
J. French Revolutionary Committee (1795)
  1. 441st session (22 June 1795): a letter from citizen Lefebvre-Villebrune; motion to print the pact "by the printing press of the Republic, in Arabic, along with the French translation", in numbers enough for the consuls in the Ports of the Levant to circulate it in the Ottoman Empire. pp. 154–155 [PDF 179–180]. attr: Guillaume 320
  2. The French "believed that the diffusion of the Pact of Muhammad would help encourage dialogue with the Turks". p. 155 [PDF 180]. fact/inf
  3. 511th session (23 Oct 1795): 1,000 copies by "the printing press of the legal office", for Committee members, all libraries of the Republic, the Ports of the Levant and European scholars; citizen Grégoire assigned the final article. p. 155 [PDF 180]. attr: Guillaume 827
  4. 514th session: Lefebvre-Villebrune removed and replaced by Mr. Legrand; "Apparently" he had removed a manuscript from the National Library. p. 155 [PDF 180]. attr: Guillaume 858 and n. 4
K. Ottomans and Turks
  1. "The Turks, it would seem, never doubted the document", meaning administrators, religious scholars and the Sultan. p. 141 [PDF 166]. inf
  2. Sultan Ibrahim I said the sacred sites had been granted "in time immemorial by Muhammad, himself, to the Greek Christians", and that he "would never violate the clauses of that treaty at any price". p. 141 [PDF 166]. attr: Lamartine 356
  3. Marana's spy: Christians reproach the Turks with violating a treaty "witnesses by our four main legal authorities, Abu Bakr, 'Uthman, and 'Ali" (only three names printed). p. 160 [PDF 185]. attr: Marana 156
  4. Marana's spy lists the privileges (peace, protection, love, exemption from taxes and tribute, freedom of conscience, freedom to marry) and the conditions (no sheltering or corresponding with enemies, no supplying arms, horses or money; receiving Muslims for three days; defending them). If Christians break these, the treaty is void. pp. 160–161 [PDF 185–186]. attr: Marana 156–157
  5. Marana was "a Marrano or a Jewish person who had been compelled to convert to Christianity". p. 160 [PDF 185]. fact
  6. The novel's purpose was to present a Turkish Muslim view of Europe and the Orient to Christian readers. p. 160 [PDF 185]. fact
  7. Marana's spy writes to "Abrahim Eli Zeid, the 'prédicateur du Serrail' or Imam of the Ottoman Porte". p. 160 [PDF 185]. attr: Marana
  8. "the vast majority of sources insist that they [the Turks] recognized it as trustworthy". p. 161 [PDF 186]. fact/inf
L. Scribe, date and related hypotheses
  1. The Najran and World covenants "were both written in the hand of Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan"; the Sinai covenant was not. p. 147 [PDF 172]. fact
  2. The Najran covenant has no date; the World covenant is dated 2 Rabi' Ashar, 4 AH. p. 147 [PDF 172]. fact
  3. The Najran covenant has thirty witnesses; the World covenant (1630) has thirty-six. p. 147 [PDF 172]. fact
  4. Selim I "was a nasibi, namely, one who is hostile towards the Household of the Prophet". p. 147 [PDF 172]. fact (author)
  5. Agoston: Ottoman propaganda portrayed the Shi'ite Safavids as "'heretics' and even 'infidels'"; since the Sunni Mamluks cooperated with them, war on the Mamluks was justified too. p. 147 [PDF 172]. attr: Agoston 93
  6. Wheatcroft: for Selim I the Safavids were "worse than the infidel", their subjects "more worthy of death than any number of Christians". p. 147 [PDF 172]. attr: Wheatcroft 50
  7. Selim's Egyptian campaign was endorsed on the grounds that "he who aids a heretic is himself a heretic". p. 147 [PDF 172]. attr: Finkel 109
  8. "many of the other covenants which remain in existence include Imam 'Ali ... as the scribe and primary witness". p. 147 [PDF 172]. fact (refers to earlier chapters)
  9. Goldziher: Umayyads "actively pursued a program of political propaganda in which hadith forgery played an important role". p. 148 [PDF 173]. attr: Brown 206
  10. Umayyad forgeries "revolved around their conflict with the partisans of Imam 'Ali and did not necessarily extend to ... foreign policy and the treatment of minorities". p. 148 [PDF 173]. inf
M. Content of the 1630 text (as quoted and translated by the author)
  1. It does not open with the basmalah. p. 162 [PDF 187]. fact
  2. Opening: "It was written by Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, the proclaimer and warner [bashiran wa nadhiran], to all the people [al-nas kaffah], ... [wadi'at Allah] ... a proof [hujjah] of Allah for the Christian religion [din al-nasraniyyah] in the eastern land and its west, its Arabs and non-Arabs [fasihiha wa 'ajamiha], near or far, known or unknown." p. 162 [PDF 187]. fact (quote)
  3. Renderings of wadi'at Allah: Van Dyke "emanated from God"; Pococke "careful guardian of the whole world"; Arundale "confidant of God, and charged with the keeping of all created beings"; M. Mauchin's rendering in Baron Marie-Joseph de Géramb "the friend of God, and that he is charged with the care of all his creatures"; Skrobucha "promises of God"; Anton F. Haddad "as a trust on the part of God". p. 162 [PDF 187]. attr: these translators
  4. Self-description: "This document [kitaban] ... constitutes an authoritative covenant ['ahdan mar'iyyan], a well-known certificate [sijlan manshuran], and a testament [wasiyyah]". p. 162 [PDF 187]. fact (quote)
  5. Violation clause: whoever breaks it "has violated the covenant of Allah ['ahd Allah], denies the oath of Allah [mithaq Allah] and has disdained his protection [dhimmah] whether he is a Sultan or anyone else". pp. 162–163 [PDF 187–188]. fact (quote)
  6. The covenant answered a request: "granted alliances ['uhud] and pledges [mawathiq] to those who requested it"; Christians placed under the safeguard of "His Prophets, His Chosen Ones [asfiya'], His Friends [awliya']". p. 163 [PDF 188]. fact (quote)
  7. Protection clause: the Prophet protects "their judges in my fortified borderlines [fi thughuri]", churches and places of pilgrimage [siyahah] everywhere, by land or sea, East or West, "the same way that I protect myself, my successors [khatimi], and the People of my Community [ahl al-millati]". p. 163 [PDF 188]. fact (quote)
  8. khatimi "literally means 'rings' or 'seals'"; Qur'an 33:40 is cited. p. 163 [PDF 188]. fact
  9. "ascribed authority [nisbatu al-amr]": the Arabic linguists the author consulted derived it from nasaba/yansubu, "to ascribe", and said it was "mostly used in Shi'ite texts". p. 164 [PDF 189]. attr: unnamed Arabic linguists
  10. Economic clause: no harm from taxes and loans ['ariyah] or land tribute [kharaj], "except what they themselves consent to give". p. 164 [PDF 189]. fact (quote)
  11. Bishops, Christians, monks, pilgrims and hermit monks may not be removed; churches may not be destroyed or their materials used for mosques or Muslim homes. p. 164 [PDF 189]. fact (quote)
  12. "[i]t is not permitted to impose a capitation [jizyah] or any kind of tax on monks or bishops only that which they are prepared to give willingly". p. 164 [PDF 189]. fact (quote)
  13. Wealthy Christians (owners of large businesses, divers, miners of precious stones, gold and silver) pay jizyah of at most "twelve dirhams per year", if they are residents and not travellers. pp. 164–165 [PDF 189–190]. fact (quote)
  14. Travellers, and residents whose place is unknown, owe no kharaj or jizyah unless they inherited land over which the ruler [sultan] has a right. p. 165 [PDF 190]. fact (quote)
  15. Labourers who cultivate the lands "are not to be taxed excessively". p. 165 [PDF 190]. fact (quote)
  16. Ahl al-dhimmah will not be obliged to go to war with the Muslims, or to give horses or arms unless they do so freely. p. 165 [PDF 190]. fact (quote)
  17. "No Christian will be made Muslim by force", citing Qur'an 29:46 within the text. p. 165 [PDF 190]. fact (quote)
  18. If a Christian commits a crime, Muslims must help, defend and protect him, and encourage the victim to pardon him or take compensation. p. 165 [PDF 190]. fact (quote)
  19. Muslims must not abandon Christians; "whatever good befell Muslims it would befall them as well". p. 165 [PDF 190]. fact (quote)
  20. Muslims must help repair churches and convents, not for reward but "by pure donation". p. 166 [PDF 191]. fact (quote)
  21. Christian girls must not be married against their parents' will; a Muslim husband must respect his Christian wife's religion and let her listen to her clerical superiors; whoever forces her "will enter into open rebellion" and is counted "among the impostors". p. 166 [PDF 191]. fact (quote)
  22. In war, no Christian may be employed as "messenger, scout, guide or spy"; whoever compels one is an "oppressor [zalim]". p. 166 [PDF 191]. fact (quote)
  23. Christians' obligations: not to spy for or shelter enemies, not to let them halt in their villages or oratories, not to supply weapons, horses or men, "including greeting them"; to host Muslims "for three days and three nights" with their animals and give them the same food; to hide a Muslim fugitive. p. 167 [PDF 192]. fact (quote)
  24. "[t]his must not be violated or altered until the hour [of the Resurrection] and the end of the world [dunya]"; unlike other covenants, it does not include insha' Allah. p. 167 [PDF 192]. fact
  25. Closes with a witness list; the scribe writes "Allah suffices as a Witness for what is contained in this document"; then praises drawn from Surah al-Fatihah. p. 167 [PDF 192]. fact
N. Content of the 1538 text
  1. Opens "In the Name of Allah, the Creator [al-Khaliq], the Living [al-Hayy], the Speaking [al-Natiq], the One who Remains after the Annihilation of Creation [al-Baqi ba'd fana' al-khaliq]". pp. 168–169 [PDF 193–194]. fact
  2. "This is a copy [nuskhah] of the covenant ['Ahd] which was written by Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib for all the Christians [nasara]"; subtitle "Copy of the Covenant [kitab al-'Ahd]". p. 169 [PDF 194]. fact (quote)
  3. Addressed "to all the Christians and all the monks"; blesses the Prophet "and his family [alihi]"; "written by the Lion [asad] and the People of His Vocation"; uses da'wat al-nasraniyyah; "a justice ['adl] and tradition [sunnah]". p. 169 [PDF 194]. fact (quote)
  4. 'Ali, not Muhammad, "bore the title the Lion of Allah", and is so called in the Covenant of 'Ali with the Armenian Nation. p. 169 [PDF 194]. fact
  5. The scribe "transcribed this covenant into 'Uthmani script from its primitive predecessor". p. 169 [PDF 194]. fact/inf
  6. Violation clause adds "disdains his religion, and merits His Maledictions". p. 169 [PDF 194]. fact (quote)
  7. Qur'an citations: 28:8 [as printed], 5:1, 3:76, 16:91, 61:2-3, 17:34, 13:25. p. 169 [PDF 194]. fact
  8. Protection clause uses "my entourage [khassati]" where 1630 has khatimi, along with "my Muslim followers [atba'i]", "land [ard]", "monasteries [al-diyar]", "businesses" and "houses of worship". p. 170 [PDF 195]. fact
  9. Shi'ites call Sunnis the 'ammah and themselves the khassah. p. 170 [PDF 195]. fact
  10. "I sacrifice myself for them ... because they are my flock [ra'iyyah]"; the shepherd image may be "the gloss of a Christian scribe". p. 170 [PDF 195]. fact (quote); inf
  11. Ascetics [zahid] are protected; no jizyah or kharaj on monks, bishops, or worshippers "who, by devotion, wear woolen clothing [al-suf] or live alone in the mountains". p. 171 [PDF 196]. fact (quote)
  12. Jizyah on non-clerics [man la yata'abbad], other than the monk and pilgrim, is "four dirhams per year or an inexpensive cloak [tawb]"; the poor are helped from the Treasury [bayt al-mal]. p. 171 [PDF 196]. fact (quote)
  13. Wealthy Christians pay at most "twelve dirhams [fiddah]" ("twelve silver dirhams"). p. 171 [PDF 196]. fact
  14. What Muslims borrow (arms, horses) "will be guaranteed by the [State] Treasury"; if lost or damaged, the Treasury compensates. pp. 171–172 [PDF 196–197]. fact (quote)
  15. Muslims must pay a Christian offender's penalty. p. 172 [PDF 197]. fact (quote)
  16. A man who forces his Christian wife against her religion "will be counted, by us, among the liars [kadhibin]". p. 172 [PDF 197]. fact (quote)
  17. Whoever employs a Christian in war "will be unjust [zaliman] towards Allah, disobedient ['asiyan] to His Messenger, and will be cast out [mutakhalliyan] from his religion". p. 172 [PDF 197]. fact (quote)
  18. Additional conditions: Christians "must not annoy them and they should be honored as long as they persist in their religion". p. 173 [PDF 198]. fact (quote)
  19. Added hadith: "Whoever is unjust after this towards a [Christian] subject [dhimmi], breaks the covenant and rejects it, I will be his enemy on the Day of Judgment". The author says this is "virtually identical" to a saying in the Sunan of Abu Dawud: "Whoever oppresses non-Muslim subjects shall find me to be their advocate on the Day of Judgment". p. 173 [PDF 198]. fact; attr: Abu Dawud
  20. Thirty witnesses (see §5). p. 173 [PDF 198]. fact
  21. "Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote this covenant." p. 174 [PDF 199]. fact (quote)
  22. "[t]he manuscript [sijl] was written on a piece of leather [jild] that was not small. It remained at the Sultan's authority and was sealed by the Prophet". p. 174 [PDF 199]. fact (quote)
  23. The Najran covenant also says it was written on leather. p. 174 [PDF 199]. fact
  24. Colophon: the "blessed book" belongs to "the great soul ... the master ... the leader ... the elder ... the scholar, Sim'an, the son of ... Fadl Allah ... known as al-Barallusi"; the writer asks readers to mention them in prayers, and "the Messiah [masih] will reward them one hundred and sixty three times". p. 174 [PDF 199]. fact (quote)
  25. The final note seems addressed to "Michel"; some of the author's Arab colleagues read yasilu ("ask") instead. p. 175 [PDF 200]. attr: author's colleagues
  26. "there is currently no complete copy of the Qur'an which dates to the time of the Prophet". p. 174 [PDF 199]. fact (author)
O. Other covenants and comparisons
  1. The 1630 content "corresponds closely" with the Najran covenant "found in the Chronicle of Seert, an ancient history compiled by Nestorian Christians". p. 146 [PDF 171]. fact
  2. The Najran and World covenants differ "in structure, vocabulary, and content". p. 147 [PDF 172]. fact
  3. The Sinai covenant has a handprint of the Prophet. p. 141 [PDF 166]. fact (implied)
  4. The 1538 leather and seal details are "very similar to those found on the Covenant ... with the Monks of Mount Sinai". p. 174 [PDF 199]. fact
  5. The 1538 witnesses "overlap with the Sinai and Najran covenants". p. 173 [PDF 198]. fact
  6. "As with the patents the Prophet provided to different Jewish communities, no two treaties were identical". p. 175 [PDF 200]. fact/inf
  7. Like the Sinai covenant, the World covenant "is not directly addressed to a particular community". p. 175 [PDF 200]. fact
P. Other claims
  1. Ibn Ishaq and other traditionists report the "two religions" saying; Hamidullah accepts it but limits it to "certain insubordinate populations". p. 154 [PDF 179]. attr: Ibn Ishaq 689; Hamidullah, Introduction 150
  2. Jews and Christians lived in the Hijaz for centuries afterwards, "even in such sacred sites such as Medina and Mecca". p. 154 [PDF 179]. attr: Hamidullah 150 ("History confirms")
  3. "The term kuffar or infidels, as employed in the Qur'an, applies to polytheists and not Christians." p. 154 [PDF 179]. fact (author)
  4. Bolívar and Martí "spoke of the superiority of the Qur'an over the American Constitution". p. 155 [PDF 180]. fact (no citation)
  5. Christian printers "were prepared to print anything that was profitable". p. 150 [PDF 175]. fact/inf
  6. Bibliander (publisher) and J. Fabricius (compiler) "were Calvinists", showing the "increased importance of the study of Islam among the reformists". p. 150 [PDF 175]. attr: Santiago-Otero 409
  7. Moriscos used Protestant arguments against Catholics; Protestants used Islamic arguments against Catholics. p. 150 [PDF 175]. fact
  8. Mamdani exposed the "good Muslim" versus "bad Muslim" dichotomy. p. 161 [PDF 186]. attr: Mamdani
  9. The "so-called Muslim rulers of Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Egypt, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, and the United Arab Emirates" side with the US and Western Europe against independent Muslim nations. p. 161 [PDF 186]. inf (opinion)
  10. Shi'ite belief: after prophethood ended, "the gate of the Imamate was opened", from 'Ali to Muhammad al-Mahdi, "the last of twelve". p. 164 [PDF 189]. fact
  11. For Shi'ites the People of the House (33:33) are the Purified Five: the Prophet, Fatimah, 'Ali, Hasan and Husayn. p. 163 [PDF 188]. fact
  12. Shi'ites treat 'adl as "the second pillar of Islam after tawhid". p. 169 [PDF 194]. fact
  13. Atba' / tabi'in properly means the followers of the Companions, not the Companions (ashab). p. 170 [PDF 195]. fact

5. Covenant details by version

5a. The 1630 printed version (Sionita / Vitray, Paris)
  • Names: al-'Ahd wa al-shurut allati sharataha Muhammad rasul Allah li ahl al-millah al-nasraniyyah; Testamentum et pactiones; Testamentum Mahometi; Treaty / Patent / Testament of Muhammad (pp. 139, 146, 149, 151).
  • Claimed date: "the second day of the month of Rabi' Ashar of the fourth year after the hijrah" (p. 147). The CE equivalent is not given by the author; his sources give 626 (Hinckelmann via Basnage, p. 158) and 625 (Twiss, pp. 159–160).
  • Place issued: not stated in the document as quoted. Ricaut (qtd. Bayle) says the treaty was made "in the monastery of the monks of Mount Carmel" (p. 153). The author says it was "supposedly" made with the Monastery of Mount Carmel (p. 164).
  • Scribe: Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan (p. 147). The author's verdict is that the scribe and the date are "almost certainly Umayyad additions" (p. 167).
  • Witnesses: thirty-six (p. 147); individual names are not listed in this chapter. Basnage's review of the 1690 Hamburg edition: "signed by thirty-three Muslims" (p. 158). Marana's spy: "four main legal authorities, Abu Bakr, 'Uthman, and 'Ali" (p. 160). Author: the list "with a few exceptions, seems reasonably sound, but ... was probably appended to it to appease hadith scholars" (p. 167).
  • Recipients: all Christians, "in the eastern land and its west, its Arabs and non-Arabs, near or far, known or unknown" (p. 162).
  • Opening/closing: no basmalah, which the author takes as Sionita's editorial suppression (p. 162). The text closes with "Allah suffices as a Witness" and praises from al-Fatihah (p. 167).
  • Source manuscript: brought by Scaliger in 1629; passed to the King, Hotman and Sionita; "eventually" in the King's library (pp. 142–143). The author identifies it with BnF Arabe 214 (p. 145), but hedges later (pp. 168, 176).
  • Publication: Paris 1630, Arabic and Latin. Credited as "published by Gabriel Sionita" (Fortescue, Layard), "Published ... by Antoine Vitray" (p. 146), or "edited ... by Antoine Vitray by Louis XIII with the collaboration of Gabriel Sionite" (Balagna). Printed without full vocalisation. Four reprints in the first year. Later editions in 1638, 1655, 1668, 1690 (Hamburg) and 1888. French translation by Scaliger in 1631; Nissel's vocalised edition; translations into Latin, French and German; French translation in Ricaut (1670); Nagy de Harsany's French translation; English translation of 1688; Lefebvre-Villebrune's French translation (1795, never printed); Grassi 1826; Miltitz 1838 (French from the English in Ricaut); Van Dyke 1881 (English from the French in Ricaut). Other renderings cited: Pococke, Arundale, Mauchin/Géramb, Skrobucha, Haddad.
  • Copy consulted by the author: a copy of Sionita's edition with invocations handwritten by Valerianus Oserole in 1659 (p. 151).
  • Text quality: the author finds its Arabic inferior to the 1538 text, with words "modified, thus completely changing the meaning" (pp. 146, 168).
  • Lexical notes (author): ahli ("families"), khatimi ("seals" → "successors"), nisbatu al-amr, which may indicate passage through "Levantine Shi'ites" (pp. 163–164).
5b. The 1538 manuscript version (BnF MS Arabe 214)

  • Names: "Charte accordée à tous les chrétiens, par Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib" (BnF index); "Copy [nuskhah] of the Covenant [kitab al-'Ahd]"; the "Pact of Muhammad in Favor of the Christian[s]" (Guillaume) (pp. 144, 145, 169).

  • Copy dates: "1254 of the Martyrs (1538 CE)". Partial completion dates 26 and 28 "Basnas" and 3 Ba'una 1254 (catalogue). Colophon: Monday, last month of Ba'una, = 27 Muharram 945 AH (author: "945 AH [1538 CE]") (pp. 144, 174).

  • Claimed date of issue: none quoted for the 1538 text. The author says it "may represent a Covenant ... with the Christians of Egypt" (p. 168).

  • Scribe of the covenant: "Ali ibn Abi Talib ... wrote this covenant" (p. 174). The text also says it was "written by the Lion [asad]" (p. 169).

  • Copyist: Girgis al-Ifrangi (George, Jacobite, "of European origin"), for the library of Yuhanna ibn Ishaq al-Batanuni (pp. 144, 175).

  • Owner: Sim'an ibn Fadl ("Fadi") Allah al-Barallusi; the author says "almost certainly a Christian" (pp. 174–175).

  • Other marks: Renaudot (note); Vansleb (seals); Girgis ibn Yuhanna al-Tamawi; Butrus ibn Diyab al-Halabi (1673); Mansur ibn Sulayman Sahyun al-Ramadi (1620); missionary to Old Cairo (1592); Gabriyal Sahyun al-Ziftawi, whom the author identifies as Sionita (pp. 144–145).

  • Location: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Department of Manuscripts; Arabe 214, formerly 385 (Regius) and Ancient Arab Collection 88. Bound 13 April 1872 (pp. 144, 146).

  • Folio location (conflicting): ff. 245–246 (de Slane via Guillaume); "Fol. 245" (catalogue); "F. 257-261" (BnF index); "sheets 257 to 262, that is, the last eleven pages" (author); "the last folio" (p. 168).

  • Recipients: "all the Christians and all the monks"; "all those who profess the Christian religion [da'wat al-nasraniyyah] in the Eastern lands and its West" (p. 169).

  • Physical form claimed in the text: written on "a piece of leather [jild] that was not small", kept "at the Sultan's authority", "sealed by the Prophet" (p. 174).

  • Witnesses (30; the author says "thirty", p. 173), as printed, in order:

    1. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq
    2. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab
    3. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan
    4. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib
    5. Abu Dharr
    6. Abu al-Darda'
    7. Abu Hurayrah
    8. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud
    9. al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Malik
    10. Fadi [Fadl?] ibn al-'Abbas al-Zahri
    11. Talhah ibn 'Abd Allah
    12. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh
    13. Sa'd ibn Ubadah
    14. Thabit ibn Qays
    15. Yazid ibn Talit
    16. 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid
    17. Farsus ibn Qasim ibn Badr ibn Ibrahim
    18. Amir ibn Zarib
    19. Sahl ibn Tamim
    20. 'Abd al-'Azim (the handwriting changes here)
    21. 'Abd al-'Azim ibn Husayn
    22. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As
    23. 'Ammar ibn Yasir
    24. Mu'azzam ibn Musa
    25. Hassan ibn Thabit
    26. Abu Hanifah
    27. 'Ubayd ibn Mansur
    28. Hashim ibn 'Abd Allah
    29. Abu al-'Azir
    30. Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib

    The BnF catalogue (via Guillaume) says "approximately thirty Companions" (p. 144).

  • Distinctive content compared with 1630 (author): Sufi-style divine names; blessing on the Prophet's family; 'adl and sunnah; khassati; atba'i; zahid; wool-wearers; 4 dirhams or a cloak for ordinary Christians; "twelve silver dirhams"; Treasury guarantee for borrowed goods; Muslims pay an offender's penalty; stronger adjectives (liars, unjust, outcasts); added hadith; 'Ali as scribe; leather and seal note; colophon; "Michel" note (pp. 168–175).

  • Publication: "never been previously published" (p. 146). The author's translation appears in this chapter.

5c. Related covenants mentioned
  • Najran covenant: in the Chronicle of Seert (Nestorian, 9th century); "discovered in a monastery in Iraq in 878 CE"; undated; scribe Mu'awiyah; 30 witnesses; written on leather (pp. 146–147, 168, 174).
  • Covenant with the Assyrian Christians: signed in the same year, 4 AH (p. 147).
  • Sinai covenant (Pactum Muhammedis): handprint; Mosheim and Döllinger call it fraudulent (pp. 141, 156–157).
  • Covenant of 'Ali with the Armenian Nation: earliest copies from the 18th century (p. 169).
  • Treaty of 'Umar (Capitulations of 'Umar): 636 (Twiss); alludes to an earlier covenant (Féraud-Giraud) (pp. 152, 160).
5d. The author's authenticity verdict and arguments

Verdict: a "distinct treaty" from the Najran covenant, "apparently produced during the same period"; its variants "are evidence of authenticity as opposed to forgery" (p. 175). The scribe and the date are later (Umayyad) additions (p. 167). The witness lists were "attached posthumously" (p. 174). He leaves open whether the 1538 text is the forerunner of the 1630 text (p. 176).

Arguments for authenticity / against forgery by Scaliger:

  1. Scaliger lacked the Arabic and Islamic learning to forge it (pp. 142–143).
  2. Scaliger was saintly and pious, with no motive, and could not fool the King's scholars (p. 143).
  3. The covenant could not help convert Muslims and seems "better suited to attract Christians to Islam" (p. 143).
  4. Christians were well treated under the Ottomans, so there was no need for a protective forgery (p. 143).
  5. The 1538 manuscript predates Scaliger by nearly a century, so he "absolutely and categorically did not forge" it (p. 145).
  6. Its previous owners and readers treated it as genuine (p. 145).
  7. Bar Hebraeus, Maris and Amrus attest its substance, so Scaliger "could not have invented something that already existed" (p. 152).
  8. Sultan Ibrahim I referred to a treaty "as old as historical memory" (p. 141).
  9. The Muslims accepted it (Mosheim, Layard, Luke) (pp. 151–152).
  10. The style differs from the Qur'an because the Prophet used different genres; the Qur'an is not "the product of Muhammad's mind and pen" (pp. 157–158).
  11. Hinckelmann, an Arabic expert, reported that scholars' doubts subsided (pp. 158–159).
  12. The 4 AH timing fits the conflict with the Jews and the need for Christian buffers against Byzantium (p. 159).
  13. Twiss: the term "conditions" fits the Qur'an and the Treaty of 'Umar; forgers would not have produced terms contrary to Muslim law (pp. 159–160).
  14. Forgers under the Fatimids would not have named Companions viewed unfavourably, nor asked for tax exemptions (p. 160).
  15. A text that is not addressed to a specific community and asks for little is unlike a forgery; such forgeries "would have been detected, denounced, and duly punished" (pp. 175–176).
  16. Similar but non-identical texts point to a common origin (p. 175).
  17. Late copies do not imply forgery (the Bukhari and Qur'an analogies) (p. 174).

Counter-arguments he addresses:

  • Ricaut's location story → rejected as geographically impossible (p. 140).
  • Bayle 1735: Scaliger forged it → rejected (pp. 142–143).
  • Grotius and others: fabricated by monks of Syria and Arabia → the author calls them prejudiced (pp. 156–157).
  • Mosheim: Muslim acceptance is worthless because they are "illiterate" → called "racist and prejudiced" (pp. 156–157).
  • The style argument (Addison's informant; the opposers in Mosheim) → "amateurish" (pp. 157–158).
  • Brought by Scaliger, therefore forged → "does not constitute proof of forgery" (p. 158).
  • Döllinger and Tychsen: it would put Christians above Muslims → "self-defeating", since Döllinger accepts the Najran covenant (p. 157).
  • Jacques and Gieseler: spurious → attributed to hostility toward Islam (p. 158).
  • Addison and Van Dyke: a temporary tactic later reversed → "evidently incorrect"; kuffar refers to polytheists (p. 154).
  • Layard and Luke's picture of opinion → "slanted" and "factually incorrect" (p. 156).
  • Guillaume: "apocryphal" → read as a shift in attitudes after the Revolution (p. 155).
  • Mu'awiyah as scribe in 4 AH is anachronistic (he converted c. 8 AH) → explained as a later alteration (pp. 147, 167, 174).
  • A copy dated 945 AH is a millennium late → it is "simply a copy" (p. 174).

6. The author's key arguments and opinions

  1. The Mount Carmel / "one day from Mecca" story (Ricaut) is geographically impossible: "this leads to absolutely nowhere of significance". Ricaut "most certainly" miscalculated. p. 140 [PDF 165]
  2. Scaliger may have found it in a Greek Orthodox monastery such as Mar Saba rather than a Carmelite house. p. 140 [PDF 165]
  3. It is "astonishing" that scholars repeated Ricaut's details as fact when Ricaut himself doubted them; for centuries they "quoted Ricaut out of context". p. 140 [PDF 165]
  4. Scaliger's wording ("fell into my hands") suggests it "was given to him"; his account of the 1628 persecution "almost seems like he provides a justification for its falsification", and the referent of "he" (Sultan or Prophet) is unclear. p. 141 [PDF 166]
  5. Christians traditionally brought out a covenant of the Prophet when persecuted. p. 141 [PDF 166]
  6. The Ottomans may have been the ones who gave Scaliger a copy, possibly as a gift from Sultan Murad to the French King. pp. 141–142 [PDF 166–167]
  7. Scaliger, the King, Hotman and Sionita all believed the covenant authentic. p. 142 [PDF 167]
  8. "I remain convinced that Father Pacifique Scaliger ... did indeed discover the covenant in a monastery in the Middle East, most probably in the Levant." p. 142 [PDF 167]
  9. "I also refuse to accept the allegation that Father Pacifique Scaliger had personally forged the manuscript." pp. 142–143 [PDF 167–168]
  10. Scaliger "does not, in my opinion, fit the profile of a person who would perpetuate a religious fraud". p. 143 [PDF 168]
  11. "If the Covenant ... is known to the world today, it is because of the efforts of Gabriel Sionita." p. 143 [PDF 168]
  12. A gifted or lucky collector may have obtained a copy for the King. p. 143 [PDF 168]
  13. The King must have regarded the Testament as "a crown jewel" of his collection. p. 144 [PDF 169]
  14. Only the author actually examined the BnF document. p. 144 [PDF 169]
  15. MS Arabe 214 is Scaliger's document and the source of Sionita's edition (the Sionita mark, the chronology). p. 145 [PDF 170]
  16. 1538 matters because of the 1536 capitulations: it was "the opportune moment for French Catholics to stake their claims to the Holy Land" with a covenant in hand, but the French did not fabricate it. pp. 145–146 [PDF 170–171]
  17. Its inclusion in an apologetic anthology does not make it fake: "Its inclusion thus makes perfect rational sense." p. 146 [PDF 171]
  18. The 1538 and 1630 versions differ in beginning and end. Covenants of the Prophet seem to have degraded over time rather than improved; the author asks why Nissel did not call Sionita out. p. 146 [PDF 171]
  19. The Najran and World covenants are "two different patents of protection", not one text altered. p. 147 [PDF 172]
  20. Selim I, a nasibi, might have replaced 'Ali's name with Mu'awiyah's; more probably the Umayyads did; or "God forbid" Mu'awiyah forged the covenants himself. p. 147 [PDF 172]
  21. Tolerance in Islam "was not aberrant or abnormal ...: it was normative." p. 148 [PDF 173]
  22. The 1630 edition was aimed "primarily at the Christians who inhabited the Ottoman Empire", but there was also a European market. p. 150 [PDF 175]
  23. Islamic ideas of tolerance "seem to have influenced" French kings such as Henri IV (Edict of Nantes). p. 150 [PDF 175]
  24. French conversions to Islam should not be dismissed as "conversions of convenience". pp. 150–151 [PDF 175–176]
  25. Valerianus Oserole may have been a convert to Islam. p. 151 [PDF 176]
  26. Scaliger sent the covenant to the King "in good faith"; he believed, or was told, that it was genuine. p. 152 [PDF 177]
  27. Renaudot is a weightier witness because he examined the original manuscript. p. 153 [PDF 178]
  28. The "Let not two religions be left" saying was attributed to the Prophet "post-factum". p. 154 [PDF 179]
  29. Van Dyke was "reacting" to the Greek war of independence and "projecting the alleged Turkish oppression of the Greeks back to the Prophet". p. 154 [PDF 179]
  30. Guillaume's disdain reflects "a shift of conscience" from Catholic kingdom to secular Republic; "so long as Muslims were powerful, they were treated with respect ... it is power and wealth that inspire respect." pp. 155–156 [PDF 180–181]
  31. Layard's statement is "slanted" and Luke's claim "factually incorrect". p. 156 [PDF 181]
  32. The arguments of Mosheim and his predecessors "are all based on prejudice"; Mosheim expresses "overtly racist and prejudiced views of Arabs and Turks". He undermines himself in a "volte-face", and an editor's footnote "further emasculates his arguments". pp. 156–157 [PDF 181–182]
  33. Döllinger's argument is "self-defeating"; he "was ignorant of the text" of the Najran covenant. p. 157 [PDF 182]
  34. The style-based arguments against the covenant are "amateurish". p. 157 [PDF 182]
  35. Scholars hostile to Islam reject any evidence that contradicts their stereotypes (Jacques, Gieseler). p. 158 [PDF 183]
  36. Hinckelmann's expert opinion "far outweighs" non-experts; he attests that critics changed their minds and reached "a consensus concerning the covenant's authenticity". pp. 158–159 [PDF 183–184]
  37. The Prophet used treaties with Christians as buffers against Byzantium and to win over Monophysites; this was "strategic intelligence", not duplicity (the "render unto Caesar" analogy). p. 159 [PDF 184]
  38. Tax exemptions "were a small price to pay to slow down the potential progress of enemy forces". p. 159 [PDF 184]
  39. Twiss's arguments are "impressive": the Treaty of 'Umar was influenced by the Testament, which was influenced by the Qur'an. p. 160 [PDF 185]
  40. Marana may have seen the original in the Royal Library; his novel suggests some Christians held the Testament over the Turks, and that some Turks doubted it. pp. 160–161 [PDF 185–186]
  41. The covenants "apply only and exclusively to People of the Book who are peaceful". They "remain authoritative and applicable until the Day of Judgment", and Muslims would demand reciprocal rights for Muslim minorities. pp. 161–162 [PDF 186–187]
  42. The basmalah's absence in 1630 is probably Sionita's editorial choice. p. 162 [PDF 187]
  43. wadi'at Allah signifies "that the Christians are Allah's trust among His Creations". p. 162 [PDF 187]
  44. wasiyyah shows that the covenant was not a fleeting, revocable accord. p. 162 [PDF 187]
  45. ahli and khatimi suggest a Shi'ite reading (the Seals of the Imamate), which "could serve as further evidence of the legitimacy of the Imamate". The 1630 copy may have passed through Levantine Shi'ite hands. pp. 163–164 [PDF 188–189]
  46. The Prophet's protection extended outside Muslim lands; he would have defended the Armenians against the Byzantines. p. 163 [PDF 188]
  47. Opposing the accord "would be an act of apostasy"; Muslims represent the Prophet by keeping it. p. 164 [PDF 189]
  48. Believers should stand together "in opposition to atheism", and against "the secular New World Order". pp. 165–166 [PDF 190–191]
  49. Religions are "ecosystems"; there is no place for syncretism; certain mixed marriages cause conflict. p. 166 [PDF 191]
  50. The Umayyad-to-Ottoman ban on church repair "was un-Islamic and in clear contradiction of the covenants of the Prophet". p. 166 [PDF 191]
  51. The war-service clause "prohibits coercion and allows for exceptions in case of voluntary service" (Mu'awiyah's navy). p. 167 [PDF 192]
  52. "Allah suffices as a Witness" implies that "the document is authentic regardless of the chain of authorities". p. 167 [PDF 192]
  53. Sionita's edition is "inferior to the source covenant". Either "Sionita's Arabic was not up to par" or his "corrections" backfired. p. 168 [PDF 193]
  54. The 1538 opening formula and the term al-asad reflect Sufi and Shi'ite influence. The 1538 formula "was probably absent from the original". p. 169 [PDF 194]
  55. Breaking covenants is "a mortal sin which merits eternal damnation" (Qur'an citations). p. 169 [PDF 194]
  56. The 1538 lexicon is "richer", "more precise", "of greater lucidity"; khassati makes more sense than khatimi. p. 170 [PDF 195]
  57. The wool-wearers clause "almost appears like an allusion to the Sufis", as if foreshadowing Umayyad decline; the Umayyads' "heirs ... are the present-day Gulf Arabs". p. 171 [PDF 196]
  58. "twelve silver dirhams" is a "sign of updating of information". p. 171 [PDF 196]
  59. The 1538 witness list is "more difficult to digest". Some witnesses may have been Jews or Christians in delegations to Medina, and the signatories were "attached posthumously". pp. 173–174 [PDF 198–199]
  60. 'Ali as scribe "agrees with the historical record", whereas Mu'awiyah is "as unlikely as it is unpalatable". Sionita may have changed the scribe's name "to appease the Ottomans". p. 174 [PDF 199]
  61. The leather writing surface suggests authorship "during the early Islamic period, prior to the availability of parchment". p. 174 [PDF 199]
  62. The owner Sim'an al-Barallusi "was almost certainly a Christian". p. 175 [PDF 200]
  63. The 1592 missionary may have carried the book "from Egypt to Mount Carmel". p. 175 [PDF 200]
  64. A European long resident in the Middle East could have learned to copy Arabic, so Girgis "al-Ifrangi" could be European. p. 175 [PDF 200]
  65. The final note shows "a Christian cleric, a mysterious Michel", urging that the Covenant be recited in congregational prayer, "mass and liturgy". p. 175 [PDF 200]
  66. The 1538 copy "was clearly not crafted during a period of persecution". p. 175 [PDF 200]
  67. Conclusion: the 1538 text may have been directed to the Coptic Christians of Egypt and the 1630 text to "the Maronites from Palestine"; "It would be premature to come to any definitive conclusions." p. 176 [PDF 201]

7. Internal inconsistencies within this section

  1. Certainty vs. hedging on the 1538 / 1630 identity. p. 145 [PDF 170]: "there is no question that this is the actual document that he [Scaliger] brought back". p. 168 [PDF 193]: "This must, of course, be the source covenant", yet "Or are we dealing with a totally different covenant?" and it "may represent a Covenant ... with the Christians of Egypt". p. 176 [PDF 201]: whether 1538 is the forerunner of 1630 "remains to be determined".
  2. Was it discovered or given? p. 141 [PDF 166]: Scaliger's words suggest "the Covenant was given to him", and "no discovery at all". p. 142 [PDF 167]: "I remain convinced that ... Scaliger ... did indeed discover the covenant in a monastery in the Middle East". p. 142 also says "Whether he received it from Carmelite or Capuchin monks or from the Sultan himself matters little."
  3. Sent vs. delivered in person. p. 142 [PDF 167]: since Scaliger travelled to Paris himself, "there would have been no need for him to send the covenant by courier". p. 152 [PDF 177]: "He sent this covenant to the King of France in good faith". p. 141–142: Scaliger "provided the document to the King" in person.
  4. Who first examined the manuscript. p. 144 [PDF 169]: "no scholar actually bothered to examine the actual document until I came to the scene", and only Guillaume "bothered to check the catalog". p. 153 [PDF 178]: Renaudot "actually went to the Bibliothèque nationale, where he examined the original manuscript" and "left notes to this effect on the manuscript itself". p. 144 also lists "A note by Renaudot" in the catalogue.
  5. Folio numbers of the covenant within Arabe 214. "folios 245-246" and "12° (Fol. 245)" (de Slane/Guillaume, p. 144) vs. "F. 257-261" (BnF index, p. 145) vs. "sheets 257 to 262, that is, the last eleven pages" (p. 146) vs. "the last folio" (p. 168). The catalogue also gives "262 fol. (f. 261 v., 262 v left blank)" and puts the copy-completion colophon at "f. 256 v".
  6. Coptic-era conversions in the catalogue data. The book equates 1254 of the Martyrs with 1538 CE and 1336 of the Martyrs with 1620 CE (both an offset of 284), but 1380 of the Martyrs with 1592 CE (an offset of 212). On the first two offsets, 1380 would not be 1592. The arithmetic uses only the book's own equivalences. p. 144–145 [PDF 169–170]
  7. The 1673 reading mark and Vansleb. The author argues the manuscript was with Sionita in Paris by 1630, so Vansleb could not have bought it in Egypt in 1671/1672 (p. 145). The same catalogue record lists a reading mark of Butrus ibn Diyab al-Halabi "dated 1673 CE" and says "Purchased by Vansleb in the Orient", with Vansleb seals. The author does not reconcile the 1673 mark with his chronology. pp. 144–145 [PDF 169–170]
  8. Who altered the scribe's name. p. 147 [PDF 172]: "possible that the Sultan [Selim I] himself modified the name of the scribe"; "could have been perpetrated by the Ottomans, but most probably by the Umayyads"; or Mu'awiyah himself forged it. p. 167 [PDF 192]: the scribe and date "are almost certainly Umayyad additions". p. 174 [PDF 199]: "Could Gabriel Sionita have changed the name of the scribe in order to appease the Ottomans". These are competing hypotheses.
  9. Status of the 4 AH date. p. 167 [PDF 192]: the date is "almost certainly [an] Umayyad addition". Yet p. 147 [PDF 172] presents it neutrally (the same year as the Assyrian covenant, a time of diplomacy), and p. 159 [PDF 184] says Hinckelmann's use of the 4 AH date "provides some important insight into the timing of the covenant".
  10. CE equivalent of 4 AH. 626 CE (Basnage/Hinckelmann, p. 158) vs. 625 CE (Twiss, pp. 159–160). Both are reported without comment.
  11. Witness counts. 1630 version: thirty-six (p. 147); 1690 Hamburg edition per Basnage: thirty-three (p. 158); 1538: thirty (p. 173), and catalogue "approximately thirty" (p. 144). The Najran covenant: thirty (p. 147). Marana's spy names "four main legal authorities" but lists three (Abu Bakr, 'Uthman, 'Ali) (p. 160).
  12. James Thayer Addison and Bayle. p. 153 [PDF 178] lists "James Thayer Addison (1887-1953 CE)" among those who treat the covenant as factual, then says "A detailed defense of the covenant was also made by Dr. Addison whose arguments were summarized by Bayle". Bayle is dated 1647-1706 in the same paragraph block. The summary itself presents the covenant as one of "Mahomet's artifices", later reversed. p. 154 calls "the views of Dr. Addison ... evidently incorrect". p. 157 reports that Addison's Arabic-skilled informant judged the treaty spurious and likely forged by Scaliger. So Addison is a "defender" in one place and a sceptic in others, and the dates make Bayle summarising a 1887–1953 Addison impossible on the book's own figures.
  13. Ricaut's position. p. 140: Ricaut "himself clearly had doubts". p. 153: Ricaut (via Bayle) "is of the same opinion with Salmasius" that it is genuine. p. 161: Ricaut "claims that 'the Turks deny that this Treaty was made'".
  14. Ricaut's translation language. p. 153–154: Miltitz used "the French translation of the English translation of the original Arabic that had been included in Ricaut's ... Histoire". p. 154: Van Dyke's translation "was made on the basis of the French translation found in Ricaut". p. 151: it "appeared in French translations in historical works, such as Sir Paul Ricaut's ... History of the Ottoman Empire". Whether Ricaut's text was English or French is left unclear.
  15. The Ottoman printing ban vs. the Ottoman press. p. 148 [PDF 173]: printing banned "from 1483 to 1729 CE", but Ibrahim Muteferrika "founded the Ottoman printing press in 1726" (same page).
  16. Date of Scaliger's Levant stay vs. the edicts. p. 141: Scaliger "headed to Syria and Mount Lebanon in 1628", and came across the covenant "between 1627 and 1628". p. 142: Murad IV issued the Capuchin edicts "in April of 1627", "the time when Scaliger ... obtained permission". The 1627 date precedes the stated 1628 arrival.
  17. Scaliger's description vs. the document's date. Scaliger says the Prophet made it "before dying" (p. 141 [PDF 166]), but the 1630 text is dated the fourth year after the hijrah (p. 147). The author does not comment.
  18. Translations of the Arabic title. "...Concluded with the Christian Community" (pp. 139, 149) vs. "...Concluded with His Christian Subjects" (p. 146).
  19. Who published the 1630 edition. "published by Gabriel Sionita" (Fortescue, p. 139; Layard, p. 151; the author, pp. 143, 146, 167) vs. "Published in Paris by Antoine Vitray" (p. 146) vs. "edited ... by Antoine Vitray by Louis XIII with the collaboration of Gabriel Sionite" (Balagna, p. 149). These may be compatible (printer vs. editor), but the attribution varies.
  20. Order of the republication years. Printed as "1655, 1638, 1668, 1690, and as late as 1888" (not chronological). p. 151 [PDF 176]
  21. Salmasius's dates. "d. 1653 CE" (p. 150) vs. "1588 or 1596-1653 CE" (p. 152). Consistent on death, uncertain on birth.
  22. Marana's dates vs. publication. Marana "(1642-1693 CE)"; "This fourth volume ... was published in 1697". p. 160 [PDF 185]. Posthumous publication is not stated.
  23. Ends "differ substantially" vs. "almost identical". p. 168: "both the beginning and the end differ substantially". p. 173: "The final warnings found in the covenant of 1538 are almost identical to those found in 1630". Probably the colophon and witness material vs. the warnings, but the wording is in tension.
  24. The 1630 source said to come from Mount Carmel, yet the conclusion says "Maronites from Palestine". p. 176. Earlier the Mount Carmel provenance is disputed (p. 140), then partly accepted ("could in fact be correct", p. 142). The 1630 text is assigned to "the Maronites from Palestine" without further argument.
  25. Scaliger and French Guiana. The friar's description says Scaliger joined "the Capuchins of the province of French Guiana" (p. 143), while the biography has him go to French Guiana only at the end of his life and die on the voyage in 1648 (p. 141).
  26. Persecution as a motive. The author suggests Christians produced the covenant in response to the 1628 persecution (p. 141). He also says Christians under the Ottomans "had never had it better" (p. 143), and that the 1538 copy was "clearly not crafted during a period of persecution" (p. 175).

8. Sources the author cites most in this section (as cited)

Approximate mention counts are from the text; the OCR varies the spellings.

  • Bayle: "Bayle, 1735: 241", "Bayle 1737: 38", "Bayle 241", "Bayle 38" (about 14). Covers the Mount Carmel story, the forgery allegation, Salmasius, Ricaut, Hinckelmann and Addison.

  • Layard (207) (about 8).
  • Pacifique de Provins / Scaliger, Relation du voyage de Perse (1631) (233-236, 405-406, 407).
