1. Section summary

Chapter 6: The Prophet Muhammad and the Assyrian Christians (pp. 177–190)

  1. The chapter opens by saying that the Covenant with the Assyrian Christians, unlike the Najran covenant, "has long been known" to Muslims of upper Mesopotamia. It was allegedly first composed in Persian (Brevick 114). The author says this should not prompt "a priori claims of forgery".

  2. Following George David Malech's History of the Syrian Nation, the covenant was granted to "Said, head of the Nazarene tribe" and his bishop "Jahb Alahah". In 1517 Patriarch "Shimon the fourth" showed it to Sultan Selim I in Baghdad. Selim took the original to the treasury in Constantinople and gave the patriarch a copy signed by himself.

  3. The author takes on suspicions of forgery or "appropriation" of the Sinai covenant: similar names to the Najran delegation, the same 1517/Selim I story as Sinai, the Persian language, a text that calls itself "The translation", 27 witnesses against 16 or 22 for Sinai, and Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan as scribe two years before he is said to have become the Prophet's scribe (630–632). He offers alternative explanations for each.

  4. He collects testimony that a firman of the Prophet was held by the Assyrian Patriarchal House. The witnesses are Wigram, Brigadier General J.G. Browne, Surma D'Bait Mar Shimum, Earl Percy, Stafford, Emhardt & Lamsa, Theodore D'Mar Shimun, Yohannan, Albert Yelda (via Siemon-Netto), and Bar Hebraeus via Assemani via Percy.

  5. He sets out the conflicting accounts of the relic's fate:

    • destroyed in Bedr Khan Beg's massacres in 1847 (Stafford, Browne), or perishing in the mid-19th century (Wigram);
    • stolen in 1845 (Surma), or stolen at Dizan and taken to Bedr Khan (Theodore);
    • carried off by Turkish troops in 1899 (Percy);
    • destroyed by Turkish rulers before a massacre of 30,000 (Yelda). The author reads this as the 1915 Assyrian Genocide.

    He speculates it may survive in private hands.

  6. He gives a biography of Bedir (Badr) Khan Beg (c. 1800–1868). He argues that Kurdish and Turkish attacks on Assyrians were nationalist and secular, not Islamic, and that the attackers "had to effectively apostatize".

  7. A long "Commentary on the Content of the Covenant" goes item by item through:

    • protection of the "Nazarene nation", churches and property;
    • negotiable tribute paid into the bayt al-mal (1 dinar for commoners, 12 for the rich; nothing from strangers or the propertyless; a tax on inheritance);
    • no forced conversion, rights of Christian women and wives, and Muslim help in building churches;
    • Christian duties: no shelter for enemies, three days' hospitality, protection of Muslim women and children;
    • forfeiture of the treaty on breach, and entrusting the document to the head of the church.

  8. The commentary carries long modern digressions, among them the Bamiyan Buddhas (2001), Saudi and Iraqi edicts of 2012, Mehmet II and Hagia Sophia (1453/1935), and the Ka'bah icons of Jesus and Mary. The author claims that many militant Muslim movements are controlled by Western and Israeli intelligence services.

  9. The Conclusions say the Assyrian, Sinai and Najran covenants are "completely compatible" and "the work of the same genius". They show Muhammad as statesman and diplomat, and the author rejects the view that the spread of Islam was imperialism.

Chapter 7: The Prophet Muhammad and the Armenian Christians of Jerusalem (pp. 191–202)
  1. The author places the Armenian covenant in a "concerted campaign" by Muhammad. In his inference, the aim was to build a buffer zone of Christian sympathizers against Byzantium and the Latins.
  2. The document, "Firman Attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, Confirming the Rights of the Armenians in the Holy Places of Jerusalem", is a paper-on-silk scroll measuring 327 x 21.5 cm. It is held in the St. James Library of the Armenian Patriarchate of Jerusalem and is little known.
  3. Armenian sources (Azadian; Krikorian via Hagopian; Belleville Armenian Church citing Zeki al-Din) say Patriarch Abraham I (638–669) went to Mecca, or in 626 went to Muhammad, to obtain it. The author thinks it was most likely obtained in Medina.
  4. He attacks Father Jerome Golubovich's 1921 book I Frati Minori, and its review in Revue Biblique, as biased. Golubovich called the Sinai Pact, the Treaty of 'Umar, Selim I's firman and the Armenian covenant forgeries, mostly of 1630–1634 under Murad IV. The author's rebuttal includes Jean Thenaud's 1512 sighting of the Sinai privileges.
  5. He reproduces in full the Firman (Achtiname) of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab to Sophronios, dated 20 Rabi' al-Awwal, 15 AH. He also reproduces in full Johannes Avdall's 1870 English translation of the Covenant of 'Ali (Safar, 40 AH; given as 660 CE by the author).
  6. His commentary on the Covenant of 'Ali points to its Shi'ite traits and argues that a Christian forger would not have produced them.
  7. He cites the Charter of Caliph Muktafi II to the Nestorian Church (1138, ed. A. Mingana), Salah al-Din's firman (1187 per Dadoyan), and the Armenian historians Samuel of Ani, Mxit'ar of Ani, Kirakos and Juanser. He sets the doubts of Sanjian, Dadoyan and R.W. Thomson against them.
  8. He argues for an "unbroken chain" or "covenantal continuity" from the Prophet through 'Umar, 'Ali, the Umayyads, Muktafi II and Salah al-Din to the 1917 edict of Sharif al-Husayn ibn 'Ali of Mecca.
  9. A polemical passage follows against "Takfiris", Wahhabis, Saudi Arabia and their "Western backers".
  10. The Conclusions note that the Patriarchate cautiously says "attributed to" and keeps the relic from public view. The author states his belief that it and the other covenants are "most likely" genuine and asks the Patriarchate to release it for study.
  11. Part II then begins: a divider page (p. 203) and an epigraph, Qur'an 3:3–4 (p. 204).

4. Factual claims (non-date), by theme

Basis tags: [Fact] = author states as fact; [Attr. X] = attributed to source X; [Trad.] = tradition; [Inf.] = author's inference; [Op.] = author's opinion.

A. Chapter 6: Origin, language and transmission of the Assyrian covenant
  1. Unlike the Najran covenant, unknown to Muslims until its rediscovery "almost one hundred years ago", the Assyrian covenant "has long been known to the Muslims from upper Mesopotamia or what is now southeastern Turkey and part of northern Iraq". p. 177 [PDF 202] [Fact]
  2. "Unlike most of the other covenants of the Prophet, the original ... was allegedly composed in the Persian language." p. 177 [PDF 202] [Attr. Brevick 114]
  3. Malech calls it the "Agreement between Prophet Mohammed and Nazarene Christians of the East". p. 177 [PDF 202] [Attr. Malech]
  4. "Mohammed wrote an epistle to Said, head of the Nazarene tribe, who were Christians, and asked him and his people to accept the teachings of Islam. Together [with] Jahb Alahah, their bishop, Said appeared before the Prophet and agreed to pay him tribute for enjoying the liberty to worship in their own way unharmed by the Islamites." p. 177 [PDF 202] [Attr. Malech 221]
  5. "The document was signed by Mohammed himself and a number of the leading Islamites. It is written in the Persian language and has been preserved among the Christians for many centuries." p. 177 [PDF 202] [Attr. Malech 221]
  6. The original was preserved by the Assyrian Christians until the time of Selim I, "only to be seized by the Sultan". p. 177 [PDF 202] [Attr. "is said"; Malech]
  7. Selim said the document "was so valuable, that it ought to be preserved in the royal treasury of Constantinople". p. 177 [PDF 202] [Attr. Malech 221]
  8. "Jahb Alahah may be a corruption of Abu Haritha while Said could be the Sayyid 'Absiso, the leaders of the delegation from Najran." p. 177 [PDF 202] [Inf.]
  9. "For some scholars", the shared characteristics with the Sinai covenant "may point to appropriation". The Assyrians may have copied the Sinai covenant, addressed to "all Christians", and come to believe it was their own; "This remains within the realm of possibility." p. 177 [PDF 202] [Attr. unnamed "some scholars"; Inf.]
  10. "The repertoire of personal names among the Christians of the time was very limited in scope." p. 178 [PDF 203] [Fact/Op.]
  11. "Of all the Caliphs, Selim I was of the most relentless in his search for religious relics." He and his agents sought ancient Qur'ans, letters of the Prophet, and items of the Prophet, his Companions or earlier prophets. p. 178 [PDF 203] [Fact]
  12. Conquered communities "often approach their new rulers to express their submission ... and to request protection or privileges". 1517 "would have been the ideal time for the Assyrian or Armenian Christians to show their copies". p. 178 [PDF 203] [Inf.]
  13. "Traditions in Muslim and Bukhari" demonstrate that the Prophet could speak Persian. p. 178 [PDF 203] [Attr. hadith collections, as characterized by the author]
  14. Salman al-Farsi "was perfectly proficient, not only in Persian but in Aramaic, and possibly Greek"; he "was not only literate". p. 178 [PDF 203] [Fact]
  15. The Persian language "does not appear to have surprised Selim I or any of his scholars". p. 178 [PDF 203] [Inf.]
  16. Had the Ottomans thought it a fake, it would have been destroyed and the forgers "put to the sword". p. 178 [PDF 203] [Inf.]
  17. The document "commences with the words: 'The translation of the holy messenger's treaty, peace be upon him and his family.'" This initial section, in Malech's version, was not translated into English. p. 178 [PDF 203] [Fact]
  18. The scribe "is said to have been Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan". p. 178 [PDF 203] [Attr. "is said"]
  19. Several native Persian-speaking professors of religious studies judged the language consistent with 17th-century Persia. One felt it "so archaic that it could conceivably have been written during the time of the Prophet". None saw any sign of forgery. p. 178 [PDF 203] [Attr. unnamed colleagues]
  20. "It has not yet been established whether the version in Malech's text was transcribed in modern or ancient times." p. 178 [PDF 203] [Fact]
  21. The English translation "is good" but "not perfectly accurate, particularly when it comes to the list of witnesses at the end". p. 178 [PDF 203] [Attr. "I am told"]
  22. The Persian covenant has 27 witnesses. "Two of the Sinai covenants have sixteen signatories and four have twenty-two." p. 179 [PDF 204] [Fact]
  23. "Muttawatir" (printed so) is the highest hadith grade, meaning passed down by many narrators. p. 179 [PDF 204] [Fact]
  24. "Assyrian tradition declares that special privileges were given to their church and their patriarch, by a firman of the Prophet himself." p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Wigram, An Introduction 310]
  25. "[T]he Prophet Mohammed ... gave the Assyrians a written firman ... according them permission to carry out their own religious observances without interference." p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Browne, n.p.]
  26. "It is a thing of common knowledge among the Mussalmans of Hakkiari that there was a special firman granted by the Prophet to our house, and therewith ... a certain special knife of his giving." p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Surma, n.p.]
  27. "The strictest Moslems ... will eat without hesitation of any animal slaughtered by a member of the Patriarchal family." p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Surma, n.p.]
  28. "The patriarchal house ... is regarded with a respect among the Moslems, which they do not show to other Christian bishops." p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Wigram, An Introduction 310]
  29. In Jelu, among the relics of the great church of Mar Zaia was "a handkerchief covered with Arabic writing which the natives believe to be a firman of the Prophet". p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Percy 645]
  30. Tradition holds that the Porte's firman to each successive Patriarch, confirming his authority over the Nestorians, was originally granted by Mahomet to Ishy Yau, then Patriarch of the East, residing at Baghdad. Assemani's Bibliotheca Orientalis, compiled for Clement XI, gives the Latin text of Bar Hebraeus's account. p. 179 [PDF 204] [Trad.; Attr. Percy 645–646]
  31. Per Bar Hebraeus (via Percy), the treaty's terms were:
    • it was negotiated with large presents through Said, Christian Prince of Najran ("Nagranensium");
    • it was a "diploma" commending Christians to Arab protection;
    • it safeguarded religion and laws and exempted them from military service;
    • it shielded Christians in Muslim households from insults to their faith;
    • it allowed them to erect churches as they pleased, with Arab help;
    • it fixed the taxes on rich and poor "with strict and minute precision". p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Percy 645–646 / Bar Hebraeus]
  32. The firman was "embossed in letters of gold, on parchment, and was written 'circle wise,' with the print of a hand in the middle". p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Surma, n.p.]
  33. An explanatory parenthesis says this is "an ancient type of Arab script": the donor's handprint was impressed in the middle and the decree written around it in one continuous spiral. p. 179 [PDF 204] [Within the Surma quotation, n.p.]
  34. "The knife had a shaft of silver, with a piece of red coral set in the pommel, and an inscription inlaid in gold on the blade." p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Surma, n.p.]
  35. "Once in the year a selected Mollah of Julamerk used to come up and read that document in the public assembly." p. 179 [PDF 204] [Attr. Surma, n.p.]
  36. The memory of the covenant "was maintained alive among both Muslims and Christians". p. 179 [PDF 204] [Inf.]
  37. "Many clerics had come to Muhammad seeking charters." p. 179–180 [PDF 204–205] [Fact/Op.]
  38. "The rights confirmed by 'Umar are clearly the very same granted in the Covenant." p. 180 [PDF 205] [Op.]
  39. Under Omar, Assyrian Church Christians had "full security as a 'millet'", "on practically the same terms, as they had received under the Persian". The terms:
    • the right to remain in the nationality and practice their religion;
    • exemption from military service;
    • churches could be repaired, but new ones not erected without permission;
    • ordinary taxes plus the 'kharj', in place of military service; monks exempt;
    • Christian girls married to Muslims "might keep their religion's rule". p. 180 [PDF 205] [Attr. Wigram, The Assyrians 33]
  40. A copy of the firman was preserved by the Patriarch of the Assyrian Church. p. 180 [PDF 205] [Attr. Stafford 95]
  41. The covenant granted the Assyrian Church freedom of religion and administration, and the right to be a millet: a protected community headed by its chief Bishop, who represented it before Muslim sovereigns. p. 180 [PDF 205] [Attr. Stafford 95]
  42. The relic "was stored in the great church of Mar Zaia in Jilu, a district located in the Hakkari region of upper Mesopotamia which consisted of some twenty Assyrian Christian villages". p. 180 [PDF 205] [Fact]
  43. "It is reported" that when the patent was raised, Muslims dropped their weapons and left the Assyrians unharmed. The Muslims knew the covenant's warning that the disobedient would be excluded from heaven's blessings. p. 180 [PDF 205] [Trad./Attr. "it is reported"]
  44. The original "was taken to Istanbul, where, unfortunately, it has yet to be located". p. 180 [PDF 205] [Fact/Attr.]
  45. "A documentary decree was issued by Mohammed and written by Ali, his son-in-law, in which he promises to the Nestorians protection and privileges ... It is now said to be in the Ottoman Museum in Constantinople." p. 180 [PDF 205] [Attr. Emhardt & Lamsa 75–76]
  46. Neither the Assyrian nor the Sinai covenant is "currently in the catalog of the collection housed in the famous Turkish museum". pp. 180–181 [PDF 205–206] [Fact]
  47. The Patriarchal family "make no mention of any such transfer" and indicate that their firman was the original. It also included a dagger given by the Prophet. p. 181 [PDF 206] [Attr. "the actual owners"]
  48. Surma was the sister of Mar Shimun XXI Benyamin. "The sacred relics of the Prophet actually belonged to her family and she relates accounts from people who had actually seen them." p. 181 [PDF 206] [Fact]
B. Chapter 6: Fate of the Assyrian firman
  1. The grant "was actually preserved until the middle of the 19th century, when Kurdish hatred of Christians overcame their reverence for the Prophet, and the grant perished in the 'Massacres of Bedr Khan Beg'". p. 181 [PDF 206] [Attr. Wigram, An Introduction 310]
  2. Stafford dates the event to 1847 and says the firman was destroyed. p. 181 [PDF 206] [Attr. Stafford 95]
  3. Browne also gives 1847. In his account the Wali of Mosul, "frightened by the tales ... of the increasing strength of the Assyrians", organized "a political massacre". Bedir Khan Beg, with Turkish troops, attacked, and the firman was destroyed. p. 181 [PDF 206] [Attr. Browne, "The Assyrians: A Debt of Honor", n.p.]
  4. The firman was stolen, not destroyed, along with the dagger. When it was shown to Bedru Khan he cursed Nurullah Beg of Julamerk for stirring him up: "Had I known that this house possessed this firman, I should never have dared to go against them." p. 181 [PDF 206] [Attr. Surma, n.p.]
  5. At Dizan the decree, "always in a satchel", was hung on a cottage post during the midday meal. When the Kurds attacked, the men went to fight in Mar Shalita Church. The satchel with dagger and decree was left behind, stolen by the Kurds and taken to Bedr Khan Beg. p. 181 [PDF 206] [Attr. Theodore D'Mar Shimun, The History]
  6. Uncle Hormizd overheard Bedr Khan Beg's son in an Istanbul coffeehouse say, "Our family possess something that is invaluable among the Muslim world." Bedr Khan's great-grandson (of Damascus, holidaying in Cyprus) said similar to an Armenian of Bohtan living in Cyprus. "There is no doubt that they were speaking about the firman stolen from Qudshanis." p. 181 [PDF 206] [Attr. Theodore D'Mar Shimun]
  7. "When the Turkish troops occupied the village at the time of my visit in 1899, this ... was the only article which they apparently thought it worth their while to carry away." p. 181 [PDF 206] [Attr. Percy 645]
  8. The covenant "may have survived in private hands to this day". p. 182 [PDF 207] [Inf.]
  9. The document "may very well have remained in the hands of the local thieves until it was confiscated by the Young Turks". p. 182 [PDF 207] [Inf.]
  10. Yelda: the firman disappeared without a trace in 1847 but was later destroyed by the Turkish rulers "before they set out to kill 30,000 Christians". p. 182 [PDF 207] [Attr. Yelda via Siemon-Netto]
  11. In the 1915 Assyrian Genocide, Turkish troops and neighboring Kurdish tribes "slaughtered scores of Christians in the region of Jilu", and survivors fled to Salmas in Iran, then spread as refugees worldwide. p. 182 [PDF 207] [Fact]
  12. The perpetrators "could not have been Muslims ... but rather, the Young Turks: a movement of secular revolutionaries who wished to emulate the West in all matters: even massacres". p. 182 [PDF 207] [Op.]
C. Chapter 6: Bedir Khan Beg and context
  1. Bedir (Badr) Khan Beg was a Kurdish leader, first leader of the Emirate of Botan (in what is now southeastern Turkey) around 1820. His breakaway state included Bahdinan in northern Iraq, and he exploited Ottoman weakness to try to forge an independent Kurdistan. p. 182 [PDF 207] [Fact]
  2. "European powers had been spreading discontent and encouraging dissent among the Christians of the Ottoman Empire." The Assyrians, like the Armenians, were seen as "a sort of fifth column". p. 182 [PDF 207] [Fact/Op.]
  3. Eastern Christians "were told that the whole world was dominated by Christian nations ... This caused discontent toward Mohammedan rulers" (83). Some placed hopes in America and Western Europe, others in Russia, "only to become seriously disillusioned" (88). p. 182 [PDF 207] [Attr. Emhardt & Lamsa 83, 88]
  4. Bedir Khan set out to exterminate the region's Christians to create a homogeneous Kurdish Muslim homeland. The mid-19th-century massacres were ended by the Turks under British and French pressure. p. 182 [PDF 207] [Fact]
  5. Bedir Khan had 40–90 sons by allegation and 22 confirmed, "many of whom continued to play an important role in Ottoman and Kurdish affairs". p. 182 [PDF 207] [Fact]
  6. "The Christians ... were always safe under true Islamic rule." p. 182 [PDF 207] [Op.]
  7. "[T]he Assyrians as well as other Christians in the Near East have never realized the value of those sacred privileges ... The trouble with these Christians was that they were left too free." p. 182 [PDF 207] [Attr. Emhardt & Lamsa 82]
  8. Percy: at first the Muslims treated the Christians in a friendly manner. When their attitude changed, it was "due not to religious antagonism but to jealousy of their superior wealth". pp. 182–183 [PDF 207–208] [Attr. Percy 645]
  9. Kurdish and Turkish targeting of Assyrians "and later the Armenians" was due to "nationalistic, secular, political, and economic considerations", not Islam. The attackers "had to effectively apostatize, as marked symbolically by the physical destruction of the firman". p. 183 [PDF 208] [Op.]
  10. "The vast majority of scholars who have written about the Assyrian Christians treat the Covenant ... as a historical fact." p. 183 [PDF 208] [Fact/Op.]
  11. "The claim of a special position is one that can hardly be substantiated under present conditions." p. 183 [PDF 208] [Attr. Wigram, An Introduction 310]
D. Chapter 6: Scribes and literacy
  1. "Mu'awiyyah did indeed act as Muhammad's scribe during the final two years of his life." p. 183 [PDF 208] [Fact]
  2. Some Sunni scholars have suggested Mu'awiyyah embraced Islam earlier. p. 183 [PDF 208] [Attr. unnamed "some Sunni scholars"]
  3. Only seventeen members of Quraysh could read and write. The literate women included Hafsah, 'A'ishah and Umm Kulthum; the literate men 'Ali, 'Umar, 'Uthman, Abu 'Ubaydah, Talhah, Abu Sufyan and Mu'awiyyah. "Certainly there were more." p. 183 [PDF 208] [Attr. al-Baladhuri via Chejne, The Arabic Language 59; 189 n.14]
  4. The Prophet sent his adopted son Zayd to learn Hebrew and Syriac, to reduce his dependence on Jewish secretaries used before the conflict with the Medinan Jews. p. 183 [PDF 208] [Attr. Zeitlin 131]
  5. The Prophet "is reported to have had at least forty-five scribes". p. 183 [PDF 208] [Attr. Azami 10]
E. Chapter 6: Content of the covenant (as quoted item by item)
  1. The covenant opens: "God has told me in a vision what to do, and I confirm His Command by giving my solemn promise to keep this agreement." p. 183 [PDF 208] [Quoted document]
  2. Item one: "To the followers of Islam ... Carry out my command, protect and help the Nazarene nation in this country of ours in their own land." p. 184 [PDF 209] [Quoted document]
  3. Eastern Christians "as late as the thirteenth century" called themselves Nasraye. Monks and priests bore the title rabban. p. 184 [PDF 209] [Attr. Jenkins 7]
  4. Item two: "Leave their places of worship in peace." Also: "help and assist their chief and their priests when in need of help, be it in the mountains, in the desert, on the sea, or at home." p. 184 [PDF 209] [Quoted document]
  5. In zones governed by the Prophet's commands, attacks on Buddhist, Shinto and Hindu sites "have never taken place"; such actions occurred "only in very recent times". p. 184 [PDF 209] [Op./Fact]
  6. Item four: "Leave all their possessions alone, be it houses or other property, do not destroy anything of their belongings ... the followers of Islam shall not harm or molest any of the members of this nation because the Nazarenes are my subjects, pay tribute to me and will help the Muslims." p. 184 [PDF 209] [Quoted document]
  7. The Prophet was dealing with "what previously was a vassal kingdom of the Byzantines". The Assyrians did not receive St. Catherine's tax-free status because they were "a fully-functioning economic hub as opposed to a monastic community". p. 184 [PDF 209] [Fact/Inf.]
  8. Item five: "No tribute, but what is agreed upon, shall be collected from them." p. 184 [PDF 209] [Quoted document]
  9. "Item four also decrees that 'their churches and buildings shall be left as they are, they shall not be altered.'" p. 185 [PDF 210] [Quoted document]
  10. "Their priests shall be permitted to teach and worship in their own way—the Nazarenes have full liberty of worship in their churches and homes." p. 185 [PDF 210] [Quoted document]
  11. Item five: "None of their churches shall be torn down, or altered into a mosque, except by the consent and free will of the Nazarenes ... If anyone disobeys this command, the anger of God and His Prophet shall be upon him." p. 185 [PDF 210] [Quoted document]
  12. Item six: the tribute shall be dedicated to promoting the spread of Islam and deposited in the bayt al-mal. p. 186 [PDF 211] [Paraphrase of document]
  13. "A common man shall pay one dinar (piece of money), but the merchants and people who own mines of gold and silver and are rich shall pay twelve dinars." p. 186 [PDF 211] [Quoted document]
  14. "Strangers and people who have no houses or other settled property shall not have taxes levied upon them." p. 186 [PDF 211] [Quoted document]
  15. "If a man inherits property he shall pay a settled sum to the bayt al-mal treasury." p. 186 [PDF 211] [Quoted document]
  16. The bayt al-mal, "the House of Money", was a Public Treasury spent on education, infrastructure, social services and military expenses. p. 186 [PDF 211] [Fact]
  17. Item seven: "The Christians are not obliged to make war on the enemies of Islam, but if an enemy attacks the Christians, the Muslims shall not deny their help, but give them horses and weapons, if they need them." p. 186 [PDF 211] [Quoted document]
  18. "The Christians are not obliged to become Muslims, until God's will makes them believers." p. 186 [PDF 211] [Quoted document]
  19. "While Muslims did not require the people they conquered to convert ... they presumed their subjects would eventually do so." p. 186 [PDF 211] [Attr. Rollin Armour 32]
  20. "More Christians embraced the faith of Muhammad of their own will than were ever forcibly converted." p. 186 [PDF 211] [Attr. Betts 10]
  21. "It is obvious that the great majority of Christians ultimately turned to Islam." p. 186 [PDF 211] [Attr. Humphreys 261]
  22. The Qur'an uses gender-inclusive "believing males" and "believing females" (3:195; 4:124; 16:97; 33:35; 40:40). This "is totally unique" in a 7th-century scripture. p. 187 [PDF 212] [Fact/Op.]
  23. Item eight: "The Muslims shall not force Christian women to accept Islam, but if they themselves wish to embrace it, the Muslims shall be kind to them." p. 187 [PDF 212] [Quoted document]
  24. Item nine: a Christian wife of a Muslim "has liberty to worship at her own church ... and her husband must not treat her unkindly on account of her religion." p. 187 [PDF 212] [Quoted document]
  25. Item ten: "If anyone disobeys this command, he disobeys God and His Prophet and will be guilty of a great offense." p. 187 [PDF 212] [Quoted document]
  26. Item eleven: "If the Nazarenes wish to build a church, their Muslim neighbors shall help them. This shall be done, because the Christians have obeyed us and have come to us and pleaded for peace and mercy." p. 187 [PDF 212] [Quoted document]
  27. "Item eleven" (as printed): "If there be among the Christians a great and learned man the Muslims shall honor him and not be envious of his greatness." p. 189 [PDF 214] [Quoted document]
  28. Item thirteen: "If anyone is unjust and unkind to the Christians he will be guilty of disobeying the Prophet of Allah." p. 189 [PDF 214] [Quoted document]
  29. Item fourteen: "The Christians should not shelter an enemy of Islam or give him horse, weapon or any other help." p. 189 [PDF 214] [Quoted document]
  30. Item fifteen: "If a Muslim is in need, the Christians shall for three days and nights be his host and shelter him from his enemies." p. 189 [PDF 214] [Quoted document]
  31. Unnumbered: "The Christians shall protect the Muslim women and children and not deliver them up to the enemy or expose them to view." p. 189 [PDF 214] [Quoted document]
  32. Item seventeen: "If the Nazarenes fail to fulfill these conditions, they have forfeited their right to protection, and the agreement is null and void." p. 190 [PDF 215] [Quoted document]
  33. Item eighteen: "This document shall be entrusted to the Christian chief and head of their church for safe keeping." The covenant ends: "The peace of God be over them all." p. 190 [PDF 215] [Quoted document]
  34. Muhammad "ended the practice of female infanticide among the Arabs". p. 189 [PDF 214] [Fact]
  35. The Assyrian Christians of Turkey and Iraq made the covenant well known to Christians and Muslims alike, unlike communities that hid their covenants. p. 190 [PDF 215] [Fact/Op.]
  36. "The lethal attacks on ... churches in Iraq ... violated the stated will of the Prophet Muhammad, who in the 7th century issued a Firman." p. 190 [PDF 215] [Attr. Siemon-Netto]
  37. The Prophet granted the Assyrians protection "out of respect for their knowledge of medicine and science". p. 190 [PDF 215] [Attr. Yelda via Siemon-Netto]
  38. Joseph Yacoub (Catholic University of Lyon) fears that terrorist bombings may accomplish "the complete de-Christianization of Iraq". p. 190 [PDF 215] [Attr. Yacoub]
F. Chapter 6: Digressions (historical and modern claims)
  1. The Bamiyan Buddhas were destroyed by the Taliban in March 2001; those involved "were inspired by Salafism". p. 184 [PDF 209] [Fact/Op.]
  2. Sufi centers in Qum, Iran, were destroyed and turned into parking lots in the early 21st century. p. 185 [PDF 210] [Fact]
  3. "In Malaysia, the Shi'ite school of Islam is outlawed and those who practice it are punished by imprisonment." p. 185 [PDF 210] [Fact]
  4. In Saudi Arabia, Twelver, Isma'ili and Zaydi Shi'ite centers "have been closed and quite often destroyed". p. 185 [PDF 210] [Fact]
  5. "In many Muslim countries, mosques only open briefly for prayers and study circles are prohibited. Religious gatherings in homes are also outlawed"; sermons are censored or imposed by a "Ministry of Religious Guidance". p. 185 [PDF 210] [Fact/Op.]
  6. "In Saudi Arabia ... the construction of Christian churches is against the law." p. 185 [PDF 210] [Fact]
  7. The Saudi Grand Mufti ruled in March 2012 that "All churches in the Arabian Peninsula must be destroyed". p. 185 [PDF 210] [Attr. Asia News]
  8. Ahmad al-Hasani al-Baghdadi's 2012 edict held that Christian women "may be legitimately taken as 'wives'". p. 185 [PDF 210] [Attr. Mahmoud]
  9. Colonial-era imperialists spread Salafism and concocted Arab nationalism to undermine the Ottoman Empire. "Many, if not most of the world's militant Muslim movements were created and remain under the control of US, British, French, and Israeli secret services." p. 185 [PDF 210] [Op./asserted as fact]
  10. Mehmet II insisted the artistic and archaeological treasures of Constantinople be protected and preserved. p. 187 [PDF 212] [Attr. Lunde 85]
  11. Mehmet II allowed the icons of Jesus, the Virgin Mary and saints to remain in the mosque beside newly added Islamic calligraphy. p. 187 [PDF 212] [Fact]
  12. "Quraysh had put pictures in the Ka'bah including two of Jesus son of Mary and Mary ... The apostle ordered that the pictures should be erased except those of Jesus and Mary." p. 188 [PDF 213] [Attr. Ibn Ishaq 552]
  13. Al-Waqidi and al-Azraqi: the Prophet placed his hand protectively over the icon of Jesus and Mary and had all other pictures erased except Abraham's. Another tradition says Abraham's image was erased because it showed him "as an old man casting lots". p. 188 [PDF 213] [Attr. Waqidi 411; Azraqi 111]
  14. Muhammad "could and did distinguish between idols devoted to polytheistic deities and icons of previous revelations". p. 188 [PDF 213] [Attr. Omid Safi 151]
  15. Ibn Hisham's version of Ibn Ishaq omits the protection of the images: "Apparently I.H. has cut out what I.I. wrote and adopted the later tradition that all the pictures were obliterated." p. 188 [PDF 213] [Attr. Guillaume 552]
  16. The images survived until the Umayyads destroyed the Ka'bah in 683 CE. p. 188 [PDF 213] [Attr. G.R.D. King 219–220]
  17. "The biographers of the Prophet and the collectors of hadith were biased, both religiously and politically." Material favorable to Christians was suppressed. p. 188 [PDF 213] [Op.]
  18. Shrines around Damascus revered by Muslims and Christians alike: the Mosque of Moses' Footprints, the birthplace of Abraham, the Cave of Abel's Blood, Adam's Cave, the Hunger Cave, the refuge of Mary and Jesus, Elias' oratory, the Cemetery of the Prophets, and others. p. 188 [PDF 213] [Attr. Bethany J. Walker, qtd. Jenkins 217–218]
  19. Bliss (1912) described these shared practices:
    • Muslims took the insane to the cave of St. Anthony at the Maronite convent of Qozhayya in Lebanon;
    • Christians went to the well at the shrine of Sheikh Hassan er Rai near Damascus;
    • barren Muslim women passed under the cloth stamped with Christ on Good Friday;
    • Christian women in Hums consulted Dervish diviners;
    • the Nuseiriyeh observed Christmas;
    • Muslims sought baptism for their children as a charm. pp. 188–189 [PDF 213–214] [Attr. Bliss, qtd. Jenkins 205]
  20. The Jews of al-Andalus invited the North African Muslims to free them from the Christian Visigoths before 711. p. 189 [PDF 214] [Attr. Levy 169]
  21. The Muslim army in Spain "met very little resistance from the Spanish Catholic masses who loathed their Germanic overlords". p. 189 [PDF 214] [Fact/Op.]
  22. "The oppressed majority ... regarded the Muslims not so much as conquerors but as saviors. The Muslims ended their slavery." p. 189 [PDF 214] [Attr. Ahmad Thomson 88]
  23. Qur'an references for respecting the signs of Allah: 22:32; 40:81; 5:29; 31:32. p. 189 [PDF 214] [Fact]
G. Chapter 7: The Armenian covenant: document and origins
  1. Muhammad reached out to the Greek Orthodox of Mount Sinai, the Copts of Egypt, the Assyrians of upper Mesopotamia, the Christians of Persia and the Armenians of Jerusalem. He had sent word to the Byzantines, who "rebuked his offers". p. 191 [PDF 216] [Fact/Op.]
  2. Muhammad's strategy "seems to have been to create a buffer zone of Greek, Assyrian, Armenian, and Persian Christian sympathizers" against the Byzantines and Western Roman Catholics. p. 191 [PDF 216] [Inf.]
  3. The covenant is known as the "Firman Attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, Confirming the Rights of the Armenians in the Holy Places of Jerusalem". p. 191 [PDF 216] [Attr. Narkiss 11, figure 2]
  4. It "has received little circulation and is generally unknown among both Armenians and Muslims". p. 191 [PDF 216] [Fact/Op.]
  5. "The scroll, which is made of paper on a silk backing, measures 327 x 21.5 cm and is housed at the St. James Library in the Armenian Patriarchate of Jerusalem." p. 191 [PDF 216] [Fact]
  6. Patriarch Abraham [I] of Jerusalem traveled to Mecca in the seventh century to secure special privileges from the Prophet. p. 191 [PDF 216] [Attr. Armenian historians / Azadian]
  7. Abraham I (638–669), "regarded by many as the first Armenian Patriarch of Jerusalem, had trekked all the way to Mecca". p. 191 [PDF 216] [Attr. Krikorian via Hagopian]
  8. Per Zeki al-Din, Abraham went to Muhammad personally in 626 and received an official document. p. 191 [PDF 216] [Attr. Belleville Armenian Church]
  9. "Abraham I appears in the full light of history", unlike some Christian figures in hadith and sirah literature. p. 191 [PDF 216] [Fact/Op.]
  10. Large numbers of leaders came to the Prophet in Medina after his return from Mecca, "to offer their submission and to seek special rights and privileges". p. 191 [PDF 216] [Fact]
H. Chapter 7: Golubovich and the review
  1. Father Jerome Golubovich's I Frati Minori nel possesso de[i] luoghi santi di Gerusalemme (1333) e i falsi firmani posseduti dai Greo-Elleni: Note e documenti per la soluzione della questione de[i] luoghi santi (1921) challenged the covenant's authenticity. p. 191 [PDF 216] [Fact]
  2. Golubovich set out to prove that the documents presented by the Greek Orthodox Church for its exclusive possession of the holy sites are spurious. p. 191 [PDF 216] [Fact/Op. ("complete lack of objectivity")]
  3. The anonymous reviewer in Revue Biblique: "we are faced with a fraud built like a war machine at the peak of the controversy over the sanctuaries of Palestine". pp. 191–192 [PDF 216–217] [Attr. L'École Pratique d'Études Bibliques 637]
  4. Golubovich concludes that the Pact or Testament of Muhammad with the monks of Mount Sinai, the Treaty of 'Umar, and the firman of Selim I "are all fake". Most of the forgeries date to 1630–1634 under Murad IV. p. 192 [PDF 217] [Attr. Golubovich via L'École Pratique 637]
  5. Golubovich alleges the frauds were authored by Cyril Lucaris; by Father Lambrinos; by his procureur Théophane, Patriarch of Jerusalem; and by his archdeacon Grégoire. The reviewer describes Grégoire as a "former Jew who, on a spite-filled day, sold the pot to the roses". p. 192 [PDF 217] [Attr. L'École Pratique 637]
  6. In the reviewer's eyes, corrupt Greek Orthodox Christians conspired with Jews, Muslims and Turks against the Catholic Church. The author calls this "far-fetched" since "Jews, Muslims, and Greek Orthodox do not even associate with one another in Jerusalem". p. 192 [PDF 217] [Op.]
  7. "The Latins ... were not the only Christians who attempted to expropriate Armenian properties and subjugate the Armenian Church; the Greeks made similar efforts." p. 192 [PDF 217] [Attr. Hagopian]
  8. Golubovich claims the Pact of Muhammad appeared around 1569 CE. p. 192 [PDF 217] [Attr. L'École Pratique 636]
  9. If Golubovich were right, the holy sites "would be returned to their earlier guardians: the Muslims". p. 192 [PDF 217] [Inf.]
  10. Thenaud (1512) said a mosque beside the Church of St. Catherine preserved Muhammad's privileges to the monks (freedom from taxation and obligations), "signed by his palm-print". p. 193 [PDF 218] [Attr. Thenaud 72]
  11. Golubovich concluded that the Armenian covenant was a fake, "along with every other document that supports their claims to the title of the holy sites". p. 193 [PDF 218] [Attr. Golubovich]
I. Chapter 7: Firman of 'Umar
  1. The "Firman Attributed to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, the Conqueror of Jerusalem in 638" is housed in the St. James Library. A handwritten Arabic copy is at the National Library in Paris. p. 193 [PDF 218] [Fact]
  2. It is also known as the "Achtiname or Ahtiname of Caliph 'Umar". It was delivered to Sophronios, the Greek Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem, on 20 Rabi' al-Awwal, 15 AH. p. 193 [PDF 218] [Fact]
  3. Text: "a contract and a pact delivered to the distinguished and most reverent Sophronios, Patriarch of the Imperial Nation, on Mount of Olives, in Jerusalem". It covers laity, clergy, monks and nuns. p. 193 [PDF 218] [Quoted document]
  4. It names the protected places as "the Kamame (the Church of the Resurrection), the Church of Bethlehem, where Jesus ... was born, the Great Church and the Cave with the three gates, the southern, northern and western ones". p. 193 [PDF 218] [Quoted document]
  5. It lists "Georgians, Abyssinians (Ethiopians), as well as Franks, Copts, Syrians, Armenians, Nestorians, Jacobians and Maronites, who will come as simple pilgrims and will belong to said Patriarch". p. 193 [PDF 218] [Quoted document]
  6. "They may have the primacy above all the others according to what was granted to them from the part of the Prophet ... who honored them with the sign of his gracious hand." p. 194 [PDF 219] [Quoted document]
  7. "All the Christian pilgrims to the All Holy Tomb, should give the Patriarch one drachma and 1/3 of a silver drachma." p. 194 [PDF 219] [Quoted document]
  8. The firman's text source is cited as "(Jerusalem Patriarchate)". p. 194 [PDF 219] [Citation]
  9. "Skeptics claim that Sophronios is not a historical figure, which is false. There were literally hundreds of patriarchs in Jerusalem at the time." p. 194 [PDF 219] [Attr. skeptics / Op.]
  10. "The original ... was also stamped with the print of the Prophet's hand, a feature found on other covenants." p. 194 [PDF 219] [Fact]
J. Chapter 7: Covenant of 'Ali
  1. 'Ali confirmed the Prophet's covenant with the Armenians "in a decree that dates from the year 660 CE". p. 194 [PDF 219] [Fact]
  2. Its title is "Covenant of 'Ali, Fourth Caliph, of Baghdad, Granting Certain Immunities and Privileges to the Armenian Nation". p. 194 [PDF 219] [Fact]
  3. Its transmission and translation:
    • translated into Armenian by Gregor Campan (1767), afterwards by M. Saragian;
    • authenticated by Joakim Gregor Bagratuni of Constantinople (1804);
    • Avdall (1869) had possessed a Cufic copy, lent to Henry Torrens, which was lost or mislaid;
    • Avdall made "a correct and faithful translation into English" from the Armenian, published in JASB 1870. p. 194 [PDF 219] [Fact / Attr. Avdall]
  4. The covenant was written by "Hashim, the son of Athap, the son of Valas" in Cufic, "in the celebrated domicile of Kharanthala, in the magnificent palace, in the month of Safar, in the fortieth year of the hijrah". p. 195 [PDF 220] [Quoted document]
  5. The petitioners and witnesses were "Jacob Sayyid 'Abdul-Shuyukh and the son of Saha, and Abraham the Priest, Bishop Isaiah, and several others, forty in number". They "rendered every assistance ... to our agent whom we had sent [to] our forts and frontiers". p. 195 [PDF 220] [Quoted document]
  6. The covenant is made "on behalf of all the tribes of Islam [so that Islam] shall prevail, and the doctrine of Christianity shall continue". It is to last "so long as the sea shall be capable of wetting wool". p. 195 [PDF 220] [Quoted document]
  7. "There shall be perpetual peace and tranquility between Christians and Musulmans." The faithful Armenians "shall resemble the Musulmans and the Mumins". p. 195 [PDF 220] [Quoted document]
  8. Its stipulations:
    • the fixed scale of taxation is to be kept, with no further demands;
    • no taking of their country;
    • priests not to be converted; monks and hermits not to be disturbed; preachers not prohibited;
    • habitations and hereditary lands not to be devastated;
    • no one shall "remove or pull down the bells from the steeples of their churches";
    • no compulsion to convert and no religious controversies;
    • Muslims to supply money for building churches and monasteries. p. 196 [PDF 221] [Quoted document]
  9. "I have entered into a Covenant of patriarchs, of prophets, which was brought down from heaven by an angel." p. 196 [PDF 221] [Quoted document]
  10. Infringers are "an unbeliever and an apostate from the divine prophet"; the disobedient "cannot remain faithful and obedient to the son of Abu Talib". p. 197 [PDF 222] [Quoted document]
  11. Kufic script is "consistent with the custom of Imam 'Ali". p. 197 [PDF 222] [Op.]
  12. "The claim that the Christians had come to the aid of Imam 'Ali is correct. The Imam, it is reported, was well-loved by the Christians." p. 197 [PDF 222] [Op./Attr. "it is reported"]
  13. The appeals to Muslims disloyal to the Imam "could only refer to the seditious Mu'awiyyah and his turn-coat followers". p. 197 [PDF 222] [Inf.]
  14. Shi'ites are "a mere ten percent of the Muslim world population" and ruled only rarely (Idrisids, Fatimids, Safavids, post-1979 Iranians). p. 198 [PDF 223] [Fact]
  15. Shi'ites believe their Imams are divinely inspired by angels and regard the Khawarij and Umayyads who fought 'Ali as apostates and infidels. p. 198 [PDF 223] [Fact]
  16. "Genuine Sunni traditions confirm the reality of divine inspiration (as distinguished from revelation ...) granted to pure and pious Muslims by means of dreams and visions." p. 198 [PDF 223] [Op./Fact]
K. Chapter 7: Later confirmations
  1. Caliph Muktafi II of Baghdad issued a Charter of Protection to the Nestorian Church in 1138 CE. It follows "the precedent of the imams and predecessors" and the Orthodox Caliphs (6), and grants the same rights as 'Ali, 'Umar and the Prophet's covenants. p. 198 [PDF 223] [Fact/Attr. Mingana ed. 6]
  2. Mingana: "Statutory intolerance was not among [official Islam's] defects." A caliph or two, "such as Mutawwakil", subjected Christians to vexatious measures, but these were "infractions of the law". "It is not the Kur'an that was the cause of persecution of Christians." pp. 198–199 [PDF 223–224] [Attr. Mingana 1–2]
  3. Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi, "a notorious nasibi", was famous for his tolerance. On conquering Jerusalem he "granted special protections to the Armenian Christians". p. 199 [PDF 224] [Fact/Op.]
  4. "Most authorities treat the Edict of Salah al-Din as historically genuine." Roman Catholic clergy, Western Orientalists and "even Armenian Orthodox authorities question the Covenant of the Prophet". p. 199 [PDF 224] [Fact]
  5. Sanjian speaks of "[t]he Firman attributed to the Prophet Mohammed", "[t]he Firman attributed to Omar Ibn al-Khattab [sic]" (Narkiss 11) and "[t]he Firman attributed to Caliph 'Ali" (13). p. 199 [PDF 224] [Attr. Sanjian in Narkiss]
  6. Dadoyan refers to the "[a]lleged 'Prophet's Oath to the Armenians'". In Armenian histories the earliest Islamic–Armenian contact concerned the status of the Armenians and Eastern Christians of Jerusalem. pp. 199–200 [PDF 224–225] [Attr. Dadoyan 60]
  7. The core of the oaths was "tolerance toward and protection of Christian communities by their Muslim rulers in return for their absolute submission and payment of taxes". p. 200 [PDF 225] [Attr. Dadoyan 60]
  8. Samuel of Ani, Mxit'ar of Ani, Kirakos and Juanser "all confirm that 'Muhammad himself made a pact with the Armenians, guaranteeing the free observance of Christianity'". p. 200 [PDF 225] [Attr. Thomson, "Muhammad" 842]
  9. Samuel's tax list: from every household "four drachmas, three bushels of xorbal, one nose-bag, one cord of hair, and one gauntlet. But from the priests, nobles and cavalry he ordered tax to be taken" (printed so). p. 200 [PDF 225] [Attr. Samuel qtd. Thomson 843]
  10. The Armenians "did not have a precise and coherent understanding of the Islamic religion"; Armenian sources on Islam "are filled with absurdities and misunderstandings". p. 200 [PDF 225] [Attr. Thomson 858 / author]
  11. "Muhammad himself was credited with an arrangement only worked out under his successors." p. 200 [PDF 225] [Attr. Thomson 842]
  12. The 1917 edict commanded Muslims to "protect and take great care of the entire Armenian, Jacobite, community", for they are "a Protected People of the Muslims [ahl al-dhimmah al-muslimin]". It cites the Prophet: "Whoever takes even a string from them, I will be his adversary on the Day of Judgment." p. 201 [PDF 226] [Quoted document]
  13. "[T]he praiseworthy keynote of tolerance that runs through" the Firman "is that of all the Muslim Caliphs, and not only one of them." p. 201 [PDF 226] [Attr. Mingana 2]
  14. Takfiris are "apostates and infidels" according to the covenants. Saudi Arabia is named as a "State player" among "armed Wahhabi terrorists". Believers must oppose them and "their Western backers, be they American, British, French, or Israeli, by any means necessary, as long as these are consonant with the traditions and laws of Islam". pp. 201–202 [PDF 226–227] [Op.]
  15. Qur'an 28:41–42 quoted ("And We made them (but) Imams inviting to the Fire ..."). p. 201 [PDF 226] [Fact]
  16. "The Armenian Patriarchate has always been careful to speak of the firman attributed to the Prophet as opposed to the firman of the Prophet" and has shown "reluctance to expose this precious relic to public view and scholarly appraisal". p. 201 [PDF 226] [Fact/Op.]
  17. Part II epigraph: Qur'an 3:3–4. p. 204 [PDF 229] [Fact]

5. Covenant details

5a. Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Assyrian Christians (Chapter 6)
Field As stated in this section
Names used "Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Assyrian Christians" (author). "Agreement between Prophet Mohammed and Nazarene Christians of the East" (Malech, p. 177). "the precious document" (Malech). "the holy messenger's treaty" (the document's opening, p. 178). "firman" (Wigram, Browne, Surma, Percy, Theodore). "a firman of the Prophet himself" (Wigram, p. 179). "diploma" (Bar Hebraeus via Percy, p. 179). "documentary decree" (Emhardt & Lamsa, p. 180). "patent", "treasured relic", "grant" (p. 180–181). "decree" (Theodore). "Firman—or letter of protection" (Siemon-Netto, p. 190)
Claimed date (AH) Not printed in this section
Claimed date (CE) Not printed as a year. The author says the covenant "dates from two years before" 630–632, the period of Mu'awiyyah's service as scribe (p. 183 [PDF 208]). "In the 7th century" (Siemon-Netto, p. 190 [PDF 215]). Given to Essvo Yabh "toward the end of the seventh" [sic] (Emhardt & Lamsa, p. 180 [PDF 205])
Place issued Not stated. Said and Jahb Alahah "appeared before the Prophet" (Malech, p. 177). The author's third hypothesis has Mu'awiyyah "present in Medina at the time" (p. 183)
Language Persian (Brevick 114; Malech 221). The document opens "The translation of the holy messenger's treaty" (p. 178). Percy describes the Jelu relic as "covered with Arabic writing" (p. 179). Surma: "letters of gold, on parchment ... 'circle wise,' with the print of a hand in the middle", called "an ancient type of Arab script" (p. 179)
Scribe "Is said to have been Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan" (p. 178; p. 183). Emhardt & Lamsa: "written by Ali, his son-in-law" (p. 180). The author's hypothesis: Salman al-Farsi "could easily have acted as the Prophet's scribe" for Farsi documents (p. 178)
Witnesses 27 ("twenty-seven witnesses", p. 179 [PDF 204]). Names not listed in this section. Malech: "signed by Mohammed himself and a number of the leading Islamites" (p. 177). The author is told the English translation of the witness list "is not perfectly accurate" (p. 178). Comparison given: "two of the Sinai covenants have sixteen signatories and four have twenty-two" (p. 179)
Recipients "Said, head of the Nazarene tribe" with "Jahb Alahah, their bishop" (Malech, p. 177). Ishy Yau, "the then Patriarch of the East, residing at Bag[h]dad", negotiated via "Said the Christian Prince of Najran" (Percy/Assemani/Bar Hebraeus, p. 179). "Nestorian Patriarch Essvo Yabh" (Emhardt & Lamsa, p. 180). "Our house", the Patriarchal House (Surma, p. 179). Item 18: "the Christian chief and head of their church" (p. 190)
Location of original/copies Original: royal treasury, Constantinople, from 1517 (Malech, pp. 177, 180). It "has yet to be located" in Istanbul (p. 180). "Now said to be in the Ottoman Museum in Constantinople" (Emhardt & Lamsa, p. 180), but not in that museum's catalog (author, pp. 180–181). Certified copy signed by Selim: "kept by the patriarch; it is still extant" (Malech 221, p. 177). Patriarchal family's firman (claimed as the original; Surma via author, p. 181): "stored in the great church of Mar Zaia in Jilu" (p. 180; Percy, p. 179); "kept among the treasures of the Patriarchate" (Surma, p. 181); carried in a satchel at Dizan; "stolen from Qudshanis" (Theodore, p. 181). A copy was preserved by the Patriarch (Stafford 95, p. 180). Fate: see §2 rows 33–45, 50–51
Published / translated Persian text with English translation in Malech's History of the Syrian Nation and the Old Evangelical-Apostolic Church of the East; no year given here. The opening line was left untranslated (p. 178). Bar Hebraeus's account is given in Latin in Assemani's Bibliotheca Orientalis, compiled for Clement XI (p. 179). The author calls for "a new, complete, translation" (pp. 178–179)
Author's verdict Treated as authentic. None of the Persian-speaking scholars "were able to see anything that indicated it was a forgery" (p. 178). In the Conclusions, the Sinai, Najran and Assyrian covenants "all appear to be the work of the same genius" (p. 190)

Author's arguments for authenticity (Ch. 6):

  1. The Persian language "should not provoke any a priori claims of forgery". It "compels ... a more in-depth analysis". p. 177 [PDF 202]

  2. Name similarities to Najran (Jahb Alahah/Abu Haritha; Said/Sayyid) are "of little significance", because the stock of Christian personal names was limited and many delegations came in the Prophet's last two years. p. 178 [PDF 203]

  3. Selim I taking it in 1517 "makes perfect chronological sense": Selim was the most relentless relic-seeker, and 1517 was the culmination of his conquests, when conquered communities would present charters. p. 178 [PDF 203]

  4. The Prophet could speak Persian (traditions in Muslim and Bukhari). Salman al-Farsi could have written it. p. 178 [PDF 203]

  5. Selim's scholars were not surprised by the Persian. A fake would have been destroyed and the forgers executed, not placed in the Treasury with a certified copy given back. p. 178 [PDF 203]

  6. If the Safavids made a Shi'ite recension, why keep Mu'awiyyah's name? p. 178 [PDF 203]

  7. Native Persian-speaking professors found no sign of forgery. One thought the language could date to the Prophet's time. p. 178 [PDF 203]

  8. Its existence "has been long attested" by Assyrian tradition, Muslim popular knowledge (Hakkari), relics, an annual public reading by a Mollah of Julamerk, and Muslim respect for the Patriarchal house. p. 179 [PDF 204]

  9. 'Umar's confirmation of the same rights (Wigram, The Assyrians 33) shows that 'Umar "entertained few doubts". p. 180 [PDF 205]

  10. Muslims knew of it: the Yohannan story of the Baghdad church burning, and Muslims dropping their weapons when the patent was raised. p. 180 [PDF 205]

  11. Surma's testimony "must take precedence over the scholarly speculations of a person like Percy". p. 181 [PDF 206]

  12. "Simply because the Covenant ... does not presently exist does not mean that it never existed": translations survive (the Declaration of Independence analogy). p. 183 [PDF 208]

  13. The Mu'awiyyah chronology problem allows three non-forgery explanations:

    • the date is mistaken, as in many documents of the period;
    • Mu'awiyyah converted earlier, as some Sunni scholars suggest;
    • Mu'awiyyah, still a polytheist, was present in Medina and acted as a "more objective" literate intermediary.

    He was among the few literate Arabs (al-Baladhuri: 17 literate Qurayshis), and the Prophet had at least 45 scribes. p. 183 [PDF 208]

  14. Its content is "completely compatible" with the Sinai and Najran covenants. p. 190 [PDF 215]

Counter-arguments the author addresses (Ch. 6):

  • (a) A Persian original is surprising. p. 177
  • (b) The account is "strangely similar" to the Najran stories. p. 177
  • (c) The "same fate" as the Sinai covenant (Selim I, 1517) "may point to appropriation", according to "some scholars". p. 177
  • (d) "Skeptics will surely suggest" that 1517 was "the ideal time to forge false charters ... and poor ones at that, since they were not even in Arabic". p. 178
  • (e) "It is odd that academics would argue that [it] was written originally in Farsi when the document itself commences with the words: 'The translation ...'". p. 178
  • (f) A possible Safavid Shi'ite recension. p. 178
  • (g) 27 witnesses against 16/22 for Sinai; a possible attempt to reach "muttawatir" grade. p. 179
  • (h) Emhardt & Lamsa may be confusing it with the Sinai covenant. p. 180
  • (i) Wigram: "the claim of a special position is one that can hardly be substantiated under present conditions". p. 183
  • (j) The "major problem": Mu'awiyyah as scribe two years before he became the Prophet's scribe. "Why, critics will naturally ask, was Mu'awiyyah acting as the Prophet's scribe?" p. 183

Related documents reproduced or cited in Chapter 7:

  • Firman (Achtiname/Ahtiname) of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.
    • Dated 20 Rabi' al-Awwal, 15 AH ("15th year of the hijrah" / "of the departure of the Prophet"); no CE equivalent given.
    • Recipient: Sophronios, "Greek Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem" / "Patriarch of the Imperial Nation". Place: "on Mount of Olives, in Jerusalem".
    • Held in the St. James Library; handwritten Arabic copy at the National Library, Paris. Text source: "(Jerusalem Patriarchate)".
    • The original was stamped with the print of the Prophet's hand (author). The text refers to "what was granted to them from the part of the Prophet ... who honored them with the sign of his gracious hand".
    • No scribe or witnesses named. pp. 193–194 [PDF 218–219]
  • Covenant of 'Ali ("Covenant of 'Ali, Fourth Caliph, of Baghdad, Granting Certain Immunities and Privileges to the Armenian Nation").
    • Dated Safar, 40 AH (document); the author gives 660 CE, "one year prior to his martyrdom".
    • Scribe: Hashim son of Athap son of Valas, writing in Cufic. Place: "the celebrated domicile of Kharanthala, in the magnificent palace".
    • Armenian notables present/petitioning: Jacob Sayyid 'Abdul-Shuyukh, the son of Saha, Abraham the Priest, Bishop Isaiah, "and several others, forty in number". The "testimony of Sayyid (Arch) Bishop and of the others" is "binding".
    • 'Ali also says he "convened together the grandees of the Musulmans and the leading men of my elders and dignitaries". No individual Muslim witnesses are named.
    • Transmission: Armenian translations by Gregor Campan (1767) and M. Saragian; authenticated by J. G. Bagratuni (1804); Avdall's Cufic copy was lost with Henry Torrens; Avdall's English translation from the Armenian appeared in JASB 1870. pp. 194–197 [PDF 219–222]
  • Firman of Salah al-Din. Images only, with captions (p. 199). Dadoyan dates his entry into Jerusalem and oath to 1187 and says the oath "is accepted as authentic". No text is reproduced.
  • Charter of Muktafi II to the Nestorian Church, 1138 CE, edited by A. Mingana. "Too long to reproduce". p. 198
  • Edict/fatwa of Sharif al-Husayn ibn 'Ali of Mecca, 1917. Quoted in part. p. 201

Author's arguments for authenticity (Ch. 7):

  1. Abraham I "appears in the full light of history". p. 191 [PDF 216]
  2. Golubovich lacks objectivity: his purpose was to strip the Greek Orthodox of the holy sites, and the reviewer's conspiracy is "far-fetched". pp. 191–192 [PDF 216–217]
  3. Golubovich is "historically inaccurate". His 1569 date for the Sinai Pact is contradicted by its removal by Selim I in 1517, by five centuries of fatwas, and by Thenaud's sighting in 1512. Its existence "predates the Ottoman Conquest of the Sinai". pp. 192–193 [PDF 217–218]
  4. The Firman of 'Umar "seems to indicate otherwise". It alludes to a prior grant by the Prophet bearing "the sign of his gracious hand". p. 193–194 [PDF 218–219]
  5. Sophronios is historical, and "no forger would have been careless enough to invent a figure that never existed". p. 194 [PDF 219]
  6. 'Ali confirmed the covenant in 660. The Covenant of 'Ali's content is "in full conformity" with the Prophet's covenants, and its Kufic script fits 'Ali's custom. p. 194, 197 [PDF 219, 222]
  7. The Covenant of 'Ali's Shi'ite traits argue against Christian forgery: divine inspiration, a covenant brought by an angel, and opponents called apostates. A Christian "could have been beheaded" for presenting it to radical Sunnis, and would not have known Shi'ite doctrine. Why would he forge an 'Ali covenant when 'Umar's would be better received? p. 198 [PDF 223]
  8. There is a "long-honored tradition of Muslim rulers of confirming the rights granted by their predecessors": Muktafi II (1138), Salah al-Din (1187), the Umayyads (703, 719), Mu'awiyah and Ibn Maslamah, up to the Sharif of Mecca (1917). An "unbroken chain" or "covenantal continuity". pp. 198–201 [PDF 223–226]
  9. Salah al-Din accepted the edicts of 'Ali and 'Umar as authentic, "and these Companions had personal knowledge of the Prophet's words and actions". p. 200 [PDF 225]
  10. Armenian Christian historians (Samuel of Ani, Mxit'ar of Ani, Kirakos, Juanser) confirm a pact. p. 200 [PDF 225]
  11. Thomson shows the Armenians misunderstood Islam, so a forgery would contain errors. Agreement with the Qur'an, Sunnah and shari'ah "suggests that their authorship has been rightly attributed". p. 200 [PDF 225]
  12. Even Dadoyan "recognizes that a long succession of Muslim rulers ... all renewed the edict". p. 200 [PDF 225]

Counter-arguments the author addresses (Ch. 7):

  • Father Jerome Golubovich (1921): the Armenian covenant, the Sinai Pact, the Treaty of 'Umar and Selim I's firman are all fakes; the Pact appeared c. 1569; most forgeries date to 1630–1634 under Murad IV, authored by Cyril Lucaris, Lambrinos, Théophane and Grégoire. pp. 191–193
  • The anonymous Revue Biblique reviewer ("a fraud built like a war machine"). pp. 191–192
  • "Politically, religiously, and economically motivated skeptics claim that Sophronios is not a historical figure." p. 194
  • "Most Sunnis will claim" that the Shi'ite features show the Covenant of 'Ali to be "a Shi'ite forgery". p. 198
  • Roman Catholic clergymen, Western Orientalists and Armenian Orthodox authorities question the covenant. Sanjian says "attributed". Dadoyan says "alleged" and calls it a "legend". p. 199–200
  • R.W. Thomson: "Muhammad himself was credited with an arrangement only worked out under his successors" (842). p. 200
  • The Armenian Patriarchate's own caution ("attributed to"). p. 201

Chapter 6
  1. A Persian original should not prompt "a priori claims of forgery". p. 177 [PDF 202]

7. Internal inconsistencies and tensions within this section (only what is in the text)

  1. Abraham I's dates against the Prophet's lifetime.
    • The book gives Abraham I's patriarchate as 638–669 (p. 191 [PDF 216]) and the Prophet's final years as 630–632 (p. 183 [PDF 208]).
    • Yet it says that "since he was Patriarch from 638 to 669 CE, he had two full years in order to obtain a firman or covenant from the Prophet" (p. 191). On the book's own dates, his patriarchate began after the Prophet's final years.
    • The 626 visit date (Zeki al-Din) also precedes 638.
  2. Place of the Armenian grant. Mecca (Azadian; Krikorian, p. 191) against Medinah (Dadoyan, p. 200). The author hedges ("most likely in Medina", p. 191).
  3. Date of 'Ali's arrangement or covenant.
    • Dadoyan: "626/4H" (p. 200 [PDF 225]).
    • The Covenant of 'Ali's text: "the month of Safar, in the fortieth year of the hijrah" (p. 195 [PDF 220]).
    • The author: "660 CE" (p. 194 [PDF 219]).
    • The book does not reconcile these. Dadoyan also places 'Ali's arrangement before 'Umar's ("a little later by Caliph 'Umar"), while the author's chain runs "from 'Umar to 'Ali" (p. 201).
  4. The Assyrian covenant's date against its scribe. The covenant "dates from two years before" 630–632, but Mu'awiyyah was scribe only 630–632 (p. 183). The author acknowledges this and offers explanations. It also sits awkwardly with his earlier remark that delegations came "during his final two years of life" (p. 178).
  5. Scribe of the Assyrian covenant. Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan (pp. 178, 183) against "written by Ali, his son-in-law" (Emhardt & Lamsa, p. 180). The author does not address the 'Ali attribution.
  6. Recipient of the Assyrian covenant. Said and bishop Jahb Alahah (Malech, p. 177); Ishy Yau, Patriarch at Baghdad, via Said the Prince of Najran (Percy/Bar Hebraeus, p. 179); Nestorian Patriarch Essvo Yabh, "toward the end of the seventh" [century] (Emhardt & Lamsa, p. 180). The last date is also in tension with a Prophet who died by 632 (p. 183).
  7. Language and material of the Assyrian document. Persian (Malech; Brevick, p. 177) against "a handkerchief covered with Arabic writing" (Percy, p. 179) against gold letters "on parchment", "an ancient type of Arab script" (Surma, p. 179). The document also calls itself "The translation of the holy messenger's treaty" (p. 178). The author notes the oddity of the translation heading only.
  8. Whether the original is in Istanbul or was held by the Patriarchal family.
    • The original was taken to Constantinople in 1517 and the patriarch kept a certified copy that is "still extant" (Malech, pp. 177, 180).
    • The family's firman was the original (Surma, as reported by the author, p. 181).
    • The family treasured it until the end of the 19th century, and it is "now said to be in the Ottoman Museum" (Emhardt & Lamsa, p. 180).
    • Two of these accounts put the original in Istanbul; Surma's puts it with the family. The author asks what happened to the certified copy (p. 180), then follows Surma.
  9. Where the relic was kept. "Stored in the great church of Mar Zaia in Jilu" (author, p. 180; Percy, p. 179). "Kept among the treasures of the Patriarchate" (Surma, p. 181). Carried in a satchel at Dizan; "the firman stolen from Qudshanis" (Theodore, p. 181).
  10. Fate and date of loss. Wigram: perished in the mid-19th century (p. 181). Stafford and Browne: destroyed in 1847 (p. 181). Surma: stolen in 1845 (p. 181). Theodore: stolen at Dizan (p. 181). Percy: carried off by Turkish troops in 1899 (p. 181). Yelda: disappeared in 1847, later destroyed by Turkish rulers before a massacre (p. 182).
    • The author both says Percy's date "seems off by nearly half a century" (p. 181) and that it "should not be so easily dismissed" (p. 182).
    • He earlier ranks Surma's testimony above Percy's "scholarly speculations" (p. 181).
    • Surma's "(1845)" also differs from the 1847 date the author gives for the massacre and Bedir Khan's defeat (pp. 181–182).
  11. Who counts as eyewitness. The author calls Surma "closely connected to the events, as opposed to a distant observer" (p. 181), but gives her dates as 1883–1975 (p. 179) for events of 1845/1847. He partly allows for this ("she relates accounts from people who had actually seen them", p. 181). Theodore D'Mar Shimun (1906–2001) narrates the Dizan theft in the first person plural ("When we went to Dizan ... our men went to fight", p. 181).
  12. 'Umar's terms against the covenant on church building. The author says the rights 'Umar confirmed "are clearly the very same granted in the Covenant" (p. 180). His Wigram quotation says Christians "might repair their churches, but might not erect new ones without permission" (p. 180). The covenant, by contrast, requires Muslim neighbors to help build churches (item 11, p. 187), as does Bar Hebraeus's version (Christians "allowed to erect churches as they pleased", p. 179).
  13. Persian or Byzantine background of the Assyrians. Wigram says the 'Umar terms matched what they "had received under the Persian" (p. 180). The author says the Prophet was dealing with "what previously was a vassal kingdom of the Byzantines" (p. 184).
  14. Military help from the Assyrian Christians.
    • The Assyrians "committed to pay taxes ... and help the Muslims when called to do so" (p. 184).
    • They "were allowed to help the Muslims, although they were under no obligation to do so" (p. 186).
    • Item 4 says "will help the Muslims" (p. 184). Item 7 says "not obliged to make war" (p. 186). Wigram and Bar Hebraeus give exemption from military service (pp. 179–180).
  15. Item numbering in the commentary.
    • "Item eleven" is given for two different clauses: church building (p. 187) and honoring "a great and learned man" (p. 189).
    • "Item four" covers possessions (p. 184) and, later, "churches and buildings shall be left as they are" (p. 185). "Item five" covers agreed tribute (p. 184) and churches not torn down (p. 185).
    • These may or may not be the same items; the text does not clarify. Items 3, 12 and 16 are never cited by number.
  16. The 'Umar firman is labelled "with the Armenian Christians". The heading says "with the Armenian Christians of Jerusalem" (pp. 192–193), but the text is addressed to Sophronios, "the Greek Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem" / "Patriarch of the Imperial Nation" (p. 193). It lists the Armenians among groups who "will belong to said Patriarch" (p. 193).
  17. Golubovich's position on the 'Umar treaty. He listed "the Treaty of 'Umar" among the fakes (p. 192). The author then offers the Firman of 'Umar as evidence against him (p. 193) without addressing whether it is the document Golubovich called fake.
  18. The author's paraphrase of Dadoyan against his quotation of her.
    • He says Dadoyan "recognizes that a long succession of Muslim rulers ... all renewed the edict" (p. 200). The quotation frames this as Armenian opinion ("This is how Armenians viewed ...", "In their opinion, the Umayyads simply 'renewed'", p. 200).
    • He says "Salah al-Din accepted the edicts of 'Ali and 'Umar as authentic" (p. 200). The quotation says Armenians "were said to have shown Salah ed-Din the oaths of 'Ali and 'Umar"; "accepted as authentic" refers to Salah ed-Din's own oath (p. 200).
  19. Does 'Ali's covenant confirm the Prophet's? The author says 'Ali's decree "confirmed" the Prophet's covenant with the Armenians (p. 194). The quoted Covenant of 'Ali does not explicitly mention a prior covenant of the Prophet with the Armenians. It speaks of "a Covenant of patriarchs, of prophets, which was brought down from heaven by an angel" (p. 196). This is an observation about the quoted text only.
  20. Title against place in the Covenant of 'Ali. The title is "Covenant of 'Ali, Fourth Caliph, of Baghdad" (p. 194). The document says it was written at "the celebrated domicile of Kharanthala" (p. 195).
  21. Mingana's quotation applied to "the Firman". Mingana edited the Muktafi II charter (p. 198). On p. 201 his remark is quoted with the bracketed insertion "the Firman", in the context of the Sharif's 1917 edict and the chain of covenants. The referent is ambiguous.
  22. Spelling variants that may matter for checking:
    • "Surma D'Bait Mar Shimum" (pp. 179, 181) against "Mar Shimun XXI Benyamin" and "Theodore D'Mar Shimun" (p. 181);
    • "Bedr Khan Beg" / "Bedru Khan Beg" / "Bedir Khan Beg" / "Bedir (Badr) Khan Beg";
    • "Jelu" (Percy) / "Jilu"; "Hakkiari" / "Hakkari";
    • "Mu'awiyyah" / "Muawiyah"; "Ishy Yau" / "Essvo Yabh";
    • "Salah al-Din" / "Salah ed-Din";
    • "Hagia Sofia"; "muttawatir" (printed so).
  23. Two characterizations of Salah al-Din. "A notorious nasibi [hater of the Household of the Prophet]" yet "famous for his tolerance and nobility of character" (p. 199). The author presents both; this is a tension of characterization, not a factual contradiction.

2. Each text version in detail

Ch. 8 — Covenant with the Monks of Mount Sinai
Sinai I — Pococke (1809), quoted from Davenport — pp. 205–206 [PDF 230–231]
  • Issuer/opening: "Muhammad the son of 'Abd Allah, the Messenger of Allah, and careful guardian of the whole world; has wrote the present instrument…" (p. 205).
  • Recipients: "all those who are in his national people, and of his own religion, as a secure and positive promise to be accomplished to the Christian nation and relations of the Nazarene, whosoever they may be, whether they be the noble or the vulgar, the honorable or otherwise" (p. 205). The provisions concern "the monks" (I–XI) and "every Christian" (XII–XVIII).
  • Date: "in the second year of the Hegira, the third day of the month of Muharram" (p. 206). No CE date.
  • Place: "at the mosque of the Prophet" (p. 206).
  • Scribe: "This present was written by the leader, the successor, 'Ali the son of Abu Talib; the Prophet marking it with his hand at the mosque of the Prophet (in whom be peace)" (p. 206).
  • Witnesses (16). Heading "Witnesses," (p. 206). OCR spellings:
    1. Ali, the son of Abu Thaleb
    2. Honiar [OCR; likely Homar, as in IV], the son of Hattavi
    3. Ziphir, the son of Abuan
    4. Saith, the son of Maat
    5. Thavitt, the son of Nesis
    6. Atnphachin [OCR; likely Amphachin], the son of Hassan
    7. Muathem, the son of Kasvi
    8. Azur, the son of jassin [Jassin]
    9. Abombaker, the son of Anibi [OCR; possibly Ambi]
    10. Kaphe Ottoman, the son of Gafas
    11. Ambtelack, the son of Messutt
    12. Phazer, the son of Abbas
    13. Talat, the son of Atnptolack [OCR; likely Amptolack]
    14. Saat the son of Abbatt
    15. Kastner the son of Abid
    16. Atnbtullack [OCR; likely Ambtullack] the son of Omar
  • Provisions: 18 numbered "chapters" (I–XVIII). A bracketed note after XI reads: "[In these eleven chapters is to be found whatever relates to the monks, as to the remaining seven chapters, they direct what relates to every Christian.]" (p. 206).
    1. (I) Any of "my nation" who breaks the promise and oath destroys the promise of God and is "worthy of the curse, whether he be the King himself, or a poor man".
    2. (II) Wherever monks settle (mountain, hill, village, habitable place, sea, desert, convent, church, house of prayer), the Prophet is "the preserver and protector of them, their goods and effects", jointly with all his people, "because they are a part of my own people, and an honor to me."
    3. (III) Officers are not to require any poll-tax or other tribute from them.
    4. (IV) No one may change their judges or governors. These remain in office "without being deported".
    5. (V) No one may molest them when they travel on the road.
    6. (VI) No one may deprive them of their churches.
    7. (VII) Whoever annuls these decrees "annuls the ordinance of God".
    8. (VIII) Their judges, governors, monks, servants, disciples and dependents pay no poll-tax and are not molested. The Prophet protects them by land or sea, east, west, north or south.
    9. (IX) Solitaries on the mountains: no poll-tax or tithes on their incomes, and no Muslim may partake of what they have.
    10. (X) When the crop is plentiful, the inhabitants must give them "a certain measure" out of every bushel.
    11. (XI) In wartime they are not taken from their dwellings or compelled to go to war, and no poll-tax is required of them.
    12. (XII) Christians who are inhabitants and able to pay the poll-tax "shall pay no more than twelve drachms."
    13. (XIII) Nothing else may be required of them. Quotes God: "'Do not molest those that have a veneration for the books that are sent from God, but rather in a kind manner give of your good things to them, and converse with them, and hinder everyone from molesting them' [29:46]".
    14. (XIV) If a Christian woman marries a Muslim man, he shall not keep her "from her church and prayers, and the practice of her religion."
    15. (XV) "That no person hinder them from repairing their churches." This is a ban on hindrance; it does not promise help.
    16. (XVI) Whoever acts contrary "becomes truly an apostate to God, and to his divine apostle".
    17. (XVII) No one shall bear arms against them, and "the Muslims shall wage war for them."
    18. (XVIII) No one of "my nation" shall act contrary "until the end of the world."
  • Stray OCR on p. 206: "1" and "-28" between XIV and XV. These may be marginalia or a page artifact.
Sinai II — Arundale (1837), from Mauchin's French — pp. 207–208 [PDF 232–233]
  • Issuer: "Mohammed-ebn-Abdallah, gives this Edict for all the world in general… the confidant of God, and charged with the keeping of all created beings."
  • Recipients: "for my nation, and for all those who are Christians; from the east and from the west, far and near; for all those that are eloquent and not eloquent, the learned and the ignorant." Violators are cursed "whoever they are, Sultan or other Musulman."
  • Date: "the 3 Moharran [sic/OCR], the second year of the Hegira, and of J.C. the 1st of August, 622" (p. 208).
  • Place: Not stated.
  • Scribe: "This Edict was written by the hand of Aby-Taleb". The name is given as Aby-Taleb only. "It is signed by the Prophet himself. Happy he who confirms." (p. 208).
  • Witnesses (22, counted by commas). Heading: "The testimonies which attest the truth of this Edict… are" (p. 208).
    1. Ali-ebn-Taleb
    2. Aboubek-rebu-Aby-Kohafey
    3. Omar ebn-el-Khattai
    4. Otman-ebn-Assan
    5. Abou-el-Daida
    6. Abou-Horeyrah
    7. AbdallahAbou-Massaoud
    8. Abbat-ebn-Abdel-Motbb
    9. Fodeyl-ebn-Abbas
    10. Zobeir-ebn-Aouan
    11. Talhat-ebn-Obeydallah
    12. Saad-ebn-Maoz
    13. Saad-ebn-Obadey
    14. Thabet-ebn-Keys
    15. MonKayetmeth
    16. Hachem-ebn-Ommyeh
    17. Hareth-ebn-Thabet
    18. Abdallah-ebn Atnrou [OCR; likely Amrou]
    19. Ebn-el-Ass
    20. Amer-ebn-Yassin
    21. Moazzam-ebn-Kerachy
    22. Abdel-Azini [OCR; likely Azim]-ebn-Hassan
  • Provisions:
    1. If "a father or a hermit" retires to a mountain, grotto, plain, desert, town, village or church, the Prophet is "behind him as his protector against all enemies, myself in person, my forces and my subjects, although these priests are cancelled by me" (sic; III renders this as "as those priests are my rayas"). "I will avoid doing them any hurt."
    2. No contributions may be taken from them "unless voluntarily".
    3. No bishop may be changed from his bishopric, priest from his priesthood, or hermit from his hermitage.
    4. None of the objects in their churches may enter the construction of mosques or Muslim dwellings.
    5. It is forbidden to exact contributions from priests, bishops or devotees. Their prerogatives are preserved everywhere, by land and sea, in all four directions.
    6. Those who sow and plant in the mountains and scattered places pay no tithes or contributions, "not even voluntarily", when the produce is for their nourishment.
    7. If they lack corn, "every house shall assist them with a measure".
    8. They are not obliged to serve in the wars or to pay imposts.
    9. Owners of goods or merchandise pay "not more than twelve drachms of silver every year."
    10. "No one must be molested; it is forbidden to enter into discussion with them by soft measures, putting aside everything disagreeable, and preserving the wing of compassion." The wording is as printed.
    11. A Christian woman who goes to the house of a Muslim "must be well treated, and allowed to perform her prayer in a church".
    12. "The Christians shall be assisted to preserve their churches and houses".
    13. They are not obliged to carry arms. "the Musulmen shall bear them for them".
    14. The ordinance is not to be disobeyed "to the end of the world."
Sinai III — Géramb (1840), from Mauchin's French — pp. 209–210 [PDF 234–235]
  • Issuer: "Mohamed ebn Abdallah has issued this edict for the whole world in general… the friend of God".
  • Recipients: "for my nation and for all those who are in Christendom, in the East, or in the West, near and afar off, for all who are eloquent and not eloquent, known and unknown". Violators: "sultan or any other Musulman."
  • Date: "the 3rd of Mohanam [OCR; Moharram], in the second year of the Hegira, and of Jesus Christ, the 1st of August, 622" (p. 210).
