  • Provisions. Same order as II, with these wording differences:
    1. A priest or hermit is protected "as those priests are my rayas [Christian subjects]".
    2. "Voluntary contributions only shall be taken from them, and they shall not be constrained to pay any."
    3. No bishop may be driven from his bishopric, "nor a priest from his religion", nor a hermit from his hermitage.
    4. Nothing belonging to their churches may be used to build mosques or Muslim dwellings.
    5. No contributions may be imposed on priests, bishops or religious men. Their privileges and "my safeguard" hold everywhere.
    6. Those who sow or plant in mountains and sequestered places pay no tithes or contributions, not even voluntarily, when the produce is for their own subsistence.
    7. If they need corn, "they shall be assisted with one measure for each house".
    8. They are not obliged to go to war or pay any taxes.
    9. "Those who possess immoveable property or merchandise shall not give more than twelve silver drachmas per year."
    10. None shall be molested, and no one shall "enter into strife with those who follow the precepts of Gospel, but behave mildly towards them".
    11. "When a Christian woman shall join the Musulmans, they shall treat her well, and permit her to go and pray in a church".
    12. "The Christians shall be assisted to preserve their churches and their houses, which will assist them to preserve their religion".
    13. They are not obliged to bear arms, and Muslims bear arms for them.
    14. The ordinance stands "until the end of the world."

  • Issuer: "this letter is addressed by Muhammad, son of Abdullah, he who proclaims and admonishes men…"

  • Recipients: "people of this faith and to all in the world who profess the Christian religion in East and West, near and far, whether they are Arabs or non-Arabs, unknown or known". Violators: "whether he be a sultan or any one so ever of the faithful of Islam."

    1. Ali the son of Abu Thaleb
    2. Homar, the son of Hattavi

  • Closing: "Praise be to all you abide by its contents, and cursed be all who do not observe it." (p. 212).

  • Provisions:

    1. If a monk or pilgrim seeks protection (mountain, valley, cave, tilled fields, plain, desert, church), "I am with him, and defend him… I, my helpers, all men of my faith, and all my followers, for these people are my followers and my protégés."
    2. They are protected "from interference with the supply of victuals".
    3. They pay no taxes "over and above what they themselves approve". No compulsion or constraint.
    4. No bishop may be removed from his bishopric, monk from his monastery or hermit from his tower, and no pilgrim may be hindered from his pilgrimage.
    5. "no church or chapel shall be destroyed".
    6. Church property may not be used to build mosques or Muslim houses.
    7. "Neither poll-tax nor impost shall be laid on monks, bishops, or hermits". They are protected everywhere.
    8. Those in the solitude of the mountains or at the holy places are free of poll-tax and of tithe or duty on what they grow for their own use.
    9. They are helped to raise a corn-crop "by a free allowance of one qadah [unit of dry measure] in every ardabb [= 6 waybah = 24 rub'a]".
    10. They are not obliged to serve in war or pay the poll-tax.
    11. Those liable to land-tax, or with resources in land or commerce, "shall not have to pay more than ten dirhams a head a year". Note: ten, not twelve.
    12. No unjust tax. "with these people of the Book there is to be no strife, unless it be over what is for the good." No Qur'an reference is given here.
    13. "We wish to take them under the wing of our mercy". Vexation is kept away from them.
    14. A Christian woman entering a Muslim household is received with kindness and given opportunity to pray in her church. "there shall be no dispute between her and a man who loves her religion."
    15. They "shall be assisted in the improvement of their churches and religious dwellings".
    16. None is compelled to bear arms, and the Muslims defend them.
    17. This holds "until the hour comes and the last day breaks upon the world."

  • Provisions:
    1. "Whenever monies [sic/OCR; probably 'monks'], devotees and pilgrims gather" (mountain, valley, den, frequented place, plain, church, houses of worship), "we are [at the] back of them and shall protect them, and their properties and their morals, by Myself, by My Friends and by My Assistants".
    2. They are exempt from the burdens others pay "as an oath of allegiance". "They must not give anything of their income but that which pleases them". They must not be offended, disturbed, coerced or compelled.
    3. Their judges may not be changed or kept from their offices. Monks may not be disturbed in their religious order, and "people of seclusion" may not be stopped from living in their cells.
    4. No one may plunder the pilgrims, destroy or spoil their churches or houses of worship, or take anything from them to "the houses of Islam".
    5. No poll-tax on their judges, monks and worshippers, and no fine, tax "or any unjust right".
    6. They are protected at sea and on land, in all four directions.
    7. No taxes or tithes from those who worship in the mountains "or from those who cultivate the Holy Lands". No interference or legal action against them.
    8. At harvest "they should be given a Kadah for each Ardab of wheat (about five bushels and a half)".
    9. For the propertied, the wealthy and merchants, the poll-tax "must not exceed twelve Dirhams a head per year (i.e. about 45 cents)."
    10. They are not forced to travel, to go to war or to carry arms. "the Islams have to fight for them."
    11. "Do no dispute or argue with them… 'Do not dispute or argue with the People of the Book but in that which is best' [29:46]".
    12. A Christian woman's marriage to a Muslim "must not take place except after her consent", and she must not be prevented from going to church for prayer.
    13. "Their churches must be honored and they must not be withheld from building churches or repairing convents."
    14. They are not to be forced "to carry arms or stones". The Islams must protect and defend them.
    15. This binds "until the Day of Resurrection and the end of the world."

  • Provisions:
    1. A monk or pilgrim seeking protection (mountain, valley, cave, tilled fields, plain, desert, church): "I am behind them… I, my helpers [a'wani], all the members of my religion [ahl al-millati], and all my followers [atba'i], for they [the monks and the pilgrims] are my protégés and my subjects [ahl al-dhimmati]."
    2. Protection "from interference with their supplies and from the payment of taxes save what they willingly renounce". No compulsion.
    3. Bishop, monk, hermit [sawma'ah = tower] and pilgrim may not be removed or hindered.
    4. "no building from among their churches… shall be destroyed, nor shall the money [mal] from their churches be used for the building of mosques or houses for the Muslims."
    5. "Neither poll-tax [jizyah] nor fees [gharamah] shall be laid on monks [ruhban], bishops [asaqifah], or worshippers".
    6. Those who withdraw to the mountains or sacred sites are free of jizyah, kharaj (land tribute) and tithe ['ushr] or duty on what they grow for their own use.
    7. They are helped to raise a crop by "one qadah… in every ardabb [= 6 waybah = 24 rub'a]".
    8. They are not obliged to serve in war or pay jizyah.
    9. Those liable to kharaj, or with land or commercial resources, pay "not… more than twelve dirhams a head per year."
    10. No unjust tax. "with the People of the Book there is to be no strife, unless it be over what is for the good [5:48]."
    11. They are under "the wing of our mercy".
    12. A Christian woman entering a Muslim household is received kindly and may pray in her church. "no dispute between her and a man who loves her religion."
    13. They are "assisted in the maintenance of their religious buildings and their dwellings [mawadi']".
    14. None is compelled to bear arms, and the Muslims defend them.
    15. This holds "until the hour comes and the world ends."
  • Colophon (p. 217): see §5.
Ch. 9 — Covenant with the Christians of Persia — Arpee 1946: 355–360 — pp. 223–226 [PDF 248–251]
  • Recipients: "all Christian nations, such as dwell throughout the world toward the eastward of Arabia and Persia, or within the bounds of them, whether they be in immediate contact with the Faithful or whether they be distant". Violators: "whether he be a king, or one of the people, whether he be a pious believer (sc., a Moslem), or only a believer (sc., a Christian)." (p. 223).
  • Date: "this Treaty was drawn up on the Monday following the first four months of the Fourth Year of the Hegira." (p. 226).
  • Place: Not stated.
  • Scribe: Not named.
  • Witnesses: None named. The text says: "In witness whereof is attached the Signature that in the presence of the Clergy and the Lords of the Nation, the Holy, Great Prophet, Mohammed, affixed, confirming the foregoing Treaty." (p. 226).
  • Structure: (a) the covenant; (b) a bracketed passage: "[Here also follows a Treaty of Mohammed… with the Christian people, a Treaty which His Majesty after the foregoing words commanded and established with the Christians…]" (p. 225); (c) commandments binding the Christians.
  • Provisions, part (a): obligations on Muslims.
    1. Muslims shall defend and aid "believers" (Christians) far or near, and throughout Christendom protect their places of worship and the dwellings of their monks and priests, everywhere (mountains, plains, towns, waste places, deserts, West and East, sea and land), both "in their faith and in their property".
    2. Muslims shall care for them "as being under our protection" and aid them in distress, "for they are a people subject to my Nation".
    3. Taxes: "not to exact more than they are able to pay, but to adjust matters with their consent, without force or violence."
    4. "Their building enterprises shall not be interfered with". Priests are not molested. They are not persecuted for faith or customs, and may pray in their own places by their own rites.
    5. Churches shall not be dismantled or destroyed, nor homes and mansions confiscated "for mosques or residences, without their consent."
    6. "No land taxes shall be exacted from them in excess of the value of four dinars, or one linen sheet". This is to be applied for the Muslims' benefit "and held as a sacred trust for public use".
    7. Poll-tax: merchants, the wealthy, open-country dwellers, pearl-fishers, and owners of mines of precious stones, gold or silver, "shall not be made to pay more than twelve dirhams."
    8. "Of those who are not of the Christian faith [and] neither conduct worship according to the Christian rite, four dirhams shall be exacted." Those who conform to that people pay no more than "the aforementioned Twelve Dirhams, provided that they dwell where all their people are resident."
    9. Travellers without permanent abode pay no land tax. The exception is an heir to property "on which the Imam has a legal claim", and even then without violence or excess.
    10. Christians are not asked to fight for Muslims, or forced to join Muslim wars. If an enemy attacks the Christians, Muslims shall defend them with horses, swords and spears.
    11. "No Christians shall be brought by force to confess Islam". There are to be no disputes "except over the better things".
    12. Muslims protect them from oppressors. If a Christian offends inadvertently, Muslims accompany him to the law-courts so that no more is exacted than God prescribes.
    13. Once the conditions are observed and the capitation tax paid, no Christian shall be tyrannized, and Christians shall not tyrannize Muslims.
    14. Muslims shall not take Christian women and maidens by force, "but only with the consent of their lords". The exception is women who freely choose to marry Muslims, "whether permanently or only for a time", out of "respect to the freewill of women".
    15. A Christian wife of a Muslim may continue in the Christian faith, attend church, and communicate with her spiritual advisers. She is not to be forced to forsake her faith.
    16. "Christians must attend to all repairs on their own churches, chapels and monasteries." If Muslims ask Christians for help, Christians shall not deny it.
    17. A Christian envoy sent to negotiate peace "between Moslems and Infidels" shall not be prevented. His service is accepted, and whoever despises him is among the wicked.
  • Provisions, part (c): commandments on Christians (pp. 225–226).
    1. Give no aid to infidels, openly or secretly. Do not receive enemies of Muslims in their houses.
    2. Do not let enemy men stop at their houses or churches. Do not harbor enemy troops or aid them "with spear, arrow, sword or horse".
    3. Do not act as guides to them or show them how to ambush. Do not keep their possessions, communicate with them or shelter them "except only under duress".
    4. A Muslim at a Christian's house "may there be entertained three days and three nights; more than that is unnecessary."
    5. Christians shall avert from Muslims the abuse of tyrants. If they must hide a Muslim, they give him a place to lie and food.
    6. Muslim women and children shall not be betrayed or shown to the enemy.
    7. Violators are "loathsome to God". The treaty binds "until such time as God shall ordain."
Ch. 10 — Covenant with the Christians of the World
World I [1630] — Rycaut (1668): 99–102 — pp. 227–229 [PDF 252–254]

  • Issuer: "Mahomet sent from God to teach mankind, and declare the Divine Commission in truth".

  • Recipients: "That the cause of Christian religion determined by God, might remain in all parts of the East, and of the West, as well amongst the inhabitants, as strangers, near and remote, known, and unknown". Violators: "whether he be a King, or any other of the faithful." The covenant is one "which the Christians have required of me".

  • Date: "the last day of the Moon of the fourth Month, the fourth year of Hegira in Medina" (p. 229).

  • Place: Medina.

  • Scribe: "the Secretary was Moavia ben abi Sofian, a Soldier of the Messenger of God" (p. 229).

  • Witnesses (4 named + "a number of others"):

    1. Abu-Bacre Assadiqu
    2. Ombar ben-alcharab
    3. Ithman benAfaw
    4. Ati [OCR; Ali] ben abi-taleb

    The list ends "... With a number of others" (p. 229). Closing: "May God remunerate those who are witnesses to this writing. Praise be to God the Lord of all creatures."

  • Provisions:

    1. Defend "their Judges in my Provinces, with my Horse and Foot, Auxiliaries, and other my faithful followers", and secure them in peace and war.
    2. Protect "their Churches, Temples, Oratories, Monasteries, and places of Pilgrimage" wherever they are (mountain, valley, cavern, house, plain, sand, any edifice).
    3. Preserve their religion and goods on land or sea, East or West, "even as I keep myself and my Scepter". Repel their enemies. "no evil touch them before it first afflict mine".
    4. Free them from the burdens confederates suffer, "either by loans of money or impositions". They pay only what they please.
    5. No bishop removed from his diocese, no Christian "compelled to renounce his faith", no "Monk his profession", no pilgrim disturbed, no "Religious man in his Cell".
    6. Churches are not to be "destroyed, or converted into Mosques".
    7. No imposition on friars or bishops, or on those not liable to taxes, "unless it be with their own consent."
    8. The tax on rich merchants, pearl-fishermen and miners of precious stones "shall not exceed above 12 shillings yearly". It falls only on "constant inhabitants", not on travellers or men of uncertain abode, unless they possess inherited land. No one is taxed beyond his ability or beyond others.
    9. Confederates are not obliged to go to war, "either to fight or discover their Armies". The Muslims "shall watch, and ward, and defend them". They need not "find Horse of Arms, unless they voluntarily famish [furnish] them", and those who do are rewarded.
    10. No Muslim shall insult them or "contend with them in anything but in kindness".
    11. If a Christian commits a crime, the Muslim shall assist, intercede, "give caution for him, and compound for his miscarriage". He shall have liberty to redeem his life. They "enjoy what the Moselmans enjoy, and suffer what they suffer".
    12. Marriage: parents are not to be compelled "to match their Daughters with Moselmans", nor molested for refusing.
    13. A Christian woman who joins a Muslim keeps "liberty of conscience". She may obey "her Ghostly Father". No threats of divorce or pressure to forsake her faith.
    14. When Christians repair churches or convents, Muslims "ought to contribute, and freely to bestow according to their ability… gratis".
    15. They shall not be oppressed or hated, or compelled "to carry Letters, or show the way".
    16. Conditions on Christians: no entertainment for "a Soldier, enemy to the Moselmans". No enemies of the Muslims lodged in their houses, churches or convents. No arms, horse or men for the enemy camp, and no correspondence with the enemy.
    17. "To any Moselman and his Beasts, they shall give three days entertainment with variety of Meat".
    18. They shall hide a Muslim in danger and not betray him.
    19. Violators lose "these privileges indulged to Bishops and Christian Monks, and to the believers of the contents of the Achoran."
    20. Observe this "until the Day of Judgment, and dissolution of the world."
World II [1630] — Van Dyck (1881) — pp. 230–232 [PDF 255–257]

  • Issuer: "Mahommed, messenger of God, sent to teach men and declare to them his Divine mission".

  • Recipients: The Christian religion "can remain free in all parts of the East and of the West, both among those who are [natives] of the country and among those who are neighbors to it, both among those who are strangers and among those who are not". Violators: "be he king, prince, or other unbeliever" (p. 230). Compare Rycaut's "or any other of the faithful".

  • Date: "the last day of the moon of the fourth month, the fourth year of the flight to Medina" (p. 232).

  • Place: Not separately stated. "Medina" appears only within "the flight to Medina".

  • Scribe: "the scribe who has drawn them up in [is] Mu'awiyyah Ibn Abi Safian, the soldier of the apostle of God" (p. 232).

  • Witnesses (4 named + "several others"):

    1. Abu Bakr es-Suddik
    2. Omar Ibn-el-Khattab
    3. Othnian [OCR; Othman] Ibn Affan
    4. AH [OCR; Ali] Ibn Abi Talib

    The list ends "and several others" (p. 232).

  • Provisions. Same sequence as I, with these differences:

    1. He promises "to protect their magistrates in my provinces" (Rycaut: "Judges").
    2. The burdens are "whether loan of silver or imports".
    3. "nor shall any Christian be constrained to renounce his faith, nor any workman his profession" (Rycaut: "Monk his profession"). The text adds "nor any monk in his cell" and "neither shall their temples be torn down or converted into mosques".
    4. "No impost shall be put upon the monks or the bishop".
    5. The tax sentence has no amount: "The tax to be demanded of rich merchants, of pearl-fishers, and of the miners who mine precious stones, gold and silver, as well as that to be demanded of other wealthy Christians, domiciled and established in fixed places, and not upon travelers…" (p. 231).
    6. Allies are not employed in military expeditions, and need not furnish horses or arms unless they choose.
    7. A Muslim must help a Christian who commits a crime, "become his surety and settle his matter; he can even redeem his life".
    8. Marriage: "the fathers and mothers shall not be forced to give their daughters in marriage to Moslems". They are not troubled "for having refused theirs sons or their daughters".
    9. A Christian wife is left her liberty of conscience and may obey "her spiritual father".
    10. Muslims must contribute to the repair of churches and monasteries "gratuitously".
    11. Muslims may not oblige Christians "to carry letters or serve as guides".
    12. Conditions on Christians: as in I. They furnish "during three days to every Moslem things necessary for his subsistence and that of his beast", and hide a Muslim in danger.
    13. Violators lose "the privileges granted to bishops and other monks; and the believers of that which is contained in the Qur'an."
    14. Observe this "till the day of judgment and till the dissolution of the world."

    27. Sad [Sa'd] ibn 'Ubadah
    28. Zayd ibn Arqarn [OCR; Arqam]
    29. Sahl ibn Bayda'
    30. Da'ud ibn Jubayr
    31. Abu al-Aliyyah
    32. Abu Ahrifah
    33. Ibn 'Usayr
    34. Hashim ibn Asiyyah
    35. Zayd ibn Arqarn [Arqam] (repeat of 28)
    36. 'Umar ibn Yamin
    37. Ka'b ibn Malik
    38. Ka'b ibn Ka'b

    The list ends "May Allah be pleased with all of them!" The closing reads: "Allah suffices as a Witness for what is contained in this document [kitaban]. Praise be to Allah, the Lord of the Worlds!"

  • Provisions:

    1. The document is an "authoritative covenant ['ahdan mar'iyyan], a well-known certificate [sijlan manshuran], and a testament [wasiyyah]". Breakers violate the "Covenant of Allah" and deny the "Oath of Allah [mithaq Allah]".
    2. He grants alliances ['uhud] and pledges [mawathiq] to those who asked, and places them under the safeguard of His Prophets, Messengers, Elect and Saints.
    3. "I protect their judges in my fortified borderlines [fi thughuri] with my horses and my men", in peace or war.
    4. "I grant security to their churches, their places of pilgrimage [siyahah]" wherever they are. He protects their religion and property "the same way that I protect myself, my successors [khatimi]…".
    5. He exempts them "from any requisitions or any onerous obligations". "I block from them the harm in the supplies which obliges the people of the pact [ahl al-'ahd] from loan ['ariyah] and land tribute [kharaj] except what they themselves consent to give."
    6. No one may remove a bishop, a Christian from his Christianity, a monk, a pilgrim or "a hermit monk from his tower".
    7. No one may destroy any part of their churches or take parts of their buildings for mosques or Muslim homes.
    8. No jizyah or tax on monks or bishops, "only that which they are prepared to give willingly."
    9. The jizyah on owners of large businesses, divers, miners of precious stones, gold and silver, and the wealthy and powerful "may not surpass more than twelve dirhams per year". This applies only to inhabitants and residents, not travellers.
    10. A traveller, or someone whose residence is unknown, pays neither kharaj nor jizyah unless he has inherited land "over which the ruler [sultan] has a monetary right". The labor force on such land is not to be "taxed excessively".
    11. The ahl al-dhimmah are not obliged to go to war with the Muslims. They are not forced to give horses or arms unless freely, and "Whoever does so will be recognized for his action."
    12. "No Christian will be made Muslim by force: And dispute ye not with the People of the Book, except with means better [29:46]. They must be covered by the wing of mercy."
    13. If a Christian commits a crime or offense, Muslims give him help, defense and protection. They pardon him and urge the victim to pardon him or accept compensation.
    14. Muslims must not abandon the Christians. Whatever good or harm befalls the Muslims befalls them too.
    15. No forced marriages. Muslims may not take Christian girls in marriage against their parents' will, or oppress families who refuse.
    16. A Muslim husband must respect his Christian wife's beliefs and give her "freedom to listen to her [clerical] superiors". Forcing her breaks the alliance of Allah.
    17. Muslims must help Christians repair churches and convents "by pure donation", not for reward.
    18. In war, Muslims will not employ any Christian "as a messenger, scout, guide or spy".
    19. Conditions on Christians: no scouting or spying for an enemy. No sheltering of enemies. Enemies may not halt "in their villages, their oratories". No weapons, horses or men for the enemy, "including greeting them".
    20. They host Muslims "for three days and three nights… with their animals", with the same food they eat themselves.
    21. They hide a Muslim in their homes or oratories and keep him concealed.
    22. Whoever contravenes this "will be cast out of the alliance between Allah and His Messenger". All are to abide by treaties "contracted with the kings, the monks [ruhban], and the Christians [nasara]".
    23. This holds "until the hour [of the Resurrection] and the end of the world".
World IV [1538] — Morrow ("2103" [sic]) — pp. 237–241 [PDF 262–266]

  • Invocation: "In the Name of Allah, the Creator [al-Khaliq], the Living [al-Hayy], the Speaking [al-Natiq], the One who Remains after the Annihilation of Creation".

  • Title inside the text: "This is a copy [nuskhah] of the covenant ['ahd] which was written by Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al Muttalib for all the Christians [nasara]." Then: "Copy [nuskhah] of the Covenant [kitab al-'ahd]". Then: "This covenant of Allah… was ordered to be written by Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Muktalib [sic]… to all the Christians and all the monks". Also "It was written by the Lion [asad] and the People of His Vocation [ahl al-millati]" (p. 237).

  • Recipients: "all the Christians and all the monks"; "all those who profess the Christian religion [da'wat al-nasraniyyah] in the Eastern lands and its West, near and far, be they Arabs or non-Arabs, known or unknown". Violators: "whether he is a Sultan or anyone else among the believers [mu'minin] and the Muslims."

  • Date of issue: None stated in the covenant. The only date is the copyist's colophon (1538 copy; see timeline and §5).

  • Place: Not stated.

  • Scribe: "'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote this covenant, and the manuscript [sijl] was written on a piece of leather [jild] that was not small. It remained at the Sultan's authority and was sealed by the Prophet" (p. 241).

  • Witnesses (30; the text says "there are thirty witnesses").

    1. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq
    2. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab
    3. 'Uthnian [OCR; 'Uthman] ibn Affan
    4. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib

  • Provisions:

    1. Anyone who keeps the covenant "holds to his Islam". Anyone who breaks it "merits His Maledictions".
    2. He grants alliances and pledges and places them under the safeguard of His Prophets, Chosen Ones [asfiya] and Friends [awliyya'].
    3. "I should protect their land ['ard], their monasteries [al-diyar], with my power… my horses, my men, my weapons… my strength… and my Muslim followers", and "protect their businesses". He secures their churches, businesses, houses of worship, and the places of their monks and pilgrims everywhere. He protects "their dhimmah, their faith [millah], and their religion [din]".
    4. "I sacrifice myself for them… because they are my flock [ra'iyyah] and the people under my protection [ahl al-dhimmati]". "No harm will reach them unless it reaches my Companions [ashabi]".
    5. He removes "the harm from taxes and loan in the supplies" except what they willingly give.
    6. No one may remove a bishop, monk, Christian, "an ascetic [zahid] from his tower" or a pilgrim. No one may destroy their churches or businesses or use their buildings for mosques or Muslim homes.
    7. No jizyah or kharaj "on monks, bishops or those who are worshippers among them, who, by devotion, wear woolen clothing [al-suf] or live alone in the mountains".
    8. The jizyah applies to Christians "who are not clerics [man la yatta'abbad] with the exception of the monk and the pilgrim in the amount of four dirhams per year or an inexpensive cloak [tawb]".
    9. The poor are helped "by means of the savings stored in the Treasury [bayt al-mal]", and helped with food if needed, "provided they willingly accept."
    10. The land tribute [jizyah al-kharaj] on big business by land or sea, pearl-diving, mining and the wealthy may "not exceed twelve dirhams [fiddah] per year", and only on inhabitants and residents.
    11. Nothing is demanded of travellers or wayfarers. Land tax falls only on landowners, without excess. The labor force is not overtaxed.
    12. Protected people "are not to engage in war". They are not forced to provide arms or horses unless freely.
    13. "what the Muslims have borrowed will be guaranteed by the [State] Treasury [bayt al-mal] until it is returned to them. If they die or are damaged, the [State] Treasury… will provide monetary compensation."
    14. "No one who practices the Christian religion will be forced to enter into Islam. And dispute ye not… [29:46]". They are under the wing of mercy.
    15. Muslims must help a Christian who commits a crime, "as well as pay his penalty for him", and encourage reconciliation.
    16. Muslims must not abandon them. They share good and bad fortune.
    17. "The girls of the Christians" are not to be forced into marriage, and are not taken against their parents' will.
    18. A Muslim husband must respect his Christian wife's religion. Otherwise he is counted "among the liars [kadhibin]".
    19. Muslims must help Christians repair churches and convents "not… with the aim of receiving any reward or debt".
    20. In war, Muslims will not employ any Christian "as a messenger, scout, guide, to show power, or for any other duty of war".
    21. Conditions on Christians: no spying, no sheltering of enemies, no halting places for enemies, no weapons, horses or men "or call for unnecessary things". "They must not annoy them and they should be honored as long as they persist in their religion and their care for their pact."
    22. They host Muslims "three days and three nights", with the same food.
    23. They hide a Muslim in need.
    24. Contraveners are cast out of the alliance. All are to abide by treaties "contracted with the monks".
    25. "The Messenger of Allah… must respect what he has granted… until the Hour of [Resurrection] arrives".
    26. "Whoever is unjust after this towards a [Christian] subject [dhimmi]… I will be his enemy on the Day of Judgment among all the Muslims."
Ch. 11 — Covenant with the Christians of Najran — Morrow (2013) — pp. 293–300 [PDF 318–325]
  • Exordium (pp. 293–297): "A covenant of protection granted by Allah and His Messenger to the People of the Book, the Christians, who belong to the religion of Najran or any other Christian sect." Other content:
    • The Jews' hostility, including "Their behavior during the days of Hunayn, the battles against the Bani Qaynuqah, the tribe of Qurayzah and Nadir" (p. 294).
    • Qur'an [5:82-83] is quoted (p. 294).
    • "The Sayyid 'Absiso [as OCR'd], Ibn Hijrah, Ibrahim the monk, and 'Isa the Bishop, came to see me, accompanied by forty horsemen from Najran" (pp. 294–295).
    • The Christians "united to wage war against the Jews" (p. 295).
    • "three people (from Sayyid Ghassani) asked me for a document that would act as a safe-conduit" (p. 296).
    • "I therefore called the leaders of the Muslims and my main Companions" (p. 296).
    • The covenant is binding "so long as water fills the ocean floor, rain falls from the sky…" (p. 296).
  • Covenant proper (pp. 297–300). Issuer: "This document has been provided by Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Messenger of Allah to all of humanity".
  • Recipients: "To Sayyid Ibn Harith ibn Ka'b, his co-religionists, and all those who profess the Christian religion, be they in East or West, in close regions or faraway regions, be they Arabs or foreigners, known or unknown." (p. 297).
  • Date: None stated.

  • Provisions:
    1. Muslims "whether or not they detain power" must preserve it "from generation to generation". No governor or holder of authority may revoke it. Believers may not impose conditions beyond those in the document.
    2. "my horsemen, my foot-soldiers, my armies, my resources, and my Muslim partisans will protect the Christians as far away as they may be located", in peace or war.
    3. Protection of their persons, "churches, chapels, oratories, the monasteries of their monks, the residences of their anchorites", wherever they are, and of "their religion and their Church".
    4. He exempts them "for [from] any requisitions or any onerous obligations".
    5. "I forbid any conquerors of the faith to rule over them during their invasions or to oblige them to pay taxes unless they themselves willingly consent."
    6. No one may remove a bishop, monk or anchorite. No one may destroy their churches or use their buildings for mosques or Muslim homes.
    7. No capitation or tax on monks, bishops, or those who "wear woolen clothing or live alone in the mountains".
    8. "a limit set of four dirhams per year that all other Christians who are not clerics, monks, or hermits need to pay. Otherwise, let them provide one outfit of stripped [sic] material or one embroidered turban from Yemen. This is to help Muslims and to contribute to the growth of the Public Treasury. Were cloth difficult for them, they should provide its equivalent price, if they themselves willingly consent."
    9. The capitation on those with income, land, large commerce, mines or wealth may "not surpass, as a whole, twelve dirhams per year", and only on inhabitants and residents.
    10. Nothing is demanded of travellers or wayfarers. Land tax falls only on owners "of inherited properties over which the ruler has a right", without excess. The labor force is not overtaxed.
    11. Members of the alliance are not obliged to go to war. "No Christian is to be constrained to provide equipment to a single Muslims [sic], in money, in arm or in horses", unless freely, and those who give will be praised.
    12. "No Christian will be made Muslim by force: And dispute ye not with the People of the Book, except with means better [29:46]."
    13. Muslims help a Christian who commits a crime. They pardon him and seek reconciliation or compensation.
    14. Muslims must not abandon them. They share good and bad fortune.
    15. No forced marriages, and no taking of Christian girls against their parents' will.
    16. A Muslim husband respects his Christian wife's religion and her freedom to listen to her clerical superiors.
    17. Muslims help repair churches and convents "by pure donation".
    18. In war, no Christian is employed "as a messenger, scout, guide or spy".
    19. Conditions on Christians, introduced as "He is also placing conditions… and I demand…": no spying, no sheltering of enemies, no halting places for enemies, no weapons, horses or men for them, "nor must they treat them well".
    20. They host Muslims "for three days and three nights… with their animals", with the same food.
    21. They hide a Muslim in need. The text prints "guide him help" (sic; World III has "give him help").
    22. Contraveners are cast out. All abide by treaties with the monks and "every other commitment that each prophet has made with his nation". This holds "until the hour of the Resurrection, Allah-willing."
Ch. 12 — Covenant with the Assyrian Christians — Malech (1910): 228–230 — pp. 313–314 [PDF 338–339]

    Closing: "The peace of God be upon them all!"

  • Provisions:

    1. Muslims are to "protect and help the Nazarene nation in this country of ours in their own land."
    2. Leave their places of worship in peace. Help their chief and priests in need, "be it in the mountains, in the desert, on the sea, or at home."
    3. Leave their houses and property alone, "because the Nazarenes are my subjects, pay tribute to me, and will help the Moslems."
    4. "No tribute, but what is agreed upon". Church buildings are left unaltered. Priests may teach and worship in their own way. "full liberty of worship in their churches and homes."
    5. No church may be torn down or turned into a mosque "except by the consent and free will of the Nazarenes".
    6. "The tribute paid the Nazarenes [sic] shall be used to promote the teachings of Islam and shall be deposited at the treasury of bayt al-mal."
    7. "A common man shall pay one dinar, but the merchants and people who own mines of gold and silver and are rich shall pay twelve dinars." Note: dinars.
    8. "Strangers and people who have no houses or other settled property shall not have taxes levied upon them." An heir pays "a settled sum to the bayt al-mal treasury".
    9. Christians are not obliged to fight Islam's enemies. If they are attacked, Muslims give "horses and weapons, if they need them, and protect them".
    10. "The Christians are not obliged to turn Moslems, until God's will makes them believers."
    11. Muslims shall not force Christian women to accept Islam, and are to be kind to those who choose it.
    12. A Christian wife of a Muslim "has liberty to worship at her own church", and is not treated unkindly.
    13. "If the Nazarenes wish to build a church, their Mohammedan neighbors shall help them."
    14. A great and learned Christian is to be honored and not envied.
    15. Christians shall not shelter an enemy of Islam or give him a horse, weapon or other help.
    16. A Christian shall host a Muslim in need "for three days and nights" and shelter him from enemies.
    17. Christians shall protect Muslim women and children "and not deliver them up to the enemy or expose them to view."
    18. If Christians fail these conditions, "the agreement is null and void."

5. Other factual claims

Sinai VI colophon (Morrow), p. 217 [PDF 242]:

  • "A copy of this covenant has been deposited in the treasury [khizanah] of the Sultan. It was signed with the seal of the Prophet, peace be upon him. It was written on a piece of leather from Ta'if."
  • "This copy, which is copied from the original, is sealed with the signature of the noble Sultan [sharif al-Sultani]. This reproduction was copied from the copy that was copied from the copy written in the handwriting of the Leader of the Believers, Ali ibn Abi Talib".
  • "With the order of the noble Sultan… which was given to a community of monks who inhabit the Mountain of Tur-Sina'i because the copy, which was copied from the copy written by the Leader of the Believers, was lost, in order that his document be a support of the Sultan's royal decrees which are evidenced by the records in the hands of the community in question."
  • "This is a reproduction of the original ['asl] without adapation [sic] [fadl wa wad]."
  • "Written by the weakest of slaves, al-Bari Nuh ibn Ahmad al-Ansari".
  • "The judge from Egypt, the Safeguarded [mahrusah], has pardoned them."
  • "Sealed with the round seal and certified. Nuh Ahmad ibn al-Ansari [signature]". Note the name is given in two forms: "al-Bari Nuh ibn Ahmad al-Ansari" and "Nuh Ahmad ibn al-Ansari".
  • "Modeled on a seal whose original [mahar] is signed with this signature."
  • "Written by the poor [faqir], Muhammad al-Qadi, from Ancient Egypt, may he be forgiven!"

Signing and sealing claims in the Sinai versions:

  • I: "the Prophet marking it with his hand at the mosque of the Prophet".
  • II and III: "It is signed by the Prophet himself".
  • V: "It was signed by the great Assistants of Mohammed".
  • VI: "signed with the seal of the Prophet".

Plate, p. 222: a Turkish-language copy of the Sinai covenant "from 1638", reproduced "by permission of St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, Egypt". The term printed is "Achtinanie" [OCR; likely "Achtiname"].

Skrobucha text, p. 211: "By permission of Oxford Universtiy [sic/OCR] Press".

Corrected Arabic method, p. 218, fn. 1: spelling and grammar "corrected", punctuation inserted, text "fully vocalized and case endings included". The footnote applies to "this and following covenants".

World IV (1538), p. 241:

  • "'Ali ibn Abi Talib… wrote this covenant, and the manuscript [sijl] was written on a piece of leather [jild] that was not small. It remained at the Sultan's authority and was sealed by the Prophet".
  • Copyist's colophon: completed on Monday, last month of Ba'una, year of the Martyrs = 27 Muharram 945 AH.
  • The book "belongs to the great soul [al-mubajjal], the master [al-mawla], the leader [al-ra'is], the elder [al-shaykh], the scholar [al-'alim], Sum'an, the son of… Fadi [Fadl] Allah… known as [al-ma'ruf] al-Barallusi."
  • The writer, "the humble [miskin], full of faults and sins", asks readers for prayers, and "the Messiah [masih] will reward them one hundred and sixty-three times." An alternate reading inserts the name "Michel" (translator's note).

6. Internal inconsistencies and points to check

  1. Typo in a source year. World IV is headed "Translation by John Andrew Morrow in 2103" (p. 237 [PDF 262]). Morrow's other translations here are dated 2013 (pp. 215, 233, 293).
  2. Sinai IV witness list. The Skrobucha 1966 translation (p. 212) prints the same 16 anglicized names as Pococke 1809 (p. 206): "Homar, the son of Hattavi… Kastner the son of Abid…". Texts II, III, V and VI give a different list of 21–22 Companion names. Check whether Skrobucha's original has Pococke's list, or whether the book supplied it.
  3. Item division differs between I and IV:
    • I: "Abombaker, the son of Anibi; Kaphe Ottoman, the son of Gafas" (p. 206).
    • IV: "Abombaker, the son of Ambi Kaphe; Ottoman, the son of Gafas" (p. 212).
  4. Who wrote the Sinai text (IV and VI). Each version says both that Muhammad wrote it and that Ali wrote it in his own hand:
    • IV (p. 212): "this letter of protection, written by Muhammad, son of Abdullah" and "written in his own hand by Ali bin Abu Talib".
    • VI (pp. 216–217): the same pairing.
  5. Name of the Sinai scribe:
    • II: "Aby-Taleb" only (p. 208).
    • III: "Aly ebn Taleb" (p. 210).
    • I, IV, V and VI: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.
  6. CE date for the Sinai text. Only II and III give a CE equivalent ("1st of August, 622"), for 3 Muharram AH 2 (pp. 208, 210). I, IV, V and VI give no CE date. Verifiers may wish to check the conversion; the book offers no others to compare.
  7. Sinai poll-tax ceiling:
    • "twelve drachms": I (p. 206).
    • "twelve drachms of silver": II (p. 207).
    • "twelve silver drachmas": III (p. 209).
    • "ten dirhams a head a year": IV (p. 212).
    • "twelve Dirhams a head per year": V (p. 214).
    • "twelve dirhams a head per year": VI (p. 216).
  8. Qur'an citation for the same clause. The "no strife with the People of the Book unless over what is for the good" clause is tagged [5:48] in VI (p. 216). IV gives no tag. The parallel clause in V and the quotation in I (XIII) are tagged [29:46].
  9. Sinai witness lists across II, III, V and VI:
    • Count: II has 22 items, splitting "Thabet-ebn-Keys, MonKayetmeth". III has 21, with "Thabet ebn Kays Mou Khayetmeth" as one.
    • V and VI drop the "Thabet ebn Kays", "Mou Khayetmeth", "Hachem ebn Omyeh" and "Ebn el Ass" forms. In their place they have "Thabit Ibn Nafees/Nafis", "Zied/Zayd ibn Thabit", "Abou Hanifa Ibn Attaba / Bu Hanifah ibn 'Ubayyah" and "Hashim Ibn Obied / Hashim ibn 'Ubayyah".
    • Order: VI moves "Harith ibn Thabit; Abd al-Azim ibn Hasan" to positions 9–10. In V they are at 19–20.
    • Name forms that differ:
      • Father of Abd Allah: "Abdullah Ibn Omar Ibn El-Aas" (V) vs "Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As" (VI).
      • Last name: "Aamir Ibn Yasir" (V) vs "Amir ibn Yasin" (VI) vs "Amer-ebn-Yassin" (II).
      • "Abou Harirat" (V) vs "Abi Hurayrah" (VI).
      • "Talhat-ebn-Obeydallah" (II/III) vs "Talhah ibn Abd Allah" (VI).
      • Third witness's father: "Otman-ebn-Assan" (II) vs "Otman ebn Hassan" (III).
  10. Divergent renderings of the same Mauchin French (II vs III):
    • "although these priests are cancelled by me" (II) vs "as those priests are my rayas" (III).
    • "it is forbidden to enter into discussion with them by soft measures" (II) vs "neither shall any enter into strife… but behave mildly towards them" (III).
  11. Church repair in the Sinai texts:
    • I: "no person hinder them from repairing their churches". This is a ban on hindrance, not a promise of help.
    • II/III: "assisted to preserve their churches".
    • IV: "assisted in the improvement".
    • VI: "assisted in the maintenance".
    • V: "not be withheld from building churches or repairing convents".
  12. Christian wife (Sinai):
    • Only V adds that the marriage "must not take place except after her consent".
    • II/III: she "go[es] to the house of / join[s] the Musulmans".
    • I: "marry a Muslim man".
  13. Church repair (Persia vs all other covenants). Persia says "Christians must attend to all repairs on their own churches, chapels and monasteries" (p. 225). Every other covenant has Muslims help or not hinder.

    • I and II: "last day of the moon of the fourth month, the fourth year" (pp. 229, 232).

1. Section summary

Chapter 13, "Examining the Authorities" (pp. 323–330 [348–355])

Morrow examines the lists of witnesses ("authorities") attached to the covenants. He says they can be read three ways: as independent chains, as offshoots of one source chain, or as late additions that do not affect the content. He goes through the witnesses on the Covenant with the Monks of Mount Sinai one by one, giving death or life dates, Sunni and Shi'i reputations, and possible corrections of misread names (Abu Hurayrah as Abu Hudayfah; Harith ibn Thabit as Hassan ibn Thabit; Abu Hanifah as Abu Hudayfah). He concludes it is a Sunni chain, inconsistent with Shi'i standards, and "relatively sound." He then examines the lists on the Covenants with the Christians of the World (1630 and 1538), Najran and Assyria. Many of these witnesses are problematic: some died before the documents could have been issued (Hamzah at Uhud, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Ja'far), some converted late (Mu'awiyyah, Abu al-'Aliyyah), and some are obscure early emigrants to Abyssinia. To reconcile early and late witnesses, he proposes that the Prophet re-issued the covenants regularly, perhaps yearly, or dictated them all in the Year of Delegations (630–631 CE). He applies hadith-science principles (consensus, "when in doubt, leave it out," Ibn Qayyim's content-based rejection criteria via Azami). He argues that the absence of developed isnads is a sign of antiquity, and that the covenants are mutawatir in wording and meaning (though not by chain), mashhur, marfu', musnad and muttasil. He adds that as written prophetic documents they are not subject to isnad rules, and places them in a category comparable to hadith qudsi. Variants are explained through the four modes of quotation in hadith literature (Azami 75–78).

Chapter 14, "Tracking the Transmissions" (pp. 331–332 [356–357])

Morrow sets out four possible modes of transmission:

  1. Multiple individual prophetic transmissions.
  2. A single source with later segmentation, where the Najran charter (the oldest surviving, 9th century CE) is copied by others.
  3. A single source with bifurcation: Najran to Egypt and the Levant; Egypt (Cairo) to Sinai, then to the Armenians of Persia, then to the Assyrians.
  4. A lost "Q source" covenant, by analogy with Bible studies.

He notes that a chronology built on the dates of surviving copies is flawed. He favours the first hypothesis: most covenants are unique and were issued by the Prophet to different denominations. He leaves open how the 1538 and 1630 Covenants with the Christians of the World are related, suggesting the 1630 copy (supposedly found at Mount Carmel) was for the Levant and the 1538 copy for Egypt.

Chapter 15, "The Covenants in Context" (pp. 333–352 [358–377])

This is a long polemical and historical survey arguing that Islam has historically treated Christians with tolerance compared with how Christians and other powers treated the conquered. It opens with anti-Muslim slurs and a Bukhari hadith against oppressing Jews and Christians. It claims the Prophet fought 68 campaigns with no more than 1,000 casualties in total, and that all his wars were just. Topics in order:

  • Early conquests: 'Umar's restraint and garrison towns; Glubb, Donner, Brockopp, Berkey and Fletcher on the absence of destruction and on Christian growth; Nestorian sources (Yeshuyab III, the Bishop of Adiabene, John bar Penkaye).
  • Early caliphs: Abu Bakr's renewal of the Najran covenant (Abu Yusuf); 'Umar's Jerusalem assurances; the genuine "Treaty of 'Umar" (al-Tabari, 15 AH) set against the "Pact of 'Umar" (al-Turtushi), which Morrow treats as a forgery, possibly of 'Umar II's era; 'Umar's 638 CE (17 AH) covenant in the Chronicle of Seert, and Addai Scher's view that it is apocryphal; Khalid ibn al-Walid's promise.
  • Mu'awiyyah's Christian ties: his navy and the Battle of the Masts (655 CE); Christian courtiers; Christian imagery on early Islamic coins.
  • Contrast with other powers: Romans (Joshel's figures), Huns, Mongols, Sassanids (614), Charlemagne (782), the Sui, Arian Visigoths.
  • Al-Andalus: the golden age; the fall of Granada (1492), which he blames on Muslim failure to obey God and on ignoring the Prophet's succession orders; the broken Capitulation of 1492; the persecution and expulsion of the Moriscos, dated year by year (1499–1614), with casualty and expulsion figures.
  • Ottomans: Mehmet II's Athos guarantees and Bosnian ahidname (1463); millet autonomy; the Mamluk–French treaty (1500); exceptions (Selim II, Selim I); the Selim I forced-conversion episodes (Eliot, Lybyer, Runciman, Gradeva); the Capitulations (1517–1923); the Ottoman Empire as a refuge.
  • Law and civilization: the shari'ah as inspiration for the Napoleonic Code; a balancing passage crediting the Catholic Church and Byzantium; the distinction between traditional shari'ah and Wahhabi/Salafi practice.
  • Close: the Chronicle of Seert's praise of Muslim rule, and a Qur'an epigraph (9:12) on p. 352.
Chapter 16, "General Conclusions" (pp. 353–364 [378–389])

Morrow concludes:

  • Neglect: the covenants were passed down from Islam's earliest days but ignored, which he blames on imperialists and Muslim scholars.
  • Authenticity: their content fully agrees with Islam, and chains are not required for primary sources.
  • Witnesses: the lists were probably appended centuries later to satisfy hadith scholars. The Persian covenant has no signatories and may predate all the others.
  • Rebuttals:
    • Sir Paul Rycaut's view that the covenant was a ploy of a weak early community.
    • The view that the short treaties in Ibn Sa'd were inflated by Christians. Morrow answers that Ibn Sa'd's treaties are summaries, and points to dating: the Najran covenant was found in 878/879 CE, the Chronicle of Seert dates to the 9th century, and the covenants are contemporaneous with Bukhari, Muslim and Nisa'i.
    • Qureishi's rejection of the Treaty of Maqnah: Qureishi assigns it to 'Abbasid Jews under al-Mutawakkil (847–861), but Ibn Sa'd died in 845.
    • Mouton's view that the Saint Catherine covenant reflects an Islam invented by monks.
  • Politics and law: he argues that the Prophet founded a state, and that Islam is political and a "democratic theocracy" that is not liberal democracy. This includes critiques of US politics (Carter, Bush, Obama, TARP) and Wahhabism, and praise of Shi'i ijtihad.
  • Forgery: the only forged prophetic letter of protection is the Jewish Cairo Geniza document.
  • Critics of tradition: he attacks Orientalist scepticism, citing Brown, Nasr, Saleh, Hawting and Cremo & Thompson. He quotes Pillsbury Dodge and Anton Haddad (who translated the Sinai covenant in 1902).
  • Closing warning: prophetic warnings that breaking covenants brings calamity, which he says explains the Muslims' loss of power and colonization. Qur'an verses on keeping covenants follow, and an epigraph (3:199) on p. 364.
Chapter 17, "Suggestions for Future Scholarship" (pp. 365–376 [390–401])

Morrow calls his book a thesis and an "essay," and states his conclusion that the covenants are genuine. He urges Muslim scholars to keep the thousand-year consensus on the Sinai covenant and to use ihtiyat (precaution) for the Najran and World covenants. His proposed research includes:

  • Notes and fatwas on the Sinai copies, with the history of their English and French translations.
  • A comparative study of Gabriel Sionita's and J. G. Nissel's editions.
  • The origin of the 1538 manuscript (MS Arabe 214, BnF): its owner, scribe and named persons, the 1592 missionary, the different handwriting of its final pages, and "Michel."
  • Possible links between Sionita and Cyril Lucaris.
  • Archival searches in Turkey, plus reported copies at Deir-Saferan (1850), an Armenian pact (1822), a Baghdad "Traité" (1822) and Nallino's charter (1899). He also calls for searching out Leon Arpee's Persian covenant.
  • Scientific dating, and even DNA testing of relics.
  • Muslim communities' correspondence. His example is the Regraga Seven Saints tradition of Morocco.
  • Comparison with Ottoman ahdname diplomatics.
  • Textual instability arising from early Arabic script, with the Qur'an protected by memorization.
  • Linguistic and dating analysis of the Arabic and Persian covenants.
  • The varying witness counts (16, 22, 32, 37–38).
  • The semantic narrowing of mu'min, muslim, mushrik, kafir and munafiq.
  • Surveys of travel, diyarat and geographical literature.
  • New translations.

The section ends with a Qur'an epigraph (2:62, p. 374), the "IV Backmatter" part title (p. 375) and an epigraph (3:77–78, p. 376).

4. Factual claims (non-date), grouped by theme

Each claim has a page and a basis tag. Quotation marks show the book's own wording.

A. Witness lists: Sinai covenant (Ch. 13)
  1. The lists of witnesses on the Sinai covenant "vary from the standard twenty-two authorities to copies which cite thirty-seven to thirty-eight and others that quote sixteen," though the content is "the same from scroll to scroll." p. 323 [348] [fact]
  2. "With rare exception, these witnesses are listed in more or less the same order." p. 323 [348] [fact]
  3. Abu Bakr "is held in the highest esteem by Sunnis but… criticized by Shi'ites for actions after the passing of the Prophet." 'Umar "ranks second only to Abu Bakr in honesty" for Sunnis but "falls short" for Shi'ites. p. 323 [348] [fact]
  4. Abu al-Darda' appears on three of the covenants and is "conspicuously absent from two." Abu Hurayrah likewise appears on only three. p. 323 [348] [fact]
  5. Abu Hurayrah's presence is "problematic as he only moved to Medina during the last few years of the Prophet's life." "Abu Hurayrah" may be a misreading of Abu Hudayfah ibn al-Yaman, or may refer to Khuways ibn Hudayfah or Salim Mawla Abu Hudayfah. p. 323 [348] [fact] + [inf/op]
  6. Ibn Mas'ud is "Respected by the Sunnis" and held "in the highest regard by Shi'ites due to his loyalty to Imam 'Ali." p. 323 [348] [fact]
  7. 'Abbas is missing from two covenants. Morrow asks: "Was he included at some later point to please the 'Abbasids?" p. 323 [348] [inf/op]
  8. "Harith ibn Thabit" is "probably a misreading of Hassan ibn Thabit." 'Abd al-'Azim ibn Hasan is "a figure I have not identified." p. 323 [348] [inf/op]
  9. Fadl ibn 'Abbas (also as the diminutive Fudayl) is "Trusted by Sunnis," "revered by Shi'ites for refusing to pledge allegiance to Abu Bakr," "fought the Europeans and the Persians and died in Syria." p. 323 [348] [fact]
  10. Talhah appears as "Talhah ibn 'Abd Allah in all but one covenant." Zubayr and Talhah are "trusted by Sunnis but loathed by Shi'ites." p. 323 [348] [fact]
  11. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah "are admired by both Sunnis and Shi'is." p. 324 [349] [fact]
  12. Thabit ibn Nafis appears on four covenants and Thabit ibn Qays on one. Thabit ibn Qays "is excoriated by Shi'ites for his role in the Saqifah." "Thabit ibn Nafis" may really be Nafi ibn al-Harith. p. 324 [349] [fact] + [inf/op]
  13. Zayd ibn Thabit is found on four covenants but absent on a fifth. p. 324 [349] [fact]
  14. One witness's name was transcribed as "Bu Hanifah ibn 'Ubayyah, Abu Hanifah ibn 'Attaba, Mou Khayetmeth, and Azur ibn Yasin." Candidates: Khuzaymah ibn Thabit; Khuwaylid ibn Asad ("who migrated to Abyssinia"); Dhu Khuwaysirah al-Tamimi, "the surname of Dhu al-Thudayyah Hurqus ibn Zuhayr al-Tamimi, the leader of the Kharijites." "a positive identification is not possible." p. 324 [349] [inf/op]
  15. Another name appears as "Hashim ibn 'Ubayyah, Hashim ibn 'Ubayd, Hashim ibn 'Abid, Hashim ibn Umayyah." It could be "Hashim ibn Utbah ibn Abi Waqqas, a Muslim army commander." p. 324 [349] [inf/op]
  16. "Mu'azzam ibn Qurayshi": "The title Muazzam is an honorific for Companions… al-Qurayshi simply indicates… the tribe of Quraysh." He cannot be identified. p. 324 [349] [fact]/[inf/op]
  17. 'Ammar ibn Yasir appears "on all but one covenant," and once as "'Amir ibn Yasin." He may be Yasir ibn Amir al-Ansi. p. 324 [349] [fact] + [inf/op]
  18. The chain "is inconsistent with Shi'ite standards of testamentary trustworthiness… This is, to all appearances, a Sunni chain of authority and, surprisingly, it seems to be relatively sound." p. 324 [349] [inf/op]
  19. If Sa'd ibn Mu'adh is removed and "Abu Hanifah" is treated as a corruption of Abu Hudayfah, "the list… would be acceptable to all Muslims." p. 324 [349] [inf/op]
B. Witness lists: Covenants with the Christians of the World (1630, 1538), Najran and Assyria (Ch. 13)
  1. These lists "commence with Abu Bakr." 'Umar follows "on every covenant but that of 1630." 'Uthman appears "on all but the covenant with the Assyrian Christians." 'Ali "is found on two of the covenants, with the exclusion of the covenant with the Christians of the World from 1630" (wording as printed). pp. 324–325 [349–350] [fact]
  2. Mu'awiyyah "follows on every manuscript but the covenant with the Christians of the world from 1538." He "was a latecomer to Islam who turned the Caliphate into a monarchy" and "single-handedly destroyed the Caliphate of the Rightly-Guided." pp. 325 [350] [fact]/[inf/op]
  3. Mu'awiyyah's absence from 1538 and appearance in 1630, "where Imam 'Ali is not featured," suggests "anti-Shi'ite Sunni tampering may be at play." p. 325 [350] [inf/op]
  4. "There is no question that post-prophetic historical events have colored accounts from the life of the Prophet." p. 325 [350] [inf/op]
  5. Abu Darda' is "on all but one covenant"; Abu Dharr "on all"; "Abu Barr" on two (most probably al-Bara' ibn Malik al-Ansari). p. 325 [350] [fact] + [inf/op]
  6. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud "appears on all of the covenants." Hamzah is on two, "Hisham ibn al-Muttalib" on another. p. 325 [350] [fact]
  7. Fadl ibn 'Abbas is on all but one. Talhah is "son of 'Ubaydullah on one and… son of 'Abd Allah on the four others." p. 325 [350] [fact]
  8. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah "appear in uniform fashion on all manuscripts." p. 325 [350] [fact]
  9. Thabit ibn Qays is on three and appears as Thumamah ibn Qays on a fourth. Zayd ibn Thabit is on two and as "Yazid ibn Thabit" on others. 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid (unidentified) is on all but one. p. 325 [350] [fact]
  10. "Sahl ibn Sufya or Sifa, Sahl ibn Bayda' or Sahl ibn Tamim" is on three covenants and absent from two. Candidates: Sahl ibn Sa'd; Sahl ibn Bayda' ("known as Shuhayl ibn Wahb ibn Rabiah"); Sahl ibn Hunayf; Sahlah bint Suhayl ibn 'Amr ("The scribes may have masculinized her"); Tamim ibn Aws al-Dari; Mundhir ibn Sawa al-Tamimi, "the ruler of Bahrayn, to whom the Prophet had written." p. 325–326 [350–351] [inf/op]
  11. Sahlah bint Suhayl and her husband "were the adopted parents of Salim Mawla Abu Hudayfah." p. 325 [350] [fact]
  12. 'Uthman ibn Ma'tun is on three covenants and appears as "'Umar ibn Mazh'un" on another. The correct identification is 'Uthman ibn Maz'un, "a foster-brother of the Prophet." p. 326 [351] [fact]/[inf/op]
  13. "Dawud ibn Jibah or David ibn Gijah" is on two covenants, possibly a Jewish or Christian witness, or Da'd bint Jahdam ibn Umayyah ibn Zarib, "mother of Suhayl ibn Bayda'," a female Companion who migrated to Abyssinia. p. 326 [351] [inf/op]
  14. Abu al-'Aliyyah is on three, with the variant "Abu al-Ghaliyyah" on another. As a tabi'i, his presence suggests "a primitive isnad from the Prophet to the Companions and then from the ashab to their followers, the tabi'in." p. 326 [351] [fact] + [inf/op]
  15. 'Abd Allah appears as son of "'Amr ibn al-Qadi" on two and of 'Amr ibn al-'As on three; he could even be 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar. p. 326 [351] [fact] + [inf/op]
  16. The next witness appears as Abu Hudayfah, Abu Hanifah or Abu Ahrifah. If it were Abu Hanifah the jurist, "the entire list… might be a late forgery. However, it would take a total incompetent to make such a mistake. In all likelihood, the name is Abu Hudayfah." p. 326 [351] [inf/op]
  17. "Ibn 'Asir, Ibn 'Usayr, Abu al-'Azir, and Ibn 'Azir" could be 'Asim ibn Thabit. p. 326 [351] [inf/op]
  18. "Ibn Rabiah" is on only two covenants. Candidates: Sa'd ibn al-Rabi'; al-Harith ibn Rabi' al-Ansari; Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi'; Abu Hudayfah ibn 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah; 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah; Rabi' ibn 'Amir; "'Uthman ibn Rabi'ah ibn Uhban ibn Wahb ibn Hudhafa, who made the first migration to Abyssinia." p. 326 [351] [inf/op]
  19. 'Ammar is on two and misidentified as "'Umar ibn Yamin" on a third. 5. Covenant details (witnesses, transmission chains, dates)

5.1 Covenant of the Prophet with the Monks of Mount Sinai (Saint Catherine)

  • Content and lists: "the content… is the same from scroll to scroll," but witness lists vary: "the standard twenty-two authorities," "copies which cite thirty-seven to thirty-eight," and "others that quote sixteen" (p. 323 [348]). Ch. 17 instead says "Some copies… feature lists of sixteen signatories while others include twenty-two," and assigns the 37–38 figure to the CW and Najran (p. 370 [395]). See §7.

  • Order of witnesses, as discussed (pp. 323–324 [348–349]):

    1. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib
    2. Abu Bakr
    3. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab
    4. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan
    5. Abu al-Darda' (on 3, absent from 2)
    6. Abu Hurayrah (on 3)
    7. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud
    8. 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib (missing from 2)
    9. "Harith ibn Thabit" (= Hassan ibn Thabit?)
    10. 'Abd al-'Azim ibn Hasan (unidentified)
    11. Fadl ibn 'Abbas / Fudayl
    12. Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam
    13. Talhah ibn 'Ubaydullah ("ibn 'Abd Allah in all but one")
    14. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh
    15. Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah
    16. Thabit ibn Nafis (on 4) / Thabit ibn Qays (on 1)
    17. Zayd ibn Thabit (on 4, absent from a 5th)
    18. "Bu Hanifah ibn 'Ubayyah / Abu Hanifah ibn 'Attaba / Mou Khayetmeth / Azur ibn Yasin"
    19. "Hashim ibn 'Ubayyah / 'Ubayd / 'Abid / Umayyah"
    20. Mu'azzam ibn Qurayshi
    21. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As (penultimate)
    22. 'Ammar ibn Yasir (final; on all but one; "'Amir ibn Yasin" on one)

    That is 22 positions as discussed. This matches "the standard twenty-two" (my count; the author does not say so explicitly).

  • Assessment: a "Sunni chain of authority… relatively sound"; inconsistent with Shi'i standards, so not a Shi'i forgery (p. 324 [349]). "more solid" than the other lists (p. 327 [352]). It "might well survive the scholarly scrutiny of Muslim hadith scholars" (p. 328 [353]).

  • Dating implications:

    • If Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (d. 627) was a real witness: "the first couple of years after the hijrah, the traditional date affixed to existing copies."
    • If Sa'd is excluded and Abu Hurayrah included: "the last few years of the Prophet's life" (p. 324 [349]).

  • Original: the witness list "reportedly did not exist on the original" (p. 328 [353]).

  • Acceptance: "deemed trustworthy for over one thousand years by scholars from all major schools of jurisprudence" (p. 365 [390]). St Catherine's holds edicts from Hanbali, Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki and Fatimid jurists supporting it (p. 365 [390]).

  • Translations: English and French versions differ. Translators may have worked from different copies, or from "the Arabic original or a Turkish translation" (pp. 365–366 [390–391]).

  • Haddad's translation: Anton F. Haddad's English translation, The Oath of the Prophet Mohammed, was published in 1902 (p. 362 [387]).

  • Pillsbury Dodge: he calls it "the famous Oath," "remarkable" and "most strange" (p. 361 [386]).

  • Mouton: calls its Islam "legendary… created from scratch by the monks" (p. 359 [384]). Morrow rejects this (pp. 359 [384]).

  • Ibn Sa'd: a "Treaty of Saint Catherine" is cited by Ibn Sa'd (784–845 CE). Morrow reads it as a summary of the full covenant (p. 354 [379]).

  • Shah-Kazemi: has published a commentary on it (p. 373 [398]).

  • Qur'an 2:63 (Mount Sinai) is linked to this covenant (p. 363 [388]).
