    • Single occurrences: Suhayl ibn Mifah; Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr; 'Ubayd ibn Mansur; 'Abd al-'Azim; 'Abd al-'Azim ibn Husayn; Mu'azzam ibn Moshe.
    • Surname "al-Najashi" attached to 'Abd al-'Azim (p. 328 [353]).
  • Witness counts (p. 370 [395]): "the two versions of the Covenant… with the Christians of the World is the same at thirty-seven or thirty-eight"; Najran has "the same number"; the Assyrian covenant "stands at thirty-two."
  • Chronological problems with the witnesses:
    • Some died early: Hamzah (Uhud 625), Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Ja'far (629), Sahl ibn Bayda' (Badr), 'Asim ibn Thabit (Badr 624), Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' (Uhud 625).
    • Some converted late: Mu'awiyyah, Abu al-'Aliyyah (a tabi'i), Jubayr ibn Mut'im (after Hudaybiyyah 628), Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi' (after the Conquest of Mecca).
    • Morrow's proposed resolutions: regular, perhaps yearly, re-issue with earlier witnesses retained "out of respect"; "early and late authorities"; or dictation of all covenants in the Year of Delegations (630–631) (pp. 325, 327, 328).
  • Common order: the common witnesses follow "the same order," which suggests either post factum production from one source chain or a common origin in the Prophet (p. 327 [352]).
  • Mu'awiyyah's position "as both scribe and witness" is "perfectly sensible" if the covenants were (re-)issued in the Prophet's last years (p. 325 [350]).
  • Ch. 16 verdict: "To all appearances, these lists of witnesses were appended to the covenants centuries after the fact in order to meet the demands of hadith scholars" (p. 353 [378]).
  • Ch. 17: "what appears as direct, first-generation, chains of narration may simply have been forged at a later point. If this were so, it would show that early Muslim scholars did not treat the hadith sciences very seriously. Chains of narration were simply padding" (p. 370 [395]).
5.3 Covenant with the Christians of the World (Testamentum et pactiones), 1538 / 1630
  • Relationship of the copies: "the covenant of 1630 included a date when its earlier incarnation was devoid of any such indicator" (p. 327 [352]).
  • Supposed date: "supposedly concluded on the fourth year of the hijrah" (pp. 353–354 [378–379]).
  • Origins: the 1630 covenant was "supposedly found at Mount Carmel" and may have been for the Christians of the Levant; the 1538 copy "could have been intended for the Christians of Egypt" (p. 332 [357]). Ch. 16 lists "Mount Carmel" among the covenant communities (p. 353 [378]).
  • Editions: Sionita (1577–1648) and Nissel (1621–1662) produced Arabic editions and Latin translations (p. 366 [391]).
  • Derivation: "appears to derive from the covenant brought to France by Father Scaliger and which dates from 1538." Morrow asks: "Did it truly come from the monks of Mount Carmel?" (p. 366 [391]).
  • The 1538 manuscript: "The Covenant which was Written by Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Muttalib for all the Christians (1538)," MS Arabe 214, BnF.
    • Owner of the library for which it was copied: Yuhanna ibn Ishaq al-Batanuni.
    • Scribe: Girgis al-Ifrangi.
    • Other named persons: Girgis ibn Yuhanna al-Tamawi, Butrus ibn Diyab al-Halabi, Mansur ibn Sulayman Sahyun al-Ramadi, Sim'an ibn Fadl Allah al-Barallusi.
    • A missionary who arrived in Old Cairo in 1592.
    • Notes made on the copy by Gabriel Sionita (date unknown).
    • The final two pages are in a different hand; the expanded witness list is not in Girgis's hand.
    • "Michel" is addressed at the end (p. 366 [391]).
  • Comparison with Najran: it "contains most of the same conditions as found in the Covenant… with the Christians of Najran." Morrow asks whether it is a separate treaty or a variant (p. 366 [391]).
  • Content points:
    • The Prophet speaks of "himself, his family [ahli], and his successors [khatimi]" (p. 355 [380]).
    • It describes the Prophet as rightful ruler of the world and affirms the Law of Moses (p. 354 [379], said of the covenants generally).
  • Rycaut thought it authentic but a deceptive ploy (Rycaut 102) (p. 353 [378]).
  • Possible courier: Cyril Lucaris may have dispatched a copy to the King of France via Father Scaliger (speculation, p. 366 [391]).
5.4 Covenant with the Christians of Najran
  • Date: the oldest such charter, "dates to the 9th century CE" (p. 331 [356]). "said to have been found in a library in 878/879 CE," "a couple of decades after the death of Ibn Sa'd." It is in the Chronicle of Seert, which "most scholars" date to the 9th century, though some say the 11th. Habib the monk's discovery story is considered fabricated by some scholars (p. 354 [379]).
  • Contemporaries: contemporary with Bukhari, Muslim and Nisa'i (9th century); predates Ibn Khuzaymah, Sharif al-Razi, Saduq and Kulayni (10th century), Mufid and Tusi (11th century), and Hurr al-'Amili and Majlisi (17th century) (pp. 354–355 [379–380]).
  • Ibn Sa'd's "Treaty of Najran": Morrow reads it as a summary. Ibn Sa'd may have had "fragments" (p. 354 [379]).
  • Abu Bakr's renewal: text in Abu Yusuf's Kitab al-kharaj (qtd. Danios) (p. 335 [360]).
  • 'Umar's 638 CE (17 AH) covenant in the Chronicle of Seert "reaffirms and reiterates the promises made by the Prophet to the Christians of Najran" (p. 338 [363]).
  • Transmission hypotheses: possible source covenant for Egypt, Sinai, Levant, Persia and Assyria (Ch. 14 hypotheses 2–3), or a stand-alone charter "received directly from the Prophet" (hypothesis 4) (p. 331 [356]).
  • Scholarly stance: Morrow recommends "ihtiyat or scholarly precaution" (p. 365 [390]).
5.5 Other covenants and charters mentioned
  • Persia: "contains no signatories—suggesting, perhaps, that it predates all of the others" (p. 353 [378]). Leon Arpee's copy has an untraced source (p. 367 [392]). In Ch. 14's third hypothesis, the Sinai achtiname "would have been copied by the Armenian Christians of Persia" (p. 331 [356]).
  • Assyria: 'Uthman is absent from its list (p. 324 [349]). Its list "stands at thirty-two" (p. 370 [395]). Ch. 14 says it was copied from the Armenian/Persian covenant (p. 331 [356]).
  • Egypt: "traces back to Cairo"; uncertain whether it preceded the Sinai covenant (p. 331 [356]).
  • Year of Delegations hypothesis: covenants to "the Sinai, Egypt, the Levant, Assyria, and Armenia, among others that are no longer extant" (p. 327 [352]).
  • Treaty of Maqnah (Maqnah/Aylah Jews): charter to a Jewish community (p. 354 [379]).
    • Clause: "Nobody will rule over you but a person from among yourselves or a member of the Household of the Prophet."
    • Accepted by Ibn Sa'd, Baladhuri, Hershfield, Yashnki, Rashprier and Hieromonk Justin; mentioned by Bar Hebraeus and (as "Diploma securitatis ailensibus") in Gibbon.
    • Rejected by Ibn Qayyim, Hamidullah and Qureshi/Qureishi (p. 355 [380]).
  • Cairo Geniza "Letter of Protection": a Jewish forgery to evade taxes, "probably inspired by the Treaty of Maqnah" (pp. 355, 359 [380, 384]).
  • Reported copies elsewhere (p. 367 [392]):
    • Deir-Saferan near Mardin (Guibert, 1850).
    • "Pact of Muhammad in Favor of the Armenians" (Zohrab, 1822).
    • Traite de Mahomet found in Baghdad (Gregory edition, 1822).
    • Nallino's Charte de Mahomet en faveur des Chretiens (1899), "certainly apocryphal" but close to "the one which is conserved by Tabari."
5.6 Caliphal and later covenants treated as continuations
  • Abu Bakr: renewal of the Najran covenant (p. 335).
  • 'Umar: Jerusalem decree (qtd. Haya 5) (p. 335); Treaty of 'Umar with Ilia', 15 AH, witnessed by Khalid ibn al-Walid, 'Amr ibn al-'As, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf and Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan (p. 337); covenant with Selenia/Nahr Bir, 638 CE / 17 AH, witnessed by 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah (pp. 338–339).
  • Khalid ibn al-Walid: church-bell promise (p. 340).
  • Granada: Treaty and Capitulation of 1492 (67 articles), broken (p. 343).
  • Mehmet II: Bosnian ahidname, 1463 (pp. 345–346).
  • Istanbul: firman to the churches at the 1453 surrender, with the documents lost in a Patriarchate fire (p. 348).
  • Ottoman Capitulations: 1517–1923 (p. 349).
  • Mamluks: treaty with France, 1500 (p. 347).
  • Ottoman ahdname format: said to imitate the prophetic covenants (p. 368).

6. The author's key arguments, conclusions and recommendations

(Kept separate from facts; all are [inf/op].)

Chapter 13
  1. The witness lists can be treated as independent chains, as offshoots of one stem, or as late additions that "in no way compromise or undermine the content." p. 323 [348]
  2. The Sinai covenant's chain is Sunni, "relatively sound," and rules out a Shi'i forgery. p. 324 [349]
  3. Mu'awiyyah's name may have been suppressed by Muslims who despised him, or his and 'Ali's names manipulated by "anti-Shi'ite Sunni tampering." p. 325 [350]
  4. The lists' obscure Companions, many of them first-hijrah emigrants to Axum, are the opposite of what a forger would choose, and point to early composition. The presence of later Companions points to later composition; regular re-issue reconciles the two. pp. 327–328 [352–353]
  5. The lists are "self-correcting" when compared: a correct reading (Abu Hudayfah) cancels an impossible one (Abu Hanifah). Using consensus and dropping disputed names gives "reasonably good references." p. 328 [353]
  6. "The issue of dating is really a modern Western preoccupation. The hadith literature is generally undated." p. 327 [352]
  7. The covenants "should be judged primarily on the basis of their content." Early Muslim acceptance, compatibility with the shari'ah and the arguments against Christian forgery "should in themselves be sufficient evidence for their legitimacy." p. 328 [353]
  8. The absence of developed isnads is "a sign of antiquity." The covenants pass every content criterion for rejecting hadith; as written, dictated documents (or as revelation) they are outside isnad rules. Variants reflect the recognized modes of quotation. pp. 329–330 [354–355]
  9. "The study of the covenants… is in its infancy. The suggestions… are hypothetical, not definitive." p. 328 [353]
Chapter 14
  1. Four transmission models. The author favours model 1, unique prophetic covenants to different denominations, as the one that "agrees the most with the historical record," and is open to revision. pp. 331–332 [356–357]
  2. A chronology based on surviving copies is "full of flaws": earlier copies may have existed back to the 7th century. p. 331 [356]
  3. Even if one source covenant was appropriated by other communities, "it would not diminish the intrinsic merit." p. 331 [356]
Chapter 15
  1. Western anti-Muslim slurs are a double standard that would not be tolerated against Jews or Blacks. p. 333 [358]
  2. The Prophet's wars were all just and defensive, "never to conquer nations." Islam "was spread both by the word and the sword," with the sword "simply used to overthrow oppressors." pp. 333–334 [358–359]
  3. Islamic conquest was liberating and non-destructive, in contrast to the Crusades and to Roman, Hunnic, Mongol, Sassanid, Carolingian, Sui and Visigothic practice. pp. 334–341
  4. The "Pact of 'Umar" is a later forgery, perhaps of 'Umar II's time and attributed to 'Umar I for authority. The Treaty in al-Tabari and the 638 CE Seert covenant reflect the real 'Umar. Scher's preference for the apocryphal over the historical reflects prejudice. pp. 336–339 [361–364]
  5. The fall of Granada and the later decline of Islamic civilization came from two causes: "the failure to fulfill God's commands" and ignoring the Prophet's orders on his succession. "nearly all of the afflictions suffered by Muslims… were the cumulative effect of a single cause: the refusal to recognize the rights of ahl al-bayt." pp. 342, 345 [367, 370]
  6. Bayazid II should have defended al-Andalus, and the ummah abandoned Andalusian Muslims just as it has abandoned Muslims in Palestine, Bosnia, Chechnya, Bangsamoro and Burma. pp. 342–343 [367–368]
  7. Ottoman tolerance was inspired by the Prophet's example and covenants. Forced conversion under Selim I was stopped by the shari'ah and specifically by the covenants. Excesses (Selim I, Selim II) were exceptions. pp. 346–348 [371–373]
  8. The Ottomans "were more than one thousand years ahead of the West." The fall of the Ottoman Empire "broke the back of the Islamic ummah." p. 349 [374]
  9. The true shari'ah helped civilize the West (via the Napoleonic Code), but the Catholic Church, Byzantium and the Christian Middle Ages also deserve credit. Traditional shari'ah must be distinguished from the Wahhabi/Salafi "perversion." pp. 349–350 [374–375]
Chapter 16

  1. The covenants "present Islam in an entirely new light" whether one considers them "authentic, weak or spurious." Their standards are "simply sublime" and superior to much of modern social organization. p. 354 [379]

  2. The witness lists were probably added centuries later, and chains are not needed for primary documents. p. 353 [378]

  3. Rycaut's "ploy" theory and the "Christians broke the terms" theory are "ill-founded": the Prophet kept making treaties until his final year, and the Maqnah/Aylah charters show he did not punish all Jews for some Medinan Jews' breaches. pp. 353–354 [378–379]

  4. Christian interpolation is implausible:

    • The extra material is "literary adornment."
    • A Christian forger would not call the Prophet ruler of the world, affirm Mosaic law, or omit any defence of Christian doctrine.
    • The time between the Najran treaty and the covenant's appearance is "too short."
    • Rival denominations with no contact could not have produced similar documents.
    • Middle Eastern Christians were ignorant of Islam, yet the covenants match the Qur'an, Sunnah and shari'ah.

    pp. 354, 359 [379, 384]

  5. Qureishi's dating of the Treaty of Maqnah is self-contradictory and chronologically impossible. Rejecting texts for "Shi'ite elements" shows Sunni prejudice. p. 355 [380]

  6. The Prophet founded a real Islamic State, and Islam is incomplete without politics. Islam is its own system, not socialist, liberal or capitalist. pp. 356 [381]

  7. Western democracy is largely illusory (Carter's remark; Bush/Obama continuity; TARP; media control per Chomsky). Islamic governance is a "democratic theocracy" with elected and accountable leaders, a possible "Supreme Court of Islamic Clerics," and normative "most tolerant" interpretations ("What is not clearly prohibited is therefore permitted"). It cannot legalize things the shari'ah forbids. pp. 357–359 [382–384]

  8. Orientalist and secular scepticism is an exercise of power and of worldview, not of evidence (Brown, Said, Nasr). Hawting concedes that the tradition cannot be disproved. pp. 359–361 [384–386]

  9. Whether Muslims or Christians are accused of inventing the covenants, the charge fails, because neither needed to forge what the Qur'an, hadith and shari'ah already provided. pp. 361 [386]

  10. The Muslims lost power and were colonized because "they violated the Covenants of Allah and His Messenger." Renewal requires following "the letter and spirit of Islam," moving forward without Salafi backwardness, toward a "True Universal Islam." pp. 362–363 [387–388]

  11. Terrorists should heed the Prophet's commands to protect non-Muslim subjects. p. 362 [387]

Chapter 17: conclusions and recommendations for future scholarship
  1. Conclusion: "the covenants of the Prophet Muhammad are genuine," reached "on the basis of meticulous and thorough examination of the evidence." p. 365 [390]
  2. Muslim scholars should maintain the consensus (ijma') on the Sinai covenant. For the Najran and World covenants, ihtiyat and compliance are "in order." p. 365 [390]
  3. The book is "a brick," to be tested by "time and the continuous process of peer review." p. 365 [390]
  4. Recommendations (pp. 365–373 [390–398]):
    1. Study the notes on the Sinai copies.
    2. Study the St Catherine fatwas (Hanbali, Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki, Fatimid).
    3. Write a history of the English and French translations and their source copies (Arabic or Turkish).
    4. St Catherine should release its early chronicles mentioning Muhammad.
    5. Compare Sionita's and Nissel's editions critically.
    6. Trace the origin of the 1538 covenant (Scaliger; Mount Carmel?).
    7. Decide whether the CW is separate from Najran or a variant.
    8. Subject all the covenants to linguistic and stylistic scrutiny.
    9. Study MS Arabe 214 and its persons (al-Batanuni, Girgis al-Ifrangi, al-Tamawi, al-Halabi, al-Ramadi, al-Barallusi, the 1592 missionary, Sionita's notes, the different hand of the last pages, "Michel").
    10. Examine the Sionita–Lucaris connection.
    11. Search Turkish archives.
    12. Search monasteries (St Catherine, St Anthony, St Paul in Egypt) and "hundreds of other such centers."
    13. Follow up the Deir-Saferan report and travel there.
    14. Carry out deliberate archaeological searches.
    15. Trace the 1822 Armenian pact, the 1822 Baghdad "Traité" and Nallino's 1899 charter.
    16. Find the source of Leon Arpee's Persian covenant.
    17. Compare all recovered copies.
    18. Apply "modern, scientific, dating methods" to the Sinai covenant and the Prophet's letters, and even DNA sequencing of the Prophet's hair and Imam Husayn's blood, to "silence… those who deny the historicity of Muhammad."
    19. Search for the Prophet's correspondence with communities that converted (e.g., the Regraga), including a possible Tifinagh Qur'an recoverable by excavation.
    20. Study the covenants alongside the Ottoman achtiname/ahdname tradition.
    21. Analyse the Arabic and Persian covenants comparatively for 7th-century usage and later developments.
    22. Have a specialist in Arabic, Persian and Turkish linguistics look for "subtle, but conclusive, signs of translation" (sin/sad confusion).
    23. Investigate the meaning of the witness numbers 16, 22 and 37–38.
    24. Study the evolution of the terms mu'min, muslim, mushrik, kafir and munafiq.
    25. Analyse the covenants from the angles of jurisprudence, political science, economics, sociology, ethics and leadership studies.
    26. Survey Arabic and Persian travel literature, diyarat (monastery) literature, geographical literature and European pilgrim itineraries (Robinson and Smith 534-553) for references to Sinai, St Catherine and the Covenant.
    27. Improve the author's translations and make new ones in other languages.
  5. The covenants' "general semantic stability" over more than half a millennium "helps to establish their trustworthiness." Unlike orally transmitted hadith, they are "transcriptions of documents dictated by the Messenger of Allah," so no chain can be demanded. p. 370 [395]
  6. Muslims "should not be overly worried" about the witness lists, "since they may merely be late additions." p. 370 [395]
  7. Early sources treated all Abrahamic believers as mu'minin. The terms narrowed over the centuries through "confessional conflict." There can be no Jewish–Christian–Muslim unity without Muslim unity, and "the powers that be" incite sectarian conflict ("Divide and conquer"; Iraq). pp. 371–372 [396–397]
  8. The ahl al-dhimmah are "a fundamental component of the Muslim community or ummah." The Mahdi may finally unite Jews, Christians and Muslims in the Family of Abraham. p. 373 [398]
  9. Morrow's findings "do not support the conclusions drawn by Patricia Crone… Gerd R. Puin, and company." The variation he found is "a lack of total textual stability which results from the phonetic shortcomings of early Arabic script," not corruption. p. 368 [393]

7. Internal inconsistencies within this section

Only discrepancies visible in the text itself.

  1. The Prophet's dates. "the Prophet (570-642 CE)" on p. 339 [364]; "the Prophet Muhammad (570-632 CE)" on p. 354 [379]. The p. 339 figure also conflicts with the section's own statement that Abu Bakr (c. 573-634 CE) succeeded the Prophet as First Caliph (pp. 324, 335). Possibly a typo or OCR error.
  2. Yusuf al-Qaradawi's birth year. "b. 1956 CE" on p. 337 [362]; "b. 1926 CE" on p. 372 [397].
  3. John of Damascus. "(c. 645 or 676-749 CE)" on p. 340 [365]; "(d. 749/764 CE)" on p. 371 [396].
  4. Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah. Printed "(1292/93-1286 CE)" on p. 355 [380]: the death year precedes the birth year.
  5. 'Umar in Jerusalem in 659 CE. 'Umar's dates are given as 579-644 CE (pp. 323, 334, 335, 338), but p. 335 [360] says Patriarch Solonio showed 'Umar the holy sites "in 659 CE." The same page dates Mu'awiyyah becoming "king" in Jerusalem to 659. The Ilia' treaty is dated 15 AH (p. 337) and 'Umar's Seert covenant 638 CE/17 AH (p. 338).
  6. Battle of the Masts. Mu'awiyyah organized the navy "while governor of Syria under the Caliph 'Umar," and it "resulted in" victory at the Battle of the Masts in 655 CE (p. 340 [365]). By the book's own dates 'Umar died in 644. This is a timing tension rather than a strict contradiction.
  7. Witness counts across chapters.
    • Ch. 13 says Sinai lists range from 22 to "thirty-seven to thirty-eight" and 16 (p. 323 [348]).
    • Ch. 17 says Sinai copies have 16 or 22, and assigns "thirty-seven or thirty-eight" to the two CW versions and Najran (p. 370 [395]).
    • Ch. 17 also calls the Assyrian list of thirty-two "One of the longest lists," though 32 is below the 37–38 cited in the same paragraph.
  8. 'Ali's presence on the second group of covenants. He is "found on two of the covenants, with the exclusion of the covenant with the Christians of the World from 1630" (pp. 324–325 [349–350]). Naming only 1630 as the exclusion implies he is on the other four, which conflicts with "two."
  9. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As. "(d. 684 CE)" on p. 324 [349]. On p. 326 [351] "the son of 'Amr ibn al-'As (c. 592-664 CE)": if those dates are meant for 'Abd Allah rather than his father, they conflict with d. 684.
  10. Counting slip. "Hashim ibn 'Asiyyah is found on three but identified as Hashim ibn 'Abd Allah on a third" (p. 326 [351]).
  11. Which covenant is oldest.
    • Ch. 14 says the Najran charter (9th c.) is "the oldest such charter" (p. 331 [356]).
    • Its third hypothesis makes the Persian (Armenian) covenant a copy of the Sinai achtiname (p. 331).
    • Ch. 16 says the Persian covenant's lack of signatories suggests "perhaps, that it predates all of the others" (p. 353 [378]).
  12. Status of the witness lists.
    • Ch. 13 treats the Sinai chain as "relatively sound," uses witnesses to date the covenants, and classes the covenants as "musnad… muttasil" (pp. 324, 329).
    • Ch. 16 concludes that the lists "were appended to the covenants centuries after the fact" (p. 353 [378]).
    • Ch. 17 says that if the chains were later forgeries "it would show that early Muslim scholars did not treat the hadith sciences very seriously" (p. 370 [395]).
  13. Relationship of the 1538 and 1630 covenants.
    • p. 327 [352] calls the 1538 covenant the "earlier incarnation" of the 1630 covenant.
    • p. 332 [357] says "the case has yet to be closed" and suggests 1630 was for the Levant and 1538 for Egypt, i.e. separate destinations.
    • p. 366 [391] says the CW "appears to derive from" the 1538 covenant.
  14. Conquest. p. 333 [358]: the Prophet "fought solely in the defense of Truth, and never to conquer nations." p. 356 [381]: "The Prophet did not simply raid, he conquered, and where he conquered he appointed governors."
  15. Same saying, two collections. "Whoever oppresses a Jew or a Christian I will testify against him on the Day of Judgment" is attributed to Sahih Bukhari (p. 333 [358]). "Whoever oppresses non-Muslim subjects shall find me to be their advocate on the Day of Judgment" is attributed to Abu Dawud (p. 362 [387]). These may be distinct reports; flagged for checking.
  16. Same verse wording, two references. "Those who believe… Jewish scriptures… the Christians, the Sabians… Last Day…" is cited as "(5:72)" on p. 341 [366] and as "(2:62)" on p. 374 [399]. The Qur'an may contain two such verses; flagged for checking.
  17. When non-Muslim rights were first encroached. p. 349 [374] says "It was only with the establishment of a secular Turkish state under Kemal Ataturk… in 1923 that the rights of non-Muslims began to be encroached upon." The preceding pages describe earlier encroachments: Selim II's confiscation of monastic estates, Selim I's forced-conversion order, and the plundering of the Bulgarian convent (pp. 347–348). The Karabell quotation on the same page also puts the turn for the worse at the empire's fraying and collapse in the early 20th century.
  18. Who chose the first caliph. Abu Bakr's "election" is "limited to a small circle of individuals… which excluded the participation of other parties" (p. 358 [383]). The same page says "The people, under the first four Caliphs, had a voice and a vote." Chapter 13 (p. 324) also describes the Saqifah as appointing Abu Bakr "without consulting with the community in any form or fashion."
  19. Morisco expulsion totals. "A total of 300,000 Moriscos… were expelled… during this second wave" (p. 345) sits beside Chejne's figures summing to "about half a million" (p. 345 [370]). Presented as alternative calculations, not reconciled.
  20. Minor imprecisions.
    • The Najran covenant found in 878/879 CE is described as "only rediscovered a couple of decades after the death of Ibn Sa'd (784-845 CE)," a gap of 33–34 years; the "Treaty of Najran… had only recently been published" (p. 354 [379]).
    • "Over five decades later, in 1899," refers back to 1822, a gap of 77 years (p. 367 [392]).
  21. Name spellings.
    • "Qureishi" (Qureishi 182, 348–351) and "Muhammad Siddique Qureshi"/"qtd. Qureshi 30" both appear (pp. 355–356).
    • "Felipe II" and "Philip II" are both used, with the same dates (p. 344).
    • "Suhayl ibn Bayda'" also appears as "Shuhayl ibn Wahb ibn Rabiah" (pp. 325–327).
    • "Abu Hudayfah ibn Utbah" also appears as "Abu Hudayfah ibn al-'Utbah" (pp. 325, 327).
    • Fortescue appears as "Fortuescue" (p. 335) and "Fortescue" (p. 340).
    • Seert appears as "Stert" (p. 338) and "Seert" (pp. 351, 354).

How this was checked. I read the whole OCR file. Then I checked it against page images:

Examples: "Yes (S)ZYes (SH)" for "Yes (S) / Yes (SH)", "About Darda" for "Aboul Darda", "Fadi" for "Fadl", and "‘Umar ibn Mazh’un Ammar" for "‘Umar ibn Mazh’un ‘Ammar".

1. Appendix I: "Witnesses to the Covenants" (pp. 377–381 [PDF 402–406])

Running heads. Page 377 carries the chapter heading "Appendix 1 / Witnesses to the Covenants". Pages 379 and 381 have the running head "Appendix 1". Pages 378 and 380 have "THE COVENANTS OF THE PROPHET MUHAMMAD". The table of contents (front matter) calls it "Appendix I: Witnesses to the Covenants • 377".

Structure. This is not one table. It is four separate tables (A–D below), each with its own header row. Every table ends with a RELIABILITY column. Rows are not numbered in the book; the "#" column is my own numbering. Wherever a column has no name in a row, the book prints the word Missing in italics.

Key / legend. No key or legend is printed anywhere in Appendix I (pp. 377–381). The abbreviations "(S)" and "(SH)" are never expanded on these pages, and neither are the terms "Unknown" and "Missing".

  • [Context from outside this section, offered as a pointer only: Chapter 13, "Examining the Authorities" (p. 323 [PDF 348]), discusses each witness's standing "by Sunnis" and "by Shi‘ites". That is consistent with S = Sunni and SH = Shi‘ite, but the appendix itself never says so.]
  • "Unknown" stands alone in the RELIABILITY column, with no (S)/(SH) split.

Total number of witnesses

  • Grand total: 130 printed rows across the four tables, and 283 named (non-Missing) cells (60 + 37 + 92 + 94).
  • Tables A and B (22 rows each) are aligned row for row and list the same witness positions. Apart from spelling, they differ substantively at rows 10, 17 and 18: row 10 has a named Skrobucha entry but Pococke Missing; row 17 has Zayd ibn Thabit in Table A but Mauchin Missing; row 18 has Bu Hanifah in Table A but "Mou Khayetmeth [?]" in Table B. The Skrobucha and Pococke columns also assign names to different rows (§6b).
  • Tables C and D (43 rows each) are also aligned row for row. In every row except one (row 34), C and D give the same reliability rating, and some rows contain only Missing placeholders. This suggests a shared master list of 43 positions. [Inference from the layout; the book does not say so.]
  • Why the count depends on the table: each column is one version of a witness list, so the number of witnesses differs by version. Examples: 22 in the Morrow (Sinai-type) list; 35 in WORLD (1630); 32 in Assyria (Malech); 29 in Najran.
  • [Context only, from outside this section: Chapter 13, p. 323 [PDF 348], says the Sinai lists "vary from the standard twenty-two authorities to copies which cite thirty-seven to thirty-eight and others that quote sixteen."]

2. Appendix II: "Possible Modes of Transmission of the Covenants" (pp. 382–383 [PDF 407–408])

Headings. Page 382 is headed "Appendix 2 / Possible Modes of Transmission of the Covenants"; p. 383 has the running head "Appendix 2". The table of contents (front matter) calls it "Appendix II … • 382". The appendix runs only pp. 382–383. Page 384 [PDF 409] is illustration 3 (see §3).

Format. The four "tables" are arrow diagrams (↓ and →). The captions of Tables 1–3 end in "(above)" and sit below their diagrams. Table 4's caption is printed at the top of p. 383, but its diagram is at the foot of p. 382.

Table 1: "Multiple Individual Prophetic Transmissions (above)" (p. 382 [PDF 407])
  • Layout: "Prophet Muhammad" at the top, a horizontal bar, then seven separate vertical arrow-columns. Left to right:
    1. Najran → (9th c. CE)
    2. Sinai → (1561 CE)
    3. Assyria → (1822 or 1845 CE)
    4. Egypt → (1538 CE)
    5. Levant → (Paris 1630)
    6. Persia → (17th c. CE)
    7. Other Christian Communities (no date printed)
  • Claim: each covenant comes independently and directly from the Prophet. No covenant derives from another.
  • The arrow-columns differ in length (Najran 1 arrow, Egypt about 5, Sinai about 6, Levant about 8, Persia about 9, Assyria about 13). [My visual count; it appears to suggest elapsed time before each copy surfaced.]
Table 2: "Single Source Transmission with Subsequent Segmentation (above)" (p. 382 [PDF 407])
  • Layout: a single vertical chain: Prophet Muhammad ↓ Najran (9th c. CE) ↓ Egypt (1538) ↓ Sinai (1561) ↓ Levant (1630) ↓ Persia (17th c. CE) ↓ Assyria (1822 or 1845 CE).
  • Claim: one line of descent. Najran derives from the Prophet, Egypt 1538 from Najran, Sinai 1561 from Egypt, Levant 1630 from Sinai, Persia from Levant, and Assyria from Persia.
  • "Other Christian Communities" does not appear in this table.
Table 3: "Single Source Transmission with Bifurcation (above)" (p. 382 [PDF 407])
  • Layout: Prophet Muhammad branches (via a horizontal bar) to Najran (9th c. CE) on the left and Other Christian Communities on the right.
  • Under Najran, the left column reads: ↓ Egypt (1538), then on the same line → Sinai (1561) → Persia (17th c. CE) → Assyria (1882 or 1845) [or possibly] Sinai (1561) → Precursor of Egypt (1538). Below that, still in the left column: ↓ Levant (1630).
  • Claim: Najran derives from the Prophet, and Egypt 1538 from Najran. The line then splits in two:
    • Branch (a): Egypt 1538 → Sinai 1561 → Persia → Assyria.
    • Branch (b): Levant 1630, reached by the down-arrow under "Egypt (1538)".
    • Bracketed alternative: "[or possibly] Sinai (1561) → Precursor of Egypt (1538)". This lets the Sinai text stand before Egypt 1538 rather than after it.
  • Uncertain reading: the ↓ to Levant sits in the same left-hand column as the Najran → Egypt arrow. It is drawn directly under "Egypt (1538)", so I read it as Egypt → Levant. It could also be read as a continuation of the Najran column.
  • Note: Assyria is dated "1882 or 1845" here. Every other place in the appendix says "1822".
Table 4: "Single Transmission from Q Source Covenant" (diagram p. 382 [PDF 407]; caption p. 383 [PDF 408])
  • Layout: Prophet Muhammad branches (via a horizontal bar) to three items: Najran (9th c. CE), Q Source Covenant, and Other Christian Communities. A second horizontal bar, drawn below and starting under "Q Source Covenant", has five down-arrows to: Egypt (1538), Levant (1630), Sinai (1561), Persia (17th c. CE), Assyrian (1822 or 1845).
  • Claim: Najran comes directly from the Prophet. A separate, hypothetical "Q Source Covenant" also comes from the Prophet, and Egypt, Levant, Sinai, Persia and Assyria each derive independently from it.
  • Layout caveat: no vertical stroke connects "Q Source Covenant" to the lower bar. The bar extends rightward beneath "Other Christian Communities", so Persia and Assyrian sit under that heading. The caption ("from Q Source Covenant") makes clear that the Q Source is the intended parent.
  • Spelling: this diagram uses "Assyrian"; Tables 1–3 use "Assyria".
Key (p. 383 [PDF 408])

The key is printed on the same line as the Table 4 caption: "Table 4: Single Transmission from Q Source Covenant Key:". The titles are in italics, and "Muhammnad" is misspelled in all seven entries.

  • Armenia appears in the key but in none of the four diagrams.
  • "Other Christian Communities" appears in Tables 1, 3 and 4 but has no key entry.
  • The sign changes: ":=" is printed for the first four labels and "=" for the last three.
