Fact-check reports

Checks on the extraction itself

3 table rows · source file QA_extraction_checks.md

Quality checks on the book extraction

These checks test whether the nine extraction files faithfully record what the book says. They were run by script against the PDF's own text layer, independently of the agents that wrote the extractions.

Check Method Result
Years land on the cited page Every 3–4 digit year in each timeline row's "Date as printed" cell was searched for on the PDF page(s) the row cites 689 of 694 years found (99.3%)
Printed page and PDF page agree Every "p. M [PDF N]" pair was tested against the page map (p. 1 = PDF 24; the scan repeats pp. 32–33 at PDF 55–58; from p. 34, PDF = p. + 25) 3,171 pairs, 0 mismatches
Quotations are verbatim Every quoted passage of 25+ characters was searched for, after normalising case, accents, hyphenation and punctuation, on the cited page(s) and the page either side 2,568 of 2,871 found verbatim (89.4%)

What the misses were. The five unmatched years were: one passage that starts on the page before the one cited (the 1403 treaty, PDF 113 rather than 114); one session number written out in words in the book ("five hundred and fourteenth"); and three rows where the "date" is a description such as "undated (before 1630)". For quotations, the unmatched 10.6% were sampled by hand. Every sampled miss was caused by the scan's text layer, not by a misquotation: doubled letters ("tthe losing … wworld"), words split across the two print columns, or brackets the agent normalised ("[w]hen" written as "When").

Page map anomaly. The PDF repeats printed pages 32–33 (PDF 55–56 and 57–58 are the same pages). One chunk label was wrong as a result (PDF 56 is p. 33, not p. 31); the extracting agent caught it and cited the correct page.

Table images. Two tables the text layer scrambled were read from page images instead: the list of Sinai copies on p. 65 (PDF 90) and the witness tables in Appendix I (PDF 402–406).

Fact-check reports

Second-opinion audit of the main findings, part 1

13 table rows · source file AUDIT_A.md

AUDIT A: independent re-verification of findings A1–A13

Book. John Andrew Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013). The book's wording was read in scratchpad/book/chunks/ (OCR). Page numbers are the printed pages.

Method. For each finding I first checked the book's exact wording. I then re-fetched the primary source myself rather than reusing the earlier agents' downloads. My copies are in scratchpad/audit/dl/. Where OCR was doubtful, I viewed the page image:

  • Cantemir p. 169
  • Napoleon Correspondance p. 219
  • the 1630 Paris print (SLUB) pp. 15–16
  • the Met catalogue pp. xvi, 60–64

The web-search quota was not used. All sources were reached by direct URL or through archive.org, K10plus or BnF catalogue APIs.

What I could not check.

  • topkapisarayi.gov.tr: DNS failure from this environment.
  • Atiya, The Arabic Manuscripts of Mount Sinai (1955): archive.org arabicmanuscript0000atiy is flagged access-restricted, so it was not opened.
  • Mauchin's "work on Egypt": not located.

Each item gives the finding as reported, what the book says, what the primary source says, and an audit verdict.

Summary of verdicts

# Verdict
A1 Confirmed. Atiya 1955, which the book cites for 975, was not checked.
A2 Confirmed.
A3 Confirmed. Cantemir's spelling is "Kioprili ogli Mustafa Pasha", not "Kiuprili". The book itself quotes "fabulously" and "true or forged".
A4 Confirmed. The contributors list is on p. xvi.
A5 Partly confirmed. The book's own date is the correct 19 Dec. "8 December" appears only inside a quotation from Tomadakis. The "endorsed / confirms the Prophet's privileges" part is confirmed.
A6 Confirmed.
A7 Confirmed.
A8 Confirmed, with qualifications. Earlier sources tie the removal to Selim's conquest without a numeral. Mauchin, Arundale's source, was not checked. The book cites Mouton for the Süleyman idea.
A9 Confirmed as far as checkable. The four letters come from TDV, not from the official palace page. No source places the Achtiname at Topkapı. The museum's own site was unreachable.
A10 Confirmed. Vansleb's journeys were 1663–64 and 1671–73, with Egypt from March 1672 to October 1673. Caveat: the 1673 reader may be the Paris-based Pierre Dipy.
A11 Confirmed.
A12 Partly confirmed. The source is Lancelot Addison, as stated. The book implies, but does not state, that "Dr. Addison" is James Thayer Addison.
A13 Confirmed, with caveats. The BnF has four 1630 records. No 1668 or 1888 edition was found, but title searches are not conclusive.

A1. The "earliest Fatimid decree of 975"

Finding as reported. The book (pp. 71, 73) dates the earliest Fatimid decree confirming the Sinai monks' privileges to 975. Specialist sources put the earliest Sinai decree at 524/1130: Stern; Heidemann, Müller & Rāġib 1997; Atiya 1950. Moritz (1918) puts it at 1134/35.

What the book says.

  • p. 71: "These decrees were issued by the Fatimids as early as 975,1109,1110,1135,1154, and 1156 CE (26)" (citing Atiya).
  • p. 71: "While the earliest of these edicts were passed by Fatimid Shi'ite jurists in 975, the latest was issued by Ottoman Sunni scholars in 1888. If the original charter was conveyed by Sultan Selim I to Istanbul after the Ottoman invasion of Egypt in 1517, Mus­lims scholars had already had access to it for 542 years."
  • p. 73: "the famous Pact of Muhammad had been confirmed by Muslims leaders and religious authorities as early as 975 CE."

What the primary sources say.

Heidemann, Müller & Rāġib, Annales islamologiques 31 (1997), p. 1. https://www.aai.uni-hamburg.de/voror/personen/heidemann/medien/heidemann-anislam-1997-sinai.pdf

  • Text: "Le Monastère de Sainte-Catherine conserve quatre-vingt-un décrets émanés des chancelleries d'Égypte et de Syrie médiévales: six remontent à la fin de l'époque fatimide (524/1130 à 553/1158)".
  • n. 2: "On trouvera l'inventaire des documents dans Atiya. Mais les publications de Stern et d'Ernst ont révélé les erreurs dont il fourmille, de dates et même de dimensions."
  • n. 6: the Balat (Istanbul) document "émane probablement du calife Al-Ḥāfiẓ, FD, … n° 4".

Princeton Geniza Project (Stern's editions).

  • Stern doc. 3: "Dhū l-Qaʿda 524 Hijrī (6 October 1130–4 November 1130 CE)". https://geniza.princeton.edu/en/documents/41382/
  • Stern doc. 4 (Istanbul metochion): "3 Rajab 529 Hijrī (19 April 1135 CE)". https://geniza.princeton.edu/en/documents/41383/

Atiya, The Monastery of St. Catherine in Mount Sinai (Cairo, preface dated February 1950), p. 51. https://archive.org/details/dli.ministry.17394

  • "A preliminary investigation shows that the oldest document is dated 524 A.H./1130 A.D."

Moritz, Beiträge zur Geschichte des Sinaiklosters im Mittelalter (1918), pp. 3–4. https://archive.org/details/beitrgezurgesc00moriuoft

  • The letters of protection run "in kaum unterbrochener Reihenfolge vom Jahre 1134 bis in das vorige Jahrhundert".
  • The oldest surviving document is "ein Firman des Fatimidenchalifen el Hafiz (526 bis 544 der Higra = 1132–1149 n. Chr.)". Moritz found it in 1910 in the monastery's branch in Balat (p. 5 n.), i.e. Stern doc. 4 (1135).
  • A footnote reports, after Cheikho, that the author of an Arabic monograph had seen in 1710 a firman "vom Jahre 508 d. H." (1114/15). Moritz marks this "(?)". The OCR is poor here.

Audit verdict: Confirmed. No source I opened attests any Sinai decree from 975. The earliest dated items are 524/1130 (Stern, Heidemann, Atiya 1950); Moritz has 1134, and an unconfirmed report of 508/1114–15. The book's citation for 975 is Atiya 1955, p. 26, which I could not open (access-restricted). The book may therefore be repeating a date error in Atiya's 1955 hand-list, which Heidemann et al. describe as full of date errors. This does not change the finding.

A2. Witness anachronisms and the "suspicious order" argument

Finding as reported. The Sinai covenant is dated 3 Muharram 2 AH. Its witnesses include Abu Hurayra (Muslim c. 7 AH) and Abu al-Dardaʾ (Muslim c. Badr or later). The Sinai lists start with ʿAli and do not include Muʿawiya. The book's p. 85 "suspicious order" argument therefore concerns the 4 AH covenants.

What the book says.

p. 85: "The order of the witnesses is especially suspi­cious, listing Abu Bakr first, 'Umar second, 'Uthman third, 'Ali, fourth, and Muawiyyah, fifth, as this is the traditional order of the Caliphs for the Sunnis." The sentence before it reads: "As far as Josee Balagna is concerned, the manuscripts witnessed by Mu'awiyyah (602-680 CE) in the fourth year of the hijrah are anomalous; however, the manu­scripts attributed to 'Ali, which were written in the second year … are 'plausible or likely'."

The Chapter 8 Sinai lists:

  • Sinai I (Pococke, p. 206) and Sinai IV (Skrobucha, p. 212) begin "Ali, the son of Abu Thaleb; Honiar [Homar], the son of Hattavi …". The names are garbled, and there is no recognisable Muʿawiya.
  • Sinai II (Arundale, p. 208): "Ali-ebn-Taleb, Aboubek-rebu-Aby-Kohafey, Omar ebn-el-Khattai, Otman-ebn-Assan, Abou-el-Daida, Abou-Horeyrah …".
  • Sinai III (Géramb, p. 210): "Aly ebn Taleb, Aboubekr Aly Kohafey, Omar ebn el-Khattab, Otman ebn Hassan, About el Darda, Abou Horeyrah …".
  • Sinai V (Haddad 1902, p. 214): "Ali Ibn Abi Talib; Abou Bekr Ibn Kahafat; Omar Ibn El-Khattab; Ottman Ibn Affan; About Darda; Abou Harirat …".
  • Sinai VI (Morrow, p. 216): "Ali ibn Abi Talib; Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah; 'Umar ibn al-Khattab; 'Uthman ibn Afjdn [Affan]; Abu al-Darda'; Abi Hurayrah …".

No Muʿawiya appears in any of the Chapter 8 texts, pp. 205–217.

The order Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, Muʿawiya is that of the 1630 / 4 AH text. Book World III, p. 236: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq; 'Umar ibn al-Khattab; 'Uthman ibn Affan; Ali ibn Abi Talib; Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan; Abu al-Darda' …".

What the primary sources say.

1630 Latin, p. 16 (SLUB image 00000022). "Abu-Bacri assadicq. Omar ben-alchatab. Othman ben-Afan. Ali ben-abi-taleb. Moauia ben-abi-Sofian. Abu-addarda. …" https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000022.tif.large.jpg

TDV "Ebû Hüreyre" (M. Y. Kandemir). https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/ebu-hureyre

  • "Ebû Hüreyre'nin 7. (628) yılın başlarında Tufeyl b. Amr ed-Devsî vasıtasıyla müslüman olduğu ve … aynı yılın muharrem ayında (Mayıs 628) Medine'ye gittiği bilinmekle beraber onun daha önce müslüman olmayıp Medine'ye İslâmiyet'i kabul etmek üzere geldiği de rivayet edilmektedir."
  • In English: he became Muslim early in year 7 through Ṭufayl. One report says he came to Medina in order to accept Islam.

TDV "Ebü'd-Derdâ" (A. Aydınlı). https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/ebud-derda

  • "Bedir Gazvesi sırasında ve ensardan en son kişi olarak müslüman olduğu rivayet edilmektedir" ("reported to have become Muslim at the time of Badr, as the last of the Ansar").

Audit verdict: Confirmed. Every Sinai list printed in Chapter 8 starts with ʿAli and lacks Muʿawiya. Sinai II, III, V and VI include Abu Hurayra and Abu al-Dardaʾ, whose conversions TDV dates to 7 AH and to the time of Badr (Ramadan 2 AH), both after Muharram 2 AH. The "Abu Bakr … Muʿawiya fifth" order matches the 1630 (4 AH) text exactly.

Context note: in the book the sentence immediately follows Balagna's remark about the 4 AH manuscripts witnessed by Muʿawiya. A reader could therefore take it as referring to those manuscripts. It sits, however, inside the Sinai chapter's argument that the Sinai witness list was added later (p. 86: "the list of witnesses may have been attached at a later period").

A3. Cantemir: which Mustafa Pasha, and how Cantemir frames the purchase

Finding as reported.

  • Cantemir (History of the Othman Empire, Tindal tr., 1734, pp. 168–169, n. 50) names "Kiuprili ogli Mustafa Pasha", i.e. Köprülüzâde Fâzıl Mustafa, grand vizier 1689–91.
  • The book (p. 72) names Merzifonlu Kara Mustafa, serving Süleyman II 1663–1666.
  • Cantemir introduces the 4,000-crown purchase with "They say, though fabulously" and calls the document Mahomet's "true or forged" instrument.

What the book says.

  • p. 72 quotes Cantemir with the name elided: "… when the Turks began to collect the Haraj upon them, and that by means of...Mustafa Pasha, who made no scruple to charge the whole Diploma with forgery … (169)".
  • p. 72 then says: "As Cantemir makes manifest, the Grand Vizier Merzifonlu Kara Mustapha Pasha, who served Sulayman II from 1663-1666, denounced the Cove­nant … as a forgery as a pretext to subject Greek Chris­tians to the kharaj".
  • pp. 10–11 quote Cantemir in full, including "They say, though fabulously, that Mahomet …" and "Mahomet's true or forged instrument, which the Emperor pur­chased of the monks for four thousand gold crowns".
  • p. 11 concludes: "Rather than being seized, it was purchased by Selim I … would not have spent such a spectacular sum on a spuri­ous document." p. 10 calls this version "the oldest of all".

What the primary sources say.

Cantemir, The History of the Growth and Decay of the Othman Empire, tr. N. Tindal, Part I (London: Knapton, "M DCC XXXIV" on the title page), Book III, annotation 50. https://archive.org/details/dli.ministry.02708 (part 4, leaves 43–44)

  • p. 168: "since I dont think it mention'd any where but in a fabulous treatise of a Sinaitish Monk, I shall here insert. They say, though fabulously, that Mahomet being of mean birth … Long after, when Sultan Selim was in Egypt, the Abbot of Mount Sinai humbly came to him with Mahomet's true or forged Instrument, which the Emperor purchased of the Monks for four thousand Gold Crowns".
  • p. 169 (page image viewed): "'Tis certain the exemption of these Monks from Tribute remain'd in force through all the Turkish dominions till the time of Soliman II. Great-Uncle of the present Emperor, when the Turks began to collect the Haraj upon them, and that by means of Kioprili ogli Mustafa Pasha, who made no scruple to charge the whole Diploma with forgery."
  • Cantemir's own numbering calls Süleyman the Magnificent "Soliman I" (running head "Book III. 10. Soliman I."), so his "Soliman II" is the sultan who reigned 1687–91.

TDV "Köprülüzâde Fâzıl Mustafa Paşa" (A. Özcan). https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/kopruluzade-fazil-mustafa-pasa

  • Appointed grand vizier "11 Muharrem 1101 / 25 Ekim 1689"; took the seal at Edirne on 8 November.
  • Reformed the cizye by a ferman of "Cemâziyelevvel 1102 (Şubat 1691)".
  • Died 1102/1691.

TDV "Süleyman II". "Osmanlı padişahı (1687-1691)". https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/suleyman-ii

TDV "Merzifonlu Kara Mustafa Paşa". https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/merzifonlu-kara-mustafa-pasa

  • Died 1095/1683 (executed 25 December 1683).
  • Was kapudan pasha 1661–1666 under Grand Vizier Fâzıl Ahmed and deputy grand vizier (kaymakam), i.e. under Mehmed IV.

Audit verdict: Confirmed.

  • Minor correction to the finding: Cantemir's spelling is "Kioprili ogli Mustafa Pasha" (page image), not "Kiuprili".
  • Kara Mustafa died four years before Süleyman II's accession. The book's "1663-1666" matches his posts under Mehmed IV, not under Süleyman II.
  • On framing: the words "fabulously" and "true or forged" are accurately reported. The book itself quotes both phrases (pp. 10–11), so it does not hide them. What it does is draw an authenticity argument from the price.

A4. "Griffith 63–64" is the Met catalogue entry by Hieromonk Justin

Finding as reported. What the book cites as "Griffith 63–64" (pp. 65, 97–98) is entry no. 37 in the Metropolitan Museum's 2012 Byzantium and Islam catalogue, written by Hieromonk Justin of Sinai.

What the book says.

  • p. 65: "According to Griffith, 'the monks of Mount Sinai presented him with the original Achtiname, bearing it into his presence on a tray, covered with green brocade …' (64)".
  • p. 97: "Sidney H. Griffith, however, has translated the word as 'parchment' (63)".
  • p. 98: "(Griffith 63-64) … '[t]he Testament was confirmed by Sultan Selim, and by subsequent rulers, to the time of Sultan Abdul Hamid II in 1904' (64)".
  • Bibliography: "Griffith, Sidney H. 'Arab Christians.' Byzantium and Islam … 2012. 60-62".

What the primary source says. Evans & Ratliff (eds.), Byzantium and Islam: Age of Transition (Met, 2012), archive.org scan: https://archive.org/details/2012-byzantium-and-islam.-age-of-transition. The page images are only 509×660 px, but the initials are legible.

  • Contributors list, p. xvi (leaf n16; V2a said p. xvii):
    • "HJS Hieromonk Justin of Sinai, Librarian, Holy Monastery of Saint Catherine, Sinai, Egypt"
    • "SHG Sidney H. Griffith, Professor, Department of Semitics, The Catholic University of America"
  • p. 60: the essay "Arab Christians, Sidney H. Griffith" begins, and catalogue entry 32 starts in the right-hand column. The catalogue entries I could read on pp. 60 and 62 end "SHG". I did not view p. 61.
  • p. 63: entry 36 ends "SHG". Entry "37. Achtiname (Testament) of Muhammad" begins and says the document "was written on parchment from Ṭāʾif by the hand of Ali ibn Abi Talib".
  • p. 64: entry 37 continues: "In 1517 … the monks of Sinai presented him with the original Achtiname, bearing it into his presence on a tray covered with green brocade … confirmed by Sultan Selim, and by subsequent rulers, to the time of Sultan Abdul Hamid II in 1904". It ends "… of the revelations of God. HJS".

Audit verdict: Confirmed. The quoted content is accurate. It comes from Hieromonk Justin's entry 37, not from Griffith; Griffith's essay is the one at pp. 60–62 that the bibliography lists.

A5. Napoleon's protection order for the monks

Finding as reported. Napoleon's protection order is Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, vol. 5, no. 3782, dated 29 frimaire an VII (19 Dec 1798). It does not mention the Prophet or the Achtiname. The book (p. 70 and elsewhere) gives 8 December and/or says Napoleon endorsed the covenant.

What the book says. p. 70:

  • "Rather than reject the Covenant, Napo­leon … endorsed its authenticity. As Tomadakis relates, '… he also issued a special decree on 8 Decem­ber, 1798 by which the privileges of Sinai were con­firmed …' (16)".
  • "In fact, the decree issued by Napoleon on 19 December 1798, in which he placed the monastery under his protection, actually confirms the privi­leges that were granted by the Prophet."

What the primary source says. Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, t. 5 (Paris: Plon, MDCCCLX), no. 3782 "ORDRE", pp. 219–220.

  • Page image viewed: "Quartier général, au Caire, 29 frimaire an VII (19 décembre 1798)". The OCR text of the napouoft scan misreads this as "10 décembre"; the naporich scan and the image both read 19.
  • Preamble: "pour qu'il transmette aux races futures la tradition de notre conquête; … Par respect pour Moïse et la nation juive …; Parce que le couvent du mont Sinaï est habité par des hommes instruits et policés".
  • Art. 3: "Ils ne seront tenus de payer aucun droit ni tribut annuel, comme ils en ont été exemptés suivant les différents titres qu'ils en conservent."
  • Muhammad, the Prophet, the Achtiname and any covenant are not named anywhere in the preamble or Arts. 1–8.
  • URLs: https://archive.org/details/correspondancede05napouoft (leaf n228) ; https://archive.org/details/correspondancede05naporich

Audit verdict: Partly confirmed.

  • Confirmed: the document number, date, place and content.
  • Confirmed: the book's claims that Napoleon "endorsed its authenticity" and that the decree "confirms the privi­leges … granted by the Prophet" are not supported by the decree's text, which refers only to "les différents titres qu'ils en conservent".
  • Not as stated: the book's own date is the correct 19 December 1798. "8 December, 1798" appears only inside the quotation from Tomadakis. The book prints it without correction, which leaves two dates on one page, but it does not adopt it.

A6. Thenaud: "compte et reliquat"

Finding as reported. Thenaud (Le voyage d'outremer, ed. Schefer 1884, p. 72) says the prior "se rendit mammelu quant on lui demanda compte et reliquat de son administration". The book (p. 19) renders this as "when asked to assume its administration".

What the book says. p. 19:

  • "In front of that church is a Mus­lim mosque which was built by prior [a prieur de leans] who became a Muslim when asked to assume its administration' (72)."
  • It continues: "the Fatimids, who were the rulers at the time, granted him the administration of the mosque on their behalf … the Covenant … was in Muslims hands from the moment the mosque was built in the 12th century CE until it fell into disuse in the 14th century".

What the primary source says. Thenaud, Le voyage d'outremer, ed. Ch. Schefer (Paris: Leroux, 1884), p. 72. https://archive.org/details/levoyagedoutreme00then

"Devant ceste église est une musquete de Mores, que fit bastir ung prieur de leans qui se rendit mammelu quant on lui demanda compte et reliquat de son administration, en laquelle sont les privilèges que Mahommet donna es caloyers, c'est assavoir immunité de tous tributz et devoirs; et sont signez de sa main, plongée en encre et assise sur ledict papier".

"Demander compte et reliquat" is accounting language: to demand a statement of account and the outstanding balance of a stewardship.

Audit verdict: Confirmed. The French says the prior turned Mamluk (renegade) when called to account for his administration. It does not say he was asked to assume the administration of the mosque. Thenaud gives no date and does not mention the Fatimids. The book's inferences about Fatimid appointment and Muslim custody from the 12th to the 14th century have no basis in this passage.

A7. Burckhardt and the AH 783 record

Finding as reported. Burckhardt (Travels in Syria and the Holy Land, 1822, pp. 543–544) used the AH 783 record to show that the mosque existed long before Selim. The book (p. 18) says Burckhardt "interprets this as proof that the mosque dates to 1381 CE".

What the book says. p. 18 quotes the AH 783 passage, via Manley and 'Abdel-Hakim 144, then says: "While Burckhardt interprets this as proof that the mosque dates to 1381 CE, to me it implies that the mosque already existed and that the monks merely hired some stranded Muslims to act as its guardians and custodians."

What the primary source says. Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (London: Murray, 1822), pp. 543–544. https://archive.org/details/b22017355

  • The monks' tradition is that the mosque "was built in the sixteenth century", after Selim's conquest.
  • "This tradition, however, is contradicted by some old Arabic records kept by the prior, in which I read a circumstantial account how, in the year of the Hedjra 783, some straggling Turkish Hadjis … were retained here, and a salary settled on them and their descendants, on condition of their becoming the servants of the mosque. The conquest of Egypt by Selim did not take place till A. H. 895. The mosque in the convent of Sinai appears therefore to have existed long before the time of Selim."

Audit verdict: Confirmed. Burckhardt does not date the mosque to 1381. He uses the AH 783 record to show that the mosque already existed then, which is the inference the book presents as its own.

Side notes:

  • Burckhardt's own "A. H. 895" for Selim's conquest is itself wrong (the conquest was 922–923 AH), but that does not affect his argument.
  • The book quotes Burckhardt second-hand, so the misreading may originate in Manley and 'Abdel-Hakim. I did not check them.

A8. When the year "1517" first appears; Moritz's "Selim or Süleyman"

Finding as reported. Among the sources checked, the explicit year "1517" for Selim's removal of the original first appears in print in Arundale (1837) and Géramb (1840). Moritz (1918) had already reported a "Selim or Süleyman" tradition and favoured Süleyman.

What the book says.

  • p. 68: "While every authority has accepted 1517 as the year in which the Covenant was taken to the capi­tal … (Ratfliff 14-15)".
  • p. 69: "If the original was indeed at Saint Catherine's between 1533-1534, then it may have been taken by Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent, who ruled from 1520 to his death in 1566 (Mouton 178)."
  • p. 67 attributes the 1517 removal also to Monconys (Le voyage 92) and Pococke (148).

What the primary sources say. Earlier sources name Selim but give no year:

  • Monconys (visit 1647; IFAO ed.): "laquelle Selin Empereur des Turcs leur osta, & l'emporta dans son thresor". https://archive.org/details/voyageenegyptede00monc
  • Cantemir 1734, p. 168: "when Sultan Selim was in Egypt".
  • Pococke 1743, vol. 1, p. 148: "in their hands to the time of Sultan Selim, who … took it from them". https://archive.org/details/b30456307_0001
  • Burckhardt 1822, p. 546: "remained in the convent until Selim the First conquered Egypt, when … he sent for it".

The first explicit "1517" I found:

  • Arundale 1837: "In [1]517, after the conquest of Egypt, Selim demanded it, and placed a copy, in parchment, certified by himself, among the archives of this monastery. M. Mauchin gives it in his work on Egypt." https://archive.org/details/illustrationsofj00arun
  • Géramb 1840, vol. 2, pp. 245–246: "In 1517, after the conquest of Egypt, Selim I. demanded it". https://archive.org/details/vol2pilgrimageto00gera

Moritz 1918, p. 5 (https://archive.org/details/beitrgezurgesc00moriuoft):

  • "Das Original selbst ist verschwunden; nach der Tradition soll es von Sultan Selim oder seinem Sohne, Sultan Suleiman, in das Staatsarchiv von Konstantinopel überführt worden sein."
  • pp. 5–6: the surviving copies date from 957 and 968 AH, and Süleyman died only in 974 AH, "so ist es höchstwahrscheinlich, daß er es gewesen ist, der diese Urkunden aus dem Kloster hat entführen lassen."

Audit verdict: Confirmed, with qualifications.

  • The numeral "1517" is absent from Monconys, Cantemir, Pococke and Burckhardt. Burckhardt and Cantemir do tie the removal to Selim's conquest of, or presence in, Egypt, so 1517 is implicit in them.
  • Arundale names Mauchin as his source. Mauchin's work was not located, so an earlier explicit "1517" in Mauchin cannot be ruled out.
  • The Moritz part is confirmed. Fairness note: the book attributes its Süleyman suggestion to Mouton (178), not to itself alone. It does not cite Moritz for it.

A9. Topkapı: letters of the Prophet in the Sacred Relics, and the Achtiname

Finding as reported. What the official Millî Saraylar / Topkapı pages and the TDV encyclopedia say about letters of the Prophet in the Sacred Relics collection: V2a reports four, to al-Muqawqis, al-Mundhir b. Sāwā, Musaylima and al-Ḥārith. Also, whether any official source says the Sinai Achtiname is there.

What the book says.

  • p. 69: the Chamber of Relics "is devoted to the holy artifacts that Selim I brought back from his conquest of Egypt in 1517. The Chamber of Relics contains the Prophet's mantle, his swords, and the letter he wrote to Muqawqis".
  • p. 69: "The possibility that the original Achtiname remains stored in some forgotten archive, perhaps in the Palace of Topkapi in Istanbul, Turkey, is tan­talizing to say the least."

What the primary sources say.

TDV "Mukaddes Emanetler" (N. Bozkurt, DİA 31, 2020, pp. 108–111). https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/mukaddes-emanetler

  • "Nâme-i saâdetler. Mukavkıs'a (nr. 21/174), Ahsâ Valisi Münzir b. Sâvâ'ya (nr. 21/397), peygamberlik iddiasında bulunan Müseylimetülkezzâb'a (nr. 21/169) ve Gassânî Emîri Hâris b. Ebû Şemir'e (nr. 21/674) gönderilen bu mektuplar …".
  • Origin of the collection: "Önemli bir kısmı Yavuz Sultan Selim'in Mısır'ı fethi sırasında ve daha sonra oradan getirilenlerden, bir kısmı devlet yetkililerinin satın almasıyla oluşan, bir kısmı da … Fahreddin Paşa'nın … İstanbul'a göndermesiyle". That is: some came with or after Selim's conquest, some were bought, some were sent from Medina by Fahreddin Paşa.
  • The article does not mention a Sinai ahidname.

TDV "Mukaddes Emanetler Dairesi" (2020). Lists "nâme-i saâdet" among the items displayed in the Arzhâne; no Sinai document. https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/mukaddes-emanetler-dairesi

TDV "Hırka-i Saâdet". No letters or Sinai document mentioned. https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/hirka-i-saadet

Millî Saraylar, Topkapı Sarayı (official page). https://www.millisaraylar.gov.tr/Lokasyon/2/topkapi-sarayi

  • It names no letters at all. It says only: "Has Oda (Mukaddes Emanetler Dairesi)" and "Burası, Yavuz Sultan Selim döneminde kutsal emanetlerin getirilmesinden sonra daha ziyade Hırka-i Saâdet Dairesi ismiyle anılmıştır."

TDV "Ahidnâme" (M. Fayda, 1988). https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/ahidname

  • "Bazı hıristiyanlar Hz. Peygamber'e nisbet edilen ahidnâmeler de uydurmuşlardır. Bunların en meşhuru … Saint Catherine Manastırı'nın ahidnâmesidir. … bu ahidnâmeyi Yavuz Sultan Selim İstanbul'a getirmiş".
  • It says nothing about where the document is today.

topkapisarayi.gov.tr. Could not be checked (DNS failure).

Audit verdict: Confirmed, as far as could be checked.

  • The four letters, with their inventory numbers, come from the TDV encyclopedia (a scholarly reference work), not from the official palace page, which lists no letters.
  • None of these sources says the Sinai Achtiname, original or copy, is at Topkapı.
  • "Four" is TDV's list. I have no evidence that it covers every letter attributed to the Prophet held at Topkapı.
  • TDV also contradicts the book's statement that the Chamber holds what Selim brought in 1517: part of the collection was purchased later or arrived from Medina in the 20th century.

A10. BnF MS Arabe 214: provenance, and Vansleb's travel dates

Finding as reported. The BnF record of MS Arabe 214 gives the provenance "Acheté par Vansleb en Orient", with Vansleb seals, a reading mark dated 1673, and a reader "Ġabriyāl Ṣahyūn al-Ziftāwī". The book (pp. 144–146) says "there is no question" that this is the manuscript Scaliger brought and Sionita printed. The finding also checks Vansleb's travel dates against the book's "1671 and 1672".

What the book says.

  • p. 144–145 reproduces the BnF "History of Conservation" ("Purchased by Vansleb in the Orient. Seals with the numbers of Vansleb … reading mark belonging to Butrus ibn Diyab al-Halabi, dated 1673 CE …"). It prints "9th of Hatur 1380" where the BnF has 1308.
  • p. 145: "[Vansleb] made his two trips in 1671 and in 1672. Since the Testa­ment of the Prophet was published in 1630 by Gab­riel Sionita, Vansleb could not possibly have purchased it in Egypt forty years later. Further­more, the manuscript contains the mark of Gabriyal Sahyun al-Ziftawi, namely, that of Gab­riel Sionita himself! … there is no question that this is the actual document that he brought back from the Middle East."

What the primary sources say.

BnF Archives et manuscrits, Arabe 214. https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877

  • "Historique de la conservation: Une notice de Renaudot. Acheté par Vansleb en Orient. Cachets au chiffre de Vansleb."
  • "marque de lecture de Buṭrus ibn Diyāb al-Ḥalabī, datée de 1673 J.-C., et de Manṣūr ibn Sulaymān Ṣahyūn al-Ramādī, datée du 14 Babā 1336 des Martyrs [1620 J.-C.] (f. 2); mention de l'arrivée d'un missionnaire au Vieux-Caire, le 9 Hatūr 1308 des Martyrs (1592 J.-C.) et marque de Ġabriyāl Ṣahyūn al-Ziftāwī (f. 2 v)".
  • Old shelfmarks: "385 (Regius)", "Ancien fonds arabe 88". Item 12: "F. 257-261 • Charte accordée à tous les chrétiens".

Vansleb, Nouvelle relation en forme de journal, d'un voyage fait en Egypte … en 1672 & 1673 (Paris 1677), pp. 1–4. https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_8n2JTTnOoMIC

  • He was at Marseille on 8 May 1671 and sailed on the 20th. He was at Aleppo from September to December 1671, then Damascus and Sidon.
  • He embarked at Sidon on 19 February (the text prints "1671"; the margin reads 1672) and reached the Damietta mouth of the Nile on the 18th of the following month. He observed Egypt "pendant vingt mois".

Pougin, Vansleb, savant orientaliste et voyageur (1869). https://archive.org/details/vanslebsavantor00pouggoog

  • p. 16: "Vansleb partit le 15 Juin 1663, et arriva au Caire en Janvier 1664. Il employa une année à visiter l'Égypte".
  • He left Egypt in mid-October 1673.
  • He sent manuscripts to Paris "dans les années 1671, 1672 et 1673".

Audit verdict: Confirmed. The BnF record reads exactly as reported, and the book quotes it while arguing against it. Vansleb's journeys were 1663–64 (Cairo from January 1664, about a year) and 1671–73 (Egypt from March 1672 to about October 1673). The book's "two trips in 1671 and in 1672" is wrong, and its rebuttal assumes the identification it sets out to prove.

Corrections and caveats:

  • V4's duration. V4's "about 12 months in Egypt (1672–73)" understates the second stay, which was about 19–20 months.
  • The 1673 reader. Wikidata Q15840509, "Pierre Dipy", has the Arabic label بطرس دياب الحلبي (Butrus Diyab al-Halabi). German Wikipedia, used only as a lead, describes him as an Aleppine Maronite in Paris who catalogued the Bibliothèque du Roi's oriental manuscripts. If he is the reader, the 1673 mark could have been made in Paris. It would then not, on its own, show that the manuscript was still in the East in 1673. The Vansleb purchase note and seals are unaffected.
  • "al-Ziftāwī". The BnF does not identify him. I did not independently verify the Zifta (Egypt) derivation of the nisba.

A11. The date in the 1630 Paris edition

Finding as reported. The 1630 Paris edition (SLUB Dresden digitised copy) dates the covenant "Monday (yawm al-ithnayn), at the completion of four months of the fourth year". The Latin reads "die Lunae ultima mensis quarti". No month is named. The book (pp. 147, 236) has "the second day of the month of Rabi' Ashar".

What the book says.

  • p. 147: "the Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World dates from the second day of the month of Rabi' Ashar of the fourth year after the hijrah."
  • World III ("[1630]", p. 236): "Written [down] by Mu'awiyyah ibn Abi Sufyan, and dictated by the Messenger of Allah on the second day of the month of Rabi' Ashar during the fourth year of the Hegira in Medina."

What the primary source says. Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Mohamedem et Christianae fidei cultores (Paris: Vitray, 1630), SLUB Dresden Hist.Turc.524 (page images viewed).

  • Arabic, pp. 15–16 (images 00000037, 00000038): "وكتب معاوية بن ابي سفيان من املا رسول الله يوم الاثنين تمام اربعة اشهر من السنة / الرابعة من الهجره بالمدينه". That is: "Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān wrote [it] at the dictation of the Messenger of God, on Monday, at the completion of four months of the fourth year of the Hijra, in Medina."
  • Latin, p. 16 (image 00000022): "Secretarius autem fuit Moauia ben-abi-Sofian, miles Nuntij Dei, die Lunae vltima mensis quarti, anni quarti Hegirae, in Medina."
  • URLs: https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000037.tif.large.jpg ; …/00000038.tif.large.jpg ; …/00000022.tif.large.jpg

Audit verdict: Confirmed. Neither the Arabic nor the Latin names a month, and neither has "second day". "Rabiʿ Ashar" is not a standard month name; the fourth month is Rabiʿ al-Akhir. That "second day" renders yawm al-ithnayn (literally "day two", i.e. Monday) is a plausible explanation, but it is an inference.

A12. "Dr. Addison"

Finding as reported. The book (pp. 153–154, 157) identifies "Dr. Addison" as James Thayer Addison (1887–1953), a defender. The cited source (A General Dictionary, Historical and Critical, vol. 1, 1735, art. "ADDISON (LANCELOT)") concerns Lancelot Addison (d. 1703). That article reports an Arabist's view that Scaliger probably forged the text.

What the book says.

  • p. 153: "The Covenant … is also treated as factual by Henri Layard …, Pedro de Madrazo …, and the Société d'Amis …, as well as James Thayer Addison (1887-1953 CE)."
  • pp. 153–154: "A detailed defense of the covenant was also made by Dr. Addison whose arguments were sum­marized by Bayle as follows: Dr Addison ... mentions the treaty of Alliance … Dr. Addison says, that we may consider it as one of Mahomet's artifices to support his authority … (241)".
  • p. 154: "The views of Dr. Addison and Van Dyke are evi­dently incorrect."
  • p. 157: "When Addison asked a person who was very skilled in the Arabic language … The reader concluded that it was very probable that the covenant had been forged by the missionary in question (Bayle 241)."
  • The bibliography lists Bayle et al., A General Dictionary, vol. 1 (1735). It has no Addison entry. Lancelot Addison is not named anywhere in the book.

What the primary source says. A General Dictionary, Historical and Critical, vol. 1 (London; the archive.org copy's title page reads "MDCCXXXIV"), art. "ADDISON (LANCELOT)", p. 241. https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_a-general-dictionary-hi_bayle-pierre_1741_1

  • The subject: "Lancelot Addison, a Minister, born at Mauldismeaburne … installed [Dean of Lichfield] June 19th 1683 … He died in 1703".
  • On the treaty, in The First State of Mahumedism: "Dr. Addison says, that we may consider it as one of Mahomet's artifices to support his authority, which was then in its infancy; but when he afterwards saw it sufficiently established, he changed his language …".
  • On the Arabist: "Dr. Addison tells us afterwards, that having asked a person very well skill'd in the Arabic tongue, what he thought of this treaty …, he replied, that when he had read it, he was of opinion it was a spurious piece, because he found nothing in the stile, which was like that of the Koran; that … this piece was brought from the East by a Capuchin, named Pacifique Scaliger; and that it is very probable it had been forged by that Missionary."

Audit verdict: Partly confirmed.

  • Confirmed: the cited article concerns Lancelot Addison (d. 1703) and reports the Arabist's forgery opinion. A 1730s dictionary cannot be summarising James Thayer Addison (b. 1887).
  • Confirmed: the quoted passage is not a defence of authenticity. Addison treats the treaty as a temporary "artifice" of Muhammad, and the book itself calls his views "evidently incorrect" (p. 154).
  • Not quite as stated: the book never explicitly says that "Dr. Addison" is James Thayer Addison. It names J. T. Addison as treating the covenant as factual, then credits "Dr. Addison" with a "detailed defense" in the next sentences. It identifies no other Addison. The conflation is implied by juxtaposition, not stated outright.
  • Minor: the copy I opened is dated 1734 on its title page, not 1735.

A13. Printing history, and the 1795 cancellation

Finding as reported. The book (p. 151) says the 1630 edition was reprinted four times in its first year, and again in 1638, 1655, 1668, 1690 and 1888. Library catalogues (VD17 etc.) show 1638 (Fabricius, Latin only), 1655 (Nissel) and 1690 (Hinckelmann), but no 1668 or 1888 edition. The 1795 French committee formally cancelled its printing order on 3 brumaire IV (25 Oct 1795).

What the book says.

  • p. 151: "Since the work sold out almost immediately, and book­stores could not meet the demand, the work was re-published four times during the first year of publication. It was republished in various editions and languages by other translators and publishers in 1655,1638, 1668,1690, and as late as 1888 CE."
  • p. 155: "Mr. Lefebvre-Villebrune was suddenly removed from the project and replaced by a certain Mr. Legrand (Guillaume 858) … To the best of my knowl­edge, the translation, publication, and dissemina­tion … never saw the light of day."

What the primary sources say.

VD17 (K10plus SRU):

  • 1638. VD17 23:259451D, Fabricius, Muhammedis Testamentum sive pacta cum Christianis in Oriente inita, Rostock: Hallervord/Meder. Language "lat" only; [4] Bl., 47 S. 4°.
  • 1690. VD17 23:259462T, Hinkelmann, Testamentum et pactiones … Arabice & Latine, Hamburg. "Text lat. und arab."; [4] Bl., 27 S.
  • 1683/84. Weber, Schediasma, which "Enth. außerdem: Muhammedis Testamentum … a M. Johanne Fabricio … olim editum Rostochii, Anno MDCXXXIIX. nunc recusum Colon. Brandenb. Anno MDCLXXXIII".
  • URL: https://sru.k10plus.de/vd17?version=1.1&operation=searchRetrieve&query=pica.tit%3DMuhammedis%20Testamentum&recordSchema=dc

GVK (K10plus):

  • Nissel, Leiden: 1655, 1660 and 1661.
  • A Nissel record dated 1641 ("Typis et Impensis Nisselianis"). Its wording ("nunc primùm figuris vocalium insignitus") matches the 1661 issue, so it is probably misdated.
  • A Gale reproduction of Fabricius dated "1838", evidently an error for 1638.
  • No 1668 or 1888 record.
  • URL: https://sru.k10plus.de/opac-de-627?version=1.1&operation=searchRetrieve&query=pica.tit%3DTestamentum%20Muhammedem&recordSchema=dc

BnF catalogue (SRU):

  • 1630: four separate records, all "A. Vitray (Parisiis)", in-4°; two give "16-16 p."; none carries an edition statement.
  • 1638: Fabricius.
  • 1655: Nissel.
  • No 1668 or 1888 record. A search for "testament de mahomet" also found the 1631 and 1645 printings of Pacifique's Voyage de Perse.
  • URL: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/api/SRU?version=1.2&operation=searchRetrieve&query=bib.title%20all%20%22Testamentum%20pactiones%22&recordSchema=dublincore

Guillaume (ed.), Procès-verbaux du Comité d'instruction publique de la Convention, vol. 6, p. 858. https://archive.org/details/procsverbauxdu06fran

  • "CINQ CENT QUATORZIÈME SÉANCE. Du 3 brumaire an IV [25 octobre 1795]."
  • The Committee withdraws its morning nomination of Lefèvre-Villebrune as "conservateur de la Bibliothèque nationale pour les manuscrits modernes" and chooses "le citoyen Legrand, auteur des Fabliaux".
  • "Le Comité … rapporte son arrêté du 1 brumaire relatif à l'impression du prétendu Traité de Mahomet avec les chrétiens, ainsi que tous autres arrêtés qui pourraient avoir le même objet, et arrête que le citoyen Lefèvre-Villebrune réintégrera sous trois jours à la Bibliothèque nationale l'exemplaire qui devait servir à l'impression".

Audit verdict: Confirmed, with caveats.

  • Confirmed: 1638 (Fabricius, Latin only), 1655 (Nissel) and 1690 (Hinckelmann, Arabic–Latin) exist.
  • Confirmed: no 1668 or 1888 edition was found in VD17, GVK or the BnF.
  • Confirmed: the printing order was formally rescinded on 3 brumaire IV (25 Oct 1795). Legrand replaced Lefebvre-Villebrune as nominee for a Bibliothèque nationale keepership, not on "the project".
  • Caveats:
    • The 1655 Leiden edition is in GVK, the BnF and Penn, not in VD17.
    • The BnF has four 1630 records. They look like duplicate catalogue records of one edition, but metadata alone cannot exclude separate issues. Nothing in them documents "four" reprints.
    • Title searches cannot detect translations embedded in other works. The book's phrase "in various editions and languages" could cover such cases; Rycaut's Present State in its 1668 edition reportedly contains an English translation (per V4; not re-checked here). So the absence of 1668 and 1888 is unproven rather than disproved.
    • The catalogues also show printings the book omits: 1645, 1660/61 and 1683/84.

Fact-check reports

Second-opinion audit of the main findings, part 2

13 table rows · source file AUDIT_B.md

AUDIT B: independent re-verification of findings B1–B13

Book: John Andrew Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013). Auditor's stance: each finding was assumed possibly wrong and re-checked against the primary text. The earlier agents' conclusions were not relied on.

How this audit was done

  • Book wording. Taken from the OCR chunks (book/chunks/*.txt) and from book/book.txt (the layout text). For B3, the printed page image was also checked: PDF p. 225, rendered from /home/cool/Documents/Turkey_Trip/_OceanofPDF.com_The_Covenants_of_the_Prophet_Muhammad_with_the_Christians_of_the_World_-_John_A_Morrow.pdf.
  • Sources. Every source below was downloaded fresh by me into scratchpad/auditB/ and searched there. I did not reuse the other agents' files.
  • Page images. Where a quotation mattered, I opened the page image: Malech pp. 221, 311 and 314; the Sharif's decree; Barakat Ahmad pp. 60–61 and 90–91.
  • Fetches that failed:
    • iranicaonline.org: 403 / Cloudflare when fetched directly. I read it through Wayback snapshots instead.
    • al-islam.org: Cloudflare, then 404.
    • EI2 is paywalled and was not consulted. TDV was used instead.
    • Narkiss (ed.), Armenian Art Treasures of Jerusalem, the book the author cites for Sanjian, was not available.
  • Calendar conversions. Tabular Islamic calendar, computed locally.

Summary of verdicts

# Short title Verdict
B1 Selim / Baghdad / "Shimon IV" in 1517 Confirmed. One small correction to the wording: Malech's list does not give 1497 for Shimon IV.
B2 Assyrian covenant dated 4 AH; Hamza and Ja'far as witnesses Confirmed
B3 Sanjian's "fabricated"; Samuel of Ani's "no tax" Confirmed (both parts)
B4 Sharif's decree is 1918, not 1917 Confirmed
B5 Barakat Ahmad misrepresented Confirmed
B6 "Poisoned mouthful" placed before the Nadir exile Confirmed (one nuance noted)
B7 Bracketed clause added to Ibn Ishaq p. 672 Confirmed (the clause is in square brackets)
B8 "Twenty-five years of silence"; Fijar called "spurious" Confirmed (nuance on which source says what)
B9 Medina Constitution names no Christians Confirmed as to the text. The book's sentence is a broader interpretive claim (see caveat).
B10 Life dates: Majlisi, Ibn Sallam, al-Kalbi, Jordac/Zaydan Confirmed (all four)
B11 Reception: Reynolds, El-Wakil, Monferrer-Sala, Sellam Confirmed. Scope note: Monferrer-Sala reviews Morrow's 2025 book, not the 2013 one.
B12 p. 112 concession; the short Najran treaty in early Muslim sources Confirmed. Nuance: the short treaty also contains religious guarantees.
B13 Moritz 1918: forgery of c. 900–1000; decrees citing the Prophet's letter Partly confirmed. The Fatimid decree says "die alten Verträge", not "Schutzschreiben des Propheten".

B1. Selim I, Baghdad and "Shimon IV" (1517)

Finding as reported. The book (p. 177, also p. 180) says that in 1517 Selim I took the Assyrian covenant from the patriarch "Shimon IV" at Baghdad. Against this:

  • Baghdad was Safavid from 1508 to 1534, and Selim never went there.
  • Shem'on IV died in 1497, and the patriarch in 1517 was Shem'on VI.
  • Malech's own list (Malech p. 314) agrees.

What the book says.

  • p. 177 (PDF 202), block quotation of Malech: "In 1517 Sultan Selim came from Constantinople to Bag[h]dad, and it is said, that Shimon the fourth, the patriarch, visited the sultan and showed him the precious document. And the sultan said that it was so valuable, that it ought to be preserved in the royal treasury of Constantinople. The patriarch had to give it up, but Selim gave him a copy of the document, signed by himself. The copy is kept by the patriarch; it is still extant—the original is in Constantinople. (Malech 221)"
  • p. 178, the author's own endorsement: "As to the claim that it was Selim I who, in 1517, insisted that the Covenant ... be preserved in the Treasury in Istanbul, it makes perfect chronological sense."
  • p. 180: "what happened, then, to the certified copy left behind by Sultan Selim I? Well, according to George David Malech, the original was taken to Istanbul in 1517."
  • Accuracy note: the book quotes Malech accurately. The Baghdad and "Shimon the fourth" details appear in that quotation on p. 177, which p. 178 endorses. p. 180 repeats only the 1517 transfer to Istanbul.

What the primary sources say.

  • Malech (1910). Item https://archive.org/details/historyofsyriann00male; I checked the page images (n246, n336, n339).
    • p. 221 matches the book's quotation. The original reads "1517 Sultan Selim came from Constantinople to Bagdad, and it is said …", with no source given.
    • p. 311: "Patriarchs: Elias IV, 1405-1433; Shimon IV, 1433-1472; Shimon V, 1472-1503."
    • p. 314: "Patriarchs: Elias V, 1503-1504; Shimon VI, 1504-1538; …"
  • Iranica, "Iraq iv. Safavid period" (Wayback: http://web.archive.org/web/20261003041726/https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-iv-safavid-period/): "After Shah Esmāʿil I took Baghdad from the Āq Qoyunlu … in 1508, the city and its environs remained in Safavid hands until the Ottomans retook the area in 1534."
  • TDV, "Selim I" (https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/selim-i):
    • It traces Selim's 1517–18 movements: Gaza "8 Zilhicce 922 (2 Ocak 1517)"; Cairo (entry 15 February [1517]); Damascus; Aleppo "11 Safer 924 (22 Şubat 1518)"; then the return to Istanbul.
    • The article never mentions Baghdad ("Bağdat": 0 occurrences).
    • Süleyman entered Baghdad on 30 November [1534] (TDV, "Süleyman I").
  • Wilmshurst, The Martyred Church (2011) (https://archive.org/details/the-martyred-church; djvu text):
    • "Shem'on IV Basidi, who died in 1497 (his epitaph has been preserved in the monastery of Rabban Hormizd …)"
    • The patriarch list gives "Shem'on VI (1504-38)".
    • "The last Nestorian patriarch to reside habitually in Baghdad was Makkikha II (1257-65)."

Audit verdict: Confirmed. All three points stand:

  • Baghdad was Safavid in 1517.
  • Selim's 1517 movements did not include Baghdad.
  • The patriarch in 1517 was Shimon VI, by Malech's own list and by Wilmshurst's.

One correction to the wording. In V5's ranked list, "Shem'on IV died in 1497, and Malech's own list on p. 314 says so" is inaccurate:

  • Malech's list (p. 311) gives Shimon IV as 1433–1472.
  • The 1497 date is Wilmshurst's, and Wilmshurst uses a different numbering (he inserts a "Shem'on III").
  • The two lists agree on what matters here: Shimon VI was patriarch from 1504 to 1538.

B2. Date and witnesses of the Assyrian covenant

Finding as reported.

  • The covenant the book reprints (Ch. 12, pp. 313–314, from Malech 1910) is dated "4th year of the Hegira".
  • The book (p. 183) dates it "two years before" 630–632.
  • Its witness list includes Hamza (killed 3 AH) and Ja'far b. Abi Talib (in Abyssinia until 7 AH).

What the book says.

  • p. 314 (PDF 339), last line of the reprint: "This agreement is written down by Moavijah Ben Sofian, according to the dictates of Mohammed, the messenger of God, in the 4th year of the Hegira in the city of Medina."
  • The signatures (p. 314) include "Hamza Ibn Almulabb … Jafar Ibn Abu Talib". The author's bracketed transliteration renders these as "Hamzah ibn al-Muttalib … Jafar ibn Abi Talib".
  • p. 183: "Mu'awiyyah did indeed act as Muhammad's scribe during the final two years of his life: from the year 630 to the year 632 CE. However, the Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Assyrian Christians dates from two years before."

What the primary sources say.

  • Malech pp. 229–230 (archive.org djvu text) has the same colophon: "…in the 4th year of the Hegira in the city of Medina." By the tabular calendar, 1 Muharram 4 AH falls in mid-June 625, so 4 AH = 625/626 CE.
  • Ibn Ishaq, tr. Guillaume (https://archive.org/details/GuillaumeATheLifeOfMuhammad; djvu text):
    • p. 375: Wahshi's account of killing Hamza at Uhud.
    • p. 389: "The battle was fought on the sabbath in mid-Shawwal". The next section is headed "THE DAY OF AL-RAJI', A.H. 3".
    • p. 526: Ja'far is among those "who stayed in Abyssinia until he sent 'Amr b. Umayya … to fetch them back … and who ultimately rejoined him in Khaybar after al-Hudaybiya". Khaybar is headed "A.H. 7" (p. 510).

Audit verdict: Confirmed.

  • 4 AH is about 4–5 years before 630, not two.
  • At 4 AH Hamza was already dead (Uhud, Shawwal 3 AH).
  • Ja'far was still in Abyssinia; he rejoined the Prophet in 7 AH.

B3. Sanjian and Samuel of Ani

Finding as reported.

  • Sanjian calls the edicts of the Prophet, 'Umar and 'Ali to the Armenians fabricated and without historical foundation; the book (pp. 199–200) cites him only for "attributed".
  • The book's quotation of Samuel of Ani (via Thomson) reads "ordered tax to be taken" where the source reads "ordered no tax".

What the book says.

  • p. 199 (PDF 224): "Avedis K. Sanjian, for example, speaks of '[t]he Firman attributed to the Prophet Mohammed, confirming the rights of the Armenians in the Holy Places of Jerusalem' (Narkiss 11), '[t]he Firman attributed to Omar Ibn al-Khattab [sic]' (11), and '[t]he Firman attributed to Caliph 'Ali' (13)."
  • p. 200 (PDF 225; checked on the page image): "…one cord of hair, and one gauntlet. But from the priests, nobles and cavalry he ordered tax to be taken, (qtd. Thomson, 'Muhammad' 843)". The word "no" is absent on the printed page, so this is not an OCR error.

What the primary sources say.

  • Sanjian, The Armenian Communities in Syria under Ottoman Dominion (Harvard 1965), p. 169 (https://archive.org/details/Sanjian1965ACSOD; djvu text):
    • "Equally unauthentic are the edicts which the Armenian patriarch of Jerusalem is alleged to have received not only from Caliph Umar I but also from the Prophet Muhammad and the orthodox Caliph Ali. All of these documents, which must have been fabricated to support rival claims to the dominical sanctuaries, have no historical foundation."
    • n. 2 (pp. 351–352) speaks of "The apocryphal charter issued to the Armenians by the Prophet Muhammad".
  • Thomson, "Muhammad and Islam in Armenian tradition", p. 843 (https://archive.org/details/thomsonmuhammadislamarmlit; djvu text): "…one cord of hair, and one gauntlet (45). But from the priests, nobles and cavalry he ordered no tax to be taken."
  • Not checked: Narkiss p. 11, the passage the book actually cites (not available). It may well say "attributed". The point stands that Sanjian's own monograph goes further.

Audit verdict: Confirmed (both parts).

B4. Date of the Sharif of Mecca's decree

Finding as reported. The decree the book dates to 1917 (p. 201) is dated 18 Rajab 1336, which is 29 April 1918.

What the book says. p. 201 (PDF 226): "In 1917, the Sharif of Mecca, al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, issued an edict which was aimed at all Muslims." The quoted text follows: "You are asked to protect and take great care of the entire Armenian, Jacobite, community … 'Whoever takes even a string from them, I will be his adversary on the Day of Judgment'…"

What the primary source says.

  • Armenian National Institute (https://www.armenian-genocide.org/Affirmation.4/current_category.1/affirmation_detail.html):
    • The entry is headed "April 29, 1918".
    • The text is addressed "to … Prince Faisal and Prince Abd al-'Aziz al-Jarba".
    • "This letter is written from Imm Al-Qura (Mecca), on 18 Rajab 1336 [April 29, 1918]".
    • The body matches the book's quotation ("Whosoever takes from them even a rope, I will be his adversary on the day of Judgment").
  • Image of the engraved document (https://www.armenian-genocide.org/uploads/Affirmation/4.jpg): I read "١٨ رجب ١٣٣٦" on line 3.
  • Tabular conversion: 18 Rajab 1336 = 29 April 1918, and 18 Rajab 1335 = 10 May 1917.

Audit verdict: Confirmed. The text the book quotes is the letter of 18 Rajab 1336 (29 April 1918). The letter is addressed to two named princes, not "all Muslims".

Not checked: whether a separate 1917 Sharifian manifesto exists (V5 cites one from Margaryan's abstract). Even if it does, the quoted text is not from it.

B5. Barakat Ahmad on executions and expulsions

Finding as reported.

  • The book (p. 41) says: "As far as Ahmad is concerned, no Jews were executed or expelled from Medina during Muhammad's life".
  • Barakat Ahmad (Muhammad and the Jews, 1979) accepts the banishment of the Banu Nadir and the execution of about 16–17 Qurayza leaders.

What the book says. p. 41 (PDF 66): "While not entirely convincing, Syed Barakat Ahmad's (d. 1988 CE) Muhammad and the Jews: A Re-Examination also cast doubts on the credibility of Ibn Ishaq's account … As far as Ahmad is concerned, no Jews were executed or expelled from Medina during Muhammad's life."

What the primary source says. Barakat Ahmad, Muhammad and the Jews: A Re-Examination (1979). PDF: https://almuslih.org/wp-content/uploads/Library/Barakat,%20A%20-%20Muhammad%20and%20the%20Jews.pdf (page images checked).

  • p. 60: "Sūrat al-Ḥashr, which was revealed after the Battle of Uḥud, in the fourth year of the Hijrah and deals with the banishment of the B. al-Naḍīr from Medina, refer to their expulsion as 'the first exile'."
  • p. 60: "While the Qur'ān mentions the B. al-Naḍīr's expulsion and the B. Qurayẓah's punishment, it does not refer to the B. Qaynuqā''s expulsion".
  • p. 91: "The leaders, Ḥuyayy b. Akhṭab, Ka'b b. Asad, Nabbāsh b. Qays and Ghazzāl b. Samaw'al were executed by 'Alī and Zubayr … The culpable leadership of a tribe of 600 to 900 men … would not normally exceed sixteen, or seventeen".
  • What Ahmad does deny is the Qaynuqa' expulsion: "the B. Qaynuqā' were not expelled during the Apostle's lifetime".

Audit verdict: Confirmed. Ahmad accepts the Nadir banishment from Medina and the execution of the Qurayza leaders. He denies only the Qaynuqa' expulsion.

B6. The "poisoned mouthful" and the Banu Nadir

Finding as reported.

  • The book (p. 39) cites a "poisoned mouthful" against the Banu Nadir before 625.
  • In Ibn Ishaq the poisoning is at Khaybar in 7 AH (Guillaume p. 516). The Nadir plot is a dropped rock (Guillaume p. 437).

What the book says. p. 39 (PDF 64): "If the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa' opposed Muhammad verbally, the Jews of Banu Nadir initiated a treacherous plot against the Prophet's life. After at least two attempts on the life of the Prophet, including an incident in which Muhammad was as close as a poisoned mouthful away from death, the Commander-in-Chief of the Muslim Community opted to exile the Banu Nadir from Medina in the year 625 CE." No source is given for the poisoning.

What the primary source says. Ibn Ishaq, tr. Guillaume (archive.org, as above).

  • p. 437 ("THE DEPORTATION OF THE B. AL-NADIR, A.H. 4"): "'Who will go to the top of the house and drop a rock on him … and rid us of him?' … 'Amr b. Jihash b. Ka'b volunteered to do this".
  • p. 516, after the conquest of Khaybar: "Zaynab d. al-Harith, the wife of Sallam b. Mishkam prepared for him a roast lamb … she put a lot of poison in it … He took hold of the shoulder and chewed a morsel of it, but he did not swallow it".
  • Nuance: Ibn Ishaq's list of rabbis (p. 239) places "Sallam b. Mishkam" under "From B. al-Nadir". So the poisoner was the wife of a Nadir man. The event is still at Khaybar, after the exile.

Audit verdict: Confirmed. In Ibn Ishaq the Nadir plot before the exile is the dropped rock. The poisoning is at Khaybar (7 AH), after the 625 exile, so the book's chronology is not supported. The Nadir link through Sallam b. Mishkam's wife is real but does not change the date.

B7. Bracketed clause in Ibn Ishaq p. 672

Finding as reported. The book (p. 52) quotes Ibn Ishaq 672 as "Fight everyone in the way of Allah [who attacked you or betrayed you]". Guillaume p. 672 has no such clause.

What the book says. p. 52 (PDF 77): "The Prophet exhorted his commander to 'Fight everyone in the way of Allah [who attacked you or betrayed you] and kill those who disbelieve in Allah' (672)."

What the primary source says. Guillaume p. 672: "Take it, Ibn 'Auf; fight everyone in the way of God and kill those who disbelieve in God. Do not be deceitful with the spoil; do not be treacherous, nor mutilate, nor kill children."

Audit verdict: Confirmed. Guillaume has no such clause. The words appear in square brackets, which conventionally mark an editorial insertion, so this is an interpolation rather than a silent change. But it is placed inside the quotation marks, it is not identified as the author's gloss, and it narrows the scope of the command.

B8. The "twenty-five years of silence" and the Fijar war

Finding as reported.

  • The book's "twenty-five years of silence" (pp. 6, 12) is contradicted by the sira: Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa'd and al-Tabari place Muhammad in Mecca at about 20 (Fijar, Hilf al-fudul), 25 (marriage) and 35 (rebuilding of the Ka'ba).
  • Ibn Sa'd quotes him: "I attended it [Fijar] with my uncles and shot arrows".
  • The book calls his Fijar participation "spurious" (p. 6).

What the book says.

  • pp. 5–6 (PDF 28–29): "As to what took place between the encounter with Bahira in 582 CE and Muhammad's marriage to Khadijah (d. 619 CE) in 595 CE, the sources are silent with the exception of spurious allegations that he participated in the Sacrilegious War or Harb al-fijar when he was twenty years of age."
  • p. 12 (PDF 35): "There is thus a period of ten years … from the time he was fifteen to the time he was twenty-five, that is unaccounted for. There is also a second period of fifteen years, from the time he was married … until he declared his prophethood, at the age of forty … These two blocks of time represent twenty-five years of silence."

What the primary sources say.

  • Guillaume p. 82: "This war broke out when the apostle was twenty years of age."
  • Ibn Hisham's note 124 (Guillaume pp. 709–710): "When the apostle was 14 or 15 years old … The apostle was present at some of these encounters, his uncles having taken him with them. He used to say that he picked up the arrows which the enemy had shot and gave them to his uncles to shoot."
  • Ibn Hisham's note 126 (p. 711): "At the age of 25 the apostle married Khadija".
  • Guillaume p. 84: "Quraysh decided to rebuild the Ka'ba when the apostle was thirty-five years of age".
  • Guillaume pp. 57–58 (Hilf al-fudul): "The apostle of God said, 'I witnessed in the house of 'Abdullah b. Jud'an a covenant…'". No age is given.
  • Ibn Sa'd, tr. Moinul Haq, vol. 1, p. 143 (https://archive.org/details/kitab-al-tabaqat-al-kabir-ibn-sad-s.-moinul-haq-h.-k.-ghazanfar-1):
    • "I attended it with my uncles and shot arrows there and I do not repent it. He was twenty years old at that time".
    • p. 144: "The oath of al-Fudul was taken after the return of the Quraysh from the battle of al-Fijar, and the Apostle of Allah then was twenty years of age."
    • Married at twenty-five ("married her when he was twenty-five years old").
    • Thirty-five at the Ka'ba rebuilding.
  • Tabari vol. 6, tr. Watt & McDonald (https://archive.org/details/the-history-of-al-tabari-vol.-6-muhammad-at-mecca-by-tabari-w.-montgomery-watt-m):
    • Marriage at 25 (Hisham b. Muhammad).
    • The Ka'ba rebuilding "fifteen years after the Sacrilegious War, when the Messenger of God was thirty-five".
    • Watt's foreword (p. xxii): these ages are "multiples of five", which "suggests that they are only approximations".

Audit verdict: Confirmed. The early sira does not leave the two periods silent. It places him at Fijar and the Hilf al-fudul (about age 20) and at the Ka'ba rebuilding (35), though thinly and with rounded ages.

Precision note on Fijar: Ibn Ishaq's own text dates the war by his age but does not itself say he fought. His participation comes from Ibn Hisham's note (at age 14/15) and from Ibn Sa'd (at age 20, in the Prophet's own words). The book gives no source for calling it "spurious".

B9. Christians and the Medina Constitution

Finding as reported. The Medina Constitution (Guillaume pp. 231–233) names Jewish groups but no Christians. The book (p. 33) says Jews and Christians "belonged to the community of believers".

What the book says. p. 33 (PDF 58): "the Prophet created an inclusive Community of Believers which included members of all the Abrahamic faiths. In the time of the Prophet, the ahl al-dhimmah, both Jewish and Christian, belonged to the community of believers." The same page adds: "While Donner is right that the Community of Believers was ecumenical and included Jews and Christians…"

What the primary source says. Guillaume pp. 231–233, "The covenant between the Muslims and the Medinans and with the Jews":

  • "The Jews of the B. 'Auf are one community with the believers (the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs) … The same applies to the Jews of the B. al-Najjar, B. al-Harith, B. Sa'ida, B. Jusham, B. al-Aus, B. Tha'laba…"
  • A search of the whole Constitution finds no "Christian", "Nazarene" or naṣārā.

Audit verdict: Confirmed as a statement about the text: the Constitution names Jewish groups only.

Caveat for fair presentation. The book's sentence is about "the time of the Prophet" in general, and the book draws the inclusion of Christians explicitly from Donner, with whom it agrees on this point. It disputes Donner only on whether Islam had a distinct identity. So this is a contested interpretive claim resting on Donner's thesis, not a misquotation of the Constitution. (V1a's remark that the book "attacks" Donner's thesis on that page is inaccurate on this specific point.)

B10. Life dates

Finding as reported.

  • al-Majlisi: the book has "1616–1689" (pp. 2, 6, 7); Iranica and TDV give 1627–1699.
  • 'Abd Allah ibn Sallam: the book has "d. 630" (p. 36); EI2 and TDV give 43/663-4.
  • "Muhammad al-Kalbi (737–819)" (p. 40): Muhammad b. al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi died 146/763. The span 737–819 belongs to his son Hisham.
  • "George Jordac or Jurji Zaydan (1861–1914)" (p. 62) conflates two men.

What the book says.

  • p. 2: "Muhammad Baqir al-Majlisi (1616-1689 CE)". p. 6: "Majlisi's (1616-1689 CE) version". p. 7: "Majlisi (1616-1689 CE)". Also p. 124: "'Allamah Majlisi (1616-1689 CE)".
  • p. 36: "al-Husayn ibn Sallam ibn al-Harith (d. 630 CE), the most learned Jewish rabbi from Yathrib".
  • p. 40: "others sources, such as Muhammad al-Kalbi (737-819 CE), make no mention of the Banu Qaynuqa' incident (Scholler 26-27)". The bibliography entry is Schöller, "Sira and Tafsir. Muhammad al-Kalbi on the Jews of Medina".
  • p. 62: "As George Jordac or Jurji Zaydan (1861-1914 CE) has eloquently expressed…". The bibliography entry is "Jordac, George. The Voice of Human Justice. Trans. M. Fazal Haq. Qum: Ansariyan, 1990."

What the sources say.

  • Majlisi:
    • Iranica, "Majlesi, Mohammad-Baqer" (Wayback: http://web.archive.org/web/20261019221009/https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/majlesi-mohammad-baqer/) gives "(b. 1627; d. 1699 or 1700)". It also notes that "Most sources agree on 1037/1627-28 as his date of birth (… the hijra year 1027/1618 in Amin … seems to be a misprint)".
    • TDV (https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/meclisi-muhammed-bakir): "1037'de (1627) İsfahan'da doğdu … 1110 (1698-99) veya (1111/1699-1700) yılında İsfahan'da vefat etti".
  • Ibn Sallam: TDV, "Abdullah b. Selâm" (https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/abdullah-b-selam): "(ö. 43/663-64) … Muâviye'nin halifeliği sırasında Medine'de vefat etmiştir". EI2 was not consulted (paywall).
  • The two Kalbis:
    • TDV, "Kelbî, Muhammed b. Sâib" (https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/kelbi-muhammed-b-saib): "(ö. 146/763)". He fought at Dayr al-Jamajim "(82/701)", so he cannot have been born in 737.
    • TDV, "Kelbî, Hişâm b. Muhammed" (https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/kelbi-hisam-b-muhammed): "Muhtemelen 120 (738) yılında Kûfe'de doğdu", "(ö. 204/819 [?])".
  • Jordac and Zaydan:
    • TDV, "Corcî Zeydân" (https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/corci-zeydan): "Corcî b. Habîb Zeydân (1861-1914)".
    • George Jordac: English Wikipedia (tertiary; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jordac) and Wikidata Q6414987 both give "(1931 – 2014)", Lebanese, author of The Voice of Human Justice, which is the book the author cites.

Audit verdict: Confirmed (all four):

  • Majlisi's dates are wrong by about a decade at both ends.
  • Ibn Sallam died in 43/663-4, not 630.
  • 737–819 are approximately Hisham's dates, not his father Muhammad's.
  • Jordac (1931–2014) and Zaydan (1861–1914) are two different people.

B11. Reception

Finding as reported.

  • Reynolds, First Things (Feb 2014), "Briefly Noted", calls the covenants late forgeries and says the earliest Sinai copies are 16th-century.
  • El-Wakil's 2016 abstract in the Journal of Islamic Studies calls forgery "the accepted understanding".
  • Monferrer-Sala, Mediterranea 11 (2026), finds Morrow's case "more persuasive as advocacy than as a decisive demonstration of authenticity".
  • Amar Sellam, who reviewed the book for AJISS, is a listed Covenants Initiative signatory.

What the primary sources say.

  • Reynolds (https://firstthings.com/briefly-noted-59/; page labelled "February 2014 Issue"):
    • "Forged by Christians intent on proving to their Muslim overlords that the Prophet himself had guaranteed their well-being and the preservation of their property, they are all quite late. The earliest copies of 'the covenant of the Prophet with the monks of Mt. Sinai' date to the sixteenth century".
    • Also: "his interest in arguing for the authenticity of these covenants is not unlike the interest of those who forged them in the first place."
  • El-Wakil, JIS 27:3 (2016), doi 10.1093/jis/etw027. Abstract via the OpenAlex API (https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1093/jis/etw027): "Morrow brought these covenants together … arguing against the accepted understanding that these are forgeries." El-Wakil himself argues for authenticity.
  • Monferrer-Sala, Mediterranea 11 (2026) 403–408 (https://journals.uco.es/mediterranea/article/download/18755/17486/60103): "its historical argumentation is more persuasive as advocacy than as a decisive demonstration of authenticity." The review is of Morrow, Muhammad and the Christians: Commemorating the Covenants of the Prophet (Academica Press, 2025), not the 2013 book.
  • Sellam:
    • The AJISS 32:2 (2015) review (https://ajis.org/index.php/ajiss/article/download/977/304) is of the 2013 book and is signed "Amar Sellam, Professeur de l'Enseignement Supérieur (retired) … Mohammed the First University, Oujda".
    • The Covenants Initiative signatory list (https://covenantsoftheprophet.org/2013/08/) includes "Dr. Amar Sellam, Mohamed I University".

Audit verdict: Confirmed. Scope note: the Monferrer-Sala quotation concerns Morrow's 2025 follow-up volume, so it should not be presented as a review of the 2013 book.

B12. The p. 112 concession and the early Muslim Najran treaty

Finding as reported.

  • On p. 112 the book concedes that the Najran covenant "appears to be completely absent in the classical Islamic sources" and that "most scholars dismiss it as dubious".
  • The early Muslim sources (Abu Yusuf, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'd, al-Baladhuri) give a short tribute treaty (2,000 robes, a loan of arms, a riba clause), not the long covenant.

What the book says. p. 112 (PDF 137): "The strongest argument that can be made against the Covenant of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of Najran resides in the fact that mention of this document appears to be completely absent in the classical Islamic sources which have survived to the present. It is on this basis that most scholars dismiss it as dubious. However, when viewed in a broader context, such a position seems eminently reactionary and intransigent."

What the primary sources say.

  • Abu Yusuf, Kitab al-Kharaj (https://shamela.ws/book/26333/88 and /89, printed pp. 84–85). It gives the copy "التي في أيديهم" (the one in their hands):
    • "على ألفي حلة … في كل رجب ألف حلة وفي كل صفر ألف حلة" (2,000 robes: 1,000 each Rajab and 1,000 each Safar)
    • "وعليهم عارية ثلاثين درعا وثلاثين فرسا وثلاثين بعيرا" (they are to lend 30 coats of mail, 30 horses and 30 camels)
    • "ومن أكل ربا من ذي قبل فذمتي منه بريئة" (whoever henceforth takes usury, my protection is withdrawn from him)
    • "جوار الله وذمة محمد … على أموالهم وأنفسهم وأرضهم وملتهم … وبيعهم … لا يغير أسقف من أسيقفيته ولا راهب من رهبانيته" (the protection of God and the dhimma of Muhammad over their property, persons, land, religion and churches; no bishop is to be moved from his see, nor monk from his monastic office)
  • Abu 'Ubayd, Kitab al-Amwal no. 517 (OpenITI: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenITI/0225AH/master/data/0224QasimIbnSallam/0224QasimIbnSallam.Amwal/0224QasimIbnSallam.Amwal.ShamAY0034007-ara1):
    • Same terms: "ألفي حلة … عارية ثلاثين فرسا، وثلاثين بعيرا، وثلاثين درعا … على أن لا ياكلوا الربا" (2,000 robes; a loan of 30 horses, 30 camels and 30 coats of mail; on condition that they do not consume usury)
    • Plus protection of "بيعهم ورهبانيتهم وأساقفتهم" (their churches, their monks and their bishops).
    • No. 518 says 'Umar expelled them because "أصابوا الربا" (they took usury).
  • Ibn Sa'd, tr. Moinul Haq, vol. 1, pp. 341–342 and 419:
    • "two thousand hullahs … If there be fighting in Yaman they will have to give as loan thirty coats of mail, thirty horses and thirty camels … provided that it is not the amount of usury".
    • Also guarantees for "their churches and places of worship", and that no bishop or monk be removed.
  • al-Baladhuri, tr. Hitti, Origins of the Islamic State pp. 100–101 (https://archive.org/details/originsofislamic01albauoft): "two thousand robes … thirty coats of mail, thirty mares and thirty camels … whosoever of them has up till now received usury, I am clear of the responsibility of his protection."
  • None of these four gives the long covenant's distinctive clauses (per-head dirham tax, Muslim help in building churches, protection of Christian wives' faith).

Audit verdict: Confirmed.

Nuance for fair wording. The short treaty is tribute-centred, but it also guarantees persons, religion, churches and the clergy's offices. "Short treaty with tribute and religious guarantees" is more exact than "tribute treaty" alone.

B13. Moritz 1918

Finding as reported.

  • Moritz (1918) dates the Sinai text to about 900–1000 and calls it a forgery.
  • He also records that Fatimid and Mamluk decrees refer to "Schutzschreiben des Propheten".

What the primary source says. Moritz, Beiträge zur Geschichte des Sinaiklosters im Mittelalter nach arabischen Quellen (1918) (https://archive.org/details/beitrgezurgesc00moriuoft; djvu text).

  • Dating: "Die Sinaiurkunde kann also nicht vor rund 900 n. Chr. entstanden sein … und können mit ziemlicher Wahrscheinlichkeit die Herstellung auf den Raum von 900—1000 begrenzen" (the Sinai document cannot have been produced before about 900 CE … and its production can, with fair probability, be limited to the period 900–1000). He suggests the time of the caliph al-Hakim.
  • Forgery:
    • "Daß die Fälschung besonders geschickt ausgeführt sei, läßt sich nicht behaupten" (one cannot claim that the forgery was particularly skilfully done).
    • Style: "ganz unmuhammedanisch, bisweilen kaum noch arabisch" (entirely un-Muhammadan, at times hardly Arabic at all).
  • What the decrees say:
    • The oldest firman, of the Fatimid caliph al-Hafiz (1132–1149), orders the governor to keep "die alten Verträge" (the old treaties). Moritz infers that only this document can be meant.
    • The Mamluk sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri's firman "vom 6. Muharram 911 (921?)" names "Schutzschreiben des Propheten und Urkunden der Chalifen" (letters of protection of the Prophet and documents of the caliphs).
    • Khair Bek (the first Ottoman governor, 926/927 AH) has "das heilige prophetische Schutzschreiben" (the holy prophetic letter of protection).

Audit verdict: Partly confirmed.

  • Confirmed: the 900–1000 dating, the forgery verdict, and the Mamluk decree's reference to the Prophet's letter of protection.
  • Inexact: "Fatimid … decrees refer to 'Schutzschreiben des Propheten'". The Fatimid decree Moritz cites speaks only of "die alten Verträge" ("the old treaties"). The explicit reference to the Prophet appears in Mamluk and early Ottoman decrees.
  • Suggested wording: "the earliest (Fatimid) decree refers to 'old treaties'; Mamluk and early Ottoman decrees refer explicitly to the Prophet's letter of protection."
