Fact-check reports

Final review of the report against the evidence

6 table rows · source file FINAL_REVIEW_of_report.md

Review of "Book Analysis Report: Timeline, Facts & Cross-Source Verification"

Under review: scratchpad/report_export.md, the report on J. A. Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013).

What the report was tested against:

  • the extraction files Covenants_Evidence_Ledger/book_extraction/ (00–09);
  • the book's OCR text scratchpad/book/chunks/*.txt (every book quotation below was re-read there);
  • the fact-check reports Covenants_Evidence_Ledger/fact_check_reports/ (V0–V7c, AUDIT_A, AUDIT_B, QA_extraction_checks).

No web sources were used.

Conventions:

  • Page numbers are the book's printed pages.
  • "Vx row Y" means the verdict row with that ID in that fact-check report.
  • Every item gives the exact report text, the problem, the evidence, and the replacement wording.

Overall judgement. The report's core findings hold up against the evidence files, including the witness anachronisms, the 1517 Baghdad story, the 1630 date, the 975 decree, and the Thenaud and Burckhardt readings. But four kinds of fault would not survive a careful reader with the book open:

  • A few statements put words in the book's mouth (items 1–2) or treat quotations as the author's own claims (item 21).
  • The headline numbers and the "confirmed by audit" claims cannot be reproduced as written (items 7–8).
  • Several "contradictions" and "not found" verdicts are overstated (items 9–12).
  • The report repeatedly leaves out concessions the book itself makes, and the strongest evidence in the book's favour that the fact-check files contain (items 3, 13–20, 26–28).

Most fixes are small. Items 1–12 should be fixed before the report is shared.

A. Statements that misrepresent the book (fix first)

1. The book never calls Hamidullah's reprint a "milestone"

Report text:

  • Errors #6, "The book says" cell: "Hamidullah's 1956 reprint of the Najran text is a milestone in its recognition".
  • Covenant-by-covenant, Najran row: "Hamidullah, whose 1956 reprint the book cites as a milestone, calls the Seert texts fabrications".

Problem:

  • The word "milestone" is not in the book's discussion of Hamidullah. In the OCR it appears only twice: on p. 114, inside a quotation from Qureshi about the Treaty of Najran recorded in the Muslim sources, and on p. 65.
  • What p. 138 actually says: "Although it was reprinted in 1956 in Muhammad Hamidullah's Majmuah al-watha'iq ... and in 2002 in Muhammad 'Amarah's al-Islam wa al-akhar, the work has not reached the wide audience that it merits."
  • The real fault, as V3 row 4.58 frames it, is an omission: the book cites the reprint without saying that Hamidullah printed the texts as forgeries.
  • V3 row 4.58 also says Hamidullah's verdict was read in his 5th edition, not the 1956 printing.
  • Neither audit checked this item.

Evidence: OCR 04_ch3_ch4.txt lines 3873–3886 (p. 138); V3 row 4.58; V3 headline findings.

Replace #6 with:

  • Book says: "The book cites Hamidullah's 1956 reprint of the Najran text (pp. xviii, 138), regretting only that the covenant 'has not reached the wide audience that it merits'".
  • Sources show: "Hamidullah includes the Seert texts as a specimen of forgery and writes that 'there is not the slightest doubt' they are fabrications (5th edition). The book does not mention this."

Replace the Najran-row sentence with: "Hamidullah, whose reprint of the text the book cites without mentioning his verdict (p. 138), calls the Seert texts fabrications."

2. Errors #8 attributes to Arpee an argument the author makes in his own voice

Report text: "| 8 | Arpee's Persia covenant has no motive for forgery (quoting Arpee) | The quotation cuts Arpee's own aside "(though by modern criticism pronounced a forgery)" | p. 99 |"

Problem:

  • On p. 99 the book quotes Arpee: the Persian text "reproduces a charter, purporting to be ... originally granted by Mohammed ... to the Monastery of St. Catherine". The ellipsis cuts the forgery aside. That quotation says nothing about motive.
  • The motive argument is on pp. 102–103, in Morrow's own voice, and it is a different claim: that Arpee himself had no motive or means to forge the text.
  • Arpee's aside refers to the underlying Sinai charter, not the Persian document.
  • V3 rates this item "Minor difference (a substantive omission)". It was never audited.

Evidence: OCR 04_ch3_ch4.txt lines 1–12 (p. 99); 04_ch3_ch4.md §5 item 6 and the "Arguments for" row ("Arpee was a serious historian with no motive ... (p. 103)"); V3 row C3-7.

Replace with: "| 8 | Quoting Arpee, the Persia text 'reproduces a charter, purporting to be ... originally granted by Mohammed ... to the Monastery of St. Catherine' | The first ellipsis removes Arpee's aside that this Sinai charter was '(though by modern criticism pronounced a forgery)' (Arpee p. 355) | p. 99 |"

Same fix in the Persia row of the covenant-by-covenant table.

  • Current: "The book's quotation of Arpee omits his remark that modern criticism called it 'a forgery'"
  • Replace: "The book's quotation of Arpee (p. 99) cuts his aside that the Sinai charter the Persian text reproduces was '(though by modern criticism pronounced a forgery)'."

B. Headline framing, chart and numbers

3. The lead paragraph overstates three points and gives nothing on the book's side

Report text: "No original survives, and each text first appears in dated evidence 250 to 1,300 years after the date it claims. Of about 1,550 checks against outside sources, 860 found the book consistent and 203 found it contradicted; the errors cluster in the evidence for authenticity. Most specialists treat the long covenant texts as later compositions, while a small group of scholars has defended them since 2016."

Problems:

  • (a) "No original survives." The files support only "no original is known to survive" or "has been found" (V2a §4: "lost or missing"; V6a §4.4: "Even its defenders concede"). The book argues the Sinai original may lie in Topkapı (pp. 65, 69). It treats the St James Armenian scroll as possibly "the original" (p. 200: "Whether the copy ... is the original Prophet's oath, a copy thereof ... is immaterial"). That scroll has never been published or examined.
  • (b) "each text first appears in dated evidence". This is not what the chart measures; see item 4. For Sinai (1512) and Armenians (1187) the dates are reports of a document, not appearances of the text. Najran's 878 is the text's own account of its discovery.
  • (c) "the errors cluster in the evidence for authenticity". No fact-check file says this, and nothing counts it. In the report's own error tables, 14 of 101 items are in the "authenticity case" table, and dozens concern Chapter 15 history and life dates. V7a–c alone hold about 45 "Inconsistent" rows on life dates, and V6b about 30 on Chapter 15. The defensible claim is about importance, not distribution, and the Errors section already makes it ("The errors that matter most concern ...").
  • (d) Balance. The lead gives only negatives. The fact-check's own neutral assessments name points for the book:
    • early Muslim sources preserve a real Najran treaty;
    • the prophetic-covenant genre is real;
    • Sinai's monks invoked a prophetic letter of protection before the Ottoman conquest.
    • Evidence: V6a §4.2 and §4.4; V0 §3.6; AUDIT_B B12, B13.
  • (e) "since 2016" leaves out Morrow (2013), the author of the book under review. V0 §3.6 says "a small, active, mostly peer-reviewed group defending it since 2016".
  • (f) The counts cannot be reproduced; see item 7.

Replace the paragraph with (keep the numbers only after the recount in item 7):

John Andrew Morrow's book argues that six covenants protecting Christians were issued by the Prophet Muhammad. No original is known to survive, and the earliest dated evidence for each covenant (a copy, a printing, or a report of such a document) comes 250 to 1,300 years after the date it claims. Of 1,551 verdicts reached against outside sources, 860 found the book consistent and 203 found it contradicted, by other sources or by its own pages. The most consequential errors concern the evidence for authenticity: the witness lists, the dating of the documents and how sources are quoted. The fact-check also confirms points in the book's favour. Early Muslim sources record a real, shorter treaty with Najran, and the monks of Sinai were invoking a prophetic letter of protection before the Ottoman conquest of 1517. Most specialists whose verdicts could be opened treat the long covenant texts as later compositions. A small group of scholars, including Morrow, has defended them, in peer-reviewed venues since 2016.

4. The chart compares unlike evidence, and on the Assyrian bar this counts against the book

Report text:

  • Line 221: "No original of any covenant survives, and each text first appears in dated evidence centuries after the date it claims."
  • Line 225: "The gap is shortest for the Najran text, which by its own story was found in 878–79, and longest for the Persian and Assyrian texts."
  • Chart data: Najran 631→878, Armenians 626→1187, Sinai 623→1512, World 625→1538, Persia 625→1881, Assyrian 625→1910.

Problem. The bars measure three different things:

Covenant Chart date What that date actually is
Sinai 1512 Thenaud's report that the privilege was kept in the monastery mosque. The earliest dated copy of the text is 957 AH / 1550–51 (Moritz). The Mamluk decree of Qansuh al-Ghawri citing "letters of protection of the Prophet" is dated 911 or 921 AH (1505 or 1515), so it may be earlier than 1512 (V2a §2b, row E4; AUDIT_B B13).
Armenians 1187 Saladin's charter, which refers to pacts of the Prophet, 'Umar and 'Ali (V5 row T78, §4.2). The Armenian text itself is unpublished and undated.
Najran 878 The text's own account of its discovery. The witness that carries that account is a chronicle of the 10th–11th century (V6a §4.3 point 4; V3 §4B).
World 1538 A manuscript of a different recension: no date, scribe 'Ali.
Persia 1881 First printing.
Assyrian 1910 First printing.

The Assyrian bar breaks the rule used for Sinai and the Armenians.

  • The report itself says "A Church of the East claim to a prophetic charter is attested from the Abbasid period" (line 233).
  • V5 §4.1: Bar Hebraeus (13th c.) and Assemani report a "diploma" obtained by Isho'yahb II with Said of Najran. "This shows the claim existed from at least the Abbasid period." V4 §4 adds that Mari and 'Amr report the same charter.
  • V5 §4.1 and V6a §4.2 point 3: the Malech text belongs to the World-covenant family, attested from 1538.
  • Scored the way Sinai and the Armenians are scored (first report of a document), the Assyrian gap would be about 650 years at most (Bar Hebraeus, 13th c.), not 1,285. Scored by its family (1538), it would be about 910.
  • As drawn, the longest bar is the product of an inconsistent rule, and that rule works against the book.
  • Caveat for fairness to the critics: V5 also says these reports do "not show that Malech's text is that charter". The same is true of Saladin's charter and the Armenian scroll. Whatever rule is chosen, it must be applied to every bar.

Replace line 221 with: "No original of any covenant is known to survive, and for each covenant the earliest dated evidence (a copy, a printing, or a report of such a document) comes centuries after the date it claims."

Add a note under the chart:

Claimed date = the date the text bears (Sinai 2 AH; World, Persia and Assyrian 4 AH). Morrow regards the 4 AH dates as later scribal additions (pp. 107, 167). The Najran text bears no date, so the book's "last year of the Prophet's life" is used. The Armenian text is unpublished, so the "626" of a tradition the book quotes is used (p. 191). The evidence points differ in kind:

  • Najran 878–79 is the text's own account of its discovery; the chronicle that carries it dates from the 10th–11th century.
  • Sinai 1512 (Thenaud) and Armenians 1187 (Saladin) are reports of a prophetic document, not copies. The earliest dated Sinai copy is 1550–51, and a Mamluk decree citing the Prophet's letters may date from 1505.
  • World 1538 is a manuscript of a different recension.
  • Persia 1881 and Assyrian 1910 are first printings. A Church of the East claim to a prophetic charter is reported much earlier (in medieval chronicles including Bar Hebraeus, 13th century), and the Assyrian text belongs to the World-covenant family attested from 1538.

Replace line 225's sentence with: "The gap is shortest for the Najran text, which by its own account was found in 878–79. It is longest for the Persian and Assyrian texts as printed (1881, 1910), though a Church of the East claim to such a charter is reported from the 13th century and the Assyrian text belongs to the World-covenant family attested from 1538."

5. Two date cells in "The six covenants" table contradict the chart and the rest of the report

(a) Armenian.

  • Report text: "None given; placed in Patriarch Abraham I's term, given as 638–669 (p. 191)".
  • Problem: the chart uses 626 as the Armenian claimed date. The book quotes "in 626" (Zeki al-Din, via the Belleville Armenian Church, p. 191) and "626/4H" and "early 630s" (Dadoyan, p. 200). Morrow himself places it "most likely in Medina, after his return" (p. 191).
  • Evidence: OCR 06_ch6_ch7.txt lines 1405–1424 (p. 191); 06_ch6_ch7.md covenant profile, "Claimed date (CE)".
  • Replace with: "None in a printed text. The book quotes traditions of 626 (Zeki al-Din, p. 191) and '626/4H' (Dadoyan, p. 200). Morrow places it in Patriarch Abraham I's term, given as 638–669, 'most likely in Medina' (p. 191)."

(b) Assyrian.

  • Report text: "No year; "two years before" Mu'awiyyah's 630–632 service as scribe (p. 183)".
  • Problem: the book's own printed text ends "in the 4th year of the Hegira in the city of Medina" (p. 314). The report says so itself in the covenant-by-covenant table (line 233) and in Errors #11.
  • Replace with: "Printed text dated '4th year of the Hegira' (p. 314). Morrow dates it 'two years before' Mu'awiyyah's 630–632 service as scribe, i.e. about 628 (p. 183)."
6. "Every specialist verdict" turns a majority into unanimity; "Both sides agree" claims more than the book concedes

Report text (line 180): "Before 2013, every specialist verdict our agents could open treats the long covenant texts as later compositions, not 7th-century documents. Since 2016 a small group, chiefly Ahmed El-Wakil and Ibrahim Zein, has defended them in peer-reviewed venues. Both sides agree that no original survives; the dispute is over what the late copies prove."

Problems:

  • V0 §3.6 limits the statement to the Sinai and Najran/Seert texts. It names Burckhardt, Ebers, Moritz, Scher and Hamidullah, and records Atiya (1950) as undecided.
  • The report's own tables list Atiya as "Undecided" (Sinai row) and Roggema as holding a "genuine core" (Najran row).
  • The World row names Salmasius, Renaudot and Hinckelmann as defenders. V4 §4 adds Twiss (1887: "haute ancienneté").
  • For the Persia text the report itself found "No specialist verdict ... beyond Dadoyan's".
  • Morrow does not agree that no original survives. He hopes the Sinai original "remains stored in some forgotten archive, perhaps in ... Topkapi" (p. 69), and says the Persian one "may simply have been misplaced or ... stolen" (p. 107).

Evidence: V0 §3.6; V2a §4; V3 §4B; V4 §4; book pp. 69, 107.

Replace with:

Before 2013, the modern specialist verdicts our agents could open on the Sinai and Najran texts (Burckhardt, Ebers, Moritz, Scher, Hamidullah, Mouton) treat them as later compositions, not 7th-century documents. Atiya (1950) left the Sinai question open. Early-modern scholars were divided over the World covenant: Grotius and Prideaux rejected it, while Salmasius, Renaudot and Hinckelmann accepted it. Since 2016 a small group, chiefly Ahmed El-Wakil and Ibrahim Zein, has joined Morrow in defending the covenants in peer-reviewed journals and with an academic press. Both sides agree that no original has been found; the dispute is over what the late copies prove.

7. The verdict counts cannot be reproduced; two category labels misdescribe their contents; "one in eight" uses the wrong base

Report text:

  • Line 238: "Most of the book's checkable statements hold up, but about one in eight is contradicted by reliable sources."
  • The table rows, including "Sources disagree with one another | 101", "Contradicted by reliable sources | 203" and "No reliable source found | 142".
  • Line 249: "Counts are verdict rows across the twelve fact-check reports, 1,551 in all".

Problems:

  • No file states the counting rule, and the figures do not reproduce.
    • The scratchpad's count_verdicts.py, run on the current reports, gives 1,728 rows: Consistent 815, Minor 155, Disputed 99, Inconsistent 181, Unverified 128, Opinion 80. Another 270 rows are unclassified, including all 81 of V2a, whose verdicts are letter codes (C/MD/I/D/U/O).
    • Two other rules (first verdict term in a Verdict column, or bold verdicts only) gave 1,710 and 1,456 rows.
    • None gives 860 / 160 / 101 / 203 / 142 / 85 = 1,551.
  • The labels do not match the categories.
    • The ledger classifier (scratchpad/ledger_script.js, lines 3–10) puts "partly / partially / mixed" verdicts in the same bin as "disputed". That bin is labelled "Sources disagree with one another", but "partly consistent" is a different finding.
    • The "unverified" bin includes "not checked", "n/a" and "no date", which is not the same as "No reliable source found".
    • The "Contradicted" bin includes rows where the book contradicts itself (e.g. V1a/V7 self-contradiction rows), not only outside sources.
  • "One in eight of the book's checkable statements".
    • 203 / 1,551 = 13%, about one in 7.6, and that base includes opinions and unverified items, which are not checkable.
    • Among checkable verdicts (1,551 − 85 − 142 = 1,324), 203 is 15%, about one in 6.5.
  • "Twelve" reports is right only if V0 is excluded, but line 388 says "Thirteen research agents".

Replace:

  • Line 238, first sentence: "Most of the book's checkable statements hold up. About 13% of all verdict rows (203 of 1,551), or 15% once opinions and unverified items are set aside, found the book contradicted, by outside sources or by its own pages."
  • Table labels:
    • "Disputed among sources, or only partly consistent | 101"
    • "Contradicted (by sources or by the book's own pages) | 203"
    • "Unverified (no source found, or not checked) | 142"
  • Line 249: "Counts are verdict rows in the twelve fact-check reports that have verdict tables (V1a–V7c; V0 covers reception), 1,551 in all, classified by the first verdict word in each row; a claim checked in two reports counts twice."
  • Before publishing, re-run the count with that stated rule and replace any figure that changes.
8. "Confirmed by the fact-check" and "re-checked by the audit" are claimed for more items than were checked

Report text:

  • Line 238: "Each item below was confirmed by the fact-check, and the 26 most serious were re-checked by a second, independent audit."
  • Line 384: "The 26 most serious findings were then re-checked by an independent audit: 23 were confirmed and 3 partly confirmed, and the corrections are reflected above."

Problems:

  • There were two audits, not one (A1–A13 and B1–B13). The report's own line 389 says "Two further agents".
  • The 26 audited findings are not "the 26 most serious". They include life dates (B10) and reviews (B11).

  • "Confirmed by the fact-check" is not true of every item:

    • #72 contradicts V7a rows 15 and 98, which rate the book's dates "Consistent".
    • #8 and #18 are rated "Minor difference" (V3 row C3-7; V1b row T98).

    • B8: the ages are rounded (Watt), and Ibn Ishaq himself does not put Muhammad in the Fijar war. See item 26.
    • B6: the poisoner was the wife of a Nadir man. See item 33.

Evidence: AUDIT_A and AUDIT_B summary tables; V3, V1b, V4 and V7a rows as cited.

Replace:

C. Verdicts stronger than the evidence

D. The book's own concessions, and the strongest evidence for its side, left out

13. Errors #1 answers the book's weakest explanation and leaves out its main one

Report text: "| 1 | Impossible witnesses can be explained by later additions to the lists, by re-issue of the covenants, or by dictation in the Year of Delegations (630–31) | No list fits any single date in the Prophet's life. ..."

Problem:

  • "No list fits any single date" rebuts the re-issue and Year-of-Delegations explanations. It does not rebut later addition.
  • Later addition is the explanation the book itself favours:
    • p. 85: "In all probability ... both the dates, the name of the scribe, and those of the witnesses were added at a later time".
    • p. 174: the signatories were "attached posthumously".
    • p. 353: "appended ... centuries after the fact".
  • That is a major concession, and the report uses it against the book in #89 while ignoring it here.
  • The pages for the Year-of-Delegations (p. 327) and re-issue (p. 328) arguments are not cited.

Evidence: OCR pp. 85, 174, 327–328, 353; V6a §4.1 and §4.3 point 1.

Replace the "book says" cell with: "The impossible witnesses are explained as later additions ('in all probability ... the dates, the name of the scribe, and those of the witnesses were added at a later time', p. 85; 'appended ... centuries after the fact', p. 353), as the result of repeated re-issue (pp. 85, 328), or by a single dictation in the Year of Delegations, 630–31 (p. 327)".

Append to the sources cell: "Neither re-issue nor a single dictation fits these lists. The later-addition explanation, which the book itself favours, concedes that the lists, dates and scribes are not original, so the body of each text has to be dated on other evidence."

Pages: "pp. 85, 115, 147, 174, 205–217, 236, 300, 327–328, 353".

14. Errors #11 and the Assyrian row present points the book itself makes as findings against it, and overstate the specialists

Report text:

  • #11: "The Assyrian covenant dates from about 628 and is an independent witness | Its own colophon reads "4th year of the Hegira". It calls itself a translation, and its scribe, date and witness order match the World covenant printed in 1630".
  • Covenant row: "It calls itself a translation and matches the World covenant family."

Replace:

  • #11, "book says": "The Assyrian covenant dates from 'two years before' Mu'awiya's 630–632 service as scribe, i.e. about 628 (p. 183). The book treats it as a separate charter, while allowing that the Assyrians may have adopted the Sinai text (p. 177)."

Its scribe, date formula and witness order match the World covenant printed in 1630, a comparison the book does not make. (The book notes that the text opens 'The translation of the holy messenger's treaty', p. 178.)"

Report text:

  • "Dated 4 AH; found by Scaliger c. 1627–28; BnF MS Arabe 214 (1538) is "no question" its source; reprinted many times"
  • "Mu'awiya (Muslim from c. 630) as scribe and Hamza (killed 625) as a witness have been flagged as anachronisms since Prideaux (1698)"

Replace:

16. Persia: the book's verdict is understated, its strongest claims are left out, and the 1881 find is credited only against the critic

Report text:

  • Six-covenants table: "Open: authenticity "cannot be disproved" (p. 107)"
  • Covenant row: "Dated 4 AH; known only from Arpee's 1946 English text; original missing; "cannot be disproved""

Problems:

The 8th-century evidence the book cites does not mention this document. ..." Then apply item 2's fix to the Arpee sentence.
17. Najran row: the scholars' positions are characterised beyond what the sources support

Report text: "Later Christian composition: Scher, Cahen, Hamidullah, Wood. Christian-written but with a genuine core: Roggema. Authentic: El-Wakil"

Problems:

Christian-written but 'not ... an absolute forgery': Roggema (seen in a snippet only). Sympathetic but conceding the witness problems: Zein and El-Wakil (2020). Authentic: El-Wakil (2016), Morrow."

18. Sinai row: the book's concession and the limits of the Topkapı check are left out

Report text:

  • "A witness, Abu Hurayra, became Muslim only around 7 AH."
  • "... and no source checked places the Sinai original there"
  • "Authentic: the monastery's tradition, Morrow, El-Wakil."

Problems:

  • The book concedes the list was "in all probability" added later (p. 85).
  • Topkapı's own website could not be reached (AUDIT_A A9: "Confirmed as far as checkable").
  • No Sinai-specific statement by El-Wakil is in the files.

Replace:

  • "A witness, Abu Hurayra, became Muslim only around 7 AH; Morrow concedes the list was 'in all probability' added later (p. 85)."
  • "... and no source checked places the Sinai original there (Topkapı's own website could not be reached)."
  • "Authentic: the monastery's tradition, Morrow; El-Wakil (on the covenants generally)."
19. Armenian row: the book is misquoted, and Saladin and Thomson are overstated

Report text:

  • "Given to Patriarch Abraham I (638–669), who "had two full years" with the Prophet". The Timeline (line 70) and #13 use the same paraphrase.
  • "Saladin's 1187 charter is genuine and is the earliest datable trace of the claim"
  • "Sanjian ("fabricated"), Thomson and Azarya treat the charters as later"

Problems:

  • The book's words (p. 191) are: "Since he was Patriarch from 638 to 669 CE, he had two full years in order to obtain a firman or covenant from the Prophet Muhammad". The 638–669 dates are quoted from Krikorian, via Hagopian. The same paragraph also quotes a tradition dating the visit to 626.
  • Saladin's charter: Sanjian says it "has all the earmarks of being authentic" (V5 row T78). The report states it as fact.
  • Thomson deals with the Armenian chroniclers' pact about "the land of Armenia", not the Jerusalem charters (V5 §4.2).

Replace:

  • Claims cell: "Given to Patriarch Abraham I, whose term the book gives as 638–669 (after Krikorian) and who, it says, 'had two full years in order to obtain a firman or covenant from the Prophet' (p. 191). The book also quotes a tradition dating the visit to 626."
  • Evidence cell: "... Saladin's 1187 charter, which Sanjian judges to have 'all the earmarks of being authentic', refers to pacts of the Prophet, 'Umar and 'Ali, and is the earliest datable trace of the claim."
  • Scholars cell: "Sanjian ('must have been fabricated') and Azarya treat the Jerusalem charters as later; Thomson explains the Armenian chroniclers' prophetic pact (about Armenia) as a later attribution. No peer-reviewed defender of a 7th-century origin was found."
  • Timeline line 70 and #13: quote the book's words as above. The verdict "Impossible" is fair for the arithmetic as printed.
20. The "Points in the book's favour" paragraph leaves out the strongest pro-authenticity evidence the files contain

Report text (line 217): "Points in the book's favour also stand. Moritz, a sceptic, records that a late Mamluk decree (Qansuh al-Ghawri, r. 1501–1516) already cites letters of protection of the Prophet, and Thenaud saw a handprinted privilege at the monastery in 1512. ..."

Problems:

  • "Thenaud saw": Thenaud reports that the mosque holds the privileges (V2a row C13 and §4: "reports"). The report treats Affagart's similar account more strictly ("He relays what the monks told him").
  • "The earlier Fatimid decrees": Moritz cites one Fatimid decree (AUDIT_B B13).
  • The decree's date (911 or 921 AH = 1505 or 1515) is known and should be given.
  • These points from the files are missing:
    • the genre is real (Ayla, Maqna; V6a §4.2 point 1);
    • the 1538 manuscript shows the World text circulating about 90 years before Scaliger (V4 §4; the book argues this on p. 145);
    • Bar Hebraeus independently reports a Najran/Isho'yahb diploma with a parallel tax structure (V3 §4B; V4 §4; V5 §4.1);
    • Saladin's 1187 charter refers to the Prophet's pact and is accepted as authentic by Sanjian (V5 §4.2);
    • Moritz thought an Ottoman removal of an "original" "möglich, sogar wahrscheinlich" (V6a §4.2 point 2);
    • El-Wakil argues it is "highly unlikely" that different communities forged the same wording (V0 §3.4; V6a §4.2 point 3);
    • even sceptics such as Döllinger and Gieseler accepted that Muhammad gave some Arabian Christians letters of protection (V4 §4).

Replace with:

Points in the book's favour also stand. Thenaud reported in 1512 that the monastery mosque held the Prophet's privileges with his handprint, as the book itself argues (pp. 19, 192). Moritz, a sceptic, records a decree of Qansuh al-Ghawri (911 or 921 AH, i.e. 1505 or 1515) that already cites "letters of protection of the Prophet", and he thought an Ottoman removal of an "original" "possible, even probable". So some claimed prophetic letter was in use before the Ottoman conquest; the earliest (Fatimid) decree refers only to "the old treaties". Written prophetic agreements with non-Muslim communities are a real genre (Ayla, Maqna). Hamidullah accepts that a short treaty with Najran existed, and even 19th-century sceptics such as Döllinger and Gieseler accepted that Muhammad gave some Arabian Christians letters of protection. The World text was circulating by 1538, about 90 years before Scaliger (p. 145). Bar Hebraeus reports a diploma for the Church of the East with terms parallel to the Seert text, and Saladin's 1187 charter to the Armenians, accepted as authentic even by Sanjian, already refers to a pact of the Prophet. El-Wakil argues that different communities are "highly unlikely" to have forged the same wording independently. None of this dates the surviving texts to the 7th century, and the monastery maintains the traditional account.

E. Quotations from the book's sources presented as the author's own claims

26. "Twenty-five years of silence" (Timeline line 46, Errors #12) overstates the sources and leaves out the book's concession

Report text:

Replace the #12 sources cell with: "The early sira places him at the Fijar war and the Hilf al-fudul at about 20 (Ibn Sa'd quotes him: 'I attended it with my uncles and shot arrows'; Ibn Hisham gives 14–15), at his marriage at 25, and at the rebuilding of the Ka'ba at 35. Fact-check reports

Reception of the book and the wider scholarship

86 table rows · source file V0_reception_and_literature.md

V0: How Morrow's book was received, and what the wider scholarship says about the "Covenants of the Prophet"

The book under check: John Andrew Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (Angelico Press / Sophia Perennis, 2013). Compiled: 2026-11-10.

0. How this report was made, and how to read it

What counts as verified. A claim counts as verified only if it came from a page or file that was actually opened. That means a WebFetch, or a PDF, OCR or JSON file downloaded and read with a tool. Search-engine snippets are never used as evidence. Where only a snippet was available, the claim is marked [snippet only – not verified].

Work done by sub-agents. Two research sub-agents worked under the same rules, and their findings are marked [SA1] or [SA2]:

  • [SA1] covered the pre-modern Najran sources and Hamidullah.
  • [SA2] covered the older European scholarship on the Sinai covenant and on Sionita's 1630 edition.

Their URL lists are reproduced in the Sources section. I re-opened six of their key claims myself and confirmed each one:

  • Addai Scher's footnote "certainement apocryphe" (Patrologia Orientalis 13 OCR).
  • Hamidullah's "fabrications" verdict (shamela.ws).
  • Moritz 1918's verdict and argument (archive.org OCR).
  • Prideaux 1698 on Muʿāwiya as secretary (archive.org OCR).
  • Burckhardt 1822's verdict (Project Gutenberg).
  • The monastery website's account.

Labels for kinds of source:

Label Meaning
PR Peer-reviewed journal or academic press
REV Book review in a journal
ADV Advocacy or interested party: Morrow's own sites, the Covenants Initiative, Christian apologetics sites
POP Journalism or popular writing
BLOG Blog
PRIM Primary source or early edition

Pages that could not be opened. Many publisher pages returned HTTP 403 or 429. These were Taylor & Francis/tandfonline, MDPI, ResearchGate, Academia.edu, Patheos, Reading Religion, Brill reference works, Gospel Coalition/Themelios, Angelico Press, and the Princeton catalogue (bot wall). For those items I report only what could be confirmed, often bibliographic metadata via the Crossref or OpenAlex APIs. Any content is reported secondhand, as quoted on another page that was opened.

One source deliberately not linked. SA1 read a few pages of Morrow's 2013 book in what appears to be an unauthorised scan on archive.org. I do not reproduce that link. Re-check those page references (c. pp. 94, 109–116) against a legitimate copy.

1.2 The author

1.3 The Covenants Initiative (2013)
  • Founding post. On covenantsoftheprophet.org, dated 11 Aug 2013 (updated 8 Feb 2021). It calls on "all Muslims, Sunni, Shi'ite, and Sufi" to sign. The declaration opens: "In response to the clash of barbarisms that is presently laying the world in ruins".
  • Wikipedia (Charles Upton article, used as a lead) says: "In 2013 Charles Upton conceived of The Covenants Initiative". It describes the Initiative as based on Morrow's book.

They also include Dr. Amar Sellam (Mohamed I University), who later reviewed the book for AJISS. Sources: covenantsoftheprophet.org/2013/08; jewishpost.com.

R1, Sellam (AJISS)

  • Praise: "With painstaking effort and much dedication invested in this groundbreaking work…".
  • On method: Morrow "insists on following a meticulously sustained stand of an academic investigator, one who presents both the pros and cons".
  • Overall: "an admirable case of a persuasive arguer".
  • He does not test the evidence himself.
  • Conflict of interest (documented):
    • Sellam is a listed Covenants Initiative signatory.
    • Morrow's 2015 interview thanks "Dr. Ammar Sellam" among colleagues credited in connection with the book's translations (lastprophet.info).

R2, Martelli (JSIS)

  • "If I should choose an adjective to define this book, it would be 'precious'."
  • She does not assess authenticity.
  • Conflict of interest: she is thanked in the same 2015 interview, and "Anna Maria Martellia" is a listed contributor to the 2017 volumes.

R3, Walsh

  • Recommends the book "for any serious student of Islam, interfaith relations".
  • Silent on authenticity.

R4, Castleton

  • Opens: "Until I was given the manuscript of this text for review, the possibility … had never occurred to me".
  • Retells the Sinai handprint story as fact.

R5, Mehraj ud Din

  • Calls it a "path breaking scholarly work". Criticises the author's "emotionally faithful" stance.
  • Reports that Seta Dadoyan holds that the covenant's authenticity "cannot be established", and that Morrow replies it is "not even disproved yet as well".

R6, Reynolds (First Things, Feb 2014)

  • Sinai covenant: "earliest copies" are 16th-century, "over nine hundred years after the death of Muhammad".
  • Assyrian covenant: 17th-century, "in an Islamic Persian script that did not exist in Muhammad's day".
  • "Christians of the world" covenant: also 16th-century.
  • Verdict: "Forged by Christians intent on proving to their Muslim overlords that the Prophet himself had guaranteed their well-being."
  • On Morrow: his "interest in arguing for the authenticity of these covenants is not unlike the interest of those who forged them."
  • April 2014 letters:
    • Upton argues "those who consider them largely genuine also have theirs [reasons]".
    • Reynolds replies they "have all of the traits of late medieval forgeries" and "simply cannot form a solid basis" for harmony. He says Christians forged them under "the constant threat of persecution under Islamic rule".

R7, Sanni (JMMA)

  • Secondhand, as quoted by the Pfander Center (ADV, evangelical):
    • "The covenants studied here … were largely obtained from monasteries or archival repositories, and their copying history goes back to the sixteenth through the nineteenth centuries (Father Scaliger's 1629 [1538] edition of the Treaty with Mt. Sinai Monks, and Gabriel Sionita's 1630 and Georg Nissel's 1655 exemplar of same)".
    • "…we find no evidence of pre-sixteenth century codices, even in Islamic sources (Ibn Sa'd's d. 845 alleged citation from the 'covenant' is unsubstantiated, p. 69)".
  • Wikipedia's Ashtiname article also cites Sanni for the point that classical Islamic texts never mention such documents.
  • Verify against the journal before quoting.

R8, Hussain (Islamic Studies)

  • Secondhand, from Morrow's rebuttal on Maydan (16 Oct 2019) and from FrontPage Magazine:
    • The covenants "are surprisingly not recorded in the classical Islamic sources".
    • "Four of them have no mention at all in Islamic sources".
    • They "cannot attain the status of a source of Islamic law if their authenticity is not established".
    • The handprint "shows the outer side of the hand, which is possible only if it is taken using a camera!"
    • He "could not find a single reference to primary sources of sirah throughout the book."
  • Morrow's replies:
    • "It is beyond dispute that the covenants of the Prophet are found in Muslim sources."
    • On the handprint: "That is called 'art.' It is a painting."
    • He says he cited al-Waqidi and Ibn Ishaq.
    • He says Islamic Studies would publish his rebuttal only with substantial changes, which he declined.

R9, Hunt. Snippet only: the book shows "an unfortunate measure of conceptual confusion". The documents reflect "the aspirations of those religious minorities who fell under the rule of his successors" more than the Prophet. Not verified.

2.2 Other critical and supportive public voices
  • Mark Durie, quoted in Christianity Today (Jayson Casper, "Covenantal Theology", 21 Dec 2018) (POP):
    • He calls the book "pious propaganda".
    • "I don't know of any serious scholar who believes [these texts] are genuine."
    • Christian communities likely produced the texts, and some stipulations reflect later Egyptian history.
  • Mustafa Akyol, same article: "Some experts dispute their authenticity… Yet to me, these covenants look convincing, at least in their general spirit."
  • Mustafa Abu Sway (Al-Quds University), same article: applies the rule that shorter texts are likelier authentic, and finds the covenants genuine in spirit.
  • Morrow's reply (The Muslim Post, 2 Jan 2019; ADV):
    • Durie "neither writes nor speaks like a scholar or an academic".
    • Supporting scholars "number in the hundreds".
    • "the lengthy documents are the most authentic, namely, the Qur'an and the Covenants of the Prophet".
  • Pakistan Supreme Court, Asia Bibi judgment (Oct 2018).
    • Justice Asif Khosa relied partly on the Sinai covenant, which he called "eternal and universal … not limited to [them] alone".
    • The judgment cited Morrow's 2013 book (Christianity Today).
    • The judgment text itself could not be opened (403).
2.3 Reception of the follow-up volumes, which defend the same thesis

Valkenberg on Islam and the People of the Book (2017). Wilhelmus (Pim) Valkenberg (Catholic University of America); review dated 29 Aug 2018, reprinted on covenantsoftheprophet.org. The original appears to be Reading Religion, but that page returned 403.

  • He grants "a multiple attestation (tawātur in hadith science) of such covenants".
  • But "the copies that have been preserved … are substantially younger than the originals". "It is therefore quite possible that the documents have a later origin and cannot be used as evidence".
  • "the Critical Studies of the Covenants of the Prophet are still in their infancy".
  • He objects to the "strong ad hominem flavor as happens in Morrow's first chapter" and says "Morrow tends to overstate his case".
  • "Many chapters … are just strings of endless citations".
  • Verdict: mixed.

Monferrer-Sala on Muhammad and the Christians (2025). Juan Pedro Monferrer-Sala (Córdoba), Mediterranea 11 (2026) 403–408, doi 10.21071/mijtk.v11i.18755 (PR; full PDF opened).

  • Morrow's argument "rests on several contested foundations".
  • It "conflates textual reception with historical origin: late Gharšūnī or Ottoman copies are treated as if they could decisively illuminate seventh-century practice".
  • It is "more persuasive as advocacy than as a decisive demonstration of authenticity."
  • He records that Morrow's own Sionita chapter lists "a substantial corpus of detractors (from Grotius and Bayle to twentieth-century scholars) some of whom alleged forgery".
  • Verdict: mixed. He praises the breadth but is not persuaded on authenticity.

Other reviews:

  • Negoiță on Zein & El-Wakil, JAAR 93:4 (Dec 2025) 740–743, doi 10.1093/jaarel/lfaf084. Only the extract is visible. It praises the "rigorous historiographical approach … systematically debunking the longstanding skepticism". Positive (extract only).
  • Armajani (Journal of Social Encounters 10:1, 2026, 219–221) and Themelios, both on the 2025 book: pages 403, content not verified. A Themelios snippet says the support "builds on tenuous arguments" [snippet only].
2.4 The overall pattern
  • The positive reviews (R1–R5) appeared in Islamic-studies, interfaith or regional-history venues. None of them weighs the manuscript or diplomatic evidence. At least two of the reviewers (Sellam, Martelli) were connected to Morrow's project.
  • The critical assessments come from:
    • Reynolds, a specialist in the Qurʾān and Christian–Muslim relations;
    • two Muslim academics (Sanni, Hussain);
    • for the sequels, Valkenberg and Monferrer-Sala.
  • Peer-reviewed defences after 2013 come almost entirely from one circle:
    • El-Wakil and Zein (HBKU College of Islamic Studies);
    • Morrow himself;
    • authors in an MDPI Religions collection on the Prophet's letters and covenants. The special-issue page appeared only in a snippet; MDPI returned 403.
  • I found no historian of St Catherine's or specialist in Islamic diplomatics who endorses Morrow's conclusions in a page I could open.

3. Other books and studies on these covenants

3.1 Pre-modern Muslim records of the Najran treaty vs. the long Christian "Covenant with the Christians of Najran" [SA1; key items spot-checked]

The short treaty in the early Muslim sources. The early Muslim sources preserve a short, tribute-centred treaty (ṣulḥ). Its terms:

  • Tribute: 2,000 robes (ḥulla), half in Rajab and half in Safar.
  • Loan for war in Yemen: 30 coats of mail, 30 horses and 30 camels.
  • Hospitality: lodging for the Prophet's envoys, up to about 20 days.
  • Protection: "جوار الله وذمة محمد" (the protection of God and the dhimma of Muhammad) over their persons, property, religion and churches (biyaʿ).
  • Clergy: no bishop or monk to be removed.
  • No army to tread their land.
  • Riba: usury is forbidden on pain of losing protection.

What each source contributes:

  • Abu Yusuf, Kitāb al-Kharāj (shamela.ws 26333/86–92) calls his text the copy "التي في أيديهم" (which is in their hands). Witnesses: Abu Sufyan, Ghaylan b. ʿAmr, Malik b. ʿAwf, al-Aqraʿ, al-Mughira. Scribe: ʿAbd Allah b. Abi Bakr. He also reports that ʿUmar moved them to "Najran of Iraq" after they acquired horses and weapons.
  • Abu ʿUbayd, Kitāb al-Amwāl nos. 517–519 (OpenITI text):
    • no. 517: a mursal isnad.
    • no. 518: ʿUmar expelled them because "أصابوا الربا في زمانه" (they took usury in his time). They settled at al-Najraniyya near Kufa, and ʿUthman cut 200 robes.
  • Ibn Zanjawayh, al-Amwāl nos. 732–733: nearly identical to Abu ʿUbayd.
  • Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt I:249: the same terms, adding "وبيعهم وصلواتهم" (their churches and their prayers).
  • al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-buldān (Hitti tr. 1916, ch. XIV):
    • Yahya b. Adam's copy reads "No attempt shall be made to turn a bishop from his office…".
    • Another copy ended "Written by ʿAli ibn-abu-Talib", and Yahya was "at a loss to know what to say".
  • Abu Dawud no. 3041: "لا تهدم لهم بيعة… ولا يفتنوا عن دينهم ما لم يحدثوا حدثا، أو يأكلوا الربا" (no church of theirs is to be demolished … nor are they to be pressed to leave their religion, so long as they commit no offence or consume usury).
  • Ibn Hishām / Ibn Isḥāq: the delegation and the refused mubāhala (mutual-curse challenge), but no treaty text.
  • Yaḥyā b. Ādam's own surviving Kharāj: no treaty text.

The long version: Chronicle of Seert (ed. Addai Scher, Patrologia Orientalis 13, 1919, pp. 600–623).

  • Claimed origin: the copy was made "sur un registre qui fut retrouvé en 265 [AH = 878–79 CE] à Rirmantha chez Habib le moine". Habib said it came from the caliphal library and was written on ox-hide with Muhammad's seal. (Spot-checked.)
  • What it adds to the short treaty:
    • fixed per-head tax rates (4 dirhams a year, 12 at most for the wealthy);
    • clergy exempt from tax;
    • "Aucun chrétien ne sera fait musulman par force" (no Christian is to be made Muslim by force);
    • no forced marriage, and a Christian wife keeps her faith;
    • Muslims to help "réparer leurs églises et leurs couvents" (repair their churches and monasteries);
    • extension to Christians "de Najran ou de toute autre secte" (of Najran or of any other sect);
    • praise for Christians who fought alongside him;
    • about 30 witnesses, ending "a écrit aussi Moʿawia ben Abi Sofian" (Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān also wrote).
  • No date is given in the Najran pact section (spot-checked).
  • The witness list cannot fit any single date. It includes Saʿd b. Muʿādh, Abū Hurayra and Jaʿfar b. Abī Ṭālib [SA1], with Muʿāwiya as writer. Saʿd b. Muʿādh died "shortly after the Battle of the Trench" (c. 627 / 5 AH). Abū Hurayra embraced Islam "around 7 AH (c. 629 CE)". Muʿāwiya converted at the capture of Mecca in 630 (though "some accounts" say secretly from 628). Jaʿfar was in Abyssinia for about twelve years and died at Muʿta in September 629. (Wikipedia, opened, used for standard dates.) This chronological argument is my inference. SA1 reports that Morrow (2013, c. pp. 109–116) discusses and tries to explain these witness objections.

Where the two versions conflict:

Issue Early Muslim sources Long Christian text
Tax Collective tribute in robes Per-head dirham tax
War obligations Najran lends arms and animals No Christian compelled to equip Muslims
Riba A central clause, and ʿUmar's stated reason for the expulsion Usury appears only as a vice of the Jews
Witnesses and scribe One set of names A different set
Document in use Abu Yusuf's text is the copy "in their hands" Surfaced only in 878–79, by its own account

Verdicts on the long version:

  • Addai Scher (1919), p. 602 n. 1 (spot-checked): "Ce pacte est certainement apocryphe. Il a été forgé par les chrétiens dans le but d'engager les musulmans à les épargner." (This pact is certainly apocryphal. It was forged by the Christians in order to induce the Muslims to spare them.) He adds that "Chaque nationalité chrétienne de l'Orient en conserve une copie plus ou moins différente" (each Christian nation of the East keeps a more or less different copy) [SA1]. On ʿUmar's related edict for Ishoʿyahb, p. 623 n. 1: "probablement aussi apocryphe" (probably also apocryphal) [SA1].
  • Muhammad Hamidullah, Majmūʿat al-wathāʾiq al-siyāsiyya (6th ed. 1407 AH), docs. 96–97, printed p. 180: "ولا يوجد أدنى شبهة في أن هذين النصين من الموضوعات" ("there is not the slightest doubt that these two texts are fabrications"). (Spot-checked: shamela.ws/book/23667/167.) His general criterion (p. 31) [SA1]: documents granting rights without duties, or mentioning things that did not exist in the Prophet's time, are fabrications, "كبعض العهود التي زعموا أنّ النبي … كتبها للنصارى واليهود والمجوس" (like some of the covenants they claim the Prophet wrote for the Christians, Jews and Magians). Note: Hamidullah accepts the short treaty (his doc. 94).
  • Lucas Van Rompay, Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage, "Nagran": the pact "gave rise to the creation of apocryphal documents, such as those preserved in the 'Chronicle of Siirt'" [SA1].
  • Philip Wood, "The Treaty between Muḥammad and the Christians of Najrān in the Chronicle of Seert: Negotiating the Rights of the Conquered and the Re-writing of the Past," Al-Masāq 33:2 (2021) 156–168, doi 10.1080/09503110.2021.1910782 (PR; abstract opened). The Chronicle "preserves an ʿAbbāsid-era re-imagination of the correspondence". The texts were "responses to Muslim efforts to produce consistent rules for non-Muslims in the caliphate". They "draw on knowledge of the Qurʾān and the Sīra to assert better rights for Christians."
  • Brandie Ratliff, Sinaiticus (Saint Catherine Foundation bulletin, 2008) [SA2; not peer-reviewed, written by a specialist]. The Najran letter "seems to have been produced by viziers of the Abbasid period, who were of Nestorian origin" (citing Massignon).
  • Morrow (2013), c. pp. 109–116 [SA1; unofficial scan; verify]:
    • He concedes that the "strongest argument" against the Najran covenant is that it "appears to be completely absent in the classical Islamic sources", which is why "most scholars dismiss it as dubious".
    • He replies there is "no logical reason" for Christians to forge it, and that Scher gave no proof.
3.2 The Sinai "Achtiname" and Sionita's 1630 "Testamentum": editions and pre-2013 studies [SA2; key items spot-checked]

Two different documents.

  • The Sinai patent is dated 3 Muḥarram AH 2, written by ʿAlī in the Prophet's mosque at Medina, with about 22 witnesses.
  • Sionita's Testamentum is dated the last day of the fourth month of AH 4, at Medina, with "Moauia ben-abi-Sofian" as secretary.
  • Wikipedia also says Sionita's text "is a different covenant … not a copy of the Ashtiname" (lead only).

PRIM: Gabriel Sionita, Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Mohamedem et Christianae fidei cultores (Paris: Antoine Vitré, 1630; Latin and Arabic) [SA2, archive.org BIU Santé scan].

  • Where the copy came from: "Religiosus Pater Pacificus Scaliger ex Capucinorum familia" obtained it by "felici … casu" (lucky chance) while working in "illis regionibus" (those regions). François Hotman had Sionita translate it.
  • No mention of Carmelites or Mount Carmel in the 1630 print.
  • Origin of the Mount Carmel story: Paul Rycaut, Present State of the Ottoman Empire (1668), II.2: "the original of which was found in the Monastery of Fryars on Mount Carmel". Bespier, quoted in Bayle, objected that it was "signed at Medina … and therefore could not be made in the monastery of mount [Carmel]".
  • Witnesses include "Moauia ben-abi-Sofian", "Abu-horain" and "Hamza ben-abdi-lmottaleb".
  • A Nissel reprint, Leiden (Elzevier) 1655, is shown in library catalogues [snippet only; the Princeton catalogue page was bot-blocked].

Early-modern verdicts on the 1630 text (each from an opened text):

  • Humphrey Prideaux, The True Nature of Imposture (1698), pp. 160–162 (spot-checked):
    • "Grotius rejects it as a Forgery; and good reason he had".
    • "there is another particular in it, which manifestly discovers the Forgery: It makes Moawias, the Son of Abu Sophian, to be the Secretary … whereas it is certain, that Moawias, with his Father Abu Sophian, was then in Arms against him; and it was not till the taking of Mecca … that they came in unto him".
    • Muhammad, just defeated at Uhud, was in no position to be asked for protection.
  • Bayle, Dictionary (English ed. 1734–38), "Mahomet", remarks AA–BB [SA2]:
    • Grotius: "forged, no doubt, by the Christians".
    • Salmasius: "I have no doubt of it's being genuine".
    • Hinckelmann and Rycaut accept it.
    • Hottinger "durst not determine".
  • Gibbon, Decline and Fall, ch. 50 n. 148 [SA2]: the patent "was admitted and reprobated by the opposite taste of Salmasius and Grotius… Renaudot urges the consent of the Mohametans… but Mosheim … inclines to believe it spurious."
  • Mosheim (tr. Maclaine) [SA2]:
    • On the Sinai edict: "undoubtedly, an artful piece of forgery" (citing Cantemir).
    • On the Sionita text: "whether it be genuine or spurious, it is certain that its contents were true".
  • Hamza's death: Hamza b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib "was killed in the Battle of Uhud on Saturday, 23 March 625 (7 Shawwal 3 AH)" (Wikipedia, opened). He therefore could not have witnessed a document dated AH 4, as Sionita's list has him doing. This is my inference from the opened dates.

PRIM/travel: Richard Pococke, A Description of the East, vol. 1 (London 1743), ch. XIV, p. 268ff. [SA2]

  • "The Patent of Mahomet, which he granted to the Monks of Mount Sinai; and to Christians in general".
  • 18 articles and 16 witnesses. Dated "in the second year of the Hegira, the third day of the month Machorem". Translated "from the modern Greek".
  • He repeats the tradition that Sultan Selim "took it from them, and granted them one under his own hand in the same terms".
  • He gives no verdict on authenticity. (Morrow's 2022 blog lists "Pococke (1743): authentic"; SA2 found no such statement in the text.)

J. L. Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (1822), pp. 546–47 (spot-checked, Project Gutenberg):

  • He records the monks' story: ʿAlī wrote it, and "Mohammed, who could not write" impressed his inked hand. Selim I took the original and left "a copy of the original certified with his own cipher".
  • His verdict: "I do not believe it to be an authentic document. None of the historians of Mohammed … mention his having been at Mount Sinai … and it is totally contrary to history that he should have granted to any Christians such privileges".
  • The document says it was written "in the mosque of the Prophet at Medina, in the second year of the Hedjra", addressed "to all the Christians". It states it was "copied from a fourth successive copy".
  • His conclusion: "the former [the monks' story] is a fable and the latter a forgery."

Georg Ebers, Durch Gosen zum Sinai (1872), pp. 287–88 [SA2]:

  • Agrees with Burckhardt that the copy is a "betrügerisches Machwerk" (fraudulent concoction).
  • Tischendorf heard the monk Kyrillos doubt the story.

PRIM/ADV: Anton F. Haddad, The Oath of the Prophet Mohammed to the Followers of the Nazarene (New York, 1902; 7 pp.; a Bahá'í publication) [SA2]:

  • An English translation that accepts the text as "his valid oath and covenant".
  • Its stated chain: from a Turkish copy rendered into Arabic by Naufal Effendi Naufal.
  • Its 22 witnesses include "Abou Harirat" (Abū Hurayra). Abū Hurayra became Muslim around 7 AH (Wikipedia, opened), and so could not have witnessed an AH 2 document. This is my inference.

PR: Bernhard Moritz, Beiträge zur Geschichte des Sinaiklosters im Mittelalter nach arabischen Quellen (Abh. Preuss. Akad. Wiss., phil.-hist. Kl., 1918 Nr. 4). Section "Der angebliche Schutzbrief des Propheten"; three copies edited and translated. Spot-checked in the archive.org OCR.

  • "Datierung, Stil und Inhalt beweisen jedes für sich allein schon [die Unechtheit]" (date, style and content each prove, on its own, that it is not genuine).
  • Date. Muhammad probably came into contact with Christians and Jews in the north only around the Tabūk expedition, AH 9. Moritz also observes that "unter den 47 Schreiben des Propheten, die sein Biograph Ibn Saʿd anführt, ein solches an die Sinaiten nicht vorkommt" (among the 47 letters of the Prophet that his biographer Ibn Saʿd cites, none is addressed to the Sinai monks).
  • Form. The text lacks the standard opening formula, and the speaking person shifts.
  • Style. "ganz unmuhammedanisch, bisweilen kaum noch arabisch zu nennen" (entirely un-Muhammadan, at times hardly Arabic at all).
  • Anachronisms [SA2]:
    • the Egyptian measures ardabb and qadaḥ;
    • "Sultan" as a title, not before c. 900 CE.
  • Likely date and motive. Probably composed about 900–1000, to protect the monks against persecution under al-Ḥākim (r. 996–1020). "Daß die Fälschung besonders geschickt ausgeführt sei, läßt sich nicht behaupten" (one cannot claim that the forgery was particularly skilfully done).
  • What he concedes from the archive [SA2]:
    • The Fatimid caliph al-Ḥāfiẓ's decree orders "die alten Verträge" (the old treaties) to be respected.
    • A Mamluk decree of Qanṣūh al-Ghūrī mentions "Schutzschreiben des Propheten und Urkunden der Chalifen" (letters of protection of the Prophet and documents of the caliphs).
    • A transfer of the original to Constantinople by Selim or Suleiman is "möglich, sogar wahrscheinlich" (possible, even probable).
    • The monastery's tradition that Selim visited Sinai is "sicher erfunden" (certainly invented).
    • Surviving copies are dated AH 957 and AH 968.
  • Bottom line: the claimed Prophetic letter was being invoked by the Mamluk period at the latest, and perhaps earlier. Moritz still judges the text a Fatimid-era forgery.

Aziz S. Atiya, The Monastery of St Catherine in Mount Sinai (Cairo 1950; popular booklet) [SA2]: undecided.

  • "it is said that the Prophet Mohammad granted the monks … a covenant".
  • "the Covenant of the Prophet, whether authentic or forged, was in some way or other renewed".
  • The archive holds more than 2,000 decrees (firmans); the oldest is dated 524/1130.
  • Not opened:
    • The Arabic Manuscripts of Mount Sinai (1955; lending-only). Morrow's blog labels it "authentic", which is unverified.
    • The PAPS article (1952).

Sinai archive inventories:

  • Heidemann, Müller & Rāġib, Annales islamologiques 31 (1997) [SA2] count 81 decrees in the archive: 6 Fatimid (524/1130–553/1158), 3 Ayyubid and 72 Mamluk.
  • The Mamluk decrees were published by Hans Ernst, Die mamlukischen Sultansurkunden des Sinai-Klosters (1960). This work was not opened: the Halle repository has a bot wall.
  • S. M. Stern's BSOAS studies (1960, 1966) and Fāṭimid Decrees (1964): abstract only, which is silent on the Prophet's covenant.

Heinz Skrobucha, Sinai (OUP 1966): NOT OPENED (lending-only). Morrow's 2019 lecture lists him among those who held the Ashtiname "apocryphal" (ADV, secondhand).

Historians of St Catherine's:

  • Jean-Michel Mouton (interview, Clio, 2002) [SA2]:
    • The visit story is a "légende" developed "à partir du IXe siècle" (from the 9th century onward).
    • It was one of the strategies "visant à légitimer l'existence du monastère au regard de la loi musulmane" (aimed at legitimising the monastery's existence under Muslim law).
    • His 1998 chapter was not available.
  • Brandie Ratliff (Sinaiticus 2008, n. 9) [SA2]: "Since the nineteenth century, scholars have questioned aspects of the document, particularly the list of witnesses; see Mouton, 177."

The monastery's own website (sinaimonastery.com, opened): the traditional view.

  • "According to the tradition preserved at Sinai, Mohammed both knew and visited the monastery".
  • A delegation requested protection "In the second year of the Hegira, corresponding to AD 623". He "placed his hand upon the document".
  • In 1517 Selim I "took the original letter of protection for safekeeping to the royal treasury in Constantinople", and left certified copies "each depicting the hand print".
  • The site does not mention any authenticity debate.

T. W. Arnold, The Preaching of Islam (1896/1913), and A. S. Tritton, The Caliphs and Their Non-Muslim Subjects (1930) [SA2]:

  • Neither discusses the Sinai or Sionita covenants in full-text searches.
  • Arnold on conquest treaties: "whether verbally authentic or not, they are significant".
  • Tritton lists the Prophet's Najran terms "whether historical or legendary" (p. 203). He mentions a commission from ʿAlī preserved at the monastery of Gubba the Outer and used at Baghdad (p. 83).
3.3 Twentieth-century specialists, as listed by Morrow himself

Morrow's 2019 lecture on johnandrewmorrow.com (ADV, opened) lists those who doubted the Ashtiname:

  • 20th century: "Some 20th century scholars concluded that the Ashtiname was apocryphal. They include Heinz Skrobucha, Louis Cheikho, Bernhard Moritz, the Encyclopedia of Islam, Lina Eckenstein, Ahmad Zaki Pasha, Muhammad Hamidullah, Philipp K. Hitti, A.F.L. Beeston, and Jean-Michel Mouton."
  • 21st century: "L'École pratique des hautes études, Christine Walsh, Caner, Brock, Van Bladel, and Price, Diarmaid MacCulloch, Brandie Ratliff, Pierre-Vincent Claverie, 'Aziz al-Azmeh, Andrew D. Magnusson, and Walter D. Ward."

In the same text he nonetheless asserts that in the 20th century "Most scholars, however, believed that the Ashtiname was authentic", and in the 19th "the vast majority of scholars asserted that it was authentic".

I did not open the individual 21st-century works, so their wording is unverified.

Seta B. Dadoyan, The Armenians in the Medieval Islamic World, vol. 1 (Routledge 2011). Ch. 2 §V.B is titled "The Alleged Prophet's Oath to the Armenians, and the Jerusalem Connection" (Routledge table of contents, opened). Her view that its authenticity "cannot be established" is known secondhand (R5).

3.4 After 2013: the pro-authenticity literature
Work Type Position Key claim (opened abstract or description)
Ahmed El-Wakil, "The Prophet's Treaty with the Christians of Najran: An Analytical Study to Determine the Authenticity of the Covenants," Journal of Islamic Studies 27:3 (2016) 273–354, doi 10.1093/jis/etw027 PR (OUP) Substantially authentic; forgery verdict "no longer tenable" Full abstract (OpenAlex): Morrow argued "against the accepted understanding that these are forgeries". After "a cross-comparison of all the covenants now available … using source-critical methods … it is argued that categorical dismissal of the covenants as forgeries is no longer tenable". Ends by endorsing Upton's "third foundational source for Islam". The abstract concedes that the prior consensus was forgery, and claims "not dismissible" rather than proven.
El-Wakil, "'Whoever Harms a Dhimmī I Shall Be His Foe…'", Religions 10:9 (2019) 516 PR (MDPI) The end-clause is authentic "it is highly unlikely for different non-Muslim communities to have forged this Prophetic statement". Hadith on non-Muslims reflect ʿAbbāsid maxims "back-projected … using fictitious isnāds".
Zein & El-Wakil, "Khālid b. al-Walīd's Treaty with the People of Damascus…," JIS 31:3 (2020) 295–328 PR Pro, by analogy Suggests a protective "written ordinance that originated with the Prophet".
Zein & El-Wakil, "Remembering the Covenants of the Prophet Muḥammad," Al-Shajarah 25:2 (2020), doi 10.31436/shajarah.v25i2.1140 PR Pro, but hedged The covenants held by non-Muslims "possess a great deal of parallels" to compacts in Muslim sources, and point to what "the original treaties of the Prophet would have reflected".
Zein & El-Wakil, The Covenants of the Prophet Muḥammad (Routledge 2022/23) Academic press Authentic "The authors argue that the claim of forgery is no longer tenable" through scribal conventions, "date-matching calculations", textual parallels and similar methods.
HBKU press release (16 Sep 2020) ADV/institutional Pro El-Wakil: "there are no solid academic grounds" for rejection; "a number of tests" can show copies are "faithful replicas". He concedes the originals do not survive.
Craig Considine, Religions 7:2 (2016) 15 PR (MDPI), sociology Assumes authenticity Uses the covenants "as a framework" to argue Muhammad "desired a pluralistic society".
Morrow, "…An Analysis of a Manuscript Copied by Fāris al-Shidyāq," Religions 12:9 (2021) 751 PR (MDPI) Pro, with a notable concession The 1857 "Shidyāq Covenant" copies the "Rylands Covenant," which "appears to be an Ottoman-issued document dating from the sixteenth or seventeenth century". It "could represent the missing link" between the Seert Najran text and Sionita's 1630 Testamentum.
Morrow, "The Covenants of the Prophet and the Subject of Succession," Religions 10:11 (2019) 593 PR (MDPI) Pro Mines the covenants for Shīʿī succession material.
Gayane Mkrtumyan, Religions 12:2 (2021) 138 (Matenadaran) PR (MDPI) Reception study Shows the documents "were recognized by Muslim authorities". This is not a 7th-century origin.
Halim Rane, Religions 13:9 (2022) 873 PR (MDPI) Reception study Interfaith actors' reception of the research. Rane is an Initiative signatory.
Abdalrahman Abulmajd, Religions 12 (2021) 450 (Aylah covenant) PR (MDPI) not opened Metadata only.
Tawfik K. Ibrahim, Islam v sovremennom mire 16:3 (2020) PR (Russian) Re-reads the short Najran jizya treaty Explicitly "in line with the reformist-modernist discourse".
3.5 After 2013: sceptical or critical scholarship
  • Reviews: Reynolds (2014), Sanni (2015), Hussain (2018), Valkenberg (2018) and Monferrer-Sala (2026). See §2.
  • Philip Wood (2021, PR) and Van Rompay (GEDSH). See §3.1.
  • Not scholarly; listed only for completeness:
    • Pfander Center, Jon Harris (ADV, evangelical): "The St. Catherine's covenant and its parallels are obvious forgeries". Suggests an Ottoman-era motive.
    • ECAW blog (2017, pseudonymous):
      • Morrow's translation dates the Sinai text to "the third of Muharram in the second year of the Prophet's Hegira", before Sinai was under Muslim rule (c. 640).
      • It exempts monks from a jizya that Morrow himself says "did not exist in the early days of Islam" (his p. 94, per the blog).
    • FrontPage Magazine (A. Harrod, 2021; POP/ADV): relays Reynolds and Hussain. It also quotes El-Wakil's 2017 thesis: the covenants "have until very recently been regarded as forgeries by both Muslim and non-Muslim academics" (secondhand).
3.6 Which view is the minority?

On the long covenants.

  • Before 2013, every specialist verdict I could open on the long Sinai and Najran/Seert texts was "forgery" or "apocryphal": Burckhardt, Ebers, Moritz, Scher and Hamidullah. Mouton calls the visit story legend.
  • Atiya (1950) is undecided.
  • Positive verdicts are early-modern (Salmasius, Rycaut, Hinckelmann, Renaudot) or advocacy (Haddad 1902).
  • El-Wakil's 2016 abstract itself calls the forgery view "the accepted understanding".
  • The authenticity position is therefore a minority view in the specialist literature. It has a small, active, mostly peer-reviewed group defending it since 2016.

On the short Najran treaty. The short tribute treaty in the Muslim sources is widely treated as reflecting a real agreement. Even Hamidullah, who rejects the Seert texts, includes it (his doc. 94), and Tritton lists its terms "whether historical or legendary". That treaty is not the long protective covenant that Morrow champions.

5. Where independent scholars directly contradict specific claims of Morrow's

Each item below gives Morrow's claim, the contradicting evidence, and where it comes from.

  1. Claim: most 19th- and 20th-century scholars held the Sinai covenant authentic. Morrow's 2019 lecture says "Most scholars, however, believed that the Ashtiname was authentic" (20th century), and "the vast majority" in the 19th.

    • Contradicted by El-Wakil, Morrow's own ally: the JIS 2016 abstract describes the "accepted understanding that these are forgeries".
    • Contradicted by Morrow's own list of 20th-century doubters (Moritz, Skrobucha, Hamidullah, Hitti, Beeston, Mouton, the Encyclopaedia of Islam).
    • Contradicted by the opened specialist verdicts: Burckhardt 1822, Ebers 1872, Moritz 1918, Scher 1919 (Najran) and Hamidullah.
    • SA1 also reports that Morrow's own 2013 book (c. p. 109–116, verify) concedes that "most scholars dismiss" the Najran covenant "as dubious".

  2. Claim: the Sinai patent dates from 2 AH (623) and was written by ʿAlī.

    • Moritz (1918): the date is impossible. Muhammad had contact with northern Christians only around 9 AH (Tabūk), and the style is "ganz unmuhammedanisch".
    • Burckhardt: no biography places Muhammad at Sinai, and the document's own text (Medina, AH 2, addressed to all Christians, copied from a "fourth successive copy") contradicts the monks' account.
    • Reynolds: the earliest copies are 16th-century.
    • Witness list: the Sinai list includes Abū Hurayra ("Abou Harirat" in Haddad), who became Muslim c. 7 AH. Ratliff and Mouton note that the witness list has been questioned since the 19th century. (The chronological point is my inference from standard dates.)

  3. Claim: the Prophet visited the Sinai monastery and stamped the document with his hand. The visit claim comes from monastic tradition, which Morrow repeats (see the Castleton review and Monferrer-Sala's summary of his 2025 book).

    • Burckhardt: no source records the visit; "the former is a fable".
    • Mouton: the visit story is a "légende" developed from the 9th century as a legitimising strategy.
    • Hussain: the handprint image shows the back of a hand. Morrow answers that it is "art … a painting", which concedes that the image is not a physical imprint.

  4. Claim: the covenants are found in Muslim sources. Morrow: "It is beyond dispute that the covenants of the Prophet are found in Muslim sources". Wikipedia summarises his view as the text being "replicated verbatim in numerous Islamic sources over more than a thousand years".

    • Hussain: "Four of them have no mention at all in Islamic sources" (secondhand).
    • Sanni: "no evidence of pre-sixteenth century codices, even in Islamic sources", and the Ibn Saʿd citation is "unsubstantiated" (secondhand).
    • Moritz: the Sinai letter is not among Ibn Saʿd's 47 Prophetic letters.
    • Morrow 2013 (per SA1): the Najran covenant "appears to be completely absent in the classical Islamic sources".
    • Partial support for Morrow: Moritz himself records that Fatimid and Mamluk decrees refer to old treaties and to "Schutzschreiben des Propheten" (letters of protection of the Prophet). So some claimed Prophetic protection letter was being invoked before the Ottomans. That is not evidence for the 7th-century text.

  5. Claim: the long Najran covenant (from the Chronicle of Seert) is authentic. The early Muslim treaty texts (Abū Yūsuf, Abū ʿUbayd, Ibn Saʿd, Balādhurī, Ibn Zanjawayh, Abū Dāwūd) give different terms:

    • a collective tribute of robes instead of per-head dirhams;
    • a duty to lend arms instead of an exemption;
    • riba as a core clause;
    • different witnesses.

    Specialist verdicts against it:

    • Scher (1919): "certainement apocryphe … forgé par les chrétiens".
    • Hamidullah: "لا يوجد أدنى شبهة … من الموضوعات" (not the slightest doubt … fabrications).
    • Van Rompay: "apocryphal documents".
    • Wood (2021): an "ʿAbbāsid-era re-imagination".

    The document's own story puts its appearance in 878–79 CE. Its witness list combines Saʿd b. Muʿādh (d. c. 5 AH), Abū Hurayra (Muslim c. 7 AH) and Muʿāwiya (Muslim 8 AH / 630). They could not all have witnessed it at one time; this is my inference.

  6. Claim: the 1630 "Covenant with the Christians of the World" (Sionita) is genuine.

    • Prideaux (1698), following Grotius: Muʿāwiya is named as secretary in AH 4, when he "was then in Arms against him" until the conquest of Mecca.
    • Hamza in the witness list: he died at Uḥud in 3 AH, a year before the stated date (my inference from the opened Wikipedia date).
    • Bespier (in Bayle): the text says Medina, not Mount Carmel.
    • The 1630 preface itself says only that a Capuchin "by a lucky chance" obtained a copy. It gives no provenance for the original.
    • Gibbon notes that Mosheim "inclines to believe it spurious".
    • Morrow's own 2021 article concludes that a related "Rylands" text "appears to be an Ottoman-issued document dating from the sixteenth or seventeenth century".

  7. Claim: the Assyrian covenant is authentic. Reynolds: the surviving copy is 17th-century, "in an Islamic Persian script that did not exist in Muhammad's day".

  8. Claim: the covenant with the Armenians of Jerusalem is authentic. Dadoyan (Routledge 2011) titles the section "The Alleged Prophet's Oath to the Armenians". Her view that authenticity "cannot be established" is secondhand (R5).

  9. Method: later confirmations by Fatimid, Mamluk and Ottoman rulers prove authenticity, and continuous copies show accurate transmission. Morrow's 2019 lecture:

    • "It has been back dated and found to be authentic";
    • "we have complete copies … from the 16th century until the 19th century".

    Against this:

    • Monferrer-Sala: this "conflates textual reception with historical origin". Late copies cannot "decisively illuminate seventh-century practice".
    • Valkenberg: the copies are "substantially younger than the originals", so "quite possible that the documents have a later origin".
    • Atiya: renewal happened "whether authentic or forged".

  10. Method: "the lengthy documents are the most authentic." This reverses the textual-criticism principle that Mustafa Abu Sway cited ("shorter documents are likely more authentic"). In the Najran case, the shorter version is the one recorded in the earliest Muslim sources (§3.1).

  11. Claim: Pococke (1743) judged the Sinai covenant authentic. This appears in Morrow's 2022 blog list. SA2 read Pococke's chapter and found no verdict on authenticity, only a report of the tradition.

  12. Presentation of the reviews. The two journal reviews Morrow's sites promote most (AJISS and JSIS) were written by people Morrow thanks for help with the translations, one of whom (Sellam) signed the Covenants Initiative. This is not a contradiction of his historical claims, but it bears on "critically-acclaimed" (the Cambridge Scholars blurb).

V1a: Verification of the front matter and Chapter 1 (printed pp. 1–33)

Book: John Andrew Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (Angelico Press / Sophia Perennis, 2013). Input: extract/01_front_ch1a.md; book wording checked against book/chunks/01_front_ch1a.txt. Out of scope (other agents): the "People with dates" lifespan table; everything about St Catherine's Monastery and Sinai; the printing history of the Covenant with the Christians of the World (Sionita to Van Dyck). Where a page could not be opened, the item is marked Unverified and section 5 says what I tried. Wikipedia appears only as a lead and is labelled when used.

Verdict scale: Consistent / Minor difference / Inconsistent / Disputed among sources / Unverified / Opinion (not checkable).
