3. Discrepancies ranked by significance

  1. "Earliest" Fatimid confirmation in 975 (pp. 71, 73) is unsupported. The specialist editions put the earliest Sinai decrees at 524/1130 (Stern; Heidemann et al. 1997; Atiya's own 1950 booklet), and Moritz 1918 at 1134/35. Heidemann et al. warn that Atiya's 1955 inventory "fourmille" with date errors. This matters because the book's "542 years of access to the original" and "one thousand years of scholarly consensus" arguments rest on 975. In addition, no Fatimid decree I could check mentions the Prophet explicitly. The earliest explicit official reference I found is late Mamluk (Qānṣūh al-Ghawrī, 1505 or 1515; Moritz p. 4).
  2. Witness anachronisms are real and broader than the two names the book discusses. Abu Hurayra was a Muslim only from 7 AH, and Abu al-Dardaʾ from about Badr (both TDV). In addition, al-ʿAbbās fought for Mecca at Badr, after the covenant's own date (Wikipedia), and ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ came to Medina after 7 AH (TDV). The book's counter-reports (an early Meccan visit by Abu Hurayra; Abu al-Dardaʾ's conversion in 623) have no source. Separately, the book's "suspicious order" argument (Abu Bakr… Muʿawiya, p. 85) applies to the 4 AH covenants, not to the Sinai lists, which start with ʿAli and lack Muʿawiya.
  3. Cantemir's vizier misidentified (p. 72). Cantemir names Köprülüzâde (Fâzıl) Mustafa Paşa, grand vizier 1689–1691 under Süleyman II, whose 1691 cizye reform fits the episode exactly. The book substitutes Merzifonlu Kara Mustafa (d. 1683) and the dates 1663–1666 (TDV for all three facts).
  4. Misattribution of the Met 2012 catalogue entry (pp. 65, 97–98). "Griffith 63–64" is cat. no. 37 by Hieromonk Justin of Sinai (HJS), not Sidney Griffith. This affects the tray/green brocade story, the "parchment" translation, the 1858 Canea copy and the 1904 Abdul Hamid II claim. The content is quoted accurately; the authority is wrong. It also means the "independent" confirmation is in fact the monastery's own librarian.
  5. Napoleon's decree: date and meaning (p. 70). The date is 19 Dec 1798, not 8 Dec. More importantly, the text mentions neither the Prophet nor the Achtiname. Saying it "confirms the privileges … granted by the Prophet" and that Napoleon "endorsed its authenticity" is interpretation.
  6. Burckhardt (pp. 68, 81–82). Burckhardt saw the Selim-certified copy in the Sinai convent at Cairo, not a display copy at the monastery. The link to the 1800/01 scroll is the author's assumption.
  7. The Süleyman hypothesis (p. 69) is presented as new, but Moritz 1918 made it, from copies dated 957 and 968 AH. Moritz also reports that tradition said "Selim or Süleyman". The claim "every authority has accepted 1517" (p. 68, citing Ratliff) is therefore wrong. Ratliff only repeats the tradition, and the explicit year 1517 appears in print only from Arundale 1837 / Géramb 1840 among the sources I opened.
  8. Moritz's base text vs the "display copy of 1800/01" (p. 97). Moritz edited from copies of 957 AH, 968 AH and an undated Cairo copy, not from an 1800/01 display copy. His apparatus also shows variants, including in the witness list, which contradicts "identical in content" (pp. 68, 74).
  9. Ratliff misrepresented (p. 81). She never links ʿAbd al-Masīḥ to the Achtiname.
  10. Affagart overstated (p. 68). He relays what the monks said and neither saw nor called it the original. On the other hand, Thenaud (1512), whom the book does not use, independently reports the same handprinted privilege in the mosque five years before 1517. This helps date the document's existence to before the Ottoman conquest; it says nothing about its authenticity.
  11. Ayyubid dates 1201/02 and 1210/11 do not match the edited decrees (592/1195, 595/1199, 609/1212-13; plus 571/1176 in Berlin).
  12. Calendar slips. "Gregorian" for a Julian date (p. 83). "625 CE = 2nd–3rd year" (p. 70). The monastery's own 2013 "AD 626", which the book reproduces without comment and the monastery has since corrected to 623. Mauchin's "1 August 622" in Ch. 8 texts II–III, which is a year off.
  13. Material and seal unanimity overstated (p. 75). "All ancient sources" do not agree. Sources variously say paper, parchment, gazelle or antelope skin, or leather from Ṭāʾif, and hand or fingers.
  14. "Fatimid school" fatwas (p. 71) have no support in the Atiya passage the book quotes.
  15. Minor: "1134" vs "1135" for the al-Ḥāfiẓ firman (Moritz vs Stern; probably the same document). Hobbs's publisher is given as "University of Austin Press".

4. Scholarly assessment of authenticity (both sides)

What the independent evidence establishes (common ground).

  • Muslim protection. From 524/1130 at the latest, Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman authorities repeatedly issued decrees protecting the monastery: 81 medieval decrees survive (Heidemann et al. 1997), and many Ottoman ones. The 1130s al-Ḥāfiẓ firman already appeals to "old treaties" (Moritz p. 4; Justin, Met p. 51).
  • Explicit references to the Prophet. Explicit reference to a prophetic letter appears in the late Mamluk decree of Qānṣūh al-Ghawrī (911/1505 or 921/1515) and in Ottoman decrees of 926–931 AH (Moritz pp. 4–5).
  • European reports. Thenaud (1512) and Affagart (1533/34) report a handprinted privilege kept in the monastery's mosque.
  • Surviving copies. All surviving copies are Ottoman-era or later. The oldest dated is 957 AH/1550 (Moritz). Specialists who discuss the text agree that the original is lost or missing.

Case for authenticity, or for a copy of a lost genuine original.

  • Who holds it. The monastery holds it as tradition (website: delegation, handprint, Selim's certified copies), and so does Morrow (2013).
  • Morrow's strongest arguments:
    • Late copies do not by themselves date a text, and the scribal notes describe a chain of copies.
    • Muslim rulers recognised the privilege continuously, across Sunni and Shiʿi dynasties.
    • The 1130s firman calls the agreements "old".
    • Genuine prophetic letters of protection to Christian and Jewish communities exist as a genre, e.g. Ayla and Maqnā.
    • Dates and witnesses may be later scribal additions to a genuine core.
  • Descriptive treatments. Hieromonk Justin and Helen Evans (Met 2012) present the Achtiname descriptively as a document "dated to the second year of the hijra" or "given … in the first years of the Muslim advance", without discussing authenticity. These are monastery-affiliated or catalogue framings rather than critical arguments.
  • Qualified "recognition" (not authenticity). Atiya (1950) expressly leaves the question open: "whether authentic or forged". Stanley (1856) thought the visit "not impossible".
  • Weakness of this side. No specialist source I opened argues for a 7th-century date on documentary, palaeographic or linguistic grounds. The pro-authenticity case rests on tradition, on continuity of recognition (which proves acceptance, not origin), and on analogy.

Case for a later composition.

  • Burckhardt (1822). No Muslim historian places Muhammad at Sinai, and the privileges (e.g. Muslims helping to rebuild churches) are "contrary to history". The document contradicts the monks' own story: it says it was written at Medina, is addressed to all Christians, and states that the original is lost. He calls the story "a fable" and the document "a forgery".
  • Moritz (1918), the fullest philological critique.
    • Content: privileges without reciprocal duties, and tax self-assessment unparalleled in Muslim practice.
    • Sinai is not named, and clauses on Christian wives and military service do not fit a monastery.
    • Egyptian measures (ardabb, qadaḥ) point to an Egyptian origin.
    • The title "Sultan" became official only in 334/945.
    • Vulgar or medieval orthography.
    • Conclusion: composed c. 900–1000, possibly under al-Ḥākim (996–1020), outside the monastery, to protect Egyptian Christians and monks; "not particularly skilful".
  • Scher & Griveau (PO 13, 1919), on the sister document (the Najran pact of 878). "Certainement apocryphe", forged by Christians to induce Muslims to spare them, with each Eastern Christian community keeping its own variant.
  • Mouton (1998, cited by Ratliff 2008 and by Morrow).
    • Anachronistic witnesses (Abu Hurayra, Abu al-Dardaʾ).
    • A Hijri-year date written before the Hijri era existed (introduced under ʿUmar c. 637/638).
    • "Nothing original": derived from the 878 Najran letter, which Massignon attributed to Nestorian-origin Abbasid viziers (Banu Makhlad).
    • In his popular article, Mouton treats the Prophet's visit as a monastic legitimising discourse from the 9th century.
  • Ratliff (2008). Reports the tradition and notes the close resemblance to the Najran letter and long-standing doubts about the witness list. She is cautious and does not accuse anyone.
  • TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi ("Ahidnâme", M. Fayda, 1988), the standard Turkish Islamic reference. "Bazı hıristiyanlar Hz. Peygamber'e nisbet edilen ahidnâmeler de uydurmuşlardır. Bunların en meşhuru … Saint Catherine Manastırı'nın ahidnâmesidir" ("Some Christians fabricated covenants attributed to the Prophet; the most famous is that of St Catherine's").
  • Additional internal evidence I checked. The witness list includes people who were not Muslims in Medina in Muharram 2 AH: Abu Hurayra, Abu al-Dardaʾ, al-ʿAbbās and ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr (A8, A10, A14).
  • Ottoman-era doubts. Köprülüzâde Mustafa Paşa (1689–91) called the "whole Diploma" a forgery, though the Sinai monks kept their exemption (Cantemir p. 169). Cantemir himself calls the instrument "true or forged" and the origin story "fabulous" (p. 168). Moritz suggests Süleyman may have made the original disappear out of suspicion.

Neutral summary.

  • The scholarly literature I could open (Burckhardt, Moritz, PO editors, Mouton via Ratliff, TDV) treats the Achtiname as a later composition. Proposed dates range from the 9th–10th century (Moritz; Mouton's derivation from the 878 Najran letter) to "some time before the 12th-century decrees".
  • The monastery and Morrow regard it as a copy of a lost genuine original.
  • What is securely documented is narrower:
    • a monastic tradition and a handprinted privilege attested by 1512;
    • centuries of Muslim protection, though explicitly tied to a prophetic letter only in late Mamluk and Ottoman decrees;
    • copies from 1550 on.
  • None of this proves composition in 623. The internal anachronisms remain unanswered except by the hypothesis that dates and witnesses were added later, a hypothesis Morrow himself adopts (p. 85).

5. Topkapı: what can be sourced

  • No source I could open says that the Sinai Achtiname (original or copy) is held, catalogued or displayed at Topkapı Palace.
    • The official Topkapı page of the Millî Saraylar (National Palaces) administration does not mention it. Topkapı has been attached to that administration since Presidential Decree no. 44 of 6 Sep 2019. The page describes the Has Oda / Mukaddes Emanetler Dairesi, called the Hırka-i Saâdet Dairesi after the relics were brought under Yavuz Sultan Selim (https://www.millisaraylar.gov.tr/Lokasyon/2/topkapi-sarayi).
    • The TDV articles "Mukaddes Emanetler" (2020) and "Mukaddes Emanetler Dairesi" (2020) do not mention it either. Their list of the Prophet's letters ("nâme-i saâdetler") in the collection names only four: to al-Muqawqis (inv. 21/174), al-Mundhir b. Sāwā (21/397), Musaylima (21/169) and al-Ḥārith b. Abī Shamir (21/674) (https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/mukaddes-emanetler ; https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/mukaddes-emanetler-dairesi).
    • Nor does the TDV "Hırka-i Saâdet" (1998) article.
  • The TDV "Ahidnâme" (1988) says only that Selim "brought it to Istanbul" and sent a translated copy back. It says nothing about where the original is today.
  • Moritz (1918) says the original "has disappeared". Tradition put it in the "Staatsarchiv von Konstantinopel".
  • Practical for a visitor. The Sacred Relics rooms (Third Court) display the relics named above, including the letter to al-Muqawqis. There is no sourced basis for expecting to see a Sinai Achtiname there. The official page (as fetched 10 Nov 2026) gives the ticket office as 09:00–17:00 and says the palace is closed on Tuesdays; check before going.
  • Side note. A Fatimid decree of the Sinai monastery (al-Ḥāfiẓ, Stern no. 4, 529/1135) was found by Moritz in 1910 at the monastery's metochion in Balat, Istanbul (Moritz p. 5 n.; Heidemann n. 6; PGP 41383). Its present location was not determined.
  • Not checked. The Topkapı museum's own domain (topkapisarayi.gov.tr) did not resolve from this environment, and the web-search quota was exhausted. So I could not search Turkish press or the Topkapı library catalogue for "Sina ahidnamesi". An inquiry to the palace library (Topkapı Sarayı Müzesi Kütüphanesi) would be the way to settle it.

6. Items not checked, and why

  • Atiya, The Arabic Manuscripts of Mount Sinai (1955). archive.org lending-only (download 401; search-inside unavailable). Its decree list (p. 26), the copy table (pp. 32–35, 80) and the quotes on pp. xviii, xxix–xxxi were checked only indirectly (Atiya 1950; Heidemann; LOC descriptions via Morrow's site).
  • Ernst (1960, Mamluk decrees) and Schwarz (1970, Ottoman decrees). Digitised at ULB Halle, but behind a bot-check; not circumvented. So the Mamluk years (E4), the Ottoman end-dates (E5–E7) and Selim's firman (C17) are unverified.
  • Hobbs, Mount Sinai (1995) and Skrobucha, Sinai (1966). archive.org lending-only. Skrobucha's summary was checked against Moritz directly; Hobbs only via Ratliff.
  • Mouton, "Les musulmans à Sainte-Catherine…" (1998). No online copy found. Checked via Ratliff's notes, Mouton's Clio article and the PO 13 edition.
  • Stern, "A Fāṭimid decree of the year 524/1130" (BSOAS 1960) and Fatimid Decrees (1964). Not openable. Used the Princeton Geniza Project records (which reproduce Stern's editions and dates) and Heidemann et al.
  • Tomadakis, Digbassanis, Manafis (eds.), Sinai: Treasures (1990); Nektarios 1980; Papamichalopoulos 1932. Not found online.
  • Library of Congress item pages (Sinai Arabic MSS 695/696, Arabic Firmans reels). HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and curl. Used Morrow's site's description (advocacy source; flagged).
  • Van Egmont & Heyman (1759), Morison (1704), M.L.M.D.C. Jeux d'esprit (1697), Fazakerley (1811 visit), Le Figaro 1986, Oumanetz/Volkoff, Davenport, Laborde's 1403 treaty, Champdor. Not located in open full text within the time available.
  • Sanni (2015) review in JMMA. Paywalled. Known only via Wikipedia (lead only).
  • Feridun Bey, Münşeât-ı Selâtîn. Listed in the TDV bibliography, and Morrow's site says it contains the Arabic Sinai text. If so it would be a c. 1575 attestation. Not checked.
  • Moritz's personal and political biography. Out of scope (other agents).
  • The Met's own website. Returned HTTP 429. The catalogue was read from the full scan on archive.org, image pages viewed directly.
  • Web-search quota. Exhausted partway through; later discovery was limited to direct URL fetches and archive.org's catalogue API.

Fact-check reports

Sinai: the monastery, mosques and travellers

135 table rows · source file V2b_sinai_monastery.md

V2b: Sinai / St Catherine's Monastery: verification report

Book: John Andrew Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013). Scope:

  • Extract 01, themes J, K and L, with the matching timeline rows and inconsistencies (book pp. 8–25 [PDF 31–48]).
  • Extract 03 (ch. 2): only the monastery's general history, the mosque, the Jabaliya, the eagle legend and early legends, and Napoleon. The Achtiname's documentary history is excluded (another agent covers it).

How to read citations:

  • Book pages are given as "p. M [PDF N]". For ch. 2, PDF = printed + 25.
  • Every verdict rests on a page or full text I actually opened. URLs are in the last column and in section 6.
  • Archive.org scans were read through their full-text (_djvu.txt) files. OCR spelling is reproduced in quotations; I normalised the long s ("ſ") only.
  • Wikipedia is used only for uncontroversial dates and is labelled "(Wikipedia)".

Calendar conversions are my own.

  • Hijri dates use the tabular Islamic calendar (epoch checked: 1 Muharram 1 AH = 16 July 622 Julian). Accuracy is ±1–2 days.
  • French Republican dates: 1 vendémiaire an VII = 22 Sept 1798.

Research limits that affected this report:

  • The session's web-search quota ran out partway through. Some items could not be located and are marked Unverified, with what I tried.
  • Hobbs, Mount Sinai (1995) is lending-restricted on archive.org, and the search-inside request returned 403.
  • Britannica, Encyclopaedia Iranica, the Guardian and Church Times returned 403 or blocked automated access.

Verdict scale: Consistent / Minor difference / Inconsistent / Disputed among sources / Unverified / Opinion / Tradition (the book reports it correctly as tradition).

1. Verification table

A. Monastery foundation and general history
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
A1 The monastery's current structure was built under Justinian (r. 527–565), "in the years immediately before the birth of Muhammad in 570" (p. 15 [PDF 38]). Established by Justinian "in the middle of the 6th century" (p. 22 [PDF 45]). Consistent (exact years disputed, see T1) Procopius, Buildings V.8: Justinian "built them a church which [they] dedicated to the Mother of God", placed "not on the mountain's summit, but much lower down", and "at the base of the mountain … a very strong fortress".<br>Michigan (Kelsey Museum): the roof beams honour Justinian and the "late Empress" Theodora; "Theodora died in 548 and Justinian in 565, so the church was completed between those years."<br>Monastery site: "The great basilica of the Transfiguration was begun in AD 542, and completed nine years later". Inscription: "For the memory and repose of our departed Empress Theodora."<br>Burckhardt (1822, p. 545): an Arabic gate inscription says Justinian built it "in the thirtieth year of his reign", i.e. Aug 556–Aug 557 by my computation.<br>Mouton (2002): "l'empereur Justinien (527-565)".<br>UNESCO: "founded in the 6th century".<br>Ševčenko, "The Early Period of the Sinai Monastery in the Light of Its Inscriptions", DOP 20 (1966) 255: the article exists (Crossref, doi 10.2307/1291249), but I could not open the text. penelope.uchicago.edu (Procopius); prod.lsa.umich.edu (Kelsey); sinaimonastery.com (catholicon); archive.org b22017355 (Burckhardt); clio.fr PDF (Mouton); whc.unesco.org/en/list/954
A2 The monastery is "built over the traditional site of the bush" (Atiya, p. 15 [PDF 38]). Consistent Monastery site: the basilica "incorporated the site of the original Chapel of the Burning Bush".<br>Mouton (2002): the church was built "à l'emplacement supposé du Buisson ardent". sinaimonastery.com (catholicon); clio.fr PDF
A3 Helena and the 330s (not claimed in the extract, but requested). Unverified as a date; tradition Wikipedia: the chapel was "ordered to be built by Empress Consort Helena" (it cites the Washington Post, 2012).<br>Sacred Destinations: "In the early 4th century, St. Helena … built the Chapel of the Burning Bush."<br>Mouton: Christians identified the summit "seulement au IVe siècle".<br>No scholarly source I opened dates a Helena foundation to the 330s. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Catherine%27s_Monastery; sacred-destinations.com; clio.fr PDF
A4 UNESCO listing 2002 (requested; not a book claim). Reference UNESCO WHC 954, "Saint Catherine Area": "Date of Inscription: 2002". Criteria (i)(iii)(iv)(vi); 60,100 ha. whc.unesco.org/en/list/954/
A5 St Catherine's body lay on Mount Catherine "for three hundred years, until it was moved to the monastery established by Emperor Justinian" (p. 22 [PDF 45]). "Rested three centuries" (p. 21 [PDF 44]). Disputed (tradition vs. history) Monastery site: angels "bore her body to the peak … where they rested until they were translated". It gives no duration.<br>Burckhardt (1822, pp. 545–546): the monks' tradition is that the relics were found "a few years after the completion of the convent".<br>Mouton (2002): "sans doute au IXe siècle, époque où l'on découvrit le corps de la sainte".<br>Art Newspaper (2000): "the saint's bones were discovered in around 800 AD".<br>From a death c. 305, the historical estimates give c. 500 years, not 300. sinaimonastery.com/…/saint-catherine; archive.org b22017355; clio.fr PDF; theartnewspaper.com (2000)
A6 Catherine (c. 282–c. 305) was "martyred nearly 500 miles away" (p. 22 [PDF 45]). Consistent (dates); Minor difference (distance) Monastery site: "born in Alexandria towards the end of the third century"; martyred "in the early fourth century" under Maxentius.<br>Great-circle distance Alexandria (Wikidata Q87: 31.1975 N, 29.8925 E) to the monastery (UNESCO: N28°33'22" E33°58'31") is ≈491 km / 305 miles (my computation). "Nearly 500" matches km, not miles. sinaimonastery.com/…/saint-catherine; wikidata Q87; UNESCO 954
A7 Christians first placed Sinai at Serbal (4th c.), relocated it in the 6th c., and "only in the 15th century" identified Mount Horeb / Jebel Musa as Sinai (p. 22 [PDF 45]). Inconsistent (the 15th-century claim) Mouton (2002): the summit "fut identifié seulement au IVe siècle de notre ère par les chrétiens, comme l'endroit où Moïse reçut les Tables de la Loi".<br>Monastery site (Holy Summit): "the Emperor Justinian ordered the construction of a three-aisled basilica at the peak of Sinai".<br>Procopius (6th c.) already calls the mountain "Sina".<br>The Serbal claim was not checked. clio.fr PDF; sinaimonastery.com/…/holy-summit; penelope.uchicago.edu
A8 The Jabaliyyah are "the Arab inhabitants of Mount Sinai" (p. 15 [PDF 38]). Their origin was requested. Consistent; origin is tradition Burckhardt (1822, p. 545), from an Arabic document kept by the monks: Justinian "sent from Constantinople some slaves, natives of the shores of the Black sea, to officiate as servants in the convent".<br>Mouton (2002): "La tradition, savamment entretenue par les moines, voulait que l'empereur Justinien ait envoyé … une centaine de militaires avec leur famille. Ces serviteurs … prirent le nom de Jabâliyya", and their descendants have been Muslim for centuries.<br>Art Newspaper: "the Jabaliya, claim to be their direct descendants". archive.org b22017355; clio.fr PDF; theartnewspaper.com
A9 Jabali tradition: Catherine became a Muslim in early Islamic times and was beheaded by her father (p. 22, Hobbs). Unverified Hobbs is not accessible (see §5). —
A10 "By 1479 CE … the Monastery … was temporarily abandoned as a result of the fall of the Byzantine Empire" (p. 23 [PDF 46]). Inconsistent / Disputed UNESCO: "used for its initial function without interruption since the 6th century".<br>Bauden (2025), Der Islam 102:2, notes on the ORBi record: in 1482 "the majority of the monks of St. Catherine were compelled to seek refuge in their metokhion" at al-Tur "after attacks by the Awlād ʿAlī tribe". That is a Bedouin attack about 30 years after Constantinople fell (1453), and a partial withdrawal. whc.unesco.org/en/list/954; orbi.uliege.be/handle/2268/336438
A11 Quoting Arabic News: the minaret "was the only high tower … until the Russian Tsar gave the monastery bells … in the 17th century" (p. 18 [PDF 41]). Inconsistent (date) Mouton (2002): the minaret was the only structure above the walls "jusqu'à la construction du clocher de l'église de la Transfiguration en 1871".<br>Art Newspaper: "a campanile was erected in 1871".<br>Sacred Destinations: "bell tower was built in 1871 by one of the monks, Gregorius. It houses nine bells given by the Tsar of Russia". The Russian gift is consistent; the century is wrong. clio.fr PDF; theartnewspaper.com; sacred-destinations.com
A12 Kingsley & Awad, 5 Sept 2013: the monastery "was forced to close its doors due to the deteriorating security situation"; "in other words, the spread of the Takfiri Jihadists" (p. 25 [PDF 48]). Consistent on the closure. Minor difference on scope and dates. Opinion on the gloss. Al-Monitor (Mohannad Sabry, 4 Sept 2013): the closure began in "the first week of August 2013" and was ordered by Egyptian security authorities. The reasons were fear of an attack, a failed attempt to kidnap a monk in June, and attacks on churches.<br>Guardian text reprinted by Coptic Solidarity (12 Sept 2013): "in July, Egyptian officials asked it to close its doors", after Morsi's removal. The monastery stayed open for services, with reopening "expected … on the 13th or the 15th".<br>So the closure was ordered by the authorities, applied to visitors, and was temporary. "Takfiri Jihadists" is the author's characterization.<br>The Guardian original and its 5 Sept date could not be opened. al-monitor.com (2013/09); copticsolidarity.org (2013/09/12)
B. The two mosques
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
B1 Minbar "built in the year 1106 CE", "donated by Shahan Shah al-Afdal"; inscription naming "Abu 'Ali al-Mansur, the Imam al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah" and "Abu al-Qasim Shahan Shah", dated "Rabi I, of the year 500" (p. 18 [PDF 41]). Consistent (the inscription wording itself was not independently opened) Egyptian Ministry of Antiquities: "built in 500 AH/1106 AD during the reign of the Fatimid Caliph al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah". The minbar is "one of only three complete surviving examples from the Fatimid Period".<br>Conversion: Rabi' I 500 ≈ 31 Oct–28 Nov 1106 (Julian).<br>Wikipedia: al-Afdal's name was "Abu al-Qasim Shahanshah", and he was "vizier of the Fatimid caliphs" (1094–1121). Wikipedia also gives al-Amir as "Abū ʿAlī Manṣūr". egymonuments.gov.eg/monuments/the-fatimid-mosque/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Afdal_Shahanshah; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Fatimid_caliphs
B2 Al-Amir "ruled from 1102 to 1131" (p. 17 [PDF 40]) vs "al-Amir (r. 1101-1130 CE)" (p. 18 [PDF 41]). p. 18 Consistent; p. 17 Minor difference Wikipedia list: no. 10, al-Amir, "1101 – 8 October 1130". His predecessor al-Musta'li's reign ended 12 Dec 1101. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Fatimid_caliphs
B3 The existing mosque was built under al-Hakim's "fourth successor, Abu Ali al-Mansur, al-Amir" (p. 17). Consistent Wikipedia list: al-Hakim (no. 6, 996–1021), then al-Zahir, al-Mustansir, al-Musta'li, al-Amir (no. 10). That makes al-Amir the fourth successor. same
B4 Summit mosque built by Emir Anushtakin "during the reign of Abu 'Ali al-Mansur (r. 996-1021 CE), the tenth of the Fatimid Caliphs" (p. 16 [PDF 39], citing Mouton 181). Inconsistent (internal conflation). The summit mosque's date is Disputed. Both al-Hakim (6th caliph, 996–1021) and al-Amir (10th, 1101–1130) bore the name Abū ʿAlī Manṣūr (Wikipedia list). The reign dates are al-Hakim's; "tenth" is al-Amir.<br>Monastery site: the summit mosque "is mentioned in 11th century descriptions of the site".<br>Hobbs, as relayed by a blog citing him: a mosque "probably built in the early 12th century (between 1101 and 1130)".<br>Mouton (2002): both mosques "remontent à la période fatimide (969-1171)".<br>Anushtakin could not be verified, because Mouton 1998 (p. 181) is not accessible. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Fatimid_caliphs; sinaimonastery.com/…/holy-summit; cannundrum.blogspot.com/2015/04/…; clio.fr PDF
B5 The Jabaliyyah "believe it dates from the rule of Caliph 'Umar" (Hobbs 634-644) (p. 16 [PDF 39]). Citation error (the claim itself is consistent) The blog summarising Hobbs: the Jabaliya "believe it dates to the rule of the Caliph 'Umar (from 634 to 644)". The book's own ch. 2 gives 'Umar "(r. 634-644 CE)". "634-644" are 'Umar's regnal years, not Hobbs page numbers. cannundrum.blogspot.com/2015/04/mount-sinai-summit-mosque.html
B6 Ch. 2, p. 75 [PDF 100] (Hobbs 161): the mosque was "apparently constructed around 1106 during the reign of al-Hakim's successor, the Fatimid Caliph al-Afdal". Its purpose may have been "a device to ward off an attack by Ottoman troops". Inconsistent Al-Afdal was vizier, not caliph (Wikipedia). The caliph in 1106 was al-Amir, al-Hakim's fourth successor (B3). "Ottoman troops" around 1106 is anachronistic by the book's own chronology, which brings the Ottomans to Sinai in 1517 (p. 23). I could not check whether the slip is Hobbs's or a transcription error. Wikipedia (al-Afdal; caliph list)
B7 The common claim that monks built the mosque to appease al-Hakim (c. 1000) "is not supported by existing evidence" (p. 17 [PDF 40]). Disputed Mouton (2002) reports this version, in the conditional: "La mosquée du monastère daterait du règne du calife Al-Hâkim (996-1021). Les moines auraient eu l'idée d'aménager cet édifice pour éviter que les hommes du calife ne détruisent le monastère."<br>Egypt Independent (2016): "built by monks during the reign of the sixth Fatimid caliph".<br>Against it: Egyptian Ministry (500/1106, al-Amir); Art Newspaper ("in 1106 … the monks hurriedly converted their refectory into a mosque"). See T2. clio.fr PDF; egyptindependent.com/?p=2470513; egymonuments.gov.eg; theartnewspaper.com
B8 Original function: "originally built as a hospice for pilgrims in the sixth century" (Freeman-Grenville/Forsyth). Also built on a chapel of St Basil (Daumas/Posniakov), or a chapel converted with only the minaret new (Champdor) (p. 19 [PDF 42]). Disputed Monastery site: "Originally it had served as the monastery refectory (from the 6th century). The structure was modified in the 11th century." Crosses were found carved into the arches.<br>Art Newspaper: refectory converted in 1106.<br>Wikipedia (citing UNESCO): "converting an existing chapel".<br>Sacred Destinations (non-scholarly): "a small Crusader chapel … between 1101 and 1106". sinaimonastery.com/…/mosque; theartnewspaper.com; Wikipedia; sacred-destinations.com
B9 "Burckhardt interprets this [the AH 783 record] as proof that the mosque dates to 1381 CE; to me it implies that the mosque already existed" (p. 18 [PDF 41]). Inconsistent (misrepresents the source) Burckhardt (1822, pp. 543–544) gives the monks' tradition that the mosque was built "in the sixteenth century" under Selim. He says the tradition "is contradicted by some old Arabic records". After the AH 783 hajjis passage, he concludes: "The mosque in the convent of Sinai appears therefore to have existed long before the time of Selim."<br>He does not date the mosque to 1381. The book presents his inference as its own.<br>The quoted passage itself is accurate. The book quotes it via Manley and 'Abdel-Hakim; the primary text is Burckhardt pp. 543–544.<br>AH 783 = 28 Mar 1381–16 Mar 1382. archive.org/details/b22017355
B10 Lindsay (1837): the mosque was "Built, for the nonce, three centuries ago, when the convent was threatened by the Paynim Soldan of Egypt" (p. 17 [PDF 40]). The author: "There was, of course, no Sultan in Egypt". Lindsay's text Unverified. The author's comment is Opinion. Burckhardt (1822, p. 543) independently records the same monastic tradition: the mosque was built in the 16th century, after Selim's conquest, "to prevent the destruction of the convent".<br>Mamluk sultans ruled Egypt until 1517; the book's ch. 2 lists the Mamluks as 1250–1517. So a "Sultan of Egypt" existed before 1517. archive.org/details/b22017355
B11 Thenaud (1512), p. 72: "a Muslim mosque which was built by prior who became a Muslim when asked to assume its administration". The author infers that the Fatimids "granted him the administration of the mosque on their behalf" and that the covenant was in Muslim hands from the 12th to the 14th century (p. 19 [PDF 42]). Inconsistent (mistranslation) Thenaud, ed. Schefer (1884), p. 72: "Devant ceste église est une musquete de Mores, que fit bastir ung prieur de leans qui se rendit mammelu quant on lui demanda compte et reliquat de son administration, en laquelle sont les privilèges que Mahommet donna es caloyers, c'est assavoir immunité de tous tributz et devoirs; et sont signez de sa main, plongée en encre et assise sur ledict papier".<br>"Quant on lui demanda compte et reliquat de son administration" means "when he was asked to render account and the balance of his administration" (an audit of his management). It does not mean being asked to assume the mosque's administration.<br>Thenaud gives no date for the prior and no Fatimid link.<br>The part saying the privileges were kept in the mosque is consistent. archive.org/details/levoyagedoutreme00then
B12 Henniker: the mosque "sanctifies the place in the eyes of the Musulman"; one person may enter on the Turkish sabbath (pp. 17, 20; Henniker 224). Consistent Henniker (1823, p. 224): "The mosque, strange as it appears adjoining to a church, is necessary to the existence of this Christian foundation — it sanctifies the place in the eyes of the Mussulman … it is even allowed for one person to enter it on the Turkish sabbath". archive.org/details/notesduringavis02henngoog
B13 The Franciscan prefect's 1722 journey: "a mosque with a turret for the Turks … near the western door of the great church … immunities granted them under the hand of the Prophet Mahomet" (p. 16 [PDF 39]). Consistent Clayton (1753): the Prefetto set out "A.D. 1722". "there is one mosch with a turret for the Turks, which stands near the western door of the great church, for the preservation of which, they say, they have several immunities granted them under the hand of the prophet Mahomet." archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_a-journal-from-grand-cai_clayton-robert_1753
B14 Stanley, who "visited Saint Catherine's in 1858": the mosques were founded "in the time of the Prophet" according to "illiterate Musulmans" (p. 16 [PDF 39], "Stanley 120"). Quote Consistent. Visit date Inconsistent. Page Minor difference (edition). Stanley, Sinai and Palestine (1868 ed.), pp. 54–55: the same wording. His advertisement says: "In the winter of 1852 and spring of 1853 … I visited the well-known scenes … in Egypt, Arabia, and Syria." The book was first published in 1856, before the visit date the book gives. archive.org/details/sinaipalestinei00stan
B15 The monastery mosque was "only officially closed in 1986" (Mouton; 'Abd al-Malik). "The SCA carried out a restoration … in 1986" (Arabic News) (p. 20). Closure "in the mid-1980s" (p. 25). "In recent decades … the closing of the mosque by the monks and the planting of a cross on its dome" (p. 19). Unverified, with conflicting later reports No source I opened mentions a 1986 closure.<br>Egypt Independent (20 June 2016): "Muslims pray inside the historic Fatimid mosque".<br>Wikipedia (citing UNESCO): "still in use today on special occasions".<br>Monastery site: "crosses carved into the crowns of the arches" were found under plaster during renovations. That is not a cross planted on the dome.<br>The book itself has the mosque closed and restored in the same year. egyptindependent.com/?p=2470513; Wikipedia; sinaimonastery.com/…/mosque
B16 The minbar is one of only three surviving Fatimid minbars, the others at Qus and Hebron (p. 18, Champdor 48). Partly verified Egyptian Ministry: "one of only three complete surviving examples from the Fatimid Period". It does not name the other two. egymonuments.gov.eg/monuments/the-fatimid-mosque/
B17 Stephens (1836): the church and mosque on the summit were in ruins; "on this sacred spot the followers of Christ and Mohammed have united in worshipping the true living God" (p. 25 [PDF 48]). Fifty monks (p. 24). Quote Consistent (one word dropped). Monk count Unverified. Stephens, Incidents of Travel (1862 Harper ed.): "Near this, also in ruins, stands a Mohammedan mosque, for on this sacred spot the followers of Christ and Mohammed have united in worshipping the true and living God." The book omits "and". I could not find "fifty" monks in this edition. archive.org/details/incidentsoftrave01step
B18 The Mosque of 'Amr ibn al-'As, built in Fustat in 642, was "the first mosque built … in Egypt [and] on the continent of Africa" (p. 17 [PDF 40]). Minor difference Egyptian Ministry: Egypt was conquered in "20 AH/640 AD"; the mosque was founded "a year later" (≈21 AH = 641/642). It is "the oldest surviving mosque in Egypt and Africa". The ministry says "oldest surviving", not "first built". egymonuments.gov.eg/monuments/mosque-of-amr-ibn-al-as/
B19 Moritz: the mosque was built "during the Crusades, around 1090 CE" (p. 18). Unverified (Moritz/Skrobucha not opened). Chronologically inconsistent. Mouton (2002): the Latin kingdom was founded in 1099, and Baldwin I (1100–1118) led the first Crusader expeditions into Sinai. "Around 1090" predates any Crusader presence. clio.fr PDF
B20 Burckhardt (1816) on the summit mosque. Relevant to the book's claim that the "period of significant decline" was the 18th to early 19th centuries (p. 25). Disputed (contrary evidence) Burckhardt (1822, pp. 566–567): "a poor mosque … held in great veneration by the Moslems, and the place of their pilgrimage. It is frequently visited by the Bedouins … Foreign Moslem pilgrims often repair to the spot". In the convent mosque, "it is only upon the occasion of the presence of some Mussulman of consequence that the call to prayers is made" (p. 544). archive.org/details/b22017355
C. al-Tur, pilgrimage, Crusades, Ottomans, Napoleonic era
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
C1 "al-Tur … replaced Clysma as the main Red Sea Port in 1058 CE" (p. 23 [PDF 46]). Disputed / Unverified Nawata, Kawatoko et al. (2012): "the port city Raya (6th-12th or 13th century AD) lies on the coast of South Sinai near al-Tur … After abandonment of this port city, al-Tur (especially al-Kilani area: 14th-20th century AD) presumed to have been established near the previous trade harbor."<br>Bauden (2025): archaeology at al-Rāyah points to abandonment in the 7th/13th century; al-Ṭūr appears in later sources; the oldest documents at the al-Ṭūr site are late 9th/15th century.<br>No source I opened gives 1058. In the Fatimid period the port appears to have been Rāya. dzvfk6x4geab4.cloudfront.net/…/ICRS2012_22A_6.pdf; orbi.uliege.be/handle/2268/336438
C2 "In 1378 CE, after a brief decline, al-Tur resumed its role as a major Red Sea port" (p. 23). Partly consistent / Unverified The 14th-century rise of al-Tur fits Nawata et al. (al-Kilani, 14th–20th c.). The year 1378 and the idea that al-Tur "resumed" a role were not found. same
C3 Aqaba and Aylah fell to the Crusaders at the beginning of the 12th century (p. 23, Peters 90). Consistent (general) Mouton (2002): "La fondation du royaume de Jérusalem en 1099 fit … du Sinaï une zone frontière"; "Baudouin Ier (1100-1118) … mena plusieurs expéditions au cœur de la péninsule". The exact year Aylah was taken was not opened. clio.fr PDF
C4 1517: Ottoman "intense fortress building … at al-Tur, Nakhl, Nuwaybah, al-Arish, and Kusayr" (p. 23). Partly inconsistent Wikipedia's list of Egyptian fortifications: "1516 AD An-Nakhl Fortress (by Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghawri)" and "1516 AD Al-Arish citadel (by Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghawri)", both Mamluk; "1893 Nuweiba Castle". It gives no dates for al-Tur or Quseir. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Egyptian_castles,_forts,_fortifications_and_city_walls
C5 Rocchetta (1598–99): "Sultan Selim had built a double wall around the Monastery" (p. 23). Unverified Not opened. For context, Mouton (2002): "Les puissantes murailles de Justinien qui enserrent encore de nos jours le monastère". clio.fr PDF
C6 Frescobaldi (1384) found 200 monks (p. 23). Unverified (text); broadly consistent Mouton (2002): about 200 monks "au Moyen Âge". clio.fr PDF
C7 "the Napoleonic expedition to Egypt in 1797-1804" (p. 24 [PDF 47]). Inconsistent Wikipedia: "28 June 1798 – 2 September 1801".<br>Art Newspaper: "After Napoleon occupied Egypt in 1798".<br>The book's own ch. 2, p. 70: "invaded by the French from 1798 to 1801". en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_campaign_in_Egypt_and_Syria; theartnewspaper.com
C8 "the 1869 construction of the Suez Canal" (p. 24). Minor difference (1869 is the opening year) Mouton (2002): "le percement du canal de Suez en 1869". clio.fr PDF
C9 Affagart (1533–34): Turks and Moors revere the place and St Catherine and built a mosque in the monastery, "in which are found the privileges which Muhammad granted" (p. 23 [PDF 46], Affagart 190–191). Consistent Affagart, ed. Chavanon (1902), pp. 190–191: "Les Turcs et Mores ont singulière dévotion à ce lieu … ont édiffié dedans le monastère une mesquite, c'est-à-dire une église et y a ung prebstre député pour la maintenir … dedans laquelle sont les previlleiges que Mahommet donna au monastère." archive.org/details/relationdeterres00affauoft
C10 Affagart: Mecca–Sinai is 14 days "by camel caravan" (p. 9 [PDF 32], Affagart 203). Minor difference Affagart p. 203: La Mecha is "environ quatorze journées par delà le mont de Sinay". He gives no mode of travel; "by camel caravan" is the book's gloss. same
C11 Napoleon's decree: "8 December, 1798" (Tomadakis, ch. 2 p. 70 [PDF 95]) vs "the decree issued by Napoleon on 19 December 1798" (same page). 19 Dec Consistent; 8 Dec Inconsistent Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, vol. 5, no. 3782, "ORDRE. Quartier général, au Caire, 29 frimaire an VII". The OCR reads "(10 décembre 1798)", but item 3783, with the same Republican date, is printed "(19 décembre 1798)". My conversion: 29 frimaire VII = 19 Dec 1798. No other Sinai order appears in the volume. archive.org/details/correspondancede05napouoft
C12 The decree content: respect for the Law of Moses and the Jewish nation; educated inhabitants; warring Bedouins barred from asylum; freedom of worship; no tribute, taxes or duties. Attributed to "Fazakerley … (378)" and "(99-100)". Napoleon's decree "actually confirms the privileges that were granted by the Prophet" (ch. 2 p. 70). Content Consistent. Attribution Minor difference. "Confirms the Prophet's privileges" is Opinion. The order: "Par respect pour Moïse et la nation juive"; "habité par des hommes instruits et policés"; Art. 1, Bedouins at war cannot "demander asile dans le couvent"; Art. 2, worship protected; Art. 3, no "droit ni tribut annuel, comme ils en ont été exemptés suivant les différents titres qu'ils en conservent"; Art. 4, customs exemption. It does not mention Muhammad.<br>Fazakerley (p. 376, not 378) only says: "we found one also from Buonaparte, when in Egypt, promising friendship and protection to the convent". archive.org correspondancede05napouoft; archive.org travelsinvarious00walp
C13 The north wall "collapsed after long and heavy rain in December, 1798" and Napoleon "assisted in the rebuilding" (ch. 2 p. 70, Tomadakis). Partly consistent; collapse date Unverified Art Newspaper: Napoleon "offered protection" and had the Justinian walls repaired. The tool's summary was that he "ordered his general to help rebuild" them.<br>Sacred Destinations: the upper wall sections "were restored on orders of Napoleon".<br>No dated source for the collapse was opened. theartnewspaper.com; sacred-destinations.com
D. Travellers: visit dates and quotations
# Book claim (page) Verdict What the source says Source URLs
D1 Monconys (1611–1665) "traveled to Mount Sinai in 1646-47". Muhammad, "a friend of one of their monks", gave a charter; signed it "with the figure of his hand"; the charter was "taken from them by Selim … who brought it to his Treasury after leaving … a copy" (p. 9 [PDF 32], "228-229"). Consistent (content and year). Minor difference (pages). Journal des voyages, Part I (Lyon: Boissat & Remeus, 1665), pp. 118–119. Marginal date "1647 / Auril", so he was at Sinai in April 1647. His informant was the archbishop: "depuis Mahomet estant amy d'vn de leurs Religieux luy donna vne pancarte de quantité de priuileges … Mahomet signa cette pancarte de la figure de sa main qu'il trempa dans de l'encre … laquelle Selin Empereur des Turcs leur osta, & l'emporta dans son thresor, apres leur en auoir laissé vne copie". Pages 228–229 presumably belong to a different edition. archive.org/details/bub_gb__ffvABn6duQC
D2 Thévenot (1633–1667), travels 1655–1663: camel driver, eagle, palm-print "on a sheet of white paper" (pp. 9–10, Relation 322–323). Unverified The original was not opened (search quota). One secondary discrepancy: Arundale (1837) quotes Wells's paraphrase of Thévenot, in which Muhammad clapped his inked hand "on the skin of a gazelle", not paper. This needs checking against Thévenot's French. archive.org/details/illustrationsofj00arun (p. 30 footnote)
D3 Morison, Relation historique (1704): Muhammad kept the monastery's camels for "a few years"; Selim took the patent to "the Treasury of the Serrail" (p. 10, Morison 105–106; p. 21, Morison 95). Unverified Not opened. —
D4 Cantemir: the story "in a fabulous treatise by a Sinaitic monk"; a cloud, not an eagle; palm "for want of a Seal"; Selim purchased the instrument "for four thousand gold crowns". The book says this version "appears to be the oldest of all" (pp. 10–11 [PDF 33–34]). Quote Consistent. "Oldest of all" is Opinion, not supported. Cantemir, History of the Growth and Decay of the Othman Empire, tr. N. Tindal (London: Knapton, 1734), Part I, p. 168, annotation 50: "since I dont think it mention'd any where but in a fabulous treatise of a Sinaitish Monk … They say, though fabulously, that Mahomet … the Abbot saw a cloud hovering over Mahomet's head … confirm'd it, for want of a Seal, with the Palm of his hand … Long after, when Sultan Selim was in Egypt, the Abbot of Mount Sinai humbly came to him with Mahomet's true or forged Instrument, which the Emperor purchased of the Monks for four thousand Gold Crowns".<br>Cantemir's text is early 18th century, and his monk's treatise is undated. Earlier dated accounts exist: Thenaud 1512, Affagart 1533–34, Monconys 1647. archive.org/details/dli.ministry.02708
D5 Fazakerley visited in 1811; "the celebrated firman of Mahomet … taken away by Sultan Selim … signed by 'Ali, and Abu Bekr" (p. 11 [PDF 34], 375–378). Consistent Walpole (ed.), Travels in Various Countries of the East (1820). The party "left Cairo on the thirty-first of January, 1811". The passage is dated "Feb. 13" and appears on p. 375. Wording matches ("Abubekr"). archive.org/details/travelsinvarious00walp
D6 Henniker (1793–1825) travelled to Sinai in 1820–21. The superior said the hand-print "is now at Constantinople, for the Gran Seignor having desired to look at it, retained it"; an eagle; "In about fifteen years afterwards …" (p. 11, Henniker 233–234). Quote Consistent. Year: not stated on the pages opened. Henniker, Notes during a Visit to Egypt, Nubia, the Oasis, Mount Sinai, and Jerusalem (London: Murray, 1823), pp. 233–234. The wording matches. The preface is dated Aug 1822, and appendix documents are dated June–July 1820, which fits 1820–21. archive.org/details/notesduringavis02henngoog
D7 "When Francis Arundale … visited the Monastery of Saint Catherine in 1831" (p. 11). Ch. 2 p. 74: "in 1831 … completes a voyage to Sinai and notes most Bedouins were Shi'ites". Year Inconsistent. Quote (p. 28) Consistent. Bedouin remark Minor difference (context). Arundale, Illustrations of Jerusalem and Mount Sinai (1837): "the day of departure being fixed for the 29th of August, 1833", with Bonomi and Catherwood.<br>p. 28: "In 1517, after the conquest of Egypt, Selim demanded it, and placed a copy, in parchment, certified by himself, among the archives of this monastery." This matches.<br>The "followers of Ali" passage (pp. 6–7) is a "short account of the general character of the Arabs" given on the Cairo–Suez stage. It is not specific to the Sinai Bedouin. archive.org/details/illustrationsofj00arun
D8 Burckhardt (1816): the monks' belief, the firman critique, 22 witnesses, "fable … forgery" (ch. 2 pp. 81–82, Burckhardt 546–47). "According to … Burckhardt … six to seven thousand monks … at the time of the Muslim conquest (546)" (p. 9 [PDF 32]). Visit and critique Consistent. Monk count Minor difference (attribution). Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (1822): journey "In the Spring of 1816". Pp. 546–547 match the book's quotes.<br>p. 546: "The prior told me that … at the time of the Mohammedan conquest, six or seven thousand monks and hermits were dispersed over the mountains". This is the prior's claim reported by Burckhardt, not Burckhardt's own finding. archive.org/details/b22017355
D9 Stanley's eagle passage (ch. 2 p. 76, "344-345"). On p. 8 [PDF 31] the same quotation is given as "As he rested with camels on Jebel Munayja at the head of Wadi ad-Dayr, an eagle …", cited "(344)" directly after Hobbs 159. Content Consistent. Wording on p. 8 Minor difference (altered quotation, unclear attribution). Stanley (1868 ed.), p. 54: "as he rested with his camels on Mount Menejia, an eagle was seen to spread its wings over his head … drawn up on the skin of a gazelle, and deposited in the archives of the convent". Stanley's footnote glosses Menejia as "That which closes up the Valley of the Convent".<br>He adds that the contract "if it ever existed, has long since disappeared; it is said, that it was taken by Sultan Selim to Constantinople, and exchanged for a copy, which however no traveller has ever seen."<br>He prefaces it: "No one can now prove or disprove the tradition" (p. 53). archive.org/details/sinaipalestinei00stan
D10 Lindsay 1837 (22 monks); Van Egmont & Heyman 1700–1723; Volney 1783–85; Harant 1598; Posniakov c. 1560; Dumas "visited the masjid" (pp. 17–24). Unverified Not opened (see §5). For Dumas, it should be checked whether he personally travelled to Sinai. —
D11 Thenaud's pilgrimage "in 1512 CE" (p. 19). Consistent Schefer's edition is of Thenaud's 1511–12 voyage, alongside the "relation de l'ambassade de Domenico Trevisan … 1512". Thenaud reached the monastery on "la vigille sainct Jehan". archive.org/details/levoyagedoutreme00then
E. Selim I and the "four thousand gold crowns"
# Book claim (page) Verdict Evidence
E1 "Rather than being seized, it was purchased by Selim I at the exorbitant amount of four thousand gold crowns. The Ottoman Caliph … would not have spent such a spectacular sum on a spurious document" (p. 11 [PDF 34]). Disputed (single, self-described "fabulous" source). The inference is Opinion. Only source found for a price: Cantemir (tr. 1734, p. 168, n. 50). He introduces the whole story with "They say, though fabulously" and calls the document "Mahomet's true or forged Instrument". He gives no year beyond "when Sultan Selim was in Egypt" (1517).<br>Other accounts I opened:<br>- Monconys 1647: Selim "leur osta" (took it from them).<br>- Fazakerley 1811: "taken away by Sultan Selim … too precious and sacred a monument to be left in Christian hands".<br>- Burckhardt 1816, monks' version: Selim "sent for it, and added it to the other relics".<br>- Henniker 1820s: the Grand Signior "having desired to look at it, retained it".<br>- Arundale 1833: "Selim demanded it".<br>- Stanley 1852–53: "it is said … taken by Sultan Selim … exchanged for a copy, which however no traveller has ever seen".<br>- Affagart 1533–34 contradicts a sale before his visit: "Les Turcs leur ont voullu donner grand argent pour avoir ce seing … mays jamays ne s'en veullent deffaire" (the Turks offered much money for the hand-sign, but the monks would never part with it), pp. 190–191.
E2 Arundale: "In 1517, after the conquest of Egypt, Selim demanded it" (p. 12). Consistent with Arundale p. 28. The book's 1831 date for Arundale is wrong (D7). archive.org illustrationsofj00arun
E3 (Ch. 2, p. 72; outside my scope, noted for the other agent.) "Merzifonlu Kara Mustapha Pasha, serving Sulayman II from 1663-1666". Flag Cantemir p. 169 (annotation) says the exemption lasted "till the time of Soliman II. Great-Uncle of the present Emperor, when the Turks began to collect the Haraj on them, and that by means of [K]ioprili ogli Mustafa Pasha". The OCR reads "ioprili ogli". So Cantemir names Köprülü-oğlu Mustafa Pasha, not Kara Mustafa. I did not verify the regnal or vizierial dates.
F. Muhammad, Sinai and the eagle legend
# Book claim (page) Verdict Evidence
F1 According to the monks and Bedouins, Muhammad visited before his revelations on a merchant journey (Hobbs 159). He "is said to have visited" (Atiya xviii) (p. 8 [PDF 31]). Tradition (reported as such) Burckhardt (p. 546): "It is a favourite belief of the monks of Mount Sinai, that Mohammed himself, in one of his journeys, alighted under the walls of the convent". Affagart (p. 191): "Les religieulx nous disrent qu'il avoyt esté en ce lieu en son vivant". Hobbs and Atiya were not opened.
F2 A "twenty-five years of silence"; "when news of Muhammad disappears in the Hijaz, news of him reappears in the Sinai"; the monks "appear … to have the missing piece" (p. 12 [PDF 35]). Opinion No dated Sinai source earlier than the 16th-century travellers was found among the sources opened. Mouton dates the monastic narrative to "à partir du IXe siècle" (F7). See §4.
F3 "recorded by a large number of pilgrims over the past millennium" (p. 12 [PDF 35]). Unverified / not supported by the sources opened The earliest traveller I opened who records the visit claim is Affagart (1533–34). Thenaud (1512) mentions the hand-signed privileges but no visit. Mouton's 9th-century date (F7) refers to a monastic discourse, not to pilgrims' records.
F4 On the Night Journey he prayed at "Medina, Mount Sinai, Bethlehem, and Jerusalem" (p. 21 [PDF 44]). Consistent with one hadith Sunan al-Nasa'i 450 (Anas b. Malik): "You have prayed in Taibah … You have prayed in Mount Sinai, where Allah … spoke to Musa … You have prayed in Bethlehem … Then I entered Bait Al-Maqdis". sunnah.com shows "Grade: Hasan (Darussalam)". Other gradings were not checked.
F5 "it is an article of faith among Muslims that the Prophet was physically present on Mount Sinai around the year 621 CE" (p. 21). Opinion / overstatement The Sinai stop rests on narrations like Nasa'i 450. Whether all Muslims treat it as an article of faith is the author's characterization; no source examined says so.
F6 Ch. 2 p. 87 [PDF 112]: "According to all of the various versions … an auspicious eagle appeared". Inconsistent (with the sources and with the book itself) Cantemir has a cloud; the book notes this itself on p. 11. Monconys, Affagart, Thenaud and Burckhardt mention no omen. The eagle appears in Henniker, Stanley and Thévenot (as paraphrased by Wells in Arundale's footnote).
F7 "The story of Muhammad at Mount Sinai does not exist in any of the surviving Arabic and Islamic sources"; stories were circulating by the mid-9th century (ch. 2 pp. 87–88). Consistent (no Islamic source). Partly consistent (9th century). Burckhardt (1822, p. 546): "None of the historians of Mohammed, who have recorded the transactions of almost every day of his life, mention his having been at Mount Sinai, neither in his earlier youth, nor after he set up as a prophet". The miraculous Night-Journey stop (F4) is a separate matter.<br>Mouton (2002): "l'élaboration, à partir du IXe siècle, d'un discours sur le passage du Prophète de l'islam à Sainte-Catherine. Mahomet, encore simple chamelier, aurait séjourné au monastère". He presents it as a monastic strategy to legitimise the monastery under Islamic law. The Istoria de Mahomet (c. 850) and Eulogius were not opened.
F8 Muhammad spent a night in the cave of Moses on Jebel Musa (Jabaliya, Hobbs 169) (p. 15). Unverified (Tradition) Hobbs is not accessible. Burckhardt (p. 567) records a footprint "stated to have been made by Mohammed's foot when he visited the mountain".
F9 The Sinai visit is placed in three different periods: ages 15–25 (p. 12), "at the age of twenty-five" (p. 21), and the decade after his marriage (p. 8). Inconsistent (internal) The travellers' versions also differ: a youth camel-driver (Cantemir, Thévenot, Henniker's "unknown youth"); a years-long stay (Morison, per the book); "in his lifetime" (Affagart). Henniker has the monk claim fulfilment "about fifteen years afterwards".
F10 Night Journey route on p. 27: "Mecca … to Syria … Palestine … and then to Mount Sinai". Inconsistent (with p. 21 and with Nasa'i 450's order) See F4: Taibah, Sinai, Bethlehem, Jerusalem.
F11 Ibn Ishaq / Ibn Sa'd / al-Tabari on the Prophet's pre-prophetic journeys. Unverified (beyond the book's own summary) Guillaume's translation on archive.org (TheLifeOfMohammedGuillaume) has unusable OCR. The fragments I could read concern the Syria journey with Abu Talib (Bahira) and the trading journey for Khadija ("he had finished his trading in Syria"), but I would not rely on that garbled text. Ibn Sa'd and Tabari were not opened.

3. Discrepancies ranked by significance

  1. Thenaud mistranslated; the inferences built on it fail (p. 19 [PDF 42]). Thenaud (1512, ed. 1884, p. 72) says the prior "se rendit mammelu quant on lui demanda compte et reliquat de son administration". He turned renegade when asked to account for his management. The book renders this as "when asked to assume its administration". On that rendering it builds three claims: Fatimid appointment of the convert prior, Muslim custody of the covenant from the 12th to the 14th century, and the Fatimids' wish that "Muslims, and not Christians, acted as the custodians". Thenaud supports none of these.

  2. Burckhardt misrepresented on the mosque's date (p. 18 [PDF 41]). The book says Burckhardt "interprets this as proof that the mosque dates to 1381 CE". Burckhardt (pp. 543–544) uses the AH 783 record to refute the monks' 16th-century story and concludes that the mosque "appears therefore to have existed long before the time of Selim". That is the very inference the book presents as its own.

  3. Selim's "purchase for four thousand gold crowns" (p. 11 [PDF 34]). The book prefers this version over all others and builds an argument for authenticity on the price ("would not have spent such a spectacular sum on a spurious document"). The only source is Cantemir (1734, p. 168, n. 50), who frames the story as told "fabulously" and the document as "true or forged". Six other accounts opened describe seizure, demand or retention. Affagart (1533–34) reports that the monks refused Turkish offers of money.

  4. Fatimid caliph conflations.

    • p. 16: the summit mosque is dated to "Abu 'Ali al-Mansur (r. 996-1021), the tenth of the Fatimid Caliphs". The reign dates are al-Hakim's (6th caliph); "tenth" is al-Amir (1101–1130). Both bore the name Abū ʿAlī Manṣūr.
    • Ch. 2 p. 75 calls "al-Afdal" a "Fatimid Caliph" and al-Hakim's "successor". He was a vizier (1094–1121) under al-Musta'li and al-Amir.
    • p. 17 gives al-Amir as 1102–1131, against 1101–1130 (and p. 18).

  5. "All versions have an eagle" (ch. 2 p. 87). This contradicts Cantemir's cloud, which the book itself reports on p. 11, and the omen-less accounts of Monconys, Affagart, Thenaud and Burckhardt.

  6. Wrong traveller dates. Arundale's visit was 1833, not 1831 (p. 11; ch. 2 p. 74). Stanley's was 1852–53, not 1858 (p. 16).

  7. Bell tower dated to the 17th century (p. 18, via Arabic News). It was built in 1871 (Mouton 2002; Art Newspaper; Sacred Destinations).

  8. "Only in the 15th century" was Jebel Musa identified as Sinai (p. 22). Christian identification of the summit dates to the 4th century (Mouton), and Justinian built a basilica on the peak in the 6th century (monastery site; Procopius).

  9. Monastery "temporarily abandoned" by 1479 because of the fall of Byzantium (p. 23). UNESCO says the monastery has been in use without interruption since the 6th century. Bauden (2025) documents a 1482 retreat of most monks to the al-Tur metochion after Bedouin (Awlād ʿAlī) attacks.

  10. Napoleonic expedition dated "1797-1804" (p. 24). It ran 1798–1801 (Wikipedia; the book's own ch. 2 p. 70 says the same).

  11. Napoleon's decree date and attribution. The book gives two dates, 8 and 19 Dec 1798. The Correspondance fixes the order at 29 frimaire an VII = 19 Dec 1798. The decree's articles are correctly summarised but attributed to Fazakerley "378". Fazakerley (p. 376) mentions only a Bonaparte document "promising friendship and protection". The order does not mention Muhammad; it refers to "différents titres" (various title-deeds).

  12. Relics of St Catherine "three hundred years" on the mountain (p. 22). Historical estimates are c. 800 or the 9th century (Art Newspaper; Mouton). Burckhardt's monks said "a few years" after the monastery was built.

  13. al-Tur replacing Clysma in 1058 (p. 23). No source found. Archaeology places the medieval port at Rāya until the 13th century, with al-Tur from the 14th century.

  14. Ottoman fort-building at five sites in 1517 (p. 23). The al-Arish and Nakhl forts are listed as Mamluk (1516, Qansuh al-Ghawri) and Nuweiba as 1893 (Wikipedia list).

  15. Citation and quotation problems.

    • "Hobbs 634-644" is 'Umar's reign, not pages.
    • p. 8 prints a Stanley quotation with "Jebel Munayja at the head of Wadi ad-Dayr" for Stanley's "Mount Menejia", cited "(344)" after Hobbs.
    • The same Stanley passage is cited as "120" (p. 16) and "344-345" (ch. 2). Both pages are 53–55 in the 1868 edition.
    • Monconys is cited as 228–229; the passage is on pp. 118–119 of the 1665 Lyon edition.

  16. Burckhardt's "six or seven thousand monks" (p. 9) presented as his own finding. It is what "the prior told me".

  17. Arundale's "followers of Ali" remark applied to the Sinai Bedouin (ch. 2 p. 74). In context it is a general remark on Arabs, made on the Cairo–Suez stage.

  18. Smaller items:

    • The monastery mosque is closed (1986) and restored (1986) on the same page, and a 2016 report describes Muslims praying in it.
    • The Night Journey route differs between p. 21 and p. 27.
    • "nearly 500 miles" should be ≈491 km / 305 miles.
    • "1869 construction" of the Suez Canal (1869 is the opening year).
    • "Fatimids (r. 901–1171)" should begin 909.

4. Neutral assessment of the "Muhammad in Sinai" thesis

What the book argues (pp. 8–16, 21; ch. 2 pp. 70, 76, 87–88).

  • There are "twenty-five years of silence" in the sira (ages 15–25 and 25–40).
  • The monks' tradition fills that gap: Muhammad was a camel-driver or caravaneer for, or a guest of, the monastery. An eagle or cloud revealed his destiny, and he gave a palm-print promise that later became the achtiname.
  • When news of him "disappears in the Hijaz, news of him reappears in the Sinai".

What the sources examined show.

  1. Islamic historical sources.

    • Burckhardt (1822, p. 546) states that "None of the historians of Mohammed … mention his having been at Mount Sinai, neither in his earlier youth, nor after he set up as a prophet".
    • The book concedes the same in ch. 2 p. 87: the story "does not exist in any of the surviving Arabic and Islamic sources".
    • The one Islamic text found that places Muhammad at Mount Sinai is a Night-Journey narration (Sunan al-Nasa'i 450, graded hasan by Darussalam). It describes a miraculous stop, not a caravan visit.
    • I could not open the sira texts themselves (Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume OCR unusable; Ibn Sa'd and Tabari not available). The book's own summary of them names journeys to Syria (Busra/Bahira; the trading journey for Khadija), not to Sinai.

  2. Christian / monastic tradition.

    • Thenaud (1512) mentions only Muhammad's hand-signed privileges kept in the mosque. He gives no visit story.
    • Affagart (1533–34) is the earliest traveller opened who reports the monks saying "qu'il avoyt esté en ce lieu en son vivant".
    • Later accounts add the camel-driver, eagle or cloud, and palm-print motifs: Monconys 1647 (via the archbishop), Thévenot (unverified), Cantemir (early 18th c., from a "fabulous treatise"), Henniker, Burckhardt ("a favourite belief of the monks") and Stanley.
    • The versions disagree on the omen (eagle, cloud, none), the material (paper, parchment, gazelle skin), Muhammad's role (friend of a monk, camel-driver, years-long servant) and the timing.

  3. Modern historians opened.

    • Mouton (2002) treats the visit as a legend, elaborated "à partir du IXe siècle" as one of the monks' strategies to legitimise the monastery under Islamic law.
    • Stanley (1856/1868) judged that "No one can now prove or disprove the tradition", while thinking Qur'anic allusions bring it "within the range of possibility".
    • Hobbs (1995), as the book quotes him, says "there are questions about whether contact took place at all". I could not open Hobbs to confirm this.

  4. The argument from silence. The "missing" years are a gap in the sources, not positive evidence of a stay in Sinai. The earliest dated monastic attestations of a visit found here are 16th-century, about nine centuries after the events. Mouton dates the narrative itself to the 9th century. The book's own placements of the visit are mutually inconsistent: ages 15–25, age 25, and the decade after his marriage.

Bottom line (neutral). The thesis rests on Christian monastic tradition recorded by European travellers from the early 16th century, and on an inference from gaps in the sira. No Islamic historical source examined records a Sinai visit (apart from the miraculous Night-Journey narration). The scholars consulted (Burckhardt, Mouton) regard the visit as a legend; Stanley regards it as unprovable. The book's claims that the monks' account "fits" and that "the evidence points to" their truthfulness are the author's opinion. The sources examined do not establish them.

Fact-check reports

Persia and Najran

188 table rows · source file V3_persia_najran.md

V3: Verification of Morrow (2013), Ch. 3 "Christians of Persia" (pp. 99–108) and Ch. 4 "Christians of Najran" (pp. 109–138), with Part II texts (Ch. 9 pp. 223–226; Ch. 11 pp. 293–311)

Inputs.

  • Extraction: extract/04_ch3_ch4.md, read in full.
  • Part II texts: extract/07_texts.md (Ch. 9 and Ch. 11 parts).
  • Raw OCR: book/chunks/04_ch3_ch4.txt, 07_texts_ch8_ch12.txt and 09_appendices_illus_biblio.txt, used where exact wording mattered.

Who opened what.

  • Rows marked [me] rest on pages I opened myself: archive.org full texts and page images, OUP, GEDSH, US government pages, Iranica via curl.
  • Rows marked [A] or [B] rest on pages opened by one of two helper research agents. Each agent was instructed to rely only on pages it opened.
  • I re-checked these helper findings myself against the source:
    • the 1881 Ter-Hovhaneants pages;
    • Hamidullah's "fabrication" verdict;
    • EI2 "Nadjrān", "Mubāhala", "Dhimma" and "ʿAbd al-Madjīd II";
    • Late Antiquity p. 753;
    • Ibn al-Mujāwir;
    • Thévenot;
    • El-Wakil 2016 and 2019;
    • Zein & El-Wakil 2020;
    • Wood 2013;
    • GEDSH on Scher.
  • [GB] means the evidence is a Google Books "search-inside" excerpt: verbatim book text, but a snippet, not a full page. Treat these as weaker.
  • Several key sources are archive.org user uploads of published books (EI2, Late Antiquity, Hamidullah, Ibn al-Mujāwir). They are cited to the printed page where visible.

Verdict key.

  • Consistent: matches independent sources.
  • Minor difference: an AH-to-CE span, a spelling, OCR, or a small detail.
  • Inconsistent: reliable sources say otherwise; what they say is given.
  • Disputed: sources disagree among themselves; each version is given.
  • Unverified: no reliable source was found or opened; what was tried is said.
  • Opinion: not checkable.

Source keys (S-…) are resolved to URLs in §6. Calendar conversions use the tabular Islamic calendar, Julian dates, ±1–2 days (calc). For example, 7 AH = 11 May 628 – 30 Apr 629; 8 AH = 1 May 629 – 19 Apr 630; 9 AH = 20 Apr 630 – 8 Apr 631; 10 AH = 9 Apr 631 – 28 Mar 632; 265 AH = 3 Sep 878 – 22 Aug 879.

Headline findings
  1. Persia: the "missing" source exists. Arpee's cited source, "Johanianz (New Julfa, 1881)", is Ter-Hovhaneants, History of New Julfa, vol. 2 (1881). On pp. 147–153 it prints an Armenian "authenticated copy of the covenant of the Prophet of the Arabs, given to the nation of the Christians or Armenians in the fourth year of the Hijra". It ends with the Monday date and "Mahamad Jafer ... one of the notable imams" confirming it against the original.
    • Dadoyan's "No such document exists in this book" is wrong.
    • Morrow's claims that the covenant "survives only in English translation" and that Arpee may have mis-referenced it are also wrong. [A; page images re-checked by me]
  2. Najran: Hamidullah calls the texts fabrications. Morrow presents Hamidullah's reprint as a milestone. Yet Hamidullah, in the Majmūʿat al-wathāʾiq itself, prints the two Seert texts with the statement "there is not the slightest doubt that these two texts are fabrications" (5th ed., docs 96–97). Morrow does not mention this. [B; re-checked]
  3. Three of Morrow's quotations omit material that cuts against his case:
    • Ibn Ishaq says the twenty Christians who came to Mecca came "from Abyssinia". Morrow's ellipsis removes this, then asserts a pre-621 Najran delegation (p. 112).
    • Arpee calls the underlying Sinai charter "(though by modern criticism pronounced a forgery)". The ellipsis on p. 99 removes this.
    • Scher's epigraph (p. 109) drops Scher's supporting reference to Al-Machriq 1909. [me]
  4. Classical sources record one undated Najran treaty, not two. That treaty has 2,000 robes, five witnesses and the scribe 'Abd Allah b. Abi Bakr or 'Ali. Morrow's separate "9 AH" and "10 AH" treaties (from Qureshi) are two recensions of the same text. Modern dating of the deputation ranges from 630 (Watt; Shahid, EI2) to 10/631–632 (Schmucker, EI2). [me]
  5. Plain date errors:
    • Turkish Republic "1916" (actually 1923).
    • Caliphate abolished "1922" (actually 1924).
    • Ja'far's return "626" (actually 7/628).
    • Khaybar "629" (actually 628).
    • Armenian deportation "1606, 150,000" (actually 1604–1605; 300,000–400,000 deported overall).
    • Arpee "1948" (actually 1946; he died in 1947).
    • Chronicle published "five years after" Scher's death (actually four: 1915 to 1919).
    • The Late Antiquity page Morrow cites contains no "999/1000 CE" source.
