3. Discrepancies ranked by significance

  1. Hamidullah's verdict suppressed (p. 138). Morrow cites Hamidullah's reprint as a step toward recognition. Hamidullah prints the two Seert texts (docs 96–97) with: "there is not the slightest doubt that these two texts are fabrications". His preface says the covenants to Christians and Magians were included "as a specimen of forgery and fabrication". Zein & El-Wakil (2020), who favour the covenants, also note that Hamidullah "expressed his misgivings". (S-HAM, S-ZE20)

  2. Persia: Dadoyan was wrong and Morrow missed the source (pp. 99, 102–103, 107). The covenant is printed in Armenian in Ter-Hovhaneants, History of New Julfa II (1881), pp. 147–153, exactly as Arpee said. This:

    • refutes Dadoyan's "No such document exists in this book";
    • makes Morrow's "survives only in English translation" and his referencing-error hypothesis wrong;
    • shifts the evidential question to the Armenian text's origin. It is presented as an "authenticated copy" with an imam's confirmation, but no older witness, Persian or Arabic, has been identified.

    Arpee's own text calls the underlying Sinai charter "by modern criticism pronounced a forgery". Morrow's p. 99 ellipsis removes that. (S-TH, S-ARP)

  3. Ibn Ishaq misquotation (p. 112). "From Abyssinia" is cut from Ibn Ishaq's account of the twenty Christians in Mecca. The resulting "first [Najran] delegation ... prior to 621 CE" rests on a reading Ibn Ishaq himself doubts. (S-II)

  4. Two Najran treaties (9 AH and 10 AH) (p. 113). The classical sources (Ibn Sa'd, Abu Yusuf, Abu 'Ubayd, al-Baladhuri) preserve one undated treaty in several recensions. Morrow's two "treaties" via Qureshi are versions of it. The deputation's date is itself disputed: 630 (Watt, Shahid) against 10 AH (Schmucker, EI2).

  5. Internal impossibility of the witness defence (pp. 115–118). Morrow dates the covenant to the Prophet's last year. Yet he defends Sa'd b. Mu'adh (d. 5/627) as a witness by placing the covenant "after the Battle of the Trench". He also says Ja'far returned in "626", when EI2 gives 7/628. On the EI2 dates, no single date fits Sa'd, Ja'far, Abu Hurayra (Muslim from 7/628–9) and Mu'awiya (Muslim from 8/630) together. The covenant's own source (the Chronicle) frames the visit c. 628–629. (S-EI2-B, S-PO13)

  6. Political dates (p. 110). Turkish Republic "1916" (actually 1923); caliphate abolished "1922" (actually 1924; the sultanate fell in 1922). (S-EI-AMII)

  7. Misused citation (p. 114). "A second Yemeni source from the year 999/1000 CE" is not on the cited Late Antiquity p. 753. Later Christian presence is still independently attested: al-Hadi's 897 treaty; bishops in the 9th–10th centuries (Shahid, EI2); Ibn al-Mujāwir in the 13th century. (S-LA, S-EI-NAJ)

  8. 'Umar's expulsion (p. 114). Morrow casts Hitti's statement as biased. Every classical source opened reports the expulsion, and EI2 says "most" of Najran's Christians went to al-Najraniyya near Kufa. Morrow is right only that some Christians stayed (Shahid). The suggestion that only the hierarchs were exiled has no source support.

  9. Scher misrepresented (p. 109). Scher gave reasons (variant copies across communities; faulty language) and a reference (Cheikho, Al-Machriq 1909). Morrow's epigraph removes the reference and then says Scher gave no argument.

  10. New Julfa (p. 99). "1606 ... over 150,000" should be 1604–05, with 300,000–400,000 deported overall and about 10,000 in New Julfa. Abbas I did not build the surviving cathedral (1653–64, under Abbas II).

  11. Arpee "1948" (p. 103). The book appeared in 1946 and Arpee died in 1947. The book's own p. 99 says 1946.

  12. Publication of the Chronicle (pp. 109, 138). It appeared four years, not five, after Scher's death. Parts I–II.1 appeared in his lifetime (1908–1911). Bar Hebraeus's summary was printed in 1877, so "first published ... 1919" holds only for the full text.

  13. Ja'far al-Sadiq "(711–36)" (Arpee's figures, repeated uncorrected); Mu'awiya in Armenia "650" (actually 652/653); "Jamal Pasha" book-burning (Shi'i tradition names al-Jazzar; rests on snippets).

  14. Witness list in Part II (p. 300). Three of Scher's names are omitted and two merged.

  15. Minor:

  • Khaybar 629;
  • CUP "1906";
  • Thévenot's dates;
  • Majlisi father/son;
  • "Bowerstock";
  • "Girangos";
  • "Birmantha" not flagged as conjectural;
  • Cahen's phrase sourced to EI2 "Dhimma", not the RHR article in Morrow's bibliography;
  • Abu Hurayra "one of the first converts" (EI2: converted 7/628–9);
  • Abbas I credited with making Shi'ism the official religion (it was Isma'il I, 1501).

4. Scholarly assessment of authenticity

4A. Covenant with the Christians of Persia (Arpee 1946; Ter-Hovhaneants 1881)

Positions found.

  • Morrow (2013): authenticity "cannot be disproved"; possibly the original of the Sinai text.
  • Dadoyan (2011): "highly dubious yet intriguing". Her stated basis, that the document is not in the cited book or the archives, is half refuted for the book; the archive claim is unverified. Her "cannot be established" refers to the oath traditions generally. [A, GB]
  • Arpee (1946): he reproduces the document. He records the Ja'far authentication, but describes the Sinai charter it reproduces as "by modern criticism pronounced a forgery". [A]
  • Hamidullah: includes "the Prophetic covenants with the Armenian Christians" in the Majmūʿa (pp. 556–560 per Zein & El-Wakil). His general verdict on covenants with Christians is "a specimen of forgery". Whether his Armenian item is this text was not checked. [me]
  • Sellam's review (AJIS 2015): does not assess the Persia covenant. [A]
  • No other scholarly verdict was found.

Strongest evidence for (early origin or authenticity).

  • A printed Armenian text (New Julfa, 1881) exists, explicitly framed as an "authenticated copy" of a covenant given "in the fourth year of the Hijra". It records confirmation by "Mahamad Jafer ... one of the notable imams". This shows a real New Julfa tradition, not a 1946 invention.
  • An older Armenian tradition of a written grant from "Mahmet" survives. Kirakos (13th c.) reports a contract with Armenia: four dram, wheat, a saddlebag, a hair rope and gloves.
  • Kirakos also records a documented 8th-century petition (John of Odzun to Hisham) securing similar freedoms.

Strongest evidence against (later composition).

  • No Arabic or Persian text and no manuscript has been identified. The earliest attested form is the 1881 printing, and Arpee says only that a 17th-century shah gave it "in copy".

  • The text is avowedly a translation and is "strikingly similar" to the Sinai covenant, which Arpee himself reports modern criticism calls a forgery.

  • Shi'i features that Morrow himself notes:

    • the ruler called "Imam";
    • "blessings of God rest upon him and his posterity";
    • temporary marriage;
    • authentication by an imam.

    These fit a Shi'i (Safavid-era) milieu of transmission. Morrow reads them as original; that is an inference either way.

  • The date (4 AH) predates any Muslim contact with Persia's Armenians.

  • The cited 8th-century evidence does not mention this document.

4B. Covenant with the Christians of Najran (Chronicle of Seert, PO 13, 1919)

Positions found.

Position Scholar Basis
Later composition Scher (1919): "certainement apocryphe", forged by Christians to gain Muslim protection Variant copies across communities; faulty Arabic; Al-Machriq 1909 [me]
Massignon (1942): forged at the Dayr Qunna circle of Nestorian scribes (Banu Makhlad) around the 265/878 "découverte" [B, GB]
Cahen (EI2 "Dhimma", 1965): "a pious fraud of Nestorian monks of the 3rd/9th century" Assertion [me]
Hamidullah (Majmūʿa): "not the slightest doubt ... fabrications" [me]
Nersessian (2001): "patent fabrication" Follows Cahen [B]
Ratliff (2008): "questioned"; produced by 'Abbasid viziers of Nestorian origin Follows Scher and Massignon [B]
Wood (OUP 2013): "far too much so to be anything other than an invention"; its "agenda was to insert the Christians, undifferentiated by denomination, into early Muslim history"; used to argue for monks' exemption from the poll tax [me]
Wood (Al-Masaq 2021): an "ʿAbbāsid-era re-imagination", responding to Muslim efforts to fix rules for non-Muslims Abstract [B]
Mixed Roggema (2009): "certainly penned by Christians, but should not be dismissed as an absolute forgery"; it echoes the Prophet's terms for Najran in Muslim sources and obligations in the Pact of 'Umar [B, GB]
Zein & El-Wakil (2020): sympathetic, but "Muʿāwiya being a scribe ... when he was not yet a Muslim, and the problematic witnesses' names are not expected to go away any time soon" [me]
Authentic Morrow (2013) —
El-Wakil (JIS 27:3, 2016, pp. 273–354): "categorical dismissal of the covenants as forgeries is no longer tenable", via source-critical cross-comparison Abstract [me]
El-Wakil (Religions 10:516, 2019): the "mistakes" (early dating, witnesses, scribe) "have all proved to be consistent anachronisms in texts inherited by non-Muslim communities"; hence "the covenants are authentic and, on the whole, textually accurate but ... deliberately suppressed or interpolated in Muslim sources" [me]
Sellam's review (AJIS 2015) Accepts them as "genuine documents" [B]
Review of Morrow's 2025 book Monferrer-Sala (2026) "more persuasive as advocacy than as a decisive demonstration of authenticity" [B]

Strongest evidence for authenticity, or for an authentic core.

  • A real treaty between Muhammad and Najran is solidly attested in the classical sources: Ibn Sa'd, Abu Yusuf, Abu 'Ubayd and al-Baladhuri, with five named witnesses, and a delegation in Ibn Ishaq.
  • The Seert exordium's details overlap with those sources: a mosque visit; a bishop called 'Isa (Bar Hebraeus: "Jesus") with the Sayyid; a delegation of tens of riders.
  • Bar Hebraeus (13th c.) independently summarizes a diploma to the Najran Sayyid and bishop with the same 4/12 tax structure. The tradition was therefore known outside the Chronicle.
  • El-Wakil argues that the shared anachronisms across covenants held by different communities, without evidence of borrowing, point to common authentic exemplars.
  • The provenance note is specific: a register found in 265/878–9 with Habib, former curator of the "house of philosophy"; yellowed ox-hide with the Prophet's seal.

Strongest evidence against.

  • No Islamic source preserves this text or anything close. El-Wakil concedes this is "certainly perplexing".
  • The terms differ in kind from the classical Najran treaty: a per-head 4/12-dirham tax and clergy exemptions, against a collective tribute of 2,000 robes.
  • The witness list cannot be reconciled with a single date: Sa'd b. Mu'adh d. 5/627 against Abu Hurayra (7/628–9) and Ja'far (7/628). Mu'awiya, a Muslim only from 8/630, appears as scribe.
  • The exordium groups Hunayn (8/630) with the Qaynuqa', Nadir and Qurayza episodes (2–5 AH).
  • The document surfaced in 878, amid 'Abbasid-era disputes over dhimmi taxation, and was recorded in a chronicle composed in the 10th century or later.
  • Its length and repetitiveness (Wood).
  • Its "incorrect" language (Scher).
  • Its own frame dates the visit to c. 628–629, which conflicts with other datings.
  • Its role in the Chronicle's arguments for clerical tax exemption (Wood).

5. Items not checked, and why

  • EI2 accessed via an archive.org upload. Brill's site returned 403. EI2 "Nadjrān", "Mubāhala", "Dhimma" and "ʿAbd al-Madjīd II" were read in the archive.org EI2 text (helper download), not on Brill.
  • Schick. No work by a "Schick" on Najran could be identified (Crossref searches). It is not used in the timeline comparison.
  • Unopened works. Bournoutian, Levy, Qureshi, Jafri, Goddard, Dobson, Hitti's Makers of Arab History p. 28, Abu Riyya, Brown, Tabataba'i, Kashif al-Ghita' and Jurdi Abisaab were not opened. Claims attributed to them are marked Unverified where no independent source was found.
  • Not located. Qureshi's Letter to the People of Najran (4.17); the 'Umar II ransom document (3.21); the 1842 fatwa (Levy); Ibn Sa'd's Maqna variant.
  • Dadoyan 2011 print pages. Pp. 60–61 and 64 n. 56 were not seen. Wording was checked against Google Books excerpts of the 2017 reprint only.
  • Roggema. Pp. 116–118 were not seen; snippets only.
  • Massignon 1942. Not read in full; snippets and secondary summaries only.
  • Cahen's 1964 RHR article. Pp. 52–58 were behind a bot wall.
  • Not accessible (403 or paywall). Sanni's 2015 review; the Christian–Muslim Relations: A Bibliographical History vol. 3 entry on the Chronicle of Seert; the full text of El-Wakil 2016 (abstract only).
  • Al-Machriq 1909 (Cheikho). Not found online, so it is unverified whether it printed a Najran text.
  • Ter-Hovhaneants II, small print. The subheading under "ՅՕԴ Թ." and the footnotes on p. 153 were not legible at scan resolution. Whether the editor comments on the document's origin or the archive is unknown. The Armenian translation is the helper's; I checked the key phrases visually.
  • Chronicle of Seert manuscript. The date of BnF arabe 6653 was not checked.
  • Lifespan rows. Out of scope, though the helper noted:
    • Abu Hurayra d. 58–59/678–79 (book: 681);
    • Majlisi (Bāqir) 1627–98 (book: 1616–1689).
  • Morrow's Mufid quotations. Checked only for the passages cited here (thirty Christians; terms; "after this year").
  • 4.60–4.71 and other opinion rows. Not checkable.

Fact-check reports

Christians of the World (1538, 1630, 1655)

151 table rows · source file V4_christians_of_world.md

V4: Verification of Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013)

Chapter 5, "The Prophet Muhammad and the Christians of the World" (pp. 139–176), and the Chapter 10 texts (World I–IV; 1538, 1630 and 1655 reproductions)

Inputs. I read the extraction extract/05_ch5.md in full and the Chapter 10 parts of extract/07_texts.md. I checked the book's exact wording for key items against book/chunks/05_ch5.txt: "folios 245-246", "Hatur 1380", "1671 and in 1672", "1688", "four times during the first year", "1655, 1638, 1668, 1690, and as late as 1888", "James Thayer Addison", "Rabi' Ashar", "Plagiarizing Grassi" and "a certain Mr. Legrand". All of these are the book's own printed text, not extraction or OCR errors.

IDs. T# is a row of the extraction's timeline table (§2). C# is a numbered claim in its §4.

Method. Every verdict rests on a page I opened, cited by URL. Where a page was blocked, I say so. Wikipedia is used only as a lead or for uncontroversial dates, and is labelled "(WP)". Rows T39–T71, T78, T97, T100, T113, T114, T119 and T123, and claims C88–C111 and C174–C177 (printing history, Franco-Ottoman context, reigns), were checked by a forked sub-agent. I condensed its findings in §1h; its full file is verify/parts/A_printing_politics.md.

Access limits. Gallica, HathiTrust, the Fihrist web front-end, Marsh's Library, the DDB Hamburg record, Encyclopaedia Iranica, Britannica, T&F, MDPI and ResearchGate blocked automated access. I therefore could not view images of BnF Arabe 214 itself. Statements about its contents rest on the BnF catalogue record and on de Slane.

Calendar method. I computed all calendar conversions with standard arithmetic:

  • Coptic year: 1 Thout AM 1 = 29 Aug 284 (Julian), with 30-day months. Check: 1 Thout 1592 AM = 11 Sep 1875 (Gregorian), as Wikipedia (WP) states.
  • Islamic year: tabular calendar, civil epoch 16 Jul 622 (Julian), leap years 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 16, 18, 21, 24, 26 and 29 of the 30-year cycle.

The script is at scratchpad/scripts/cal.py.

1. Verification table

1a. The 1630 Paris edition and the later printings
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
T89 / C1 / C3 Published in Paris, 1630, by Antoine Vitray as al-'Ahd wa al-shurut allati sharataha Muhammad rasul Allah li ahl al-millah al-nasraniyyah; Latin Testamentum et pactiones (pp. 139, 146) Consistent The title page of the SLUB Dresden copy (Hist.Turc.524) reads: Arabic العهد والشروط التي شرطها محمد رسول الله لاهل الملة النصرانية; Latin "TESTAMENTUM ET PACTIONES INITAE INTER MOHAMEDEM ET CHRISTIANAE fidei cultores. PARISIIS, Excudebat ANTONIUS VITRAY, Linguarum Orientalium, Regis Typographus. In Collegio Longobardorum. M.D.C.XXX." Collation 16 + 16 pp. (Latin, then Arabic). The Arabic colophon (Ar. p. 16) reads: "completed in the city of Paris … at the hands of the humble Antoine Vitray (انطون ويتراي), entrusted with the printing of the … King of France, in the year 1630 of our Lord Jesus Christ". The Penn record (British Library copy) agrees: 16, 16 pp., Latin version by Gabriel Sionita. https://digital.slub-dresden.de/id308498003 ; https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000007.tif.large.jpg ; https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000038.tif.large.jpg ; https://digital.slub-dresden.de/oai/?verb=GetRecord&metadataPrefix=mets&identifier=oai:de:slub-dresden:db:id-308498003 ; https://www.deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de/item/3G5LMC2QXW4IEXZS4FQGOK6DXQDI3MZA ; https://find.library.upenn.edu/catalog/9970353303503681
07 §1 #16, §6 #25 Ch. 10 reproduction caption: "Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Mohamedem Apostolum Dei, et Christianae fedei cultores", Paris: Antoine Vitre, 1630 (p. 265) Minor difference "Apostolum Dei" is in the Latin caption title on p. 5 of the print ("…inter Mohamedem Apostolum Dei, & Christianae fidei cultores"), not on the title page. The word is "fidei", not "fedei". The printer's name is spelled VITRAY on the title page (the man is usually known as Antoine Vitré). https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000011.tif.large.jpg
C14 / T88 / T91 "This is the famous Testament of Mohammed, published by Gabriel Sionita (Paris, 1630)" (Fortescue 92 n. 5) (p. 139) Consistent Fortescue, The Lesser Eastern Churches (1913), p. 92 n. 5 is quoted verbatim. https://archive.org/details/lessereasternchu00fortuoft
T90 / C58 "Edited in Paris in 1630 by Antoine Vitray … with the collaboration of Gabriel Sionite"; Vitray thanks Michel Le Jay for the Arabic, Syriac and Samaritan type; "the Arabic ones were those of Savary" (Balagna 67) (pp. 149–150) Consistent (Le Jay); Unverified (Savary types) The printer's preface "Typographus Lectori" (pp. 3–4): "Cum liberalitate eximia generosissimi illius viri D. Le Iay, Typographeium iam habeam Arabicis, Syriacis, Samaritanis, aliisque … characteribus … instructum". That the Arabic founts were Savary de Brèves's is not stated in the preface. I did not open Balagna. https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000009.tif.large.jpg
T92 The work "sold out almost immediately" and "was re-published four times during the first year" (p. 151) Unverified (no evidence found) The union catalogues (VD17 and GVK, K10plus) list only the single 1630 Paris printing. Their records are duplicates of one edition: 16, 16 pp. I found no 1630 reissue in any catalogue I opened. https://sru.k10plus.de/opac-de-627?version=1.1&operation=searchRetrieve&query=pica.tit%3DTestamentum%20Mohamedem&recordSchema=dc
T95 Republished in 1638 by "other translators and publishers" (p. 151) Consistent, with a qualification VD17 23:259451D: Johann Fabricius (1608–1653), Muhammedis Testamentum sive pacta cum Christianis in Oriente inita, Rostochii: Hallervord / Meder, 1638, [4] Bl., 47 S., 4°, Latin only. Bayle (1737), Mosheim and Rehatsek all describe it as a Latin-only edition. https://sru.k10plus.de/vd17?version=1.1&operation=searchRetrieve&query=pica.tit%3DMuhammedis%20Testamentum&recordSchema=mods ; https://archive.org/details/dictionaryhi_bayl_1738_04 ; https://archive.org/details/jasb-volume-13-for-1877-issue-no-35
T102 / T104 1655 republication; Nissel criticises Sionita's lack of vowels and republishes the text fully vocalised (pp. 146, 151; Ch. 10 caption p. 281: "Elsevier: Lugduni Batavorum, 1655") Consistent Penn record: "sive, Testamentum inter Muhamedem legatum Dei, et Christianae religionis populos olim initum … opera et studio Johannis Georgii Nisselii", Lugduni Batavorum: Ex officina Johannis Elsevier, 1655. GVK has the same edition ("[6] Bl., 16 S., S. 5–14, 11 S., [8] Bl."). A manuscript copy of the title, bound in the SLUB copy, says the text is "nunc primum figuris vocalium nobilitatus" and exposes the "grandia errata" of the Paris edition, and ends "Anno CIↃIↃCLV in 4to". Not mentioned by Morrow: GVK also lists Nissel's Leiden printings of 1660 and 1661 ("Testamentum, sive Foedus … ante mille & quinquaginta circiter annos … nunc primùm figuris vocalium insignitus"). https://find.library.upenn.edu/catalog/9979393712203681 ; https://sru.k10plus.de/opac-de-627?version=1.1&operation=searchRetrieve&query=pica.tit%3DTestamentum%20Muhammedem&recordSchema=mods ; https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000005.tif.large.jpg
T105 1668 republication (p. 151) Unverified VD17 and GVK title searches found no 1668 edition. 1668 is the date of a Rycaut English edition containing the treaty (see T106). The book may mean that, but this cannot be confirmed. as T92 ; https://archive.org/details/presentstateofot00ryca_0
T110 1690 "Hamburgh edition", reviewed by Basnage de Beauval in Histoire des ouvrages des savans (pp. 151, 158) Edition: Consistent. Review: partly verified VD17 23:259462T: Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Muhammedem et Christianae fidei cultores Arabice & Latine, Hamburgi: Henning Brendeke, 1690, [4] Bl., 27 S., 4°, ed. Abraham Hinkelmann, dedicated to Andreas Beier. Bayle cites the review as "Work of the Learned, Octob. 1690, pag. 80", which is consistent with the book's "Basnage 81–82". I could not open the review itself (the Halle copy is bot-blocked). The book's bibliography gives "Rotterdam: Leers, 1698", which is evidently a collected volume rather than the original 1690 issue. https://unapi.k10plus.de/?id=gvk:ppn:718463234&format=dc ; https://sru.k10plus.de/vd17?version=1.1&operation=searchRetrieve&query=pica.tit%3DTestamentum%20pactiones&recordSchema=mods ; https://archive.org/details/dictionaryhi_bayl_1738_04
T128 Republished "as late as 1888 CE" (p. 151) Unverified No 1888 edition was found in the catalogues searched. as T92
(omitted by book) — Additional printings Morrow does not list 1645: Pacifique's Le Voyage de Perse reissued "Avec … le Testament de Mahomet" (Paris: La Coste; GVK). 1683/84: Gottfried Weber, Schediasma de Testamento Muhammedis, quod vulgo dicitur (Coloniae Brandenburgicae: G. Schultze), which "Enth. außerdem" a reprint of Fabricius's 1638 Muhammedis Testamentum ("nunc recusum … MDCLXXXIII") (VD17). https://sru.k10plus.de/opac-de-627?version=1.1&operation=searchRetrieve&query=pica.tit%3Dtestament%20mahomet&recordSchema=dc ; https://sru.k10plus.de/vd17?version=1.1&operation=searchRetrieve&query=pica.tit%3DMuhammedis%20Testamentum&recordSchema=mods
C59 Sionita published it "without full vocalization and case endings" (p. 146) Consistent The 1630 Arabic pages are largely unvocalised (pp. 3–16 viewed). Nissel's 1655/1661 titles advertise vocalisation "for the first time". https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000025.tif.large.jpg
C60 Translated into Latin, French and German (p. 150) Consistent Latin: 1630 and 1638. French: Pacifique 1631; the Briot translation of Rycaut (GVK lists 1696 and 1709 Briot editions). 1b. Pacifique de Provins ("Scaliger") and the story of the find
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
C32 / people René de l'Escale dit Pacifique de Provins, b. 1588, d. 1648 (p. 141) Consistent BnF authority: "Pacifique de Provins (capucin, 1588-1648)". CCFR record of the 1631 Relation: author "Pacifique de Provins, De l'Escalle, père". The 1630 preface calls him "Pater Pacificus Scaliger ex Capucinorum familia". https://data.bnf.fr/fr/10742253/pacifique_de_provins/ ; https://ccfr.bnf.fr/portailccfr/ark:/16871/0013238542 ; https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000009.tif.large.jpg
T76 1622: Scaliger arrives in Constantinople, then travels through Egypt, the Holy Land and Syria (Pouillon) (p. 141) Consistent (departure only) Relation (1631): "Nous fismes voile … des Isles de Marseille le iour S. Vincent vingt-deuxiesme Ianuier mil six cens vingt-deux". The Constantinople arrival itself was not seen. https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZRtL0ZuZGeQC
T77 1623: returns to Italy and meets Gregory XV about the Capuchin missions; then goes to Paris (p. 141) Consistent Relation, c. p. 250 (OCR page number unclear): "ayant informé la Sainteté du Pape Grégoire quinzième, & la sacrée Congrégation … de Propaganda Fide" … then Paris. (Gregory XV died in July 1623.) https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZRtL0ZuZGeQC
T80 / C35 April 1627: Murad IV's two edicts for the Capuchins (Aleppo, then the whole Empire) (p. 142) Consistent Relation: one command written "à la fin du mois de Regeb, en l'année 1036, & des Chrestiens mil six cens vingt-sept le quinziesme Avril"; another "Donné en la cité d'Alep, le premier du mois de Chaban l'an mil trente six … Avril, mil six cens vingt-sept". https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZRtL0ZuZGeQC
T83 / C33 1628: Scaliger "headed to Syria and Mount Lebanon"; missions in Aleppo and Cyprus, then Baghdad and Isfahan (Pouillon) (p. 141) Minor difference By his own Relation, Pacifique was already in Aleppo from an August (most likely 1626, since he reports "un an entier" of opposition before the April 1627 edicts). He left Aleppo "environ le vingtiesme iour de Iuin mil six cens vingt-huict" and reached Baghdad after 52 days. A Persian command is dated October 1628. WP dates the Isfahan mission to 1627. So "1628 to Syria" is too late. Persia in 1628 is right. https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZRtL0ZuZGeQC ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacifique_de_Provins
T81–T82 / C27 The Testament "fortuitously fell into my hands"; the "violent but passing" tax persecution of "this past year, 1628" (pp. 140–141) Consistent Relation, pp. 405–406: "une chose très-rare qui m'est tombée fortuitement entre les mains … le Testament de Mahomet … cette année passée mil six cens vingt huict il s'esleva une bourrasque & persecution de bourse sur les Ecclesiastiques & marchands Chrestiens". The following clause ("les prenant en sa sauvegarde … il fit les pacts") is ambiguous as to who "il" is, as the book notes. The 1630 preface independently says he obtained it "foelici … casu" while working "in illis regionibus". https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZRtL0ZuZGeQC ; https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000009.tif.large.jpg
C5 / C28 / T94 / C41 1631 Relation du voyage de Perse; final piece "Pièce très rare et curieuse qui est le Testament de Mahomet"; the Turks call it his "main ou signature", made "avant mourir", authenticated by a secretary or notary (pp. 140–142) Consistent CCFR: Paris, Nicolas & Jean de La Coste, 1631, (2) f., 415 p., (6) f.; the title ends "Avec le Testament de Mahomet que les Turcs appellent sa main & signature qu'il fit avant que de mourir". Text pp. 405–415. https://ccfr.bnf.fr/portailccfr/ark:/16871/0013238542 ; https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZRtL0ZuZGeQC
C26 The Relation does not mention Mount Carmel as the place of discovery (p. 140) Consistent The only "Carmel" in the text is a topographic mention in the Holy Land itinerary. Neither the Testament section nor the 1630 preface names any place. https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZRtL0ZuZGeQC
T84 Scaliger leaves the Ottoman Empire in 1629 and goes to Paris (p. 141) Consistent (indirect) The Relation's "cette année passée … 1628" implies he was writing in 1629. Publication followed in 1631. https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ZRtL0ZuZGeQC
T85 In Paris "from 1629 to 1645", witnessing "edition after edition" (p. 142) Unverified / Opinion Only Paris 1630, Rostock 1638 (Latin) and his own 1645 reissue fall in this window (see 1a). as 1a
T98–T99 1645 to the Antilles; 1646 back to Paris, then Guiana (p. 141) Consistent Grunberg (PUR 2015): "Le capucin Pacifique de Provins part de La Rochelle en 1645, arrive à la Guadeloupe le 15 mai 1645 … avant de retourner en France durant l'été 1646." Binasco's monograph title (2006) covers "Levante, Acadia e Guyana, 1622-1648". https://books.openedition.org/pur/89698 ; https://nome.unak.is/previous-issues/issues/vol3_1/ferrara.html
T101 Dies in 1648 on the voyage to Guiana (p. 141) Year: Consistent. Circumstances: Unverified BnF authority gives 1648. The manner of death was not found in an opened source. https://data.bnf.fr/fr/10742253/pacifique_de_provins/
T106 / C18 / C25 Ricaut 1670 (French): treaty "found in a convent belonging to the monks of Mount Carmel … close to Mount Lebanon, and at one day's journey from Mecca, where Muslim pilgrims perform their Qurban"; "it is said" the original went to the King's Library (p. 140) Consistent Rycaut, Present State of the Ottoman Empire (English, 1668 ed.), p. 99: "the original of which was found in the Monastery of Fryars on Mount Carmel, neer Mount Libanus (which is within one days journey of Mecha, and is the place where the Mahometan Pilgrims make their Corban or Sacrifice …) and, as it is said, was transported to the Kings Library in France; which because it is ancient, and of curiosity …". Grassi (1825) quotes the French version (Riccaut "tome I, page 189"): "proche le mont Liban, à une journée de la Mecque … On dit que cet original a été porté dans la bibliothèque du roi". The 1670 Briot translation itself and its p. 320 were not opened. https://archive.org/details/presentstateofot00ryca_0 ; https://archive.org/details/charteturqueouo01grasgoog
C23 (geography) / p. 140 critique Ricaut's location is geographically impossible Consistent (with earlier precedent) The critique is old. Bayle (1737), note 149, reports Bespier's remark: "This is not at all probable; nay the treaty is signed at Medina, as the piece says; and therefore could not be made in the monastery of mount Carmel." https://archive.org/details/dictionaryhi_bayl_1738_04
T136 / C15 17th–19th-century sources say Scaliger found it in a Carmelite convent (Bayle; Van Dyke 85) (pp. 139–140) Consistent The General Dictionary (1735) vol. 1, art. "Addison (Lancelot)": "from the original, which it is said was found in a monastery of mount Carmel". Döllinger (Eng. tr. 1840, II, 95): Scaliger "received [it] from the Carmelites in Palestine". Van Dyck (1881), p. 85 (from Grassi): "found in a convent, belonging to the Carmelite order". A divergent version: Rehatsek (1877, p. 97 n. 141a) says he obtained it "from Arab Capuchin monks". https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_a-general-dictionary-hi_bayle-pierre_1741_1 ; https://archive.org/details/historyofchurcht02dl ; https://archive.org/details/cu31924007490422 ; https://archive.org/details/jasb-volume-13-for-1877-issue-no-35
T137 "There was a Catholic monastery at Mount Carmel during the time of Scaliger. Chronologically, the claim is correct" (p. 139) Inconsistent (lead source; needs confirmation) WP, "Stella Maris Monastery": the hermits left after the fall of Acre (1291); "In 1631 the Discalced branch of the Order returned to the Holy Land, led by the Venerable Father Prosper", who had a small monastery built on the promontory. The article mentions no Carmelite presence between 1291 and 1631 (its 1631 sentence is uncited; it lists Giordano 1994 for detail). On this evidence there was no Carmelite house there in 1627–28, when Pacifique obtained the text. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stella_Maris_Monastery
T135 / C48 17th–18th-century sources agree that Scaliger brought the text to Europe (p. 139, p. 142) Consistent 1630 preface: "Copiam illius Europae fecit … Pacificus Scaliger". Also Bayle (1737) art. Mahomet rem. [AA]; Mosheim; Gieseler; Döllinger; Rehatsek. URLs above
C42 Bayle (1735: 241) alleged that Scaliger personally forged the manuscript (p. 142) Minor difference (attribution) "Bayle 1735" is A General Dictionary, Historical and Critical, vol. 1 (London 1735), an English expansion of Bayle (the book's own bibliography confirms this). The passage is in the article "ADDISON (LANCELOT)". It reports that Dr. Lancelot Addison asked "a person very well skill'd in the Arabic tongue", who judged the piece spurious and thought it "very probable it had been forged by that Missionary". It is not Bayle's own allegation. https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_a-general-dictionary-hi_bayle-pierre_1741_1

1d. BnF MS Arabe 214 (the "1538" manuscript) and its dates
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
T55 / C63 / C67 MS Arabe 214, an anthology dated 1254 of the Martyrs (1538); formerly 385 (Regius) and Ancien fonds arabe 88 (p. 144) Consistent BnF Archives et manuscrits: "Arabe 214 • 385 (Regius) • Recueil … 1538"; old shelfmarks "385 (Regius)" and "Ancien fonds arabe 88". Calendar check: Bashans and Ba'una of AM 1254 fall in May–June 1538. https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877 ; https://archive.org/details/cataloguearabes00bibluoft
T56 / C69 Copy made for Yuhanna ibn Ishaq al-Batanuni by Girgis al-Ifrangi (ff. 114, 125), completed on 26 Bashans (f. 220), 28 Bashans (f. 231v) and 3 Ba'una 1254 (f. 256v) (p. 144) Consistent The BnF record has exactly this. Tabular 27 Muharram 945 = Tuesday 25 June 1538, a normal one-day offset between tabular and observed months. computation; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coptic_calendar ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabular_Islamic_calendar
C68 Physical description: 17 lines; written area 210 × 135 mm; Western paper; 262 ff. (261v and 262v blank); Coptic foliation; Egyptian hand; rubricated titles; 285 × 210 mm; brown calf binding with Napoleon I cipher (p. 144) Consistent Word for word with the BnF record. https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877
T125 The MS was bound on "April 13, 1872" (p. 146) Unverified The BnF describes a "Reliure veau raciné brun, dos maroquin rouge au chiffre de Napoléon Ier", which is a First Empire binding. A 13 April 1872 date may be a later stamp or restoration, but I could not see it (Gallica blocked). https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877
C7 / C63 / C65 / C76 Folio location of the charter: "folios 245-246" (de Slane via Guillaume); "12° (Fol. 245)"; BnF index "F. 257-261"; "sheets 257 to 262, that is, the last eleven pages" (pp. 144–146) Minor difference (catalogues differ) De Slane, p. 55 (page image checked): "12° (Fol. 245.) Copie de la charte accordée par Mahomet … avec les signatures d'environ une trentaine des Compagnons. C'est une des nombreuses rédactions de ce document apocryphe." He gives no "245–246". The modern BnF record: item 12 at "F. 257-261", with item 11 at ff. 232–256v, consistent with the 256v colophon. Ff. 257–261r is about 9 written pages, not "eleven". https://archive.org/download/cataloguearabes00bibluoft/page/n70_w1600.jpg ; https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877
C64 / C71 / C86 Copyist George, Jacobite, "of European origin"; "nothing in his writing indicates … a French writer" (p. 144–145, 175) Consistent De Slane: "le copiste … se nommait Georges, qu'il était de la religion jacobite et d'origine européenne; mais rien dans son écriture n'indique l'écrivain franc." https://archive.org/details/cataloguearabes00bibluoft

T108 / C70 Reading mark of Butrus ibn Diyab al-Halabi "dated 1673 CE" (f. 2) (p. 145) Consistent BnF: "marque de lecture de Buṭrus ibn Diyāb al-Ḥalabī, datée de 1673 J.-C." https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877
T75 Mark of Mansur ibn Sulayman Sahyun al-Ramadi, "14 Baba 1336 of the Martyrs (1620 CE)" (p. 145) Minor difference (calendar) The book follows the BnF ("14 Babā 1336 des Martyrs [1620 J.-C.]"). But 14 Baba (Paopi) 1336 AM = 12 Oct 1619 (Julian) / 22 Oct 1619 (Gregorian). For Thout to early Tubah the CE year is AM + 283, not + 284. computation; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coptic_calendar ; https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877
T66 Note of a missionary's arrival in Old Cairo, "9th of Hatur 1380 of the Martyrs (1592 CE)" (pp. 145, 175) Inconsistent (transcription error) + calendar slip The BnF record reads "le 9 Hatūr 1308 des Martyrs (1592 J.-C.)". Morrow transposed the digits (the book's own text has 1380; it is not an OCR error). 1380 AM would be 1663. And 9 Hatur 1308 = 6 Nov 1591 (Julian), so the BnF's own "1592" is one year off. Morrow's reading of the 1592 missionary as carrying the book "from Egypt to Mount Carmel" (p. 175) is his inference. https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877 ; computation
C70 / C74 Mark of "Gabriyal Sahyun al-Ziftawi" (f. 2v) "is that of Gabriel Sionita himself!" (p. 145) Disputed / unsupported The BnF gives "Ġabriyāl Ṣahyūn al-Ziftāwī" without identifying him. Al-Ziftāwī is a nisba from Zifta (Zefta), a town in the Gharbia governorate of the Egyptian Nile Delta. Sionita was born at Ehden in Lebanon (GEDSH; Catholic Encyclopedia: "Edden on the Lebanon") and went to Rome as a child. The same manuscript carries the surname Ṣahyūn for an Egyptian reader (Manṣūr ibn Sulaymān Ṣahyūn al-Ramādī, 1619), so the name alone does not point to Sionita. https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zefta ; https://gedsh.bethmardutho.org/al-Sahyuni-Jibrail ; https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/06331a.htm
C73 / T107 Renaudot's inference that Vansleb bought the MS is "chronologically incorrect", because Vansleb made "his two trips in 1671 and in 1672" (p. 145) Inconsistent (1) The BnF record states as provenance: "Une notice de Renaudot. Acheté par Vansleb en Orient. Cachets au chiffre de Vansleb". (2) Wansleben's Egyptian journeys were 1663–64 (for Ernst of Saxe-Gotha) and, for Colbert, from Marseille on 20 May 1671, reaching Damietta in March 1672 and spending about 12 months in Egypt (1672–73). Brill's editions are titled Travels in the Levant, 1671–1674 and Travels in Turkey, 1673–1676 (WP). A purchase in the 1670s is coherent with the seals and with the 1673 reading mark. It is incompatible with the MS being in Paris in 1629–30. https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Michael_Vansleb
C75 / C39 "There is no question that this is the actual document that he [Scaliger] brought back" (p. 145) Inconsistent with the evidence (and hedged by the author himself on pp. 168, 176) Against the identification: the Vansleb provenance and seals; the 1673 reading mark; the Egyptian nisba of "al-Ziftāwī"; and the textual divergence. The 1630 print has 36 witnesses, scribe Mu'awiya, a date and no basmala. The 1538 text has 30 witnesses, scribe 'Ali, no date and a Sufi-style invocation. Also, Cambridge UL MS Dd.11.33, ff. 37b–44a, contains "Two copies of the covenant made by Muhammad the Apostle of God with the Christians. Transcribed by Antoine Vitre, superintendent of the Imprimerie Royale" (Browne's 1900 hand-list no. 691, via Fihrist). This is an exemplar tied to the printer himself. Morrow's later work (2021; 2025 per Monferrer-Sala) places the 1630 text in a "Mu'awiyah lineage" with other copies (Rylands/Shidyāq; Cambridge). https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877 ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fihristorg/fihrist-mss/master/collections/cambridge%20university/Dd_11_33.xml ; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.3390/rel12090751 ; https://journals.uco.es/mediterranea/article/download/18755/17486/60103

1e. Date and wording of the covenant (Chapter 5 and the Chapter 10 texts)
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
T11 / C172; Ch. 10 World III p. 236 The 1630 covenant is dated "the second day of the month of Rabi' Ashar of the fourth year after the hijrah" (p. 147; World III: "…in Medina") Inconsistent (mistranslation) The 1630 Arabic (pp. 15–16) reads: وكتب معاوية بن ابي سفيان من املا رسول الله يوم الاثنين تمام اربعة اشهر من السنة الرابعة من الهجرة بالمدينة, i.e. "on Monday (yawm al-ithnayn), at the completion of four months of the fourth year of the Hijra, in Medina". The 1630 Latin (p. 16) reads "die Lunae ultima mensis quarti, anni quarti Hegirae, in Medina". No month name occurs. "Second day" appears to render yawm al-ithnayn (Monday) literally, and "Rabi' Ashar" is not a month name. The intended month (the fourth) is Rabi' al-Akhir. https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000037.tif.large.jpg ; https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000038.tif.large.jpg ; https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000022.tif.large.jpg

Van Dyck 1881 p. 87 has "the last day of the moon of the fourth month, the fourth year of the flight to Medina". Both took "die Lunae" (Monday) as "day of the moon". https://archive.org/details/presentstateofot00ryca_0 ; https://archive.org/details/cu31924007490422
T13 / T14 4 AH = "626" (Hinckelmann via Basnage, p. 158); 4 AH = "625" (Twiss, pp. 159–160) 625: Consistent. 626: Minor difference (AH→CE) Tabular: 4 AH = 13 Jun 625 – 1 Jun 626 (Julian). The 1630 Arabic has عمار بن ياسين (Latin "Omar ben-iamin"). https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000036.tif.large.jpg ; https://digital.slub-dresden.de/data/kitodo/testetpai_308498003/testetpai_308498003_tif/jpegs/00000037.tif.large.jpg

"Voetius, Hoornbeek, Bespier, and many other ministers embrace this opinion". Prideaux (via Bayle rem. [BB]): "Grotius rejects this capitulation as a forgery, and not without reason" (the 4 AH date after Uhud; Mu'awiya as secretary). Bayle himself, in the article text: "Proofs of the forgery may be drawn from the piece itself." https://archive.org/details/dictionaryhi_bayl_1738_04
C149 (Mosheim) / C113 / C150 / C151 Mosheim is an opponent; quotes from Mosheim 254–255 and an editor's note (pp. 151–152, 156–157) Quotes: Consistent. Label: Disputed Mosheim, Institutes (Murdock tr., 1839), I, pp. 450–451: "though some learned men doubt the authenticity of this instrument, yet the Mohammedans do not call it in question". In n. 3 he finds the Grotian forgery hypothesis "not incredible" and Muslim acceptance "of little weight" ("rude and illiterate Mohammedans"), rejects the style argument ("he might have employed his secretary"), and concludes "however dubious the Testament itself may be, the subject matter of it is not doubtful". The bracketed note signed "Schl." (Schlegel) calls it "a formal compact … with the Nestorians and Monophysites". Rehatsek (1877) says Mosheim "gives no opinion of his own, but states that Renaudot believed it to be genuine". So: a doubter, not a firm opponent. https://archive.org/details/institutesofeccl183901mosh ; https://archive.org/details/jasb-volume-13-for-1877-issue-no-35
C128 / C130 / C154 / §7 #12 "James Thayer Addison (1887–1953)" treats the covenant as factual; "A detailed defense … was also made by Dr. Addison whose arguments were summarized by Bayle"; Addison's Arabist informant thought Scaliger forged it (pp. 153, 154, 157) Inconsistent (wrong person and wrong position) "Bayle 1735: 241" is the General Dictionary I (1735), art. "ADDISON (LANCELOT)": Lancelot Addison (d. 1703), Dean of Lichfield, author of The First State of Mahumedism (2nd ed. London 1687). That article says Dr. Addison treats the treaty as "one of Mahomet's artifices to support his authority", later revoked, and reports his Arabist informant's judgment that it was "a spurious piece" probably "forged by that Missionary" (Scaliger). Neither a defence nor a 20th-century author. https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_a-general-dictionary-hi_bayle-pierre_1741_1
T112 / C167 Marana's L'Espion vol. 4 published 1697; Marana (1642–1693) (p. 160) Date: Consistent. Authorship: Disputed WP (citing Ballaster 2005; Betts 1984): Marana wrote vol. 1 (1684–86); a French edition of the later volumes appeared 1696–97. The later volumes are attributed variously to Marana or to Midgley and Bradshaw. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letters_Writ_by_a_Turkish_Spy
T109 "The English … would wait until 1688 before circulating an English translation" (p. 146) Inconsistent The English translation is in Rycaut's Present State, opened in the 1668 edition, pp. 99–102. An EEBO copy dated 1667 is on archive.org; the first edition is 1666–67. Twiss (1887, p. 431 n.) cites a later "Londres, 1688" edition, probably the source of the 1688 date. https://archive.org/details/presentstateofot00ryca_0 ; https://archive.org/details/bim_early-english-books-1641-1700_the-present-state-of-the_rycaut-paul-sir_1667 ; https://archive.org/details/ledroitdesgensou01twis
C139–C142 / T13 Basnage's review of the 1690 edition: Grotius doubted it; Hinckelmann says doubts subsided; "signed by thirty-three Muslims"; 4 AH = 626 (p. 158) Unverified (review not opened) Bayle cites the review (Oct. 1690, p. 80). The 1630 print has 36 witnesses, so "33" is either Basnage's count or a different edition's. https://archive.org/details/dictionaryhi_bayl_1738_04
C124 Nagy de Harsány treated it as trustworthy (pp. 152–153) Unverified Not opened. —
1g. Reception, 19th–20th centuries, and the 1795 Committee
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
T4 / T5 / C115 Fortescue 92: Yeshu'yab II "was said to have gone to see Mohammed"; Luke 68: Ishu-yahb II "is said to have" visited the Prophet; the charter is "generally regarded in the West as of dubious authenticity but accepted by early Moslem writers as genuine" (pp. 139, 152, 156) Consistent Fortescue (1913) p. 92. Luke, Mosul and its Minorities (1925) p. 68, which adds "Published in Paris by Gabriel Sionita in 1630". https://archive.org/details/lessereasternchu00fortuoft ; https://archive.org/details/mosulitsminoriti0000harr
T6 / T7 / T37 / C29 / C117 Bar Hebraeus (via Rehatsek 97) and Amrus (98) on Jesujab's diploma; Layard 207: "The substance of this treaty is given by three Syriac authors" (pp. 151–152) Consistent as reported (but note what the "substance" is) Rehatsek, JBBRAS XIII (1877), pp. 97–98, gives the Barhebraeus and 'Amru accounts as quoted. n. 141a: Sionita 1630, Fabricius 1638, Hinkelmann 1690; "brought to Europe by Pacificus Scaliger, who had obtained it from Arab Capuchin monks. Grotius believed the document to be spurious, and Salmasius genuine". Layard, Nineveh and its Remains (1849) I, ch. VIII n., is as quoted. The "substance" Layard and Luke describe (exemption from military service, 12 vs 4 coins, Christian women in Muslim service) is that of the Nestorian Isho'yahb/Najran charter, not the specific 1630 text. https://archive.org/details/jasb-volume-13-for-1877-issue-no-35 ; https://archive.org/details/b29350207_0001
C114 / C148 Layard: "rejected as a forgery by several European critics … its authenticity is admitted by early Mohammedan and Eastern Christian writers"; admits a Nestorian treaty (pp. 152, 156) Consistent Layard 1849 I: "which, however, it is right to state, has been rejected as a forgery by several European critics, whilst its authenticity is admitted by early Mohammedan and Eastern Christian writers". This is reporting, not a personal verdict, so Morrow's dual labelling (defender/neutral) reflects real ambiguity. https://archive.org/details/b29350207_0001
C152 / C153 / T93 Döllinger: the Testament Scaliger brought, "printed in Paris since 1630", and the Sinai document "all shows signs of being fictitious"; they would put Christians above Muslims, "as Tychsen observes"; he admits the Najran letter (p. 157) Consistent (opponent) Döllinger, History of the Church (Cox tr., 1840) II, p. 95 n.: "The so-called will of Muhammed, which the capuchin missionary, Pacificus Scaliger, received from the Carmelites in Palestine, and which was printed at Paris in 1630, and several times later … bear upon them every sign of invention … as Tychsen remarks, the condition of the Christians would have been better than that of the Muhammedans". In the main text he accepts Elmakyn's report of letters of peace given to the Nestorians of Negran through Jesujab II. (Morrow cites the 1842 French translation, p. 291; the English translation was used here.) https://archive.org/details/historyofchurcht02dl
C156 / C9 Gieseler: both the Testamentum et pactiones and the Pactum Muhammedis "are spurious" (p. 158) Consistent (opponent) Gieseler, Text-Book of Church History (1857) I, section on Islam and the Eastern churches, n. 7 (the book cites p. 563 n. 7): "though doubtless both the Testamentum et pactiones initae inter Mohammedem et christianae fidei cultores (first brought from the East by the Capuchin Pacificus Scaliger, and printed at Paris 1630, 4to, and often afterward), and the Pactum Muhammedis, quod indulsit Monachis montis Sinai et Christianis in universum … are spurious." He accepts that Muhammad had granted "letters of freedom" to some Arabian Christians. https://archive.org/details/textbookofchurch01gies
C155 Jacques 203: both documents are spurious (p. 158) Unverified; identity established The book's bibliography: Edwin E. Jacques, The Albanians: An Ethnic History (McFarland, 1995). Not opened. He is not a specialist on the subject. book/chunks/09_appendices_illus_biblio.txt
T14 / T18 / C143–C146 Twiss: "conditions" "perfectly harmonious with the Qur'an"; the Testament (625) and 'Umar's capitulations (636); forgers would have avoided contradicting Muslim law; possibly a bilateral treaty (pp. 159–160) Consistent, with a nuance Twiss, Le droit des gens (1887), pp. 431–432, as summarised. But Twiss also writes that the authenticity "a été mise en doute", calls it "le soi-disant testament", and claims only "haute ancienneté". His argument runs from antiquity, not proof. For the 'Umar date, Gieseler gives 637 ("Omar, at the taking of Jerusalem, 637"). https://archive.org/details/ledroitdesgensou01twis ; https://archive.org/details/textbookofchurch01gies
T122 / C131–C133 Grassi, Charte Turque (1826): commentary on the "Traité de Mahomet avec les Chrétiens" (75–89); the Testament "a political and moral masterpiece"; front page "The Charter of Muhammad only is inviolable…" (pp. 153, 155) Minor difference (date); quotes Consistent; one nuance archive.org copy, tome II: Paris, P. Mongie aîné, 1825. Van Dyck also cites "Paris, 1825, tome 2, pp. 74 to 89". The 1826 Dupont issue cited by Morrow was not seen. P. 75: "Ce traité doit être considéré comme un chef-d'œuvre de politique, et comme un monument rare de sagesse, de morale et de tolérance". The epigraph reads "La Charte mahométane seule est inviolable … obligatoires pour le riche, pour le pauvre, pour le prince lui-même". That refers to Islamic law in general, not the Testament. https://archive.org/details/charteturqueouo01grasgoog ; https://archive.org/details/cu31924007490422
T124 / C134 Miltitz, Manuel des consuls (1838), II, 496–499, prints "Privilège accordé par Mahomet aux Chrétiens", a French translation of Ricaut (p. 153) Unverified / Disputed (location) I could not find the piece in the OCR of the archive.org volumes I opened (vol. II, pts. 1–3; the metadata gives 1837, and the text cites 1838 works). Twiss (1887, p. 431 n.) places the French text in "Manuel des consuls … t. I, App. n° 1, Berlin, 1837". https://archive.org/details/manueldesconsul02miltgoog ; https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_Bo4OAAAAQAAJ ; https://archive.org/details/ledroitdesgensou01twis
T126 / C135–C137 1881: "Edward A. Van Dyke", US consular clerk at Cairo; translation based on the French in Ricaut; "considered by many as apocryphal" (87), but "he himself believed that it was genuine"; Muir reference (p. 154) Facts: Consistent. Spelling: Van Dyck. "Believed genuine": Unsupported Capitulations of the Ottoman Empire: Report of Edward A. Van Dyck, Consular Clerk … at Cairo (Washington: GPO, 1881), Appendix 1, "Mahommed's Will or Command", pp. 85–87. It is headed "[See 'Charte Turque', by M. Grassi, Paris, 1825, tome 2, pp. 74 to 89.]" and gives the text "as it has been given in the work of M. Riccaut". It ends "[Note.—This treaty is considered by many as apocryphal.]" and refers to Muir. The introductory paragraphs are Grassi's French in translation, so there is no separate statement of Van Dyck's own belief. https://archive.org/details/cu31924007490422
C138 / T146 "Plagiarizing Grassi (75), Van Dyke writes" the "masterpiece" line; Van Dyke was "reacting" to the Greek war, "projecting the alleged Turkish oppression of the Greeks back to the Prophet" (p. 154) Inconsistent Van Dyck credits Grassi at the head of the appendix, so this is not plagiarism. The Greek-war sentence ("It is by this Sûrah … that the Turks behaved with such cruelty in the war of Greek independence") translates Grassi 1825, p. 76: "la cruauté qui leur est justement reprochée dans la guerre actuelle avec les Grecs". It is Grassi writing during the war, not Van Dyck in 1881. https://archive.org/details/cu31924007490422 ; https://archive.org/details/charteturqueouo01grasgoog
T115 / C159 22 June 1795, 441st session: letter from Lefebvre-Villebrune; the pact to be printed in Arabic with a French translation for the consuls in the Levant (Guillaume 320) (pp. 154–155) Consistent Guillaume VI: "QUATRE CENT QUARANTE ET UNIÈME SÉANCE, Du 4 messidor an III [22 juin 1795]". The Committee, "lecture faite d'une lettre du citoyen Lefèvre-Villebrune … de rendre public … le pacte fait entre Mahomet et les chrétiens, l'an 4 de l'hégire, arrête que ledit pacte sera imprimé à l'imprimerie de la République, en arabe, avec la traduction française … distribué aux consuls de la République dans les Échelles du Levant". (4 messidor III = 22 June 1795.) https://archive.org/details/procsverbauxdu06fran
T116 / C161 23 Oct 1795, 511th session: 1,000 copies by the legal office's press for Committee members, all libraries, the Levant ports and European scholars; Grégoire charged with the last article (Guillaume 827) (p. 155) Consistent (Grégoire's name not legible in the OCR) "CINQ CENT ONZIÈME SÉANCE, Du 1er brumaire an IV [23 octobre 1795]": "la traduction faite par le citoyen [Lefèvre-]Villebrune du Pacte de Mahomet en faveur des chrétiens sera imprimée à l'imprimerie [du dépôt] des lois au nombre de mille exemplaires … membres du Comité … toutes les bibliothèques de la République … Échelles du Levant … savants de l'Europe". Page 827 (p. 828 follows). https://archive.org/details/procsverbauxdu06fran
T117 / C162 514th session (no date given): Lefebvre-Villebrune "suddenly removed from the project and replaced by a certain Mr. Legrand"; reproached for removing a manuscript (Guillaume 858 and n. 4) (p. 155) Inconsistent in detail "CINQ CENT QUATORZIÈME SÉANCE, Du 3 brumaire an IV [25 octobre 1795]" (evening). The Committee withdrew its morning nomination of Lefebvre-Villebrune as keeper of modern manuscripts at the Bibliothèque nationale and chose instead "le citoyen Legrand, auteur des Fabliaux" for that post. Separately, it "rapporte son arrêté du 1er brumaire relatif à l'impression du prétendu Traité de Mahomet … ainsi que tous autres arrêtés qui pourraient avoir le même objet" and ordered Lefebvre-Villebrune to return within three days "l'exemplaire qui devait servir à l'impression" and Adam's manuscript translation of Athenaeus. Note 4: "Il semble qu'on ait fait grief à Lefebvre de Villebrune d'avoir déplacé un manuscrit … mais il avait pu s'y croire autorisé"; the Athenaeus manuscript was probably the main cause. https://archive.org/details/procsverbauxdu06fran
T118 "To the best of my knowledge" the translation was never published (p. 155) Consistent (and explained) The printing order was formally rescinded on 3 brumaire IV (25 Oct 1795). https://archive.org/details/procsverbauxdu06fran
C116 / C128 (Madrazo, Société d'Amis) / C129 / C123 Féraud-Giraud 36; Madrazo 123; Annales de la Religion 112–113; SDUK 362 Unverified Not opened. —

T39 / T40 / C100 / C105 Ottoman printing "banned … from 1483 to 1729", "punishable by death" (p. 148) Disputed among sources The claim traces to André Thevet (1584). Feodorov (2023) says no Ottoman document has been found; Schwartz (2017) argues there "never was such a ban". The Müteferrika firman is dated 5 Jul 1727 and his first book 1729. https://library.oapen.org/bitstream/20.500.12657/76898/1/9783110786996.pdf ; https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/332F7012F00F4D7D87C3EB268E451DF6/core-reader
T44 First Arabic press in the Vatican, early 16th c. (p. 148) Inconsistent The first Arabic movable-type book is the 1514 "Fano" (probably Venetian) Horologion. The Vatican press dates from 1587. Feodorov pp. 9–10, 17 (URL above)
T45 1514 Fano book: "first known Islamic book printed in the West", patron Julius II (p. 150) Inconsistent ("Islamic"); Disputed (place/patron) It is a Christian Book of Hours (BnF: "Diurnal … à l'usage des Jacobites"). Julius II died in Feb 1513. https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb368264623 ; Feodorov
T48 Genoa 1516 polyglot Psalter (p. 150) Consistent BnF record. https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb305135983
T53 / T61 / C107 A French-printed Qur'an c. 1536 with Henri II arms, bound 1549, in the BnF; "the French were the first to machine press the Qur'an" (p. 149) Inconsistent No such printed edition is known. The first printed Arabic Qur'an is Paganini, Venice, 9 Aug 1537 – 9 Aug 1538. Nothing matching was found in BnF SRU searches. Feodorov p. 12 ; https://online-exhibitions.library.columbia.edu/exhibits/show/quran/qurans/printed
T54 Paganini Qur'an 1537/38 "apparently burned" (p. 149) Date: Consistent. Burning: Disputed/Unverified Copy rediscovered in 1987 (Nuovo). Contemporary explanations of its disappearance "vary widely". https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paganino_Paganini
T50 / T51 / C88 1536 capitulations (Jean de La Forêt) granting protection of the Holy Places (p. 145, 148) Disputed (1536); Inconsistent (Holy Places) The 1536 text is contested or regarded as a draft (ratified 1569). The Jerusalem clauses first appear in Arts. IV–V of the 1604 capitulations. Twiss (1887) dates the first treaty to 1535. https://heritage.bnf.fr/bibliothequesorient/en/capitulations ; https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/12488a.htm ; https://archive.org/details/ledroitdesgensou01twis

T100 Du Ryer's French Qur'an 1647 (p. 151) Consistent BnF record. https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb33327671k

T114 Müteferrika's press 1726 (p. 148) Minor difference 1726 petition; 1727 firman; 1729 first book. Feodorov pp. 90–91

3. Discrepancies ranked by significance (most serious first)

  1. The identification of BnF Arabe 214 as the manuscript Scaliger brought and Sionita printed (pp. 144–146; "there is no question", p. 145). This is the chapter's central documentary claim, and the evidence runs against it.

    • The BnF's own record gives the provenance as "Acheté par Vansleb en Orient", with Vansleb seals. Wansleben was in Egypt in 1663–64 and 1672–73.
    • The record carries a reading mark dated 1673.
    • The mark Morrow reads as Sionita's belongs to a "Ġabriyāl Ṣahyūn al-Ziftāwī". Zifta is in the Egyptian Delta; Sionita was from Ehden, Lebanon.
    • The 1538 text differs from the 1630 print in its opening, scribe ('Ali vs Mu'awiya), date (none vs Monday at the end of the 4th month, 4 AH) and witnesses (30 vs 36).
    • A Cambridge manuscript (UL Dd.11.33) contains "two copies of the covenant … transcribed by Antoine Vitré", the 1630 printer.
    • Morrow's rebuttal of the Vansleb provenance ("chronologically incorrect") depends on wrong travel dates (1671/1672) and on assuming the conclusion. He himself hedges on pp. 168 and 176, and his 2021 and 2025 work places the 1630 text in a separate "Mu'awiyah lineage".
    • Sources: BnF record; de Slane p. 55; SLUB images; Fihrist TEI for Dd.11.33; Crossref (Morrow 2021); Monferrer-Sala 2026.

  2. The covenant's date is mistranslated (p. 147; World III, p. 236). The 1630 Arabic has yawm al-ithnayn tamām arbaʿat ashhur min al-sana al-rābiʿa ("Monday, at the completion of four months of the fourth year"). The Latin has "die Lunae ultima mensis quarti". The book's "second day of the month of Rabi' Ashar" names a non-existent month and turns "Monday" into "second day". This matters because Morrow builds dating arguments on it (the Jewish conflict; "the same year as the Assyrian covenant"). On the CE side, 625 (Twiss) is right for the stated month; Hinckelmann's 626 is not.

  3. "Dr. Addison" is misidentified, and his position reversed (pp. 153–154, 157). The book lists James Thayer Addison (1887–1953) among those who treat the covenant as factual and credits "Dr. Addison" with a "detailed defense … summarized by Bayle". The source ("Bayle 1735: 241" = General Dictionary I, 1735, art. "ADDISON (LANCELOT)") is about Lancelot Addison (d. 1703), Dean of Lichfield. He treated the treaty as a temporary "artifice" and reported an Arabist's view that Scaliger probably forged it. The roster of "defenders" is inflated accordingly. Relatedly, the allegation that Scaliger forged the text (p. 142) is the informant's, as reported in the Addison article, not Bayle's own.

  4. The publication history is overstated (p. 151; p. 146).

    • No evidence was found for "four times during the first year".
    • No 1668 or 1888 edition was found.
    • The 1638 printing is Fabricius's Latin-only text.
    • Printings in 1645, 1660, 1661 and 1683/84 are omitted.
    • The "1688" English translation is a later edition. Rycaut printed an English translation in 1666–68.

    The book uses the inflated history to argue strong demand and early European acceptance.

  5. The Coptic dates in the MS are mis-transcribed and mis-converted (pp. 145, 175). The BnF reads 9 Hatur 1308; Morrow prints 1380, which would be 1663. The BnF's conversions, copied by Morrow, are each one year late: 14 Baba 1336 is 1619, not 1620, and 9 Hatur 1308 is 1591, not 1592. The 1254 = 1538 conversion, and the Monday 24 June 1538 colophon, are correct.

  6. The Mount Carmel chronology (p. 139). The book says Ricaut's claim is "chronologically … correct" because a Catholic monastery stood on Mount Carmel in Scaliger's day. A lead source (WP) says the Carmelites returned only in 1631, after Pacifique's 1627–28 stay. This needs a specialist source (Giordano 1994) for confirmation. Note also that the Medina dating already contradicted Mount Carmel in Bespier's 17th-century critique.

  7. Van Dyck (p. 154).

    • His appendix explicitly credits Grassi (1825), so "plagiarizing" is wrong.
    • The "war of Greek independence" sentence is Grassi's (1825), not Van Dyck's own reaction in 1881.
    • There is no textual basis for "he himself believed that it was genuine".
    • His name is spelled Van Dyck.

  8. The 1795 Committee (p. 155). Lefebvre-Villebrune was not "replaced by Mr. Legrand" on the project. Legrand replaced him as nominee for keeper of modern manuscripts at the Bibliothèque nationale. The printing order itself was formally rescinded on 3 brumaire IV (25 Oct 1795), the "prétendu Traité". The other session dates and numbers are correct.

  9. Printing-history claims used as context (pp. 148–150; fork).

    • A French printed Qur'an c. 1536, and "the French were the first": no evidence. The first is Venice 1537–38.
    • The 1514 "Islamic book" is a Christian Horologion.
    • The Ottoman printing "ban" is disputed.
    • The 1536 capitulations with Holy Places protection: the 1536 text is contested, and the Holy Places clauses come only in 1604.
    • Chejne's dates for Aleppo and Lebanon are wrong.

  10. Classification of scholars. Mosheim is labelled an opponent. His text calls the Testament "dubious" and finds the forgery hypothesis "not incredible", but rejects the style argument and accepts its "subject matter". Rehatsek (1877) says he "gives no opinion of his own". Layard reports both views rather than endorsing one. Twiss argues from antiquity while calling it the "soi-disant testament". Morrow's other labels match the texts opened: Salmasius, Hinckelmann, Renaudot and Sionita as defenders; Hottinger as neutral; Grotius, Voetius, Hoornbeek, Bespier, Prideaux, Bayle, Döllinger and Gieseler as opponents.

  11. Smaller points.

  • Vansleb's travel years.
  • Pacifique's arrival in Syria (1626/27, not 1628).
  • Sionita's chair (1614, not 1618).
  • Grassi's date (1825, not 1826).
  • The folio numbers in Arabe 214.
  • The Chronicle of Seert (10th–11th c., not 9th).
  • Grassi's "Charte mahométane" epigraph refers to Islamic law, not the Testament.
  • Lamartine names an Austrian envoy, not "European diplomats".
  • World III lists 38 witnesses (a duplicated Zayd ibn Arqam and a split name) where the print has 36.

4. Scholarly assessment of authenticity (both sides, neutrally stated)

What is not in dispute.

  • An Arabic text titled al-ʿAhd wa-l-shurūṭ was printed in Paris in 1630 from a copy Pacifique de Provins brought from the Levant, with a Latin version commissioned by Hotman.
  • A related but distinct recension of a "charter granted to all Christians" was copied in Egypt in 1538 in a Coptic/Jacobite apologetic anthology (BnF Arabe 214).
  • De Slane (1883–95) already called it "one of the numerous redactions of this apocryphal document".

Arguments and authorities for authenticity, or at least for early origin.

  • Renaudot (1713). The Testament is found "in various manuscripts". Even Muslims do not doubt it. Those who call it spurious are only "moderately versed" in Arabic literature. He holds that Christian affairs were in fact ordered according to its provisions. (https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_r5tk9rAzY6AC)

  • Salmasius and Hinckelmann (per Bayle 1737). Salmasius held it a genuine "league and covenant", linking it to Elmacin's report that Muhammad granted Christians safe-conduct for tribute. Hinckelmann held the same opinion. (https://archive.org/details/dictionaryhi_bayl_1738_04)

  • Twiss (1887). Whatever its authenticity, the document is of "haute ancienneté". Its term "conditions" fits Islamic law. Forgers would have avoided wording inadmissible in Muslim courts. (https://archive.org/details/ledroitdesgensou01twis)

  • Manuscript evidence. The 1538 manuscript shows that a version circulated about 90 years before 1630, so Scaliger did not invent the genre in 1628–29. Further copies exist in Cambridge (Dd.11.33) and Manchester (Rylands, per Morrow 2021). Morrow (2021) suggests the Rylands/Shidyāq covenant could be "the missing link" between the Najran covenant of the Chronicle of Seert and the 1630 Testamentum. (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fihristorg/fihrist-mss/master/collections/cambridge%20university/Dd_11_33.xml ; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.3390/rel12090751)

  • Parallels with the Nestorian charter tradition. The substance parallels the charter for Isho'yahb II and the Christians of Najran reported by Bar Hebraeus, Mari and 'Amr (Layard 1849; Rehatsek 1877). Even sceptics such as Döllinger and Gieseler accepted that Muhammad gave some Arabian Christians letters of protection. (https://archive.org/details/b29350207_0001 ; https://archive.org/details/jasb-volume-13-for-1877-issue-no-35 ; https://archive.org/details/historyofchurcht02dl ; https://archive.org/details/textbookofchurch01gies)

  • Recent defenders.

    • Morrow (2013 and later).
    • Zein and El-Wakil, The Covenants of the Prophet Muḥammad (Routledge 2022/23). The reviewer Negoiță (JAAR 93:4, 2025) describes the book as "systematically debunking the longstanding skepticism", using "transmission nuances, calendar synchronization, and scribal convention analyses".
    • Sellam (AJIS 2015) reviewed Morrow 2013 favourably.
    • Considine (Religions 2016) uses the covenants as a framework for pluralism.

    (https://academic.oup.com/jaar/article/93/4/740/8316999 ; https://www.ajis.org/index.php/ajiss/article/view/977 ; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.3390/rel7020015)

Arguments and authorities for later composition or forgery.

  • Internal anachronism. Mu'awiya is named as secretary in 4 AH, but he joined Islam at the conquest of Mecca (8 AH/630), or at most at Hudaybiyya (628). Prideaux (1697, via Bayle rem. [BB]) made this point. Morrow himself concedes that the scribe and date are later "Umayyad additions" (p. 167).
  • Historical implausibility (Prideaux). In 4 AH, soon after Uhud, Muhammad was not powerful enough for anyone to seek his protection on such terms. Provenance contradiction (Bespier, via Bayle): a text "signed at Medina" cannot have been made at Mount Carmel.
  • Content too favourable to Christians. Grotius: "haud dubie a Christianis suppositum, ut sub obtentu tanti nominis Musulmanis aequioribus uterentur". Tychsen and Döllinger: it would put Christians in a better condition than Muslims; it bears "every sign of invention". Gieseler: "doubtless … spurious". Mosheim found the hypothesis of fabrication by Syrian and Arabian monks "not incredible", comparing the Sinai patent, which he thought "beyond all controversy fraudulently drawn up". (https://archive.org/details/dictionaryhi_bayl_1738_04 ; https://archive.org/details/historyofchurcht02dl ; https://archive.org/details/textbookofchurch01gies ; https://archive.org/details/institutesofeccl183901mosh)
  • Style and attestation.
    • Lancelot Addison's Arabist found nothing Qur'anic in its style and suspected Scaliger (General Dictionary I, 1735). Mosheim discounted the style argument.
    • Morrow concedes (p. 139) that the text is absent from Islamic sources.
    • It survives in Christian manuscripts and in divergent redactions: two scribes, differing witness lists, dated and undated forms.
    • The 1630 publication followed a 1628 fiscal "persecution" of Levantine Christians, which Pacifique himself links to the text.
  • Catalogue and archival judgments. De Slane (1883–95): "document apocryphe". Guillaume (1907): "document apocryphe", "prétendu Traité". The Revolutionary Committee rescinded its own printing order in October 1795.
  • The parent Najran tradition. Philip Wood dates the Chronicle of Seert to the 10th–11th century and has a 2021 study whose title treats the Najran treaty as a "re-writing of the past" (Al-Masāq 33:2; I read only the title and metadata). This bears on Morrow's argument (pp. 146–147, 175) that the World covenant shares an ancient origin with the Najran text. (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/9781444338386.wbeah30539 ; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1080/09503110.2021.1910782)
  • Assessment of Morrow's method. Monferrer-Sala's review of Morrow's 2025 sequel (Mediterranea 11, 2026, pp. 403–408): "the work at times conflates textual reception with historical origin … its historical argumentation is more persuasive as advocacy than as a decisive demonstration of authenticity". (https://journals.uco.es/mediterranea/article/download/18755/17486/60103)

When and by whom, if later. The sources opened propose these alternatives (none is proven):

  • Christians generally, to win milder treatment (Grotius).
  • Monks of Syria or Arabia (the Grotian view, as Mosheim reports it).
  • The Carmelites in Palestine, as the source of Scaliger's copy (Döllinger's provenance).
  • Scaliger himself (Addison's informant, 1678/1687). The 1538 manuscript rules this out for the genre, though not for the specific 1630 recension.
  • For the Najran parent text, an Abbasid-era Church of the East milieu (Wood 2021, from its title; the 878 "discovery" is reported by the Chronicle, which another agent is checking).

Neutral summary. The documentary record supports three points:

  1. Versions of a "charter of Muhammad to all Christians" circulated among Arabic-speaking Christians by 1538.
  2. The 1630 recension contains at least one clear anachronism (Mu'awiya as scribe in 4 AH) and has no Islamic attestation.
  3. Opinion has been divided since 1630.

On the authorities opened here, most specialist historians from Grotius to Gieseler and the BnF cataloguers judged the text apocryphal. Renaudot, Salmasius, Hinckelmann and, among moderns, Morrow and Zein & El-Wakil defend an authentic core. Monferrer-Sala's 2026 review judges Morrow's approach "more persuasive as advocacy than as a decisive demonstration of authenticity".

5. Items not checked, and why

  • Images of BnF Arabe 214. Gallica blocks automated access (Cloudflare 403). I therefore could not verify, from the manuscript itself:
    • the 1538 wording, the 30 witnesses, the change of hand and 'Ali as scribe;
    • the colophon text and the "Michel" reading;
    • the f. 2v mark, and the 13 April 1872 binding date.
  • Basnage de Beauval's review (Oct. 1690), including the "33 witnesses" and "626": no accessible copy (Halle is bot-blocked); only Bayle's citation of it was seen.
  • Morrow's secondary sources, not opened (lending-restricted, paywalled or not found):
    • Pouillon, Bernard, Balagna, Goujet, Thenaud/Schefer, Hamilton & Richard, Toomer, Göçek, Chejne, Hadjiantonious;
    • Madrazo, the Société d'Amis' Annales de la Religion, Féraud-Giraud, the SDUK;
    • Jacques (The Albanians), Nagy de Harsány, Marana vol. IV;
    • the 1670 Briot edition of Rycaut, p. 320; Döllinger's French translation (1842), p. 291 (the English translation was used instead).
  • Miltitz pp. 496–499: not located in the OCR of the volumes opened.
  • Catalogue pages for the 1638 edition (Czech national library 502; Marsh's Library and DDB blocked by bot-checks). Covered instead by VD17 via SRU.
  • CMR entries (Moukarzel, "Testamentum et pactiones…"; "Gabriel Sionita"; "Pacifique de Provins"; "Relation du voyage de Perse"): paywalled. Only their existence and metadata were seen (https://doi.org/10.1163/2451-9537_cmrii_com_29350 ; …_29347 ; …_28368 ; …_28369).
  • Wood 2021 (Al-Masāq) and Morrow 2021 (Religions): full texts blocked (T&F, MDPI). Only Crossref metadata and, for Morrow, the abstract were used.
  • The Carmelite 1281 constitution and the 1631 Carmelite return: only a WP lead was opened for the return.
  • Ch. 5 rows outside this section's documentary focus: Najran 878, the Assyrian covenant, early-Islamic narrative rows and lifespans are left to other agents. Detailed checking of Morrow's clause-by-clause Arabic translations, beyond the opening, date, scribe, witnesses and close of the 1630 print, was not attempted.
  • Valerianus Oserole's 1659 annotations: a private copy, not checkable.
  • Printing-history quotations (Göçek, Chejne, Ágoston, Wheatcroft, Finkel, Boullata): see the fork's file, §3.

Fact-check reports

Assyrian and Armenian covenants

207 table rows · source file V5_assyrian_armenian.md

V5: Checking Morrow (2013), Chapter 6 (Assyrian Christians) and Chapter 7 (Armenian Christians of Jerusalem) against independent sources

Book: John Andrew Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013), pp. 177–204.

Input: the extraction scratchpad/extract/06_ch6_ch7.md. IDs used below:

  • T = row of its timeline table (§2);
  • C = item in its factual-claims list (§4).

The book's wording was checked against book/chunks/06_ch6_ch7.txt. The Assyrian covenant text was checked at PDF pp. 338–347 of 07_texts_ch8_ch12.txt.

Method

  • Every verdict rests on a page that was opened, either by me or by one of four sub-checks whose working files are listed below. Search snippets were not used as evidence.
  • Full texts came from archive.org, read as djvu text with page images where pagination mattered. Other sources were GEDSH online, Encyclopaedia Iranica, open-access journals, and Wayback snapshots.
  • Wikipedia is used only as a lead, or for uncontroversial dates, and is labelled where used.
  • Calendar. AH→CE conversions use the tabular Islamic calendar (epoch 16 July 622, Julian), cross-checked with the Aladhan API. Treat them as ±2 days.
  • Before marking an item Inconsistent, I checked for OCR misreadings (several against the book's page images) and calendar spans, and looked for a second source.

Working files. Full detail and extra quotations are in these files, all in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-cool-Documents-Turkey-Trip/7546f7f6-5b83-4cbe-bfaf-72579fbd2e97/scratchpad/verify/parts/:

  • A_assyrian_sources.md: Ch. 6 sources;
  • B_ottoman_kurdish.md: Ottoman, Kurdish and Church-of-the-East chronology, and the digressions;
  • C_islamic_chronology.md: early-Islamic chronology, 'Umar, 'Ali, Muktafi;
  • D_armenian_golubovich.md: Armenian material, Golubovich, Thenaud, Avdall, Thomson, the Sharif.

Verdict legend

  • Consistent: independent sources agree.
  • Minor difference: a spelling slip, an AH/CE span, a wrong page, or a small overstatement.
  • Inconsistent: reliable sources say otherwise; the row says what they say.
  • Disputed: sources disagree with each other; the row gives each version.
  • Unverified: no reliable source could be opened; the row says what was tried.
  • Opinion: not checkable as fact.

But the cited article says "The massacre of 30,000 Christians in 1847 was succeeded by another in 1896. In 1915 ... 250,000 Assyrians", and attributes the destruction belief to "Assyrians", not Yelda. https://gedsh.bethmardutho.org/Hakkari ; https://archive.org/details/massacres-resistance-protectors-muslim-christian-relations-in-eastern-anatolia-d ; CT (as T9)
T51 The covenant was destroyed "at some later point" than 1845/47 but before 1915 (p. 182) Opinion, unsupported This inference rests on merging the two relics (T45) and on misdating Yelda's massacre (T50). as T45, T50
T52 1935: Hagia Sophia turned into a museum (p. 187) Minor difference Council of Ministers decree of 24 Nov 1934; opened as a museum on 1 Feb 1935 (Akan 2020; EOE "1934"). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/1184889 ; EOE
T53 1990s: Muslims visited the Virgin of Seidnaya (p. 189) Consistent with Jenkins Jenkins p. 205 (citing Dalrymple). Jenkins
T54 "End of the twentieth century": Canada recognised Quebec as a nation; Spain recognised Catalonia, Galicia and the Basque Country as autonomous (p. 184) Quebec Inconsistent. Spain Consistent House of Commons motion "the Québécois form a nation within a united Canada", adopted 27 Nov 2006. Spain: Basque and Catalan statutes of 18 Dec 1979; Galicia, 6 Apr 1981. https://www.noscommunes.ca/Content/House/391/Journals/087/Journal087.PDF ; https://boe.es/boe/dias/1979/12/22 ; https://www.boe.es/eli/es/lo/1981/04/06/1
T55 March 2001: the Taliban destroyed the Bamiyan Buddhas, inspired by Salafism (p. 184) Date Consistent; "Salafism" is Opinion UNAMA: destroyed "by the Taliban regime in March 2001". https://unama.unmissions.org/en/node/61683
