1. Verification table

1A. Chapter 13: witness dates, conversions and identifications

TDV URLs have the form https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/<slug>; the slug is given in brackets. "IH" = Ibn Hisham (OpenITI line numbers of the downloaded file in brackets).

# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source
1 'Ali d. 661 (p. 323) Consistent d. 40/661 TDV [ali]
2 Abu Bakr c. 573–634 (p. 323) Consistent d. 13/634 TDV [ebu-bekir]
3 'Umar 579–644; 'Uthman 577–656 (p. 323) Consistent d. 23/644; d. 35/656 TDV [omer], [osman]
4 Abu al-Darda' d. 652 (pp. 323, 325) Consistent d. 32/652 (variant 31/651). Reportedly converted "during the Badr campaign, as the last of the Ansar" (Ramadan 2 AH, c. March 624). The conversion date matters for the Sinai list (row 1C-1). TDV [ebud-derda]
5 Abu Hurayrah 603–681; moved to Medina "during the last few years of the Prophet's life" (p. 323) Death: Minor difference. Move: Consistent Converted early 7 AH (628) via Tufayl b. 'Amr; came to Medina in Muharram 7 (May 628); d. 58/678 (variants 57, 59). Morrow's own point (he cannot fit an AH 2 document) is correct. His suggestion that Abu Hurayra "may have been in Medina on a voyage at an earlier date" has no source. TDV [ebu-hureyre]
6 "Abu Hudayfah ibn al-Yaman" d. 656, proposed reading for "Abu Hurayrah" (p. 323) Minor difference (name) The Companion is Hudhayfa b. al-Yaman, kunya Abu 'Abd Allah, d. 36/656 at al-Mada'in. "Abu Hudhayfa b. al-Yaman" conflates him with Abu Hudhayfa b. 'Utba. TDV [huzeyfe-b-yeman]
7 Salim mawla Abi Hudhayfa died fighting Musaylima under Abu Bakr (p. 323) Consistent Killed at al-Yamama, 12/633, beside Abu Hudhayfa b. 'Utba TDV [salim-mevla-ebu-huzeyfe], [ebu-huzeyfe]
8 Ibn Mas'ud d. c. 650 (p. 323) Minor difference d. 32/652–53 in Medina TDV [abdullah-b-mesud]
9 al-'Abbas d. 652/653 (p. 323) Consistent d. 32/653. Conversion is disputed: TDV reports he became Muslim secretly early on and stayed in Mecca; he fought on the Meccan side at Badr, was captured, and declared his Islam openly only around the conquest of Mecca. TDV [abbas--sahabi]
10 Hassan b. Thabit d. 674 (p. 323) Disputed among sources TDV gives 40/660, 50/670 or 54/674 (header "60/680 [?]"). Morrow's 674 = one of the reported years. Converted c. 622 (after the second 'Aqaba) at about 60. TDV [hassan-b-sabit]
11 Zubayr 594–656; Talha d. 656; Camel 656 (p. 323) Consistent Both d. 36/656. Talha killed at the Camel, Jumada II 36 / Dec 656. Both were very early converts. TDV [zubeyr-b-avvam], [talha-b-ubeydullah]
12 Sa'd b. Mu'adh d. 627, "died during the conflict with the Medinan Jews" (p. 324) Consistent Converted c. 621. Wounded at the Trench; died after the Banu Qurayza judgement, 5/627. TDV [sad-b-muaz]
13 Sa'd b. 'Ubada died "during the rule of Abu Bakr" (p. 324) Inconsistent Refused allegiance to Abu Bakr and 'Umar; left Medina early in 'Umar's caliphate and died at Hawran in 14/635 or 15/636, i.e. under 'Umar. Wikipedia (second source, labelled): "d. 637", "c. 635–637", after moving to Syria under 'Umar. TDV [sad-b-ubade]; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sa%27d_ibn_Ubadah
14 Nafi' b. al-Harith, "the Prophet Muhammad's physician", d. 670 (p. 324) Disputed / Minor difference TDV: the Arab physician was his father al-Harith b. Kalada (d. 13/634); Nafi' is named only as a Companion son. Wikipedia's al-Harith article likewise does not call Nafi' a physician, though "Nafi ibn al-Harith" appears in its navigation list of 7th-century physicians. TDV [haris-b-kelede]; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Harith_ibn_Kalada
15 Zayd b. Thabit c. 610–c. 660 (pp. 324–325) Minor difference b. 611 (11 years before the hijra); d. 45/665 preferred (variants 51, 55) TDV [zeyd-b-sabit]
16 Khuzayma b. Thabit d. 657, died for 'Ali at Siffin (p. 324) Consistent d. 37/657. An early Medinan convert. TDV [huzeyme-b-sabit]
17 'Abd Allah b. 'Amr b. al-'As d. 684 (p. 324); "c. 592–664" attached to him on p. 326 p. 324 Consistent; p. 326 internal conflict (see 1D-2) d. 65/684–85 (variants 63–69). Born c. 7 years before the hijra; converted before his father and moved to Medina only after 7 AH. This conversion date is decisive for the Sinai (AH 2) and World (AH 4) lists. TDV [abdullah-b-amr-b-as]
18 'Ammar c. 570–c. 657 (pp. 324, 326) Consistent d. 37/657 at Siffin, aged about 93 TDV [ammar-b-yasir]
19 "'Amir ibn Yasin" may be Yasir b. 'Amir al-'Ansi, who converted 610–613 (p. 324) Consistent on conversion. The identification is chronologically impossible Yasir, 'Ammar's father, was tortured to death in Mecca, "probably 615 CE", before any Medinan document. TDV [ammar-b-yasir]
20 al-Bara' b. Malik d. 640 at Tustar (p. 325) Minor difference Martyred at the siege of Tustar; d. 20/641 TDV [bera-b-malik]
21 Anas b. Malik c. 612–709/712 (p. 325) Consistent b. 612; d. 93/711–12 (variants 90–95) TDV [enes-b-malik]
22 Hamza 568–625, martyred at Uhud, so "a covenant he witnessed would need to predate this event" (p. 325) Consistent (dates and logic) b. 569/570; d. 3/625 at Uhud (7 Shawwal 3 AH ≈ 23 Mar 625). This rules him out of the World (AH 4) and Assyrian (AH 4) lists, both of which name him. TDV [hamza]
23 Sahl b. Bayda', a muhajir, sought refuge in Abyssinia and "died in the Battle of Badr" (p. 325) Inconsistent IH names Suhayl b. Bayda' (= Suhayl b. Wahb b. Rabi'a) among the first ten emigrants to Abyssinia [IH 5368] and among the Badr participants [IH 12665]. The Badr martyr was his brother Safwan b. Bayda' [IH 13124]. Sahl b. Bayda' appears in Mecca in the boycott episode [IH 6416]. The book merges three brothers. IBN HISHAM
24 Sahl b. Hunayf d. c. 658 (p. 325) Consistent d. 38/658–59 in Kufa TDV [sehl-b-huneyf]
25 Sahla bint Suhayl and Abu Hudhayfa b. 'Utba in the first hijra; Abu Hudhayfa d. 633 (p. 325) Consistent Both are in IH's first group of ten [IH 5352–5354]. Abu Hudhayfa was killed at al-Yamama, 12/633. IBN HISHAM; TDV [ebu-huzeyfe]
26 Tamim al-Dari d. 661 (p. 325) Consistent d. 40/661. Converted only in 9 or 10 AH (after Tabuk). TDV [temim-ed-dari]
27 'Uthman b. Maz'un died in the Prophet's lifetime; "a foster-brother of the Prophet" (p. 326) Death Consistent; "foster-brother" Unverified d. 2/624, after Badr, "the first muhajir to die in Medina". TDV does not call him a foster-brother. TDV [osman-b-mazun]
28 Abu al-'Aliya converted under Abu Bakr; a tabi'i (p. 326) Consistent Converted during Abu Bakr's caliphate; d. 90/709 TDV [ebul-aliye-er-riyahi]
29 'Abd Allah b. 'Umar c. 614–693 (p. 326) Consistent b. 3rd year of prophethood; d. 73/693 TDV [abdullah-b-omer-b-hattab]
30 'Asim b. Thabit died at Badr, 624 (p. 326) Inconsistent At Badr he killed 'Uqba b. Abi Mu'ayt [IH 11790]. He was killed later at al-Raji', which IH heads "Yawm al-Raji' fi sanat thalath" [IH 16325, 16350–16363]; TDV gives d. 4/625. IBN HISHAM; TDV [asim-b-sabit]
31 Sa'd b. al-Rabi' died at Uhud, 625 (p. 326) Consistent d. 3/625 at Uhud TDV [sad-b-rebi]
32 Abu al-'As b. al-Rabi' converted "after the Conquest of Mecca" (p. 326) Inconsistent IH: "qubayla l-fath" (shortly before the conquest) he lost his caravan to a Muslim raid, returned the goods in Mecca, declared his Islam and went to the Prophet [IH 12052–12081]. TDV: his wife was restored to him in Muharram 7 (628); d. 12/634. IBN HISHAM; TDV [ebul-as]
33 'Amir b. Rabi'a "was one of the leaders of the group that returned to Medina in 615 CE" (p. 326) Inconsistent (anachronism) The first Abyssinian emigrants who came back in c. 615 returned to Mecca. TDV on 'Uthman b. Maz'un, their leader, says they returned to Mecca on a false rumour of the Meccans' conversion. 'Amir went to Medina only after the Prophet's hijra (622). TDV [osman-b-mazun], [amir-b-rebia]
34 Hisham b. al-'As died at Yarmuk, 635 (p. 326) Disputed among sources TDV: fought and died at Ajnadayn, 13/634. Some accounts place him at Yarmuk, which is normally dated 15/636. TDV [hisam-b-as-b-vail]
35 Ka'b b. Malik died in 'Ali's reign (p. 326) Disputed among sources TDV: "most historians" give 50/670. Variants are a year before 40/660, 51 or 54. Only the minority date falls under 'Ali. TDV [kab-b-malik]
36 Ja'far d. 629, "during the early years of the hijrah" (p. 326) Date Consistent; wording Inconsistent Killed at Mu'ta, 8/629. He was in Abyssinia until he rejoined the Prophet at Khaybar (7 AH). 8 AH is not "early". TDV [cafer-b-ebu-talib]
37 Hurqus b. Zuhayr fought in the conquest of Persia under 'Umar, later led the Kharijites, "reproached by the Prophet" (p. 326) Consistent; identification Disputed Sent by 'Umar to Ahwaz. A Kharijite commander killed at Nahrawan, 38/658. His conversion date is unknown (perhaps before 6 AH if he was at Hudaybiya). Identification with Dhu al-Khuwaysira rests on "some reports" (Ibn Hajar). TDV [hurkus-b-zuheyr]
38 Usama b. Zayd 615–673; Zayd b. Arqam d. 685, "one of the earliest converts" (pp. 326–327) Minor difference Usama: b. 614, d. 54/674. Zayd b. Arqam: b. c. 612, too young for Uhud, d. 66/686 or 68/688. A child Medinan convert is not "one of the earliest converts". TDV [usame-b-zeyd], [zeyd-b-erkam]
39 Jubayr b. Mut'im became Muslim after Hudaybiya, 628 (p. 327) Consistent 628 (some say at the conquest) TDV [cubeyr-b-mutim]
40 Mus'ab b. 'Umayr: first envoy to Yathrib; killed at Uhud (p. 327) Consistent d. 3/625 at Uhud TDV [musab-b-umeyr]
41 "Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr" on one list "refers to Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr" (p. 327) Opinion. Either reading is chronologically impossible for the Najran list Mus'ab b. al-Zubayr was born 27–37 AH (647–657) (TDV). Mus'ab b. 'Umayr d. 3/625. SEERT's Arabic reads مصعب بن جبير, with variant مصعب بن الزبير in the note. TDV [musab-b-zubeyr]; SEERT p. 617
42 "Hashim ibn 'Ubayyah/'Ubayd…" (Sinai) could be Hashim b. 'Utba b. Abi Waqqas (p. 324) Plausible: SEERT's Najran list has هاشم بن عتبة. But it creates a new anachronism for the Sinai date TDV: Hashim b. 'Utba "became Muslim on the day Mecca was conquered" (8/630); d. 37/657. SEERT p. 618; TDV [hasim-b-utbe]
43 "Ibn Zubayr / Ibn Jubayr / Ibn Jamir" could be Nafi' b. Jubayr or Jubayr b. Mut'im (p. 327) Minor difference (an identification the cited edition already settles) SEERT prints خوات بن جبير (Khawwat b. Jubayr), an Ansari Companion b. c. 587, d. 40/660–61 (TDV). SEERT p. 618; TDV [havvat-b-cubeyr]
44 Witnesses who joined "the first hijrah to the Kingdom of Axum": Abu Hudhayfa, Sahla, 'Amir b. Rabi'a, 'Uthman b. Maz'un, Zubayr, Suhayl b. Bayda', Ja'far, Ibn Mas'ud, Mus'ab b. 'Umayr (p. 327, citing Ibn Ishaq 146–150) Consistent if "first hijrah" means the Abyssinian emigration as a whole; Minor difference if it means the first party IH's first party of ten includes Abu Hudhayfa and Sahla, Zubayr, Mus'ab, 'Uthman b. Maz'un, 'Amir b. Rabi'a and Suhayl b. Bayda' [IH 5349–5370]. Then "Ja'far went out, and the Muslims followed one another" [IH 5372]. Ibn Mas'ud is in the later list [IH 5429]. IBN HISHAM
45 'Amr b. Umayya b. al-Harith joined the Abyssinian hijra and "died in Abyssinia"; Abu 'Ubayd[a] b. al-Jarrah joined it (p. 328) Consistent IH lists 'Amr b. Umayya b. al-Harith b. Asad among the emigrants [IH 5410] and among those who died in Abyssinia [IH 20113–20114, 20188]. It lists Abu 'Ubayda b. al-Jarrah among the emigrants of Banu al-Harith b. Fihr [IH 5516]. Neither is in the first party of ten. IBN HISHAM
46 Umayna bint Khalaf b. As'ad, wife of Khalid b. Sa'id (p. 328) Consistent IH: "Khalid b. Sa'id … with his wife Umayna bint Khalaf b. As'ad" IBN HISHAM [5384–5385]
47 Year of Delegations = 630–631 (p. 327) Consistent 9 AH ≈ 20 Apr 630 – 8 Apr 631. Landau-Tasseron: "The Year 9 A.H. is known as 'ām al-wufūd". calendar; Landau-Tasseron 1986 abstract (OpenAlex)
48 Mu'awiya "a latecomer to Islam"; scribe and witness (p. 325) Consistent b. 602/603; "became Muslim with his father at the conquest" (8/630); afterwards served as the Prophet's scribe. (Wikipedia, used as a lead in V0, mentions accounts of an earlier secret conversion from 628; I did not find this in TDV.) TDV [muaviye-b-ebu-sufyan]
49 Salman, Abu Dharr, Bilal, Jabir would be a forger's choices (p. 327) Opinion — —
1B. Chapter 13: what the lists contain, checked against the printed editions
# Book claim (page) Verdict What the editions show Source
1 The Sinai lists "vary from the standard twenty-two authorities to copies which cite thirty-seven to thirty-eight and others that quote sixteen" (p. 323) 22 and 16: Consistent. 37–38 for Sinai: not found, and contradicted by the book's own p. 370 HADDAD prints 22 names. POCOCKE prints 16. GERAMB/ARUNDALE (Mauchin) print 21 (no Zayd b. Thabit). On p. 370 the book itself assigns 37–38 to the World and Najran covenants, not to Sinai. HADDAD; POCOCKE; GERAMB pp. 247–248; ARUNDALE pp. 29–30
2 "With rare exception, these witnesses are listed in more or less the same order" (Sinai, p. 323) Minor difference The sequences match only partly. HADDAD runs 'Ali, Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayra … with "El-Harith Ibn Thabit, Abdoul Azim Ibn Haasan" in 19th–20th place. Mauchin has Hareth b. Thabet 17th and 'Abd al-'Azim last. Pococke's two columns read in a different order. Appendix I re-sorts all columns into one order, which hides this. as above
3 'Umar follows Abu Bakr "on every covenant but that of 1630" (p. 324) Inconsistent SIONITA 1630 prints عمر بن الخطاب (Arabic p. 14, line 1) and "Omar ben-alchatab" (Latin p. 16). Morrow's own Appendix I (Table C) shows 'Umar present in 1630 and Missing in the 1655 (Nissel) column. The text probably confuses 1630 with 1655. SIONITA (page images); Appendix I
4 'Ali is on two covenants, "with the exclusion of the covenant with the Christians of the World from 1630" (p. 325) Inconsistent SIONITA 1630 prints علي بن أبي طالب (Arabic p. 14) / "Ali ben-abi-taleb". SEERT's Najran list has 'Ali; MALECH's Persian list has him (per colleague's Part A); the English list does not. Appendix I again shows 1630 with 'Ali and 1655 without. SIONITA; SEERT p. 617; Part A
5 Mu'awiya appears on 1630 "where Imam 'Ali is not featured", so "anti-Shi'ite Sunni tampering may be at play" (p. 325) Opinion resting on a false premise 'Ali is on the 1630 list, directly before Mu'awiya (عثمان بن عفان / علي بن أبي طالب / معاوية بن سفيان). SIONITA
6 'Uthman "on all but the covenant with the Assyrian Christians" (p. 324) Minor difference MALECH's English list lacks 'Uthman, but his Persian list has him (Part A), and Morrow's own "ASSYRIA (Morrow)" column (Table D row 3) has him. MALECH p. 229; Part A; Appendix I
7 Mu'awiya "on every manuscript but … 1538" (p. 325) Consistent for the editions opened SIONITA: scribe and witness. SEERT: writer only ("a écrit aussi Mo'âwia ben Abi Sofiân" / وكتب معوية بن أبي سفيان). MALECH: witness and writer. The 1538 MS was not opened. SIONITA; SEERT p. 618; MALECH pp. 229–230
8 Abu Dharr "on all"; Ibn Mas'ud "on all"; Sa'd b. Mu'adh and Sa'd b. 'Ubada "in uniform fashion on all manuscripts"; Ja'far on four (pp. 325–326) Consistent for SIONITA, SEERT, MALECH All three editions have Abu Dharr (أبو اذر / Abou 'dh-Dharr / Abuzar), Ibn Mas'ud, both Sa'ds and Ja'far. as above
9 Hamza "on two" (p. 325) Minor difference Hamza is on SIONITA 1630 and MALECH, and on Morrow's own 1655 column. SEERT's Najran list lacks him. SIONITA; MALECH; SEERT
10 Abu Hurayra "on two and … 'Abu Harifah' on a third" (p. 327) Minor difference SEERT has أبو هريرة. SIONITA 1630 has أبو هرين ("Abu-horain") in the place where MALECH has "Abubra". Morrow's Table C omits this name from the 1630 column entirely (row 8 is Missing in all three columns). SIONITA; SEERT; MALECH
11 "The names of the common witnesses on all of these covenants seem to follow the same order" (p. 327) Consistent (and analytically important; see §4) SEERT and MALECH run in nearly the same sequence: Abu Bakr, 'Umar, ['Uthman, 'Ali,] Abu Dharr/Abu al-Darda', … Ibn Mas'ud, al-'Abbas/Ibn 'Abbas, Fadl, Zubayr, Talha, Sa'd b. Mu'adh, Sa'd b. 'Ubada, Thumama/Thabit b. Qays, Zayd b. Thabit, 'Abd Allah b. [Zayd/Yazid], … 'Uthman/'Umar b. Maz'un, … Abu al-'Aliya, 'Abd Allah b. 'Amr/'Umar, Abu Hudhayfa/Harifa, … Hashim, … Ka'b b. Malik, Hassan, Ja'far. SIONITA's two-column layout gives the same names in a similar order. SIONITA and MALECH also share the scribe (Mu'awiya) and the date formula (Monday, end of the 4th month of AH 4, Medina). SIONITA; SEERT pp. 617–618; MALECH pp. 229–230
12 "Talhah … son of 'Ubaydullah on one and … son of 'Abd Allah on the four others" (p. 325) Consistent SEERT (French): "Talha ben 'Obeïd Allah". SIONITA: طلحة بن عبد الله. MALECH: "Tilha Ibn Abdullah". as above
13 The Sinai list "reportedly did not exist on the original" (p. 328) Unverified No source is given. Burckhardt (via V0) reports the monks' copy was itself "copied from a fourth successive copy". MORITZ calls the surviving texts a "tertiäre Abschrift" (tertiary copy). V0; MORITZ
1C. Chapter 13: hadith-science terms and rijal ratings [SA-3; two quotations spot-checked by me]
# Book claim (page) Verdict What the handbooks say Source
1 The covenants "are not mutawatir by chain. They are, however, mutawatir by words and mutawatir according to meaning" (p. 329) Inconsistent with the definitions Mutawatir is a property of transmission at every level of the isnad. Ibn al-Salah: «لا بد في إسناده من استمرار هذا الشرط في رواته من أوله إلى منتهاه» (this condition must hold among its transmitters from beginning to end). Lafzi and ma'nawi are subtypes of that same mass transmission. Al-Suyuti, Tadrib (I re-opened this): «لفظي: وهو ما تواتر لفظه. ومعنوي: وهو أن ينقل جماعة يستحيل تواطؤهم على الكذب وقائع مختلفة تشترك في أمر» (verbal: its wording is mass-transmitted; by meaning: a group who cannot have colluded in lying transmit different events that share one element). The Shi'i dirayah handbook (al-Shahid al-Thani, al-Ri'aya) says the same. Agreement between copies of one document is not independent mass transmission. Ibn al-Salah, Muqaddima naw' 30; al-Suyuti, Tadrib; al-Ri'aya (OpenITI)
2 Unlike most ahadith (ahad, "on the authority of a single witness"), the covenants are mashhur (p. 329) Inconsistent Ahad means anything short of tawatur, however many narrators (Ibn Hajar, Nukhba: «وكلها - سوى الأول - آحاد», all of them except the first [mutawatir] are ahad). Mashhur is a kind of ahad: more than two chains at every level. In the loose sense of "widely known" it can describe a text with no isnad at all and then carries no authenticating weight. Ibn al-Salah gives famous but baseless examples, among them «من آذى ذميا فأنا خصمه» (whoever harms a dhimmi, I am his adversary). Nukhba; Ibn al-Salah; al-Ri'aya
3 The covenants are marfu' (p. 329) Consistent only in the trivial sense Marfu' = attributed to the Prophet, whether the chain is connected or broken. It implies nothing about authenticity. Ibn al-Salah naw' 6; Nukhba
4 The covenants are musnad and muttasil (p. 329) Inconsistent Both terms describe a connected chain. Muttasil: «الذي اتصل إسناده فكان كل واحد من رواته قد سمعه ممن فوقه» (whose isnad is connected, each transmitter having heard it from the one above). Musnad (Nukhba): «مرفوع صحابي بسند ظاهره الاتصال» (a Companion's report from the Prophet with an apparently connected chain). The covenants have no chain from the witnesses to the surviving copies. Ibn al-Salah naws 4–5; Nukhba; al-Ri'aya
5 "The absence of a fully developed isnad is not a sign of forgery; on the contrary, it is a sign of antiquity" (p. 329) Opinion (not a rule of the discipline) Ibn al-Salah treats a text found in someone's handwriting (wijada) as belonging to the broken (munqati'/mursal) category, «غير أنه أخذ شوبا من الاتصال» (though it has a tinge of connection). Ibn al-Salah
6 Letters "to kings, rulers, chieftains" are "not subject to the rules of isnad" (pp. 329–330) Inconsistent with practice Sahih Muslim transmits the letter to Heraclius with a full isnad: 'Abd al-Razzaq ← Ma'mar ← al-Zuhri ← 'Ubayd Allah ← Ibn 'Abbas ← Abu Sufyan (Kitab al-jihad). It transmits the letters to Kisra, Qaysar and the Negus via Qatada ← Anas. Sahih Muslim (OpenITI)
7 The covenants may form a category "similar to … al-ahadith al-qudsiyyah" (p. 330) Opinion; no support in the discipline Hadith qudsi are transmitted «آحاداً … مع إسناده لها عن ربه» (as ahad, with his isnad back to his Lord) (Ibn Hajar al-Haytami). They are therefore not exempt from isnad criticism. al-Jurjani, Ta'rifat; al-Haytami, al-Fath al-mubin
8 When two equally strong hadith conflict, "the permissible prevails over the prohibitive" (p. 328) Inconsistent (a minority view presented as the rule) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam (I re-opened this): «فذهب الأكثر كأصحابنا وأحمد بن حنبل والكرخي والرازي … إلى أن الحاظر أولى» (most, including our school, Ahmad b. Hanbal, al-Karkhi and al-Razi, hold that the prohibitive takes precedence). Al-Zarkashi, Ibn Qudama and al-Suyuti agree («قدم التحريم في الأصح», prohibition takes precedence on the soundest view). Preferring the permissive is attributed to a minority (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Wahhab). al-Amidi; al-Zarkashi; Ibn Qudama; al-Suyuti, al-Ashbah
9 Ibn Sirin: "they did not ask about the isnad, but when … fitnah arose, they said 'Name to us your men'" (p. 329, via Azami 33) Consistent, but truncated Sahih Muslim, Muqaddima, bab 5 continues: «فينظر إلى أهل السنة فيؤخذ حديثهم، وينظر إلى أهل البدع فلا يؤخذ حديثهم» (the people of the Sunna are looked to and their hadith taken; the people of innovation are looked to and theirs not taken). The chapter heading: «باب في أن الإسناد من الدين» (the isnad is part of religion). Azami p. 33 not checked. Sahih Muslim
10 "The Qur'an itself is transmitted without chains of authority" (p. 329) Misleading Usul defines the Qur'an by tawatur (mass transmission): al-Sarakhsi, «المنقول إلينا … نقلا متواترا» (what has been transmitted to us by mass transmission). al-Sarakhsi, Usul
11 Sunni ratings in Appendix I ("Yes (S)") and the claim that 'Uthman is "criticized by both Sunni and Shi'ite authorities for his administrative shortcomings" (p. 323) Ratings: uninformative. 'Uthman: misleading for the Sunni side Sunni doctrine holds all Companions 'udul (just). Ibn Hajar, al-Isaba: «اتفق أهل السنة على أن الجميع عدول» (Sunnis agree that all of them are just); likewise Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and al-Khatib. So "Yes (S)" is automatic for any genuine Companion, Mu'awiya included. The real Sunni test is identity and date. Ibn al-'Arabi, al-'Awasim, defends 'Uthman and calls the charges dependent on «رواية كذابين» (the reports of liars). Isaba; Isti'ab; Kifaya; al-'Awasim
12 Ibn Mas'ud held "in the highest regard by Shi'ites due to his loyalty to Imam 'Ali" (p. 323); Appendix "Yes (SH)" Disputed among Shi'i sources; contradicted by the main rijal authorities Al-Kashshi (from al-Fadl b. Shadhan): «ابن مسعود خلط ووالى القوم» (Ibn Mas'ud mixed with and allied himself to that party). Al-'Allama al-Hilli puts him among the doubtful. Al-Khu'i: «لم يثبت أنه والى علياً» (it is not established that he was loyal to 'Ali). But al-Saduq's Khisal lists him among the twelve who objected to Abu Bakr. al-Kashshi; Khulasa; al-Khu'i; Khisal
13 Appendix I rates Zayd b. Thabit, Hassan b. Thabit, Ka'b b. Malik, Usama "Yes (SH)" Inconsistent / Disputed Al-Mufid, al-Jamal, names Zayd and Hassan b. Thabit among those «ممن ظاهر عليه بالعداوة» (who openly showed enmity to 'Ali). Al-Khu'i cites al-Kafi against Zayd. Al-Tabari and al-Mas'udi list Hassan, Ka'b and Zayd as 'Uthmanis who held back from 'Ali; TDV also says Ka'b did not pledge to 'Ali. Al-Kashshi lists Usama among ahl al-wuquf (those who held back); al-Hilli suspends judgement on him. al-Mufid; al-Khu'i; al-Tabari; al-Mas'udi; TDV [kab-b-malik]
14 Thabit b. Qays "excoriated by Shi'ites for his role in the Saqifah" (p. 324) Inconsistent Al-Hilli's Khulasa lists him in Part 1 (relied-upon). Al-Khu'i cites a report of him praising 'Ali. On the Sunni side, Ibn Hajar suggests he was the Ansar's spokesman at the Saqifa, arguing their case, not Abu Bakr's. Khulasa; al-Khu'i; Fath al-Bari
15 Sa'd b. 'Ubada "a close Companion of Imam 'Ali" (p. 324) Unsupported He refused allegiance to Abu Bakr (Isti'ab; TDV). No source links him closely to 'Ali; possibly a confusion with his son Qays. Isti'ab; al-Khu'i; TDV
16 Fadl b. 'Abbas "revered by Shi'ites for refusing to pledge allegiance to Abu Bakr" (p. 323) Partly supported Al-Ya'qubi lists him among those who held back from Abu Bakr. He is not among Khisal's twelve. Shi'i rijal list him without evaluation. al-Ya'qubi; al-Khu'i
17 'Abd Allah b. 'Amr "despised by Shi'ites for the crimes he committed in the name of the Umayyads" (p. 324) Unsupported Al-Kashshi (via al-Khu'i) gives only his remark to Mu'awiya about 'Ammar and «إني معكم ولست أقاتل» (I am with you but I do not fight). The Isti'ab: he swore he struck no blow at Siffin. al-Khu'i; Isti'ab
18 Sahl b. Hunayf "a partisan of 'Ali who refused to pay allegiance to Abu Bakr"; Khuzayma sided with 'Ali; Abu Dharr, 'Ammar, Salman revered (pp. 324–325) Consistent All of them are among Khisal's twelve objectors. Sahl was 'Ali's governor of Medina. Abu Dharr and 'Ammar are among the "four pillars" (al-Tusi via al-Khu'i). Khisal; al-Khu'i; al-Kashshi
19 Zayd b. Arqam "refused to acknowledge Abu Bakr"; "son of the first martyrs" (p. 327) Unverified / unsupported He is not in Khisal's or al-Ya'qubi's lists. The Isti'ab describes him as an orphan raised by Ibn Rawaha; "the first martyrs" were 'Ammar's parents (TDV). Isti'ab; TDV [ammar-b-yasir]
20 Appendix ratings of 'Ali "No (SH)" (Tables A, B), Abu Bakr "Yes (SH)" (Table A), Sa'd b. Mu'adh "No (SH)" (Tables C, D) Inconsistent (evident errors) 'Ali is the first Imam of the Shi'a. The Khisal twelve objected to Abu Bakr. Al-Khu'i grades a hadith on Sa'd b. Mu'adh's «جلالة» (eminence) as sound. Khisal; al-Khu'i
21 The Sinai chain is "a Sunni chain of authority and … relatively sound"; removing Sa'd b. Mu'adh and reading Abu Hudhayfa for Abu Hanifa makes it "acceptable to all Muslims" (p. 324) Inconsistent with the dates At the covenant's own date (3 Muharram 2 AH ≈ 7 July 623), Sa'd b. Mu'adh is one of the few unproblematic witnesses: he was alive until 5 AH. The impossible ones are Abu Hurayra (Muslim 7 AH), 'Abd Allah b. 'Amr b. al-'As (Muslim after 7 AH), al-Fadl b. al-'Abbas and al-'Abbas (in Mecca; al-'Abbas fought for Quraysh at Badr), and Abu al-Darda' (converted at Badr, months later). If Morrow's own identification of "Hashim" with Hashim b. 'Utba is used, add him (Muslim 8 AH). See §2. TDV (see 1A)
1D. Chapter 13 internal inconsistencies relevant to the argument
# Point Verdict Detail
1 Status of the witness lists Internal inconsistency Ch. 13 calls the Sinai chain "relatively sound", uses the witnesses to date the covenants, and classes the covenants as musnad/muttasil (pp. 324, 329). Ch. 16 says the lists "were appended … centuries after the fact" (p. 353). Ch. 17 says they "may merely be late additions" (p. 370). The book uses the lists as evidence when they help and discards them when they do not.
2 'Abd Allah b. 'Amr b. al-'As Internal inconsistency "d. 684" on p. 324, but "(c. 592–664 CE)" printed after "the son of 'Amr ibn al-'As" on p. 326. TDV gives 'Abd Allah d. 65/684–85. The p. 326 dates fit his father 'Amr.
3 Witness counts (p. 323 vs p. 370) Internal inconsistency + Inconsistent with editions p. 323 gives Sinai 22 / 37–38 / 16. p. 370 gives Sinai 16 / 22 and World and Najran 37–38, and calls Assyria's 32 "one of the longest". The editions have SIONITA 36 names; SEERT 31 witnesses plus Mu'awiya as writer; MALECH 31 (English, page image checked) and 33 (Persian, per Part A).
4 Year of Delegations hypothesis (p. 327) vs the documents' own dates Opinion contradicted by the texts SIONITA's colophon: «يوم الاثنين تمام اربعة اشهر من السنة الرابعة من الهجرة بالمدينة» (Monday, end of four months of the fourth year of the hijra, at Medina) = c. Sept–Oct 625. MALECH's English: "in the 4th year of the Hegira in the city of Medina". HADDAD, GERAMB and POCOCKE all date Sinai to 3 Muharram 2 AH. None of the dated texts points to 9 AH.
5 "All evidence indicates that the original copies of the covenants were in correct Classical Arabic" (p. 329) Inconsistent with the editors' judgements Scher, on the Seert Najran pact (PO 13 p. 602 n. 1): "Celle-ci est rédigée dans une langue peu sûre et incorrecte" (this one is written in an uncertain and incorrect language). Moritz, on the Sinai text: "Der … ungelenke, häufig unklare Stil ist ganz unmuhammedanisch, bisweilen kaum noch arabisch zu nennen" (the clumsy, often unclear style is entirely un-Muhammadan, at times hardly to be called Arabic) (MORITZ, section "Der angebliche Schutzbrief des Propheten"). There are no "original copies" whose language could be checked.
1E. Chapter 14: the four transmission models and their dates (and Appendix II, which diagrams them)
# Book claim (page) Verdict What the sources show Source
1 The Najran charter is "the oldest such charter of protection", dating "to the 9th century CE" (p. 331; App. II "Najran (9th c. CE)") Disputed / Minor difference The 9th-century date is the text's own claim: SEERT p. 601 says the copy was made from a register "retrouvé en 265 à Rirmantha chez Habib le moine" (found in [AH] 265 at Rirmantha, at the house of Habib the monk). Scher's note: 878–879; tabular conversion 3 Sept 878 – 22 Aug 879. No 9th-century witness survives. The Chronicle of Seert is dated "probably … the tenth century" (Wood 2013) or "vers 1036" (Mouton & Popescu-Belis 2005); its single manuscript is 13th-century (Wood, citing Scher) [SA-1]. Wood (2021) calls the text "an ʿAbbāsid-era re-imagination". SEERT; Wood 2021 abstract (OpenAlex); [SA-1]
2 The 1630 covenant, "supposedly found at Mount Carmel, may have been provided to the Christians of the Levant" (p. 332) "Supposedly" fair. Levant destination: Opinion with weak basis SIONITA's printer's preface (pp. 3–4) says only that the Capuchin Pacificus Scaliger "in illis regionibus … foelici id nanciscitur casu" (came upon it by lucky chance in those regions). Mount Carmel is not mentioned. The Carmel story first appears in Rycaut 1668, Bk II ch. 2, pp. 99–100: "the original of which was found in the Monastery of Fryars on Mount Carmel, neer Mount Libanus (which is within one days journey of Mecha …)". That geography is garbled. Morrow himself later asks "Did it truly come from the monks of Mount Carmel?" (p. 366). SIONITA; Rycaut (archive.org)
3 The 1538 covenant "could have been intended for the Christians of Egypt" (p. 332; App. II "Egypt (1538)") Opinion. Copy date Consistent MS BnF Arabe 214 is dated 1254 of the Martyrs (1538) and was copied by "Georges", a Jacobite, for a named owner (SLANE p. 55; BnF record per colleague). Coptic-era dating shows an Egyptian copying milieu, not the original addressee. De Slane: "une des nombreuses rédactions de ce document apocryphe" (one of the many recensions of this apocryphal document); "avec les signatures d'environ une trentaine des Compagnons" (with the signatures of about thirty Companions). SLANE (page image)
4 Sinai copy "1561" (App. II) Minor difference MORITZ: the surviving copies "in den Jahren 957 d. H. (aus Ägypten) und 968 d. H. (aus Konstantinopel) angefertigt" (made in 957 AH from Egypt and 968 AH from Constantinople), plus an undated Cairo copy. 957 AH begins Jan 1550; 968 AH = Sept 1560 – Sept 1561. "1561" fits the 968 copy, not the earliest dated copy (1550). MORITZ
5 Assyria "1822 or 1845" / "1822 or 1845–1847" (App. II; "1882 or 1845" in Table 3) Inconsistent as copy dates; "1822/1882" vary internally 1845/1847 are not dates of a surviving copy. In the book's own Ch. 6–7 they are dates for the reported loss of the Patriarchate's firman in Bedr Khan Beg's massacres. The colleague's Part A found earlier dating: 1843 (Yohannan 1916, p. 78; Theodore d'Mar Shimun) and "1843–46" (GEDSH, Hakkari). The only dated text available, MALECH (1910), dates the document itself to "the 4th year of the Hegira". "1822" corresponds to no Assyrian copy. The only 1822 item the book cites is a pact for the Armenians that the French consul at Baghdad gave to the Société asiatique (1G-5). The "Traité de Mahomet de Bagdad" is an 1882 mention of a geometry treatise (1G-6). Table 3's "1882" therefore coincides with the real date of that item and may not be a simple misprint. Book chunk 06 (Ch. 6–7); Part A; MALECH p. 230
6 Model 1 (separate, independent prophetic issuances) "agrees the most with the historical record" (pp. 331–332) Opinion; the textual evidence points the other way Three of the "independent" covenants share one witness list in largely the same order (1B-11). SIONITA and MALECH also share the scribe (Mu'awiya) and an identical date formula (Monday, end of the fourth month, AH 4, Medina; Part A confirms the same colophon in Malech's Persian). SEERT shares the list order and ends "a écrit aussi Mo'âwia". Shared errors and order are the classic sign of a common written ancestor (models 2–4), not of separate dictations. SIONITA; MALECH; SEERT; Part A
7 A chronology based on surviving copies is "full of flaws"; earlier copies may go back to the 7th century (p. 331) Opinion (true in principle, unsupported in fact) Copy dates are indeed only termini ante quem. But no pre-878 attestation of any of these texts has been produced. The Sinai document is absent from Ibn Sa'd's 47 letters (MORITZ). Ibn Sa'd's Najran treaty differs in substance from the Seert text ([SA-1]; 1F-3). MORITZ; [SA-1]
8 "Early Islamic accounts unanimously agree that the Prophet sent and received emissaries" (p. 331) Consistent Sahih Muslim transmits the letters to Heraclius, Kisra and the Negus with isnads [SA-3]. 9 AH is "the year of the delegations" (Landau-Tasseron). [SA-3]; Landau-Tasseron 1986
9 App. II key: "Armenia (1538 CE)" Unverified / internal The key gives the Armenian covenant the same date as Egypt, but it appears in no diagram. Not checked further (the Armenian covenant is outside Part III). —
10 Persia "(17th c. CE)" (App. II). Ch. 14 model 3 says the Sinai achtiname "would have been copied by the Armenian Christians of Persia". Ch. 16 says the Persian covenant's lack of signatories suggests it "predates all of the others" (p. 353) 17th c. and model 3: Consistent with Arpee. "Predates all others": Inconsistent with Arpee Arpee (1946, App. III, p. 355) says the Persian text reproduces the charter "to the Monastery of St Catherine", given "in copy" by the Shah to the Armenian bishop of New Julfa in the 17th century, and "by modern criticism pronounced a forgery" [SA-2]. The book's own chapters disagree with each other on this point (see also extract §7 no. 11). https://archive.org/download/historyofarmenia00arpe/historyofarmenia00arpe_djvu.txt
1F. Chapter 16: the rebuttals [SA-1, with my spot-checks marked ✔]
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source
1 Rycaut "recognize[s] the Covenant … as authentic" but sees a ploy of weakness: "made a false peace … only to violate it" (p. 353, "Rycaut 102") Consistent, with nuance ✔ Rycaut p. 102: "This Covenant … (howsoever denyed by the Turks to have been the act and agreement of Mahomet) is yet by very good Authors taken for real, and to have been at that time confirmed when his Kingdom was weak … But mark how well Mahomet in the sequel observed this Law …". He attributes authenticity to "very good Authors" and records the Turkish denial. https://archive.org/stream/presentstateofot00ryca_0/presentstateofot00ryca_0_djvu.txt
2 Ibn Sa'd "cites the Treaty of Saint Catherine and the Treaty of Najran" (pp. 354–355) Inconsistent (Sinai) ✔ MORITZ: "unter den 47 Schreiben des Propheten, die sein Biograph Ibn Sa'd anführt, ein solches an die Sinaiten nicht vorkommt" (among the 47 letters of the Prophet that Ibn Sa'd quotes, none is addressed to the Sinai monks). SA-1 searched the full Tabaqat and found no Sinai treaty. The nearest is the letter to Yuhanna b. Ru'ba of Ayla. MORITZ; Ibn Sa'd (OpenITI)
3 Ibn Sa'd's treaties "contain virtually the same clauses" as the covenants; the rest is "literary adornment" (p. 354) Inconsistent Ibn Sa'd's Najran treaty (I:218–219) has a collective tribute of 2,000 robes, a loan to the Muslims of 30 mail coats, 30 horses and 30 camels "if there is war in Yemen", and a riba clause. The Seert text (PO 13 pp. 612–614) has a per-head tax of 4 dirhams (12 for the rich), clergy exempt, Christians "pas tenus de sortir avec les musulmans pour combattre" (not obliged to go out to fight with the Muslims) and "qu'aucun chrétien ne soit contraint de pourvoir à l'équipement d'un seul musulman … en armes ou en chevaux" (no Christian to be compelled to equip a single Muslim, with arms or horses). That reverses the loan clause. It has no robes and no riba clause. Only the general protection and clergy clauses overlap. TDV's Najran article independently summarises the treaty as 2,000 garments a year plus hosting envoys. Ibn Sa'd (OpenITI); SEERT; TDV [necran]
4 Najran covenant "said to have been found in a library in 878/879", "only rediscovered a couple of decades after the death of Ibn Sa'd" (p. 354) Minor difference It was found at Rirmantha, at Habib the monk's; the copy was said to come from the "bibliothèque de philosophie" he had kept. AH 265 = 878–79. The gap after Ibn Sa'd's death (Jumada II 230 / Feb 845) is 33–34 years, not "a couple of decades". SEERT p. 601 ✔; calendar ✔
5 The Chronicle of Seert: "most scholars believe that the work dates from the 9th century", some say 11th (p. 354) Disputed; "most scholars: 9th century" not supported Wood (OUP 2013): "probably composed in the tenth century". Mouton & Popescu-Belis (2005): "écrite vers 1036" (written around 1036). Wikipedia (lead only): 9th–11th century, attribution to Isho'dnah of Basra contested. [SA-1]: https://academic.oup.com/book/26826/chapter/195820115 ; https://journals.uco.es/cco/article/download/14818/13228/29104
6 The Najran covenant is "contemporaneous with Bukhari, Muslim and Nisa'i" (p. 354) Opinion It rests on accepting the text's own 878 discovery story. The earliest witness is the Chronicle (10th/11th century) in a 13th-century manuscript. as row 5
7 Qureishi assigns the Treaty of Maqna to 'Abbasid Jews under al-Mutawakkil, but al-Mutawakkil "only ruled from 847 to 861" and Ibn Sa'd (784–845) already cites it (p. 355) Dates Consistent. Qureishi's words Unverified. The rebuttal may miss its target Al-Mutawakkil: allegiance Dhu al-Hijja 232 (Aug 847) to Shawwal 247 (Dec 861). Ibn Sa'd: b. 168, d. 4 Jumada II 230 (Feb 845) (al-Dhahabi, Siyar). Ibn Sa'd I:211 does contain the Maqna letter, with "برئتم … من كل جزية" (you are freed … from all jizya) and the household clause. But the long exemption texts (the Geniza/Khaybar family) are dated later: Ibn Kathir says the Khaybar letter surfaced "after 300 AH"; Encyclopaedia Judaica places the Geniza letter in al-Hakim's reign. So an 'Abbasid or Fatimid date is not impossible if Qureishi meant those texts. Qureshi's book exists (Lahore 1989; New Delhi 1991), but its text was not reachable. [SA-1]: al-Dhahabi; Ibn Sa'd; Ibn Kathir; EJ "Khaybar" ✔; Open Library
8 The Maqna treaty is accepted by Ibn Sa'd and al-Baladhuri, and "rejected by Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah, Muhammad Hamidullah and Muhammad Siddique Qureshi due to … 'Shi'ite elements'" (p. 355) Partly Inconsistent Hamidullah accepts the Ibn Sa'd/Baladhuri Maqna text (his doc. 33). He calls only the Geniza version (doc. 34) "مفتعل" (fabricated). Ibn Qayyim's Ahkam ahl al-dhimma and al-Manar al-munif do not discuss Maqna. He rejects the Khaybar exemption letter, on ten grounds that include its witnesses. [SA-1]; Ibn Qayyim ✔
9 Al-Baladhuri "claimed to have received a copy of the treaty from a person who had seen it in Maqnah" (p. 355) Minor difference ✔ Baladhuri (Hitti tr. p. 93): "An Egyptian told me that he saw with his own eye the statement that the Prophet wrote them on a red parchment … which he copied and dictated to me". No place of viewing is given. https://archive.org/details/originsofislamic00balarich
10 Gibbon: "Diploma securitatis ailensibus is attested by Ahmed Ben Joseph … but Abulfeda … as well as Elmacin … only mention peace and tribute" (p. 355) Minor difference in the quotation. Misapplied The note (ch. 50 n. 148) concerns Ayla's Christians, not the Jews of Maqna. Gibbon reports the Sionita patent only through others' opinions, ending with Mosheim, who "inclines to believe it spurious". [SA-1]: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/735/pg735.txt
11 The Cairo Geniza "Letter of Protection from the Prophet" is "a fake, probably inspired by the Treaty of Maqnah", forged "for the purpose of evading taxes", "never admitted as authentic", "proven to be a fake by both Muslim and non-Muslim scholars" (pp. 355, 359) Mostly Consistent; "never admitted as authentic" Inconsistent First edited by Hirschfeld (JQR o.s. 15, 1903, pp. 167–181). Addressed "to Hanina and the people of Kheibar and Maqna", it exempts them from the tax. Hirschfeld defended it ✔: "it is out of the question to assume that it was a Jewish fabrication"; he dated the fragment to "the tenth century, if not still earlier". EJ ✔: "recognized by most scholars as a forgery … composed at the time of the caliph Al-Ḥākim bi-Amr Allah (ca. 1010)". Hamidullah (doc. 34): fabricated. Gil (2004, p. 291): "Sometimes the Muslim rulers accepted the argument of the Jews who said that they were Khaybaris". Ibn Taymiyya (via Ibn Qayyim) says such documents had long been accepted and the jizya waived. Gil History pp. 29–30 n. 27 and Goitein p. 185: Unverified. https://archive.org/details/jstor-1450432 ; https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/khaybar ; [SA-1]
12 "To my knowledge, the only prophetic letter of protection which was forged in the history of Islam was produced, not by Christians, but by Jews" (p. 359) Inconsistent (as a statement of the scholarship) (a) The Khaybar Jews' jizya-exemption letter was exposed by al-Khatib al-Baghdadi (5th/11th c.). Yaqut, Mu'jam al-udaba' ✔, says a Jew produced a letter claiming the Prophet had lifted the jizya from Khaybar, "with the witnesses of the Companions, and that it was in the hand of 'Ali b. Abi Talib". Al-Khatib said «هذا مزور … في الكتاب شهادة معاوية بن أبي سفيان، ومعاوية أسلم يوم الفتح وخيبر كانت في سنة سبع، وفيه شهادة سعد بن معاذ وكان قد مات يوم الخندق في سنة خمس» (this is forged … the document has the witness of Mu'awiya, who became Muslim on the day of the Conquest, while Khaybar was in year 7; and the witness of Sa'd b. Mu'adh, who died at the Trench in year 5). The account is also in al-Dhahabi, Siyar, and Ibn Kathir. Ibn Taymiyya refuted it again in Damascus in 701 AH. Ibn Qayyim ✔: "كذب مختلق بإجماع أهل العلم من عشرة أوجه" (a fabricated lie by the consensus of the scholars, on ten grounds); its forgers "وضعوا فيه شهادة سعد بن معاذ ومعاوية بن أبي سفيان" (put into it the witness of Sa'd b. Mu'adh and Mu'awiya). This is the Jewish forgery family the book means, but it was recognised long before the Geniza. (b) Christian-held covenants called forged by specialists: Scher on the Seert Najran pact ("certainement apocryphe … forgé par les chrétiens", certainly apocryphal … forged by the Christians); Hamidullah on the Seert texts (docs. 96–97, "من الموضوعات", among the fabrications) and on covenants for Christians and Magians in general; Moritz on the Sinai covenant; Mouton & Popescu-Belis ("un texte apocryphe"). The book may disagree with these verdicts, but it cannot say none exists. Yaqut, Dhahabi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Qayyim (OpenITI) [SA-1]; V0 §3
13 Mouton holds that the covenant's Islam is "legendary" and "created from scratch by the monks" (p. 359, "Mouton 177") Exact wording Unverified; gist fair; Morrow's rebuttal misses Mouton's thesis The cited chapter exists ("Les musulmans à Sainte-Catherine au Moyen Âge", 1998, pp. 177–182) but is not online. Clio interview (2002): the visit story is a "légende" developed "à partir du IXe siècle". Mouton & Popescu-Belis 2005: "un texte apocryphe dont il fallait retrouver l'origine dans les environs de Bagdad au IXe siècle" (an apocryphal text whose origin is to be sought near Baghdad in the 9th century), forged by Nestorian monks of Dayr Qunna for the Banu Makhlad viziers, later adapted at Sinai. That is not "invented from scratch by the Sinai monks". [SA-1]: Clio PDF; https://journals.uco.es/cco/article/download/14818/13228/29104 ; EPHE publication list
14 Middle Eastern Christians "were grossly ignorant of Islamic history and beliefs" and the rival denominations "had virtually no contact", so they could not have forged texts consonant with the Qur'an (p. 359) Opinion, contradicted by specialist scholarship and by the book itself Wood (2021): the Seert texts "draw on knowledge of the Qurʾān and the Sīra". Mouton & Popescu-Belis: Nestorian secretaries at the 'Abbasid court. The book itself cites Patriarch Timothy I of Baghdad on Islam (p. 371). Wood 2021 abstract; [SA-1]
15 Those who think the covenants forged are "in many cases the same people who maintain that the hadith literature is entirely fictitious, and that the Qur'an itself was forged" (p. 359) Opinion, not borne out by the critics actually on record The opened verdicts come from Hamidullah (a Muslim scholar who accepts the short Najran and Maqna treaties), al-Khatib, Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Qayyim (on the Khaybar letter, by the same witness test), Scher (editor of the Seert text), Moritz, Burckhardt and Mouton. None of these verdicts rests on rejecting the hadith corpus or the Qur'an. V0; [SA-1]
16 Anton F. Haddad published an English translation of the Sinai covenant in 1902 (p. 362) Consistent ✔ "New York: Board of Counsel, 1902", 7 pages. HADDAD
1G. Chapter 17: research leads and the Regraga tradition [SA-2, with my spot-checks marked ✔]
# Book claim (page) Verdict What the sources show Source
1 Sionita (1577–1648) and Nissel (1621–1662) "produced Arabic editions and Latin translations" of the Testamentum; Sionita's and Nissel's versions should be compared (p. 366) Edition existence Consistent. Nissel's role: Minor difference. Nissel's birth year: Disputed Nissel's 1655 edition exists: "Lugduni Batavorum: Ex officina Johannis Elsevier, 1655", 16 pp., British Library copy, reproduced by Cengage (Penn and Wisconsin catalogues). The catalogue summary says the Arabic text is "noviter recusus … è regione versione Latinâ (Gabrielis Sionitæ)". So Nissel reprinted Sionita's Arabic with Sionita's Latin and made no new translation. Sionita 1577–1648 (GND 104043857). Nissel d. 1662 (GND 121226646; BnF; ADB). His birth year is given as 1621 (EMLO via Wikidata), 1623 (ECARTICO) or "ca. 1624" (bibliasacra). https://find.library.upenn.edu/catalog/9979393712203681 ; https://search.library.wisc.edu/catalog/9913221075502121 ; https://lobid.org/gnd/104043857.json ; https://lobid.org/gnd/121226646.json ; https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb11997022q
2 The 1538 covenant (BnF MS Arabe 214) "appears to derive from the covenant brought to France by Father Scaliger". The book names the owner al-Batanuni, the scribe Girgis al-Ifrangi, and al-Tamawi, al-Halabi, al-Ramadi, al-Barallusi; a missionary who arrived in Old Cairo in 1592; notes by Sionita; "the final two pages in a different handwriting"; and "Michel" (p. 366) Names: Consistent. Sionita, Scaliger, "Michel" and the different hand: not in the record. Scaliger derivation: Inconsistent with the record The BnF record has al-Batanuni, the scribe Girgis al-Ifranji, al-Tamawi (f. 1v), Butrus b. Diyab al-Halabi's reading mark dated 1673 (f. 2), al-Ramadi's mark 14 Baba 1336 AM [1620], al-Barallusi (f. 262), and the missionary's arrival in Old Cairo 9 Hatur 1308 AM [1592]. It does not mention Sionita: the only "Gabriel" is "Ġabriyāl Ṣahyūn al-Ziftāwī" (f. 2v). It has no Scaliger, no "Michel" and no note on a different hand. It says "Acheté par Vansleb en Orient" (bought by Vansleb in the East; Wansleben 1635–1679). The manuscript was therefore still in the Near East in 1673, after Sionita's 1630 edition and his death in 1648. It cannot be the copy Scaliger brought to France before 1630. The 1538 colophon is at f. 256v, before the charter (ff. 257–261; de Slane's older foliation puts the charter at fol. 245). De Slane calls the charter "une des nombreuses rédactions de ce document apocryphe" (one of the many recensions of this apocryphal document) ✔. https://archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cc894877 (saved copy); SLANE; https://lobid.org/gnd/search?q=Wansleben+Johann+Michael
3 Lucaris sent the Codex Alexandrinus to Charles I; Lucaris and Sionita were contemporaries, "both connected to Protestants"; "Perhaps Cyril Lucaris was involved in dispatching a copy … by means of Father Scaliger" (p. 366) Codex: Minor difference. Contemporaries: Consistent. Sionita "connected to Protestants": Unverified. Lucaris–Scaliger link: Opinion Catholic Encyclopedia: Lucar sent the codex "as a present to King James I … James died before the gift was presented, and Charles I, in 1627, accepted it". The same encyclopedia refers to "the Calvinistic confession of Cyril Lucaris". Its Sionita article mentions no Protestant ties. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04080c.htm ; https://newadvent.org/cathen/04312c.htm ; https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/06331a.htm
4 Guibert (1850): Deir-Saferan, "15 km north-west of Mardin", residence of a Jacobite patriarch; "It is said that the charter of Muhammad … is conserved in a convent" (p. 367) Entry wording: Unverified (Guibert's page could not be opened; snippet only). Report: recycled hearsay. Geography: Inconsistent The same stock entry appears in earlier and later gazetteers (all opened). Worcester's Geographical Dictionary (Boston 1823): "10 NW. Mardin. Here is a convent, in which, it is said, the original charter remains, by which Mahomet confirmed the free toleration of worship to the Christians". There are 1828 and 1829 French dictionaries. Larousse (1870): "à 15 kilom. N.-O. de Mardin … On y conserve, dit-on, dans un couvent, la charte de Mahomet". So it is not an independent 1850 report. Dayr al-Za'faran lies about 5 km east-south-east of Mardin (Columbia MCID: "5 km east of Mardin"; Syriaca.org coordinates 37.2994, 40.7926). It was the patriarchal seat from 1293 until after WWI (Syriaca, citing GEDSH). https://syriaca.org/place/69.html ; https://mcid.mcah.columbia.edu/mapping-mesopotamian-monuments/deyrul-zafarandeir-al-zafaran-monastery ; archive.org: geographicaldict01worc, LarousGrdictionnXIX06bnf, bub_gb_6qi5kQ2eRFQC, bub_gb_8jGtf3VvUQ0C
5 1822: Journal asiatique received a "Copy of the Pact of Muhammad in Favor of the Armenians, which an interlinear translation in Greek... by M. J. Zohrab, an Armenian doctor" (p. 367, "Société Asiatique 116") Inconsistent ✔ (page image read) Journal asiatique t. 1 (1822), p. 116, "Ouvrages offerts". Under "Par M. Rousseau, consul de France à Bagdad" the list ends "… Copie du pacte de Mahomet, en faveur des Arméniens, avec la traduction interlinéaire en turc". The next entry begins "— Par M. J. Zohrab, docteur arménien: Eusebii Cæsariensis et Samuelis Aniensis Chronica …". The translation is Turkish, not Greek. The donor is Rousseau, French consul at Baghdad. The book's ellipsis merges two separate donor entries. Year, volume and page are correct. https://archive.org/download/in.gov.ignca.26090/page/n118.jpg
6 "In the same year [1822], the Bulletin des sciences mathématiques et astronomiques made a passing mention of a Traité de Mahomet, found in Baghdad, which had appeared in an edition by Gregory … unclear whether this was the same as the Pact … or a different covenant" (p. 367, "Darboux et al. 145") Inconsistent ✔ (page image read) The book's own bibliography dates the source 1882. Bull. des sciences mathém., 2e série, t. VI (June 1882), p. 145, is a review of Heiberg's Litterargeschichtliche Studien über Euklid. The reviewer says Heiberg finds Euclid's On Divisions "non pas dans le Traité de Mahomet de Bagdad, qu'a recueilli l'édition de Gregory, mais bien dans un écrit du Ms supplément arabe 952" (not in the Treatise of Muhammad of Baghdad, which Gregory's edition included, but in a text of MS supplément arabe 952). This is a geometry treatise by "Machometus Bagdedinus", printed in David Gregory's Oxford Euclid of 1703 (Archibald 1915, p. 2 n. 11, page image read by SA-2). It is not a covenant, has nothing to do with 1822, and was not "found in Baghdad". https://archive.org/download/s2bulletindessci06fran/page/n164.jpg ; https://archive.org/download/euclidsbookondiv00archuoft/page/n13.jpg
7 1899 Actes du XIIe Congrès des orientalistes: "M. Nallino presented the Arabic text … of a Charte de Mahomet en faveur des Chrétiens" — "certainly apocryphal", but "it does not differ much from the one which is conserved by Tabari" (p. 367, "clxxxviii") Quotations Consistent; attribution Minor difference Actes (Rome 1899), t. I, p. CLXXXVIII: "M. Nallino présente le texte arabe et la traduction française d'une Charte (apocryphe certainement) de Mahomet en faveur des Chrétiens; texte et traduction qui ont été envoyés au Congrès par le Père Pierre de la Mère de Dieu, supérieur de la Mission des Carmes à Baghdâd … signée par le Prophète et par les principaux de ses compagnons, tels que Abû Bekr, 'Omar, 'Othmân, 'Alî, Mo'âwiya etc.; elle ne diffère pas beaucoup de celle qui nous est conservée par Tabarî". Nallino was presenting a text sent by the Carmelite superior in Baghdad. "Over five decades later" understates the gap: 1822 to 1899 is 77 years. "Arts" should read "Acts". https://archive.org/download/1899proceedings01inteuoft/page/n193.jpg
8 The provenance of Leon Arpee's Covenant with the Christians of Persia "so far, has eluded" scholars (p. 367); the Persian covenant "contains no signatories", suggesting it "predates all of the others" (p. 353) Minor difference / Opinion Arpee, A History of Armenian Christianity (1946), App. III, p. 355, states a provenance: "preserved in the archives of the Armenian Bishop of New Julfa, rendered here from the version of Johanianz (New Julfa, 1881) … purporting to be (though by modern criticism pronounced a forgery) originally granted by Mohammed (625 A.D.) to the Monastery of St Catherine … The Shah of Persia in the seventeenth century gives this document in copy to the Armenian Bishop of New Julfa." Arpee thus treats it as a copy of the Sinai charter. "No signatories, so earlier" is an inference against Arpee's own account. https://archive.org/download/historyofarmenia00arpe/historyofarmenia00arpe_djvu.txt
9 The Regraga "Seven Saints" travelled to the Prophet in Mecca; they descend from "three disciples of Jesus, Hamij, Harid, and Hirt"; Fatima's "rajrajah"; the Daour visits "forty-four saints over thirty-nine days"; they introduced the Qur'an, "most probably … in Tifinagh"; "Islam … was widespread in the Maghreb for decades prior to the Arab conquests" (pp. 367–368; no citation in the book) The tradition is real but legendary. Several of Morrow's details are Unverified or unsupported; the Tifinagh Qur'an is the author's conjecture Real tradition: Doutté, En tribu (1914), pp. 360–361, 369: seven ancestors went to the Prophet, and Sidi Ouasmin was sent "pour convertir les Chiâd'ma". Treated as legend: Cornell, Realm of the Saint (1998), pp. 49–51: the tales "had begun to be circulated" "by the early Almoravid period" to promote the Masmuda tradition, and "modern historians … can find no evidence that any of these saints … predated the Barghwata polity in Tamesna, which was founded in 124/741-2". Moroccan press (le360, 2018) frames it "Selon le mythe…" (according to the myth) and gives the "rajraja" etymology. Hachim (le360, 2022) says Fez 'ulama' of the 17th century doubted the "apostles of Jesus" thesis. Unsupported: the names "Hamij, Harid, Hirt", the Prophet answering in Berber, the Tifinagh Qur'an, and "the first to introduce the Qur'an". Minor difference: the Daour has 44 stages over 39 days, or 44 days, per le360 and Hachim. https://archive.org/download/entribu00doue/entribu00doue_djvu.txt ; Cornell (archive.org user upload, vincent-cornell-realm-moroccan-sufism; not linked as authoritative) ; https://fr.le360.ma/lifestyle/culture-legendes-et-traditions-il-etait-une-fois-le-daour-des-regraga-162610/ ; https://fr.le360.ma/blog/la-chronique-de-mouna-hachim/sept-hommes-dici-et-dailleurs-263699/
10 Atiya xii: the 1950 expedition aimed "not so much to discover new material as to make accessible … the unworked resources of this remarkable library" (p. 366) Consistent (wording); page Unverified The phrase is in the Foreword signed by Wendell Phillips (November 1954), seen only through archive.org's in-book search excerpt. The book is lending-restricted, so p. xii itself was not seen. archive.org full-text search, arabicmanuscript0000atiy [SA-2]
11 "The Monastery of Saint Catherine contains a large body of edicts, passed by jurists from the Hanbali, Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki, and Fatimid schools … supporting the contents of the Covenant" (p. 365) Partly Consistent MORITZ and V0: Fatimid and Mamluk decrees refer to "Schutzschreiben des Propheten" (letters of protection from the Prophet), and Khair Bek's firman of 926 AH speaks of "das heilige prophetische Schutzschreiben" (the holy prophetic letter of protection). Rulers' decrees, then, not jurists' fatwas from all four madhhabs as such. A breakdown by madhhab was not checked. MORITZ, section "Der angebliche Schutzbrief des Propheten"
12 The Sinai covenant "has been deemed trustworthy for over one thousand years by scholars from all major schools" (p. 365) Opinion; contradicted for the scholarly literature Muslim scholars on record against the long covenants: Hamidullah (V0). Morrow himself concedes "most scholars" doubt the Najran covenant (V0). The oldest attestations of a Sinai "prophetic letter" are Fatimid and Mamluk administrative references (MORITZ). V0; MORITZ
13 The Ottoman ahdname structure "appear[s] to imitate the structure of the covenants of the Prophet" (p. 368) Opinion Not checked against Ottoman diplomatics. Note that Morrow's 2021 article dates a related "Rylands" text to the Ottoman period (V0). V0
14 The Hieromonk Justin of Sinai essay (Evans & Ratliff 2012, pp. 50–51) treats the Maqna treaty as "historical fact" (Ch. 16, p. 355) Unverified The Met catalogue copy found has unusable OCR, and the Met site returned 429. —

2. Witness feasibility table

Reference dates, as the documents state them:

  • Sinai: 3 Muharram AH 2 ≈ 7 July 623, written by 'Ali "in the worship place of the Prophet" (HADDAD, GERAMB, POCOCKE).
  • World (1630): Monday, end of the 4th month of AH 4 ≈ 10 Sept – 8 Oct 625, Medina, Mu'awiya scribe (SIONITA).
  • Assyrian: MALECH's English dates it "the 4th year of the Hegira in the city of Medina", with Mu'awiya as scribe. Part A reads the same colophon in the Persian. The 8–10 AH range used in this brief is not the document's own date; it is also tested.
  • Najran: the Seert text is undated. The Najran delegation came in 9 AH (631) per TDV [necran]; 9–10 AH is used here.

"Y" = a Muslim, alive, and (as far as known) able to be in Medina. "N" = impossible for the reason given. "?" = uncertain. "child" = in Medina but a minor.

What the table shows:

  • No single date fits any list.
    • The Sinai list (AH 2) contains at least five impossible witnesses: Abu Hurayra, Abu al-Darda', al-'Abbas, al-Fadl and 'Abd Allah b. 'Amr. A sixth, Hashim b. 'Utba, applies if Morrow's identification is accepted.
    • The World 1630 list (AH 4) contains at least nine: Mu'awiya as scribe, Hamza, Ja'far, 'Uthman b. Maz'un, Abu al-'Aliya, both Ibn 'Abbas entries, Fudayl and 'Abd Allah b. 'Amr. Abu Hurayra is a tenth if أبو هرين is read that way.
    • The Najran list (AH 9–10) contains at least five: Sa'd b. Mu'adh, Ja'far, 'Uthman/'Umar b. Maz'un, Mus'ab and Abu al-'Aliya.
    • The Assyrian list fails at AH 4 (Mu'awiya, Hamza, Ja'far, Abu al-'Aliya and others) and again at AH 8–10 (Hamza, Sa'd b. Mu'adh, 'Uthman b. Maz'un, Abu al-'Aliya).
  • Some witnesses never fit any date in the Prophet's life. Abu al-'Aliya converted after the Prophet's death. Mus'ab b. al-Zubayr (as printed) was born after it.
  • Morrow's own fixes do not resolve this. He proposes yearly re-issue with dead witnesses kept "out of respect", or a single dictation in the Year of Delegations (p. 327). Neither explains a post-prophetic convert, a scribe who was not yet a Muslim on the document's own date, or the fact that the dated texts give AH 2 and AH 4 rather than AH 9.
  • Classical Muslim scholars used this exact test. They exposed the Khaybar exemption letter because it carried the witness of Sa'd b. Mu'adh, who had died at the Trench, and of Mu'awiya, who was not yet a Muslim at Khaybar (Ibn Qayyim; Yaqut, citing al-Khatib) (1F-12). Both names also stand on the Seert Najran list.
  • Morrow concedes the conclusion. He writes that "many of them were not Muslims at the time, some were dead" (p. 353) and that the lists were "appended … centuries after the fact" (p. 353).

3. Discrepancies ranked by significance

Ranked by how much each one bears on the book's central claim that the covenants are authentic.

  1. No witness list fits any date in the Prophet's life (pp. 323–328, 353). At the Sinai date (AH 2), Abu Hurayra, Abu al-Darda', al-'Abbas, al-Fadl and 'Abd Allah b. 'Amr were not yet Muslims in Medina. At the World date (AH 4), the named scribe Mu'awiya was a pagan in Mecca, and Hamza, 'Uthman b. Maz'un and Ja'far were dead or abroad. Abu al-'Aliya converted after the Prophet's death. At the Najran date (AH 9–10), Sa'd b. Mu'adh, Ja'far, 'Uthman b. Maz'un and Mus'ab were dead or unborn. The book's Ch. 13 nonetheless calls the Sinai chain "relatively sound" and treats Sa'd b. Mu'adh as the problem; at AH 2 he is one of the few unproblematic names. Classical Muslim critics (al-Khatib, Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Qayyim) rejected the Khaybar exemption letter on this same test, citing the same names, Sa'd b. Mu'adh and Mu'awiya. Evidence: §2; TDV; SEERT; SIONITA; 1F-12.

  2. The hadith-science terms are misapplied (pp. 328–330). The book makes five errors:

    • It says the covenants are "mutawatir by words and meaning but not by chain". Tawatur is defined by the chain at every level, and lafzi/ma'nawi are subtypes of it.
    • It calls them musnad and muttasil without any chain.
    • It glosses ahad as "a single witness", which is incorrect.
    • It says letters to rulers are exempt from isnad, which Sahih Muslim contradicts.
    • It gives the conflict rule in reverse: the majority prefer the prohibitive.

    Evidence: Ibn al-Salah, al-Suyuti, Ibn Hajar, al-Shahid al-Thani, al-Amidi, al-Zarkashi, Ibn Qudama, Sahih Muslim [SA-3; two spot-checked].

  3. The claimed continuity with Ibn Sa'd fails (pp. 354–355). Ibn Sa'd has no Sinai treaty (MORITZ: not among his 47 letters; [SA-1] full-text search). His Najran treaty differs from the Seert text on the core fiscal and military clauses. Robes are paid collectively instead of a per-head tax. The Muslims receive an arms loan instead of the Christians being exempted from equipping them. The riba clause is absent from Seert. These are not "literary adornment".

  4. "The only prophetic letter of protection which was forged … was produced … by Jews" (p. 359). This is contradicted in two ways:

    • The Khaybar exemption letter was exposed as forged by Muslim scholars from the 11th century on.
    • Specialists have judged Christian-held covenants forged: Scher, Hamidullah, Moritz, de Slane, Mouton.

    "Never admitted as authentic" is also false. Ibn Taymiyya and Gil report that such documents were accepted for a time, and Hirschfeld, who first edited the Geniza letter, defended it.

  5. 'Umar and 'Ali are said to be absent from the 1630 covenant (pp. 324–325). Both are printed in Sionita's 1630 Arabic and Latin lists. The error supports an inference of "anti-Shi'ite Sunni tampering", which therefore rests on a false premise. The book's own Appendix I shows the absence belongs to the 1655 column.

  6. The book's own textual evidence undercuts Model 1, independent issuance (pp. 327, 331–332). World 1630, the Assyrian covenant and Seert Najran share a witness list and order. The World and Assyrian texts also share the scribe and an identical colophon (AH 4, Monday, end of the fourth month, Medina). This points to a common written ancestor.

  7. Appendix I mis-transcribes the editions (pp. 377–381):

    • Najran: Hashim b. 'Utba, 'Abd Allah b. Hafaf and Mus'ab are omitted, and Khawwat b. Jubayr is truncated.
    • "Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr" is placed in the Malech column; it belongs to Seert.
    • Sionita 1630: one name is split into two, two names are dropped, and "Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (twice)" is wrong.
    • The Pococke/Skrobucha forms are mapped to the wrong witnesses (the two Sa'ds swapped; Zubayr given as Sa'd b. 'Ubada; Sa'd b. 'Ubada given as Zayd b. Thabit).
    • There is no S/SH legend, and some ratings are clear errors: 'Ali "No (SH)".

  8. The Chapter 17 research leads are mis-cited (pp. 366–367).

    • The 1822 Journal asiatique pact. The interlinear translation is in Turkish, not Greek. The donor is the French consul at Baghdad, Rousseau, not Zohrab.
    • The "Traité de Mahomet … found in Baghdad". This is an 1882 review mentioning a geometry treatise by "Machometus Bagdedinus", which David Gregory printed in his 1703 Euclid. It is not an 1822 covenant report.
    • Guibert's Deir-Saferan entry. It recycles a gazetteer line dating back at least to 1823, and it gives the wrong direction and distance.
    • Nallino in 1899. He presented a text sent by the Carmelite superior of Baghdad. The Actes call it "apocryphe certainement" (certainly apocryphal).
    • BnF Arabe 214. The manuscript was bought in the East by Vansleb and carries a reader's mark dated 1673. It therefore cannot be the copy Scaliger brought to France before 1630. Its catalogue record mentions no Sionita, no "Michel" and no second hand.
    • Arpee's Persian covenant. Its provenance is stated: New Julfa, a 17th-century copy given by the Shah. Arpee describes it as a copy of the Sinai charter "by modern criticism pronounced a forgery". This undercuts the book's suggestion (p. 353) that the Persian text "predates all of the others".

    Evidence: 1G; page images of JA 1822 p. 116 and BSM 1882 p. 145 read by me.

  9. The witness counts are wrong (p. 370). World is given as 37–38, but Sionita prints 36. Najran is given as "the same", but Seert has 31 plus the writer. Assyria is given as 32, but Malech has 31 in English and 33 in Persian.

  10. "Correct Classical Arabic" (p. 329) contradicts both editors. Scher calls the Seert pact's language "peu sûre et incorrecte" (uncertain and incorrect). Moritz calls the Sinai text "bisweilen kaum noch arabisch" (at times hardly Arabic at all).

  11. The Chronicle of Seert is not 9th-century by "most scholars" (p. 354). Wood (2013) has "probably … the tenth century"; Mouton & Popescu-Belis (2005) have "vers 1036". The 878–79 date is the text's own discovery claim.

  12. Mouton's thesis is misrepresented, and the rebuttal misses it (p. 359). Mouton and Popescu-Belis trace the text to Nestorian circles near Baghdad in the 9th century, not to invention "from scratch" by the Sinai monks. Morrow's counter-argument, that Christians were ignorant of Islam, does not engage that thesis.

  13. The Maqna paragraph misattributes positions (p. 355):

    • Hamidullah accepts the Ibn Sa'd/Baladhuri Maqna letter; he rejects only the Geniza version.
    • Ibn Qayyim's verdict concerns the Khaybar letter, not Maqna.
    • Baladhuri's informant was "an Egyptian", and the text gives no place of viewing.
    • The Gibbon note concerns Ayla's Christians, not the Jews of Maqna.
    • The Qureishi rebuttal is chronologically valid only against the short Ibn Sa'd letter.

  14. Biographical errors used in the witness discussion (pp. 324–326):

    • Sahl b. Bayda' did not die at Badr; Safwan did, and Suhayl survived.
    • 'Asim b. Thabit died at al-Raji', not Badr.
    • Abu al-'As converted before the conquest.
    • 'Amir b. Rabi'a "returned to Medina in 615": the return was to Mecca.
    • Sa'd b. 'Ubada died under 'Umar, not Abu Bakr.
    • Ja'far's death in 8 AH is described as "early years".
    • Yasir b. 'Amir, who died c. 615 in Mecca, is proposed as a witness.
    • "Abu Hudayfah ibn al-Yaman" conflates Hudhayfa b. al-Yaman with Abu Hudhayfa b. 'Utba.

  15. Several Shi'i reputations are misstated (pp. 323–324; App. I):

    • Ibn Mas'ud is said to be held in the "highest regard … due to his loyalty to 'Ali". Al-Kashshi, al-Hilli and al-Khu'i say otherwise.
    • Thabit b. Qays is said to be "excoriated" for the Saqifa. He is in fact relied upon in al-Hilli's Khulasa.
    • Zayd b. Thabit, Hassan b. Thabit and Ka'b b. Malik are rated "Yes (SH)". Al-Mufid and others name them as 'Uthmanis or as hostile to 'Ali.
    • 'Abd Allah b. 'Amr's "crimes" are unsupported.

  16. The Regraga tradition is presented as history, without any citation (pp. 367–368). The tradition is real, but specialists treat it as an Almoravid-era legend. Cornell (1998): there is "no evidence that any of these saints … predated the Barghwata polity … founded in 124/741-2". Several details have no source: the names "Hamij, Harid, Hirt", the Prophet answering in Berber, a Tifinagh Qur'an, and "the first to introduce the Qur'an". The inferences drawn from it, that the complete Qur'an existed in Mecca and that the Prophet knew all languages, are the author's own.

  17. Appendix II dates (pp. 382–383):

    • Sinai "1561" is the 968 AH copy; the earliest dated copy is 957 AH, i.e. 1550.
    • Assyria "1845/1847" are loss dates; Part A gives 1843 as better supported.
    • "1882" is a misprint.
    • Armenia appears in the key but in no diagram.

4. Neutral assessment of the authenticity argument (Chapters 13–16)

4.1 What the book argues

Chapters 13–16 rest on six claims:

  • The witness lists are on the whole sound, or at worst late additions that do not touch the content.
  • The covenants are mass-transmitted (mutawatir) in wording and meaning and, as dictated documents, exempt from isnad criticism.
  • Their content agrees with the Qur'an, the Sunna and the shari'a.
  • Ibn Sa'd's short treaties are summaries of the long texts.
  • Christians had neither the knowledge nor the motive to forge them, and the only known forged protection letter is Jewish.
  • The several covenants were issued independently to different communities (Model 1).
4.2 Strongest points in the book's favour
  1. The genre is real. Written prophetic agreements with non-Muslim communities are well attested.
    • The short Najran treaty appears in Abu Yusuf, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'd and al-Baladhuri (V0 §3.1; TDV [necran]).
    • The Ayla and Maqna letters are in Ibn Sa'd and al-Baladhuri ([SA-1]; Hitti p. 93).
    • Michael Lecker describes the Prophet's letters to tribes and rulers as "a sizable corpus of source material", preserved by "many people, both prominent and unknown" (abstract of "The Preservation of Muḥammad's Letters", repr. 2022, doi 10.4324/9781003278894-10).
    • A Christian community holding some prophetic document is therefore historically plausible, and for Najran it is documented.
  2. The Sinai claim is old. Moritz (1918), though he judged the text forged, records that the Mamluk and early Ottoman decrees refer to letters of protection "from one of the first four caliphs and the Prophet himself". The rulers named are Qaitbay, Qansuh, Khair Bek and Suleiman; Khair Bek's firman of 926 AH (1520) names "das heilige prophetische Schutzschreiben" (the holy prophetic letter of protection). A Fatimid decree of al-Hafiz orders "the old treaties" respected (V0). Moritz also thought the Ottoman removal of an "original" "möglich, sogar wahrscheinlich" (possible, even probable). The monastery thus invoked a prophetic grant before its earliest dated copy (1550).
  3. The texts are related, not independent inventions. World 1630, the Assyrian text and Seert Najran share a witness list and order (§1B-11), and World and Assyria share a scribe and colophon. Separate denominations did not each invent a document from nothing; something was transmitted between them. This is the basis of El-Wakil's argument that a clause shared across communities is "highly unlikely" to have been forged by each (Religions 2019, via V0).
  4. The content draws on Islamic norms, especially protection of churches and clergy, which the short Muslim-recorded treaties also contain.
  5. Some peer-reviewed support exists since 2013. El-Wakil (JIS 2016, OUP) argues "categorical dismissal of the covenants as forgeries is no longer tenable". Zein & El-Wakil (Routledge 2022) argue the same. The question is not closed in the literature.
4.3 Strongest points against the book's case
  1. The witness lists fail the test classical Muslim scholarship itself uses. Every list examined is impossible at every date in the Prophet's life (§2).
    • Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi rejected the Khaybar exemption letter, which was "in the hand of 'Ali", precisely because it carried the witness of Mu'awiya ("أسلم يوم الفتح", who became Muslim on the day of the Conquest) and Sa'd b. Mu'adh ("مات يوم الخندق في سنة خمس", who died at the Trench in year 5) (Yaqut).
    • Ibn Qayyim called it "كذب مختلق بإجماع أهل العلم" (a fabricated lie, by the consensus of the scholars), and his grounds include the same two witnesses. Ibn Taymiyya declared it forged in 701 AH (1F-12).
    • Both names stand on the Seert Najran list.
    • The book's Ch. 13 ruling that the Sinai chain is "relatively sound" overlooks five impossible witnesses (1C-21).
    • By Ch. 16 the book itself concedes the lists were "appended … centuries after the fact".
  2. The hadith-science defence misuses the discipline's terms.
    • Mutawatir, mashhur, musnad and muttasil are properties of chains. They cannot be claimed for texts that have none.
    • Letters to rulers were transmitted with isnads (Sahih Muslim).
    • The conflict rule the book cites is the minority view; the majority prefers the prohibitive.
    • All four points come from Sunni and Shi'i handbooks alike ([SA-3]; 1C).
  3. The claimed continuity with Ibn Sa'd does not hold.
    • Ibn Sa'd has no Sinai letter. Moritz: none among his 47 letters.
    • His Najran treaty and the Seert covenant differ on the central fiscal and military terms: a robe tribute against a per-head tax, and an arms loan to Muslims against an exemption from equipping them. The riba clause is missing from Seert (1F-3).
    • These are substantive differences, not "literary adornment".
  4. There is no pre-878 attestation, and specialist verdicts are negative.
    • By its own account the long Najran text surfaced in 265/878–79 and survives in a chronicle of the 10th or 11th century.
    • Wood (2021) reads it as "an ʿAbbāsid-era re-imagination" that draws "on knowledge of the Qurʾān and the Sīra".
    • Mouton & Popescu-Belis (2005) place the origin of the Najran/Sinai text family near 9th-century Baghdad (1F-13).
    • Scher (1919), Moritz (1918), de Slane ("document apocryphe") and Hamidullah reach the same negative conclusion. Hamidullah is a Muslim scholar who accepts many prophetic documents, including the short Najran and Maqna texts.
  5. The motive argument is weak.
    • Protective and tax-exempting documents had obvious value to the communities that held them. Ibn Taymiyya reports that forged exemption documents had long been accepted and the jizya waived ([SA-1]). Gil notes rulers "sometimes" accepted Khaybari claims.
    • The book's premise that Eastern Christians were ignorant of Islam conflicts with the Nestorian-secretary thesis (Mouton/Massignon) and with Wood's analysis.
  6. The shared textual features point to adaptation. The common witness list, scribe and colophon (1E-6) are what one expects if one text was adapted for several communities, which is Scher's observation that "chaque nationalité chrétienne de l'Orient en conserve une copie plus ou moins différente" (each Christian nation of the East keeps a more or less different copy; PO 13 p. 602 n. 1, re-read by me). They are not what one expects from separate dictations to separate communities.
  7. Methodological standards.
    • Wadad al-Qadi's study of early Islamic letters insists on genre-specific criteria for authenticity (chapter introduction, pp. 215–276, Gerlach reissue 2021).
    • Landau-Tasseron shows how compilers reshaped the accounts of the year-9 delegations (BSOAS 1986, abstract).
    • The book applies neither diplomatic analysis (formulae, script, material) nor redaction analysis. Its strongest tools are content agreement and analogy with hadith, and §1C shows the analogy is misapplied.
  8. The data are handled loosely in places. Appendix I has mis-transcriptions (1H). The claim that 'Ali and 'Umar are absent from 1630 is false (1B-3/4) yet supports a "tampering" inference. The witness counts are wrong (1D-3).
4.4 Overall (my assessment, offered as such)
  • What the book shows. The prophetic-covenant genre is real. A Najran agreement existed. Christian communities from the 9th century on (Najran/Seert) and in Mamluk–Ottoman Sinai held and successfully invoked texts in the Prophet's name.
  • What it does not show. It does not establish that the extant long texts go back to the Prophet. Its central evidential moves fail when checked against the sources it invokes:
    • the witness lists;
    • the hadith-science classification;
    • the Ibn Sa'd comparison;
    • the "only forgery was Jewish" claim.
  • The best-supported reading. The positions most compatible with the material I opened are the mainstream pre-2013 view and a cautious middle view:
    • Mainstream view: the long covenants are later compositions, 9th century or later, by their own testimony and on internal evidence.
    • Middle view: they may preserve memories of genuine prophetic protection agreements, as Valkenberg and the hedged Zein & El-Wakil 2020 piece suggest (V0).
  • Where the case stands. The pro-authenticity case remains a minority position in the specialist literature. Even its defenders concede that no original survives. Morrow's own 2021 article dates a related "Rylands" text to the 16th–17th century Ottoman period (V0).
