1.5 Theme H: conduct of other powers (pp. 340–341, 349) (helper C)
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
C109 [C10] "Since time immemorial, it was considered the right of the conqueror to kill and enslave the conquered. In some extreme examples, such as the Aztecs, the conquered were ritually sacrificed to the gods. Those who were not slaughtered were subjected to heavy taxes, including payment in the form of slaves." (p. 340) Opinion (sweeping generalisation). The Aztec example is Consistent. Davíd Carrasco, "Aztec Religion", Encyclopedia of Religion (1987): in Aztec myth "warfare was established so that human beings could be captured and sacrificed to nourish the Sun"; the New Fire ceremony used "a heart sacrifice of a war captive"; subject city-states "paid tribute". Strictly, the Aztecs mostly sacrificed war captives rather than whole conquered populations. The Roman material in 1a-1d supports the general point about enslavement. encyclopedia.com (aztec-religion)
T122 [C1a] Block quote "(Joshel)": "In 177 BCE, during his campaign in Sardinia, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus killed or enslaved 80,000 of the island's inhabitants" (p. 341) Minor difference Joshel's own sentence (OL search-inside): "In 177 BCE during his campaign in Sardinia, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus killed or enslaved 80,000 of the island's inhabitants (Livy 41.28.9). So many captives flooded the slave market…". Livy 41.28 (Latin) quotes the dedication tablet: "in ea prouincia hostium caesa aut capta supra octoginta milia" ("over 80,000 enemies killed or captured"). Livy places the tablet "eodem anno", which is the year of the elections for the consuls of 173 BCE, so the tablet dates to 174 BCE. The campaign covered 177 and 176 BCE: Livy 41.12 records 12,000 killed in 177, and Livy 41.17 records 15,000 killed and Gracchus kept in the province as proconsul "eo anno". Gracchus triumphed in 175 (Wikipedia, citing Broughton MRR 1:397-402; labelled lead). So the figure is "more than 80,000 killed or captured", for 177-176 BCE, and comes from Gracchus's own victory tablet. The wording matches Joshel. The minor issues: "enslaved" glosses "captured", and "177" names only the campaign's first year. thelatinlibrary.com/livy/liv.41.shtml; openlibrary.org/search/inside.json (q="inhabitants (Livy", "In 177 BCE, during his campaign", "Sempronius Gracchus killed or enslaved"); en.wikipedia.org (Gracchus consul 177, raw)
T123 [C1b] "In 167 BCE the Roman senate granted the victorious Roman general in Greece the right to sack seventy cities on the west coast of Greece: 150,000 persons were enslaved" (p. 341) Consistent with the ancient sources. Minor difference from Joshel's wording. Joshel (OL search-inside): "the right to sack seventy cities in Epirus (on the west coast of Greece): 150,000 persons were enslaved (Livy 45.34.5)". The book drops "in Epirus" and the citation without marking the change. Livy 45.34: the senate gave the army "praedam Epiri ciuitatium, quae ad Persea defecissent"; "centum quinquaginta milia capitum humanorum abducerentur … ea fuere oppida circa septuaginta". Polybius 30.15, via Strabo 7.7.3 (LacusCurtius): Paulus "destroyed seventy cities of the Epeirotes (most of which … belonged to the Molossi), and reduced to slavery one hundred and fifty thousand people". Plutarch, Aem. 29: "in a single hour a hundred and fifty thousand persons were made slaves, and seventy cities were sacked". Paton's Loeb translation of Polybius 30.15 reads "seventy cities in Macedonia, most of them belonging to the Molotti"; the Molossi/Molotti are Epirote. Scheidel (2007, p. 6) calls this "the largest recorded tally for a single operation that may bear some semblance to reality". thelatinlibrary.com/livy/liv.45.shtml; penelope.uchicago.edu Strabo 7G*; Polybius 30*; Plutarch Aemilius*; OL search-inside; Scheidel PDF (Wayback)
T126 [C1c] "In the Jewish War in 66-70 CE … 97,000 people were enslaved" (p. 341) Consistent, with a minor qualification Josephus BJ 6.9.3 (= 6.420), Whiston translation: "the number of those that were carried captive during this whole war was collected to be ninety-seven thousand; as was the number of those that perished during the whole siege eleven hundred thousand". The same passage says captives over 17 were sent "to the Egyptian mines", some were given to the provinces "to be destroyed upon their theatres", and those under 17 "were sold for slaves". So "captives" covers forced labour, death in the arena and sale, not only enslavement. Scheidel gives the war as AD 66-73: "Josephus gives a total of 97,000 enslavements for the former". Joshel's text (OL search-inside): "In the Jewish War in 66-70 CE, to take…". gutenberg.org/cache/epub/2850/pg2850.txt; Scheidel PDF; OL search-inside
T125 [C1d] Imperial-era wars bringing captives (Augustus: Alpine tribes and Spain; Tiberius: Rhine; Claudius: Britain; Parthians; Trajan: Dacia; Marcus Aurelius: Danube) Consistent (confirmed as Joshel's text) Joshel (OL search-inside): "Augustus's wars against the Alpine tribes and in Spain, Tiberius's wars along…"; "campaigns against the Parthians, Trajan's wars in Dacia (Figures 25-26, 29, 31), and Marcus Aurelius's campaign across the Danube all brought…". Scheidel independently notes that the Alpine Salassi were enslaved in 25 BC ("the entire surviving population of 44,000 was sold into slavery", Strabo 4.6.7), cites Florus 2.52 on the Cantabrians, and mentions Trajan's "putative" 500,000 Dacian slaves (Lydus), which he calls suspect. OL search-inside; Scheidel PDF
T124–T126 (quote fidelity) [C1e] Block-quote fidelity: "Revolts in the provinces, though rarer, too, resulted in enslavements" Minor difference Joshel: "Revolts in the provinces, although more rare (or underreported), also resulted in enslavements." The book's block quote also silently omits Joshel's sentences "So many captives flooded the slave market…" and "In 57 BCE Julius Caesar sold 53,000 of the Aduatuci into slavery", together with her Livy citations. It is a condensed paraphrase presented as a verbatim quotation. OL search-inside
C110 [C1f] Joshel quote: "men and women brought into the empire in the long-distance slave trade not only lost their natal cultures, they became outsiders…" (p. 341) Unverified Search-inside queries for "lost their natal cultures", "natal cultures", "like their goods, became plunder" and "became outsiders" "defeated enemies" returned no hit in Joshel. That proves nothing either way, because the OCR index may be incomplete. OL search-inside
T122–T126 (context) [C1g] Reliability of ancient enslavement figures (modern scholarship) n/a (context) Scheidel 2007: "while particular reports may well be exaggerated, they nevertheless cumulatively understate the actual scale of slave-making"; later tallies "are suspect … either because they mirror earlier totals … or simply because of their enormous size" (Caesar's 1 million; Trajan's 500,000). Scheidel PDF (web.archive.org copy of princeton.edu/~pswpc/pdfs/scheidel/050704.pdf)
C111 [C2a] Huns pillaged churches and monasteries, slew monks and "sexually assault[ed] virgins" (Ferrill) (p. 341) Minor difference (on "sexually assaulting"). The attribution to Ferrill is Unverified. The primary source usually quoted is Callinicus, Life of Hypatius, on the Hun invasion of 447. In E. A. Thompson's translation (OL search-inside): "they took captive the churches and monasteries and slew the monks and maidens in great numbers", followed by "Perhaps the holy writer has exaggerated somewhat in saying that a hundred towns were captured". Other books render it "slew the monks and virgins" (Craughwell; Rice). Every rendering I found says the Huns killed the virgins or maidens, not that they raped them. A separate text by Jerome lists the Huns among many peoples who "sacked, devastated, raided, raped" provinces (quoted in an OL search-inside hit from O'Grady), but it does not single out the Huns. I could not open Ferrill's Fall of the Roman Empire: The Military Explanation (archive.org item fallofromanempir0000arth is restricted). OL search-inside (q="slew the monks", "took captive the churches and monasteries", "Perhaps the holy writer has exaggerated", "maidens in great numbers")
C112 (scorched earth) [C2b] "Like the Chinese and the Mongols, the Huns adopted a scorched earth policy which aimed at preventing their enemies from ever rising again" Opinion (generalisation) No specific checkable claim. Thompson's caution about exaggeration in the Christian sources (2a) applies. —
C112 (salt) [C2c] "Romans and Mongols alike used to sow with salt the territory of defeated populations so that nothing could grow there again" Inconsistent for the Romans. Unverified for the Mongols. The well-known Roman case, Carthage, is a modern myth. R. T. Ridley, "To be Taken with a Pinch of Salt: The Destruction of Carthage", Classical Philology 81.2 (1986) 140-146 (Crossref verified); B. H. Warmington, "The Destruction of Carthage: A Retractatio", CP 83.4 (1988) 308-310; S. T. Stevens, CP 83 (1988) 39-41; P. Visonà, CP 83 (1988) 41-42. A biography of B. L. Hallward (OL search-inside) notes that Ridley "rejected BLH's assertion that the ruins of Carthage were sown with salt. See Classical Philology, vol. 81, 1986". The Wikipedia article "Salting the earth" (used only as a lead) says the story entered scholarship through Hallward's chapter in CAH 1st ed. (1930) and that "there are no ancient sources for it". I could not open the JSTOR or UChicago pages. I found no attestation of Mongol salting in any source consulted, and Wikipedia's list of salting cases has no Mongol case. api.crossref.org (4 DOIs); OL search-inside; en.wikipedia.org (Salting_the_earth, raw); jstor.org/stable/269786 FAILED; journals.uchicago.edu FAILED
— (p. 341, Tacitus allusion) [C2d] "Like the Romans, they would create deserts of destruction and death and call it peace" Consistent (as an allusion) Tacitus, Agricola 30, in the speech the historian gives the Caledonian chief Calgacus: "Auferre trucidare rapere falsis nominibus imperium, atque ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant." It is a Roman historian's rhetoric placed in an enemy's mouth, not a Roman self-description. thelatinlibrary.com/tacitus/tac.agri.shtml
T127 [C4] "During the days of the Prophet, regional and world powers included Byzantium, the Sassanid Empire …, the Visigoths in Spain, … the Franks in France, and the Sui Dynasty in China" (p. 341) Minor difference Britannica, Sui dynasty: "(581-618 ce) … the succeeding Tang dynasty (618-907)". Muhammad c. 570-632 (Wikipedia, labelled; uncontroversial). The Sui overlap only 570-618; for the Prophet's last 14 years China was ruled by the Tang, which the book leaves out. Visigothic kingdom "destroyed in 711 by the Arabs" (New Catholic Encyclopedia). Sasanian Khosrow II reigned 590-628 (Britannica). "Franks in France" is anachronistic but harmless; I did not check it separately. web.archive.org Britannica Sui-dynasty, Khosrow-II; encyclopedia.com (NCE "Visigoths"); en.wikipedia.org Muhammad (raw)
T128 (date) [C5a] "In 614, during the final phase of the Sassanid-Byzantine War, the city of Jerusalem was laid siege" (p. 341) Minor difference Britannica (Khosrow II) dates the war from Maurice's murder (602) to Heraclius's 628 campaign and Khosrow's execution (628): "in 614 Jerusalem fell". 614 falls in the middle of the war, during the Persian ascendancy, not in its "final phase" (622-628). Sebeos dates the siege to 19 days ending "ten days after Easter". web.archive.org Britannica Khosrow-II; attalus.org Sebeos ch. 24
T128 (massacre) [C5b] "the Persians are alleged to have slaughtered Christians and desecrated holy sites"; "contentious … object of scholarly debate" (p. 341) Consistent The literary sources are unanimous about a massacre but disagree on the numbers (see Table 2). G. Avni, BASOR 357 (2010) 35-48 (abstract via OpenAlex): "A careful evaluation of the archaeological record reveals a number of mass graves around the city walls which may be attributed to the conquest and the massacre of the Christian population. At the same time, no evidence was found for the destruction of buildings and monuments…". Britannica (Khosrow II) still says "The Holy Sepulchre was destroyed", and the archaeology contradicts it. E. Horowitz, Jewish Social Studies 4.2 (1998) 1-39 (Crossref metadata only) studies how modern historians handled the claim that Jews took part in the massacre. api.openalex.org (Avni abstract); api.crossref.org; tertullian.org (Conybeare); attalus.org; archive.org Macler; archive.org de Boor
C114 [C6] "While Islam preached an eye for an eye, such relatively moderate notions were unheard of in Europe" (p. 341) Inconsistent Roman law, Twelve Tables VIII: "Si membrum rup[s]it, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto" ("If he has broken a limb, unless he makes a settlement with him, let there be retaliation in kind"). Hebrew Bible, Exodus 21:23-25 (JPS): "life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth…". The Qur'an's own talion verse, 5:45, presents the rule as prescribed in the Torah ("In the Torah We prescribed for them … an eye for an eye", Abdel Haleem) and adds remission as charity. Early medieval Germanic law in Europe often used monetary composition instead of talion. Salic Law XLI.1: "If any one shall have killed a free Frank … he shall be sentenced to 8000 denars". The principle was well known in Europe, in Roman law and in the Bible read throughout Christendom. thelatinlibrary.com/12tables.html; sefaria.org API Exodus 21:23-25; api.quran.com 5:45; avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/salic.asp
T129 [C7] "in the year 782, Charlemagne slaughtered 4,500 Saxons in response to the death of two envoys, four counts, and approximately twenty nobles" (p. 341) Consistent with the Frankish annals. The modern debate is minor and set out in col. 4. The revised annals ("Annales q. d. Einhardi") for 782: "legatorum duo, Adalgisus et Geilo, comitum quattuor aliorumque clarorum atque nobilium usque ad viginti interfecti" (two envoys, four counts and up to twenty other distinguished nobles killed at the Süntel). They continue: "usque ad quattuor milia D [quingenti] traditi super Alaram fluvium in loco, qui Ferdun vocatur, iussu regis omnes una die decollati sunt". The original Royal Frankish Annals have the Saxons hand over the "malefactores … ad occidendum IIII D [= 4,500]; quod ita et factum est". Variant: MSS D1 and D3 read "quattuor milia". The original annals present the Süntel battle as a Frankish victory ("victores extiterunt Franci"); the revised version admits a defeat. Annales Fuldenses: "quattuor milium et quingentorum hominum decollatione". Kurze's MGH edition, note 3, records the 19th-century doubts: "Omnes occisos esse negant W. de Bippen (1889) et Fr. Dieck (1894); in numero mendum esse Ulmann … arbitratur". The "decollare → delocare" (beheaded → relocated) scribal-error theory is reported by Chamberlin (OL search-inside: "had written, or intended to write, delocare (to relocate or remove) and not decollare") and by German popular-history books. Barbero (2004, pp. 46-47, as quoted in Wikipedia, which I did not open in the original) judges that "None of these attempts has proved credible". Wikipedia also reports Lintzel (exaggeration), Bachrach (figure "generally accepted"), Becher (2003, p. 67: a smaller number of executions accompanied by deportations) and Nelson (legal vengeance). I did not open those books. archive.org annalesregnifran00anna (Kurze 1895, MGH SRG 6) djvu text; OL search-inside ("delocare", "Verden" "delocati"); en.wikipedia.org Massacre_of_Verden (raw, lead only)
T130 [C8] "The Sui people were equally ruthless. When their troops entered Nanjing, and the last emperor of the southern Chen surrendered, they razed the city to the ground" (p. 341) Consistent on the razing. Minor difference on "surrendered" and on timing. Sui shu 31 (Dili zhi), on the prefecture whose seat was Jiankang (modern Nanjing): "平陳，詔並平蕩耕墾，更於石頭城置蔣州" ("after Chen was pacified, an edict ordered it entirely levelled and ploughed for cultivation; Jiang prefecture was set up instead at Shitou"). Chen shu 6: the last ruler, Chen Shubao, fled with palace women to a well, got into it, and "及夜，為隋軍所執" ("at night he was seized by the Sui army"). He was captured rather than formally surrendering, and the levelling followed by imperial edict after the conquest (589). Britannica says Wendi overwhelmed Chen in 589, which "had put up only token resistance", and then exempted the new population "from 10 years of taxes to help ensure their loyalty". That is context against a simple "ruthless" label. A Time-Life volume has almost the book's wording (OL search-inside: "Coldly, Wendi razed the entire city of Jiankang, the 300-year-old capital"). zh.wikisource.org 隋書/卷31, 陳書/卷6; web.archive.org Britannica China/The-Sui-dynasty, Wendi; OL search-inside
T131 (Arian) [C9a] "the Arian Visigoths in Spain were notoriously intolerant towards Jewish people, adopting an official church-state policy of systematic anti-Semitism" (p. 341) Inconsistent (wrong confessional period) Encyclopaedia Judaica, "Spain" (S. Schwarzfuchs): the anti-Jewish policy followed "the conversion of their king Reccared, originally an Arian, to Catholicism (587)… As in the case of all other subjects, the policy was to have them adopt Catholicism, which had by then become the state religion." New Catholic Encyclopedia: "With the acceptance of the Catholic faith by Reccared … the end came for Arianism in Spain; and Arius was anathematized in 589". Bachrach, Early Medieval Jewish Policy (OL search-inside): "Until 589 the Visigoths were Arian Christians, and scholars generally agree that they pursued a policy of tolerance toward the many Jewish…". Ziegler, Church and State in Visigothic Spain (1930): under the Arian kings Jews lived under the Breviary of Alaric. Restrictions applied (no Christian slaves, no new synagogues, no public office, death for proselytising Christians), but Jews "were free to practise their cult … and were not to be disturbed in Sabbath or festival observance". "Beyond this legislation … the Visigothic kings of the Arian period do not appear to have made laws in regard to the Jews". Ziegler calls this "tolerance of the Arian sovereigns". The persecution the book describes was by Catholic Visigothic kings and the Councils of Toledo. encyclopedia.com (EJ "Spain"; NCE "Visigoths"); archive.org churchstateinvis00zieg djvu; OL search-inside (Bachrach)
T131 (measures) [C9b] Circumcision, Sabbath and other rites outlawed; forced conversion and baptism; exorbitant taxes; property confiscated; public flogging (p. 341) Consistent, but all under the Catholic kings from 589 to 711 EJ "Spain": Third Council of Toledo (589) ordered children of mixed marriages baptised. Sisebut: "From 613 they were ordered to be baptized or leave the kingdom". Recceswinth (653): "prohibiting circumcision and forbidding them to celebrate the Sabbath and the festivals". Erwig (12th Council of Toledo, 681): forced baptism; refusers penalised "by having their belongings seized, by corporal punishment, and finally by exile". Egica: "their taxes were considerably increased". 17th Council (694): Jews "declared as slaves and their possessions confiscated". The Visigothic Code XII.2.5 and XII.2.7 (Scott translation) ban Passover, Sabbath and circumcision. EJ also notes these laws "were honored more in the breach than in the observance". encyclopedia.com EJ "Spain"; web.archive.org libro.uca.edu/vcode/vg12-2.htm
T131 (executions) [C9c] "publicly flogged and even executed simply for being Jewish" (p. 341) Minor difference (overstated) Visigothic Code XII.2.12 (Scott numbering): anyone who defies the anti-Jewish laws "shall be either stoned to death, or burned by such of his own countrymen as may have entered into an agreement to do so", unless the king commutes the sentence to slavery and confiscation. EJ (Recceswinth) says converts had to pledge "to execute themselves those of their erring brethren who backslid into Judaism". The death penalty was therefore written into law for practising Judaism or relapsing after baptism. I found no source documenting actual executions, or death "simply for being Jewish" as such, and EJ stresses weak enforcement. web.archive.org libro.uca.edu vg12-2; encyclopedia.com EJ "Spain"
C116 [C3] "The Huns … would kill anyone who committed a serious crime. Theft would result in the expropriation of the thief's property. Even minor crimes resulted in cruel punishment involving the crushing of bones." (p. 349) Unverified for the European Huns. The wording matches Sima Qian's description of the Xiongnu. Shiji 110 (Xiongnu liezhuan), 2nd-1st c. BCE: "其法，拔刃尺者死，坐盜者沒入其家；有罪小者軋，大者死" ("their law: whoever draws a blade a foot [from the sheath] dies; one convicted of theft has his household/property confiscated; lesser offences are punished by ya, major ones by death"). Commentators disagree on ya (軋). Hanshu yinyi and Fu Qian say it means cutting the face with a blade. Ru Chun says beating. Yan Shigu says "軋者謂輾轢其骨節，若今之厭踝者也" (crushing the bone joints, like present-day ankle-pressing). Burton Watson's translation (OL search-inside, Records of the Grand Historian): "Anyone convicted of theft has his property confiscated. Minor offenses are punished by flogging"; Ebrey's Chinese Civilization sourcebook also has "flogged". Britannica (Xiongnu): "Others believe that the Xiongnu are the Huns … Though possible, this view cannot be substantiated." I found no Priscus-type source on European Hun criminal law. The book transfers a Chinese account of the Xiongnu to the Huns of the European "barbarian invasions", and picks the most severe reading of ya. zh.wikisource.org 史記/卷110 and 史記三家註/卷110; OL search-inside ("draws his sword a foot", "has his property confiscated" "minor"); web.archive.org Britannica Xiongnu
C113 "the Byzantine Romans, who considered themselves civilized, were as savage as the so-called Barbarians hordes" (p. 341) Opinion — —
1.6 Theme I: al-Andalus, Granada and the Moriscos (pp. 341–345) (helper A)

Page note: helper A labelled rows A32–A39 "p. 345". They are on printed p. 344 (second column), as in the extraction, and are corrected here.

# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
T132 / C117 [A1] Jews and Christians of al-Andalus "generally experienced a golden age of peace and prosperity over the course of nearly eight centuries"; rulers "intolerant towards those who were not Maliki Sunnis" but "extremely tolerant and benevolent towards Jews and Christians" (p. 341) Opinion / Disputed among sources Supporting: Brit. "ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III": "Christian and Jewish communities flourished during ʿAbd al-Raḥmān's tolerant reign." Brit. "Spain – Muslim Spain": Jews under the conquest "were no longer persecuted". The same article confirms Maliki rigour: the state "rested … on a foundation of the most rigid Islamic orthodoxy as interpreted by the Malikite (Mālikīyah) school, which in Al-Andalus manifested special characteristics of a hyperconservative nature." Against "eight centuries" of peace: (a) Martyrs of Córdoba. Brit. "Spain – Muslim Spain" says Mozarabs "began to publicly revile the Prophet … punishable by death from 850 onward … The conflict ended in 859–860 … [and] led to the execution of 53 people." (b) Granada 1066. Encyclopaedia Judaica (via Jewish Virtual Library): Joseph ha-Nagid "fell victim to a mass revolt in 1066 in which the [Jewish] community of Granada perished along with him", with "more than 1,500 householders" killed according to a later testimony. (c) Almohads. Brit. "Maimonides": the Almohads "captured Córdoba in 1148, leaving the Jewish community faced with the grim alternative of submitting to Islam or leaving the city." (d) Brit. "Spain – Muslim Spain": Christians and Jews "came next in the social hierarchy, but their numbers decreased in the course of time." See section 3 for the historiographical debate. https://web.archive.org/web/20261021061814/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Abd-al-Rahman-III ; https://web.archive.org/web/20261013212104/https://www.britannica.com/place/Spain/Muslim-Spain ; https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/granada ; https://web.archive.org/web/20261011102438/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Moses-Maimonides
T133 [A2] "'Abd al-Rahman III (r. 912-961 CE)" let the defeated Jews and Christians keep their religion, language and culture (p. 342) Consistent (one wording issue) Brit.: "reigned as hereditary emir … of Córdoba from October 912 and took the title of caliph in 929"; died "October 15, 961". Tolerance: see A1. Wording: "having defeated the Jews and Christians" is loose. His wars were against Leon and Navarre and against muwallad and crypto-Christian rebels such as Ibn Ḥafṣūn (Brit.). No war against Jews is described. same Brit. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III URL
C118 [A3] "it was under Muslim rule that the Hebrew language experienced a revival" (p. 342) Consistent in substance (the word "revival" is not checked) Brit. "Samuel ha-Nagid" (Granada, 993–1055/56): "Talmudic scholar, grammarian, philologist, poet". Brit. "Spain – Culture of Muslim Spain": the Jews "had become culturally Arabized. They also pursued their own religious studies; the works of Moses Maimonides … are a good example of the cultural brilliance of the Andalusian Jews." I found no opened source that uses the word "revival". https://web.archive.org/web/20260115144555/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Samuel-ha-Nagid ; https://web.archive.org/web/20260930200314/https://www.britannica.com/place/Spain/Culture-of-Muslim-Spain
C119 [A4] Jews, Christians and Muslims translated Greco-Roman classics and scientific tracts, "giving a powerful impetus to the European Renaissance" (p. 342) Partly consistent / Opinion Joint work under Muslim rule is attested. Brit. "Culture of Muslim Spain": a revision of Dioscorides' Materia medica "ordered by al-Naṣir [ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III], on which Jews, Arabs, and Christians collaborated"; Averroës' Aristotle commentaries "had great influence on Jewish and Christian thinkers, including Thomas Aquinas". However, the large Arabic-to-Latin movement happened largely under Christian rule. Brit. "Gerard of Cremona": he "went to Toledo [kingdom of Castile]… About 80 translations from the Arabic have been attributed to him". "Impetus to the Renaissance" is an interpretive claim. Brit. Culture URL above; https://web.archive.org/web/20250908035425/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gerard-of-Cremona
C120 [A5] "many Christian communities sided with the Muslims, and fought side to side … against the less civilized Christians from the north" (p. 342) Opinion / Unverified as stated No opened source describes Christian communities siding with Muslims for the reason given. Documented examples are of a different kind. Brit. "Spain – The Almoravids": the Almoravids "had to hire Christian mercenaries"; the Cid "first served as a mercenary in the ṭāʾifa of Zaragoza". Evidence pointing the other way: Brit. "Mozarab": Mozarabs "eventually relocated in the north"; Brit. "Muslim Spain": Ibn Ḥafṣūn led "muwallad and even Mozarabic discontent" against Córdoba. https://web.archive.org/web/20260921074536/https://www.britannica.com/place/Spain/The-Almoravids ; https://web.archive.org/web/20261013170327/https://www.britannica.com/topic/Mozarab ; Brit. Muslim-Spain URL
C121 [A6] Book titles: The Ornament of the World … "by Maria Rosa Menoscal"; Convivencia … by Mann, Glick, Dodds (p. 342) Consistent, except a misspelling Open Library: The Ornament of the World, María Rosa Menocal, first published 2002, Little, Brown. Convivencia, Vivian B. Mann, Thomas F. Glick, Jerrilynn D. Dodds, 1992, George Braziller with the Jewish Museum. The book's bibliography repeats "Menoscal". https://openlibrary.org/search.json?title=ornament+of+the+world&author=menocal ; https://openlibrary.org/search.json?title=convivencia&q=glick
T134 [A7] The Emirate of Granada "came to an end after more than seven hundred years of real and effective rule" (p. 342) Minor difference (conflation) Brit. "Naṣrid dynasty": the Nasrids "ruled Granada from 1238 to 1492", about 254 years. "More than seven hundred years" fits Muslim rule in Iberia, not the emirate. Brit. "Muslim Spain" refers to "Arabs who had entered Spain in 712 under Mūsā". https://web.archive.org/web/20261013172838/https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nasrid-dynasty
— (p. 342) [A8] Granada fell "for the same reasons that the Huns razed Baghdad" (p. 342) Inconsistent (factual slip) Brit. "Hülegü": the Mongol ruler who "in 1258 … seized and largely destroyed Baghdad". The Huns had no part in it. https://web.archive.org/web/20261027133408/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hulegu
T135 [A9] "The last Caliph of the Umayyads, 'Abd al-Rahman I, escaped to found the Emirate of Cordoba in 756 CE" (p. 342) Inconsistent (the 756 date is fine) Brit. "Marwān II": "the last of the Umayyad caliphs (reigned 744–750)", killed 750. Brit. "ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I": "a member of the Umayyad ruling family of Syria who founded an Umayyad dynasty in Spain". He fled the ʿAbbāsid massacre and was "attacking and defeating the governor of Al-Andalus in 755 and making Córdoba his capital". He never held the title of caliph. https://web.archive.org/web/20260924111004/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Marwan-II ; https://web.archive.org/web/20261004183658/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Abd-al-Rahman-I
T136 [A10] The emirate "was declared a Caliphate in 929 CE, under his successor, 'Abd al-Rahman III, in response to a threat from the Fatimids" (p. 342) Consistent (motive partly; "successor" is loose) Brit. "ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III": he assumed the caliphal title in 929. "His reasons were, internally, to enhance his prestige and, externally, to counter the Fāṭimid claim to this honour." He was a later descendant (grandson of ʿAbd Allāh), not ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I's immediate successor. Brit. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III URL
T137 [A11] Bayazid II (r. 1481–1512) "committed his forces to Cyprus" instead of defending al-Andalus (p. 342) Inconsistent (reign dates consistent) Reign 1481–1512: Brit. "Bayezid II". Cyprus: Brit. "Caterina Cornaro": the Venetians "forced the queen to abdicate (1489)". Brit. "Cyprus – Ottoman rule": "A Turkish invading force landed in Cyprus in 1570 … the following year Famagusta fell". So Cyprus was Venetian, and the Ottomans took it only in 1570–71. What Ottoman forces were doing: TDV-Turan: the Ottoman–Mamluk war "1485'te başlayan … 1491'de anlaşmaya varıldı" (began 1485; agreement reached 1491). TDV-Turan also says help to Granada could not be given because of "Osmanlı deniz gücünün zayıflığı ve Cem olayı" (Ottoman naval weakness and the Cem affair), but "Kemal Reis kumandasındaki bir filo İspanya sahillerini vurmuş" (a fleet under Kemal Reis struck the Spanish coasts). TDV-Bostan: Kemal Reis was sent in 892/1487 "Güneybatı İspanya'yı vurmakla" (to strike south-western Spain) and plundered Málaga. Brit. "Bayezid II": he "committed only a modest force against the Mamluks", fearing a Christian alliance built around his brother Cem. https://web.archive.org/web/20261025213530/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Bayezid-II ; https://web.archive.org/web/20260105232846/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Caterina-Cornaro ; https://web.archive.org/web/20261028211115/https://www.britannica.com/place/Cyprus/Ottoman-rule ; https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/bayezid-ii ; https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/kemal-reis
T138 [A12] Bayazid II "sending his navy to al-Andalus in 1492 CE to evacuate the Jews" (p. 342) Unverified / Disputed (I found no documentary support) Brit. "Bayezid II" says only that he "welcomed Jews expelled from Spain … He encouraged their immigration". It says nothing about a fleet. TDV-Turan: Kemal Reis's fleet "Endülüs müslümanlarının bir kısmını Afrika sahillerine ve Osmanlı ülkesine taşımıştı" (carried some Andalusian Muslims to the African coast and Ottoman lands), while "yahudilerden bir kısmı da Osmanlı topraklarına sığınarak" (some Jews took refuge in Ottoman lands). No ships are mentioned for the Jews. TDV-Bostan: in 897/1492 Kemal Reis raided the French coast and the Balearics, then Malta, and returned to Gallipoli. No evacuation is mentioned. Popular sources (Wikipedia "Kemal Reis" lead; +972 Magazine 2018) state the rescue without citing evidence. TDV URLs above; Brit. Bayezid URL; https://www.972mag.com/when-the-sultan-took-in-jewish-refugees/ ; lead only: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kemal_Reis&action=raw
T139 [A13] "Of the 500,000 original inhabitants of Granada, 100,000 died fighting … or were enslaved, 200,000 fled (mostly to North Africa), and 200,000 stayed behind" (p. 343) Inconsistent (500,000 is far above scholarly estimates; the breakdown has no source) Ladero 1968 (article pp. 481–490; section "La población del reino de Granada"): "no parece muy arriesgado cifrar en 300.000 personas en números redondos la población del reino de Granada en los años anteriores a su conquista". Granada city was about 50,000 (Torres Balbás), and Cisneros reckoned "unas 50.000 ánimas" in the city and Vega around 1500. Núñez Muley c. 1565 counted "50.000 vecinos moriscos … es decir, 250.000 personas". Cortés Peña 2009: "los 300 000 musulmanes que, se calcula, habitaban el reino antes del comienzo de la guerra … reducido en 1502 a unos 165 000". Lea p. 31 n.: the Moorish population of the city c. 1499 "was estimated at 40,000". The book cites no source for its figures. https://app.dipalme.org/pandora/high.raw?id=0000004037&name=00000001.original.pdf ; https://books.openedition.org/ausonius/1803?lang=en ; https://archive.org/download/moriscosofspaint00leahuoft/moriscosofspaint00leahuoft_djvu.txt
T140 [A14] The Treaty of Granada was "signed and ratified" between Boabdil "(1459-1533 CE)" and Fernando and Isabel, and granted religious, cultural and linguistic freedom (p. 343) Consistent (Boabdil's dates disputed) CODOIN 8 p. 421 prints the Simancas original: "Capitulación de la toma é entrega de Granada. Fecha en el Real de la Vega de Granada á 25 dias del mes de noviembre de 1491", agreed "con el alcaide Bulcacin el Muleh, en nombre de Muley Baaudili Rey de Granada". The BRAH review of Garrido Atienza (1910) gives the same place and date. Brit. "Muḥammad XII": he "surrendered, on January 2, 1492". Terms: Chejne p. 6 lists "the preservation of their law, mosque … freedom of travel and worship; and the use of their language and customs". Boabdil's dates: Brit. gives "died 1527". Al-Maqqari (Gayangos II, 390) says he died in Fez in 940 AH, printed "(A.D. 1538)". By tabular conversion, 940 AH began 23 July 1533 (my calculation). So "1533" matches al-Maqqari's Hijri year, and the 1538 in Gayangos is probably a misprint or OCR slip. I did not check the 1459 birth year. https://archive.org/download/colecciondedocum08tick/colecciondedocum08tick_djvu.txt ; https://www.cervantesvirtual.com/research/las-capitulaciones-para-la-entrega-de-granada-0/01be4774-82b2-11df-acc7-002185ce6064.pdf ; https://web.archive.org/web/20251119070444/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Muhammad-XII ; https://archive.org/download/historyofthemoha032395mbp/historyofthemoha032395mbp_djvu.txt
T140 / C126 [A15] The treaty "was soon broken … on the pretext that covenants with 'infidels' were not binding" (p. 343) Breach: Consistent. Stated pretext: Disputed (the sources give a different justification) Breach: al-Maqqari (Gayangos II, 391): "Not many years elapsed before the Christians violated the treaty". Chejne p. 6: "soon subjected to strictures in violation of the terms". Justification given in the sources: the 1499–1501 rebellion was treated as forfeiting the treaty. Brit. "Spain – The conquest of Granada": they "considered themselves to have been released by the rebellion from their previous guarantees". Chejne p. 7: the revolt "gave the monarchy an excuse for declaring the terms of capitulations null and void". Lea p. 35: "the opportunity of annulling the capitulations was not to be lost". Al-Maqqari (p. 391) also cites priests' writings on compelling converts to return to their old faith. The general doctrine that pledges to infidels do not bind is cited from Hamidullah. I did not check Hamidullah. Gayangos URL; Chejne: https://archive.org/download/chejne-anwar.-islam-and-the-west.-the-moriscos-a-cultural-and-social-history-1983/ ; https://web.archive.org/web/20261017192945/https://www.britannica.com/place/Spain/The-conquest-of-Granada ; Lea URL
T141 / C124–C125 [A16] "The terms of surrender negotiated by the Muslims in the Capitulation of 1492 CE contained sixty-seven articles", followed by a quotation (al-Maqqari 389) (p. 343) Quotation: Consistent. "Sixty-seven": Disputed among sources. "Of 1492" and the bracketed gloss: Minor errors The quotation matches Gayangos II, 388–389: "The capitulation contained sixty-seven articles, among which were the following …". The quote starts on p. 388, not 389. The book omits some clauses (for example, that no Christian or Jew in office under the late sultan should rule over them). Article counts: the Castilian text from Simancas (CODOIN 8, pp. 421–436) runs to 47 articles, which the editors numbered ("La capitulación original no tiene numerados los artículos"). CODOIN's note says the privilegio rodado version printed by Bermúdez de Pedraza (1638) lacks one article and adds eight, which would give about 54. The BRAH review says the same: "falta uno de ellos y se aumentan ocho nuevos". A separate agreement on Boabdil's own interests, dated the same day, is printed at CODOIN 8, pp. 411ff. Spanish Wikipedia says "77 artículos" (lead only). The document is dated 25 Nov 1491, not 1492. Gloss: the book's "[Spanish Muslims who refused to convert to Christianity]" is wrong. Brit. "Mudejar" defines them as Muslims "who remained in Spain after the Reconquista", from Arabic "mudajjan, 'permitted to remain'". Gayangos URL; CODOIN 8 URL; BRAH PDF URL; https://web.archive.org/web/20261013192917/https://www.britannica.com/topic/Mudejar ; lead only: https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Capitulaciones_de_Granada&action=raw
T142 [A17] Wiegers block quote: "According to the capitulations drawn up by Ferdinand and Isabella … within the space of seven years these generous terms had been broken. (10)" (p. 343) Not found in the cited source (the claim itself is consistent) The sentence does not appear anywhere in Wiegers 1994. I searched the full text, including pp. 9–11. Wiegers p. 9 actually says: "Once again, a capitulation seemed to guarantee the existence a stable Mudejar minority. This, however, was not to be." He goes on to describe the bearing of arms being banned and Cisneros's arrival in 1498. The substance (terms broken by about 1499) agrees with Wiegers and the sources in A15. The book's bibliography does list Wiegers 1994 (Brill). Where the quoted wording comes from remains unknown. It may be Boase 1990, which I could not access. https://archive.org/download/alj_20231221/Alj_djvu.txt
T143–T144 [A18] Cisneros "started to forcibly convert Muslims, burn Islamic books"; "the Muslims of Albaicin, Granada revolted in 1499" (p. 343) Consistent Wiegers p. 9: Cisneros's method "in December 1499 led to a revolt in the Albaicin … which spread to the Alpujarras and had to be put down by military force, in 1501". Lea pp. 30–35 and Chejne p. 6 ("had all Arabic religious books burned"). Wiegers, Lea, Chejne URLs
T145 [A19] "In 1500 CE, many Muslims were compelled to convert" (p. 343) Consistent Lea pp. 35–39: Albaicín baptisms after the revolt; Ferdinand's general pardon to converts of 26 Feb 1500; the Alpujarras rebels "consenting to baptism" in 1500. Lea URL
T146 [A20] "In the Capitulations of 1500-1501, Muslims were prohibited from ritually slaughtering animals and were banned from bathing" (p. 343) Unverified No opened source records such clauses in 1500–1501. Lea pp. 37–41 describes the 1500–1501 terms as incentives and conditions: a cédula of 30 July 1500 promising converts tax equality; the 1501 Ronda/Sierra Bermeja terms allowing emigration for 10 doblas; disarmament on 1 Sept 1501. Bans on baths are documented later, in the Edict of Granada of 1526 (Lea p. 216) and the 1567 Pragmática (Mármol I, 145; Lea p. 229). Bans on slaughter appear in an edict after 1524 (Chejne p. 9). Lea, Chejne, Mármol URLs
T147 [A21] "On October 12th, 1501, all Arabic and Islamic books in Granada were burned" (p. 343) Inconsistent (two events conflated; "all" overstated) The burning was Cisneros's, in 1499–1500. Lea p. 32: "five thousand were brought to him … the whole were publicly burnt, save a few on medicine". Eisenberg 1992 n. 28: "No se conoce la fecha exacta, aunque parece probable que fue en enero o febrero de 1500". Eisenberg also quotes Vallejo's count of "más de 4 ó 5 mil volúmenes". 12 October 1501 is the date of a royal order on Arabic books. Wiegers p. 10 n.: "At first Arabic books on medicine etc. were excepted from this prohibition: see AGS RGS, 12 October 1501, f. 13", published in Ladero Quesada, Los Mudéjares de Castilla, doc. 146. Lea, Wiegers URLs; https://web.archive.org/web/20160406123737/http://users.ipfw.edu/jehle/deisenbe/Other_Hispanic_Topics/Cisneros_y_la_quema_de_los_manuscritos_granadinos.htm
T148 [A22] "In 1501, the Spanish authorities gave the Muslims an ultimatum: convert to Christianity or be expelled" (p. 343) Consistent Lea p. 39 (early 1501): "Ferdinand issued a proclamation that all who would not be converted must leave the kingdom within ten days". Chejne p. 7: "In 1501 a royal ordinance was issued calling for the conversion of the Muslims of Granada". Lea, Chejne URLs
T150 [A23] "In 1502, the ultimatums were extended to the mudejares of Castile and Leon" (p. 344) Consistent Lea pp. 43–44: "on February 12, 1502, was issued the pragmatica … all Moors were ordered to quit the kingdoms of Castile and Leon by the end of April — that is, all males over the age of fourteen and females over twelve". Wiegers p. 9: "In February 1502 the Mudejars of Castile … were offered the choice between conversion, emigration or death". Brit. "Morisco": "In 1502, offered the choice of baptism or exile". Lea, Wiegers; https://web.archive.org/web/20261013155004/https://www.britannica.com/topic/Morisco
T151 [A24] "In 1508, Arabic and Islamic dress was prohibited by law" (p. 344) Unverified (year) No opened source gives 1508. Lea p. 216 n.: "The wearing of Moorish garments had been forbidden under Ferdinand, but the prohibition was suspended until, in 1518, Charles ordered it enforced and again suspended it". Chejne p. 7: "In 1516, Cisneros … instituted an ordinance calling for the abandonment of Moorish dress and customs … rescinded". The English Wikipedia "Morisco" lead gives 1508; that is a lead only, not a source. Lea, Chejne URLs; lead: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morisco&action=raw
T152 [A25] "Between 1511 and 1513 a series of decrees were passed prohibiting the production, sale, and consumption of halal meat" (p. 344) Unverified Not found. The 1511 and 1513 decrees I did find are on other subjects. Lea p. 42 and p. 191: the arms edict was repeated in 1511 and 1515. A UNAM chapter (2019) cites cédulas of 20 June 1511 and 29 July 1513 on godparents at baptisms. Chejne p. 9: a post-1524 edict banned the "manner of slaughtering animals". Lea p. 207 mentions undated laws forbidding Moriscos to be butchers, "repeated as late as 1595". Lea, Chejne URLs; https://archivos.juridicas.unam.mx/www/bjv/libros/11/5148/11.pdf
T153 (Navarre) [A26] Mudéjars of Navarre forced to convert or leave "by 1515" (p. 344) Consistent Wiegers p. 9: "In 1515 the new Castilian legislation was made applicable to Navarre when that was incorporated into the Spanish crown." Lea p. 55: Navarre was conquered in 1512 and brought under the 1502 edict; most emigrated, and "as early as 1516" Tudela had 200 empty houses. Wiegers, Lea URLs
T153 (Aragon) [A27] Mudéjars of Aragon forced to convert or leave "by … 1525" (p. 344) Minor difference Lea p. 87: the general edict of 25 Nov 1525 ordered the Moors of Valencia out "by December 31, 1525, and those of Aragon and Catalonia by January 31, 1526". Wiegers p. 10: "In 1526 the general conversion of all Muslims in Aragon and Valencia was decreed". Brit. "Morisco": "in 1526 the Muslims of Valencia and Aragon were similarly forced to convert". Lea, Wiegers, Brit. Morisco URLs
T154 [A28] "In 1525, forced conversions were declared to be legally and religiously valid, and Charles V … extended the decree of expulsion or conversion to Muslims in all of his kingdoms" (p. 344) Consistent Lea p. 78: a junta in Madrid, attended by the emperor on 23 March 1525, upheld the Germanía baptisms, and a cédula of 4 April 1525 "declared the baptized Moors to be Christians". Wiegers p. 10: "a Junta of theologians confirmed it in 1525". General edict: see A27. Lea, Wiegers URLs
T155 [A29] "In 1526 and 1527, he introduced even more restrictive legislation": clothing, amulets, jewellery, circumcision (Chejne 9); weapons; Islamic marriages (p. 344) Consistent, with an omission Lea pp. 214–216: the Edict of Granada, 7 Dec 1526. It forbade "the use of Arabic and the wearing of Moorish dress"; banned Moorish-style jewels and baths; required Christian midwives at births; ordered doors open "on feast-days, Fridays, Saturdays and during weddings"; banned Moorish names; checked licences to bear arms. A papal brief transferring the Inquisition to Granada is dated 7 July 1527 (Lea p. 215 n.). Chejne p. 9 lists "Arabic language, clothing, amulets, jewels, circumcision, manner of slaughtering animals". Omitted by the book: the edict was suspended for payment. Lea p. 217: the Moriscos "raised 80,000 ducats … he suspended it". Chejne p. 9: "rescinded in return for a payment of ninety thousand ducados". Lea p. 230: "Forty years before they had been similarly threatened and had succeeded in buying themselves off". Lea, Chejne URLs
T156 [A30] "In 1565, Felipe II outlawed speaking, reading, and writing in Arabic; nullified all contracts written in Arabic; obliged the Moriscos to dress like Christians; prohibited … the headscarf or the veil; banned Morisco music and dances; outlawed all celebrations on Friday; forbade … Muslim names; … henna; and banned and destroyed public baths" (p. 344) Date: Inconsistent. Contents: Consistent, with minor differences Date: 1565 was the year of Archbishop Guerrero's provincial council (Lea p. 226). Mármol I, 142: "mandó su Magestad el año de mil quinientos sesenta y seis hacer una junta en la villa de Madrid". The Pragmática was proclaimed "el primero dia del mes de Enero del año … mil quinientos sesenta y siete" (Mármol I, 150; Lea pp. 228, 230). Contents (Mármol I, 143–145; Lea p. 229): Castilian to be learned within three years, after which no one might "hablar, leer, ni escrebir en publico ni en secreto en arábigo"; contracts in Arabic void; Arabic books to be handed in within 30 days; no new Moorish garments; women to go "las caras descubiertas"; doors open at weddings, "los viernes en la tarde y todos los dias de fiesta"; no zambras or leilas; no Moorish names; no henna; artificial baths "se derribasen luego", public and private. Minor differences: there was no general ban on "all celebrations on Friday". The bans covered zambras and leilas (Lea: "on Fridays and feast-days"; Mármol: "en ninguna manera") and the open-door rule. The baths ban covered private baths as well as public ones. https://archive.org/download/historiadelrebel01mr/historiadelrebel01mr_djvu.txt ; Lea URL
C128 [A31] The headscarf or veil was "normative even for the Christian women of the time" (p. 344) Partly supported / Opinion Mármol I, 144–145: the junta expected the Moriscas, to avoid going unveiled, to switch to "mantos y sombreros, como se había hecho en el reyno de Aragón". Chejne p. 20, summarising Núñez Muley's 1567 protest: "Our women's clothes follow local traditions (traje de provincia), as Castilians and other provincials wear their own traditional clothing." Lea p. 130 n.: a Morisca on trial pleaded that henna "was not specially a Moorish custom, for Christian women frequently stained their nails and hair". I opened no source on Christian women's veiling customs. Mármol I, Chejne, Lea URLs
T157 [A32] The 'aqiqa was outlawed; children were forcibly baptized; Moriscos were obliged to attend mass (p. 344) Partly verified Lea p. 216: the 1526 edict required that "all births were to be watched by Christian midwives to see that no Moorish rites were performed". Lea p. 214: "they had their children baptized and then washed off the chrism"; "they went to mass to escape the fine" (p. 213). None of the sources I opened names the ʿaqīqa itself. Lea URL
C129 [A33] Wiegers quotations: legislation "was directed not only against religion, but against all manifestations of traditional culture, such as all oral and written use of Arabic" (10); bathing banned (10); an Arabic-script book was a possible corpus delicti (11) (p. 344) Consistent Wiegers p. 10: "In 1567 new legislation in Granada was directed not only against religion, but against all manifestations of traditional culture, such as all oral and written use of Arabic and traditional dances (zambras)." Wiegers p. 10: "The possession of Islamic books was prohibited, followed by prohibitions of customs which were supposed to be connected with Islam, such as bathing." Wiegers p. 11: "manuscripts written in 'letra morisca' were viewed as possible corpora delicti". Lea p. 131: possession of Arabic books "was almost conclusive pr[oof]". Wiegers, Lea URLs
C130 (doors) [A34] Muslims "were also expected to keep their doors open, particularly on Fridays" (p. 344) Consistent Lea p. 216 (1526 edict) and p. 229 (1567); Mármol I, 145. See A29–A30. Lea, Mármol URLs
C130 (pork, bathing) [A35] Christians offered pork to Moriscos to test them; refusal led to the Inquisition and torture; "a failure to smell foul" could lead to torture (p. 344) Partly consistent; rhetorical framing is Opinion Lea p. 130: "Abstinence from pork and wine was of course a highly suspicious circumstance, which frequently appears in the trials". Lea p. 129: "cleanliness was regarded as a suspicious circumstance — doubtless from the Moorish habit of bathing". Bartolomé Sánchez (Toledo 1597) was tortured, and Miguel Cañete (1606) "for washing himself in the fields". No source supports the claim that Christians "found it comical to randomly offer pork". Lea URL
T158 (trigger) [A36] Philip II "decreed that all Morisco children were to be turned over to Christian priests to be educated, leading to the Alpujarras uprising" (p. 344) Inconsistent / Unverified The sources name the 1567 Pragmática (and the silk crisis) as the trigger, not a decree on children. Brit. "Spain – Philip II": "In 1567 a decree was published … On Christmas Day, 1568, they rose". Wiegers pp. 10–11; Lea pp. 228–230. The Pragmática's articles (Mármol I, 143–145) contain no clause on handing over children. Schools teaching Castilian to children go back to 1526 (Lea p. 216) and were suggested again in 1566 (Mármol I, 148). The children-related pragmática came during the war. Lea pp. 239–240: when captives were enslaved, boys "under 10 and girls under 11" were exempted and "given in charge to Christians for support and instruction". Brit. Philip-II: https://web.archive.org/web/20261030074727/https://www.britannica.com/place/Spain/Philip-II ; Mármol I, Lea, Wiegers URLs
T158–T159 [A37] Alpujarras uprising "lasted from 1568 to 1571"; suppressed by Don Juan de Austria (p. 344) Consistent; end date Disputed among sources Lea p. 240: the revolt broke out in late December 1568. Lea p. 261: the last rebel king Aben Aboo was killed in March 1571. Bernabé Pons 2020: "Second War of Granada (1568–1571)". Chejne p. 10: "1568-1570". Wiegers p. 11: "After its suppression in 1570". Brit. "Morisco": "They revolted in 1569; after two years of war". Don Juan's command: Lea pp. 254–260. See timeline item A-T10 (§2.3). Lea, Chejne, Wiegers, Brit. Morisco; https://www.ieg-ego.eu/en/threads/europe-on-the-road/forced-ethnic-migration/luis-fernando-bernabe-pons-expulsion-of-the-muslims-from-spain
T160 [A38] Galera "was raised [razed] to the ground and sprinkled with salt, and all its 2,500 inhabitants, including women and children, were slaughtered" (quoted as Wiegers 11) (p. 344) Razing and salting: Consistent. "All 2,500 slaughtered": Inconsistent. Attribution: not found in Wiegers Mármol, an eyewitness ordered to carry out the razing, II, Libro VIII, chs 5–6 (the 1797 ed. prints "2^S"/"2^p", apparently pp. 248–249): Galera taken after the mine of "diez dias del mes de Febrero" [1570]. Over "dos mil y quatrocientos hombres de pelea" were killed; Don Juan's guards killed "mas de quatrocientas mugeres y niños"; "quatro mil y quinientas" women and children survived as captives, from Galera, Orce, Castilleja and elsewhere. Don Juan "mandó … que la villa fuese asolada y sembrada de sal". Lea p. 255 gives the same figures (400 women and children "butchered", 4,500 "preserved as slaves"). The quotation is not on Wiegers p. 11. The figure "all of the 2,500 inhabitants were slaughtered" appears in English Wikipedia "Galera, Granada", which cites a school textbook (Pendrill 2002). https://archive.org/download/historiadelrebel02mr/historiadelrebel02mr_djvu.txt ; Lea, Wiegers URLs; lead: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Galera,_Granada&action=raw
T161 / C131 [A39] After the revolt the Crown "forcibly deported and resettled 84,000 Moriscos from Granada and Castile" (p. 344) Disputed among sources; minor misreading Wiegers p. 11: "about 84,000 Moriscos were deported and scattered throughout Castile". That means from Granada into Castile; the book's "from Granada and Castile" misreads it. Chejne p. 11: "Some fifty thousand Granadans were rounded up and redistributed". Lea p. 259 gives the order of 28 Oct 1570 and the routes, but no total. The English Wikipedia lead says 80,000–90,000, citing Lapeyre, Harvey and Vincent; I did not open those. Wiegers, Chejne, Lea URLs
T162 / C132 [A40] "In 1609, the final decision to expel the Moriscos was taken on the grounds of national security", with accusations of conspiring with North Africa and the Ottomans (pp. 344–345) Consistent Wiegers p. 11: the decision "was taken in 1609 … mainly justified on grounds of national security, viz. an alleged Morisco conspiracy with foreign powers". Lea p. 315: the Council of State's consulta of April 1609, with "fear of the Moors and Muley Cidan". Brit. "Timeline of the Spanish Inquisition": "April 9, 1609 — Philip III … signs a decree expelling the Moriscos". Valencia edict published 22 Sept 1609 (Lea p. 320). Wiegers, Lea; https://web.archive.org/web/20260211040105/https://www.britannica.com/list/timeline-of-the-spanish-inquisition
T163 [A41] Expulsion of the Jews in 1492 "completed in one step" (p. 345) Consistent (broadly) Brit. Timeline: "Ferdinand and Isabella issue the Alhambra Decree, which announces the expulsion of all Jews from Spain" (31 March 1492). I did not check earlier local expulsions. Brit. Timeline URL
T164–T165 [A42] "The Moriscos of Valencia were the first expelled in 1609, followed by the Moriscos of Castile in 1614" (p. 345) Inconsistent Lea: Valencia edict 22 Sept 1609 (p. 320). Andalusia and Granada edict sent 9 Dec 1609, published 12 Jan 1610 (p. 345). Old and New Castile, La Mancha and Extremadura: cédula of 28 Dec 1609 permitting departure, then an edict of 10 July 1610 (pp. 349–351). Aragon and Catalonia: edicts published 29 May 1610 (p. 339). Remnants, including the old Castilian Moriscos antiguos: orders of 22 March and 3 May 1611 (p. 351). Murcia and the Val de Ricote: cédula 19 Oct 1613, proclamation 4 Jan 1614 (pp. 356–357). Bernabé Pons 2020 gives the same order. Castile was not last in 1614; only the Murcia/Ricote remnant was. Lea, Bernabé Pons URLs
C133 [A43] Moriscos "were forced to leave Spain without their money or goods. They were even forced to leave their children behind" (p. 345) Minor difference / partly consistent The terms varied by edict. Valencia: "what they could carry on their backs" (Lea p. 320). Andalusia: they could sell their movables and carry the proceeds as merchandise (p. 345). Castile: sale of movables allowed (p. 349). July 1610: money and jewels allowed if half was surrendered (p. 351). Children: the Catalonia edict (and later Castile and Andalusia) kept children under seven whose parents went to infidel lands (pp. 339, 345). In Valencia, children could go with their parents (see A44). Lea URL
T166 [A44] "Morisco children under the age of seven were to serve the religious establishment, while … children over the age of seven were to be sold as slaves to Cristianos viejos" (Boase 13) (p. 345) Inconsistent with the edicts Valencia edict (Lea p. 321): "Children under four years of age desiring to remain could do so with consent of their parents"; children under six of Old Christian fathers stayed. Chejne p. 13 agrees: "children under four provided that their parents consented". Later edicts kept children under seven going to infidel lands (Lea pp. 339, 345). No edict sold children over seven as slaves. Related facts that may lie behind the claim: Ribera's 1602 memorial urged that children under seven be distributed "to whom the king could grant them as slaves" (Lea p. 322 n.). Children captured in the Valencian revolts were sold "for 8, 10, 12 and 15 ducats apiece", although "the king decided that he did not grant them as slaves". For these captured children, "Philip decided that those over 7 should be expelled and the rest be kept" (Lea p. 324 n.). The gloss "families which had been Christians for over a thousand years" for Old Christians is the book's own; no source checked supports it. Lea, Chejne URLs
T167 [A45] "Between October 1609 and July 1611 … over 50,000 Moriscos died resisting forcible expulsion, while over 60,000 died during their passage abroad by land or sea, or at the hands of their co-religionists" (Boase 12) (p. 345) Traced to a contemporary source; wording differs slightly; no modern confirmation I could not access Boase. The figures go back to Aznar Cardona (1612), a pro-expulsion contemporary. At scan leaf 418 he says those "que dellos han muerto desventuradamente por estos montes, caminos [y ma]res desde el Octubre del año de mil seyscientos y nueve … hasta el Iulio de mil seyscientos y onze … son mas de cincuenta mil". That is, they died "miserably" in mountains, roads and seas; he does not say "resisting". At leaf 454 he says that after leaving Spain more than sixty thousand perished, "por estos mares … caminos … y otros á manos de sus amigos los Alarbes". The OCR is poor but readable at these points. Brit. Timeline repeats the figures as "Contemporary accounts estimate that some 50,000 are killed while resisting expulsion while another 60,000 die before reaching their destinations." Lea p. 334 gives a single example: about 3,000 killed at the Vall de Laguar in Nov 1609. I found no modern overall death count. https://archive.org/download/bub_gb_q9F5NeL42jEC/bub_gb_q9F5NeL42jEC_djvu.txt ; https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_q9F5NeL42jEC (leaves 418, 454, located with archive.org search-inside); Brit. Timeline; Lea URL
T168 [A46] "A total of 300,000 Moriscos, most of whom were from modern-day Aragon, Catalonia, and Valencia, were expelled … eventually reaching the Ottoman Empire and Morocco" (p. 345) Consistent (rounded); destinations incomplete Lapeyre 1959, as reproduced in Chejne's own note 67 (p. 179): Valencia 117,464; Catalonia 3,716; Aragon 60,818; Castile, Mancha and Extremadura 44,625; Murcia 13,552; Andalusia 29,939; Granada 2,026; total 272,140. The Crown of Aragon share (181,998) is about 67%, so "most" is right. Brit. "Spain – Reign of Philip III": "By 1614 some 275,000 Moriscos had been forced to leave Spain." Brit. "Morisco" and Brit. Timeline: about 300,000. Bernabé Pons 2020: "a figure between 275,000 and 300,000 people expelled or dead during the process is widely accepted". Destinations: Brit. "Morisco": "mainly in Algeria, Tunisia, and Morocco". Wiegers p. 11 adds the Ottoman Empire and Egypt, "but above all … Morocco and Tunisia". Chejne, Wiegers URLs; https://web.archive.org/web/20260808082714/https://www.britannica.com/place/Spain/The-reign-of-Philip-III ; Brit. Morisco, Brit. Timeline, Bernabé Pons URLs
T169 [A47] "Of the 500,000 Muslims from Granada, only 10,000 to 15,000 remained after the expulsion of 1609" (p. 345) Unverified; its base figure is unsupported No source found for 10,000–15,000. The base of 500,000 is not supported (see A13). Lapeyre (via Chejne n. 67) counts only 2,026 expelled from Granada in 1610, because most Granadans had been deported in 1570 (A39). The claim also conflicts with the book's own p. 343 ("200,000 stayed behind"). Chejne URL
T170 [A48] "According to the lowest estimate, one fifth of the Morisco population perished … According to other writers, two-thirds to three-quarters" (Boase 12) (p. 345) Unverified for the whole population; "two-thirds/three-quarters" goes back to contemporary claims about deportees in North Africa Lea p. 364: "the statement of the Comendador … of Oran, that what between disease and the atrocities of the Arabs two-thirds of those deported had perished. In fact, the general estimate was that the proportion was at least three-quarters." Those figures concern deportees landing in North Africa, not the whole Morisco population. I found no source for the "one fifth" figure. Lea URL
T171 [A49] "110,000 Moriscos left Andalusia, Murcia, and Hornachos; some 50,000, Cataluna; 120,000, Aragon; 250,000, Castile, Mancha, and Estremadura" for a total of "about half a million" (Chejne 13) (p. 345) Quotation accurate, but selective Chejne p. 13 has these words, but just before them he gives Valencia: "it is estimated that 125,000 were sent to North Africa". The book leaves this out. The four quoted figures add up to 530,000; with Valencia the total is 655,000. Chejne nevertheless writes "about half a million, although there is no general agreement". Chejne's own notes (p. 179) say the Catalonia figure "appears exaggerated. Lapeyre … puts it at 3717" and that Lapeyre "places [Aragon] at 60818". They also give Lapeyre's total of 272,140. Chejne URL
S7-19 [A50] Internal: the book gives 300,000 (A46) and "about half a million" (A49) side by side without reconciling them Inconsistent within the book Standard documentary figures: Lapeyre 272,140; Brit. 275,000 (Spain article) or about 300,000 (Morisco and Timeline articles); Bernabé Pons 275,000–300,000. Higher figures are older or contemporary: Danvila "something less than 500,000" (as reported by Lea p. 359); Aznar "más de seyscientos mil" (leaf 454); others listed by Lea p. 359 range from 120,000 to 3,000,000. Chejne's half-million rests on regional figures that his own notes question. Lea, Chejne, Aznar URLs

T198 The Capitulations, granting Christians commercial rights "and custody of certain holy places", "remained current from 1517 to their abolishment by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923" (p. 349) Inconsistent (start date). End date: Minor difference. Holy places: Minor difference (later grants) İnalcık (TDV "İmtiyâzât"). Start: the first Ottoman capitulation went to the Genoese c. 1352 (text lost); the earliest surviving text is dated 7 June 1387; Venetian grants followed in 1403, 1419, 1430, 1446 and 1479/1481. "Yavuz Sultan Selim, 1517'de Memlük sultanları tarafından Venedik'e verilen kapitülasyonları yeniledi" (in 1517 Selim renewed the Mamluk grants to Venice). The 1536 French draft (de la Forest) was never ratified, and "Fransa ile genel tasdikli kapitülasyon 1569 kapitülasyonudur" (the first ratified French capitulation is that of 1569). Holy places: French protection of pilgrims and monks came in 1604; Catholics regained some holy places by a 1690 decree; the broadest grant was 1740. End: an Ottoman ferman of 8 Sept 1914 abolished the capitulations unilaterally; Sèvres restored them; "Lozan Antlaşması ile (24 Temmuz 1923) müttefik devletler kapitülasyonların lağvını kabule mecbur oldular" (at Lausanne the Allies had to accept the abolition). https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/imtiyazat

1.8 Theme K: shari'ah, law and Western civilization; close of chapter (pp. 349–352)
# Book claim (page) Verdict What independent sources say Source URLs
T203 / C166 [C13a] "the shari'ah … was the inspiration for the Napoleonic Code (though some scholars attempt to trace this Code back to the Laws of Justinian and other sources), and thus the forerunner of modern Western law in France and Quebec" (pp. 349-350) Inconsistent with mainstream legal history. A minority pro-influence claim exists (see Section 3). Lloyd Bonfield, "Napoleonic Code", Encyclopedia of Modern Europe: the drafting commission included "two … experts in customary law, while two others were scholars of the ius commune"; "The code as it was finally promulgated in 1804 relied upon both sources, the Roman and the customary law, though most modern scholars believe that the former predominates"; "the civil codes of Louisiana and Quebec … have been inspired by it". So Roman-law and customary-law origins are the mainstream view, not a fringe attempt as the book implies. Quebec (Canadian Encyclopedia): the 1866 Civil Code of Lower Canada derived "the majority of the Code's rules from the Custom of Paris, brought to New France in 1663", relied "heavily" on Pothier and only "to a lesser extent on various commentaries on the Code Napoléon"; "For form, the commissioners adopted the model of the 1804 Code Napoléon". The Maliki text usually cited as the conduit, Khalil's Mukhtasar, was translated by N. Perron as Précis de jurisprudence musulmane … selon le rite mâlékite. It was published "par ordre du gouvernement" in the Exploration scientifique de l'Algérie pendant les années 1840, 1841, 1842 (Paris, Imprimerie nationale, 1848/1849), decades after the 1804 Code and tied to French Algeria, not to Bonaparte's Egyptian expedition. encyclopedia.com (Napoleonic Code, Bonfield); thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/civil-code; archive.org prcisdejurispru00unkngoog (title page); journals.qu.edu.qa FAILED; Britannica FAILED (403 and Wayback 429)
C167 [C13b] Ireland "known as 'The Isle of Saints and Scholars'" (p. 350) Consistent Traditional epithet. Archbishop John Healy's Insula sanctorum et doctorum, or Ireland's Ancient Schools and Scholars (1890; archive.org records). A travel book (OL search-inside) says Ireland "in the 6th-8th centuries was famed as the 'Isle of Saints and Scholars'". archive.org advancedsearch (Healy); OL search-inside
C168 [C13d] "the Greco-Roman lore Islam helped re-introduce into the West was, of course, largely that preserved by the Christian scholars of the Byzantine Empire" (p. 350) Minor difference Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy" (rev. 2026): Greek learning had long been assimilated by "the Christian elites of Syria" (schools of Edessa, Nisibis, Qenneshre). This "tradition of learning … lay in the background of the Christians of Syria who took part in the translation movement fostered by the early ʿAbbasid Caliphate". The key translator was "the Nestorian Christian physician and scientist Hunayn ibn Ishaq (d. 873)". Christian mediation is well supported, but the mediators were mainly Syriac-speaking Christians, many of them outside Byzantium or in churches at odds with it, rather than "scholars of the Byzantine Empire" as such. plato.stanford.edu/entries/arabic-islamic-greek/
T205 / C169 [C13e] Christian civilisation began to emerge under the Merovingians; "Dark Ages" not as dark as portrayed (p. 350) Opinion Interpretive, not checkable as fact. —
C170 [C13c] "atrocious punishments such as hanging, drawing and quartering were practiced in Europe up until modern times" (p. 350) Consistent The Forfeiture Act 1870, s. 31, repealed the parts of 30 Geo. III c. 48 and 54 Geo. III c. 146 requiring that treason judgments "include the drawing of the person on a hurdle … and, after execution, the severing of the head from the body, and the dividing of the body into four quarters". Dictionary of Welsh Biography: the Chartists Frost, Williams and Jones "on 16 January 1840 were condemned to be hanged and quartered for treason, but the sentence was changed to one of transportation for life". The sentence was thus still pronounced in 1840 and remained law until 1870. I did not verify when it was last actually carried out (1817/1820). legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/Vict/33-34/23/section/31/enacted; biography.wales/article/s-FROS-JOH-1784
