3. Discrepancies ranked by significance

Ranking criteria: (1) how far the error changes the historical picture or the chapter's argument; (2) whether a quotation or source is misattributed; (3) whether it is a plain factual slip; (4) minor dating, wording or OCR issues.

Tier 1: substantive errors that bear on the chapter's argument
  1. The Capitulations' dates and scope are wrong (p. 349; T198). The book says they "remained current from 1517 to their abolishment by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923" and granted "custody of certain holy places".
    • İnalcık (TDV "İmtiyâzât") dates the first Ottoman capitulation to c. 1352 (Genoa); the earliest surviving text is of 1387.
    • In 1517 Selim I only renewed the Mamluk grants.
    • The first ratified French capitulation is 1569; the 1536 draft was never confirmed.
    • The holy-places privileges came in 1604, 1690 and 1740.
    • The Ottomans abolished the capitulations unilaterally on 8 Sept 1914; Lausanne (24 July 1923) made the Allies accept that.
  2. The persecution blamed on the "Arian" Visigoths was carried out by Catholic Visigoths (p. 341; T131) [C9a–C9c].
    • Encyclopaedia Judaica ("Spain") and the Visigothic Code put the forced baptisms (613), the bans on circumcision and the Sabbath (653), the confiscations, the punitive taxes and the enslavement (694) after Reccared's conversion in 587/589.
    • Ziegler (1930) and Bachrach (via OL search-inside) describe the Arian kings as comparatively tolerant.
    • The book's later praise of the Catholic Church (p. 350) sits awkwardly with this misattribution.
  3. "Only … in 1923" did non-Muslim rights begin to be encroached upon (p. 349; T201; S7-17).
    • Britannica: the Hamidian massacres of 1894–96 killed hundreds of thousands; Adana 1909 about 20,000; the Armenian Genocide of 1915–16 600,000 to more than 1,000,000.
    • The book's own pp. 347–348 and the Karabell sentence it quotes immediately afterwards also contradict "only … in 1923".
  4. Two quotations are attributed to Wiegers but are not in Wiegers (pp. 343–344; T142 [A17], T160 [A38]). Both helper A and the lead agent checked Wiegers 1994 pp. 9–11.
    • Neither "within the space of seven years these generous terms had been broken" nor the Galera sentence is there.
    • On Galera itself: the eyewitness Mármol (II, Bk VIII) and Lea p. 255 give more than 2,400 fighting men killed, more than 400 women and children killed, and 4,500 women and children enslaved. The town was razed and salted.
    • "All its 2,500 inhabitants … slaughtered" matches English Wikipedia, which cites a school textbook.
  5. Several statements about the Morisco expulsion contradict the edicts and the documentary record (p. 345).
    • Children (T166) [A44]: no edict sold children over seven as slaves.
    • Sequence (T164–T165) [A42]: the expulsion ran Valencia 1609 → Andalusia, Castile, Aragon and Catalonia 1610 → Murcia and Ricote 1613–14, not "Castile in 1614".
    • "50,000 died resisting" (T167) [A45]: this traces to the pro-expulsion writer Aznar Cardona (1612), who says they "died miserably", not "resisting".
    • "Two-thirds to three-quarters" (T170) [A48]: this is a contemporary estimate for deportees in North Africa (Lea p. 364), not for the whole Morisco population.
    • Totals: the book gives 300,000 and "half a million" (S7-19). Lapeyre counts 272,140; Britannica and Bernabé Pons give 275,000–300,000. The book's Chejne quotation leaves out Chejne's own Valencia figure and Chejne's notes questioning the regional totals.
  6. 'Umar's visit to Jerusalem is dated "659 CE" (p. 335; T96; S7-5). 'Umar died in 644. All the source dates for the surrender fall between 634/5 and 638. "659" is the book's own date for Mu'awiya (T98) and was probably transferred from there.
  7. Battle of the Masts "while governor of Syria under the Caliph 'Umar" (p. 340; T116; S7-6).
    • Baladhuri says 'Umar refused Mu'awiya a naval expedition, and the first expedition came under 'Uthman (AH 28).
    • The battle (655, or AH 31/34) fell in 'Uthman's caliphate.
    • Theophanes names Abu'l-A'war as the fleet commander.
  8. "The Caliph 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Marwan … known for his love of the Christians" (p. 336; T99). He was governor of Egypt, not caliph (LC authority). Fortescue, whom the book cites elsewhere, records him extorting 100,000 dinars from Patriarch John III by torture, taxing monks and forbidding new monastic vocations (p. 229).
  9. The Prophet's 1,000-casualty total (p. 333; T78). No source was found for it, and it conflicts with the traditional figures. The Qurayza execution alone is put at 600–900, or 400–900 in Kister's survey (prior check V1b). The campaign count "68" differs from Ibn Ishaq's 65 and Ibn Sa'd's 74.
Tier 2: plain factual errors (the source contradicts the book)
  1. Granada's population (p. 343; T139) [A13]. The book gives 500,000, split into 100,000, 200,000 and 200,000. Scholars estimate about 300,000 for the whole kingdom before the war (Ladero 1968; Cortés Peña 2009) and about 165,000 by 1502. The city's Moorish population was about 40,000–50,000.
  2. Bayezid II "committed his forces to Cyprus" (p. 342; T137) [A11]. Cyprus was Venetian (1489–1570/71), and Ottoman forces were fighting the Mamluks in 1485–91. Kemal Reis did raid Spain in 1487 (TDV). The 1492 fleet to evacuate Jews (T138) [A12] is not documented in TDV or Britannica.
  3. Pragmática dated "1565" (p. 344; T156) [A30]. It was proclaimed on 1 January 1567, after the 1566 Madrid junta; 1565 was the provincial council. The book also makes a "decree turning children over to priests" the trigger of the Alpujarras revolt (T158) [A36], but no such clause is in the Pragmática.
  4. "On October 12th, 1501, all Arabic and Islamic books in Granada were burned" (p. 343; T147) [A21]. Cisneros burned the books in 1499–1500. 12 October 1501 is the date of a royal order on Arabic books that exempted medical works (Wiegers p. 10 n.).
  5. "Eye for an eye … unheard of in Europe" (p. 341; C114) [C6]. Talion is in the Twelve Tables (VIII.2) and Exodus 21:23–25.
  6. Wrong collection and verse reference (S7-15, S7-16). The "oppresses a Jew or a Christian" hadith is not in Bukhari; the nearest text is Abu Dawud 3052, about any mu'ahid, with mixed gradings (C73) [C12a]. The verse cited as "5:72" is 2:62 (C115) [C11a].
  7. The shari'ah as "the inspiration for the Napoleonic Code" (pp. 349–350; T203) [C13a]. Mainstream legal history (Bonfield) traces the Code to Roman law and French customary law. Perron's Maliki translation appeared in 1848–49, after the Code. The Quebec code of 1866 rests on the Custom of Paris.
  8. "Hun" criminal law (p. 349; C116) [C3] is Sima Qian's description of the Xiongnu (Shiji 110). The "crushing of bones" is only Yan Shigu's gloss.
  9. "Romans … used to sow with salt" (p. 341; C112) [C2c]. The Carthage salting is a modern myth (Ridley 1986; Warmington 1988). No Mongol case was found.
  10. Slips in the al-Andalus passage (p. 342). 'Abd al-Rahman I was not "the last Caliph of the Umayyads" (T135) [A9]; Marwan II was. It was the Mongols in 1258, not "the Huns", who razed Baghdad [A8]. The Emirate of Granada did not last "more than seven hundred years" (T134) [A7]; the Nasrids ruled 1238–1492.
  11. Qum as one of 'Umar's garrison towns (p. 334; T82). Iranica: Qum was largely untouched for 60 years after 644, and Arabs first settled there permanently in 685–96.
  12. Mamluk–French "treaty … in Cairo in 1500" (p. 347; T184). The documented Mamluk grant to the French and Catalans is of 1507 (IFAO).
  13. The Fojnica ahdname described as "the original" (p. 345; T174). The displayed document is partly a later renewal: radiocarbon dates the upper part to 1665–1808 (Horvatinčić et al. 2017). The consensus is that the text is authentic and the grant was issued in 1463 (Sekulić).
  14. Lebanon "still almost half Christian" (p. 334; C81). Statistics Lebanon (US State Dept 2023 report) gives 30.5% of the citizen population.
Tier 3: misquotation, selective quotation and context omitted
  1. The Treaty of 'Umar's harvest clause is reversed (T106). The book has "Nothing shall be taken from them after their crops have been harvested"; Tabari XII has "before their harvest is reaped".
  2. Quotations shortened without ellipsis, changing their force:
    • Eliot: "… privileges granted by the conqueror by enormous presents" (T188).
    • Lybyer: "nine centuries before Selim" dropped; "religion" changed to "creed" (T189).
    • Scher: "probablement aussi apocryphe" (T112).
    • Joshel's block quote: condensed, with "in Epirus" dropped (T123–T126) [C1e].
    • Chronicle of Seert: the sentence "they destroyed the fire-temples" is left out of the praise passage (T207).
    • Chejne: the Valencia figure is omitted (T171) [A49].
  3. The JVL/EJ quotation on the Pact of 'Umar stops before EJ's next point (C93). EJ goes on: "Recent research … considers many of its provisions to be consistent with the early years of the conquest" (Noth, Cohen).
  4. Quotations whose own context cuts against the use made of them:
    • Isho'yahb III's praise of the Arabs (T89) comes in a letter rebuking the Christians of Mazun for converting to keep half their property.
    • Fortescue frames the "Bishop of Adiabene" report as part of "legends … made deliberately to persuade the Moslem conqueror" (T90). Fortescue also names the 1630 "Testament of Mohammed" in this context.
    • Wigram's "eternity of dullness, enlivened only by occasional risk of massacre" (C149) is cited as support.
  5. "'Umar … brought Jews back" (p. 338; T111) conflicts with the Tabari treaty the book prints on p. 337 ("None of the Jews shall reside with them"). The sources disagree (El-Awaisi pp. 58–59).
  6. Selim I "attempted to exterminate all the partisans of the Household of the Prophet" (p. 348). TDV (Emecen) rejects the 40,000 figure and says the targets were mainly Safavid propagandists.
  7. Nuseibeh custody through "'Ubadah ibn al-Samit" (p. 335). This is family tradition, and the family's own accounts name Abdullah b. Nusaybah and also point to Saladin's time. The key is physically held by the Joudeh family.
Tier 4: minor dating, naming or OCR
  1. Minor dating and naming points:
    • Mu'awiya made king in 659 versus July 660 (AG 971 spans both).
    • Almoravids 1040 versus c. 1054; Almohads 1121 versus 1130.
    • 614 was mid-war, not the "final phase" [C5a].
    • The Sui overlap the Prophet's life only until 618 [C4].
    • Chen Shubao was captured, not "surrendered" [C8].
    • 'Uthman's wife Na'ila was a Christian who converted before the marriage, not simply "a Jacobite Christian".
    • "Selenia" should be Seleucia; "Scher 201-203" should be [301]–[303].
    • The Prophet is printed 570–642 on p. 339.
    • "Menoscal" should be Menocal; "ansar" should be amsar; "Solonio" should be Sophronius.
    • The Capitulation was dated 25 Nov 1491; the Simancas text has 47 articles against al-Maqqari's 67 [A16]. The gloss on "Mudejares" is wrong [A16].
    • The Aragon conversion was 1525/26 [A27].
    • The Alpujarras revolt is variously said to have ended in 1570 or 1571 [A37].
    • The 84,000 Granadans were deported "throughout Castile", not "from Granada and Castile" [A39].
  2. Book page numbers that differ from the editions opened: Eliot 247–248 (1900 ed. pp. 271–272); Wigram 34 (1929 ed. pp. 78–79); al-Maqqari 389 (quotation starts p. 388) [A16]. The book may have used other editions.

4. Contested framings (both sides, brief, cited)

  1. Islamic conquest compared with other powers (pp. 334–341).
    • For: Donner and Avni are reported as finding little archaeological destruction. Avni (abstract): the Islamic conquest "had only a minor effect" on Jerusalem's layout [C, §3]. Many of the Roman, Frankish, Persian and Hun atrocities the book cites are attested in ancient sources (Livy, Josephus, the Royal Frankish Annals, Sebeos) [C1a–C7].
    • Against or qualifying: Several comparison claims are wrong: Arian persecution, Roman salting, Hun law and talion. The book sets Islamic norms (Qur'an, covenants) against other powers' worst practice, while omitting Islamic-side episodes recorded in its own sources. These include Qurayza (V1b), Mazun's conversions under fiscal pressure (Isho'yahb III), the Chronicle of Seert's note that the conquerors destroyed fire-temples, and 'Abd al-'Aziz's extortions (Fortescue). Modern figures are often self-reported or partisan (Scheidel; Thompson) [C, §3].
  2. The Crusades as extermination (p. 335). Book (via Mamdani): "the point of the Crusades was not to convert Muslims but to exterminate them." Britannica: the objectives were "to check the spread of Islam, to retake control of the Holy Land …, to conquer pagan areas, and to recapture formerly Christian territories". (The chapter does not discuss the 1099 sack of Jerusalem, so it was not checked.)
  3. Authenticity of the Pact of 'Umar (pp. 336–339).
    • Forgery or late: de Goeje and Caetani ("invention of a later age", Arnold p. 57); Tritton ("no one knew what the covenant of 'Umar was", p. 12); Bernard Lewis ("can hardly be authentic", via Wikipedia lead).
    • Early roots: Noth (stipulations rooted in the conquest treaties); Cohen (a petition-and-decree form that medieval Muslims would accept as authentic); Levy-Rubin (formalised in the early 'Abbasid period out of earlier surrender agreements and pre-Islamic models). Sources: EJ; CUP description.
    • The book reports only the first group, and takes from JVL/EJ the half of the entry that suits it.
  4. Authenticity of the Tabari Jerusalem treaty (p. 339). The book says "historians approve" it.
    • Fabrication: Caetani (via Tritton p. 114); Goitein and Hitti (via El-Awaisi).
    • Reliable kernel: Gil (via El-Awaisi).
    • Undecided: Kennedy (2007, p. 92), "we cannot be sure" (prior check C_islamic_chronology).
  5. The Seert covenants (pp. 338–339). Morrow attributes Scher's verdict to "prejudice". Scher (PO 13 p. 623 n. 1) calls the Najran covenant and the 'Umar edict "deux faux" (two forgeries). Wood (2013, 2021) and Wilmshurst (2011) also treat them as 'Abbasid-era or later Christian productions (see V5 §4; V0). The defence of authenticity comes mainly from Morrow's circle (V5).
  6. Al-Andalus as a "golden age" (pp. 341–342).
    • For: Menocal 2002; Convivencia 1992; Britannica on 'Abd al-Rahman III's "tolerant reign".
    • Against: Fernández-Morera 2016 (summarised by R. V. Young in Modern Age, a conservative journal). Episodes cited include the Córdoba martyrs (850–859/60, 53 executed), the Granada massacre of 1066 and the Almohad ultimatum of 1148 [A1; A, §3].
  7. The Ottoman "millet system" and Ottoman tolerance (pp. 346–349).
    • For: Bodin's 1606 testimony to four religions tolerated at Pera; Lybyer's account of the Sacred Law protecting Christians; Mehmed II's grants (Gennadios, the 1461 Armenian patriarchate tradition) (Bodin; Lybyer; TDV "Millet").
    • Qualifying: Braude's "Foundation Myths of the Millet System" (cited by Ortaylı in TDV "Millet", which notes "dispute" over the dates). Selim I's punishment of Kızılbaş, Selim II's 1568 confiscations, and the 19th–20th-century massacres (TDV; Kermeli; Britannica).
    • The book's own evidence (pp. 347–348) undercuts its claim (p. 349) that encroachment began only in 1923.
  8. Bayezid II's "rescue fleet" of 1492 (p. 342). It is widely repeated in popular and Turkish public sources (e.g. +972 Magazine). The scholarly encyclopedia articles opened (TDV Bayezid II, TDV Kemal Reis, Britannica) say only that Jews were welcomed; TDV says Kemal Reis carried Andalusian Muslims [A12].
  9. The Fojnica ahdname as a "human rights declaration" (p. 345). The "326 years before 1789 … 485 years before 1948" formula is a modern Bosniak and Turkish public trope. Sekulić calls it "curious, if anachronistic" (New Lines, 2022). The book repeats it without comment.
  10. Verden 782 (p. 341). The numbers are in the annals. Exculpatory readings ("delocati" for "decollati") are generally rejected (Barbero via Wikipedia; Chamberlin), while the scale is debated: Lintzel and Becher versus Bachrach (via Wikipedia, not opened) [C7; C, §3].
  11. The Napoleonic Code (pp. 349–350). A pro-Maliki-influence article in a Qatar University journal exists but could not be opened. The mainstream view is Roman plus customary law (Bonfield). The book's wording treats the mainstream as a fringe "attempt" [C13a].

V7a — Verification of people's dates in Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013)

Input list: people/people_1a.md (155 rows; rows numbered 1–155 in file order). Checked 10 Nov 2026.

Method. Every verdict rests on pages that were opened and read, not on search snippets. The URL of each page is in the last column. The sources used:

  • Authority files: GND (Deutsche Nationalbibliothek), read as lobid.org JSON (https://lobid.org/gnd/<id>.json, the same record as https://d-nb.info/gnd/<id>), and BnF catalogue authority records.
  • Encyclopaedias: Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed. (Brill abstract pages on referenceworks.brill.com), TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi (a peer-reviewed Turkish encyclopaedia of Islam), Encyclopaedia Iranica, the Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org), Treccani DBI, the old DNB on Wikisource, Magyar életrajzi lexikon, Russkij biograficheskij slovar'.
  • Primary texts: digitised on archive.org or Gutenberg.
  • Wikidata entity JSON: each claim is cited together with its own source.

Wikipedia was used only for: the Volney travel dates, the summary of the scholarly debate on Vegetius, and confirming that Bangash's date has no source. Each of these is labelled in its row.

Access limits. Britannica, Oxford DNB, Library of Congress (id.loc.gov) and VIAF all refused automated access (403/502/404), so LoC/ODNB data appear only where Wikidata cites them. The shared web-search budget ran out near the end.

Who checked what. Rows 10, 19, 32–33 (travels), 36, 41, 43–45 (travels), 47–51, 58, 60, 62–65, 68, 71–73, 75, 78, 87–89, 99, 104, 119, 122, 126, 129, 139–141, 143, 146–148, 151, 155 were researched by two helper agents, who opened the cited pages. Their key claims were spot-checked by re-opening:

  • BnF on Safdar Husayn
  • GND on Musavi Lari
  • Iranica on Petrus de Monte, Pacifique de Provins and A. ʿAlawi
  • Stanley's Sinai and Palestine
  • Arundale's Illustrations

All spot-checks confirmed the helpers' readings.

AH→CE. A Hijri year spans two Gregorian years. A one-year difference that comes from that overlap is graded "Minor". Garbled OCR in the printed dates (e.g. "16161689", "QE", "Vegeitus", "1951CE") was read in the obvious way and the dates checked. No row needed the separate verdict "OCR issue".

Deaths after publication (not errors). Patricia Crone d. 2015; F. E. Peters d. 2020; John L. Esposito d. 15 Jul 2026 (GND/BnF).

2. Inconsistent and Disputed rows (most significant first)

Inconsistent (12 rows)

  1. Row 97 — 'Abd Allah ibn Sallam, "d. 630". EI2 and TDV both give 43/663-4, and BnF gives 663. The book is 33 years early. EI2 also records his activity under 'Umar and 'Uthman, which rules out a death in 630.
  2. Row 135 — "George Jordac or Jurji Zaydan (1861–1914)". These are two different men. 1861–1914 are Jurji Zaydan's dates (EI2, TDV). The quoted work on 'Ali is by George Jordac (Jurj Jurdaq), 1931–2014 (BnF, GND).
  3. Row 102 — "Muhammad al-Kalbi (737–819)". Muhammad b. al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi died 146/763 (TDV). 737–819 belong to his son Hisham Ibn al-Kalbi (BnF, TDV). The book's own source (Schöller) is about Muhammad.
  4. Row 13 — al-Majlisi, "1616–1689" (pp. 2, 6, 7). Iranica gives b. 1627, d. 1699 or 1700. GND gives 1627–1698 and TDV d. 1110/1698-99. Both ends are about 11 years early.
  5. Row 51 — Sayyed Safdar Husayn, "1932–1989". The book cites his Histoire des premiers temps de l'Islam (1991). BnF's record for that author is 1868–1949, with an explicit warning not to confuse him with Safdar Husain Najafi. The book has mixed up two men.
  6. Row 152 — Ja'far al-Sadiq, "(711–36)" (Arpee's figures, repeated by the book). He was born 83/702 and died 148/765, and his imamate ran from 117/735 or 114/732 (Iranica, TDV, BnF). "711–36" fits neither his life nor his imamate.
  7. Row 58 — A. P. Stanley "visited Saint Catherine's in 1858". Stanley's own Sinai and Palestine (1856) puts the visit in winter 1852 and spring 1853 (at Feiran on 9 Mar 1853). The DNB agrees. A book published in 1856 cannot describe an 1858 visit.
  8. Row 54 — "Abu 'Ali al-Mansur (r. 996–1021), the tenth of the Fatimid Caliphs". The reign is al-Hakim's, but al-Hakim was the 6th Fatimid caliph. The 10th was al-Amir (1101–1130), who had the same name, Abu 'Ali al-Mansur (TDV). The book has merged the two.
  9. Row 41 — Musavi Lari, "1925–2013". GND gives b. 1935. WikiShia gives b. 1314 SH (= 1935/36) and d. 9 Mar 2013. The 1925 probably comes from al-islam.org's mis-conversion "1314/1925".
  10. Row 59 — 'Amr ibn al-'As, "592–664". EI2 says he was "over ninety" at his death (c. 42/663), so he was born before c. 573. GND gives c. 570 or c. 575. The death year 664 is fine (TDV 43/664).
  11. Row 114 — Abu Hurayrah, "603–681". EI2 gives d. 57, 58 or 59 AH (probably 58/678 or 59), aged 78. TDV gives 58/678. GND gives 602–679 and BnF 601?–677?. No source checked gives 681.
  12. Row 50 — Francis Arundale "visited ... in 1831" (pp. 11, 21). He went to Egypt in 1831 (DNB). His own Illustrations show the caravan leaving Cairo for Sinai on 29 Aug 1833.

Disputed among sources (9 rows)

  1. Row 106 — 'Umar ibn al-Khattab b. 579. Sources give GND 568, BnF 581, TDV c. 583 and Britannica (via Wikidata) c. 586. No source checked gives 579. The death year 644 is consistent.
  2. Row 96 — Salman al-Farisi d. 654. TDV says end of 35 or start of 36 AH (656) and notes other dates. Islamskiy ents. slovar' gives 657. No source checked gives 654.
  3. Row 21 — al-Ya'qubi d. 897/898. GND and BnF give 897, which matches the book. TDV says after 292/905, and OpenITI gives 905.
  4. Row 45 — Monconys b. 1611. The current BnF and GND records give 1608. Older data (ULAN, RKD, the earlier BnF record via Wikidata) give 1611. His travel dates are consistent.
  5. Row 9 — André du Ryer c. 1580–1660. GND agrees with the book. BnF gives "15..–1688?" and LIBRIS 1688.
  6. Row 8 — Hermann of Carinthia c. 1100–c. 1160. BnF gives 1110–1154. Other records give a birth of c. 1100 or 1110 and a death of c. 1143 or c. 1160.
  7. Row 148 — Ahmad 'Alawi 'Amili d. 1644. Iranica: "d. between 1054/1644 and 1060/1650". 1644 is only the earliest possible year.
  8. Row 108 — Vegetius, "end of the 4th century". This is one side of a scholarly dispute: dedication to Theodosius I (379–395) or Valentinian III (430s). BnF/GND give 383?–450?.
  9. Row 69 — St Catherine c. 282–c. 305. She is a legendary figure (GND: "Fiktive Gestalt"). The Catholic Encyclopedia gives no years. The dates are traditional and appear only in Wikipedias.

Minor differences (14 rows; ±1 year or AH conversion)

  • Life dates off by one year or by AH conversion: rows 3, 4, 17, 18, 40, 84 (Hoyland: authority files say b. 1966), 101, 128 (Tindal: GND 1687 vs BnF 1688) and 133.
  • Row 26: John of Damascus' birth year is uncertain.
  • Row 38: George Hamartolos is better dated to the mid-9th century or the 860s than to the late 9th.
  • Row 56: al-Amir, p. 17's "1102–1131" (p. 18 is correct).
  • Row 32: Thévenot's Levant travels were 1655–1659, not 1655–1663.
  • Row 49: Henniker was at Sinai in April 1820; no source supports 1821.

3. Places where the book contradicts itself or confuses people

  • al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah. p. 17: "ruled from 1102 to 1131 CE". p. 18: "r. 1101-1130 CE". p. 18 is correct (TDV 1101–1130).
  • "Abu 'Ali al-Mansur". On p. 16 the name, al-Hakim's reign (996–1021) and the ordinal "tenth Fatimid caliph" are combined. On p. 17 the same name is applied to al-Amir. Both caliphs did bear the name, but the p. 16 description merges two rulers.
  • al-Hakim's reign. A block quotation on p. 79 [PDF 104] gives "Caliph Hakim (AD 996-1020)", against the author's own "r. 996–1021" (pp. 16–17). This is a quoted source, not the author, but it is left uncorrected.
  • "George Jordac or Jurji Zaydan" (p. 62). The book treats two different authors as one person.
  • "Muhammad al-Kalbi (737–819)" (p. 40). The book gives the son's (Hisham's) dates to the father, whom its own cited source (Schöller) discusses.
  • Sayyed Safdar Husayn (p. 12). The dates given are those of a different man (Safdar Husain Najafi), not of the author of the cited book.
  • Name variants only, dates consistent:
    • "John L. Esposito" (pp. 28, 47) vs "John F. Esposito" (p. 60)
    • "Girangos" (p. 99) vs "Giragos" (p. 103) Vartabed
    • "Petrus de Monte" (p. 100) vs "Petrus del Monte" (p. 101)
    • "Walid ibn al-Malik" (p. 62) for al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik
  • Repeated people where the book is self-consistent:
    • Ibn Sa'd: "d. 845" (p. 1) and "c. 784–845" (p. 4)
    • Ibn Ishaq: 704–761/770, at every occurrence
    • 'Amr ibn al-'As: "592–664" (p. 17) and "d. 664" (pp. 50, 58); the birth year is wrong in both places that give it
    • Imam 'Ali: "d. 661" (p. 45) and "r. 656–661" (p. 62)
    • 'Abd al-Malik: pp. 33 (twice) and 34
    • Peters, Armstrong, Donner, Crone, Esposito (all "b." dates)
    • Salah al-Din: pp. 19, 61
    • Selim I: pp. 9–12, 23, 61
    • Cantemir: pp. 10, 61
    • al-Waqidi: pp. 28, 41
    • Hisham: pp. 25, 103
    • Greffin Affagart: pp. 9, 23, 61
    • Arundale: "1831" on both p. 11 and p. 21, consistently wrong
    • Scaliger: elsewhere in the book "(d. 1648)" and "(1588–1648)", which agree with BnF and Iranica

4. Unverified rows

  • Row 99 — Qays 'Abd al-Rashid "575–661". He is a legendary Pashtun ancestor and no reliable source gives him dates. What was tried:
    • No GND or BnF record exists.
    • Iranica's "AFGHAN" entry does not mention him.
    • Wikidata's 575 has no reference, and its 661 is inferred from a Wikipedia category.
    • The dates appear to originate in Wikipedia.
  • Row 117 — Khalid ibn al-Walid "592–642". The death year 642 is confirmed (TDV 21/642; GND). No reliable source for a birth year was found:
    • The GND record and the EI2 abstract give none.
    • Wikidata's 586 comes only from Italian Wikipedia.
  • Row 119 — Zafar Bangash "b. 1950". No authority file dates him:
    • LoC nr89007088 has no date.
    • There are no GND, BnF or IdRef records.
    • English Wikipedia infers 1950 from a 2003 newspaper giving his age as 52, which allows 1950 or 1951. That newspaper is paywalled and could not be opened.

Partial caveats inside otherwise-graded rows:

  • Row 6: Nissel's birth year 1621 is attested only by EMLO; ECARTICO gives 1623; GND and BnF give no birth year.
  • Row 63: the 1106 minbar date for al-Afdal rests on one source (Moritz 1918).
  • Row 72: Rochetta's 1598–99 journey dates are confirmed, but the source checked does not mention a Sinai visit.
  • Row 115: 'Amr's command in Sinai in 634 was not separately checked.

Fact-check reports

People and dates, batch 2

174 table rows · source file V7b_people.md

V7b: People list 1b, fact-check of dates

Book: John Andrew Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013). Input: scratchpad/people/people_1b.md (155 rows, chapters 3-7, pp. 110-201). Checked: 2026-11-10.

How the rows were checked

Every verdict rests on a page or record I actually opened. These are the sources:

  • Wikidata entity records, retrieved through the API. I noted each claim's own reference (GND, BnF, Britannica and so on).
  • GND (Deutsche Nationalbibliothek) authority records, read through lobid.org/gnd/<id>.json.
  • BnF authority headings, from data.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb<id>.
  • TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi (islamansiklopedisi.org.tr), a peer-reviewed scholarly encyclopaedia. It gives AH/CE death dates in its headers.
  • Wikipedia, used only where marked:
    • modern uncontroversial dates;
    • patriarch lists (the Church of the East list follows Wilmshurst);
    • three event dates: the abolition of the caliphate, the Toulon wintering, and the Fano printing;
    • Ja'far as a second source after TDV;
    • Berthold, Samuel of Ani and Bedir Khan.
  • Single pages from Store norske leksikon, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani) and WikiShia.

Sources I could not use:

  • Britannica returned 403.
  • id.loc.gov (LoC) returned 403 behind Cloudflare.
  • VIAF and the Iranica search are JavaScript-only.
  • The session's web-search budget ran out partway through. After that I only opened known URLs and searched Wikidata and GND.

Verdict rules:

  • Minor difference: ±1 year, an AH→CE conversion difference, or an approximate birth year.
  • Disputed among sources: the standard references disagree, and the book follows one of the versions.
  • Inconsistent: no source I checked supports the book's date, confirmed with at least two sources.
  • N/A: the row gives no date.

2. Inconsistent and Disputed rows, most significant first

Inconsistent
  1. Row 24, 'Allamah Majlisi (Muhammad Baqir), "1616-1689". The real dates are b. 1037/1627 and d. 1110/1698-99 or 1111/1699-1700 (TDV; GND 1627-1698). Both ends are about 11 years early. The book may have mixed him up with his father's generation.
  2. Row 149, Samuel of Ani, "wrote in the 13th century". He was a 12th-century historian: GND d. 1179; Wikidata c. 1105-c. 1185; Wikipedia. The book is a century late.
  3. Row 11, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, "return 626". He returned from Abyssinia at the conquest of Khaybar, 7/628 (TDV "Ca'fer b. Ebu Talib" and "Hayber"). Wikipedia gives summer 628.
  4. Row 9, Abu Hurayrah, "603-681". He died in 58/678, with 57/677 or 59/679 also reported (TDV). BnF gives d. 677? and GND d. 679. No source gives 681.
  5. Row 127, "Shimon the fourth", patriarch in 1517. Shemon IV died in 1497. The patriarch in 1517 was Shemon VI (1504-1538), per the Wikipedia list and Wikidata citing Wilmshurst. The lists number the Shemon patriarchs differently, so this may be a numbering mismatch.
  6. Row 51, Johann Michael Vansleb, "1635-1676". He died on 12 Jun 1679 (GND; BnF heading 1635-1679).
  7. Row 45, Berthold, "died in 1188". He died c. 1195 (Store norske leksikon; Wikipedia). Wikidata gives 1195 or 1198.
  8. Rows 3 and 121, Ibn Ishaq, "704-761/770". The standard death date is 150/767 or 151/768 (TDV; GND 768; BnF 767?). TDV lists 153/770 and 154/771 only as minority variants. 761 is not attested in any source checked.
  9. Row 138, Essvo Yabh (Ishoyahb), "toward the end of the seventh [century]". No Ishoyahb was patriarch then. Ishoyahb II served 628-645/646 and Ishoyahb III 649-659 (Wikipedia list; GND; Wikidata). If the book meant the seventh year of the Hijra, 628 fits Ishoyahb II.
  10. Row 40, Khalid ibn al-Walid, born "592". TDV gives c. 583-587 ("35-39 years before the Hijra") and Wikidata 586. His death in 642 is correct. This is low significance because the birth year is approximate anyway.

Other dating errors in these rows that are not life or reign dates:

  • Row 1. Atatürk "abolished the Caliphate in 1922": the sultanate was abolished on 1 Nov 1922 and the caliphate on 3 Mar 1924 (Wikipedia "Abolition of the Caliphate"). This is the most visible event-date error in the batch, though Atatürk's own dates (1881-1938) are correct.
  • Row 98. Julius II is called "patron of the 1514 Fano printing", but he died on 21 Feb 1513 (GND, BnF, Wikidata). At most he founded or patronised the press.
Disputed among sources (the book follows one version)
  1. Row 117, Salman the Persian, "d. 654". TDV gives 35-36/656 and says other dates exist. Wikidata gives 657. I found 654 in no source, so this is close to Inconsistent.
  2. Row 21, al-Sarakhsi, "d. c. 1096". The usual date is 483/1090-91 (TDV; GND; BnF). Some biographies say "around [4]90", and the book follows that minority version.
  3. Row 19, 'Ali al-Rida, born "765". BnF gives 765? and TDV lists 148/765 as one variant. But TDV, GND and Wikidata prefer 153/770. His death in 203/818 is agreed.
  4. Row 65, André Du Ryer, "c. 1580-1660". GND gives 1580-1660, but BnF gives "15..-1688?".
  5. Row 90, Henri Basnage de Beauval, "1657-1710". BnF gives 1657-1710, but GND and Wikidata give a 1656 birth.

3. Does the book contradict itself about the same person?

Dates: no direct contradiction found. Every person who appears in several rows gets the same life or reign dates each time:

  • Mu'awiyah: pp. 115, 116, 147, 178, 183
  • Ibn Ishaq: p. 112 "761/770" and p. 188 "761/70", the same dates abbreviated
  • al-Baladhuri: pp. 120, 183
  • 'Umar: pp. 114, 193
  • 'Ali: pp. 147, 160, 194-200
  • Selim I: pp. 147-148, 177
  • Karen Armstrong: pp. 128, 186
  • Muhammad: pp. 152, 183
  • Pacifique de Provins: pp. 139-152
  • Henri IV: pp. 149, 150
  • Sulayman: pp. 148, 175
  • Renaudot: p. 145 and p. 153, the latter only an OCR join
  • Murad IV: "r. 1623-1640" on p. 142 and the "1630-1634" period on p. 192. These do not conflict; the second is a sub-period.

Hedges and small wording differences:

  • Salmasius. The book gives "d. 1653" on p. 150 and "1588 or 1596-1653" on p. 152. The death year agrees; the second page adds an unsupported alternative birth year.

Chronological tensions inside the book's own narrative (flag for the user):

  • 'Umar. On p. 193 he is the "conqueror of Jerusalem in 638" (TDV agrees: 17/638). Yet his firman to Sophronios is dated 20 Rabi' al-Awwal 15 AH, about 636, roughly two years before the capitulation the book itself dates to 638.
  • Abraham I, Armenian Patriarch of Jerusalem. On p. 191 he is "Patriarch from 638 to 669", but he is also said to have visited the Prophet "in 626" to obtain privileges. The visit falls 12 years before his patriarchate, and the Prophet died in 632 (BnF, GND).
  • Mu'awiyah. On p. 115 he "might not yet have been a Muslim" when he witnessed the Najran covenant. On pp. 147 and 183 he "embraced Islam before the conquest of Mecca (8 AH/630)" and was the Prophet's scribe 630-632. Whether these clash depends on the date the book assigns to the Najran covenant, which is not in this list.
  • Baron de Slane. Row 114 gives "catalogue 1883-1895", but de Slane died in 1878 (BnF, GND). These are the posthumous publication dates, not years he was working.

4. Unverified rows and why

The session's web-search budget ran out partway through. After that I tried only Wikidata search (wbsearchentities), GND search (lobid), VIAF autosuggest and direct Wikipedia titles.

  • Rows 100, 101, 102 and 107 (Girgis al-Ifrangi, Mansur ibn Sulayman Sahyun al-Ramadi, Butrus ibn Diyab al-Halabi, Valerianus Oserole). These are copyists and readers known only from notes in the manuscript or printed copy. I found no authority record in Wikidata or GND. The dates come from the book's reading of the manuscript and can only be checked against the manuscript itself (BnF MS Arabe 214 and the copy of Sionita's edition).
  • Row 113 (Edward A. Van Dyck). The GND record (1052800505) and the Wikidata item (Q111473359) exist but carry no dates. The 1881 date is the year of his consular report, which I did not open.
  • Row 130 (Theodore D'Mar Shimun, "1906-2001"). Not found in Wikidata, GND or Wikipedia (direct title). VIAF autosuggest gave nothing usable.
  • Row 137 (Ahmad al-Hasani al-Baghdadi, fl. 2012). Not found in Wikidata or Wikipedia under any spelling I tried. The 2012 edict is unverified.
  • Rows 150 and 151 (Gregor Campan, fl. 1767; Joakim Gregor Bagratuni, fl. 1804). No Wikidata or GND record. Both are known only through Avdall's 1870 article in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, which I did not open.
  • Also partly unverified (counted as Consistent):
    • Row 110: "Mr. Legrand" could not be identified; Grégoire's part is fine.
    • Rows 42, 115 and 146: the publication years (Hamidullah's 1956 edition, Guillaume's Procès-verbaux, Golubovich's 1921 book) were only checked against the authors' lifespans.
  • Row 155 (Albert Yelda) is marked N/A because the book gives no date.

Fact-check reports

People and dates, batch 3 (Sinai and Part III)

239 table rows · source file V7c_people.md

V7c — People's dates in Morrow, The Covenants of the Prophet Muhammad with the Christians of the World (2013): Chapter 2 (Sinai) and Part III

Input: people/people_batch2.md. It has 196 rows, numbered 1–196 in file order:

  • rows 1–65 come from extract 03_ch2;
  • rows 66–196 come from extract 08_ch13_ch17.

Checked 10 Nov 2026.

Method. Every verdict rests on a page or API record that I opened in this session. Search-engine snippets were not used, and no WebSearch call was made. The sources:

  • TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi. Full article text was fetched and the birth, death and conversion passages were read.
  • GND authority records. Each cited ID was re-fetched individually as https://lobid.org/gnd/<id>.json.
  • BnF authority and bibliographic records, read through the BnF SRU API. They are cited by ark.
  • Wikidata entity JSON. References are given for each date claim.
  • Primary texts, fetched by me from archive.org and Gutenberg:
    • Arundale's Illustrations;
    • Walpole's Travels (1820), which contains Fazakerley's account;
    • Burckhardt's Travels in Syria;
    • Patrologia Orientalis 13 (Chronicle of Seert).
  • English, French and Hebrew Wikipedia, and English Wikisource, used only where noted. These are labelled "Wikipedia-level".

The printed wording of disputed items was checked against the book's own page text in book/pages and book/book.txt.

Grading.

  • AH→CE overlap. A Hijri year spans two CE years, so a one-year difference caused by that overlap is graded Minor difference.
  • Approximate dates. A date marked "c." that lies within about 3 years of the reference is also Minor difference. Larger gaps are Inconsistent.
  • Before marking Inconsistent, a second independent source was checked in every case.
  • Rows with two printings. Where the book prints the same person twice and one printing is right and the other wrong, the row is graded Inconsistent and the reference column explains which printing is wrong.

Access limits.

  • The Wikidata Query Service was rate-limited to 1 request/min, and the wbgetentities API returned HTTP 429. Wikidata was therefore read entity by entity through Special:EntityData.
  • The Library of Congress and HathiTrust returned 403.
  • No TDV entry was found for 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Hisham ibn al-'As, Sahl ibn Sa'd, al-Mu'tamid, al-Mutawakkil or Jaqmaq. Other sources were used for these.

Deaths after publication (not errors). Lewontin (2021), F. E. Peters (2020), Bernard Lewis (2018), Patricia Crone (2015), Qaradawi (2022), Robert Irwin (2024) and John Adair (2025). Juan Vernet died in 2011, before the book appeared; the book gives only "b. 1923".

2. Inconsistent and Disputed rows, most significant first

Inconsistent (20)

  1. Row 125 – the Prophet "570-642 CE" (p. 339). He died in 632 (GND, Wikidata). The book itself prints 570–632 on p. 354 and dates his death 19 years before 651 on p. 85.
  2. Rows 31/71 – Abu Hurayrah "603-681" (pp. 83, 323). He died in 58/678; the variants are 677 and 679 (TDV, GND, BnF). No source gives 681. He reached Medina only in Muharram 7 AH, which is 5 years after the Sinai date.
  3. Row 48 – al-Mu'tamid "nominal Caliph 878-885" and "(r. 877; 878-879)" (p. 86). He reigned 870–892. The book's figures are the dates of his viziers al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Makhlad. These are the very men Mouton's forgery thesis rests on.
  4. Row 161 – Ibn Qayyim "1292/93-1286" (p. 355). The death date is printed before the birth date. Correct: 1292–1350.
  5. Row 116 – Qaradawi "b. 1956" (p. 337). Correct: 1926, as the book itself gives on p. 372.
  6. Row 96 – 'Asim ibn Thabit "died at Badr (624)". He was killed at al-Raji' in 4/625. The error affects the book's identification of the witness "Ibn 'Asir".
  7. Row 98 – 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah "returned to Medina in 615". The 615 emigrants returned to Mecca. Medina before 622 is impossible.
  8. Rows 20/64 – Kara Mustafa "served Sulayman II from 1663-1666". In those years he served Mehmed IV, as kapudan pasha and acting grand vizier. Suleiman II reigned 1687–1691, after Kara Mustafa died in 1683.
  9. Row 54 – al-Biruni "937". Correct: b. 973 (TDV, GND, BnF).
  10. Row 148 – "Sir Charles Eliot (1801-1875)". These are the dates of Admiral Charles Elliot. The author of Turkey in Europe lived 1862–1931.
  11. Row 28 – Leo Frobenius "1873-1973". He died in 1938.
  12. Row 15 – Fatimids from "901". Correct: 909.
  13. Row 38 – Ibn Qutaybah "828-885". He died in 276/889 (TDV, GND, BnF).
  14. Row 126 – Khalid ibn al-Walid "592". Correct: b. 583–587 (TDV); Wikidata 586.
  15. Row 25 – al-Afdal called "the Fatimid Caliph" and al-Hakim's successor. He was vizier 1094–1121. The caliph in 1106 was al-Amir, and al-Hakim's successor was al-Zahir.
  16. Row 23 – Arundale's Sinai voyage "1831". By his own account he left Cairo for Sinai on 29 Aug 1833.
  17. Row 99 – Hisham ibn al-'As "died 635 at Yarmuk". Yarmuk was in 15/636; 13/634 was Ajnadayn.
  18. Row 80 – Zayd ibn Thabit "d. c. 660". Reported years are 45, 51 or 55 AH (665+); only English Wikipedia gives 660.

Disputed among sources (16)

  1. Rows 22/68 – 'Umar b. 579. Sources give 568 (GND), 581? (BnF), ≈583 (TDV) and c. 586 (Wikidata/Britannica). None gives 579.
  2. Row 127 – John of Damascus "c. 645 or 676" and "d. 749/764". TDV lists 640, 645, 655–660, 675 (the majority) and 679 for the birth, and 749 for the death. No source supports 764.
  3. Row 79 – Nafi ibn al-Harith "d. 670, the Prophet's physician". The physician was his father al-Harith ibn Kalada, who died either 13/634 (TDV's preference) or 50/670. The son's death is given as 634–635 by current English Wikipedia.
  4. Row 93 – 'Amr ibn al-'As "c. 592". GND ca. 570/575; Wikipedia c. 573; TDV implies c. 603. No source gives 592.
  5. Row 69 – 'Uthman b. 577. TDV: six years after the Year of the Elephant (≈576); GND 574; BnF 570?.
  6. Row 75 – Hassan ibn Thabit d. 674. Reported dates are 660, 670, 674 and c. 680 (TDV); GND 660.
  7. Row 32 – Abu al-Darda' converted 623 or 624. TDV supports 624 (at Badr). No source checked supports 623.
  8. Row 112 – Mu'awiya "king in Jerusalem 659". Wikipedia: late 660/early 661 and July 661.
  9. Row 140 – al-Maqqari b. 1578. Sources give 1577? (BnF), 1582 or later (TDV) and 1591 (GND).
  10. Row 6 – Monconys b. 1611. BnF and GND now give 1608.
  11. Row 83 – 'Ammar b. c. 570. TDV's "about 93 at Siffin" implies c. 564.
  12. Row 157 – Ibn Sa'd b. 784. GND, BnF and Wikidata give 784; TDV gives 777.
  13. Row 61 – Barthélemy's find "1850". The EI2 quotation gives 1850; another source quoted on the same Wikipedia page gives 1858. The place is also given as Akhmim, not "near Saide".
  14. Row 16 – Ayyubids 1174–1249. The usual dating is 1171–1250. The book's end points are events, not dynastic limits.
  15. Row 18 – Ottomans 1517–1805. 1805 is Muhammad Ali's appointment. The eyalet formally lasted until 1867.

3. Places where the book contradicts itself about the same person

Person Conflicting printings Which is right
The Prophet Muhammad 570–642 (p. 339) vs 570–632 (p. 354); p. 85 dates his death 19 years before 651, i.e. 632 632
Yusuf al-Qaradawi b. 1956 (p. 337) vs b. 1926 (p. 372) 1926
John of Damascus "c. 645 or 676–749" (p. 340) vs "d. 749/764" (p. 371) Death is 749 per all checked sources; 764 is unsupported
Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah "1292/93–1286" (p. 355) contradicts itself (death before birth) 1292–1350; 1286 is Bar Hebraeus' death year, printed immediately before
al-Mu'tamid "nominal Caliph 878–885" and "(r. 877; 878–879)", in adjacent sentences on p. 86 Neither: he reigned 870–892
al-Afdal "the Fatimid Caliph al-Afdal", al-Hakim's successor (p. 75, Hobbs passage) vs "Shahan Shah al-Afdal, a powerful chancellor of the Fatimid Empire" (p. 75, from Skrobucha) Chancellor/vizier
al-Hakim r. 996–1021 (author) vs AD 996–1020 (Skrobucha quotation) 1021 (TDV); the quote is a minor slip
Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman "Hudayfah ibn al-Yaman (d. 656)" (p. 84) vs "Abu Hudayfah ibn al-Yaman (d. 656)" (p. 323) Same date; the kunya on p. 323 is wrong
Abu al-Darda' conversion "after Badr in 624" vs "one year after the hijrah … 623" (p. 83) The book reports two versions without choosing; TDV supports 624
Ja'far ibn Abi Talib "d. 629 CE" vs "died during the early years of the hijrah" (p. 326) 8 AH (629) is not the "early years"

Checked and found consistent across their repetitions:

  • 'Ali (d. 661);
  • 'Umar (r. 634–644 / 579–644);
  • Mu'awiya (d. 680 / 602–680);
  • Ibn Sa'd (d. 845 / 784–845);
  • Selim I;
  • Hamidullah;
  • 'Umar II;
  • al-Mutawakkil;
  • Abu Hurayrah (603–681 on both pages, consistently wrong);
  • Caetani;
  • Arundale ("1831" on p. 74 and also on p. 11, consistently wrong).

4. Witnesses whose reference dates conflict with a covenant's claimed date of issue

The covenant dates are the book's own:

Covenant Claimed date
Sinai 3 Muharram 2 AH ≈ 7 Jul 623
Christians of the World ("CW") 4 AH ≈ Jun 625 – Jun 626
Najran 9–10 AH ≈ Apr 630 – Mar 632

The witness lists are as the book gives them: Sinai on pp. 323–324 (and p. 74 for Mu'awiya); the "second group" on pp. 324–327, which covers CW 1630, CW 1538, Najran, Assyria and one further text.

Witness (row) Covenant Conflict Source
Abu Hurayrah (31, 71) Sinai Converted and came to Medina in Muharram 7 AH (May 628), about 5 years after 2 AH. The book admits this (p. 323) TDV ebu-hureyre
Mu'awiya (21, 112) Sinai (fifth witness, p. 74); CW 1630 Converted with his father during the conquest of Mecca (8/630). That is after both 2 AH and 4 AH. It is not a problem for Najran TDV muaviye-b-ebu-sufyan
Abu al-Darda' (32, 70) Sinai Converted at the time of Badr (Ramadan 2 AH ≈ Mar 624), about 8 months after 3 Muharram 2 AH TDV ebud-derda
'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib (74) Sinai Fought for the Quraysh at Badr and was captured; he did not emigrate to Medina; formal conversion is perhaps Jan 630. In Muharram 2 AH he was a non-Muslim (at least openly) in Mecca enwiki Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib
'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As (82) Sinai (penultimate witness); also on three second-group texts Born c. 615. Converted before his father, but went to Medina only after 7 AH. His father converted on 1 Safar 8 / 31 May 629. So he was absent in 2 AH and 4 AH TDV abdullah-b-amr-b-as ; TDV amr-b-as
Hamzah (88) Second group (on two texts) Killed at Uhud, 3/625. That is before 4 AH and before 9–10 AH, so it is a conflict whichever two texts carry him. The book admits this TDV hamza
Ja'far ibn Abi Talib (100) Second group (on four of five texts) In Abyssinia until he joined the Prophet at Khaybar (7/628); killed at Mu'ta (8/629). Conflicts with CW (4 AH) and with Najran (9–10 AH) TDV cafer-b-ebu-talib
Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (78) All second-group manuscripts, including Najran d. 5/627, before 9–10 AH. No conflict with Sinai or CW. The book notes the problem TDV sad-b-muaz
Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' (97), proposed by the book for "Ibn Rabiah" Second group d. 3/625 at Uhud, before CW and Najran TDV sad-b-rebi
'Asim ibn Thabit (96), proposed for "Ibn 'Asir" Second group d. 4/625 at al-Raji': borderline for CW (same year) and a conflict for Najran. The book's "died at Badr 624" would make it worse TDV asim-b-sabit
Jubayr ibn Mut'im (103), proposed for "Ibn Jubayr" Second group Converted 628 (or at the conquest of Mecca), after CW's 4 AH TDV cubeyr-b-mutim
Tamim al-Dari (92), proposed for "Sahl ibn Tamim" Second group Converted 9 (630) or 10 (631) AH, after CW's 4 AH; acceptable for Najran TDV temim-ed-dari
Abu Dharr (85) All second-group texts Emigrated to Medina after Uhud (3/625) or after the Trench (5/627). On the second report he was not in Medina in 4 AH. This is a possible conflict with CW only TDV ebu-zer-el-gifari

No date conflict was found for the other dated witnesses:

  • 'Ali, Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman;
  • Ibn Mas'ud, Zubayr, Talhah;
  • Hassan ibn Thabit (converted 622, TDV);
  • Zayd ibn Thabit (aged about 12 in 623), Khuzaymah, 'Ammar;
  • al-Bara' ibn Malik, Abu Hudhayfa ibn 'Utba, Hisham ibn al-'As;
  • Sahl ibn Hunayf, Usamah, Zayd ibn Arqam.

Claims inside otherwise verified rows that I did not check:

  • the "552 CE" birth year for the Prophet attributed to "a few Western historians" (row 65);
  • Griffith's statement that Abdul Hamid II confirmed the Testament in 1904 (row 58; the date only falls within his reign);
  • that Rincon's 1532 visit was at Belgrade (row 152);
  • that Abraha's 552 campaign was "near Mecca" (row 44; the inscription refers to central Arabia).
